### [1] [STATERA: Hidden Mass Estimation via Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematics using Frozen Temporal Tubelets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00003)
*Animesh Varma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces STATERA, a method for center-of-mass (CoM) localization of opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from monocular videos, addressing the challenge of inferring hidden physical properties when visual cues are unreliable due to self-occlusion. The method adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer. The HiddenMass Benchmark (50K simulation + 63 real-world sequences) is introduced to support this task.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance struggle to infer hidden physical properties (like center-of-mass) from motion because surface cues and point tracking become unreliable under self-occlusion. This is a fundamental limitation for understanding object physics from visual observation alone.

Method: STATERA adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and introduces a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. The approach uses a unique supervision strategy (phase-aware vs phase-agnostic targets) and is evaluated on the proposed HiddenMass Benchmark containing 50K MuJoCo trajectories and 63 real-world sequences with physically calibrated CoM ground truth.

Result: In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma reduces normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, phase-aware supervision (STATERA-50K-Crescent) is the only method showing consistent movement toward true hidden offset, improving physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%, despite introducing a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error.

Conclusion: Frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation. There exists a fundamental trade-off in sim-to-real transfer: phase-aware targets enable meaningful physics capture but risk bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets are more stable but may collapse toward safe centroids.

Abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark, comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.

</details>


### [2] [Emergent Object Binding Has a Finite Spatial Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00006)
*Mayank Singal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Pretrained Vision Transformers encode object binding information in patch embeddings. This IsSameObject signal decays exponentially with spatial distance between patches, with a finite length scale and nonzero floor, suggesting object binding emerges from self-supervised pretraining alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The aggregate accuracy of decoding IsSameObject from frozen patch embeddings hides the true structure of the signal. The researchers wanted to understand why binding behaves differently across various conditions (object size, occlusion, class similarity) by examining the spatial structure of the binding signal.

Method: Tested binding decoding across three probe families, two datasets (ADE20K, COCO), and two backbones (DINO, CLIP). Mapped various behaviors while controlling for confounds. Examined how binding probability decays with patch distance, fit the decay to exponential models, and tested effects of object size, occlusion, class similarity, and part-whole relationships.

Result: Binding is local: probability of decoding two patches as bound falls off monotonically with distance, following an exponential decay with finite length scale and nonzero floor. This local interpretation accounts for: (1) weakened binding on large objects, (2) reduced separation between same-class objects vs different classes, (3) grouping of parts with wholes, (4) no effect from occlusion when object size controlled. Different depth organization between DINOv2 and DINOv3 for horizon and floor.

Conclusion: Object binding emerges from self-supervised pretraining alone, and the binding signal has a specific local spatial structure (exponential decay with finite range). This local coherence interpretation explains multiple behavioral patterns that aggregate accuracy scores obscure, indicating the finding is a property of the representation rather than the decoder.

Abstract: Pretrained Vision Transformers encode whether two image patches belong to the same object. This IsSameObject signal is decodable from frozen patch embeddings at high accuracy, which suggests that object binding emerges from self-supervised pretraining alone. We show that this single accuracy number hides the structure of the signal. Binding is local: the probability that two patches of the same object are decoded as bound falls off monotonically with the distance between them and levels off at a nonzero floor, a falloff well described by an exponential with a finite length scale. This decay holds across object sizes, across three families of probe, on both ADE20K and COCO, and across DINO and CLIP backbones, which indicates that it is a property of the representation rather than of the decoder. Reading binding as local spatial coherence with a finite range accounts for a set of behaviors that the aggregate score leaves unexplained: binding weakens on large objects, separates distinct objects of the same class less reliably than objects of different classes, and groups object parts with their wholes. It is, by contrast, unaffected by occlusion once object size is controlled. We map each behavior with confounds controlled. As a preliminary observation, the horizon and its floor are organized at different depths in DINOv2 and DINOv3, which we report as suggestive given the small number of layers probed and the confound between the two models.

</details>


### [3] [Soundwich: Video Generation with Layered and Controllable Audio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00691)
*Zhuo Ning,AmirHossein Naghi Razlighi,Sagi Polaczek,Daniel Cohen-Or,Ali Mahdavi-Amiri*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Soundwich is a training-free framework that converts a frozen joint audio-video flow-matching model into a multi-track audio stem generator, enabling separate editable audio tracks (speech, music, sound effects, ambient) synchronized with video.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current joint audio-video generative models produce audio as a single mixed track, limiting source-level control. Practical workflows require separate editable tracks for speech, music, sound effects, and ambient sounds.

Method: Soundwich uses three key innovations: (1) explicit temporal activity control for each audio stem, (2) a shared scene representation that maintains global audiovisual context while preserving source separation, and (3) cross-modal routing between each audio stem and its visual source to improve consistency.

Result: Experiments and human evaluations demonstrate improved temporal control, source separation, and naturalness while enabling flexible source-level editing within coherent audiovisual generation.

Conclusion: Soundwich successfully enables independent retiming, muting, replacing, or remixing of audio stems while maintaining synchronization with video, bridging the gap between generative models and practical audiovisual editing workflows.

Abstract: Recent joint audio-video generative models can synthesize realistic videos with synchronized sound, but typically generate audio as a single mixed track. This limits source-level control and differs from practical audiovisual workflows, where speech, music, sound effects, and ambient sounds are represented as separate editable tracks. We introduce Soundwich, a training-free framework that transforms a frozen joint audio-video flow-matching model into a generator of multiple synchronized, independently editable audio stems coupled to a shared video. Soundwich generates separate audio stems with explicit control over their temporal activity. To keep separately generated sounds coherent, we introduce a shared scene representation that communicates global audiovisual context across stems while preserving their source-level separation. We further route cross-modal interactions between each audio stem and its corresponding visual source, improving audiovisual consistency. The resulting stems remain synchronized with the video and can be independently retimed, muted, replaced, or remixed. Experiments and human evaluations show improved temporal control, source separation, and naturalness, while enabling flexible source-level editing within coherent audiovisual generation. Code is available at https://github.com/CodyNing/Soundwich.

</details>


### [4] [Spatial Lifting for Dense Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00017)
*Mingzhi Xu,Tao Zhou,Yong Li,Yizhe Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Spatial Lifting (SL) is a novel methodology that lifts 2D images into a higher-dimensional space (e.g., 3D) and processes them using networks designed for that higher dimension (e.g., 3D U-Net). This counter-intuitive approach achieves better performance on dense prediction tasks while reducing inference costs and drastically lowering the number of model parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense prediction tasks in computer vision (e.g., segmentation) typically operate in the original input space. The authors propose that lifting inputs to a higher-dimensional space can paradoxically lead to more efficient models with fewer parameters while achieving better performance.

Method: The methodology involves: (1) Lifting standard 2D inputs into a higher-dimensional space (e.g., 3D), (2) Processing with networks designed for that higher dimension (e.g., 3D U-Net), (3) Leveraging intrinsically structured outputs along the lifted dimension for dense supervision during training, (4) Enabling single-forward-pass self-consistency-based quality and uncertainty estimation at test time.

Result: The method achieves good performance on benchmark tasks compared to conventional approaches, while reducing inference costs and drastically lowering the number of model parameters.

Conclusion: Spatial Lifting offers a simple and general modeling strategy that provides a promising path toward more efficient, accurate, and reliable deep networks for dense prediction tasks in vision.

Abstract: We present Spatial Lifting (SL), a novel methodology for dense prediction tasks. SL operates by lifting standard inputs, such as 2D images, into a higher-dimensional space and subsequently processing them using networks designed for that higher dimension, such as a 3D U-Net. Counterintuitively, this dimensionality lifting allows us to achieve good performance on benchmark tasks compared to conventional approaches, while reducing inference costs and \textbf{drastically lowering the number of model parameters}. The SL framework produces intrinsically structured outputs along the lifted dimension. This emergent structure facilitates dense supervision during training and enables single-forward-pass self-consistency-based quality and uncertainty estimation at test time. Spatial Lifting introduces a simple and general modeling strategy that offers a promising path toward more efficient, accurate, and reliable deep networks for dense prediction tasks in vision.

</details>


### [5] [Supervising Sound Localization by In-the-wild Egomotion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01388)
*Anna Min,Ziyang Chen,Hang Zhao,Andrew Owens*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A method for learning binaural sound localization using egomotion as a supervisory signal, where camera motion provides weak but plentiful supervision combined with traditional binaural cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sound localization is important for audio-visual understanding, but supervised learning requires expensive labeled data. The authors propose using naturally occurring camera motion (egomotion) as a free supervision signal to learn sound direction prediction.

Method: The method trains an audio model to predict sound directions consistent with visual estimates of camera motion obtained from multi-view geometry. This weak supervision is combined with traditional binaural cues. A dataset of real-world audio-visual videos with egomotion was created for evaluation.

Result: The model successfully learns from real-world data and performs well on sound localization tasks.

Conclusion: Egomotion can serve as an effective supervisory signal for learning binaural sound localization, enabling models to learn from abundant unlabeled real-world data without requiring manual annotation.

Abstract: We present a method for learning binaural sound localization using egomotion as a supervisory signal. Over the course of a video, the cameras direction to a sound source will change as the camera moves. We train an audio model to predict sound directions that are consistent with visual estimates of camera motion, which we obtain using traditional methods from multi-view geometry. This provides a weak but plentiful form of supervision that we combine with traditional binaural cues. To evaluate this method, we propose a dataset of real-world audio-visual videos with egomotion. We show that our model can successfully learn from real-world data and that it performs well on sound localization tasks

</details>


### [6] [Encoded but Disconnected: Decomposing Vision-Language Model Failures under a Patching Null](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00024)
*Genpei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: First study to systematically test causal role of mid-layer representations across three vision-language models (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B). Despite mid layers encoding ground-truth answers in 68-91% of errors, this signal is not causally active: residual-stream patching yields 0% non-trivial flip at layer level on all architectures, with only one exception (InternVL3 head). Three distinct failure modes are identified and learnable above 60% accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether mid-layer representations in vision-language models are causally relevant to final predictions -- i.e., whether encoded information is actually used by the model. This addresses a fundamental assumption in interpretability research that "seeing" the correct answer in internals means the model "knows" it.

Method: Experiments across three VLM architectures using POPE benchmark. Methods include: (1) probing mid-layer representations for ground-truth answer encoding; (2) residual-stream patching at layer and head levels to test causal activity; (3) classifying errors into three failure modes using learned classifiers; (4) testing intervention responses based on architecture prior direction.

Result: Mid layers encode ground-truth in 68-91% of errors, yet patching yields 0% non-trivial flip at layer level across all models. At per-head level: Qwen shows 0/12,600 patched forwards successful; only InternVL3 layer-20 head-2 shows effect (self-attending, non-vocab, localized, p<1e-4). Three failure modes (Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override) are learnable above 60% on all architectures. Architecture prior direction predicts which intervention elicits category-specific response.

Conclusion: Mid-layer representations encode but do not use correct answers -- the "encoding ≠ causality" gap is universal in these VLMs. The three failure modes are mechanistically real (verified via oracle labels), providing evidence they are not mere statistical artifacts. However, these findings are presented as evidence of mechanistic reality, not as a deployable mitigation method.

Abstract: Across three vision-language model architectures (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B), we report a universal negative finding for mid-layer interpretability. On POPE -- the benchmark common to all three -- the mid layers encode the ground-truth answer in 68-91% of errors, yet this signal is not causally active for the final prediction: residual-stream patching yields 0% non-trivial flip at the layer level on all three architectures, and on two of three at the per-head level (Qwen: 0/12,600 patched forwards). The lone exception, InternVL3 layer-20 head-2, is a non-vocab, self-attending head whose effect is localized to that specific head (p < 1e-4). Despite the null, the errors separate operationally into three failure modes -- Perception Failure, Encoded-but-Disconnected, Prior-Override -- learnable above 60% on all three architectures, and the architecture's prior direction predicts which of two interventions elicits a category-specific response. We report these mitigation effects under oracle labels as evidence the categories are mechanistically real, not as a deployable method.

</details>


### [7] [Exploring Weaknesses of Generative Image Watermarks against Latent Frequency Masking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02010)
*Kirill Aistov,Khaled Abud,Irina Serzhenko,Egor Kovalev,Aleksey Yakushev,Aleksandr Akimenkov,Dmitry Obydenkov,Yury Markin,Sergey Lavrushkin,Dmitriy Vatolin,Anastasia Antsiferova*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper introduces "Latent Frequency Masking," an attack that removes invisible watermarks from AI-generated images by manipulating Fourier coefficients in the latent representation. The attack has two variants - a fast Gaussian noise version and a diffusion-based version for better image quality. Evaluation against 6 watermarking methods shows the attack can remove or weaken watermarks while preserving perceptual quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Invisible watermarking is used to trace AI-generated images, but its robustness against adaptive removal attacks is not well understood. The authors aim to identify a practical attack surface (latent-frequency manipulation) that current watermarking methods may not defend against.

Method: The proposed Latent Frequency Masking attack works by: 1) Replacing selected Fourier coefficients in the latent representation of watermarked images, 2) Using either Gaussian noise sampling (efficient) or diffusion regeneration (better preservation). The paper also provides a theoretical distortion bound.

Result: The attack successfully removes or substantially weakens several watermarks while preserving perceptual quality and achieving favorable runtime compared with existing attacks. This demonstrates latent-frequency manipulation as a practical vulnerability.

Conclusion: Latent-frequency manipulation represents a practical attack surface for generative image watermarking. The authors recommend including such attacks in future robustness evaluations of watermarking systems.

Abstract: Invisible watermarking has become a central tool for tracing AI-generated images, but its robustness against adaptive removal attacks remains an open security question. We introduce Latent Frequency Masking, an attack that erases watermark evidence by replacing selected Fourier coefficients in the latent representation of a watermarked image. The replacement can be sampled from Gaussian noise for efficiency or derived from diffusion regeneration for improved image preservation. We provide a theoretical distortion bound relating the change between the reconstructed adversarial image and the masked latent-frequency perturbation. We evaluate the proposed attack against six diffusion watermarking methods on images generated from DiffusionDB and MS-COCO prompts. Latent Frequency Masking removes or substantially weakens several watermarks while preserving perceptual quality and achieving favorable runtime compared with existing attacks. These results identify latent-frequency manipulation as a practical attack surface and highlight the need to include such attacks in robustness evaluations of generative image watermarking.

</details>


### [8] [Domain generalization and synthetic data in object detection: the enabler, the probe, and the gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00030)
*Elfi I. S. Hofmeijer,Ella P. Fokkinga,Friso G. Heslinga,Klamer Schutte,Jörgen M. Karlholm*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an object detection-centric review of Domain Generalization (DG), focusing on the role of synthetic data from three perspectives: as an enabler through diversification/alignment strategies, as a probe for identifying failure modes, and as a challenge (synthetic-to-real gap). It identifies limitations in current DG approaches and argues for representation-aware methods addressing both localization and classification under domain shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Object detection models experience performance degradation under distribution shifts (weather, environment, appearance changes), yet DG research specifically for object detection is scarce despite additional challenges around localization and multi-scale representations. Synthetic data offers a promising tool to support DG through large-scale diverse sample generation.

Method: This paper provides a comprehensive review examining synthetic data's role in DG from three complementary perspectives: (1) as an enabler using diversification and alignment strategies to improve robustness, (2) as a probe enabling controlled experimentation to identify failure modes, and (3) analyzing the synthetic-to-real gap when deploying synthetic-trained models on real-world data.

Result: The review identifies limitations of current DG approaches for object detection, particularly the need for methods that explicitly address both localization and classification under domain shift.

Conclusion: Future research in DG for object detection requires representation-aware methods that explicitly handle both localization and classification under distribution shifts, moving beyond current approaches that may not adequately address these dual challenges.

Abstract: Object detection models often experience performance degradation when deployed under distribution shifts, caused by for example changes in weather type, operational environment, or object appearance. Domain Generalization (DG) aims to develop models that remain robust under such shifts and generalize well to unseen domains. DG research specifically focused on object detection models is scarce, although these models face additional challenges around localization and multi-scale representations. Synthetic data is a promising tool to support in DG, by enabling large-scale generation of diverse new samples. In this paper, we present an object detection-centric review of DG and examine the role of synthetic data from three complementary perspectives. First, synthetic data acts as an enabler of DG through diversification and alignment strategies that aim to improve robustness to distribution shifts. Second, it serves as a probe that enables controlled experimentation to identify and understand failure modes. Third, we discuss the synthetic-to-real gap, a particularly challenging form of domain shift that arises when models trained on synthetic imagery are deployed on real-world data. Through reviewing these perspectives, we identify limitations of current DG approaches for object detection and argue that future research requires representation-aware methods that explicitly address both localization and classification under domain shift.

</details>

*Kaizhen Tan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Street-view imagery is increasingly used to infer urban attributes, but predictive accuracy alone does not reveal how much a photograph contributes beyond data already available for the same place. We compare image-based predictions with existing urban data across seven attributes from five public resources and three VLMs. The same urban units are evaluated using images, task context, nearby observations, and public records, while image replacements and conflicting records test source reliance. Existing urban data matched or exceeded image-only models for road damage, curb ramps, and house price, while neighbouring official statistics nearly matched the best image result for population. Images were more informative for building type, building function, and low-rise floor count. For floor count, image advantage increased by 5.7 percentage points per doubling of distance to the nearest labelled building and declined for tall buildings whose rooflines often fell outside the frame. Models frequently followed conflicting records. OpenFACADES floor annotations were generated with OpenStreetMap floor values and showed the opposite height-dependent error pattern from image-only reruns. Street-view image value therefore depends on visual legibility and local data coverage. Comparing images with existing urban data can guide image collection and clarify the provenance of derived urban maps.

### [10] [DSSR-3D: Decoupled Reasoning for View-Dependent Referring in 3D Gaussians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00040)
*Thanh-Khoi Nguyen,Thien-Phuc Tran,Minh-Triet Tran*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DSSR-3D introduces an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, using two interfaces (pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning) that enable zero-shot transfer without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting methods for open-vocabulary referring segmentation embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose.

Method: The framework is formalized as two interfaces: pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning. This is instantiated with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step. No retraining of the underlying semantic field is required.

Result: Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods with no additional training beyond the base semantic field. The method transfers zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. A new benchmark (ViewRef-GS) and augmented Ref-LERF are proposed for evaluation.

Conclusion: DSSR-3D successfully enables view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields through a training-free approach, offering a plug-and-play solution that works with existing semantic fields and provides a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding.

Abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have enabled open-vocabulary and referring segmentation by distilling semantic knowledge from 2D foundation models into 3D representations. However, existing referring fields embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. We propose DSSR-3D, an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields, formalized as two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - such that any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation, requiring no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no reliance on discrete geometric proxies such as bounding boxes. We instantiate the two interfaces with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step, and show they transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. We further propose ViewRef-GS, a benchmark isolating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, evaluated jointly with an augmented Ref-LERF to provide a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding. Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field

</details>


### [11] [Reachability Is Not Generalization: Understanding Verb--Noun Decomposition in Assembly Action Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00064)
*Changyi Li,Yu Xiao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper analyzes how verb-noun decomposition performs in generalizing to unseen action combinations in assembly tasks. The authors find that while decomposition escapes the "atomic ceiling" (the zero-probability problem for unseen combinations), it only partially generalizes beyond this - performance remains tied to training data co-occurrence patterns, and failures concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component (usually nouns).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is that atomic action classifiers assign zero probability to unseen combinations of familiar components. Verb-noun decomposition is the prevailing solution, but it was unclear how well it generalizes under compositional shift (unseen combinations).

Method: The authors conducted a systematic analysis across three assembly datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, and IMPACT). They studied: (1) how decomposition generalizes beyond the atomic ceiling, (2) the relationship between generalization and training data co-occurrence structure, (3) the impact of vocabulary asymmetry, and (4) the effect of shared-encoder training on component entanglement.

Result: Key findings: (1) Decomposition escapes the atomic ceiling but only partially generalizes beyond it; (2) Unseen-composition performance is strongly tied to training data co-occurrence structure - much of the gain comes from interpolation within densely supported regions rather than true recombination; (3) Failures concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component; (4) IMPACT's verb-heavy vocabulary reverses the bottleneck from nouns to verbs; (5) Shared-encoder training introduces component entanglement, encouraging reliance on co-occurrence patterns that transfer poorly to unseen compositions, trailing independent recombination by up to 6.0× in harmonic mean.

Conclusion: Decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice. The connected sources of error are: primitive support (limited training support for components), vocabulary asymmetry (the larger vocabulary component becomes the bottleneck), and component entanglement (from shared encoders). The authors provide a portable diagnostic framework for studying compositional recognition beyond aggregate accuracy.

Abstract: Assembly actions are compositional: they combine a manipulation with a part or tool. In deployment, systems routinely encounter novel combinations of familiar components, yet an atomic action classifier assigns every unseen combination exactly zero probability by construction. The prevailing solution is verb--noun decomposition, which predicts components separately and recombines them to reach unseen actions. While widely adopted, how decomposition generalizes under compositional shift remains poorly understood. We present a systematic analysis of verb--noun decomposition across three assembly datasets (MECCANO, HAViD, and IMPACT). Although decomposition escapes the atomic ceiling, its generalization extends only partially beyond it. Unseen-composition performance remains strongly tied to the co-occurrence structure of the training data, indicating that much of the observed gain arises from interpolation within densely supported regions of the compositional space rather than from unconstrained recombination. Across datasets, failures consistently concentrate on the larger-vocabulary component, and IMPACT's verb-heavy vocabulary reverses the bottleneck from nouns to verbs. We further show that shared-encoder training introduces component entanglement, encouraging reliance on co-occurrence patterns that transfer poorly to unseen compositions and trailing independent recombination by up to $6.0\times$ in harmonic mean. Taken together, these findings explain why decomposition achieves only partial compositional generalization in practice. By identifying primitive support, vocabulary asymmetry, and component entanglement as connected sources of error, we provide a portable diagnostic framework for studying compositional recognition beyond aggregate accuracy. Code: https://github.com/hisalaheiyo/assembly.

</details>


### [12] [What Builds the Scene? Luminance Dominates Geometry Formation in 3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00749)
*Rezvan Joshaghani,Steven Cutchin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates how luminance and chroma contribute to geometry learning in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by training models with different channel supervision and comparing reconstruction quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard 3DGS learns geometry and appearance jointly from RGB supervision, making it difficult to isolate how luminance and chroma individually contribute to the learned representation.

Method: The authors train models under different channel supervision (luminance-only, chroma-only, RGB), freeze non-appearance parameters (position, scale, rotation, opacity), re-estimate appearance with the same solver, and compare held-out reconstruction across 11 benchmark scenes with 4 independent runs each.

Result: Geometry learned from luminance alone performs 0.085 dB below RGB-trained geometry. Chroma can be recovered to original quality after freezing geometry. Higher-order spherical harmonics improve PSNR by 1.44 dB for luminance vs 0.19 dB for chroma. Chroma-only supervision produces geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse than luminance-only supervision. Densification partially explains this gap.

Conclusion: Geometry formation in standard 3DGS is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive. Much chromatic appearance can be recovered after spatial support has formed.

Abstract: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) learns geometry and appearance jointly from RGB supervision, making it difficult to isolate how luminance and chroma contribute to the learned representation. We study this by training models under different channel supervision, freezing their non-appearance parameters (position, scale, rotation, and opacity), and re-estimating appearance with the same solver before comparing held-out reconstruction. Across eleven benchmark scenes with four independent runs each, geometry learned from luminance alone supports held-out reconstruction 0.085 dB below RGB-trained geometry on average. If chroma is deleted from a trained model, a sufficiently expressive solver can re-fit it on the frozen geometry to the original quality or slightly better. Higher-order spherical harmonics contribute much more reconstruction quality to luminance than to chroma, improving PSNR by 1.44 dB versus 0.19 dB on average, although on mirror-like surfaces hue does still change with viewpoint. The luminance advantage is even larger when geometry is being formed. Chroma-only supervision produces geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse than luminance-only supervision after the same appearance solve; densification explains part of this gap. Overall, geometry formation in standard 3DGS is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive, and much of the chromatic appearance can be recovered after spatial support has formed.

</details>


### [13] [Robust Online Aero-Engine Blade Defect Detection via Dual-Alignment Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00067)
*Zhaoyang Wang,Haiyong Chen,Dongying Li,Yining Wang,Huapeng Wu,Xinwei Lv,Atik Shahariar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ABDD is an online adaptive detection framework for aero-engine blade defect inspection that addresses domain shift challenges through test-time adaptation. It uses a Dual-Alignment Strategy combining feature-statistics and pseudo-box alignment, an Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism to handle unreliable pseudo labels, and a Sparse Dilated Mona module for parameter-efficient delta tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The reliability of deep defect detectors in aero-engine blade manufacturing degrades due to domain shifts caused by varying production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds. This is particularly challenging because sparse defects make pseudo-label-based adaptation vulnerable to noisy or missing predictions.

Method: The proposed ABDD framework employs three key components: (1) Dual-Alignment Strategy that jointly adapts global visual style and local defect morphology by combining feature-statistics alignment with pseudo-box alignment; (2) Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism that evaluates pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy to reduce error accumulation; (3) Sparse Dilated Mona module for parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting. Evaluation uses RT-DETR + Swin-T architecture.

Result: ABDD consistently improves detection robustness under domain shifts on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD datasets across multiple domain-shift scenarios. The method's practicality is further validated on an industrial inspection platform.

Conclusion: Test-time adaptation with dual-alignment and uncertainty-aware filtering effectively addresses domain shift challenges in aero-engine blade defect detection, achieving robust performance in industrial deployment settings.

Abstract: Reliable visual inspection is essential for quality assurance in aero-engine blade manufacturing, where defect appearance may vary across production lines, imaging conditions, blade poses, and surface backgrounds. Such domain shifts cause a mismatch between training and deployment data and degrade the reliability of deep defect detectors in online inspection. This problem is particularly challenging because aero-engine blade images usually contain sparse defects, making pseudolabel-based adaptation vulnerable to noisy or missing predictions. To address this issue, we propose Aero-engine Blade Defect Detector (ABDD), an online adaptive detection framework based on test-time adaptation. ABDD introduces a Dual-Alignment Strategy to jointly adapt global visual style and local defect morphology by combining feature-statistics alignment with pseudo-box alignment. To reduce error accumulation from unreliable pseudo labels, an Uncertainty-aware Box Filtering mechanism evaluates pseudo boxes using classification confidence, classification entropy, and localization entropy. In addition, a lightweight Sparse Dilated Mona module enables parameter-efficient delta tuning while limiting source-domain forgetting. ABDD is evaluated on CD-AeBD and HD-AeBD under multiple domain-shift scenarios, with TTA strategies compared under a unified RT-DETR + Swin-T architecture. Experiments show that ABDD consistently improves detection robustness under domain shifts, and its practicality is further validated on an industrial inspection platform.

</details>


### [14] [A Framework for Egocentric and Exocentric Procedural Understanding via Temporal Segmentation and Semantic Abstraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00069)
*Vivek Chavan,Jörg Krüger*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory (Work Environment Model) by detecting event boundaries using multiple contextual signals and encoding segments into compact, auditable event cards with evidence linkages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon ego/exo video data is rich in procedural evidence but suffers from redundancy, noise, and high processing/retention costs. Existing methods rely on fixed windows or visual novelty alone, which are inadequate for capturing meaningful procedural boundaries.

Method: Inspired by event segmentation theory, the framework detects boundaries using multimodal signals including visual context changes, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence. Each detected segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. Implementation uses frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders with a local language model.

Result: The framework enables compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints through incremental WEM updates.

Conclusion: The proposed WEM framework provides a principled approach to procedural memory encoding from multimodal video. Future work outlines evaluation criteria for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.

Abstract: Long-horizon ego/exo data contains rich procedural evidence, but are redundant, noisy, and costly to process or retain. We propose a compact framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory, implemented as a Work Environment Model (WEM). Inspired by event segmentation theory, we detect boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence, rather than fixed windows or visual novelty alone. Each segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. These event cards incrementally update the WEM, enabling compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints. We instantiate the design with frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders and a local language model, and outline evaluation criteria for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.

</details>


### [15] [LiteReality-Agent: An Agentic System for Interactable 3D Indoor Scene Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01863)
*Zhening Huang,Yueyan Li,Johnathan Chiu,Xiaoyang Lyu,Matt Zhou,Yuxin Yao,Joan Lasenby,Shangzhe Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LiteReality-Agent is an agentic system that reconstructs real indoor environments as realistic, articulated, and simulation-ready 3D scenes from RGB-D scans. It formulates 3D reconstruction as a coding problem where a coding agent uses specialized tools to iteratively edit a Python script (Room.py) that produces a 3D digital twin of the room.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to create high-quality, simulation-ready 3D reconstructions of real indoor environments for embodied AI tasks. Current frontier models like Astra and Fable produce reconstructions that lack sufficient geometric accuracy, visual realism, and simulation compatibility. The authors view this as a building block for robust real-to-sim systems.

Method: The core method treats 3D reconstruction as a coding problem. A coding agent gathers evidence using specialized tools and iteratively edits a Python script (Room.py) that can be executed to produce a 3D digital twin. The system uses an observe-edit-verify harness that supports evidence gathering, measurement, verification, layout optimization, simulation readiness, and quality control throughout the reconstruction process.

Result: LiteReality-Agent produces reconstructions that are more geometrically accurate, visually realistic, and simulation-compatible than those generated by recent frontier models (Astra and Fable). The system provides a robust orchestration framework with specialized tools, structured workflows, and verification mechanisms that improve reconstruction quality and reliability.

Conclusion: LiteReality-Agent is a practical and important building block for robust real-to-sim systems. It represents a strong orchestration framework for future agents as capabilities continue to improve. Both source code and data-capture application are publicly available.

Abstract: We present LiteReality-Agent, an agentic system for reconstructing real indoor environments as realistic, articulated, and simulation-ready 3D scenes from RGB-D scans. At its core, LiteReality-Agent formulates 3D reconstruction as a coding problem, in which a coding agent gathers evidence using specialised tools and iteratively edits a Python script, Room.py, which can be executed to produce a 3D digital twin of the room. With this formulation, we develop a robust observe-edit-verify harness that supports evidence gathering, measurement, verification, layout optimisation, simulation readiness, and quality control throughout the reconstruction process. LiteReality-Agent produces high-quality reconstructions suitable for simulation and downstream embodied AI tasks. Furthermore, as agent capabilities continue to improve rapidly, the system introduced by LiteReality-Agent remains a strong orchestration framework for future agents: it equips them with specialised tools, structured workflows, and robust verification mechanisms that substantially improve reconstruction quality and reliability. We demonstrate that LiteReality-Agent produces reconstructions that are more geometrically accurate, visually realistic, and simulation-compatible than those generated by recent frontier models, such as Astra and Fable. We therefore view LiteReality-Agent as a practical and important building block for robust real-to-sim systems. Both the source code and the data-capture application are publicly available. Code:https://github.com/LiteReality/LiteReality-Agent/

</details>


### [16] [DramaAgent: Agentic Storytelling Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00097)
*Ting Huang,Biao Wu,Ronghao Chen,Zeyu Zhang,Tengfei Cheng,Qizhen Lan,Huacan Wang,Hao Tang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DramaAgent is a hierarchical agentic framework for long-form text-to-video-and-audio generation that introduces an upper-level control layer to decompose generation into story planning, persistent character conditioning, scene-wise synthesis, and reflection-guided repair. It maintains reusable story and character states across scenes and diagnoses/repairs failures like identity drift and audio-visual mismatch.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion and autoregressive models struggle with coherent long-form story videos, suffering from narrative drift, unstable character identity, weak cross-scene continuity, and audio-visual mismatch over extended sequences. There was a need for a controllable approach to long-form audiovisual generation.

Method: DramaAgent uses a hierarchical, agentic, model-agnostic framework with four key components: (1) story planning for narrative structure, (2) persistent character conditioning for identity consistency, (3) scene-wise synthesis for generation, and (4) reflection-guided targeted repair for diagnosing and fixing failures like identity drift, missing scene semantics, temporal discontinuity, and cross-modal mismatch.

Result: Experiments across multiple video generation backbones show that DramaAgent improves long-horizon coherence, character consistency, narrative fidelity, and scene-level audio-visual consistency over direct generation and strong baselines.

Conclusion: Hierarchical agentic control is a practical and effective direction for controllable long-form audiovisual generation, offering a novel approach that augments existing video backbones rather than modifying them.

Abstract: Recent diffusion and autoregressive models have substantially improved text-to-video generation, yet producing coherent long-form story videos with consistent characters and aligned audio remains challenging. Existing methods often suffer from narrative drift, unstable character identity, weak cross-scene continuity, and audio-visual mismatch over extended sequences. We propose DramaAgent, a hierarchical, agentic, and model-agnostic framework for long-form text-to-video-and-audio generation. Rather than improving the underlying video backbone itself, DramaAgent introduces an upper-level control layer that decomposes generation into story planning, persistent character conditioning, scene-wise synthesis, and reflection-guided targeted repair. The framework maintains reusable story and character states across scenes, diagnoses failures such as identity drift, missing scene semantics, temporal discontinuity, and cross-modal mismatch, and repairs problematic clips in a stage-specific manner. Experiments across multiple video generation backbones show that DramaAgent improves long-horizon coherence, character consistency, narrative fidelity, and scene-level audio-visual consistency over direct generation and strong baselines. These results suggest that hierarchical agentic control is a practical direction for controllable long-form audiovisual generation. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/DramaAgent. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/DramaAgent.

</details>


### [17] [MosaiChunk: Compositing Spatio-Temporal Memory for Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02153)
*Yiwen Zhang,Haocheng Xi,Michael Tian-Yue Liu,Alexei A. Efros,Hadar Averbuch-Elor,Qianqian Wang,Haiwen Feng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MosaiChunk introduces a spatio-temporal memory mechanism that composes a mosaic of selected historical key-value (KV) entries to address context window limitations in long-horizon autoregressive video generation. It uses a lightweight router to select historical sections under a fixed memory budget, and is evaluated on RememBench with both T2V and I2V settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon autoregressive video generation is limited by a finite context window. When objects or scenes fall out of context, fine-grained visual details may be lost and difficult to recover upon reappearance.

Method: MosaiChunk composes a mosaic of selected historical KV entries across space and time. The generator is kept frozen, and only a lightweight router is learned to determine which historical sections to include in the mosaic under a fixed active-memory budget. Evaluation is performed on RememBench, a new benchmark with T2V and I2V splits for long-horizon revisits.

Result: MosaiChunk consistently improves revisit consistency over both sliding-window inference and whole-chunk retrieval under matched memory budgets, across both T2V and I2V settings.

Conclusion: The proposed spatio-temporal memory mechanism effectively addresses context window limitations in long-horizon video generation by selectively retaining historical visual details through a learned router.

Abstract: Long-horizon autoregressive video generation is limited by a finite context window. When an object or scene falls out of context, its fine-grained visual details may be lost and difficult to recover upon reappearance. To retain access to such visual details, we introduce MosaiChunk, a spatio-temporal memory mechanism that composes a mosaic of selected historical key-value (KV) entries across space and time. Our approach is motivated by the observation that a frozen video generator can directly consume such non-contiguous historical KV and recover the corresponding visual content. We therefore keep the generator fixed and learn only a lightweight router that determines which historical sections to include in the mosaic under a fixed active-memory budget. We further introduce RememBench, a benchmark of long-horizon revisits with prompt-driven text-to-video (T2V) and camera-driven image-to-video (I2V) splits. Our experiments show that MosaiChunk consistently improves revisit consistency over both sliding-window inference and whole-chunk retrieval under matched memory budgets, across both T2V and I2V settings.

</details>


### [18] [A Low Grounding Score Is Not an Ungrounded Judge: Identifying the Perceptibility Confound in Multimodal Oversight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00111)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether counterfactual probes of visual grounding actually measure what they claim to. The authors find that the Verdict Grounding Score has a systematic false alarm problem: it can only make a judge appear less grounded than it actually is, because the score is capped by how perceptible the edit is. They show this missing quantity can be identified from three quantities already collected during the audit, making false-alarm rates directly measurable. Empirical testing on nine judges confirms these predictions, and they recommend that detection probes on unedited images should always accompany counterfactual scores to certify false alarms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model judges are increasingly used to supervise multimodal systems at scale, filtering training data, selecting outputs, and providing rewards for reasoning models. However, trusting these judges requires verifying they actually use visual evidence (visual grounding). The authors aim to check whether a counterfactual probe of visual grounding measures what it claims to, as this check itself is worth scrutinizing.

Method: The authors formalize the counterfactual probe as the Verdict Grounding Score. The probe edits the image so the ground truth flips, holds the reasoning trace fixed, and asks whether the verdict follows. They analyze the theoretical properties of this score and show it has a systematic one-sided error: the score can only make a judge appear less grounded than it actually is. Under stated assumptions, they demonstrate the missing quantity can be identified from three quantities already collected in the audit protocol.

Result: The predicted ordering holds strictly across all nine judges audited. The typical judge acts on only about half of the edits whose attribute it can otherwise resolve. Applying a conservative rejection threshold certifies several cells as false alarms outright, including a judge that detects injected errors essentially every time while still scoring as if it had not used the image at all.

Conclusion: The key recommendation is that an image-side counterfactual score should never be reported alone. A detection probe on the unedited image upper-bounds the score, certifies its false alarms, and costs nothing extra to run. This makes proper auditing of visual grounding in model judges feasible and prevents discarding usable overseers due to false alarms.

Abstract: Model judges now supervise multimodal systems at scale, filtering training data, selecting outputs, and supplying the reward that shapes multimodal reasoning models. Trusting one means first checking that it uses its evidence, and that check is itself worth scrutinizing, so we ask whether a counterfactual probe of visual grounding measures what it claims to. The probe edits the image so the ground truth flips, holds the reasoning trace fixed, and asks whether the verdict follows. We formalize it as the Verdict Grounding Score and show it cannot be read the way such scores are read. A verdict responds only to an edit that reaches the judge's decision-relevant reading, so the score is capped by how perceptible the edit is, and unless editing makes the attribute easier to read, the error is one-sided: the score can only make a judge look less grounded than it is. The practical failure is therefore a false alarm, an auditor discarding a usable overseer. Under assumptions we state, we show this missing quantity is not merely bounded but identified from three quantities the same audit protocol already collects, which makes the false-alarm rate directly measurable rather than merely a concern. Auditing nine judges, we find the predicted ordering holds strictly across our entire primary pool, and the typical judge there acts on only about half of the edits whose attribute it can otherwise resolve. Applying a conservative rejection threshold certifies several cells as false alarms outright, the clearest being a judge that detects the injected error essentially every time while still scoring as if it had not used the image at all. The rule that follows is that an image-side counterfactual score should never be reported alone: a detection probe on the unedited image upper-bounds it, certifies its false alarms, and costs nothing extra to run.

</details>


### [19] [Evaluating the Robustness of Anti-UAV Detection under Controlled Fog Degradation: Fog-Aware Training and Clear-Sky Tradeoff](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00141)
*Gur Levy Birkental,Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari,Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents the first severity-controlled fog benchmark for vision-based anti-UAV detection, revealing that detection performance degrades sharply and non-linearly with fog severity (96% mAP@0.5:0.95 drop), and that fog-aware training significantly improves robustness but cannot prevent collapse under extreme fog conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-based anti-UAV systems must function in poor visibility conditions, but existing benchmarks only use clear-sky footage. Previous robustness studies treated adverse weather as a simple present/absent condition, failing to understand how fog severity impacts ground-to-air UAV detection.

Method: The researchers created a synthetic fog benchmark at ten severity levels applied to the RGB modality of the Anti-UAV300 dataset. They compared a clear-trained YOLOv5m baseline against a fog-aware model trained on both clear and foggy images.

Result: Detection performance degrades sharply and non-linearly, with degradation front-loaded across light-to-moderate fog (beta ≈ 0.05-0.10). There is a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog, primarily due to lost recall and confidence. On mAP@0.5, this collapse exceeds the most extreme rain degradation reported in prior benchmarks. Fog-aware training improves detection across all severities (up to +0.320 mAP@0.5:0.95) with only a 9.1% clear-sky accuracy drop, but cannot prevent collapse under extreme fog. Reliability is lost within a narrow visibility range.

Conclusion: Simple clear vs adverse weather tests underestimate operational risk. The study highlights the need for severity-controlled benchmarks to properly assess anti-UAV system performance in real-world conditions where visibility varies significantly.

Abstract: Vision-based anti-UAV systems must function in poor visibility, yet most benchmarks use only clear-sky footage, and previous robustness studies treat adverse weather as a simple present/absent condition. As a result, the impact of fog severity on ground-to-air UAV detection remains poorly understood. This work presents the first severity-controlled fog benchmark for this task: synthetic fog at ten severity levels is applied to the RGB modality of the Anti-UAV300 dataset, comparing a clear-trained YOLOv5m baseline to a fog-aware model trained on both clear and foggy images. Detection performance drops sharply and non-linearly: degradation is front-loaded across light-to-moderate fog (beta approximately 0.05-0.10), with a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog, mainly due to lost recall and confidence. On the comparable metric (mAP@0.5), this collapse exceeds the most extreme rain degradation reported in the closest prior benchmark. Fog-aware training boosts detection across all severities (up to +0.320 mAP@0.5:0.95) with only a 9.1% drop in clear-sky accuracy, raising the threshold for reliable detection while not preventing collapse under extreme fog. Since reliability is lost within a narrow visibility range, simple clear vs adverse tests underestimate operational risk.

</details>


### [20] [GPEC: Efficient Pre-LLM Gaussian Process Embedding Correction for Cardiac Video Caption Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00196)
*Arefeh Rezaei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GPEC is a modular pre-LLM error-correction method that improves visual representations for cardiac ultrasound caption generation by learning a residual correction between the visual projection layer and language model, using sparse variational Gaussian Process with annotation-guided targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show performance decline in specialized medical imaging domains like echocardiography, despite their strong potential in general video understanding. Current approaches may not effectively handle the unique characteristics of cardiac ultrasound data.

Method: GPEC inserts a correction module between the visual projection layer and language model of VideoChat2. It learns a residual correction using sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points, natural-parameter variational updates, and block-wise linear kernel. The target is constructed by converting structured video annotations into qualitative attributes, generating fixed-format reference captions, and mapping them into the language-model embedding space. Original VideoChat2 components remain frozen.

Result: GPEC improves caption similarity and content alignment compared to original VideoChat2. The method adds less than 0.05 seconds of inference-time overhead per video while not requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained multimodal backbone.

Conclusion: GPEC can effectively improve caption generation in specialized medical video domains with minimal computational cost, offering a modular solution that enhances medical video understanding without requiring extensive retraining of the base model.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for video understanding and caption generation, but their performance may decline in specialized medical imaging domains such as echocardiography. This work introduces Gaussian Process Embedding Correction (GPEC), a modular and computationally efficient pre-LLM error-correction method that improves the visual representations used by VideoChat2 for cardiac ultrasound caption generation. GPEC is inserted between the visual projection layer and the language model and learns a residual correction that moves the projected visual representation toward an annotation-guided target. The target is constructed by converting structured video annotations into qualitative attributes, generating a fixed-format reference caption, and mapping it into the language-model embedding space. The correction is modeled using a sparse variational Gaussian Process with inducing points, natural-parameter variational updates, and a block-wise linear kernel, while the original VideoChat2 components remain frozen.The method is evaluated using representation-level, caption-level, content-oriented, and execution-time metrics by comparing the original VideoChat2 with VideoChat2 + GPEC under identical input and reference conditions. Results show improved caption similarity and content alignment after applying the proposed correction. Furthermore, GPEC adds less than 0.05 s of inference-time overhead per video in the evaluated setting. These findings indicate that GPEC can improve caption generation in specialized medical video domains with minimal computational cost, without requiring end-to-end fine-tuning of the pretrained multimodal backbone.

</details>


### [21] [Query Independent Variable Rate Visual Token Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00204)
*Hongbo Zhang,Zihao Yang,Liuyang Song,Daqian Yang,Haoyang Yao,Yan Wen,Zhengtao Yao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A transform coding approach for visual-token compression in vision-language models that keeps all tokens but allocates variable bit rates across them using rate-distortion optimization, creating a single compressed representation that serves any query rather than being question-dependent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current methods treat visual-token compression as a token selection problem (keep/discard) ranked by attention the language model pays tokens, which makes the ranking dependent on the question. This is problematic for multi-turn conversations or caching scenarios where one compressed representation must serve multiple queries.

Method: Expose each token's measured distortion-rate curve and distribute a fixed bit budget across tokens using exact integer rate-distortion optimization. No text enters the pipeline, ensuring one compressed representation serves any query.

Result: At equal bit budgets on two datasets and two capacities, it better preserves the model's output distribution and answers than uniform-rate coding, closed-form water-fill, and distortion-ranked pruning. It matches attention-ranked pruning on the question it was tuned for, and outperforms it when the compressed image must answer a different question about the same image.

Conclusion: Transform coding with rate-distortion optimization provides a more versatile compression approach than selection-based methods, as it creates a single compressed representation that works across different queries rather than being optimized for a specific question.

Abstract: Visual-token compression for vision--language models is posed almost entirely as a selection problem: decide which tokens to keep and discard the rest. The criteria that work best rank tokens by the attention the language model pays them, which makes the ranking a function of the question being asked. That is invisible in a single-turn benchmark and decisive whenever a compressed representation is written once and read many times, as when it is cached across the turns of a conversation or transmitted between a device and a server. We take the other half of the classical transform-coding toolkit instead: keep every token and vary its rate. A transform code exposes each token's measured distortion--rate curve, and a fixed bit budget is distributed across tokens by exact integer rate--distortion optimisation on those curves. No text enters the pipeline, so one compressed representation serves any query. At equal bit budgets, on two datasets and two capacities, it preserves the model's output distribution and its answers better than uniform-rate coding, the closed-form water-fill and distortion-ranked pruning. It matches attention-ranked pruning on the question pruning was tuned for, and overtakes it once the compressed image must answer a different question about the same image.

</details>


### [22] [Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion U-Net for Magnetic Resonance Imaging Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00279)
*Eirini Cholopoulou,Dimitrios E. Diamantis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes MRFFU-Net, a novel deep learning architecture for MRI segmentation that incorporates a Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion (MRFF) module into U-Net-like frameworks. The MRFF module is integrated at all levels of the encoder-decoder structure along with attention mechanisms and skip connections to capture both fine-grained details and global contextual information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current U-Net architectures struggle with preserving fine-grained details and global contextual information in MRI segmentation, where anatomical structures have irregular boundaries and variations in shape, contrast, and scale.

Method: The proposed MRFF module is integrated into all levels of an encoder-decoder structure, combined with attention mechanisms and skip connections to extract features at multiple resolutions.

Result: MRFFU-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics on two benchmark MRI datasets: CSF segmentation in spinal MR scans and left atrium cardiac segmentation from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) challenge.

Conclusion: The MRFFU-Net architecture demonstrates effectiveness in MRI segmentation by successfully capturing both fine-grained details and global contextual information through its multi-resolution feature fusion approach.

Abstract: The segmentation of anatomical structures in medical images and particularly in MRI scans, is essential for clinical diagnosis and monitoring disease progression. While Deep Learning (DL) architectures, such as U-Net and its extensions are very effective in medical image segmentation tasks, they often struggle with preserving fine-grained details and global contextual information. This is especially challenging for MRI data segmentation, where anatomical structures are characterized by irregular boundaries and variations in shape, contrast, and scale. To address this challenge, we propose a novel DL architecture for MRI segmentation across different anatomical structures. Specifically, the architecture introduces a module, named Multi-Resolution Feature Fusion (MRFF), that can be easily integrated into any U-Net-like architecture. The MRFF is integrated in all levels of an encode-decoder structure, along with attention mechanisms and skip connections to extract features at multiple resolutions, enabling the model to capture both fine-grained details and global contextual information. We evaluate the MRFFU-Net on two publicly available benchmark MRI datasets of different anatomical targets; one for Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) segmentation in spinal MR scans, and one for left atrium cardiac segmentation, from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) challenge. Experimental results indicate that MRFFU-Net outperforms state-of-the-art models across multiple evaluation metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness in MRI segmentation.

</details>


### [23] [LENS-GRF: Permutation-Invariant Lesion Evidence Network with Gated Residual Fusion for Acne Severity Grading and Multi-Rater Clinical Oracle Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00294)
*Muhammad Muhtasim Shahriar,M. F. Mridha*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LENS-GRF is an interpretable multi-stage framework for automated four-class acne severity grading that combines global facial context (Vision Transformer) with fine-grained lesion evidence (Lesion Set Transformer) through Gated Residual Fusion. Achieved 95.89% accuracy with ground-truth annotations on ACNE04, but only 35-47% accuracy in zero-shot evaluation on PLSBRACNE01, revealing significant domain shift and annotation variability challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Acne severity grading requires both whole-face context and fine-grained lesion evidence, but existing methods lack interpretability and struggle with cross-domain generalization. The authors propose combining global Vision Transformer priors with local lesion set encoding to achieve interpretable multi-stage grading.

Method: LENS-GRF integrates: (1) Adaptive Facial Skin Segmentation for region extraction; (2) Global Vision Transformer for whole-face context; (3) Permutation-invariant Lesion Set Transformer encoding localized lesion patches and spatial geometry; (4) Gated Residual Fusion that adaptively controls local residual contribution. The gate mechanism can reduce to global prediction only when gate equals zero.

Result: On ACNE04: 80.82% accuracy with YOLOv11s detector; 95.89% ± 0.59% accuracy and QWK of 0.9753 with ground-truth annotations. On PLSBRACNE01 (200 subjects, 600 views): 35.00% accuracy (automated) vs 42.50% (global baseline). With ground-truth lesions on 148-subject cohort: best oracle accuracy 47.97%, highest oracle QWK 0.5799. Pairwise oracle agreement ranged 49.32%-66.22%. Data audit found 15 cross-split duplicates including 5 with conflicting labels.

Conclusion: While LENS-GRF achieves high accuracy on ACNE04 with ground-truth lesions (95.89%), cross-domain generalization remains challenging (35% on PLSBRACNE01). The gap between oracle analysis (47.97%) and automated performance reveals significant detector domain shift, annotation variability, and cross-criterion label inconsistency issues. The framework demonstrates the importance of both global context and local lesion evidence, but domain adaptation and standardized annotation criteria remain critical challenges.

Abstract: Automated acne severity grading requires both whole-face context and fine-grained lesion evidence. We propose LENS-GRF (Lesion Evidence Network with Set-Transformer and Gated Residual Fusion), an interpretable multi-stage framework for four-class acne severity grading. The method combines Adaptive Facial Skin Segmentation and a global Vision Transformer prior with a permutation-invariant Lesion Set Transformer that encodes localized lesion patches and spatial geometry. Gated Residual Fusion adaptively controls the local residual contribution and reduces to the global prediction when the gate is zero. On ACNE04, fully automated LENS-GRF with YOLOv11s achieved 80.82% accuracy; with ground-truth lesion annotations, it achieved 95.89% +/- 0.59% accuracy and a Quadratic Weighted Kappa of 0.9753. A data-integrity audit identified 15 cross-split duplicate image pairs, including five with conflicting severity labels. In locked zero-shot evaluation on the full PLSBRACNE01 cohort (200 subjects, 600 views), automated LENS-GRF achieved 35.00% accuracy versus 42.50% for the global baseline. On the 148-subject common cohort used for three-dermatologist oracle analysis, ground-truth lesion inputs increased the best oracle accuracy to 47.97%, while the highest oracle QWK was 0.5799. Pairwise oracle agreement ranged from 49.32% to 66.22%, highlighting detector domain shift, annotation variability, and cross-criterion mismatch.

</details>


### [24] [Decoding the Disaster: Multi-Task Geospatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models and Crowdsourced Imagery for Disaster Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00302)
*Wenping Yin,Fabian Desuer,Ziqi Liu,Naixia Mou,Weijia Li,Pedram Ghamisi,Xiao Xiang Zhu,Hao Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes GRDisaster, a multi-task Geospatial Reasoning Disaster mapping framework that leverages vision-language models (VLMs) to understand, geolocalize, and reason over crowdsourced disaster imagery. It uses a new benchmark dataset of 26,340 images with cross-view triplets (VGI, SVI, RSI) to enable cross-view geolocalization and disaster damage assessment through spatial reasoning indicators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Crowdsourced imagery provides timely, fine-grained street-level observations for disaster mapping but is often unstructured, spatially ambiguous, and lacks reliable geographic metadata, making manual geolocalization and interpretation labor-intensive and difficult to scale.

Method: GRDisaster combines deterministic and probabilistic cross-view geolocalization with multi-view fusion to associate VGI images with georeferenced SVI and RSI. It introduces two sets of spatial reasoning indicators: (1) for cross-view geolocalization validation using structural, environmental, and global-scene cues, and (2) for disaster damage assessment with expert-verified annotations to assess disaster severity.

Result: The framework provides the first systematic investigation and unified evaluation framework for examining how VLM-based spatial reasoning can transform crowdsourced disaster imagery into actionable GeoAI through cross-view geolocalization validation, interpretable spatial reasoning, and damage-aware severity assessment.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates the potential of VLMs in transforming crowdsourced disaster imagery into actionable geospatial intelligence, enabling more scalable and interpretable disaster response mapping.

Abstract: Crowdsourced imagery provides timely, fine-grained, street-level observations for disaster mapping, complementing conventional remote sensing imagery (RSI) during emergency response. However, such imagery is often unstructured, spatially ambiguous, and lacks reliable geographic metadata, making manual geolocalization and interpretation labor-intensive and difficult to scale. This work proposes a multi-task Geospatial Reasoning Disaster mapping framework, namely GRDisaster, to examine the potential of vision-language models (VLMs) in understanding, geolocalizing, and reasoning over crowdsourced disaster imagery. GRDisaster is built on a newly curated benchmark dataset derived from PhotoMappers, comprising 26,340 images organized into human-validated volunteered geographic information (VGI), street-view imagery (SVI), RSI cross-view triplets covering multiple disaster events from 2018 to 2024. The framework combines deterministic and probabilistic cross-view geolocalization with multi-view fusion to associate VGI images with georeferenced SVI and RSI. It introduces two sets of spatial reasoning indicators for cross-view geolocalization validation and disaster damage assessment. These indicators use structural, environmental, and global-scene cues to validate cross-view correspondences and visually observable damage evidence with expert-verified annotations to assess disaster severity, improving the interpretability of VLM outputs. To our knowledge, this study provides the first systematic investigation and unified evaluation framework for examining how VLM-based spatial reasoning can transform crowdsourced disaster imagery into actionable geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) through cross-view geolocalization validation, interpretable spatial reasoning, and damage-aware severity assessment.

</details>


### [25] [Watch Your Speech: Text-aware Video-to-Speech Synthesis with Textual Conditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01012)
*Gunwoo Lee,Yoori Oh,Yoseob Han*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Watch Your Speech (WYS) is a video-to-speech synthesis framework that addresses the one-to-many mapping problem by incorporating textual conditioning as an explicit linguistic cue. It uses an attention-based embedding fusion module and conditional flow matching for high-fidelity speech generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The fundamental challenge in video-to-speech synthesis is the inherent one-to-many mapping problem, where visual dynamics from silent talking-face videos often lack sufficient information to uniquely determine the corresponding utterance, leading to ambiguity in speech generation.
