Method: The proposed WYS framework integrates textual conditioning through: 1) An attention-based embedding fusion module that synergistically combines textual context with video sequences, and 2) A conditional flow matching objective for high-fidelity speech generation.

Result: Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 datasets show WYS achieves state-of-the-art results in audio-visual synchronization (LSE-C/D) while maintaining highly competitive word error rate (WER). Subjective evaluations confirm near-human naturalness speech generation.

Conclusion: Textual conditioning effectively mitigates visual ambiguity in video-to-speech synthesis, enabling content-controlled speech generation with superior audio-visual synchronization and naturalness. The approach establishes a new paradigm for integrating linguistic cues in visual speech synthesis.

Abstract: Video-to-speech synthesis aims to generate natural-sounding speech from silent talking-face videos while ensuring phonetic accuracy. A fundamental challenge in this task is the inherent one-to-many mapping problem, where visual dynamics often lack sufficient information to uniquely determine the corresponding utterance. To address this, we propose Watch Your Speech (WYS), a video-to-speech synthesis framework that incorporates textual conditioning as an explicit linguistic cue to mitigate visual ambiguity. Our framework features an attention-based embedding fusion module that synergistically integrates textual context with video sequences, coupled with a conditional flow matching objective for high-fidelity speech generation. Extensive experiments on the LRS2 and LRS3 datasets demonstrate that WYS achieves superior performance, establishing new state-of-the-art results in audio-visual synchronization (LSE-C/D) while maintaining highly competitive textual accuracy (WER). Subjective evaluations further confirm that our model generates speech with near-human naturalness, validating the effectiveness of textual conditioning in content-controlled video-to-speech synthesis. Project page: https://github.com/gunwoo5034/Watch-your-Speech

</details>


### [26] [Beyond Pixel Reconstruction: Retrieval-Guided Glyph-Aware Restoration for Low-Resource Manchu Historical Documents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00315)
*Ting Huang,Dongdong Wang,Mingqiu Liang,Siyang Lu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a retrieval-guided glyph-aware restoration framework for historical Manchu documents that addresses the limitation of existing pixel-level reconstruction methods by explicitly incorporating glyph-level structural knowledge through exemplar retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Historical Manchu documents preserve invaluable linguistic and cultural heritage, but their digitization is hindered by severe degradations and scarcity of paired training data. Existing restoration methods focus on pixel-level reconstruction, which produces visually plausible results but fails to preserve the structural identity of Manchu glyphs.

Method: The proposed method retrieves relevant glyph exemplars to provide structural guidance during restoration and integrates this information into the reconstruction process. This approach explicitly incorporates glyph-level structural knowledge beyond pixel reconstruction to improve recovery of degraded character structures under low-resource conditions.

Result: Extensive experiments on Manchu historical documents demonstrate that the proposed approach improves both image restoration quality and glyph-level fidelity compared with existing restoration methods.

Conclusion: The results highlight the importance of incorporating character-aware structural priors for reliable restoration of low-resource historical documents.

Abstract: Historical Manchu documents preserve invaluable linguistic and cultural heritage, yet their digitization is hindered by severe degradations and the scarcity of paired training data. Existing document restoration methods primarily optimize pixel-level reconstruction, which can produce visually plausible results while failing to preserve the structural identity of Manchu glyphs. To address this limitation, we propose a retrieval-guided glyph-aware restoration framework that goes beyond pixel reconstruction by explicitly incorporating glyph-level structural knowledge. Our method retrieves relevant glyph exemplars to provide structural guidance during restoration and integrates this information into the reconstruction process, improving the recovery of degraded character structures under low-resource conditions. Extensive experiments on Manchu historical documents demonstrate that the proposed approach improves both image restoration quality and glyph-level fidelity compared with existing restoration methods. These results highlight the importance of incorporating character-aware structural priors for reliable restoration of low-resource historical documents.

</details>


### [27] [EgoRefine: Ego-Referenced Predictive Alignment and Trajectory-Conditioned Reliability-Aware Fusion for Asynchronous Collaborative Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00319)
*Lingzhao Kong,Yongsheng Zang,Yu Kang,Kailun Yang,Jie Fu,Yukun Zuo,Zhiyong Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EgoRefine is a novel framework for asynchronous collaborative 3D object detection that addresses temporal misalignment issues in cooperative perception. It introduces an ego-referenced predictive alignment module that uses current ego features to guide cooperative trajectory prediction, and a trajectory-conditioned reliability-aware fusion module that adaptively reweights features based on alignment quality. The method outperforms TraF-Align by 1.6% AP@0.5 and 2.9% AP@0.7 on V2V4Real and DAIR-V2X-Seq datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Collaborative perception enables connected agents to share observations for extended sensing range and occlusion mitigation. However, asynchronous communication causes temporal delays in cooperative features. Existing prediction-based methods compensate using only the transmitting agent's history, leaving residual misalignment with the ego agent's current observation, and current fusion approaches overlook spatial variations in alignment quality.

Method: EgoRefine consists of two key modules: (1) Ego-referenced Predictive Alignment module - uses current ego feature to guide cooperative trajectory-field prediction and refines sampling offsets along an ego-referenced trajectory direction; (2) Trajectory-conditioned Reliability-aware Fusion module - treats trajectory discrepancy between ego and cooperative streams and directional refinement magnitude as alignment cues to condition feature relations and adaptively reweight streams before convolutional fusion.

Result: EgoRefine outperforms TraF-Align by 1.6 points on AP@0.5 and 2.9 points on AP@0.7 on V2V4Real and DAIR-V2X-Seq datasets.

Conclusion: The ego-referenced approach effectively reduces residual misalignment in asynchronous collaborative perception, and the reliability-aware fusion module successfully leverages alignment quality cues to improve detection performance.

Abstract: Collaborative perception enables connected agents to share complementary observations for 3D object detection, extending sensing range and mitigating occlusion. Under asynchronous communication, however, cooperative features arrive with temporal delay. Existing prediction-based methods compensate for these features mainly from the transmitting agent's own history, leaving residual misalignment with the ego agent's current observation; subsequent fusion also often overlooks spatial variations in alignment quality. We propose EgoRefine, an ego-referenced predictive alignment and reliability-aware fusion framework for asynchronous collaborative perception. Its Ego-referenced Predictive Alignment module uses the current ego feature to guide cooperative trajectory-field prediction and refines the sampling offsets along an ego-referenced trajectory direction. Its Trajectory-conditioned Reliability-aware Fusion module treats the trajectory discrepancy between the ego and cooperative streams and the directional refinement magnitude as alignment cues, using them to condition the relation between aligned features and adaptively reweight the two streams before convolutional fusion. Experiments on V2V4Real and DAIR-V2X-Seq show that EgoRefine outperforms TraF-Align by 1.6 and 2.9 points on average in AP@0.5 and AP@0.7, respectively. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/godk0509/EgoRefine.

</details>


### [28] [LEGO-OPD: Factorized Teacher Composition for Multimodal On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00333)
*Jaeyun Shin,Hangeol Chang,Jong Chul Ye*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LEGO-OPD introduces a factorized teacher composition approach for multimodal on-policy distillation, separating language prior (from Language Expert) from visual grounding (from Grounding Expert) using Bayesian formulation, with adaptive calibration to control visual supervision strength at each decoding prefix.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-teacher OPD approaches combine LLM and VLM teachers for complementary supervision, but directly using VLM's full predictive distribution entangles visual grounding signals with the VLM's language prior, preventing independent transfer of grounding information. Increasing visual supervision improves perception but risks degrading language reasoning.

Method: LEGO-OPD uses a generalized Bayesian formulation where the Language Expert provides a prior over candidate tokens, and the Grounding Expert contributes a visual likelihood that updates this prior (rather than transferring the complete predictive distribution). This factorized composition allows independent control of language reasoning and visual grounding. Adaptive calibration is introduced using the grounding expert's image-induced prediction shift as a prefix-dependent reference to determine optimal visual supervision strength.

Result: Experiments with Qwen3 models show LEGO-OPD consistently outperforms single- and multi-teacher OPD baselines on both multimodal and text-only reasoning tasks. It improves initial student's visual perception while preserving text-only reasoning capabilities.

Conclusion: LEGO-OPD successfully addresses the trade-off between visual grounding and language reasoning in multimodal distillation by factorizing teacher expertise and using adaptive calibration, achieving superior performance across both multimodal and text-only tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) aims to improve visual grounding while preserving the strong reasoning capabilities of language models. Recent multi-teacher approaches combine LLM and VLM teachers to provide complementary supervision. However, directly using a VLM's full predictive distribution entangles its visual grounding signal with its own language prior, preventing the grounding information from being transferred independently. Conversely, increasing the strength of visual supervision can improve perception but may overemphasize visual evidence and degrade language reasoning. To address this trade-off, we introduce LEGO-OPD, which selectively composes factors from a Language Expert and a Grounding expert into One teacher distribution for multimodal OPD. Under a generalized Bayesian formulation, the language expert provides a prior over candidate tokens, while the grounding expert contributes a visual likelihood that updates this prior, rather than transferring its complete predictive distribution. This factorized composition allows language reasoning and visual grounding to be controlled independently. We further introduce adaptive calibration to determine how strongly the visual likelihood should update the language prior at each decoding prefix. Specifically, LEGO-OPD uses the grounding expert's image-induced prediction shift as a prefix-dependent reference, preventing both insufficient and excessive visual supervision. Experiments with Qwen3 models show that LEGO-OPD consistently outperforms the evaluated single- and multi-teacher OPD baselines on both multimodal and text-only reasoning tasks. Moreover, it improves the initial student's visual perception while preserving text-only reasoning.

</details>


### [29] [Vmem-$\varphi$: Low-Compute Out-of-Distribution Detection in Spiking Neural Networks from Membrane-Potential Statistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00350)
*Arul Rana,Agrim Tripathi,Shoaib Ahmed Dipu,Md. Shaown Miah,Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed,Sayeed Shafayet Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes using subthreshold membrane potential (V_mem(t)) as an internal signal for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) processing event-camera data. The approach introduces the Gen1-C benchmark (six sensor-motivated corruption tests at five severity levels) and the Multi-Descriptor Deviation (MDD) method that operates on membrane-potential statistics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SNNs offer energy-efficient processing for event-camera data, but OOD detection remains challenging. Existing methods rely on model outputs unavailable in object detection SNNs or are unsuitable for low-compute deployment scenarios.

Method: The approach uses subthreshold membrane potential V_mem(t) as an internal signal for OOD detection. Simple per-channel statistics are derived from membrane dynamics. The proposed Multi-Descriptor Deviation (MDD) is a corruption-blind method that operates on these membrane-potential statistics within a bounded 64-frame observation window.

Result: At the highest corruption severity, MDD achieves AUROC > 0.88 on five of six corruptions using only a 64-frame observation window. The remaining corruption shows the smallest effect on the underlying detector.

Conclusion: Temporal membrane-potential dynamics can provide an effective and low-cost signal for OOD detection in SNN-based event perception, making it suitable for low-compute deployment scenarios.

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an energy-efficient approach to processing event-camera data, yet out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains challenging in this setting. Existing OOD detection methods often depend on model outputs or computational components that are unavailable in object detection SNNs or are poorly suited to low-compute deployment. To that effect, we show that the subthreshold membrane potential \(V_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)\) provides a useful internal signal for detecting distribution shifts. Simple per-channel statistics derived from these membrane dynamics enable OOD detection. To evaluate this approach, we introduce Gen1-C, an event-camera corruption benchmark developed upon the Prophesee Gen1 automotive detection dataset, containing six sensor-motivated histogram-level stress tests at five severity levels. We further propose the Multi-Descriptor Deviation (MDD), a corruption-blind method that operates on membrane-potential statistics. At the highest corruption severity, MDD achieves an AUROC of more than 0.88 on five of the six corruptions using only a bounded 64-frame observation window. Notably, the remaining corruption is also the one that has the smallest effect on the underlying detector. These results show that the temporal membrane-potential dynamics can provide an effective and low-cost signal for OOD detection in SNN-based event perception.

</details>


### [30] [From Image Latent Space to Fuzzy Rules: Interpretable Analysis of Gastrointestinal Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00414)
*Michael D. Vasilakakis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A prototype-based fuzzy-rule framework is proposed to interpret patch-level features from pretrained foundation models (ViT-S/16) in medical imaging, without fine-tuning. Class-specific prototypes are learned via clustering, and patch features are expressed as prototype similarities classified by human-readable fuzzy IF-THEN rules. The method achieves comparable accuracy to black-box classifiers while providing interpretability, and can analyze synthetic medical images by identifying which real prototypes/rules a generator reproduces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding how latent representations of pretrained foundation models encode clinically relevant information in medical imaging remains an open challenge, limiting their deployment in safety-critical domains where interpretability is essential.

Method: 1) Extract patch-level features from frozen ViT-S/16 backbone (final two blocks) pretrained on ImageNet-1K and GastroNet-5M; 2) Learn class-specific prototypes via clustering in feature space; 3) Express patch features as prototype similarities; 4) Classify using fuzzy rules with linguistic IF-THEN conditions; 5) Apply to WCE classification, GI endoscopy classification, and colonic polyp segmentation; 6) Compare against kNN, kernel SVM, and linear probing under identical frozen features.

Result: Without backbone fine-tuning, the proposed method reaches accuracy comparable to black-box classifiers. Domain-specific pretraining (GastroNet-5M) yields features that are both discriminative and symbolically compressible. The extracted rules can identify which real prototypes/rules a synthetic medical image reproduces or fails to reproduce, localizing departures from real tissue.

Conclusion: The framework provides a transparent, depth-resolved view of how foundation models organize clinically relevant structure, achieving competitive accuracy without fine-tuning while enabling interpretable rule extraction and synthetic image analysis.

Abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large-scale datasets demonstrate strong transferability to medical imaging tasks. However, understanding how their latent representations encode clinically relevant information remains an open challenge in safety-critical domains. This study proposes a prototype-based fuzzy-rule framework that interprets the patch-level features produced by the inner layers of pretrained foundation models, without any fine-tuning. Class-specific prototypes are learned by clustering in the feature space, yielding compact visual patterns. Patch features are then expressed as prototype similarities and classified by fuzzy rules with linguistic IF-THEN conditions that are human readable. The framework is applied across the final two blocks of ViT-S/16 backbones pretrained on ImageNet-1K and GastroNet-5M, and benchmarked against k-nearest neighbours, kernel SVM, and linear probing under identical frozen features, on wireless capsule endoscopy classification, gastrointestinal endoscopy classification, and colonic polyp segmentation. The experimental analysis shows that the proposed method, without backbone fine-tuning, reaches accuracy comparable to these black-box classifiers, and that domain-specific pretraining yields features that are both discriminative and symbolically compressible. Because the resulting rules are extracted from real data and expressed in interpretable terms, they are further used as an instrument to investigate synthetic medical images, providing a human-readable account of which real prototypes and rules a generator reproduces or fails to reproduce, localising where a synthetic image departs from real tissue rather than summarising it with a single score. The framework thus offers a transparent, depth-resolved view of how foundation models organise clinically relevant structure, together with a practical downstream use of the extracted rules.

</details>


### [31] [Scores That Hold, Benchmarks That Leak: Measuring Dataset Contamination in Public Brain-Tumor MRI Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00421)
*Bhanu Prakash Vangala,Sowmya Guda,Latha Peddi,Navya Vangala*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper reveals severe data contamination in public brain tumor MRI datasets used for deep learning benchmark. Despite reported accuracies exceeding 98%, the authors demonstrate that a significant portion of test sets are not independent from training data at image, patient, and acquisition-source levels. Surprisingly, removing leaked images does not significantly reduce measured performance, suggesting that high accuracy may not reflect true tumor recognition capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses a critical gap in medical imaging deep learning research: while accuracy metrics on public benchmarks are high, there's no assessment of whether these benchmarks properly separate test from training data. The authors argue that dataset integrity—defined as independence at image, patient, and source levels—is a fundamental but overlooked dimension of benchmark quality.

Method: The authors introduce a three-layer contamination framework: (1) duplicate leakage (near-twin images), (2) patient leakage (same patient in train and test), and (3) source-label leakage (non-anatomical features like file headers). They audit three widely used brain tumor corpora using a chest-radiograph negative control, testing nine architectures across three evaluation conditions to quantify contamination's effect on performance.

Result: Contamination was severe at every layer: 28.8% of the dominant corpus's official test split has near-twin images in its training split; one corpus leaks 22.3% of test images byte-identically; 95.5% of traceable test images share a patient with training; and file-header features alone classify tumor vs. no-tumor at 0.959 balanced accuracy (matching fine-tuned ResNet). Notably, removing all identified leaked test images leaves balanced accuracy essentially unchanged.

Conclusion: Dataset integrity is a distinct, measurable axis of benchmark quality that cannot be certified by stable leaderboard performance. Reported accuracy on these contaminated corpora does not establish that models have learned to recognize tumors rather than exploit dataset-specific cues. The authors release contaminated-file lists, recovered patient identifiers, and deduplicated splits for future research.

Abstract: Automated classification of brain tumors from MRI is a heavily published application of deep learning in medical imaging, with reported accuracies on public benchmarks routinely exceeding 98%. However, accuracy does not capture a critical dimension of benchmark quality: dataset integrity, defined as the independence of test from training data at the image, patient, and acquisition-source levels. We introduce a three-layer contamination framework comprising duplicate, patient, and source-label leakage to assess the public corpora on which this literature rests. We audit the three most widely used corpora against a chest-radiograph negative control and quantify each layer's effect on measured performance across nine architectures and three evaluation conditions. Contamination is severe at every layer: 28.8% of the dominant corpus's official test split has a near-twin in its own training split, a second corpus leaks 22.3% of its test images byte-identically, 95.5% of traceable test images share a patient with training, and file-header features containing no anatomy separate tumor from no-tumor at 0.959 balanced accuracy, at parity with fine-tuned ResNet backbones. The unexpected result is that removing every identified leaked test image leaves balanced accuracy essentially unchanged: stable performance after deduplication does not establish benchmark integrity. Our findings establish dataset integrity as a distinct, measurable axis of benchmark quality that a stable leaderboard cannot certify. For biomedical research, reported accuracy on these corpora alone does not establish that a model has learned to recognize tumors rather than exploit dataset-specific cues. We release the contaminated-file lists, recovered patient identifiers, and deduplicated splits.

</details>


### [32] [PACT: End-to-End Learning of Human Pose, Contacts, and Forces from Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00451)
*Rikhat Akizhanov,Yangsong Zhang,Nikolai Kaliazin,Peter Wolf,Yoshihiko Nakamura,Pascal Fua,Fabio Pizzati,Ivan Laptev*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PACT is an end-to-end model that jointly estimates human pose, contacts, and contact forces from monocular video by augmenting a foundation model with learnable tokens and temporal transformers, outperforming staged approaches and introducing a new climbing benchmark (ForceWall) with ground-truth force sensors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches separate visual pose reconstruction from contact and force estimation, which limits joint reasoning and propagates errors between stages. This separation is problematic because human motion, environmental contacts, and interaction forces are governed by common physical laws that should be reasoned about jointly.

Method: PACT augments a human reconstruction foundation model with learnable contact-force tokens and a temporal transformer that integrates visual features with world-space motion. Joint prediction heads refine human poses and estimate contacts and forces, while physics-based supervision encourages consistency between reconstructed motion and interaction forces. A data annotation pipeline combines contact labeling with physics-based motion and force optimization to produce training supervision from synthetic and real-world videos.

Result: Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art contact and force estimation, outperforming staged reconstruction approaches and generalizing to interactions beyond the training distribution.

Conclusion: End-to-end joint learning is an effective approach to recovering human motion and physical interactions from video, supporting the value of unified reasoning about pose, contact, and forces.

Abstract: Human motion, environmental contacts, and interaction forces are governed by common physical laws, yet existing approaches typically separate visual pose reconstruction from contact and force estimation. This separation limits joint reasoning and can propagate errors between stages. We introduce PACT, an end-to-end model that jointly learns to estimate human pose, contacts and contact forces from monocular video. Our approach augments a human reconstruction foundation model with learnable contact-force tokens and a temporal transformer that integrates visual features with world-space motion. Joint prediction heads refine human poses and estimate contacts and forces, while physics-based supervision encourages consistency between the reconstructed motion and interaction forces. To address the scarcity of force annotations, we develop a data annotation pipeline that combines contact labeling with physics-based motion and force optimization, producing training supervision from synthetic and real-world videos. We also introduce a real-world climbing benchmark ForceWall with climbing videos and corresponding ground-truth contact forces obtained from the force sensors. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art contact and force estimation, outperforming staged reconstruction approaches and generalizing to interactions beyond the training distribution. These results support end-to-end joint learning as an effective approach to recovering human motion and physical interactions from video.

</details>


### [33] [PixelDense: Dense Prediction as Representation Alignment for Pixel Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00483)
*Lehan Yang,Daiqing Qi,Wenhao Zhang,Avery Li,Yiqing Yang,Yifan Li,Yu Kong,Haitian Zheng,Zhifei Zhang,Zhe Lin,Varun Jampani,Sheng Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PixelDense introduces a dual-projection architecture for representation alignment in diffusion transformers, separating semantic teachers (DINOv2, SAM2) from geometric teachers (Depth Anything v2, Metric3D v2) with an orthogonality penalty, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks including GenEval, DPG-Bench, and HPS v2.1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Representation alignment (REPA) accelerates diffusion transformer training but relies on semantic encoders. Recent work shows spatial structure—not global semantics—is the key alignment factor. Dense-prediction foundation models trained on spatial structure (SAM2 for segmentation, Depth Anything v2 for depth, Metric3D v2 for surface normals) were unexplored as REPA targets. Additionally, simply combining multiple teachers fails due to gradient conflict in a single projection stream.

Method: PixelDense routes semantic teachers (DINOv2, SAM2) through a semantic projection stream and geometric teachers (Depth Anything v2, Metric3D v2) through a geometric projection stream. A weight-space orthogonality penalty enforces that the two streams occupy disjoint subspaces, preventing gradient interference. Teachers remain frozen during training and are dropped at inference.

Result: PixelDense outperforms all baselines: PixelGen-XXL's GenEval Overall improves from 0.7927 to 0.8093. Achieves up to 53.1% PQ gain in panoptic segmentation and 36.0% depth AbsRel reduction at τ=0.5. Reaches baseline's peak GenEval 1.23x faster from random initialization. In SDEdit editing, raises background PSNR by up to 2.2 dB while preserving more layout.

Conclusion: Separating semantic and geometric alignment targets into distinct projection streams with orthogonality constraints is crucial for leveraging multiple dense-prediction teachers. This approach unlocks complementary benefits from both semantic and spatial structure supervision without gradient interference, establishing a new paradigm for representation alignment in diffusion models.

Abstract: Representation alignment (REPA) accelerates diffusion transformer training, but its alignment targets are almost exclusively semantic encoders such as DINOv2 and CLIP. Recent analysis points to spatial structure, not global semantics, as the carrier of the alignment effect, yet dense-prediction foundation models trained to predict that structure remain overlooked as REPA targets. In pixel-space diffusion, SAM2, Depth Anything v2, and Metric3D v2 each outperform the DINOv2-only GenEval baseline, with the two geometric teachers leading the segmentation teacher. A flat sum of all four teachers, however, lands below the best single geometric teacher, as semantic and geometric gradients compete for one denoiser projection. We introduce PixelDense, which routes DINOv2 and SAM2 through a semantic projection stream, routes Depth Anything v2 and Metric3D v2 through a geometric projection stream, and adds a weight-space orthogonality penalty that keeps the two streams in disjoint subspaces. All four teachers are frozen during training and dropped at inference. Applied to PixelGen and DeCo with a single recipe, PixelDense improves GenEval, DPG-Bench, and HPS v2.1, raises PixelGen-XXL's GenEval Overall from 0.7927 to 0.8093, and beats every single-teacher and unfactored multi-teacher variant. In partial-noise reconstruction, independent panoptic, depth, and surface-normal probes show up to 53.1% PQ gain and 36.0% depth AbsRel reduction at $τ=0.5$ across COCO and Flickr30K. From random initialization, PixelDense also reaches the baseline's peak GenEval 1.23x faster. In SDEdit editing on PIE-Bench, PixelDense keeps more of the source background and layout at every edit strength, raising background PSNR by up to 2.2 dB.

</details>


### [34] [Memorizon: Training World Models Beyond Their Context Window](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00544)
*Tingting Liao,Xuezhi Liang,Hao Li,Guangyi Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Memorizon enables long-span supervision for streaming world models without quadratic attention costs by using a retrieval-based memory bank. Training samples span any length but are scored only on last k chunks, which retrieve top-K latents by camera co-visibility, forming a bounded bank (kK). This allows revisiting supervision without including every intervening frame.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Streaming world models need to render places consistently across repeated visits. However, supervising such revisits requires training samples spanning minutes, and dense attention over full spans incurs quadratic costs, making long-span supervision computationally expensive.

Method: The method decouples supervision span from attention span: (1) Training samples cover spans of any length but are scored only on last k chunks; (2) Each scored chunk retrieves its own top-K latents by camera co-visibility; (3) The union of retrieval requests forms a shared memory bank bounded by kK, keeping sequence length bounded regardless of span length; (4) At shortest span, this equals conventional training.

Result: Going from 100 to 400 seconds adds only 12% to step time. Retrieval raises revisit consistency on every split vs sliding-window baseline. A span reaching the first visit of each return adds 24-30% improvement, at some cost in image quality. Filling the bank from another episode lowers revisit correlation by 83%, confirming the model uses retrieved information.

Conclusion: Memorizon successfully enables long-span supervision for streaming world models while keeping attention costs bounded. The retrieval mechanism allows the model to access relevant past information without incurring quadratic costs, significantly improving revisit consistency with minimal computational overhead.

Abstract: Streaming world models should render a place consistently across repeated visits. Directly supervising such revisits requires training samples that capture both visits, often spanning minutes. Yet dense attention over the full span incurs quadratic costs, making long-span supervision expensive. Memorizon breaks this coupling: long spans are needed for supervision, but not for attention, since the two visits can share a forward pass without including every intervening frame. A training sample covers a span of any length but is scored only on its last $k$ chunks. Instead of tokenizing the history before them, each scored chunk retrieves its own top-$K$ latents by camera co-visibility, and the union of these requests forms a shared bank. The bank is bounded by $kK$, so the sequence stays bounded however long the span; at the shortest span the recipe is exactly conventional training. Adding the bank raises the cost of a step once; beyond that, a longer span costs little, and going from 100 to 400 s adds 12% to the step time. Against a sliding-window baseline, retrieval raises revisit consistency on every split, and a span long enough to reach the first visit of each return adds a further 24% to 30%, at some cost in image quality; beyond that span, more length no longer helps. Filling the bank from another episode lowers revisit correlation by 83%, so the model uses what it retrieves. Project page: https://tingtingliao.github.io/memorizon

</details>


### [35] [PhysVista: Benchmarking Physical Intelligence in VLMs via a Perception-Reasoning-Assessment Loop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00559)
*Xinge Peng,Yiting Lu,Tianwu Zhi,Wen Wen,Jianzhao Liu,Xin Li,Zhibo Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhysVista is a benchmark that evaluates physical intelligence in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) through a closed cognitive loop framework, assessing perception, reasoning, and physical plausibility assessment together rather than in isolation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks suffer from fragmented evaluation, focusing on isolated cognitive stages while overlooking the synergy between perception, reasoning, and physical judgment. This limits the ability to diagnose whether VLMs can reliably evaluate physical authenticity of generative models.

Method: PhysVista uses a closed cognitive loop framework inspired by human seeing-reasoning-assessment process. It jointly evaluates physical state perception, physical dynamics reasoning, and physical plausibility assessment. It distinguishes event-level reasoning (what happens) from scale-level reasoning (how things happen) for fine-grained analysis. The benchmark includes both real-world and AI-generated videos.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse VLMs reveal substantial limitations in physical reasoning and plausibility assessment, highlighting a persistent gap between visual recognition and genuine physical understanding.

Conclusion: There is a significant gap between visual recognition and genuine physical understanding in current VLMs, pointing toward the need for more principled designs for physically grounded multimodal intelligence.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, yet whether they truly capture the physical consistency underlying real-world dynamics remains unclear. Existing benchmark paradigms often suffer from fragmented evaluation, focusing on isolated cognitive stages while overlooking the inherent synergy between perception, reasoning, and physical judgment. The lack of a holistic perspective limits the ability to diagnose whether VLMs can reliably evaluate the physical authenticity of emerging generative models. To address these issues, we introduce PhysVista, a benchmark designed to evaluate physical intelligence in VLMs through a closed cognitive loop framework inspired by the human seeing-reasoning-assessment process. PhysVista restores this loop by jointly evaluating physical state perception, physical dynamics reasoning, and physical plausibility assessment. It further distinguishes event-level reasoning and scale-level reasoning to enable fine-grained analysis of physical understanding. In addition, PhysVista incorporates both real-world and AI-generated videos, allowing evaluation across diverse domains and emerging generative scenarios. Extensive experiments across a diverse set of VLMs reveal substantial limitations in physical reasoning and plausibility assessment, highlighting a persistent gap between visual recognition and genuine physical understanding, and pointing toward more principled designs for physically grounded multimodal intelligence.

</details>


### [36] [FORTE: Adaptive Scoring and Exact Keyframe Selection for Long-Video Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00573)
*Haifeng Huang,Biyin Xu,Chunsheng Xin,Yang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FORTE is a training-free framework for query-aware keyframe selection in long video understanding. It addresses the limitation of fixed candidate pools by using adaptive relevance scoring via Gaussian-process prediction and global keyframe optimization to maximize relevance and temporal coverage. The method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on four long-video QA benchmarks across various scoring budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing score-based keyframe selection methods rely on fixed, uniformly sampled candidate pools, preventing evidence outside this pool from being selected. With limited relevance-scoring budget, there is a need to adaptively allocate evaluations to promising frames while exploring underrepresented temporal regions.

Method: Two-stage approach: (1) Adaptive relevance scoring using Gaussian-process relevance predictor that exploits temporal locality and banded kernel structure to reduce computation from O(n³) to O(n) for fixed bandwidth; (2) Global keyframe optimization that selects final keyframes by maximizing an objective capturing measured relevance and temporal coverage, with an exact algorithm leveraging logarithmic coverage structure running in linear time.

Result: FORTE achieves the highest observed mean accuracy among compared selectors under every tested scoring budget on four long-video question-answering benchmarks. It demonstrates consistent effectiveness across different relevance scorers and downstream MLLMs.

Conclusion: The proposed training-free framework successfully addresses the keyframe selection problem by adaptively allocating scoring budgets and optimizing for both relevance and temporal coverage. Its strong performance across diverse benchmarks and model configurations validates the approach as an effective solution for enabling MLLMs to process long videos efficiently.

Abstract: Query-aware keyframe selection enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to process long videos using only a small set of question-relevant frames. Existing score-based methods, however, typically search within a fixed, uniformly sampled candidate pool, preventing evidence outside this pool from ever being selected. Given a limited relevance-scoring budget, the key challenge is to allocate evaluations adaptively to promising frames while continuing to explore underrepresented temporal regions. We introduce FORTE, a training-free framework that addresses this challenge through two stages: adaptive relevance scoring and global keyframe optimization. Starting from sparse, uniformly distributed observations, our efficient Gaussian-process relevance predictor estimates relevance for unscored frames, exploiting temporal locality and the approximately banded kernel structure to reduce the core computation from cubic to linear time in the number of frames for fixed bandwidth. The scoring stage then selects which frames to score next by balancing predicted relevance with temporal coverage, prioritizing promising regions while also exploring less-represented parts of the video. The optimization stage selects the final keyframes by maximizing an objective that jointly captures measured relevance and temporal coverage. We derive an exact algorithm that leverages the logarithmic coverage structure to identify the optimal subset of the scored candidate pool in time linear in the pool size, for a fixed final-frame budget. Experiments on four long-video question-answering benchmarks show that FORTE achieves the highest observed mean accuracy among the compared selectors under every tested scoring budget. Further evaluations demonstrate its consistent effectiveness across different relevance scorers and downstream MLLMs.

</details>


### [37] [Gestalt: Large Multimodal Interplay Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00576)
*Zequn Yang,Yu Miao,Haotian Ni,Ziheng Chen,Chengxiang Huang,Dongzhan Zhou,Kai Chen,Qi Zhang,Ji-Rong Wen,Yake Wei,Di Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Gestalt is a new large multimodal model paradigm that uses a multimodal interplay pyramid to organize modeling from modality-specific processing through cross-modal alignment to deeper integration, employing a unified discrete diffusion framework with interplay tokens.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current large multimodal models focus on adding modalities but overlook the distinct characteristics of each modality and their relations. Human multisensory perception has multistage property, which inspired the proposed approach.

Method: The paper proposes a multimodal interplay pyramid that organizes multimodal modeling into three stages: modality-specific processing, cross-modal alignment, and deeper multimodal integration. Gestalt uses a unified discrete diffusion framework with an interplay-partitioned architecture and learnable interplay tokens to mediate cross-modal exchange and integration. The pyramid also structures data organization and training strategy.

Result: Strong performance across image generation, multimodal understanding, and text-only evaluation, significantly improving cross-modal integration while preserving modality-specific information.

Conclusion: Gestalt effectively harnesses the strengths of diffusion-based multimodal models and offers a promising path toward unified multimodal intelligence by improving cross-modal integration while preserving modality-specific features.

Abstract: In this paper, we propose Gestalt, a new paradigm of large multimodal model built around multimodal interplay. Despite rapid advances, large multimodal models are reaching a bottleneck: existing approaches focus primarily on accommodating additional modalities while overlooking the distinct characteristics of each modality and the relations among them. Motivated by the multistage property of human multisensory perception, we propose a multimodal interplay pyramid that organizes multimodal modeling as a progression from modality-specific processing, through cross-modal alignment, to deeper multimodal integration. Guided by this pyramid, Gestalt adopts a unified discrete diffusion framework and an interplay-partitioned architecture, with learnable interplay tokens mediating cross-modal exchange and integration. The pyramid also structures its data organization and training strategy. Strong performance across image generation, multimodal understanding, and text-only evaluation shows that Gestalt significantly improves cross-modal integration while preserving modality-specific information, effectively harnessing the strengths of diffusion-based multimodal models and offering a promising path toward unified multimodal intelligence.

</details>


### [38] [Discrete Annotation, Continuous Preference: Rethinking Supervision for Accurate and Generalizable Aesthetic Image Cropping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00582)
*Ziqing Zhang,Xiao Liu,Kai Liu,Jianze Li,Weihang Zhang,Linghe Kong,Yulun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Continuous Preference Field (CPF) framework to address fundamental limitations in aesthetic image cropping datasets and evaluation. It introduces CPIC (a VLM-based cropping model trained with GRPO using CPF rewards) and CPICD (a recalibrated benchmark dataset), achieving state-of-the-art performance and improved out-of-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing aesthetic image cropping datasets suffer from two critical flaws: (1) human subjectivity in annotations, and (2) rigid discreteness confined to fixed sampling grids. These issues limit model accuracy, generalization, and distort fair evaluation across benchmarks.

Method: The authors propose CPF to model human cropping preference as a multi-peaked, continuous, and sharp field over the crop space. CPF recovers dense preference from discrete annotations through: (1) peak clustering, (2) off-lattice refinement, (3) negative shaping, and (4) field assembly. Based on CPF, they train CPIC, a VLM-based cropping model optimized via GRPO with CPF reward. They also introduce CPICD to recalibrate existing ground-truth boxes by correcting grid-bound artifacts across mainstream benchmarks.

Result: CPIC achieves state-of-the-art performance with exceptional out-of-domain generalization. CPICD establishes a rigorous and reliable evaluation foundation. Extensive experiments and user studies demonstrate the superiority of CPF, CPIC, and CPICD.

Conclusion: The Continuous Preference Field approach successfully addresses long-standing problems in aesthetic image cropping by providing continuous preference modeling, overcoming template collapse, and establishing reliable benchmarks. The code, model, and data are publicly available.

Abstract: Aesthetic image cropping aims to identify the optimal crop of an image in terms of aesthetics and composition. While supervision based on annotated data is fundamental, the field has been hindered by a long-standing problem: existing datasets suffer from (1) human subjectivity and (2) rigid discreteness confined to fixed sampling grids. These flawed annotations not only limit the accuracy and generalization of trained models but also severely distort fair evaluation. To overcome this, we propose to model human cropping preference as a multi-peaked, continuous, and sharp field over the crop space. We introduce the Continuous Preference Field (CPF), which recovers a dense preference landscape from discrete annotations through (1) peak clustering, (2) off-lattice refinement, (3) negative shaping, and (4) field assembly. Based on this, we train CPIC, a VLM-based cropping model optimized via GRPO with the CPF reward, which overcomes template collapse, achieving state-of-the-art performance and exceptional out-of-domain generalization. Finally, to resolve the long-standing benchmark evaluation crisis, we introduce CPICD, a comprehensive recalibration of existing ground-truth boxes. By leveraging the CPF to correct grid-bound artifacts across mainstream benchmarks, CPICD establishes a rigorous and reliable foundation for future cropping research. Extensive experiments and user studies demonstrate the superiority of our CPF, CPIC, and CPICD. Code, model, and data are available at https://github.com/zzqingz/CPIC.

</details>


### [39] [Just Align $\bm{x}$: Aligning Predictions, Not Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00600)
*Yuyao Zhang,Yuwei Hu,Ziyang Mai,Yu-Wing Tai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: JAx (Just Align x) is a prediction-supervision method for diffusion training that aligns clean-image predictions across noise levels instead of aligning intermediate representations. It couples a noisier student observation with a cleaner observation through Markov degradation, preserving the JiT input distribution while providing lower-variance training targets. The method achieves consistent FID improvements and accelerated convergence on ImageNet 256x256 across JiT-B/16, L/16, and H/16 models without external encoders or architecture changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Representation alignment has become effective for accelerating diffusion training, but its benefits do not reliably transfer to pixel-space clean-image prediction. The prior method JiT uses auxiliary feature alignment which improves access to semantic features while reducing access to image variation needed for clean-image prediction, creating a mismatch between the auxiliary objective and the denoising task. The key insight is that auxiliary supervision should improve the prediction target itself rather than impose a separate representation target.

Method: JAx introduces prediction-supervision that aligns clean-image predictions across noise levels. It couples a noisier student observation with a cleaner observation through a Markov degradation that preserves the original JiT input distribution. Under this coupling, the oracle prediction from the cleaner state has the same conditional mean as the optimal JiT target while its conditional target covariance is no greater. This preserves the population JiT objective up to a constant while providing a lower-variance training target. For practical implementation with an imperfect EMA teacher, JAx combines ground-truth supervision with a reliability-gated coupling band that selects nearby teacher states based on prediction risk.

Result: On ImageNet 256x256, JAx consistently improves FID and accelerates convergence across JiT-B/16, L/16, and H/16 models, without external encoders or changes to architecture/sampling procedure. Gradient diagnostics show reduced minibatch gradient variance. Ablations demonstrate that gains cannot be explained by time reweighting alone.

Conclusion: Prediction-space supervision provides a simple and principled alternative to representation alignment for pixel-space generative models. The key principle is that auxiliary supervision should improve the prediction target itself rather than impose a separate representation target.

Abstract: Representation alignment has become an effective way to accelerate diffusion training, but its benefits do not transfer reliably to pixel-space clean-image prediction. In JiT, we find that auxiliary feature alignment can improve access to semantic features while reducing access to image variation needed for clean-image prediction, creating a mismatch between the auxiliary objective and the denoising task. This suggests a different principle: auxiliary supervision should improve the prediction target itself rather than impose a separate representation target. We introduce JAx (Just Align x), a prediction-supervision method that aligns clean-image predictions across noise levels. JAx couples a noisier student observation with a cleaner observation through a Markov degradation that preserves the original JiT input distribution. Under this coupling, the oracle prediction from the cleaner state has the same conditional mean as the optimal JiT target, while its conditional target covariance is no greater. Thus, oracle prediction alignment preserves the population JiT objective up to a constant while providing a lower-variance training target. To make this construction practical with an imperfect EMA teacher, JAx combines ground-truth supervision with a reliability-gated coupling band that selects nearby teacher states based on prediction risk. On ImageNet 256x256, JAx consistently improves FID and accelerates convergence across JiT-B/16, L/16, and H/16, without an external encoder or changes to the architecture or sampling procedure. Gradient diagnostics further show reduced minibatch gradient variance, while ablations demonstrate that the gains cannot be explained by time reweighting alone. These results show that prediction-space supervision provides a simple and principled alternative to representation alignment for pixel-space generative models.

</details>


### [40] [HAWK: Rethinking Multimodal Drafting for Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00623)
*Wenhan Yang,Anirudh Rao,Ashwin Chandra*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HAWK is a speculative decoding framework designed to accelerate large vision-language models (LVLMs) by addressing two key limitations: (1) drafters' difficulty using multimodal information, and (2) the mismatch between drafter and target predictions during multi-step drafting. It uses representation similarity to select informative target layers, provides compressed visual hidden states to the drafter, and trains the drafter to model how target predictions shift after its own proposals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding achieves significant speedups for LLMs but remains less effective for LVLMs due to two limitations: (1) lightweight drafters struggle to leverage rich multimodal information, and (2) standard distillation only supervises the drafter along the original training trajectory without modeling how target predictions shift after the drafter's proposals, causing increasing disagreement in later steps.

Method: HAWK addresses these limitations through three key innovations: (1) Uses representation similarity to select informative target layers and learns how to combine their hidden states; (2) Provides the drafter with compressed visual hidden states from the target model instead of raw visual tokens, making visual information easier for shallow drafters to use; (3) Trains the drafter to capture how target predictions change after its own proposals, improving agreement with the target during multi-step drafting.

Result: On SmolVLM-256M across ten multimodal benchmarks, HAWK raises average acceptance length from 3.32 to 4.08 and speedup from 2.19x to 2.60x over EAGLE-3 under greedy decoding, and from 2.89 to 3.41 and 1.92x to 2.19x under sampling.

Conclusion: HAWK significantly improves speculative decoding for LVLMs by better utilizing multimodal information and modeling prediction shifts, achieving substantial speedups over prior methods like EAGLE-3 under both greedy decoding and sampling.

Abstract: Speculative decoding has achieved substantial lossless speedups for LLMs, but remains less effective for large vision-language models (LVLMs), where lightweight drafters struggle to use rich multimodal information. A second limitation is that standard distillation supervises the drafter only along the original training trajectory, without modeling how target predictions shift after the drafter's own proposals. As drafting moves away from this trajectory, the drafter can increasingly disagree with the target, reducing acceptance in later steps. We propose HAWK to address both limitations. HAWK uses representation similarity to select informative target layers and learns how to combine their hidden states. For visual information, it directly provides the drafter with compressed visual hidden states from the target model instead of raw visual tokens, making the visual information easier for a shallow drafter to use. HAWK also trains the drafter to capture how target predictions change after its own proposals, improving its agreement with the target during multi-step drafting. On SmolVLM-256M across ten multimodal benchmarks, HAWK raises average acceptance length from 3.32 to 4.08 and speedup from 2.19x to 2.60x over EAGLE-3 under greedy decoding, and from 2.89 to 3.41 and 1.92x to 2.19x under sampling.

</details>


### [41] [VisionQ: VLM-as-a-Judge Taxonomy, Dataset and Benchmark for Qualitative Analysis in Computer Vision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00666)
*Vu Dinh Xuan,Duc-Hai Nguyen,Minh-Dung Dao,Vu Quynh Giao,Quang Hong Nguyen,Binh-Son Hua,Barry O'Sullivan,David Murphy,Hoang D. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VisionQ is the first benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on criterion-conditioned visual discrimination, using peer-reviewed CV comparison figures with hand-annotated visual criteria. It comprises 1,409 papers, 1,800+ figures, and 3,911 data points, with a 51-leaf taxonomy of visual criteria. The best VLM achieves only 63.1% accuracy (vs 32.2% chance).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VLM benchmarks score only scalar quality or overall preference, allowing judges to be rewarded for picking the preferred image for wrong visual reasons. There was no benchmark that evaluates whether a VLM selects the correct image based on the specific visual criterion stated by the authors.

Method: 1) Built a corpus of 1,409 CVPR/ICCV papers with 1,800+ validated comparison figures and 3,911 hand-annotated data points linking method crops to author-stated visual claims. 2) Created a six-axis, 51-leaf taxonomy of visual criteria. 3) Developed criterion-conditioned evaluation protocol hiding method names, captions, and paper identity. 4) Trained VisionQ-Judge using DPO on symmetric evidence pairs (Gemma-4-E4B base).

Result: VisionQ-Judge reduces last-option predictions by 7.0 percentage points and improves accuracy by 2.5pp on held-out test set. Evaluating 20 open-/closed-source VLM judges shows the strongest achieves only 63.1% accuracy (chance level 32.2%), with reliability varying sharply across criteria.

Conclusion: VisionQ establishes a new task (criterion-conditioned visual discrimination) and provides the first benchmark grounded in peer-reviewed visual criteria. Current VLM judges still have significant room for improvement, with substantial variation in performance across different visual criteria.

Abstract: Qualitative comparison figures are central evidence in computer vision papers, and vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used to judge them. Yet existing benchmarks score only scalar quality or overall preference, so a judge can be rewarded for picking the preferred image for the wrong visual reason. We introduce VisionQ, the first benchmark built from peer-reviewed CV comparison figures that grounds every judgment in a named visual criterion: each question states the criterion, and a judge is credited only when it selects the output the authors identify as best on that criterion. We call this task criterion-conditioned visual discrimination. VisionQ comprises (1) a corpus of 1,409 CVPR and ICCV papers with 1,800+ validated comparison figures and 3,911 hand-annotated data points linking method crops to author-stated visual claims; (2) a six-axis, 51-leaf taxonomy of the visual criteria behind qualitative judgment; (3) a criterion-conditioned evaluation protocol that hides method names, captions, and paper identity and reports accuracy per criterion; and (4) VisionQ-Judge, a DPO-tuned Gemma-4-E4B judge trained on symmetric evidence pairs, which reduces last-option predictions by 7.0pp and improves accuracy by 2.5pp on a held-out test set. Evaluating 20 open- and closed-source VLM judges, we find that the strongest reach only 63.1% accuracy (chance 32.2%) and that reliability varies sharply across criteria. Code: https://github.com/ReML-AI/visionq. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/visionq-anon-2026/VisionQ-1k.

</details>


### [42] [Harnessing Vision-Language Models for Perceptual Quality Assessment and Autonomous Content Adjustment in Augmented Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00677)
*Elias Rotondo,Lin Duan,Yanming Xiu,Sangjun Eom,Conrad Li,Maria Gorlatova*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents an automated framework using vision-language models (VLMs) to evaluate and predict the visual fidelity of AR scenes, addressing the limitations of costly and inflexible user studies in AR evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AR head-mounted displays face challenges with constrained scene geometry, spatial jitter, and temporal instability. Traditional user studies for AR visual quality evaluation are expensive, lack scalability, and are inflexible during iterative design processes.

Method: The researchers introduced RateAR, a benchmark of AR images and videos across diverse scenes and conditions with high reliability (ICC(2,5) >= .90). They evaluated 11 commercial VLMs on this benchmark, conducted an ablation study on prompting strategies, and built an automated AR content adjustment system tested in a 21-participant user study.

Result: VLM-based quality predictions strongly correlated with human subjective judgments, achieving Spearman's rank-order correlations up to 0.8695. Contextual prompting yielded better alignment with human ratings. Over 90% of participants found the system improved placement and size coherence of virtual content.

Conclusion: Vision-language models can effectively evaluate and predict AR visual fidelity as perceived by users, offering a scalable and automated alternative to traditional user studies for AR content evaluation and refinement.

Abstract: Advancements in augmented reality (AR) continue to foster innovative solutions, facilitating novel methodologies within educational systems, healthcare delivery, and risk-mitigation protocols. However, optimizing for end-user immersion and comfort remains challenging, as AR head-mounted displays contend with constrained scene geometry, spatial jitter, and temporal instability. User studies are the standard AR evaluation method for visual quality, but their cost, diminishing scalability, and inflexibility pose bottlenecks during iterative application design. To address this problem, we present an automated framework for AR content evaluation and refinement, built on vision-language models (VLMs), to evaluate and predict the visual fidelity of AR scenes as perceived by users. First, we introduce RateAR, a benchmark of AR images and videos collected across diverse scenes and environmental conditions, with good-to-excellent reliability (ICC(2,5) >= .90) across perceptual factors, including object placement, scale, and shadow consistency. Subsequently, we evaluate eleven commercial VLMs on the crafted benchmark. Results support that VLM-based quality predictions strongly correlate with human subjective judgments, achieving Spearman's rank-order correlations of up to 0.8695. An ablation study further suggests that, compared to other prompting strategies, our contextual prompting yields better alignment with human ratings while balancing introduced complexity cues. Building on these findings, we construct an automated AR content adjustment system and conduct a 21-participant user study. More than 90% of participants found that the system improved placement and size coherence of virtual content.

</details>


### [43] [SemanTok: Predictable Semantic Tokens for Efficient Autoregressive Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00686)
*Mikhail Dereviannykh,Vikram Voleti,Simon Donne,Mallikarjun Byrasandra Ramalinga Reddy,Shimon Vainer,Mark Boss*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SemanTok introduces a novel flexible video tokenizer that uses frozen DINO features as semantic targets, reconstructing them from each token prefix. This approach achieves state-of-the-art performance with a 201M model matching or beating models 3.4× its size, while maintaining semantic alignment on out-of-distribution data and improving generation fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing flexible video tokenizers only apply representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, which the decoder can partially meet from its noised input. The authors aim to improve semantic alignment and video fidelity by explicitly enforcing semantic consistency at every token prefix level, not just at the decoder hidden states.

Method: SemanTok feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight reconstruction heads that predict these semantic features from each retained token prefix alone. This ensures semantic alignment at every level of the token hierarchy, with coarse tokens carrying global semantics and fine tokens adding pixel-level details.

Result: A 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model 3.4× its size. Larger SemanTok models further improve fidelity. The method maintains semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and provides higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. Short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and yield better generation fidelity.

Conclusion: SemanTok successfully combines high semantic alignment with video fidelity by enforcing DINO feature reconstruction at every token prefix. The approach achieves superior efficiency (smaller model size, better performance) and better generation quality through coarse-to-fine tokenization, where semantic information is concentrated in early tokens and pixel details are deferred to later tokens.

Abstract: Recent video-based world models pair the scalability of autoregressive (AR) prediction with the visual quality of diffusion models. The choice of scene tokenizer is paramount for the optimal performance of each of these, both in terms of fidelity and semantics. Flexible-length, coarse-to-fine tokenizers yield exactly that: the first coarse tokens carry the clip's global semantics while later tokens further specify details. Existing flexible tokenizers only apply a representation-alignment (REPA) loss on early decoder hidden states, a target the decoder can partly meet from its noised input instead. We introduce SemanTok, a flexible video tokenizer that feeds frozen DINO features into its encoder and adds lightweight heads that reconstruct them from each retained token prefix alone. SemanTok achieves high semantic alignment and video fidelity at every AR model size: a 201M SemanTok AR model matches or beats a VideoFlexTok AR model $3.4\times$ its size, and larger SemanTok AR models further improve fidelity. It keeps semantic alignment on out-of-distribution classes and gives the decoder higher semantic alignment at every noise level, including pure noise. It performs well in both reconstruction and generation, and its short token prefixes are cheaper to predict and give better generation fidelity, with pixel detail deferred to later tokens.

</details>


### [44] [FedMAD: Modulation-Aware Directional Aggregation for Federated Learning in Remote Sensing Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00693)
*Barış Büyüktaş,Begüm Demir*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FedMAD is a personalized federated learning framework for remote sensing image classification that addresses data heterogeneity by separating global representation parameters from client-specific adaptation parameters, using lightweight modulation modules and a modulation-aware directional aggregation strategy to suppress conflicting updates while enhancing consistent adaptation behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning (FL) in remote sensing enables collaborative model training across decentralized data archives without direct data access. However, FL performance significantly degrades when data distributions are heterogeneous across clients, which is common in remote sensing due to geographical differences, seasonal changes, and varying image acquisition and atmospheric conditions.

Method: The proposed FedMAD framework separates globally shared representation parameters from client-specific adaptation parameters. This is achieved by integrating lightweight modulation modules and local batch normalization layers into the backbone network. While globally shared parameters are collaboratively optimized, client-specific parameters remain local to preserve domain-specific features. Additionally, FedMAD introduces a modulation-aware directional aggregation strategy that dynamically adjusts the importance of each client's contribution based on the alignment of local modulation updates, suppressing conflicting updates from heterogeneous data distributions while enhancing contributions from clients with consistent adaptation behaviors.

Result: Experimental results on BigEarthNet-S2 and EuroSAT datasets demonstrate that FedMAD outperforms state-of-the-art FL algorithms under heterogeneous remote sensing data distributions.

Conclusion: FedMAD effectively addresses the challenge of data heterogeneity in federated learning for remote sensing image classification by separating global and local parameters and using modulation-aware aggregation, achieving superior performance compared to existing FL methods.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) has recently attracted increasing attention in remote sensing (RS) since it enables collaborative model training across decentralized RS image archives without requiring direct access to local data. However, FL performance significantly degrades when the data distributions between clients are heterogeneous, which often occurs due to geographical differences, seasonal changes, and varying image acquisition and atmospheric conditions. To address this challenge, in this letter, we propose a novel personalized FL framework (denoted as FedMAD) for RS image classification problems. The proposed framework separates globally shared representation parameters from client-specific adaptation parameters to preserve client-specific features while maintaining globally transferable representations. This is achieved by integrating lightweight modulation modules and local batch normalization layers into the backbone network. Although globally shared parameters are collaboratively optimized between clients, client-specific parameters remain local to preserve domain-specific feature characteristics. In addition, FedMAD introduces a modulation-aware directional aggregation strategy that dynamically adjusts the importance of aggregation for each client according to the alignment of local modulation updates. This allows the global optimization process to suppress conflicting client updates originating from heterogeneous data distributions while enhancing the contribution of clients with consistent adaptation behaviors. The experimental results obtained on the BigEarthNet-S2 and EuroSAT datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedMAD compared to state-of-the-art FL algorithms under heterogeneous RS data distributions. The code of the proposed framework will be publicly available at https://git.tu-berlin.de/rsim/fedmad.

</details>


### [45] [Personalized Image Generation with Reasoning and Reflection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00737)
*Bo Ni,Ngoc N. Tran,Qinwen Ge,Franck Dernoncourt,Seunghyun Yoon,Samyadeep Basu,Sungchul Kim,Puneet Mathur,Nedim Lipka,Tong Yu,Yu Wang,Ryan A. Rossi,Tyler Derr*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first unified benchmark for personalized image generation from user histories, comprising two tasks (Personalized Scene Generation and Personalized Creative Generation) with a multi-axis evaluation protocol. It proposes PEARL, a method coupling a multimodal reasoner with a frozen image generator, which achieves 15% improvement across personalization metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current personalized image generation is narrowly focused on conditional synthesis from visual exemplars, missing the richer personal context (reviews, posts, images, captions, metadata) that users accumulate over time. A truly personalized generator should leverage this entire history to produce images aligned with user's lifestyle and aesthetic preferences.

Method: PEARL couples a multimodal reasoner with a frozen image generator in an interleaved reason-reflect loop, optimized with differential data reward. The benchmark includes two complementary tasks: (1) Personalized Scene Generation - placing a given object in a scene reflecting user's preferences/lifestyle (for e-commerce); and (2) Personalized Creative Generation - generating novel images on specified topics faithful to user's aesthetic/visual identity (for social media).

Result: PEARL outperforms strong baselines across both tasks, achieving an average improvement of 15% across personalization metrics.

Conclusion: This work establishes the first unified benchmark for personalized image generation from user histories, demonstrating that leveraging rich user context beyond curated visual exemplars enables more personalized and contextually aligned image generation. The proposed PEARL method shows significant improvements over baselines.

Abstract: Personalized image generation has remained narrowly focused on conditional synthesis from curated visual exemplars, rather than capturing who a user is. In practice, however, a user's personal context is much richer, comprising reviews, posts, images, captions, and metadata accumulated over time. A truly personalized generator should leverage this history to produce images aligned with the user's lifestyle and aesthetic preferences. To this end, we introduce the first unified benchmark for personalized image generation from user histories. The benchmark comprises two complementary tasks and a multi-axis evaluation protocol that assesses target fidelity, visual quality, user distinguishability, semantic alignment with the user's history, and task-specific utility. Grounded in real-world e-commerce and social media settings, the benchmark includes: (1) Personalized Scene Generation, which places a given object in a scene that reflects a user's preferences and lifestyle, motivated by personalized product presentation; and (2) Personalized Creative Generation, which generates a novel image on a specified topic that is faithful to a user's aesthetic and visual identity, motivated by social media content creation. We further propose PEARL, which couples a multimodal reasoner with a frozen image generator in an interleaved reason-reflect loop optimized with differential data reward. Across both tasks, PEARL outperforms strong baselines, achieving an average improvement of 15% across personalization metrics.

</details>


### [46] [Video Evidence Indexing: Learning Where to Look from Video Previews for Token-Budgeted Long-Video Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00757)
*Haowen Guan,Shengzhi Li,Shichao Pei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses long-video question answering by proposing Token-budgeted Video Evidence Indexing (VEI), a method that uses a low-resolution video preview for global coverage and selectively extracts high-resolution frames (evidence set) for final reasoning, constrained by a limited visual token budget. A privileged self-distillation training approach is used to address missing frame-level supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-video question answering is limited by two key challenges: (1) the high cost of visual tokens when processing long videos, and (2) the fixed context width of current Vision-Language Models (VLMs). While a long-video question may require broad temporal coverage, the supporting evidence for the answer is often concentrated in only a compact set of moments.

Method: The authors propose a three-stage inference pipeline: (1) Video Preview provides cheap global coverage using low-resolution frames, (2) Video Evidence Indexing (VEI) acts as a policy that jointly performs evidence localization (finding question-relevant moments) and budget planning (deciding where to spend limited high-resolution frame budget), and (3) Answer Generation combines both inputs for final VQA. For training without frame-level supervision, they adopt privileged self-distillation where an answer-aware teacher guides the test-time policy on student-generated indexing traces. A single policy is trained to support previews at 1, 6, 12, and 24 visual tokens per frame.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that Video Evidence Indexing improves accuracy under limited visual budgets, and self-distillation further improves both QA accuracy and temporal evidence localization performance.

Conclusion: The proposed VEI method effectively addresses the token budget constraint in long-video QA by intelligently selecting a compact set of high-resolution evidence frames from a low-resolution preview. The privileged self-distillation approach enables training without expensive frame-level annotations while improving both answer quality and evidence localization accuracy.

Abstract: Long-video question answering is limited by the high cost of visual tokens and by the fixed context width of current VLMs. A long-video question may require broad temporal coverage, but the answer is often supported by only a compact set of moments. To locate these moments efficiently, we propose token-budgeted Video Evidence Indexing (VEI): given a dense low-resolution Video Preview, the model constructs a compact high-resolution Evidence Set for final reasoning. We treat VEI as a policy that must jointly solve \textit{evidence localization}, which finds question-relevant moments, and \textit{budget planning}, which decides where to spend the limited high-resolution frame budget. We implement this idea with an inference pipeline: the Video Preview provides cheap global coverage, Video Evidence Indexing constructs the Evidence Set, and Answer Generation combines both inputs for final VQA. To address missing frame-level supervision, we adopt privileged self-distillation, where an answer-aware teacher guides the normal test-time policy on student-generated indexing traces. We explore previews at 1, 6, 12, and 24 visual tokens per frame, training a single policy that supports all four resolutions. Experiments show that Video Evidence Indexing improves accuracy under limited visual budgets, and self-distillation further improves both QA accuracy and temporal evidence localization.

</details>


### [47] [VTV-FM: Flow Matching through Variational Terminal-Velocity Closure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00785)
*Haoyang Jiang,Yuheng Li,Di Yang,Yanhai Xiong,Haipeng Chen,Yi He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VTV-FM is a second-order flow matching framework that addresses the limitation of first-order bridges in flow matching by introducing a variational approach to derive terminal velocity from static data, improving transport geometry and generation quality across various domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current flow matching methods use first-order (linear) bridges between source and target distributions, which cannot model curved motion, acceleration, or changing directions. Second-order phase-space dynamics could help, but require terminal-velocity information that static datasets don't provide.
