Method: The paper proposes Variational Terminal-Velocity Flow Matching (VTV-FM), which derives missing velocity by minimizing acceleration energy, yielding a closed-form closure for static data. The same minimum-acceleration variational construction defines the OT pairing cost and acceleration targets used for training.

Result: VTV-FM improves transport geometry and generation quality over first-order and high-order FM baselines on low-dimensional datasets, PDE-governed physical fields, and CIFAR-10.

Conclusion: The variational approach successfully enables second-order flow matching without requiring terminal-velocity information, providing better modeling of curved motion and acceleration while maintaining computational tractability through the closed-form solution.

Abstract: Flow matching (FM) learns generative transport by fitting continuous-time motion from a simple source distribution to the data distribution. Most existing methods use first-order bridges: once a source and a target sample are paired, the path is a straight motion with constant velocity. FM with optimal transport (OT) improves the pairing, but the bridge itself remains linear, limiting its ability to model curved motion, acceleration, and changing directions. A natural remedy is to use second-order phase-space dynamics; however, learning the bridge requires target-side terminal-velocity information that static datasets do not provide. We propose Variational Terminal-Velocity Flow Matching (VTV-FM), a second-order FM framework that derives the missing velocity by minimizing acceleration energy, yielding a closed-form closure for static data. The same minimum-acceleration variational construction also defines the OT pairing cost and the acceleration targets used for training. Experiments on low-dimensional datasets, PDE-governed physical fields, and CIFAR-10 show that VTV-FM improves transport geometry and generation quality over first-order and high-order FM baselines.

</details>


### [48] [Paying for Too Many Tokens? Valid and Cost-Efficient Multimodal LLM Annotation with Simple Heuristics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00809)
*Zhixi Zhu,Kristina Gligoric*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper systematically evaluates cost-saving heuristics for Vision-Language Model (VLM) video annotation in computational social science tasks. The study examines whether heuristics that reduce token costs (frame sampling, image grids, single modality) preserve downstream inference validity, finding that accuracy and validity often diverge, and that a single 2×8 image grid using shot-transition detection can achieve full-video understanding at ~15% of the token cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video annotation with VLMs is expensive (millions of tokens for 60-second videos), but researchers lack guidance on which cost-saving heuristics preserve downstream conclusions. This study addresses this gap by evaluating heuristics across accuracy, inference validity, and cost dimensions.

Method: Systematic evaluation of three heuristics (frame sampling, image grid compression, single modality) on short-form videos for two CSS tasks (sentiment and topic classification). Each configuration evaluated across three axes: classification accuracy, downstream inference validity, and per-video token cost.

Result: 1) Accuracy and validity diverge - highest-accuracy configuration can produce wrong conclusions. 2) Text alone can yield strong performance - adding modalities doesn't always add signal. 3) A single 2×8 image grid using shot-transition detection achieves full-video understanding (κ within ~0.05) at ~15% token cost.

Conclusion: Cost can be decoupled from video length for short-form videos. Guidelines derived enable cost-aware VLM annotation in CSS while preserving inference validity.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable video annotation at scale, but costs accumulate quickly: processing a typical 60-second short-form video at one frame per second requires millions of tokens. To reduce costs, researchers rely on heuristics such as sampling a subset of frames, compressing videos into image grids, or using only a single modality. However, it remains unclear which heuristics save cost, and whether they preserve the downstream conclusions these annotations enable. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic evaluation of these heuristics using short-form videos, on two computational social science (CSS) tasks: sentiment and topic classification. We evaluate each configuration along three axes the literature typically treats separately: classification accuracy, validity of downstream inference, and per-video token cost. First, we find that accuracy and validity diverge: the highest-accuracy configuration can produce wrong conclusions. Second, modality value is not guaranteed: text alone can yield strong performance, indicating that adding modalities can add cost without adding signal. Finally, we find that cost can be decoupled from video length when annotating short-form videos: a single $2\times8$ image grid built via simple shot-transition detection approaches full-video understanding ($κ$ within~.05), at $\sim 15\%$ of the token cost. Based on these findings, we derive guidelines that can enable cost-aware VLM annotation in CSS.

</details>


### [49] [Video Generation Models: A Survey of Post-Training and Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00812)
*Chaoyu Li,Xiaoyi Gu,Yogesh Kulkarni,Eun Woo Im,Mohammadmahdi Honarmand,Zeyu Wang,Juntong Song,Fei Du,Xilin Jiang,Kexin Zheng,Tianzhi Li,Fei Tao,Pooyan Fazli*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This survey provides the first comprehensive review of post-training and alignment strategies for video generation models, addressing the challenge of making pretrained video models follow human intent while maintaining temporal coherence and physical constraints. The authors propose a taxonomy of four categories (supervised fine-tuning, self-training/distillation, preference/reward-based, and inference-time methods) and discuss datasets, benchmarks, evaluation practices, and open challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained video models struggle with reliably following human intent, maintaining temporal coherence, and satisfying physical/safety constraints. Video generation alignment faces unique challenges (error accumulation, motion-appearance coupling, multi-objective trade-offs, limited temporal supervision) that differ from image/text generation, motivating systematic post-training strategies rather than retraining from scratch.

Method: The authors frame post-training as a unifying framework and distinguish between implicit alignment (where alignment signals are indirectly enforced) and explicit alignment (where alignment signals are directly enforced). They organize existing approaches into four broad categories: (1) supervised fine-tuning methods, (2) self-training and distillation methods, (3) preference- and reward-based methods, and (4) inference-time methods.

Result: The survey presents a coherent taxonomy that provides a structured conceptual foundation for understanding how alignment signals shape model behavior across both training and deployment. It reviews commonly used datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation practices, and identifies open challenges including scalable reward design, long-horizon temporal consistency, stability-expressiveness trade-offs, and safety-aware generation.

Conclusion: This survey aims to provide practical guidance for advancing controllable and reliable video generation models by establishing a systematic framework for understanding post-training and alignment techniques in video generation.

Abstract: Video generation has rapidly progressed from short, low-quality clips to high-resolution, long-duration sequences with complex spatiotemporal dynamics. Despite strong generative priors learned through large-scale pretraining, pretrained video models often fail to reliably follow human intent, maintain temporal coherence, or satisfy physical and safety constraints. Compared with image and text generation, alignment in video generation presents unique challenges, including error accumulation over time, motion-appearance coupling, multi-objective trade-offs, and limited supervision for temporal properties. These challenges motivate systematic post-training strategies that adapt pretrained models without retraining them from scratch. In this survey, we present the first comprehensive review of post-training and alignment in video generation models. We frame post-training as a unifying framework and distinguish between implicit alignment and explicit alignment based on how alignment signals are enforced. From this perspective, we organize existing approaches into four broad categories: supervised fine-tuning methods, self-training and distillation methods, preference- and reward-based methods, and inference-time methods. This taxonomy provides a coherent view of how alignment signals shape model behavior across both training and deployment. Beyond methodological advances, we review commonly used datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation practices, and discuss open challenges such as scalable reward design, long-horizon temporal consistency, stability-expressiveness trade-offs, and safety-aware generation. This survey aims to provide a structured conceptual foundation and practical guidance for advancing controllable and reliable video generation models.

</details>


### [50] [Align Then Reason: A Multimodal Lip-Sync Judge for Dubbing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00825)
*Rui Liu,Bhavin Jawade,Haoqi Li,Shivam Mehta,Karan Saxena,Yinghong Lan,Cameron R. Wolfe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ATR is a multilingual lip-sync judge that first establishes monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and phonetic units, then uses an LLM to reason over this alignment for final judgment. It improves mean AUC by 45.9-59.4% across different LLM families and sizes on a seven-language benchmark, and generalizes to unseen languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dubbing quality control requires reference-free judgment of whether candidate text matches speaker's lip motion in content and timing, using only silent video and text. Existing visual speech recognizers and video-language models, even when fine-tuned for lip reading, remain largely insensitive to temporal errors.

Method: Align Then Reason (ATR): 1) Establish monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and phonetic units of candidate text; 2) Use alignment scorer to provide LLM with both local evidence per phonetic unit and calibrated global alignment score; 3) LLM reasons jointly about content and timing to make final judgment.

Result: On seven-language benchmark: +59.4%, +50.2%, +50.8% mean AUC over Qwen3.5 SFT baselines with 2B, 4B, 9B reasoners. Generalizes across LLM families: +45.9% (LLaMA-3.1-8B), +46.6% (Mistral-7B). Transfers to three unseen MuAViC languages. Downstream: dub-line reranking +52.0%, script-to-clip assignment +17.7% over best lip-reading baseline.

Conclusion: ATR successfully addresses temporal error detection in lip-sync by combining alignment-based local evidence with LLM reasoning. The method achieves significant improvements across multiple LLM families and sizes, generalizes to unseen languages, and performs well on real dubbing downstream tasks.

Abstract: Dubbing quality control requires a reference-free judge that can determine whether a candidate text line matches a speaker's visible articulation in both content and timing, using only silent video and text because dubbed audio may not yet exist. Existing visual speech recognizers and video-language models are poorly suited to this setting: even when fine-tuned to recover spoken content from lip motion, they remain largely insensitive to temporal errors. We introduce $\textit{Align Then Reason}$ (ATR), a multilingual lip-sync judge that first establishes a monotonic alignment between frame-level lip representations and the phonetic units of the candidate line, then reasons over this alignment to make the final judgment. An alignment scorer provides the LLM with both local evidence for each phonetic unit and a calibrated global alignment score, enabling it to reason jointly about content and timing. On a seven-language benchmark, our method improves mean AUC over the corresponding Qwen3.5 SFT baselines by 59.4%, 50.2%, and 50.8% with 2B, 4B, and 9B reasoners, respectively. The gains generalize across LLM families, reaching mean AUC improvements of 45.9% and 46.6% over the best baseline for LLaMA-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, respectively. They also transfer across datasets to three unseen MuAViC languages. Furthermore, we evaluate on two downstream tasks built from real dubbing lines. On dub-line reranking, ATR-9B outperforms the best lip-reading baseline by 52.0%, while on script-to-clip assignment, ATR-9B improves over the best lip-reading baseline by 17.7%.

</details>


### [51] [Geometric Similarity in VLM Low-Level Vision Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00848)
*Shao-Jun Xia,Huixin Zhang,Zhen Lei,Anlan Sun,Yuner Zhang,Xiaoyang Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces GeoSim, a unified four-level framework for analyzing how vision-language models (VLMs) organize hidden-layer representations across 24 low-level image restoration tasks. It compares autoregressive models and diffusion transformers to understand their representational geometry and transferability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The field lacks understanding of how VLMs organize hidden-layer representations for pixel-level perception, and whether different architectures (AR models vs DiTs) share common geometric organization. This knowledge is essential for building transferable, unified restoration VLMs and adapters.

Method: GeoSim framework analyzes task-conditioned representations across four levels: (1) global similarity, (2) local geometry, (3) sparse feature decomposition, and (4) topological verification. Applied to hidden states in AR models and feature maps in DiTs across same- and cross-task/model settings.

Result: The study reveals organizing principles of low-level visual representations while exposing limits in cross-task and cross-model agreement. GeoSim provides an interpretability lens for probing latent transferability and diagnosing model limitations.

Conclusion: GeoSim serves as a diagnostic tool for understanding representational similarity in low-level vision VLMs, enabling better design of unified restoration models and adapters by identifying where cross-task and cross-model transferability succeeds or fails.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as powerful candidates for universal vision backbones, with representative architectures including autoregressive (AR) models and diffusion transformers (DiTs). Yet, adapting them efficiently for all-in-one low-level image restoration remains a challenge. Crucially, the field lacks an understanding of how VLMs organize hidden-layer representations and whether these structurally distinct paradigms share a common geometric organization for pixel-level perception. Such shared organization is a prerequisite for building highly transferable, unified restoration VLMs and adapters. In this paper, we systematically investigate representational similarity across 24 low-level tasks spanning 5 categories. We propose GeoSim, a unified four-level framework that analyzes task-conditioned representations from global similarity, local geometry, sparse feature decomposition, and topological verification perspectives. Our formulation applies to the analysis of hidden states in AR models and feature maps in DiTs across same- and cross-task/model settings. Our results reveal the organizing principles of low-level visual representations while exposing their limits in cross-task and cross-model agreement. Ultimately, GeoSim provides an interpretability lens for probing latent transferability in low-level vision and diagnosing model limitations in task- or model-specific scenarios.

</details>


### [52] [SmoothOperator: Enhancing Representations for Fine-grained Open-set Recognition via Modulated Label Smoothing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00851)
*Thiru Thillai Nadarasar Bahavan,Yu Xia,Sachith Seneviratne,Saman Halgamuge*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SmoothOperator (SmoothOP) is a plug-in method that assigns sample-specific label smoothing coefficients based on "prominence" - an embedding-space metric measuring how distinctly a sample's class stands out against competitors. This addresses the limitation of fixed smoothing coefficients in existing spherical representation learning methods for Open Set Recognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current spherical representation learning methods for OSR use uniform label smoothing across all samples, ignoring individual differences in embedding quality. The alignment-uniformity structure in these methods means label smoothing acts as an alignment dial, but a fixed coefficient treats all samples equally regardless of how well each is already embedded.

Method: SmoothOP computes "prominence" for each sample by measuring how clearly the sample's own class stands out against its strongest competing class in the embedding space. Samples with high prominence receive strong smoothing (reducing alignment/relaxing pull), while samples with low prominence receive less smoothing. The method integrates into four existing spherical representation learning methods with minimal training overhead.

Result: On the Semantic Shift Benchmark, SmoothOP-augmented variants generally outperform base objectives across datasets, degrees of semantic shift, and OSR post-processors, with gains of up to 4.7% in AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy.

Conclusion: The proposed plug-in approach effectively personalizes label smoothing per sample based on embedding characteristics, providing consistent improvements across multiple baselines, datasets, and evaluation metrics in open set recognition tasks.

Abstract: Open Set Recognition (OSR) aims to enable models to accurately classify known classes while rejecting samples from unseen classes. A key challenge in OSR lies in the inability to model the unbounded distribution of unknown classes during training, often leading to the misclassification of samples from these classes. Rather than modeling unknowns, recent work shapes the feature space so that known classes are compact and well separated, and spherical representation learning methods have achieved strong results this way. Label smoothing has been identified as one of the key drivers of this success, yet it applies the same coefficient to every training sample, regardless of how well each sample is already embedded. We show that the spherical representation learning objectives used in OSR share a single alignment--uniformity structure in which labels enter only through the alignment term. Label smoothing therefore acts as an alignment dial, and a fixed coefficient sets this dial to the same value for every sample. We propose a plug-in, SmoothOperator (SmoothOP), which sets the smoothing coefficient of each sample from its \textbf{prominence}, an embedding-space signal measuring how clearly the sample's own class stands out against its strongest competing class. Our method integrates into four existing spherical representation learning methods at minimal training overhead. SmoothOP assigns strong smoothing to samples with high prominence, which reduces their alignment and relaxes their pull. On the Semantic Shift Benchmark, SmoothOP-augmented variants generally outperform their base objectives across datasets, degrees of semantic shift, and OSR post-processors, with gains of up to 4.7\% in AUROC, OSCR, and closed-set accuracy.

</details>


### [53] [Lang3DSeg: Annotation-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation with Point Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00855)
*Cigdem Kokenoz,Amir Salarpour,Alkim Domeke,Christopher Salas,Pedram MohajerAnsari,Long Cheng,Mert D. Pesé,Bing Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Lang3DSeg is a point transformer-based method for open-vocabulary 3D LiDAR semantic segmentation that achieves state-of-the-art results (52.8% mIoU on nuScenes, 41.4% on SemanticKITTI) among annotation-free methods, using a novel class-priority rule and depth gap truncation to correct 2D-to-3D projection errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised LiDAR segmentation relies on expensive manual annotation and closed taxonomies, while existing open-vocabulary methods use voxel-based sparse convolutions and point transformers have been limited to indoor environments with dense 3D data.

Method: Lang3DSeg uses a point transformer backbone for outdoor 3D LiDAR segmentation, trained from scratch without geometric pre-training. It addresses depth ambiguity in 2D-to-3D label projection by applying a class-priority rule for compositing masks and truncating each projected instance at the first gap in its depth distribution.

Result: Achieves 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes validation and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, the highest among published annotation-free methods on both benchmarks. Inference runs in real-time on single LiDAR sweeps without requiring vision-language models.

Conclusion: Point transformers can serve as effective backbones for outdoor open-vocabulary LiDAR segmentation, and explicit correction of 2D-to-3D projection errors (rather than averaging over sequences) significantly improves performance. The method enables real-time annotation-free semantic perception.

Abstract: Accurate 3D semantic perception is critical for safe autonomous navigation. However, supervised LiDAR segmentation remains tied to closed taxonomies and to the cost of point-wise manual annotation. Open-vocabulary methods avoid that cost by projecting the output of 2D vision-language models onto LiDAR and distilling it into a 3D network. These methods rely almost exclusively on voxel-based sparse convolutions, and point transformers have so far been limited to indoor environments, where 3D data is dense and bounded. We present Lang3DSeg, which establishes a point transformer as the backbone for annotation-free open-vocabulary segmentation of outdoor 3D LiDAR, and is trained from scratch without geometric pre-training. This training paradigm necessitates addressing the inherent noise in 2D-to-3D label projections; specifically, naive projection often suffers from depth ambiguity, where points behind an object are erroneously assigned its semantic label. We therefore composite masks using an explicit class-priority rule and truncate each projected instance at the first gap in its depth distribution, correcting the projection error directly rather than averaging it over registered sequences. Lang3DSeg achieves 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes validation and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, the highest among published annotation-free methods on both benchmarks. Every 3D semantic segmentation is on a single LiDAR sweep, and inference operates in real-time without running vision-language models.

</details>


### [54] [CtrlWAM: Controllable World Action Models with Aligned Intent and Foresight](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00859)
*Chensheng Peng,Wenhao Ding,Ran Tian,Zewei Zhou,Jef Packer,Maximilian Igl,Peter Karkus,Yan Wang,Masayoshi Tomizuka,Boris Ivanovic,Marco Pavone,Yuxiao Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CtrlWAM addresses a training mismatch in World Action Models (WAMs) where perturbed actions imply counterfactual futures but noised video remains tied to ground truth. The method executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with noised visual consequences, using warped video-action noise schedules and extending to multi-agent streams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard WAM training adds noise to both actions and video simultaneously, creating a mismatch: perturbed actions imply counterfactual future visuals while noised video stays tied to GT recording. In low-noise regimes, scene geometry and dynamic behavior remain visible from noisy future frames despite added noise, causing training inconsistency.

Method: 1) Execute perturbed actions in a simulator and pair with noised visual consequences for joint WAM learning; 2) Introduce warped video-action noise schedules to keep visual layout responsive as action predictions evolve; 3) Extend action interface from ego-only control to variable number of agent streams for unified multi-agent representation.

Result: Driving experiments: more accurate action forecasts, closer agreement between generated video and actions, better command following. Robotics experiments: stronger motion fidelity and controllability. Matched controls support benefit of off-path renders for command following and manipulation fidelity.

Conclusion: CtrlWAM achieves more controllable world action model through simulator-based training with perturbed actions, warped noise schedules, and multi-agent support, demonstrating improved action forecasting accuracy, video-action consistency, and command following across driving and robotics domains.

Abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict actions (intent) and visual future (foresight). Standard training adds noise to recorded actions and video simultaneously, but such training paradigms introduce a mismatch: perturbed actions imply counterfactual future visual, while the noised video remains tied to the GT recording. In low-noise regime, the scene geometry and even the dynamic behavior remain clearly visible from the noisy future frames despite the added noise. We present CtrlWAM, which executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with their noised visual consequences for joint WAM learning. To accommodate the different denoising requirements of video and actions, we introduce warped video--action noise schedules that aim to keep visual layout responsive as action predictions evolve. We further extend the action interface from ego-only control to a variable number of agent streams, allowing a unified model to represent predicted or commanded futures for multiple agents. Driving experiments show more accurate action forecasts, closer agreement between generated video and actions, and better following of supplied commands; robotics experiments show stronger motion fidelity and controllability. Matched controls support the benefit of off-path renders for command following and manipulation fidelity. Together, these findings contribute to a more controllable world action model. Project page: https://ctrl-wam.github.io/

</details>


### [55] [Machine Translation for Sign Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00881)
*Ozge Mercanoglu Sincan,Anton Pelykh,Edward Fish,Harry Walsh,JianHe Low,Karahan Sahin,Oline Ranum,Sobhan Asasi,Steven Emery,Richard Bowden*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A comprehensive review of sign language machine translation, covering the evolution from isolated sign recognition to end-to-end translation systems, examining linguistic properties, technical challenges, and ethical considerations, with emphasis on interdisciplinary collaboration with deaf communities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite substantial progress in sign language machine translation over the past decade, significant challenges remain: limited datasets compared to spoken-language resources, inadequate evaluation metrics, and the fundamental difficulty of capturing the simultaneous, multi-layered, and three-dimensional structure of sign languages. Additionally, ethical considerations around data governance, community involvement, and appropriate use require attention.

Method: This is a comprehensive review paper synthesizing interdisciplinary perspectives spanning computer vision, sign language linguistics, and deaf studies. It traces the evolution of recognition, translation, and production systems while examining linguistic properties that make sign languages computationally unique.

Result: The review identifies key advances driven by pose estimation, transformer architectures, and large-scale dataset collection. It analyzes ongoing technical challenges including dataset limitations, evaluation metric inadequacies, and the complexity of sign language structure. The paper also addresses ethical considerations around data governance and community involvement.

Conclusion: Continued progress in sign language machine translation requires sustained collaboration across computer vision, sign language linguistics, and deaf studies fields, with meaningful involvement of deaf communities throughout the research process.

Abstract: Sign language machine translation has progressed substantially over the past decade, evolving from isolated sign recognition to end-to-end translation systems. Advances in pose estimation, transformer architectures, and large-scale dataset collection have driven progress, yet challenges remain. Datasets are limited compared to spoken-language resources; evaluation metrics inadequately capture the linguistic quality of output; and models must capture the simultaneous, multi-layered, and three-dimensional structure of sign languages. This manuscript provides a comprehensive review that seeks to balance technical challenges with stakeholder considerations. We examine the linguistic properties that make sign languages computationally unique, trace the evolution of recognition, translation, and production systems, and analyze ongoing technical challenges. Crucially, we address ethical considerations around data governance, community involvement, and appropriate use. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives spanning computer vision, sign language linguistics, and deaf studies, our analysis emphasizes that continued progress requires sustained collaboration across these fields and with deaf communities.

</details>


### [56] [EyeTAG: Eye Trajectory-Aware Gaze Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00922)
*Jungmin Lee,Niamat Ullah,Yoseob Han*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EyeTAG proposes a causal multi-frame gaze estimation framework that uses an explicit first-order gaze prior by differentiating recent predictions into a kinematic token. This approach reduces jitter and removes systematic saccade bias by modeling motion explicitly rather than implicitly within appearance features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-frame gaze estimation methods suffer from output jitter due to predicting each frame independently. Existing multi-frame methods reduce jitter but learn motion implicitly inside appearance features, never treating gaze trajectory as an explicit variable. This limits their ability to properly model temporal motion dynamics.

Method: EyeTAG is a causal multi-frame framework built around an explicit first-order gaze prior. At each time step, it differentiates its own recent predictions and feeds the resulting trajectory back as a compact kinematic token. This token is translation-invariant in gaze space, carrying subject-invariant motion rather than personal gaze offsets. Face and eye streams provide visual evidence, fused by cross-attention and a causal Transformer decoder.

Result: EyeTAG reduces mean angular error by about 1.0° on Gaze360 and performs on par with the strongest baseline on EVE (2.56° vs 2.58°). Within-model ablations show that the differential formulation, rather than temporal context alone, removes the systematic saccade bias that persists even with an absolute gaze-history prior.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling gaze trajectory as a differential kinematic token is more effective than implicit motion learning in appearance features. The translation-invariant nature of the differential token makes it subject-invariant, and this formulation specifically addresses saccade bias that absolute gaze-history priors cannot eliminate.

Abstract: Gaze estimation under natural head-eye motion underpins applications from driver monitoring to human-computer interaction. Single-frame methods predict each frame independently, so consecutive outputs fluctuate as jitter. Multi-frame methods reduce this, but they learn motion implicitly inside appearance features, so the gaze trajectory is never an explicit variable. We propose EyeTAG (Eye Trajectory-Aware Gaze Estimation), a causal multi-frame framework built around an explicit first-order gaze prior: at each step it differentiates its own recent predictions and feeds the resulting trajectory back as a compact kinematic token. Because differencing is translation-invariant in gaze space, this token carries subject-invariant motion rather than personal gaze offsets. Face and eye streams supply visual evidence, fused by cross-attention and a causal Transformer decoder. EyeTAG reduces the mean angular error by about 1.0$^\circ$ on Gaze360 and performs on par with the strongest baseline on EVE (2.56$^\circ$ vs. 2.58$^\circ$). Within-model ablations, which keep the encoder and the rest of the architecture fixed and vary only the gaze history, show that the differential formulation, rather than temporal context alone, removes the systematic saccade bias that persists even with an absolute gaze-history prior. Our code is available at https://github.com/peter8366/EyeTAG.

</details>


### [57] [Joint Branch-Space Transform Coding for Diffusion Activation Quantization with Classifier-Free Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00930)
*Mingrun Jiang,Yuejia Liu,Zishan Shao,Ting Jiang,Qinsi Wang,Hancheng Ye,Yixiao Wang,Rui-Feng Wang,Kangning Cui,Yixuan Chen,Fan Yang,Xiang Cheng,Hai Li,Yiran Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces branch-space transform coding for post-training quantization of diffusion models with Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG). The method rotates matched CFG branches via a 2x2 orthogonal matrix to exploit cross-activation structure, and GCBT provides a closed-form solution incorporating CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current diffusion model quantization treats conditional and unconditional branch activations independently, leaving cross-activation structure unexploited. The authors observe that matched CFG activations form a strongly correlated 2D source, and the choice of branch coding basis significantly affects quantization fidelity under fixed bit budget.

Method: The authors propose branch-space transform coding, which rotates matched CFG branches via an offline-derived 2x2 orthogonal matrix. They further derive GCBT (Guidance-Correlation Branch Transform), which jointly incorporates the CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments, admitting a closed-form per-layer solution without gradient optimization or angle search.

Result: Applied on top of existing diffusion PTQ methods, GCBT yields statistically significant fidelity gains in most evaluated comparisons with no statistically significant degradation, while leaving the underlying host quantization pipeline unchanged.

Conclusion: Exploiting cross-activation structure between CFG branches through transform coding is an effective approach for improving diffusion model quantization, achieving fidelity gains without modifying the host quantization pipeline.

Abstract: Post-training quantization for diffusion models increasingly exploits timestep, feature, and layer structure. While recent work has begun incorporating CFG structure into diffusion quantization, activation quantization still operates independently across conditional and unconditional coordinates, leaving cross-activation structure unexploited. We show that matched CFG activations form a strongly correlated two-dimensional source and that, under a fixed bit budget, the choice of branch coding basis materially affects quantization fidelity. Motivated by this observation, we introduce branch-space transform coding, which rotates matched CFG branches via an offline derived 2x2 orthogonal matrix, requiring minimal modifications to model parameters or the quantization pipeline. We further derive the Guidance-Correlation Branch Transform (GCBT), which jointly incorporates the CFG guidance direction and cross-branch second moments. Under an equal-rate quantization-noise surrogate, GCBT admits a closed-form per-layer solution without gradient optimization or angle search. Applied on top of existing diffusion PTQ methods, GCBT yields statistically significant fidelity gains in most evaluated comparisons with no statistically significant degradation, while leaving the underlying host quantization pipeline unchanged.

</details>


### [58] [A Matched-Budget Audit Framework for Recaptioned Image-Text Supervision Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00952)
*Giyeong Oh,Junghun Park,Yuhan Bae,Youngjae Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces a matched-budget audit framework for evaluating recaptioned image-text corpora used in text-to-image training, addressing the challenge of auditing supervision distributions at scale. The framework evaluates captions across five axes at a fixed budget of B=64, using controllable basic units (CBU) as the standard metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the difficulty of evaluating recaptioned corpora at scale, as existing methods (length-correlated proxies and downstream benchmarks) fail to capture caption-register artifacts and are entangled with training choices, making it hard to audit the quality and characteristics of these supervision distributions.

Method: The authors propose a reusable matched-budget audit framework that evaluates recaptioned supervision distributions D_{π,V_c,C} at a fixed text budget of B=64. The framework reports a five-axis profile covering: (1) prompt-side coverage, (2) image-conditioned faithfulness, and (3) caption-surface health, with CBU as the common claim unit. They instantiate this framework on seven paired comparisons across five public source corpora, using Qwen and Gemma as judges.

Result: Across four cross-corpus pairs, the released surface raises supported CBU per caption by +3.39 to +6.36 under both Qwen and Gemma judges. On CC12M, the framework exposes a long-vs-dense frontier that is consistent across both judges and four budgets. The audited multi-source recap corpus (~490M) and audit-artifact bundle are released.

Conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to audit recaptioned supervision distributions, revealing that dense captions (with proper quality control) can significantly increase supported CBU per caption. The approach demonstrates consistent findings across different judges and budgets, and enables better understanding of caption quality in large-scale T2I training data.

Abstract: Recaptioned image-text corpora are now standard for text-to-image (T2I) training, with vision--language model (VLM) captioners replacing sparse alt-text by dense descriptions. A recaptioned corpus is a supervision distribution induced by a documented captioning policy ($π$), captioner ($V_c$), and source corpus ($C$). Length-correlated proxies miss caption-register artifacts and downstream T2I benchmarks entangle the corpus with training choices, so this distribution is hard to audit at corpus scale. We introduce a reusable matched-budget audit framework for recaptioned supervision distributions $D_{π,V_c,C}$: at a fixed text budget of $B = 64$ it reports a five-axis profile spanning prompt-side coverage, image-conditioned faithfulness, and caption-surface health, with claimed controllable basic units (CBU) as the common claim unit. We instantiate the framework on seven paired comparisons over five public source corpora. Across the four cross-corpus pairs, the released surface raises supported CBU per caption by $+3.39$ to $+6.36$ under both Qwen and Gemma Judges, and on CC12M the same framework exposes a long-vs-dense frontier that is consistent across both judges and four budgets. We release the audited multi-source recap corpus ($\approx$ 490M) together with the audit-artifact bundle.

</details>


### [59] [Two Clocks in Diffusion MLLMs: When Answers Stabilize Before Rationales Unfold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00953)
*Keuntae Kim,Yong Suk Choi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates temporal dynamics in masked diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), specifically examining when answer candidates stabilize relative to rationale generation in visual question-answering tasks. The study distinguishes between retrospective stabilization and token commitment, and measures how these timing events relate to rationale unfolding across different benchmarks and prompting strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be understanding the internal generation process of masked diffusion MLLMs, particularly the temporal relationship between when answers stabilize versus when rationales are generated. This addresses a gap in understanding how these models process information temporally during inference.

Method: The study employs three visual question-answering benchmarks (M3CoT, ScienceQA, V*Bench/LaViDa). Methods include: (1) Analyzing single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa runs to measure rationale canvas completion at stabilization; (2) V*Bench experiments varying block length from 128 to 8; (3) EOS-enabled prompting with direct instructions on Nemotron and LaViDa; (4) Symmetric decomposition to separate coverage from conditional accuracy components; (5) Matched-canvas image ablations to measure visual sensitivity alongside answer stabilization.

Result: Key findings: (1) 89.4-98.1% of rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block, EOS-suppressed runs; (2) Reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%, affecting answer coverage and observation window; (3) EOS-enabled prompting improves Nemotron's accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M3CoT and ScienceQA but reduces LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points; (4) Coverage accounts for the larger absolute component of prompting differences than conditional accuracy; (5) The method successfully separates answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity as distinct temporal readouts.

Conclusion: The study concludes that answer stabilization and rationale unfolding are temporally distinct processes in masked diffusion MLLMs. Coverage changes (rather than conditional accuracy) are the primary driver of prompting differences across benchmarks. The proposed measurements successfully distinguish these three dimensions: answer stabilization timing, rationale generation, and visual sensitivity, providing a framework for understanding generation dynamics in these models.

Abstract: An answer candidate in a masked diffusion MLLM can stabilize while its rationale is still unfolding. We distinguish retrospective stabilization of the logged candidate from token commitment, and examine these two clocks relative to rationale generation. Analyzing our results across three visual question-answering benchmarks, we find that 89.4-98.1% of the rationale-side canvas remains unwritten at stabilization in single-block, EOS-suppressed LaViDa runs. On V*Bench, reducing block length from 128 to 8 changes this fraction from 89.4% to 1.7%, together with answer coverage and the eligible observation window. Under EOS-enabled prompting, direct instructions improve Nemotron's overall accuracy by 15.0 and 19.5 percentage points on M3CoT and ScienceQA, but reduce LaViDa/V*Bench accuracy by 11.0 points. A symmetric decomposition associates the larger absolute component of each change with coverage rather than conditional accuracy. Matched-canvas image ablations measure visual sensitivity alongside answer stabilization, separating the two temporal readouts. Together, these measurements distinguish answer stabilization, rationale unfolding, and visual sensitivity, and identify coverage as the larger component of the prompting differences.

</details>


### [60] [Video-Index: A Curated Meta-Benchmark for Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00960)
*Enxin Song,Yinuo Xu,Shusheng Yang,Wenhao Chai,Jiatao Gu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces the "attack pyramid" framework to audit 115 video benchmarks for shortcut vulnerabilities, revealing that models can achieve near-full accuracy without seeing video frames on 35 benchmarks. The authors release Video-Index, a curated benchmark of 840 verified difficult items across four capability groups, where Claude Opus 5 outperforms open-source models by over 37 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video benchmarks claim to measure video understanding capabilities, but models can exploit shortcuts in answer options, question text, or partial visual evidence rather than truly understanding video content. This raises serious concerns about the validity of current video benchmark evaluations.

Method: The authors propose the "attack pyramid" - five levels of shortcut attacks with increasing access to each benchmark item. They audit 115 video benchmarks using this framework, conduct temporal probes on 51 benchmarks, identify near-duplicate questions, and screen 505,518 QA pairs from 112 benchmarks. They use agents to transform evaluation requests into specifications, with a deterministic selector and red-team gate for reproducible benchmarks.

Result: On 35 benchmarks, attackers that never see any frame approach full-video accuracy. On 51 benchmarks with temporal probes, shuffled frames retain a median 96% of full-video accuracy. Near-duplicate questions comprise at least half the items in 63 benchmarks. Video-Index contains 210 hardest verified items in each of four capability groups (840 items total from 76 sources). Claude Opus 5 outperforms all open-source models by over 37 percentage points, with agent tools adding ~20 percentage points, yet all systems still have room for improvement.

Conclusion: Current video benchmarks suffer from significant shortcut vulnerabilities. The attack pyramid provides a systematic framework for auditing benchmarks. Video-Index offers a more robust evaluation benchmark, though even the best systems (Claude Opus 5 with agents) still show room for improvement in efficiency and accuracy on this harder benchmark set.

Abstract: A video benchmark should reward the capability it claims to measure, yet models can exploit answer options, question text, or partial visual evidence. We introduce the attack pyramid, five levels of shortcut attacks with increasing access to each item, and audit 115 video benchmarks with it. On 35 benchmarks, attackers that never see a frame approach full-video accuracy. On 51 benchmarks with temporal probes, shuffled frames keep a median 96% of full-video accuracy. Near-duplicate questions make up at least half the items in 63 benchmarks. We screen 505,518 question-answer pairs from 112 of them into an audited pool. Agents turn evaluation requests into specifications, and a deterministic selector with a red-team gate composes reproducible benchmarks. We release Video-Index, the 210 hardest verified items under these attacks in each of four capability groups, 840 items from 76 sources. With the same fixed input, Claude Opus 5 outscores every open-source model by over 37 percentage points, and agent tools add about 20 more, yet all systems leave room to improve efficiency and accuracy. Blog: https://www.enxinsong.com/blog/video-index/ GitHub: https://github.com/Espere-1119-Song/Video-Index Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Video-Index/Video-Index

</details>


### [61] [RelationVGGT: Visual Geometry Transformers for 3D Spatial Relation Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00970)
*Minsu Kim,Jaesung Choe,Jiwoo Lee,Yu-Chiang Frank Wang,Seon Joo Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces RelationVGGT, a feed-forward framework for 3D spatial relation segmentation that segments target objects based on a visual subject specification and relational text query without category names or camera poses. It combines visual foundation models with 3D geometry models and uses a relation transformer for cross-view prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing 3D reconstruction and semantic understanding methods focus on object-centric perception and neglect spatial relations between objects. The authors address this gap by formulating a new task: segmenting targets based on spatial relations to a visually specified subject, without requiring category names or per-scene optimization.

Method: RelationVGGT integrates semantic features from a visual foundation model with geometry-aware representations from a 3D geometry foundation model. It uses a relation transformer for subject-conditioned, cross-view relation prediction. The method is pose-free (no known camera poses required) and feed-forward (no per-scene optimization). The paper also provides an automated annotation pipeline using ScanNet++ with VLMs and LLMs for scalable training data generation.

Result: The paper presents a novel framework that can segment targets across multiple views based on spatial relations to a subject, without requiring category names or camera poses. The automated annotation pipeline enables scalable training data generation.

Conclusion: RelationVGGT represents a step toward more holistic 3D scene understanding by incorporating spatial relations between objects. The proposed approach demonstrates the feasibility of feed-forward, pose-free multi-view relation segmentation, and the annotation pipeline enables scalable training data generation for this new task.

Abstract: Recent advances in 3D reconstruction have progressed from per-scene optimization to feed-forward inference, and semantic scene understanding has followed suit -- yet existing methods remain confined to object-centric perception, neglecting spatial relations between objects. We formulate 3D spatial relation segmentation in a feed-forward, pose-free multi-view setting: given a visually specified subject and a relational text query, the model segments the target across views without receiving its category name. To this end, we propose RelationVGGT, a novel feed-forward framework that integrates semantic features from a visual foundation model with geometry-aware representations from a 3D geometry foundation model and leverages a relation transformer for subject-conditioned, cross-view relation prediction -- requiring neither per-scene optimization nor known camera poses. We additionally provide a fully automated annotation pipeline built on ScanNet++ with VLMs and LLMs, enabling scalable training data generation for this new task.

</details>


### [62] [Concept Driven Domain Adaptation: Finding an Abstract Needle in a Haystack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00973)
*Haiming Zhao,Tai Wang,Kun Zhang,Xicheng Peng,Zhiyang Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses a gap in video retrieval for science education: existing methods assume queries describe observable events, but teachers need to retrieve specific visual examples that demonstrate abstract scientific concepts. The authors propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework that adapts vision-language models to bridge the abstraction gap between curriculum concepts and documentary video evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Science teachers search for video excerpts by querying abstract concepts they intend to teach, but existing language-based video retrieval methods assume queries describe observable events. This mismatch creates a fundamental limitation when educators need to find concrete visual phenomena that instantiate underlying scientific principles—a problem termed "concept-to-example video retrieval."

Method: The proposed CDDA framework operates in three stages: (1) Structure the textual embedding space using textbook and teacher-handbook example-concept pairs as semantic anchors; (2) Transfer this concept-aware geometry to documentary visuals using a frozen visual encoder; (3) Jointly adapt both encoders with sparse visual concept supervision. From a geometric perspective, this staged alignment reduces text-concept and vision-concept angular gaps.

Result: CDDA outperforms several competitive multimodal baselines on a curated middle-school physics retrieval benchmark, including Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, while maintaining concrete image-text matching performance after adaptation.

Conclusion: The three-stage concept-level adaptation successfully bridges the abstraction gap between curriculum concepts and documentary visuals. CDDA achieves pedagogically-oriented concept retrieval without sacrificing the pretrained model's ability to match concrete image descriptions, demonstrating the effectiveness of treating concepts as intermediate semantic anchors.

Abstract: Science teachers frequently search for documentary excerpts not by describing what appears on screen, but by querying the abstract concepts they intend to teach. This use case exposes a limitation of existing language-based video moment retrieval methods, which typically assume that queries describe observable events, whereas instructional search requires retrieving concrete visual phenomena that instantiate an underlying scientific principle. We study this setting as concept-to-example video retrieval, an abstract-needle-in-a-haystack problem where compact curriculum concepts must be grounded in temporally sparse documentary evidence. To bridge this abstraction gap, we propose Concept-Driven Domain Adaptation (CDDA), a three-stage framework for adapting two-tower vision-language models to concept-level retrieval. CDDA treats concepts as intermediate semantic anchors: it first structures the textual embedding space with textbook and teacher-handbook example-concept pairs, then transfers this concept-aware geometry to documentary visuals under a frozen visual encoder, and finally jointly adapts both encoders with sparse visual concept supervision. From a geometric perspective, this staged alignment reduces text-concept and vision-concept angular gaps, thereby encouraging concept-level adaptation while preserving the pretrained model's concrete image description alignment. On a curated middle-school physics retrieval benchmark, CDDA achieves stronger pedagogically oriented concept retrieval than several competitive multimodal baselines, including Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, while maintaining concrete image-text matching after adaptation.

</details>


### [63] [VIEScore2: Unified Image Evaluation with Spatially Grounded Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00994)
*Xianda Du,Max Ku,Weiming Ren,Zhi Rui Tam,Chunlin Ren,Ping Nie,Min-Hung Chen,Wenhu Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VIEScore2 is a unified evaluator for image generation and editing tasks that jointly predicts quality scores and defect locations in a single model pass by representing images as an N×N grid. It achieves an overall-score SRCC of 0.601, outperforming Gemini-3-Flash (0.491), and excels at defect localization across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing synthetic image evaluators only provide scalar quality scores without identifying which image regions support those scores. This limits interpretability and actionable feedback for image generation and editing tasks.

Method: VIEScore2 represents images as an N×N grid and uses a text-native grid representation for heterogeneous spatial supervision. Training uses 38K examples across score-only, localization-only, and joint supervision. Training starts with supervised fine-tuning, then applies GRPO with rewards combining cell-level Dice overlap, score accuracy, and output-format validity. A parameter-free parser converts structured predictions into readable explanations.

Result: VIEScore2 achieves an overall-score SRCC of 0.601, compared with 0.491 for Gemini-3-Flash (strongest zero-shot VLM baseline). For defect localization, it outperforms general-purpose VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators on 3 of 6 benchmarks in per-image grid IoU and ranks among top three on five benchmarks, including datasets beyond its training sources.

Conclusion: VIEScore2 successfully provides both quality scores and defect localization in a unified model, demonstrating superior performance over zero-shot VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators while maintaining generalization to out-of-domain datasets.

Abstract: Existing synthetic image evaluators typically provide only a scalar quality score and do not identify the image regions that support it. We introduce VIEScore2, a unified evaluator for image generation and editing tasks with optional conditioning images. VIEScore2 represents an image as an N x N grid and jointly predicts quality scores and defect locations in a single model pass. Its text-native grid representation provides a common interface for heterogeneous spatial supervision and enables directly verifiable post-training objectives. We train on 38K examples spanning score-only, localization-only, and joint supervision across generation and editing tasks. Starting from supervised fine-tuning, we further apply GRPO to improve defect localization using rewards that combine cell-level Dice overlap, score accuracy, and output-format validity. A parameter-free parser converts the structured predictions into readable explanations. On the primary suite, VIEScore2 achieves an overall-score SRCC of 0.601, compared with 0.491 for Gemini-3-Flash, the strongest zero-shot general-purpose VLM baseline under matched inputs. For defect localization, VIEScore2 outperforms both general-purpose VLMs and specialized spatial evaluators on three of six benchmarks in per-image grid IoU and ranks among the top three on five, including datasets beyond its training sources.

</details>


### [64] [VASC: Value-Aware Sparse Attention with Cross-Layer Memory for Efficient 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01013)
*Junyi Wu,Fanqing Kong,Leyang Chen,Shaoqiu Zhang,Yulun Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VASC is a training-free sparse attention method for feed-forward 3D vision models (like VGGT) that addresses quadratic complexity issues and value redundancy in existing sparse methods. It combines value-aware block selection with execution-aware cross-layer memory to improve efficiency while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feed-forward 3D vision models like VGGT have quadratic global attention, making long image sequences expensive. Existing sparse methods may favor highly attended but value-redundant regions, leading to inefficient computation allocation.

Method: VASC introduces two key components: (1) Value-aware block selection that integrates pooled query-key relevance with neighboring value contrast to reduce redundancy while preserving query-relevant and distinctive content; (2) Execution-aware cross-layer memory that tracks unserved demand across layers and updates based on actual execution, enabling previously underserved blocks to compete under fixed computation budget.

Result: Experiments on 7Scenes and NeuralRGB-D datasets with VGGT and π³ show improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality compared with FasterVGGT, together with up to 2.29× faster inference than dense VGGT.

Conclusion: VASC provides an effective training-free solution for sparse attention in 3D vision models, achieving a good balance between computational efficiency (up to 2.29× speedup) and accuracy (improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality) compared to existing dense and sparse methods.

Abstract: Feed-forward 3D vision models such as VGGT have achieved remarkable progress, unifying camera estimation and dense scene reconstruction in a single pass. However, their quadratic global attention makes long image sequences expensive, while existing sparse methods may favor highly attended yet value-redundant regions. To address these limitations, we introduce VASC, a training-free sparse attention method combining value-aware block selection and execution-aware cross-layer memory. Our value-aware block selection integrates pooled query--key relevance with neighboring value contrast, reducing redundancy while preserving query-relevant and distinctive content. Cross-layer memory tracks unserved demand across layers and updates this state according to actual execution, enabling previously underserved blocks to compete under a fixed computation budget. Experiments on 7Scenes and NeuralRGB-D with VGGT and $π^3$ demonstrate improved pose estimation and reconstruction quality compared with FasterVGGT, together with up to $2.29\times$ faster inference than dense VGGT. Code is available at https://github.com/kosakayamahoo-design/VASC.

</details>


### [65] [FutureWorlds: Learning Robotic World Models from Alternative Futures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01019)
*Hao Wu,Shengju Qian,Weiyan Wang,Fan Xu,Fan Zhang,Yuanpeng He,Qingsong Wen,Yuxuan Liang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FutureWorlds is a framework for robotic world models that unifies candidate construction, history maintenance, and learning from relative quality. It uses a multimodal discrete autoregressive model with diverse beam search to generate diverse candidate futures, combined with MemSPO to optimize the world model using group-relative advantages from video trajectory rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key challenges in robotic world models are: (1) similar candidate predictions limit informative quality comparisons, and (2) diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of their individual histories. Current methods struggle to effectively utilize alternative predictions as learning signals.

Method: FutureWorlds uses a multimodal discrete autoregressive model with diverse beam search during reinforcement learning to construct candidate futures that balance confidence and diversity. Candidate-specific bounded memory preserves scene states to ensure matching histories between generation and policy scoring. MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization) converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages to optimize the world model.

Result: On RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa datasets, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12% respectively, relative to the strongest baseline. Only 200 MemSPO updates further improve generation quality and support continued prediction beyond the training horizon. Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and optical-flow evaluation confirm gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction and more consistent object states.

Conclusion: FutureWorlds successfully addresses the challenges of candidate comparison and history maintenance in robotic world models. The framework achieves significant improvements in prediction quality across multiple benchmarks, with gains that transfer to motion prediction and object state consistency. The approach enables continued improvement beyond the training horizon with minimal updates.

Abstract: Robotic world models predict action-conditioned future scenes, providing a foundation for understanding action outcomes. However, turning alternative predictions into useful learning signals remains challenging: similar candidates limit informative quality comparisons, while diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of their individual histories. We introduce FutureWorlds, a framework that unifies candidate construction, history maintenance, and learning from relative quality. Built on a multimodal discrete autoregressive model, FutureWorlds uses diverse beam search during reinforcement learning to construct candidate futures that balance confidence and diversity. Candidate-specific bounded memory preserves scene states and ensures that generation and policy scoring use matching histories. We further propose MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization), which converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages to optimize the world model. On RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset. Under fixed evaluation configurations, only 200 MemSPO updates further improve generation quality and support continued prediction beyond the training horizon. Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and optical-flow evaluation show that these gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction and more consistent object states. Project page and code: https://github.com/Alexander-wu/FutureWorlds.

</details>


### [66] [Towards Automatic Video Annotation with ASH: Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Tracking and Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01022)
*Arash Rocky,Q. M. Jonathan Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses limitations in memory-attention-based Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) methods, specifically high memory requirements restricting to short clips and inefficient single-prompt design for multi-category tracking. The authors propose two contributions: Generalized Presence Token (GPT) for efficient multi-prompt processing (O(N) to O(1) image encoding cost) and Annotation and Segmentation Handler (ASH) for arbitrary-length video processing via overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based identity matching. The resulting SAM3-ASH pipeline achieves SOTA HOTA on MOTS20 under zero-shot conditions while maintaining competitive performance across 7 benchmarks with GPU memory under 25GB.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-attention-based VIS methods have two key limitations: (1) substantial memory requirements confine them to short video clips, and (2) single-prompt inference design makes multi-category open-vocabulary tracking computationally prohibitive. The work aims to enable fully automated tracking annotation of arbitrary video in a training-free manner.

Method: Two technical contributions: (1) GPT reformulates SAM3's inference pipeline to process N text prompts simultaneously via virtual prompt batching, reducing image encoding cost from O(N) to O(1) without modifying learned components; (2) ASH extends any memory-attention VIS tracker to arbitrary length sequences through overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based inter-chunk identity matching, requiring no dataset-specific training.

Result: SAM3-ASH achieves state-of-the-art HOTA on MOTS20 under fully zero-shot conditions and remains competitive with trained specialists across seven additional benchmarks, while peak GPU memory consumption stays below 25 GB.

Conclusion: The proposed SAM3-ASH establishes a practical baseline for scalable, training-free automated video annotation, successfully addressing memory constraints and enabling efficient multi-category open-vocabulary tracking.

Abstract: Memory-attention-based Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) methods have demonstrated strong zero-shot tracking capability, yet their substantial memory requirements confine them to short video clips and their single-prompt inference design makes multi-category open-vocabulary tracking computationally prohibitive. This work introduces two contributions toward fully automated tracking annotation of arbitrary video. The Generalized Presence Token (GPT) reformulates SAM3's inference pipeline to process N text prompts simultaneously via virtual prompt batching, reducing image encoding cost from O(N) to O(1) with no modifications to any learned component. The Annotation and Segmentation Handler (ASH) extends any memory-attention VIS tracker to sequences of arbitrary length through overlapping temporal chunks with IoU-based inter-chunk identity matching, requiring no dataset-specific training. Instantiated on SAM3, the resulting pipeline -- SAM3-ASH -- achieves state-of-the-art HOTA on MOTS20 under fully zero-shot conditions and remains competitive with trained specialists across seven additional benchmarks, while peak GPU memory consumption stays below 25 GB, establishing a practical baseline for scalable, training-free automated video annotation.

</details>


### [67] [Bootstrapping Video Interaction Generation with Synthetic State Transitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01039)
*Jiho Jang,Jinyoung Kim,Nojun Kwak,Kyungjune Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A framework for generating synthetic video datasets of controllable physical interactions, using structured taxonomy and image editing models to create start/end state anchors, combined with a novel State-Guided Sampling (SGS) technique to produce seamless videos and reduce generation artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video generative models struggle to portray plausible physical interactions and state transitions, limiting applications in robotics and VR/AR.

Method: 1) Structured taxonomy for interaction categorization
2) Image editing models to create explicit start and end state images as visual anchors
3) State-Guided Sampling (SGS) - novel sampling technique to mitigate artifacts in conditional generation
4) Automated evaluation system aligned with human judgments

Result: Fine-tuning a base model on the synthetic dataset significantly enhances its ability to generate plausible physical interactions.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully creates high-quality synthetic interaction data, addressing the critical bottleneck in video generation for physical interactions.

Abstract: While recent video generative models can synthesize high-fidelity videos, they struggle to portray plausible physical interactions and the resulting state transitions, a critical bottleneck for applications in robotics and VR/AR. To address this, we introduce a framework to generate a scalable synthetic dataset of controllable interactions. Our pipeline leverages a structured taxonomy and state-of-the-art image editing models to create explicit `start' and `end' state images, which serve as visual anchors for the interaction. To generate a seamless video utilizing these anchors, we propose State-Guided Sampling (SGS), a novel sampling technique that mitigates artifacts common in naive conditional generation. Furthermore, we develop and validate a new automated evaluation system that aligns with human judgments to ensure data quality. Experiments show that fine-tuning a base model on our dataset significantly enhances its ability to generate plausible interactions.

</details>


### [68] [Towards Subject Consistency over Dynamic Subject Sets in Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01052)
*Tongcheng Zhang,Jun Zhu,Jianfei Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces DynSC-Eval, a novel evaluation framework for assessing subject consistency in long-duration video generation. It dynamically tracks subjects throughout their visible lifespans and measures consistency using six complementary metrics, addressing a critical gap in existing evaluation methods that fail to capture consistency issues in longer videos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video generation evaluation metrics fail to adequately assess subject consistency in longer videos (5s, 15s, 60s). Existing metrics obscure substantial consistency differences between models. There is a need for dynamic subject tracking that evaluates consistency over the entire visible lifespan of subjects rather than using static evaluation approaches.

Method: The paper introduces DynSC-Eval framework that: (1) Dynamically tracks eligible subjects throughout their visible lifespans; (2) Measures local continuity and global identity preservation using six complementary object-level metrics; (3) Explicitly detects inconsistency events. Synthetic experiments inject inconsistency events to validate sensitivity. The method is applied to post-training using DiffusionNFT with rewards constructed from DynSC-Eval metrics, tested on an autonomous-driving testbed. Curriculum learning extends generation to 10s and 30s.

Result: On 5s generation, the approach reduces six inconsistency metrics by an average of 13.82% for Wan-2.1-1.3B and 5.66% for SANA-2B, with improvements also on ReSim I2V model. Consistency optimization remains effective when extending to 10s and 30s while preserving other capabilities. The framework demonstrates both sensitivity to injected inconsistencies and reveals substantial subject consistency differences across models that conventional metrics miss.

Conclusion: DynSC-Eval provides a more accurate and comprehensive evaluation of subject consistency in video generation. The framework successfully identifies model weaknesses that existing metrics overlook. Post-training with DynSC-Eval rewards effectively improves subject consistency, and this improvement scales to longer video durations (10s, 30s) through curriculum learning without sacrificing other generation capabilities.

Abstract: We argue that as video generation extends to longer durations, subject consistency should be evaluated over \textit{dynamic subject sets}. We therefore introduce \textbf{DynSC-Eval}, an evaluation framework that dynamically tracks eligible subjects throughout their visible lifespans and measures local continuity and global identity preservation using six complementary object-level metrics, with explicit detection of inconsistency events. To validate its effectiveness, we design synthetic experiments that actively inject inconsistency events, demonstrating both the sensitivity of DynSC-Eval and the limitations of existing metrics. Evaluations of diverse models on 5s, 15s, and 60s video generation further reveal substantial subject consistency differences that are obscured by conventional metrics. Beyond evaluation, we construct rewards from DynSC-Eval and apply DiffusionNFT post-training in an autonomous-driving testbed. On 5s generation, our approach reduces the six inconsistency metrics by an average of 13.82\% for Wan-2.1-1.3B and 5.66\% for SANA-2B, with improvements also observed on the I2V model ReSim. Qualitative comparisons further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. We then extend generation to 10s and 30s through curriculum learning and show that consistency optimization remains effective while largely preserving other capabilities.

</details>


### [69] [HierGF: Hierarchical Gaussian Fields via Geometry-perception Message Passing for Sparse-view 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01056)
*Bi'an Du,Zhimin Zhang,Daizong Liu,Baoquan Chen,Wei Hu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: HierGF addresses sparse view 3D reconstruction by converting limited observations into structured pseudo-supervision through a hierarchical geometry-perception approach, featuring a two-stage backbone network, learnable confidence network, and geometrically consistent densification module to enhance multi-view consistency with very few input views.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparse view 3D reconstruction faces two major challenges: 1) too few images for matching, making multi-view consistency difficult; 2) insufficient view coverage leading to missing parts in under-sampled regions. Existing methods rely on limited reprojection errors and regularization terms, prone to overfitting and inconsistent appearances, while using heuristic density control in geometrically under-sampled regions.

Method: The paper proposes Hierarchical Gaussian Fields (HierGF) with three key components: 1) A two-stage geometry-perception backbone network that transforms coarse 3D geometric information and additional 2D generative priors into structured pseudo-supervision; 2) A learnable confidence network to guide gradients toward cross-view consistent content; 3) A geometrically consistent densification module to improve reconstruction of multi-view alignment and under-sampled regions.

Result: The method enhances multi-view consistency with very few input views by moving beyond fixed priors and heuristic density control, providing reliable guidance for under-sampled regions.

Conclusion: HierGF successfully addresses sparse view 3D reconstruction by revisiting the problem from a hierarchical geometry-perception perspective and converting limited observations into reliable self-generated supervision, effectively solving the challenges of limited views and under-sampled regions.

Abstract: Sparse view 3D reconstruction is an important and common scenario in multimedia applications, such as augmented reality/virtual reality (AR/VR) content creation, cultural heritage digitization, and certain robotic applications, where only a limited number of randomly captured views may be available. However, sparse views contain only limited 3D information, posing two major challenges:1) too few images are available for matching, making it difficult to build multi-view consistency; 2) insufficient view coverage leads to a lack of information in under-sampled regions, resulting in missing parts of object structure. Existing methods mostly still rely on limited reprojection errors and regularization terms, which are prone to overfitting to a single view and inconsistent appearances across views. In geometrically under-sampled regions, they often rely on heuristic density control, lacking reliable guidance and often resulting in blurring and structural holes.To address these issues, this paper proposes Hierarchical Gaussian Fields (HierGF), which revisits sparse-view reconstruction from a hierarchical geometry-perception perspective and converts limited observations into reliable self-generated supervision beyond fixed priors and heuristic density control. In particular, we transform coarse 3D geometric information and additional 2D generative priors into structured pseudo-supervision through a two-stage geometry-perception backbone network, thereby enhancing multi-view consistency with very few input views. In addition, we introduce a learnable confidence network to guide gradients toward cross-view consistent content, and a geometrically consistent densification module to improve the reconstruction of multi-view alignment and under-sampled regions.

</details>


### [70] [Overcoming Kernel Redundancy for Scaling Logic Gate Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01069)
*Sejin Park,Hongjae Lee,Changwoo Han,Seung-Won Jung*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates width scaling in differentiable logic gate networks. The authors identify that naive width scaling leads to kernel redundancy and performance saturation. They propose a dynamic logic kernel framework with input-dependent routing that promotes specialization across kernel groups, focusing adaptation at the first gate level where redundancy is most pronounced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core motivation addresses a key gap in logic gate network research: while scaling model capacity is a central principle in deep neural networks that typically improves performance, this scaling behavior remains underexplored in logic gate networks. The authors aim to determine whether similar scaling benefits can be achieved in logic gate networks.

Method: The authors propose a dynamic logic kernel framework that reorganizes kernel utilization through input-dependent kernel routing. This approach promotes specialization across kernel groups, enabling better utilization of increased width.
