To address these limitations, we propose One-step Deshadow Diffusion via Reward guidance (ODDR), a new framework that achieves efficient and high-fidelity shadow removal without relying on real-world paired supervision. Our method begins with One-step Deshadow Diffusion (ODD), a baseline model trained on synthetic shadow data for efficient one-step shadow-free reconstruction. We further adapt ODD into ODDR using ShadowReward. In contrast to traditional, annotation-heavy approaches, ShadowReward is the first reward model for shadow removal trained entirely without human annotation. It learns to mimic human perceptual judgments by ranking synthetically generated images with controlled degradations, such as texture distortion and boundary artifacts. This reward-guided fine-tuning enables ODDR to close the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Extensive experiments show that ODD achieves strong performance without relying on real-world paired supervision, and ODDR further improves the results, narrowing the gap to fully supervised methods trained on real-world paired data while maintaining higher computational efficiency as a single-step model.

</details>


### [94] [STAGE: Subspace-Targeted Affine Generative Erasure for Text-to-3D Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01302)
*Karol Dziekan,Przemysław Spurek,Dawid Malarz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STAGE is a training-free, closed-form framework for erasing target concepts (shape, material, object) in native text-to-3D generators by applying stage-aware editing to either structural stage, appearance stage, or both, achieving a composite score of 66.7 vs 53.2 for the best baseline on TRELLIS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing closed-form concept erasure methods were designed for 2D image diffusion and assume a single generative pathway where geometry and texture are edited together. However, native 3D generators synthesize structured 3D representations directly rather than by lifting 2D samples, violating this assumption. Shape and object concepts must be erased in the structural stage while material concepts must be erased in the appearance stage, requiring a stage-aware editing approach.

Method: STAGE formulates concept erasure in native text-to-3D as a stage-aware editing problem. It confines each edit to the low-dimensional subspace spanned by the differences between erase and anchor embeddings. The method relaxes the norm-preserving (orthogonal) constraint of prior editors into a least-squares affine correction that maps target activations onto safe anchors subject to a penalty on the displacement of retained prompts. The correction can be applied to the structural stage, the appearance stage, or both.

Result: On TRELLIS (the standard open native 3D generator), across 15 shape, material, and object concepts, STAGE achieves a composite score of 66.7, versus 53.2 for the strongest adapted baseline. The composite score balances forgetting the target concept against preserving everything else, aggregating CLIP-based semantic and physical metrics.

Conclusion: The stage at which an edit must be applied is determined by concept type - shape and object concepts require editing in the structural stage while material concepts require editing in the appearance stage. STAGE successfully handles this distinction, significantly outperforming prior adapted methods on native 3D generators.

Abstract: Concept erasure suppresses a target concept while preserving behavior on unrelated inputs. Existing closed-form methods were designed for 2D image diffusion and assume a single generative pathway, so one edit must cover geometry and texture at once. Native 3D generators, which synthesize structured 3D representations directly rather than by lifting 2D samples, violate this assumption. We show that shape and object concepts must be erased in the structural stage of the pipeline and material concepts in the appearance stage. We therefore formulate erasure in native text-to-3D as a stage-aware editing problem and introduce STAGE, a training-free, closed-form framework. STAGE confines each edit to the low-dimensional subspace spanned by the differences between erase and anchor embeddings, and relaxes the norm-preserving (orthogonal) constraint of prior editors into a least-squares affine correction that maps target activations onto safe anchors subject to a penalty on the displacement of retained prompts. The correction applies to the structural stage, the appearance stage, or both. We find that the stage an edit must reach is determined by concept type. On TRELLIS, the standard open native 3D generator, across 15 shape, material, and object concepts, STAGE reaches 66.7 on a composite score that balances forgetting the target concept against preserving everything else, aggregating CLIP-based semantic and physical metrics, versus 53.2 for the strongest adapted baseline.
  Code: https://github.com/gmum/STAGE/
  Project Page https://gmum.github.io/STAGE/

</details>


### [95] [ARROW: Arbitrary Reconstruction and Tracking of 4D Observations in the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01314)
*Ilya Fradlin,Christian Schmidt,Jens Piekenbrinck,Karim Knaebel,Gonzalo Martin Garcia,Bastian Leibe*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ARROW is a feed-forward model that unifies 3D reconstruction and 3D point tracking from arbitrary image sets (moving camera, multiple video streams, or images at different times). It uses a novel order-invariant querying approach for associating queries with observations across arbitrary inputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic scenes captured from different viewpoints, times, and visibility changes require establishing correspondence. Existing methods struggle to unify 3D reconstruction and 3D point tracking across these diverse input types.

Method: 1) Novel order-invariant querying approach enabling association of queries with observations across arbitrary inputs; 2) Training with diverse input sets improves generalization to multiple tasks including multi-view tracking.

Result: State-of-the-art 3D tracking on WorldTrack and TAPVid-3D; outperforms dedicated multi-view trackers on RGB-only MVTracker benchmark; remains competitive in 3D reconstruction tasks.

Conclusion: A unified feed-forward model can achieve superior performance across multiple tasks (3D reconstruction and tracking) when trained with diverse input sets, demonstrating strong generalization capabilities.

Abstract: Dynamic scenes may be captured by a moving camera, multiple video streams, or images taken at different times. These observations reveal complementary aspects of scene geometry and motion, yet bringing them together requires establishing correspondence across viewpoints, capture times, and visibility changes. We introduce ARROW, a feed-forward model that unifies 3D reconstruction and 3D point tracking from arbitrary image sets. At its core is a novel order-invariant querying approach, which allows the association of queries with observations across arbitrary inputs. We show that exposing the model to more diverse sets of inputs during training results in improved task performance. Moreover, the resulting model is capable of generalization to a wider range of tasks including multi-view tracking. Trained with this strategy, ARROW establishes a new state of the art in 3D tracking on WorldTrack and TAPVid-3D and outperforms dedicated multi-view trackers on an adapted RGB-only MVTracker benchmark, while remaining competitive across 3D reconstruction tasks. Code and weights are publicly available.

</details>


### [96] [CLASP: Continual Low-rank Adapters for Spatially Placed Concepts from One Hypernetwork](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01331)
*Wojciech Gromski,Patryk Krukowski,Jan Miksa,Maciej Zieba,Przemysław Spurek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A rehearsal-free method for continual personalization of text-to-image diffusion models using a single fixed-size hypernetwork that generates concept-specific adaptations without expanding model parameters, while also integrating spatial control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual personalization methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting or require storing additional per-concept parameters that grow with the concept stream, limiting scalability to long sequences of tasks.

Method: A fixed-size hypernetwork that dynamically produces concept-specific adaptations for a frozen diffusion model, preserving previously learned concepts without model expansion. The framework integrates spatial control into personalization without additional per-concept components.

Result: Strong retention of previously learned concepts and reliable spatial grounding, matching or improving upon existing methods while maintaining parameter footprint independent of the number of learned concepts.

Conclusion: The proposed approach enables scalable continual personalization with a constant parameter footprint (aside from compact concept representations), effectively balancing new concept acquisition with retention of previously learned concepts.

Abstract: Continual personalization of text-to-image diffusion models requires sequentially acquiring new concepts while retaining previously learned ones. However, existing methods either suffer from catastrophic forgetting or rely on storing additional concept-specific parameters and spatial components, causing their parameter footprint to grow with the concept stream. This limits their ability to scale to long sequences of personalization tasks. We propose a rehearsal-free approach that uses a single fixed-size hypernetwork to continually personalize a frozen diffusion model. Instead of expanding the model as new concepts are acquired, the hypernetwork dynamically produces the concept-specific adaptations required for personalization while preserving previously learned concepts. Our framework further integrates spatial control into the personalization process, allowing users to specify where a personalized concept should appear without introducing additional per-concept components. This formulation enables continual personalization with a parameter footprint that remains independent of the number of learned concepts, aside from compact concept representations. Experiments demonstrate strong retention of previously learned concepts and reliable spatial grounding, matching or improving upon existing methods while scaling effectively to long streams of personalization tasks.

</details>


### [97] [MMVistaReason: Toward Open-Data and Post-Training Recipes for Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01352)
*Juekai Lin,Honglin Lin,Yuqian Yuan,Xiaolong Wu,Jie Cao,Liang Liang,Yunqi Cao,Yun Zhu,Wenqiao Zhang,Lijun Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MMVistaReason (MVR) is a post-training recipe for open multimodal reasoning models that addresses challenges in data quality, supervision construction, difficulty balancing, and cross-domain interference through three components: broader capability coverage across Analytical and Real-World reasoning groups, efficient SFT/RL data construction with staged cleaning and difficulty-aware teacher distillation, and specialize-then-integrate training via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). The method achieves 72.8 average score on 15 benchmarks with a 4B model, outperforming larger models while using fewer training samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open multimodal reasoning models face challenges in post-training due to: (1) uneven data quality, (2) inefficient supervision construction, (3) imbalanced difficulty, and (4) cross-domain interference. The authors aim to create a systematic, scalable approach to reliable multimodal reasoning using open data.

Method: Three-component approach: (1) Capability coverage across Analytical (structured reasoning) and Real-World (visual perception/spatial grounding) reasoning groups; (2) Efficient data construction via staged cleaning/annotation for SFT data (MVR-SFT-528K) using difficulty-aware cascaded teacher distillation and answer-likelihood-based trajectory selection, and scale-specific frontier filtering for RL data (MVR-RL-63K); (3) Specialize-then-integrate training: train complementary RL experts then consolidate via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD).

Result: MVR-4B achieves 72.8 average score on 15 multimodal benchmarks, outperforming Qwen3.5-9B (Instruct) and MMFineReason-8B with ~70% fewer samples. MVR-9B achieves 74.4 average, surpassing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Instruct). Key findings: smaller models benefit more from selected supervision; larger models are robust to trajectory variation and mixed-domain interference; mixed-domain RL causes benchmark-level negative transfer; MOPD provides consistent capability integration with KL direction varying across model scales.

Conclusion: Systematic open-data construction and capacity-aware post-training provide a practical and scalable path toward reliable multimodal reasoning. The capacity-dependent interaction between supervision difficulty, trajectory quality, and model capacity is a key finding, suggesting different training strategies for different model scales.

Abstract: Open multimodal reasoning models have benefited from large-scale reasoning supervision, yet reliable post-training remains challenging due to uneven data quality, inefficient supervision construction, imbalanced difficulty, and cross-domain interference. We introduce MMVistaReason (MVR), an open-data post-training recipe with three components: (1) broader capability coverage across complementary Analytical and Real-World reasoning groups, emphasizing structured reasoning versus visual perception and spatial grounding; (2) efficient SFT and RL data construction, standardizing heterogeneous open data through staged cleaning and annotation, combining difficulty-aware cascaded teacher distillation with answer-likelihood-based trajectory selection to construct MVR-SFT-528K, and applying scale-specific frontier filtering for MVR-RL-63K; and (3) specialize-then-integrate training, which trains complementary RL experts and consolidates their capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Our analyses reveal a capacity-dependent interaction between supervision difficulty, trajectory quality, and model capacity: smaller students benefit more from selected supervision, while larger students are robust to trajectory variation and mixed-domain interference. Mixed-domain RL introduces benchmark-level negative transfer, whereas MOPD provides consistent capability integration, with the preferred KL direction varying across model scales. Across 15 multimodal benchmarks, MVR-4B achieves an average score of 72.8, outperforming Qwen3.5-9B (Instruct) and MMFineReason-8B while using about 70% fewer samples than MMFineReason. Scaling to 9B improves the average to 74.4, surpassing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Instruct). Overall, MMVistaReason demonstrates that systematic open-data construction and capacity-aware post-training provide a practical and scalable path toward reliable multimodal reasoning.

</details>


### [98] [Smoother Flow Matching via Contrastive Trajectory Repulsion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01408)
*Ziqi Jiang,Zhenqi He,Long Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CoFlow introduces contrastive learning into Flow Matching to explicitly repel trajectories during training, reducing trajectory crossings that cause high local Lipschitz constants in velocity fields. It formulates a repulsive drift term from SDE perspective and derives an equivalent stochastic interpolant formulation, significantly improving FID in few-step inference on ImageNet 256x256 with no added training overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Trajectory crossing is a critical bottleneck in Flow Matching (FM). Previous works address it indirectly through post-hoc distillation or endpoint coupling without explicitly regulating intermediate trajectories. Crossing points induce high local Lipschitz constants in the target velocity field, causing two problems: (1) neural networks struggle to fit high-frequency signals due to spectral bias, and (2) drastic velocity variations lead to severe numerical integration errors in few-step inference.

Method: CoFlow introduces contrastive learning paradigm into FM to explicitly repel trajectories during training. From a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) perspective, a repulsive drift term is injected to actively guide the forward process of positive samples away from negative trajectories, effectively reducing local Lipschitz constants. An equivalent stochastic interpolant formulation is derived, providing a simple and tractable design space to control the influence of negative samples.

Result: On ImageNet 256x256, CoFlow significantly reduces FID compared to standard FM in few-step inference (e.g., 20 steps), with no added training overhead.

Conclusion: CoFlow effectively reduces local Lipschitz constants of the velocity field through contrastive learning, improving generation quality in few-step inference without additional computational overhead.

Abstract: Trajectory crossing remains a critical bottleneck in Flow Matching (FM), and previous works typically view these crossings from a theoretical optimization perspective causing velocity averaging. They attempt to address it indirectly by post-hoc distillation or endpoint coupling, without explicitly regulating the intermediate trajectories. In this paper, we introduce a new network learning perspective: crossing points inherently induce large local Lipschitz constants in the target velocity field, leading to two drawbacks. First, high Lipschitz constants correspond to high-frequency signals in the velocity field that neural networks struggle to fit due to spectral bias. Second, they also imply drastic velocity variations, leading to severe numerical integration errors in few-step inference. To alleviate this, we propose CoFlow, a framework that introduces the contrastive learning paradigm into FM to explicitly repel trajectories during training, thereby lowering the local Lipschitz constants of the velocity field. Specifically, we formulate CoFlow from a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) perspective by injecting a repulsive drift term. This drift actively guides the forward process of positive samples away from negative trajectories, effectively reducing the local Lipschitz constant. Furthermore, we derive an equivalent stochastic interpolant formulation from this SDE, providing a simple and tractable design space to control the influence of negative samples. Extensive experiments on ImageNet 256x256 demonstrate that CoFlow significantly reduces FID compared to standard FM in few-step inference (e.g., 20 steps), with no added training overhead. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/HKUST-LongGroup/CoFlow

</details>


### [99] [Localisation-Aware Uncertainty for Pretrained Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01409)
*Charmaine Barker,Daniel Bethell,Simos Gerasimou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GRACE is a lightweight post-hoc uncertainty estimation method for object detectors that works without retraining or modifying the base detector. It uses saliency-guided curriculum learning to train an evidential meta-model that estimates uncertainty for each predicted bounding box by combining localization error, modification level, and prediction instability signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying object detectors in real-world scenarios faces challenges from distribution shift and adversarial attacks. Existing uncertainty estimation methods require detector retraining, architectural modifications, or multiple inferences, which are often infeasible or computationally expensive. There is a need for a lightweight, post-hoc approach that can identify when object localizations should be considered uncertain without modifying the base detector.

Method: The proposed GRACE method works in three key stages: (1) Automatic identification of localization-relevant features from the frozen detector, (2) Saliency-guided modification to construct a progressively challenging curriculum, (3) Training an evidential meta-model using detection-level targets combining localization error, modification level, and prediction instability. The method requires no changes to the detector architecture and preserves original localization outputs.

Result: GRACE achieves up to 22% relative improvement in TP-FP AUROC compared to the strongest comparator under adversarial attacks, while maintaining in-distribution detection performance. The method is effective across different adversarial attack strengths.

Conclusion: The paper presents a practical solution for uncertainty estimation in object detection that avoids expensive retraining or architectural changes. By using a post-hoc meta-model with curriculum learning, GRACE can reliably identify uncertain detections under distribution shift and adversarial conditions, making it suitable for deployment in real-world safety-critical applications.

Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for deploying object detectors when distribution/covariate shift and adversarial attacks may occur. Existing approaches often require detector retraining, architectural modification, or repeated inference, which may be infeasible or incur significant overheads. We introduce a lightweight post-hoc evidential meta-model that learns when object localisations should be considered uncertain while keeping the base detector frozen. Our approach automatically identifies localisation-relevant features and uses saliency-guided modification to construct an increasingly challenging curriculum. Detection-level targets combine localisation error, modification level, and prediction instability to guide an evidential meta-model to estimate uncertainty for each predicted bounding box. Our approach requires no changes to the detector and preserves its original localisation outputs. Across adversarial attacks and evaluated strengths, GRACE improves TP-FP AUROC by 22% relative to the strongest comparator in some cases while maintaining in-distribution detection performance.

</details>


### [100] [MWOP: Modality-aware Width-wise Operation Pruning for Efficient MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01434)
*Xudong Wang,Hao Wu,Haozhe Hu,Peiran Yin,Xinghao Chen,Yunpu Ma,Wei Zhang,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MWOP is a fine-grained operation pruning method for multimodal LLMs that independently prunes attention paths (V2V, T2V, T2T) and FFN channels for visual and textual inputs, achieving 1.6× prefill speedup with 99.7% performance retention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs incur high inference costs when processing long visual-textual sequences. Existing operation compression methods treat attention heads and FFN channels as unified units, ignoring finer-grained redundancy across modality-interaction paths and visual/textual executions.

Method: MWOP uses first-order Taylor criterion to independently prune V2V, T2V, and T2T attention paths within each layer, and separately selects FFN channels for visual and textual inputs. FFN importance is re-evaluated after attention pruning, followed by LoRA-based recovery training. Implementation includes path-sparse Triton attention kernels and compact visual-side FFN execution.

Result: On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, MWOP achieves 1.6× prefill speedup with 99.7% average performance retention across 12 benchmarks. Combined with token compression methods, it increases prefill speedups from 2.0× and 1.9× to 2.9× and 2.7× respectively. Results on Qwen2.5-VL-7B demonstrate cross-architecture applicability.

Conclusion: MWOP preserves token sequence while reducing attention and FFN computation, making it complementary to token compression. It effectively exploits fine-grained redundancy across modality interactions and achieves significant speedups without substantial performance degradation.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) incur substantial inference costs when processing long visual-textual sequences. While existing operation compression methods exploit modality-level redundancy, they largely treat computation within attention heads and shared feed-forward network (FFN) channels as unified units, leaving finer-grained redundancy underexplored. We find that redundancy varies both across modality-interaction paths within the same attention head and across visual and textual executions of the same FFN channel. Based on these findings, we propose Modality-aware Width-wise Operation Pruning (MWOP), which independently prunes visual-to-visual (V2V), text-to-visual (T2V), and text-to-text (T2T) attention paths within each layer, and separately selects FFN channels for visual and textual inputs. A first-order Taylor criterion guides the pruning process, with FFN importance re-evaluated after attention pruning and LoRA-based recovery training. To translate the resulting fine-grained sparsity into practical acceleration, we further develop path-sparse Triton attention kernels and compact visual-side FFN execution. MWOP preserves the token sequence while reducing attention and FFN computation, making it complementary to token compression and enabling simultaneous reduction of sequence length and per-token computation. On LLaVA-OneVision-7B, MWOP alone achieves a $1.6\times$ prefill speedup with 99.7\% average performance retention across 12 benchmarks. Combined with two representative token compression methods, it further increases their prefill speedups from $2.0\times$ and $1.9\times$ to $2.9\times$ and $2.7\times$, respectively. Results on Qwen2.5-VL-7B further demonstrate its applicability across architectures. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/MWOP.

</details>


### [101] [The Impact of Processing Parameters on High-Accuracy Measurements in UAV Photogrammetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01438)
*Paweł Ćwiąkała,Edyta Puniach,Elżbieta Pastucha,Wojciech Gruszczyński*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This study systematically evaluates 768 processing variants of UAV photogrammetry workflows to assess how Bundle Block Adjustment parameter settings affect 3D accuracy and deformation measurements. Results show RMSE ranges from 16mm to 303mm, with GCP number, camera calibration corrections, and PPK GNSS being the most influential factors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While UAV photogrammetry is increasingly used for high-accuracy applications like landslide monitoring and microrelief transformation, the influence of processing workflow parameters (particularly Bundle Block Adjustment settings) remains insufficiently explored. This study addresses this gap with a large-scale, practice-oriented assessment.

Method: Systematic full-factorial evaluation of 768 processing variants applied to ten UAV datasets collected over 1.5 years in a 220 ha study area. Eight key parameters were analyzed, including the number of ground control points, camera calibration corrections, and Post-Processing Kinematic GNSS methods.

Result: The best variant achieved RMSE of 16mm while the weakest reached 303mm. Most influential factors were: (1) number of GCPs, (2) additional camera calibration corrections, and (3) PPK GNSS method for camera projection center coordinates. Random displacement errors remained stable (RMSE ~6-7mm), but systematic errors were reduced by over half in all axes. Vertical median absolute error decreased from 14mm to 7mm in optimized vs. baseline configuration.

Conclusion: This study provides the first large-scale assessment of how processing parameter selection shapes accuracy of both photogrammetric products and deformation indices. The results offer actionable guidance for developing more robust and repeatable UAV photogrammetry workflows for high-precision monitoring applications.

Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry is increasingly used in applications requiring high accuracy, such as determining ground surface changes caused by landslides, mining, or microrelief transformation. While acquisition strategies have been widely studied, the influence of the processing workflow-particularly Bundle Block Adjustment parameter settings-remains insufficiently explored. This study addresses this gap through a systematic, full-factorial evaluation of 768 processing variants applied to ten UAV datasets collected over 1.5 years in a 220 ha study area. Eight key parameters were analysed. The results show substantial variability in final 3D accuracy: the best performing variant achieved a root mean square error (RMSE) of 16 mm, whereas the weakest reached 303 mm. The most influential factors were the number of ground control points, the application of additional camera calibration corrections, and the use of the Post-Processing Kinematic GNSS method for determining camera projection center coordinates. The study also evaluates how workflow optimization affects the accuracy of displacement, tilt changes, and horizontal strain determination. While random displacement errors remained stable (RMSE of ~6-7 mm), systematic errors were significantly reduced by over half in all axes, with vertical median absolute error decreasing from 14 mm to 7 mm in the optimized configuration compared to the baseline previously used by the authors. This study provides the first large-scale, practice-oriented assessment of how processing parameter selection shapes the accuracy of both photogrammetric products and deformation indices determination. The results offer actionable guidance for developing more robust and repeatable UAV photogrammetry workflows tailored to high-precision monitoring.

</details>


### [102] [Uncertainty-Guided Handshake: Efficient Human-in-the-Loop Refinement for Surgical-Grade Glioma Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01452)
*Samuel Hart,Ahmad Yahya,Ahmed Karam Eldaly*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a Hybrid Structural-Aleatoric Human-in-the-Loop framework for glioma segmentation that uses Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) uncertainty and hierarchical topological filtering to detect and correct structural failures in automated medical image segmentation, achieving sub-2.0 mm HD95 and significantly improving tumor boundary accuracy with minimal human intervention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-of-the-art automated medical image segmentation models suffer from localized, catastrophic failures that preclude safe clinical deployment. Existing interactive segmentation frameworks require prohibitive cognitive and temporal workloads. The authors aimed to bridge the gap between automated baseline performance and surgical-grade precision.

Method: The framework extracts voxel-wise Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) uncertainty and applies hierarchical topological filtering to proactively isolate high-risk structural anomalies. Evaluation was performed on a challenging out-of-distribution clinical stress-test cohort (N = 362) under a simulated Human Oracle.

Result: The framework improved Whole Tumor (WT) Dice from 0.891 to 0.914 and reduced HD95 from 5.82 mm to 4.76 mm. For Tumor Core, mean HD95 was reduced from 17.96 mm to 14.83 mm, with TC Dice improving to 0.356. These improvements were achieved with a median interactive workload of just 11.3% of the target volume.

Conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates a highly Pareto-efficient pathway for safely deploying clinical AI in neuro-oncology, achieving surgical-grade precision while requiring minimal human oversight. The method effectively rescues severe boundary failures with limited interactive workload, representing a promising approach for clinical AI deployment.

Abstract: While state-of-the-art automated models for medical image segmentation achieve high mean performance, they frequently suffer from localized, catastrophic failures that preclude safe clinical deployment, particularly in neuro-oncology. Interactive segmentation frameworks mitigate this by incorporating human oversight, but traditionally impose prohibitive cognitive and temporal workloads by requiring clinicians to manually search for errors. In this project, we present an efficient, Hybrid Structural-Aleatoric Human-in-the-Loop framework for glioma segmentation that bridges the gap between automated baseline performance and surgical-grade precision, achieving sub-2.0 mm HD95 on curated benchmarks while providing safety-net routing for structural failures across real-world clinical data. By extracting voxel-wise Test-Time Augmentation (TTA) uncertainty and applying hierarchical topological filtering, our method proactively isolates high-risk structural anomalies. We comprehensively evaluated our approach on a challenging out-of-distribution clinical stress-test cohort (N = 362). Operating under a simulated Human Oracle, the framework improved the Whole Tumor (WT) Dice score from 0.891 to 0.914 and reduced the 95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95) from 5.82 mm to 4.76 mm. Critically for surgical safety, the system rescued severe boundary failures in the Tumor Core, reducing mean HD95 from 17.96 mm to 14.83 mm (improving absolute TC Dice to 0.356). These spatial rescues were achieved while demanding a median interactive workload of just 11.3% of the target volume. Acknowledging this as a simulated upper bound lacking real-world cognitive friction, the framework nevertheless demonstrates a highly Pareto-efficient pathway for safely deploying clinical AI.

</details>


### [103] [FiVOS: A Fish Segmentation Algorithm Based on Interactive Video Object Segmentation and Filter Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01480)
*Yuqing Duan,Song Zhang,Shili Zhao,Daoliang Li,Ran Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes FiVOS, an improved interactive video object segmentation method specifically designed for fish behavior monitoring in aquaculture. The method addresses limitations of existing deep learning approaches by using a mask block filter with rule-based thresholding and serialized noise filters to detect, correct, and eliminate erroneous propagated masks. Two fish-specific datasets were constructed to address data scarcity. FiVOS achieves state-of-the-art performance in fish video segmentation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With the expansion of aquaculture, precise fish behavior monitoring is critical for improving farming efficiency. Existing deep learning-based video segmentation methods overlook dynamic correlations between video frames. While Interactive Video Object Segmentation (IVOS) offers high-precision segmentation with minimal user effort, its application in aquaculture is limited due to data scarcity, error accumulation, and mask loss over long sequence propagation caused by high intra-class similarity among fish.

Method: FiVOS employs two key components: (1) a mask block filter enabling early detection and correction of erroneous propagated mask blocks, with filtering accuracy enhanced through a rule-based thresholding approach; and (2) serialized noise filters to further eliminate erroneous mask noise, improving model robustness. Two fish-specific datasets were constructed to address the data scarcity issue in aquaculture scenarios.

Result: Experimental results demonstrate that FiVOS achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in fish video segmentation tasks, providing robust technical support for fish behavior research.

Conclusion: The proposed FiVOS method successfully addresses the challenges of error accumulation and mask loss in fish video segmentation, offering a reliable tool for fish behavior monitoring in aquaculture environments. Its SOTA performance validates the effectiveness of the mask block filter and serialized noise filters approach.

Abstract: With the continuous expansion of aquaculture, precise and efficient monitoring of fish behavior has become increasingly critical for improving farming efficiency and reducing economic losses. In particular, with the ongoing enhancement of computational capabilities in deep learning models, vision-based fish segmentation methods are garnering growing attention. By analyzing video segmentation results, fish behavior can be effectively tracked, thereby providing reliable data support for the precise regulation of aquaculture environments. However, existing deep learning-based video segmentation methods for aquaculture scenarios often overlook the dynamic correlations between video frames. In contrast, Interactive Video Object Segmentation (IVOS) employs an interaction-propagation scheme to achieve high-precision segmentation while minimizing user effort, thereby enhancing monitoring efficiency. Yet, IVOS applications in aquaculture remain limited due to data scarcity, and are susceptible to error accumulation and mask loss over long sequence propagation due to high intra-class similarity. In response, this paper proposes an improved interactive video object segmentation method (FiVOS) and constructs two fish-specific datasets. FiVOS utilizes a mask block filter to enable early detection and correction of erroneous propagated mask blocks, enhancing filtering accuracy through a rule-based thresholding approach. Additionally, it serializes noise filters to further eliminate erroneous mask noise, thereby improving model robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that FiVOS achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in fish video segmentation tasks, providing robust technical support for fish behavior research.

</details>


### [104] [SALD: Self-Referenced Advantage Learning for Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01496)
*Aryan Das,Surjo Dey,Koushik Biswas,Swalpa Kumar Roy,Moloud Abdar,Arnab Bhattacharya,Vinay Kumar Verma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SALD introduces a self-referenced training framework for diffusion models that generates training signals by comparing predictions at two different noise levels (easy lower-noise path vs. harder higher-noise path) using the same model, without requiring external teacher networks or additional parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing language model adaptation uses teacher networks driven by student parameters to obtain training signals. This work investigates whether diffusion models can identify self-referenced training signals without external demonstrations or teacher networks, based on the "internal-reference principle."

Method: SALD evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels using the same model. The lower-noise path (easier) provides a reference without gradient tracking, while the higher-noise path (harder) provides the training gradient. The difference between two path errors adapts the hard-path objective. Three components: (1) Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts relative error into differentiable sample-level weights; (2) Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) accumulates relative difficulty across training to adapt future gap between noise levels; (3) Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) compares residual power spectra to construct frequency-derived latent-element weights.

Result: Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in generation quality. Component-wise ablations quantify contributions of proposed components.

Conclusion: SALD achieves improved generation quality without external teacher networks, additional trainable parameters, or modifications to inference procedures. All components share a single set of model parameters, making it a parameter-efficient self-training approach for diffusion models.

Abstract: Recent work on language-model adaptation has shown that single models can obtain informative training signals by evaluating their behavior in demonstrationor feedback-augmented contexts, with the help of a teacher network, which is driven by the student's learned parameters. Inspired by this internal-reference principle, we investigate how diffusion models can identify self-referenced training signals without external demonstrations or teacher networks. We introduce SALD, a self-referenced training framework that evaluates each image-caption pair at two noise levels using the same model. The easier, lower-noise path is evaluated without gradient tracking to provide a reference, while the harder, higher-noise path provides the training gradient. Rather than directly distilling the easy-path prediction, SALD uses the difference between two path errors to adapt the hardpath objective. The proposed Advantage-Guided Diffusion (AGD) converts this relative error into a differentiable sample-level weight. Temporal Advantage Memory (TAM) accumulates relative difficulty across training and adapts the future gap between the two noise levels. Spectral Advantage Decomposition (SAD) further compares the residual power spectra of the two paths and constructs a differentiable, frequency-derived latent-element weight. All components share a single set of model parameters, requiring neither an external teacher network nor additional trainable parameters during training or inference, and no modification to the inference procedure. Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in generation quality, while component-wise ablations quantify the contributions of the proposed components.

</details>


### [105] [VTR-Bench: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Text Rendering in Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01499)
*Yu Huang,Jungang Li,Zhiyuan Wang,Yonghua Hei,Song Dai,Jiayu Yang,Deyuan Liu,Xiang Zheng,Xiaoshuang Shi,Hao Cheng,Kaidi Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VTR-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating visual text rendering in AI-generated videos. It addresses the overlooked problem that video generation models often produce visually realistic videos but fail to accurately render text within the scene. The benchmark includes 300 prompts across 5 scenarios and introduces a Keyframe-Guided Agentic Framework for iterative refinement. Testing 11 state-of-the-art models reveals widespread difficulties, with the best model achieving a 25% word error rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing video generation benchmarks focus on visual quality, aesthetic appeal, and physical plausibility, but neglect text rendering accuracy. Since text is essential for conveying information in everyday scenes (signs, advertisements, labels), a generated video may look realistic but contain incorrect or illegible text, limiting practical applicability.

Method: 1) VTR-Bench: 300 prompts across 5 scenario categories (advertisements, scientific videos, etc.) with concrete application contexts. 2) Automated evaluation pipeline with human alignment: assesses text fidelity through carrier-specific transcription and scene/motion requirements through prompt-specific chain-of-query. 3) Keyframe-Guided Agentic Framework: Director agent coordinates image and video generation with visual evaluation, guiding iterative refinement and candidate selection through visual feedback.

Result: Experiments on 11 state-of-the-art video generation models reveal widespread difficulties in accurately rendering scene text. The best-performing model records an overall word error rate (WER) of 0.250 (25% error rate), indicating significant challenges across all models tested.

Conclusion: Visual text rendering is a key challenge for current video generation models. The VTR-Bench benchmark and Keyframe-Guided Agentic Framework provide practical tools for systematic evaluation and improvement. This work highlights the need for future research to address text rendering as a critical dimension of video generation quality.

Abstract: Recent video generation models can produce highly realistic videos from natural language instructions, with visual quality approaching cinematic standards. Existing evaluation benchmarks, however, predominantly assess visual quality, aesthetic appeal and physical plausibility, while paying limited attention to text, an essential medium for conveying information in everyday scenes. A generated video may appear visually compelling and feature lifelike subjects, yet still render the text within the scene incorrectly. To address this overlooked dimension, we introduce \textbf{VTR-Bench}, a systematic benchmark for evaluating the \textbf{V}isual \textbf{T}ext \textbf{R}endering capabilities of video generation models. VTR-Bench situates text within concrete application scenarios, such as advertisements and scientific videos, with 300 carefully constructed prompts spanning five scenario categories. We develop an automated evaluation pipeline with human alignments that separately assesses text fidelity through carrier-specific transcription and scene and motion requirements through a prompt-specific chain of query. Beyond evaluation, we introduce a \textbf{Keyframe-Guided Agentic Framework} in which a Director agent coordinates image and video generation with visual evaluation, guiding iterative refinement and candidate selection through visual feedback. Experiments on 11 state-of-the-art models reveal widespread difficulties in accurately rendering scene text, with the best-performing model recording an overall word error rate (WER) of 0.250. We further analyze text rendering failures to characterize the challenges faced by current video generation models. These findings highlight visual text rendering as a key challenge for video generation and demonstrate a practical path toward improvement. Code is available at https://github.com/hardenyu21/VTR-Bench.

</details>


### [106] [FedCKA: Representation-Guided Layer Personalization for Federated 3D Perception Across Driving Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01510)
*Jolle Verhoog,Ali Burak Ünal,Holger Caesar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FedCKA is a federated learning approach for 3D object detection in autonomous vehicles that uses Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to dynamically handle the trade-off between global model consensus and local client personalization. It computes layer-wise feature similarities to create client-specific aggregation masks, selectively sharing representation-consistent layers while keeping client-specific layers local.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robust 3D perception in intelligent vehicles is needed under domain shifts (time, location, weather), but training data is scarce in some environments. While federated learning enables privacy-preserving collaborative training, traditional approaches rely on a single global model that struggles with heterogeneous data distributions across clients. Existing personalization methods use fixed layer partitions or ratios, limiting adaptation to client-specific divergence.

Method: FedCKA computes layer-wise feature similarities between local client models and the global consensus model during training using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). These similarity scores are converted into client-specific aggregation masks that selectively share representation-consistent layers while preserving client-specific adaptation.

Result: FedCKA outperforms established federated baselines (FedBN, FedRep, FedSelect) on a unified multi-domain benchmark based on nuScenes, improving average NDS (NuScenes Detection Score) by 7 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

Conclusion: FedCKA offers a promising direction for robust federated 3D perception across domain shifts in location, weather, and illumination, providing both a comparative benchmark and a flexible approach to handle the personalization-globalization trade-off in heterogeneous federated learning.

Abstract: Robust perception in intelligent vehicles demands 3D object detectors that remain dependable under domain shifts, such as changes in time of day, location, or weather. However, due to costly annotation and rare shifts, some environments lack sufficient data to train a standalone detector. Federated learning offers a privacy-preserving framework for collaborative model training, enabling clients to benefit from shared learning across diverse environments. Yet, this framework traditionally relies on a single global consensus model, which struggles to perform across heterogeneous local data distributions. Local conditions are better captured by adapting a subset of the model, but many personalization approaches rely on predefined layer partitions or fixed personalization ratios, thereby limiting adaptation to client-specific divergence. To reduce this rigidity, we propose FedCKA, a Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)-based strategy that dynamically handles the personalization-globalization trade-off. Specifically, FedCKA computes layer-wise feature similarities between local client models and the global consensus model during training. By converting layer-wise similarity scores into client-specific aggregation masks, FedCKA selectively shares representation-consistent layers. Evaluation on a unified multi-domain benchmark based on nuScenes shows that FedCKA outperforms established federated baselines, including FedBN, FedRep, and FedSelect, improving average NDS by 7 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The findings offer both a comparative benchmark and a promising direction for robust federated 3D perception across shifts in location, weather, and illumination. Code is available at https://github.com/j-verhoog/FedCKA.

</details>


### [107] [VoxelSynth3D: Interpretable Volumetric Image-Domain Metal Artifact Reduction with a Paired Synthetic CLINIC-Metal Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01512)
*Amritesh Banerjee,Abdul Basit,Renil Renji Joseph,Nouhaila Innan,Muhammad Shafique*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VoxelSynth3D is a training-free 3D image-domain framework for reducing metal artifacts in postoperative musculoskeletal CT scans. It combines support masking, normalized tissue synthesis, deviation gating, and restricted edge refinement to correct metal-induced artifacts while preserving implant voxels. The method was evaluated on a synthetic dataset (Synthetic CLINIC-Metal) and 75 real cases, showing RMSE reduction from 801.48 to 786.18 HU.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metal artifacts in postoperative musculoskeletal CT obscure bone-implant and adjacent soft-tissue interfaces, making clinical assessment difficult. Existing metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods often require unavailable raw projections or learned models that may not generalize across different scanners and implants. This work aims to develop a training-free, case-consistent method that works directly on reconstructed CT volumes without these limitations.

Method: VoxelSynth3D combines four key techniques: (1) support masking to identify implant voxels, (2) normalized tissue synthesis for artifact-free tissue estimation, (3) deviation gating to control correction strength, and (4) restricted edge refinement to preserve structural integrity. The framework operates on reconstructed CT without requiring raw projections or training data. Evaluation was performed on Synthetic CLINIC-Metal (constructed from no-metal CTPelvic1K volumes with clean targets, metal/artifact masks, fixed seeds, and patient-level splits) and 75 unpaired real metal cases for qualitative evaluation.

Result: On 40 held-out cases, VoxelSynth3D reduced RMSE from 801.48 to 786.18 HU, achieving a paired gain of 15.30 HU (95% CI 11.68-19.23). The method improved every case and exceeded the evaluated 3D Gaussian smoother by 13.58 HU. Clean-edge agreement decreased next to metal but exceeded input beyond 5 mm. Spacing-aware sensitivity analysis retained aggregate broad-region improvement and identified near-metal calibration as a target for future improvement.

Conclusion: VoxelSynth3D provides case-consistent within-distribution tissue-error reduction with a localized structural tradeoff. The training-free approach offers better generalization potential across different scanners and implants compared to learned methods. The method achieves consistent improvement across all tested cases while maintaining artifact reduction in regions beyond 5 mm from metal implants.

Abstract: Metal artifacts in postoperative musculoskeletal CT obscure bone-implant and adjacent soft-tissue interfaces. Many metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods require unavailable raw projections or learned models that may shift across scanners and implants. We present VoxelSynth3D, a training-free 3D image-domain framework for reconstructed CT. The framework combines support masking, normalized tissue synthesis, deviation gating, and restricted edge refinement. Detected implant voxels are preserved in the output, while correction targets metal-induced artifacts in the surrounding tissue. We also construct Synthetic CLINIC-Metal, a controlled paired synthetic evaluation resource, from no-metal CTPelvic1K volumes with clean targets, metal/artifact masks, fixed seeds, and patient-level splits; 75 unpaired real metal cases receive qualitative/no-reference evaluation only. The operating point was fixed in a near-flat validation basin. With exact-mask oracle localization, all methods share a metal-excluded tissue ROI. On 40 held-out cases, VoxelSynth3D reduced RMSE from 801.48 to 786.18 HU (paired gain 15.30 HU, 95% CI 11.68-19.23), improving every case and exceeding the evaluated 3D Gaussian smoother by 13.58 HU. Clean-edge agreement decreased next to metal but exceeded input beyond 5 mm. Thus, VoxelSynth3D provides case-consistent within-distribution tissue-error reduction with a localized structural tradeoff. Spacing-aware sensitivity retained aggregate broad-region improvement and identified near-metal calibration as a target.

</details>


### [108] [SuperMotion: Source-Preserving Denoising for Text-Driven Human Motion Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01517)
*Fa-Ting Hong,Peter Wonka*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SuperMotion proposes a Source-Preserving Denoising framework for text-driven human motion editing that explicitly reuses the source motion at each reverse step to preserve temporal detail. It uses a preservation gate to control source reuse across frames and dimensions, and a clean-space source anchor to inject temporal details that denoising tends to smooth away.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion-based motion editors rely on learned conditioning for preservation but lose temporal detail as denoising proceeds. The goal is to preserve unedited content while realizing requested text-guided changes.

Method: 1) Align source motion to output timeline and predict a preservation gate controlling reuse across frames and feature dimensions. 2) Clean-space source anchor blends predicted clean motion with aligned source using the preservation gate. 3) Pass corrected estimate to sampling posterior. 4) Supervise anchored estimate against editing target with temporal high-frequency loss on second temporal differences. No explicit edit masks required.

Result: Achieves 33.20% full-pool R@1 on MotionFix, reduces temporal-detail attenuation, and preserves motion dynamics while realizing requested changes.

Conclusion: The learned preservation gate is responsible for the performance gain, effectively reusing source to retain unedited content. The clean-space source anchor injects sample-level temporal detail that reconstruction-trained denoisers tend to smooth away.

Abstract: Text-driven human motion editing aims to realize a requested change while preserving compatible source content. Existing diffusion editors rely largely on learned conditioning for preservation of the unedited part, yet their outputs can lose temporal detail as denoising proceeds. We propose the \textbf{Source-Preserving Denoising framework (SuperMotion)}, which explicitly reuses the source at each reverse step for source preservation. We first align the source motion to the output timeline and predict a preservation gate that controls reuse across frames and feature dimensions. A clean-space source anchor then utilizes the learned preservation gate to blend the predicted clean motion with the aligned source and passes the corrected estimate directly to the sampling posterior. Because the aligned source is a realized motion rather than a regression output, the anchor injects sample-level temporal detail that a reconstruction-trained denoiser tends to smooth away. To learn effective source reuse, we supervise the anchored estimate against the editing target and match its second temporal differences through a temporal high-frequency loss. These objectives require no explicit edit masks. Extensive experiments show that SuperMotion improves editing accuracy, reaching 33.20\% full-pool R@1 on MotionFix, while reducing temporal-detail attenuation and preserving motion dynamics as it realizes the requested changes. Ablations confirm that the learned preservation gate is responsible for the gain and that it reuses the source to retain the unedited content properly.

</details>


### [109] [Synthetic training for long-tail haemorrhagic lesion segmentation in data-scarce settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01542)
*Yuan Cao,Sumeet Dash,Antonia Zachariadis,Stefanie Schreiber,Katja Neumann,Jose Bernal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A synthetic training framework for automated segmentation of cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) that requires no real lesion annotations, using procedural lesion synthesis based on clinical priors and radiological descriptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the critical challenge of limited available positive cases and voxel-level annotations for haemorrhagic lesion segmentation in cerebral small vessel disease, by eliminating the need for real annotated training data.

Method: The framework uses anatomical brain parcellations with spatial augmentation and voxel resampling, procedurally inserts cSS and CMB labels using clinical priors on lesion location and morphology, and synthesizes images through randomized intensity assignment, blurring, and Rician noise simulation. Models were trained on dynamically generated image-label pairs.

Result: For cSS, the hypointensity constrained model achieved AUPRC of 0.284 vs 0.083 (Frangi filter) and AUROC of 0.907 vs 0.731. For CMBs, explicit synthesis of blood vessels as lesion mimics improved AUPRC to 0.538 vs 0.004 and AUROC to 0.999 vs 0.968, compared to classical baseline.

Conclusion: The synthetic training framework is a feasible strategy for data-scarce haemorrhagic lesion segmentation, successfully addressing the annotation scarcity problem in medical imaging.

Abstract: Cerebral microbleeds (CMBs) and cortical superficial siderosis (cSS) are imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease, but their automated segmentation is limited by the scarcity of positive cases and voxel-level annotations. We propose a synthetic training framework for long-tail haemorrhagic lesion segmentation that requires no real lesion annotations for training and leverages radiological description of the lesions. Starting from anatomical brain parcellations, the framework applies spatial augmentation and voxel resampling, procedurally inserts cSS and CMB labels using clinical priors on lesion location and morphology, and synthesises images through randomised intensity assignment, blurring, and Rician noise simulation. Models were trained on dynamically generated image-label pairs and evaluated against manual delineations in 10 cSS cases and 13 CMB cases. The proposed configurations outperformed classical filter baselines. For cSS, the hypointensity constrained model achieved higher AUPRC and AUROC than the Frangi filter (AUPRC: 0.284 vs 0.083; AUROC: 0.907 vs 0.731). For CMBs, explicit synthesis of blood vessels as lesion mimics improved performance over the classical baseline (AUPRC: 0.538 vs 0.004; AUROC: 0.999 vs 0.968). These results support our proposal as a feasible strategy for data-scarce haemorrhagic lesion segmentation.

</details>


### [110] [Revisiting Cross-Reconstruction for Generalizable Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01544)
*Bingjian Yang,Shilei Zhao,Zheng Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes an artifact-oriented disentanglement framework for robust image forgery detection that preserves artifact diversity rather than enforcing alignment. The method uses semantically aligned cross-generator reconstruction with masked frequency-aware reconstruction to learn transferable forensic representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing image forgery detectors suffer from poor generalization to unseen manipulation methods due to limited ability to capture transferable forensic cues. Prior cross-reconstruction methods align heterogeneous artifacts across generators and exclude artifact representations during reconstruction, overlooking the inherent diversity and visual cues of manipulation artifacts.

Method: The framework preserves diverse artifact characteristics through semantically aligned cross-generator reconstruction, incorporates artifact representations into the reconstruction process, and introduces a masked frequency-aware reconstruction strategy to emphasize manipulation-related residuals while reducing semantic interference.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate improvements under both cross-dataset and cross-generator evaluation settings. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of artifact diversity preservation and artifact-aware cross-reconstruction.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully learns transferable forensic representations from diverse artifacts by preserving artifact diversity rather than enforcing alignment, with the masked frequency-aware reconstruction strategy effectively emphasizing manipulation-related residuals.

Abstract: Existing image forgery detectors often suffer from generalization to unseen manipulation methods due to the limited ability to capture transferable forensic cues. Recent cross-reconstruction based methods attempt to improve generalization through semantic-artifact disentanglement, but typically align heterogeneous artifacts across generators and exclude artifact representations during reconstruction, which may overlook the inherent diversity and visual cues of manipulation artifacts. In this work, we revisit cross-reconstruction and introduce an artifact-oriented disentanglement framework for robust image forgery detection. We argue that \textbf{artifact diversity}, i.e., the intrinsic variations of manipulation artifacts introduced by different generation processes, contains complementary forensic cues rather than undesirable domain variations. Instead of enforcing explicit artifact alignment, our framework preserves diverse artifact characteristics through semantically aligned cross-generator reconstruction. Furthermore, we incorporate artifact representations into the reconstruction process and introduce a masked frequency-aware reconstruction strategy to emphasize manipulation-related residuals while reducing semantic interference. This design enables the model to learn transferable forensic representations from diverse artifacts. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate improvements under both cross-dataset and cross-generator evaluation settings. Further analysis and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of artifact diversity preservation and artifact-aware cross-reconstruction.

</details>


### [111] [PAGER: Partial-to-global Alignment via Geometric and Relational Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01589)
*Akira-Miranda Adeyomi Adeniran-Lowe,Binod Singh,Lars Arnold Dethlefsen,Lazaros Nalpantidis,Theodora Kontogianni*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses a representation mismatch problem between pretrained 3D encoders (trained on globally reconstructed scenes) and embodied systems that must reason from partial, viewpoint-dependent observations in camera coordinates. The authors introduce PAGER, a label-free adaptation method that aligns partial-view features with a frozen global 3D semantic space using matched-point feature alignment and relational supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained 3D encoders are developed on globally reconstructed scenes in a consistent world coordinate frame, but embodied systems must reason from partial, viewpoint-dependent observations in camera coordinates. This shift exposes a severe representation mismatch that causes significant performance degradation (72.47 mIoU on full scenes vs 2.57 mIoU on single-frame inputs).

Method: PAGER (label-free adaptation method) aligns partial-view features with a frozen global 3D semantic space using only paired partial/global geometry. It learns lightweight adaptation modules while keeping the pretrained encoder and global segmentation probe frozen. Key components: (1) matched-point feature alignment anchors partial features to global counterparts, (2) relational supervision preserves similarity structure with respect to global representation. Global geometry provides supervision only during training; inference operates directly on partial observations.

Result: PAGER without partial-view labels outperforms label-supervised PEFT on both Sonata and Concerto encoders. In zero-shot ScanNet→ScanNet++ transfer, PAGER achieves 53.93 mIoU vs 48.09 mIoU for fully fine-tuned Sonata, demonstrating that preserving the frozen global representation can improve cross-dataset transfer.

Conclusion: Coordinate-frame mismatch is a dominant source of performance degradation but cannot be fully resolved through canonicalization alone (gravity alignment only recovers to 41.64 mIoU). PAGER effectively bridges the gap between global pretrained representations and partial-view observations through lightweight adaptation, achieving superior performance compared to both label-supervised PEFT and fully fine-tuned methods, while preserving the frozen global representation benefits for cross-dataset transfer.

Abstract: Pretrained 3D encoders are typically developed on globally reconstructed scenes expressed in a consistent world coordinate frame, whereas embodied systems must reason from partial, viewpoint-dependent observations in camera coordinates. We show that this shift from globally learned 3D feature spaces to realistic partial observations exposes a severe representation mismatch, which we find consistently across representative state-of-the-art encoders, including Sonata and Concerto. A frozen Sonata encoder with a global linear probe achieves 72.47 mIoU on full ScanNet scenes, but 2.57 mIoU on single-frame camera-coordinate inputs. Training-free gravity alignment recovers performance to 41.64 mIoU, showing that coordinate-frame mismatch is a dominant source of degradation but cannot be fully resolved through canonicalization alone. We introduce PAGER, a label-free adaptation method that aligns partial-view features with a frozen global 3D semantic space using only paired partial/global geometry. It learns lightweight adaptation modules while keeping the pretrained encoder and global segmentation probe frozen. Matched-point feature alignment anchors partial features to their global counterparts, while relational supervision preserves their similarity structure with respect to the global representation. Global geometry provides supervision only during training. Inference operates directly on the partial observation. Without partial-view labels, PAGER outperforms label-supervised PEFT on both Sonata and Concerto, and in zero-shot ScanNet$\rightarrow$ScanNet++ transfer surpasses fully fine-tuned Sonata ($53.93$ vs.\ $48.09$ mIoU), suggesting that preserving the frozen global representation can improve cross-dataset transfer.

</details>


### [112] [Before It Fades: Reinforcing Temporal Representations at Inference Time in VideoLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01595)
*Youngwoo Shin,Yusung Ro,Minseo Kim,Junmo Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VideoLLMs fail to maintain temporal information from intermediate layers to output. The paper introduces Temporal Activation Injection (TAI), a training-free method that extracts the temporal divergence vector at intermediate layers and reinjects it into subsequent layers to improve temporal reasoning performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VideoLLMs struggle with temporal reasoning - reversing video frame order often doesn't change predictions, even though it should invert temporal answers. This is a persistent weakness across architectures that needed investigation.

Method: The authors defined the temporal divergence vector τ_l as the layer-wise representational difference induced by reversing temporal order. They tracked its magnitude across layers to identify where temporal information is acquired but lost. Their solution, Temporal Activation Injection (TAI), extracts τ_l at the peak divergence layer and reinjects it into subsequent layers following the measured decay pattern.

Result: The temporal divergence peaks at intermediate layers and progressively diminishes toward output, confirming that VideoLLMs acquire temporal information at intermediate layers but fail to maintain it to the output. TAI consistently improves temporal reasoning across three VideoLLMs and four benchmarks with negligible impact on non-temporal tasks.

Conclusion: Temporal information is acquired but progressively fades in VideoLLMs. TAI, a training-free intervention, effectively addresses this issue by reinjecting temporal signals at appropriate layers, providing a general solution to improve temporal reasoning without additional training.

Abstract: Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) receive frames in sequential order and interpret how visual content evolves along the temporal axis, yet temporal reasoning remains a persistent weakness across architectures. Reversing the frame order of a video, a transformation that should invert temporal answers, often leaves the final prediction unchanged. We investigate where this failure originates by defining the temporal divergence vector $τ_l$, the layer-wise representational difference induced by reversing temporal order. Tracking its magnitude across layers reveals a consistent temporal divergence profile where the divergence peaks at intermediate layers and progressively diminishes toward the output. We confirm this peak is specific to temporal reasoning and functionally critical for predictions, establishing that VideoLLMs acquire temporal information at intermediate layers but fail to maintain it to the output. This progressive fading motivates our method, Temporal Activation Injection (TAI), which extracts $τ_l$ at the peak of the profile for each input and reinjects it into subsequent layers following the measured decay. TAI requires no training and consistently improves temporal reasoning across three VideoLLMs and four benchmarks with negligible impact on non-temporal tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/Before-It-Fades.

</details>


### [113] [Hob-VL: A Benchmark for Visually Grounded Boolean Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01605)
*Yuzhou Wang,Emile Anand,Ijay Narang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Hob-VL is a benchmark for visually grounded Boolean reasoning, comprising 6,000 Yes/No questions and 1,000 object-identification questions across 1,000 generated scenes and 46 photographs. The benchmark evaluates whether Boolean rules hold in images or identifies objects satisfying Boolean descriptions, with questions featuring misleading cues and nested logical operations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current visual reasoning models struggle with composing multiple visual observations and returning consistent answers to logically equivalent questions. Existing benchmarks lack sufficient focus on Boolean reasoning with complex logical operations. This work aims to expose failures in visual reasoning through a carefully designed benchmark with executable reference answers.

Method: The benchmark was constructed with 6,000 human-verified balanced Yes/No questions, each defined by Boolean combinations of ten visual statements across 1,000 generated scenes and 46 diverse labeled photographs, plus 1,000 object-identification questions. Question families were designed to challenge reasoning through misleading local cues and nested logical operations, including both symbolic and natural-language presentations. Eight model configurations were tested with thinking disabled/minimized, plus a thinking-enabled GLM configuration.

Result: Boolean accuracy ranges from 48.52% to 50.57% across eight model configurations, while identification accuracy reaches at most 43.0%. A thinking-enabled GLM configuration achieves uneven gains while retaining substantial errors and inconsistencies.

Conclusion: Hob-VL exposes significant failures in current visual reasoning models on Boolean tasks, with accuracies near random chance (50%) for Boolean questions and even lower for identification tasks. The benchmark reveals that even thinking-enabled models struggle with consistent logical reasoning, highlighting the need for improvement in visual grounding and Boolean reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Reliable visual reasoning requires composing multiple visual observations and returning consistent answers to logically equivalent questions. We introduce Hob-VL, a benchmark for visually grounded Boolean reasoning. Hob-VL comprises two tasks: (1) evaluating whether a Boolean rule holds in an image, and (2) identifying the (unique) object satisfying a Boolean description. Hob-VL contains 6,000 human-verified balanced Yes/No questions, each defined by a Boolean combination of ten visual statements, across 1,000 generated scenes and 46 diverse labeled photographs, along with 1,000 object-identification questions over the same photographs. Our question families are deliberately constructed to challenge reasoning through misleading local cues and nested logical operations, and include symbolic and structured natural-language presentations. Across eight model configurations with thinking disabled or minimized, Boolean accuracy ranges from 48.52% to 50.57%, while the identification accuracy reaches at most 43.0%. A thinking-enabled GLM configuration achieves uneven gains while retaining substantial errors and inconsistencies. Hob-VL exposes these failures through executable reference answers and matched evaluations.

</details>


### [114] [Oneira: From Open-Ended Generation to Open-World Interaction in Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01614)
*Xindi Yang,Baolu Li,Liam Lee,Zhenfei Yin,Songxin Zhang,Zhuoyang Song,Xu Jia,Jianfei Cai,Tien-Tsin Wong,Bingyi Jing,Mengyue Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Oneira is an interactive video world model that closes the loop between generation and interaction through an explicit world state managed by a coding agent. It addresses two key requirements: Open-World Interactivity (newly generated entities become actionable) and Persistent State (interaction outcomes persist in the environment).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current generative video world models can synthesize open-ended environments but lack full interaction capabilities. When a generated world expands, newly created content should be actionable by agents, and changes made by the agent should become persistent parts of the environment rather than transient visual effects.

Method: Oneira uses an explicit, extensible world state managed by a coding agent. Given the current observation and an action or high-level goal, the agent: (1) reads the world state, (2) grounds relevant entities, (3) plans the interaction, and (4) writes the outcome back into a world state table. When exploration reveals new objects, the agent incorporates them from generated observations, allowing the interaction space to expand. Previously induced state changes are carried across video segments. The updated world state is rendered along the camera action trajectory into a coarse conditioning video, from which a video generator fills in appearance, motion, and interaction details.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that Oneira enables direct and consistent interaction with newly generated objects while preserving the effects of prior interactions over long horizons.

Conclusion: Oneira successfully implements Open-World Interactivity and Persistent State in interactive video world models, enabling agents to interact with newly generated content and maintain persistent effects of their actions across the generated world.

Abstract: Generative video world models can now synthesize open-ended environments that agents can navigate and interact with in simple ways. Yet open-ended generation does not imply full interaction: as a generated world expands, newly created content through navigation should expand what the agent can act upon, and as the agent changes the world, those changes should become persistent parts of the environment rather than transient visual effects. We characterize these two requirements as Open-World Interactivity, where newly generated or encountered entities are incorporated into the actionable world, and Persistent State, where interaction outcomes are committed to the world state and continue to influence subsequent observations and interactions. We present Oneira, an interactive video world model that closes the loop between generation and interaction through an explicit, extensible world state managed by a coding agent. Given the current observation and an action or high-level goal, the agent reads the world state, grounds the relevant entities, plans the interaction, and writes its outcome back into a world state table. When exploration reveals new objects, the agent incorporates them from generated observations, allowing the interaction space to expand with the generated world. Meanwhile, previously induced state changes are carried across video segments, making the consequences of interaction persistent parts of subsequent world evolution. The updated world state is rendered along the camera action trajectory into a coarse conditioning video, from which a video generator fills in the appearance, motion, and interaction details not represented in the state. Experiments show that Oneira enables direct and consistent interaction with newly generated objects, while preserving the effects of prior interactions over long horizons. Project page: https://madaoer.github.io/projects/oneira

</details>


### [115] [Beyond Domain-Level Adaptation: Margin-Oriented Semantic-Appearance Interaction Correction for Personalized Federated Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01625)
*Wentao Yue,Qingyu Mao,Tianyou Lai,Ahmed M. Abdelmoniem,Qilei Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MOSAIC addresses domain heterogeneity in federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning of vision-language models by identifying and correcting class-domain residuals that harm decision margins, using a low-rank adapter with globally shared class factors and private domain factors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated personalized methods treat each domain as a class-agnostic transformation, but this abstraction is insufficient because cross-domain displacement varies across semantic classes, and only a subset of class-domain residuals damages the image-text decision margin.
