Method: MOSAIC constructs a decision-aware harmfulness score measuring whether a training-derived class-domain residual favors a competing text prototype over the true class. It uses a low-rank residual adapter with globally shared class factors and residual basis while keeping domain factors client-private. An image-conditioned gate controls candidate-wise correction, and harmful-pair-aware reweighting prioritizes decision-relevant residuals during local optimization.

Result: MOSAIC consistently improves macro-client top-1 accuracy across all evaluated domain-shift and joint domain-label-shift settings on Office31, OfficeHome, and DomainNet100.

Conclusion: By addressing the fine-grained class-domain interactions rather than treating domains as class-agnostic, MOSAIC effectively handles domain heterogeneity in federated vision-language model fine-tuning while preserving privacy and parameter efficiency.

Abstract: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables distributed clients to adapt pretrained vision-language models without sharing raw data or updating the full backbone. Its effectiveness, however, is limited by domain heterogeneity across clients. Existing personalized methods separate globally shared knowledge from client-specific style, but they largely treat each domain as a class-agnostic transformation. We show that this abstraction is insufficient: the cross-domain displacement associated with a fixed domain varies across semantic classes, and only a subset of these class-domain residuals damages the image-text decision margin. We therefore propose Margin-Oriented Semantic-Appearance Interaction Correction (MOSAIC), which first constructs a decision-aware harmfulness score that measures whether a training-derived class-domain residual favors a competing text prototype over the true class. It then models fine-grained class-domain interactions with a low-rank residual adapter whose class factors and residual basis are globally shared while domain factors remain client-private. An image-conditioned gate further controls candidate-wise correction, and harmful-pair-aware reweighting prioritizes decision-relevant residuals during local optimization. Extensive experiments on Office31, OfficeHome, and DomainNet100 demonstrate that MOSAIC consistently improves macro-client top-1 accuracy across all evaluated domain-shift and joint domain-label-shift settings.

</details>


### [116] [Fusing Visual and Textual Representations via Multi-layer Fusing Transformers for Vietnamese Visual Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01637)
*Cong Phu Nguyen,Huy Tien Nguyen,Tung Le*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of Visual Question Answering research for Vietnamese by proposing a Multi-layer Fusing Transformer model with cross attention module that combines multi-modality features from different layers. The model achieves competitive results on the ViVQA dataset, contributing to the advancement of VQA technology for Vietnamese language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a significant research gap: while Visual Question Answering (VQA) has been extensively studied for English, there have been very few similar efforts for other languages, particularly Vietnamese. This gap presents both a challenge and opportunity for advancing VQA technology in the Vietnamese language context, with potential applications in education, healthcare, and entertainment for Vietnamese-speaking populations worldwide.

Method: The paper proposes a Multi-layer Fusing Transformer model that utilizes a cross attention module to combine multiple modality features (images and texts) from different layers into an aggregated representation. This architecture extracts information from low-level to high-level features, enabling comprehensive cross-modal understanding.

Result: The model achieves promising results against competitive baselines on the ViVQA dataset for Vietnamese language, demonstrating the effectiveness of the multi-layer fusing approach with cross attention mechanism.

Conclusion: The proposed Multi-layer Fusing Transformer model with cross attention module represents a significant advancement in Vietnamese VQA research. By achieving promising results against competitive baselines on the ViVQA dataset, this work addresses the research gap in non-English VQA and opens pathways for practical applications in education, healthcare, and entertainment for Vietnamese-speaking populations.

Abstract: In recent decades, artificial intelligence has made significant progress in understanding and interacting with images. One of the important applications of this technology is Visual Question Answering (VQA), a research field that requires computers to understand and answer questions about images in a natural manner. Despite extensive research and development in VQA for English, there have been very few similar efforts made for other languages, especially Vietnamese. This gap presents a significant challenge and opportunity for the advancement of VQA technology in the Vietnamese language context. By bridging this gap, the field of Vietnamese VQA not only enriches the diversity of research in artificial intelligence but also enables practical applications in various domains, such as education, healthcare, and entertainment, catering to Vietnamese-speaking populations worldwide. Thus, the exploration and development of Vietnamese VQA systems hold immense potential for advancing both research and practical applications in the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing. In this paper, we propose a Multi-layer Fusing Transformer model utilizing a cross attention module to combine multiple modality features of images and texts from different layers in an aggregated representation. Our architecture allows us extract information from low level to high level. Through detailed experiments and ablation studies, our model achieves promising results against the competitive baselines in ViVQA dataset for Vietnamese language.

</details>


### [117] [Not All Error Yields to Scale: Where Scaling Stops in Vision-Language Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01640)
*Xinye Zhao,Yunkai Dang,Yunchen Wu,Wenbin Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes the "Separable Law" to address the fixed-budget trade-off in Vision-Language Models between processing more visual information (higher resolution/more tokens) and using a larger language backbone for complex reasoning. The law is fitted on 26 models (InternVL and QwenVL, 1B-72B parameters) across four high-resolution benchmarks (224px to 8K images).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models face a fundamental trade-off between visual detail and reasoning capability under fixed compute budgets. Existing research provides no guidance on optimal backbone size vs. input resolution combinations, especially for high-resolution deployments. The authors seek a principled way to decide how much a model should see at high resolution given its reasoning requirements.

Method: The authors propose the Separable Law, which describes how VLM performance changes with language backbone size and visual token count. They fit this law to empirical measurements from 26 InternVL and QwenVL models across four high-resolution benchmarks with image sizes ranging from 224 pixels to 8K. They also combine it with a cost law to derive a closed-form rule for compute allocation.

Result: Key findings: (1) Scaling responses can be predicted from the skill requirements of questions; (2) A substantial fraction of questions never respond to scaling; (3) Both model families gain similarly from larger backbones, but their gains from more visual tokens differ sharply; (4) The law identifies model and image sizes that perform close to the best feasible choice under the same budget.

Conclusion: The Separable Law provides a principled framework for deciding how much visual information a VLM should process given its reasoning requirements. When deployment is limited to available configurations, the law can identify near-optimal model and image size combinations within compute budgets. The authors hope this work enables more systematic deployment decisions for VLMs in high-resolution applications.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) face a fixed-budget trade-off between processing more visual information for fine-grained perception and using a larger language backbone for complex reasoning. Existing studies do not tell us which combination of backbone size and input resolution to deploy, especially in high-resolution deployments. To address this gap, we propose the Separable Law that describes how VLM performance changes with language backbone size and visual token count. We fit the law to measurements from 26 InternVL and QwenVL models, with language backbone sizes from 1B to 72B, on four high-resolution benchmarks with image sizes from 224 pixels to 8K. We find that the questions responding to scaling can be predicted from the skill they require, while a substantial fraction never responds at all. We also find that the two model families gain similarly from a larger backbone, while their gains from more visual tokens differ sharply. Combined with a cost law, the Separable Law gives a closed-form rule for allocating compute between backbone size and visual tokens. When deployment is limited to available configurations, the law identifies model and image sizes that perform close to the best feasible choice under the same budget. We hope our work offers a principled way to decide how much a model should be allowed to see at high resolution, given what it must reason about.

</details>


### [118] [DiVid: Diagnosing Dimension-Specific Diversity Collapse in Video Generation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01661)
*Huanran Hu,Zihui Ren,Dingyi Yang,Zhinan Song,Guozheng Wu,Tiezheng Ge,Qin Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DiVid is a diagnostic framework that measures video generation diversity across six interpretable dimensions (Semantic, Style, Subject, Scene, Motion, Camera) to identify where and why diversity collapses, revealing that even high-performing models fail on Motion and Camera dimensions due to two bottlenecks: default mode convergence and realization gaps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video generation models produce similar outputs when repeatedly sampled from the same prompt, limiting creative exploration. Current diversity metrics are too coarse (global scalars) to identify where diversity collapses in spatiotemporal space.

Method: Decompose video generation diversity into six interpretable dimensions measured through a reproducible computer-vision pipeline. Evaluate representative models systematically, analyze alongside quality and instruction faithfulness, and use controlled prompt interventions to identify bottlenecks.

Result: Diversity is highly dimension-specific: models with strong global diversity scores still collapse on specific factors, particularly Motion and Camera. These rankings persist after filtering unfaithful generations. Two fundamental bottlenecks identified: (1) default mode convergence - models fall back to dominant patterns under open-ended prompts; (2) realization gaps - models fail to faithfully realize diverse, explicitly requested alternatives, especially for temporal factors. Larger faithfulness losses for temporal factors highlight difficulty of controlling motion and camera variation through text alone.

Conclusion: DiVid shifts the study of diversity from measuring "whether" it exists to diagnosing "where and why" it collapses, providing actionable directions for dimension-aware training objectives and control signals to improve diverse and controllable video generation.

Abstract: Despite remarkable progress, video generation models often produce highly similar outputs when repeatedly sampled from the same prompt, limiting their usefulness for creative exploration. Existing diversity evaluations primarily rely on global scalar metrics, which obscure where diversity collapses in the spatiotemporal space of videos. We introduce DiVid, a dimension-level diagnostic framework that decomposes video generation diversity into six interpretable dimensions: Semantic, Style, Subject, Scene, Motion, and Camera. Each dimension is measured through a reproducible computer-vision pipeline and analyzed alongside quality and instruction faithfulness to examine potential trade-offs. Systematic evaluation of representative video generation models reveals that diversity is highly dimension-specific: models with strong global diversity scores still collapse on specific factors, particularly Motion and Camera. These rankings persist after filtering unfaithful generations, indicating genuine capability differences rather than off-prompt outputs. Beyond measurement, controlled prompt interventions identify two fundamental bottlenecks: default mode convergence, where models fall back to dominant patterns under open-ended prompts; and realization gaps, where models fail to faithfully realize diverse, explicitly requested alternatives, particularly for temporal factors. The larger faithfulness losses for temporal factors highlight the difficulty of controlling motion and camera variation through text alone. DiVid thus shifts the study of diversity from measuring whether it exists to diagnosing where and why it collapses, and provides actionable directions for dimension-aware training objectives and control signals. The framework will be released to facilitate future research on diverse and controllable video generation.

</details>


### [119] [Do MLLM Judges Judge the Edit? Auditing Bias in Image Editing Evaluation with Verified Quality Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01670)
*Yuan Huang,Zirui Song,Xiuying Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EditJudgeBias is a benchmark introduced to audit biases in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) used as automated judges for image editing evaluation. The benchmark contains 1,196 real editing samples with 13 quality-preserving cues injected across four evaluation sites, using calibrated validators and human inspection to verify quality preservation. Experiments on five MLLM judges reveal that quality-preserving cues cause measurable shifts beyond each judge's noise floor, with candidate order swaps reversing up to 60.9% of pairwise decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs are increasingly used as automated judges for instruction-based image editing and as reward signals for model training. However, systematically auditing whether these judges are influenced by cues irrelevant to editing quality is challenging because visual interventions may themselves alter the quality being evaluated. A judgment shift can be attributed to bias only when the intervention is verified to preserve the underlying editing quality.

Method: The authors introduce EditJudgeBias, a counterfactual benchmark with verified quality preservation, comprising 1,196 real editing samples and 13 cues injected across four evaluation sites. Quality preservation is verified using calibrated multimodal validators, controls, and human inspection. Five MLLM judges are audited along three complementary dimensions: (1) invariance to quality-preserving cues, (2) agreement with human judgments, and (3) stability of pairwise preferences. Observed shifts are evaluated against each judge's own zero-dose and re-query noise floors rather than against zero.

Result: Quality-preserving cues move every judge beyond its own noise floor. Fabricated majority opinions increase ratings. Irrelevant visual elements cause larger shifts than whole-image manipulations. Swapping candidate order reverses up to 60.9% of pairwise decisions. Edit-region cues also tend to reduce human agreement. The three measures characterize judges differently, showing that robustness cannot be captured by a single metric.

Conclusion: All tested MLLM judges exhibit measurable biases when evaluated with quality-preserving cues. The study demonstrates the importance of evaluating MLLM judges against their own noise baselines rather than absolute zero, and suggests that multiple complementary metrics are needed to capture judge robustness comprehensively.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for instruction-based image editing and as reward signals for model training. However, systematically auditing whether these judges are influenced by cues irrelevant to editing quality is challenging because visual interventions may themselves alter the quality being evaluated. A judgment shift can therefore be attributed to bias only when the intervention is verified to preserve the underlying editing quality. To address this challenge, we introduce EditJudgeBias, a counterfactual benchmark with verified quality preservation, comprising 1,196 real editing samples and 13 cues injected across four evaluation sites. We verify quality preservation for the requested edit using calibrated multimodal validators, controls, and human inspection. We then audit five MLLM judges along three complementary dimensions: invariance to quality-preserving cues, agreement with human judgments, and stability of pairwise preferences. Importantly, observed shifts are evaluated against each judge's own zero-dose and re-query noise floors rather than against zero. Experiments show that quality-preserving cues move every judge beyond its own noise. Fabricated majority opinions increase ratings, irrelevant visual elements cause larger shifts than whole-image manipulations, and swapping candidate order reverses up to 60.9% of pairwise decisions. Edit-region cues also tend to reduce human agreement. The three measures characterize judges differently, showing that robustness cannot be captured by a single metric.

</details>


### [120] [When Text-to-Image Helps Editing: The Effects of Conditioning During Denoising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01681)
*Lidia Troeshestova,Alexander Ustyuzhanin,Sergey Kastryulin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper investigates how to improve unified models that handle both instruction-based image editing and text-to-image (T2I) generation. The authors discover that source attention declines during denoising in pure editing mode, and propose "task switching" - temporarily switching to T2I mode during specific intervals - to leverage the model's T2I capabilities while maintaining editing conditioning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified models are trained for both image editing and T2I generation, but standard editing pipelines maintain source-image conditioning throughout the entire denoising process. The authors question whether editing can benefit from T2I capabilities and aim to study how conditioning effects vary across different edits and denoising stages.

Method: The researchers analyzed three unified editors across four benchmarks. They observed that in pure editing, source attention declines for some edits over the sampling trajectory. Based on this observation, they proposed "task switching" - switching to the T2I task for bounded intervals during the denoising process. This allows the model to leverage its T2I capabilities while maintaining editing conditioning.

Result: Switching to the T2I task for bounded intervals improves edit quality across all three unified editors and four benchmarks, while mean perceptual preservation remains close to pure editing across all three models. The timing of the switch sets the balance between edit quality and preservation.

Conclusion: Unified editors benefit from using both conditioning modes they are trained for (editing and T2I). The timing of the task switch determines the trade-off between edit quality and source preservation. This approach provides a simple yet effective way to improve unified image editing models.

Abstract: Unified models are trained for both instruction-based image editing and text-to-image (T2I) generation, but standard editing pipelines keep source-image conditioning throughout denoising. We ask whether editing can benefit from T2I, and study how the effects of conditioning vary across edits and denoising stages. In pure editing, source attention declines for some edits over the sampling trajectory. This observation led us to task switching, which lets the model draw on its T2I capabilities. Across three unified editors and four benchmarks, switching to the T2I task for bounded intervals improves edit quality, while mean perceptual preservation remains close to pure editing across all three models. Unified editors therefore benefit from using both conditioning modes they are trained for, and the timing of the switch sets the balance between quality and preservation.

</details>


### [121] [Architectural Sampling: Test-Time Scaling via Computational Diversity in Frozen Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01687)
*Akshit Singh,Shyam Marjit,Wei Lin,Leonid Karlinsky,M. Jehanzeb Mirza*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces "architectural sampling," a training-free method that generates diverse candidate responses by reusing different blocks of decoder layers during forward computation, rather than using the same computation path for all candidates as in conventional temperature sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional test-time scaling methods like temperature sampling generate all candidates along the same fixed computation path, limiting computational diversity. The authors aim to introduce computational diversity without modifying model weights or adding parameters.

Method: Architectural sampling varies the location and repetition count of decoder layer blocks during forward computation, creating distinct computation paths for different candidates. This is a training-free approach that reuses selected blocks of decoder layers to generate diverse outputs.

Result: Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, architectural sampling improves pass@9 by 6.58 percentage points over standard-path temperature sampling at the same nine-candidate budget. Reusing early layers yields the strongest gains, and the improvement persists even under greedy decoding. The method produces candidates with lower lexical overlap and improves accuracy when used as rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning.

Conclusion: Architectural sampling extends benefits beyond candidate coverage, demonstrating more effective learning from a model's own outputs. The approach provides computational diversity without any training or parameter modification, making it a practical improvement for test-time scaling.

Abstract: Test-time scaling often seeks better answers by sampling multiple responses from a frozen model, yet conventional temperature sampling generates every candidate along the same fixed computation path. We introduce architectural sampling, a training-free method that generates candidates through distinct forward computations by reusing selected blocks of decoder layers. Varying the block location and repetition count introduces computational diversity without updating model weights or adding auxiliary parameters. Across five Qwen checkpoints and twelve multimodal benchmarks, architectural sampling improves pass@9 over standard-path temperature sampling by 6.58 percentage points on average at the same nine-candidate budget. Reusing early layers yields the strongest gains, and the improvement in candidate coverage persists even under greedy decoding. The resulting candidates show lower lexical overlap and improve accuracy when used as rollouts for label-free test-time reinforcement learning. These findings extend the benefits of our architectural sampling beyond candidate coverage, demonstrating more effective learning from a model's own outputs.

</details>


### [122] [MEGA: Object-Level Mesh Extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting via Spatial Visual Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01707)
*Liwei Liao,Yingkui Zhang,Qianqian Tong,Ronggang Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MEGA proposes a novel "segment-then-mesh" framework for extracting object-level, watertight meshes from 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. It uses Spatial Visual Distillation (SVD) to leverage 3DGS as a teacher for training a mesh reconstruction model, achieving state-of-the-art performance in object-level 3D occupancy recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mesh extraction methods from 3DGS focus on scene-level extraction, failing to represent object-level occupancy and often producing non-watertight surfaces. This limits applications requiring precise geometric boundaries for individual objects.

Method: The framework uses Spatial Visual Distillation (SVD) which treats 3DGS as a teacher, sampling diverse camera poses and rendering corresponding views of each segmented object. These observations train a mesh reconstruction model through photometric supervision, combined with a mask-guided neural surface reconstruction module.

Result: MEGA achieves state-of-the-art performance in recovering accurate object-level 3D occupancy on widely used benchmarks. It enables complex physical interactions by combining high-quality object-level meshes for geometric occupancy with 3DGS representations for photorealistic rendering.

Conclusion: MEGA successfully bridges the gap between implicit 3DGS representations and explicit mesh geometry, enabling object-level watertight mesh extraction that supports physical interactions while maintaining photorealistic rendering capabilities.

Abstract: Mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) aims to endow 3D Gaussians with accurate geometric structures, enabling explicit and precise 3D occupancy. However, existing methods primarily focus on scene-level mesh extraction, making them unable to represent object-level occupancy and often resulting in non-watertight surfaces. To overcome these limitations, we propose \textbf{MEGA} (\underline{M}esh \underline{E}xtraction from \underline{GA}ussians), a ``segment-then-mesh'' framework for extracting object-level, watertight meshes from complex 3DGS scenes. At the core of MEGA are \textbf{Spatial Visual Distillation (SVD)} and a mask-guided neural surface reconstruction module. SVD treats the 3DGS model as a teacher, sampling diverse camera poses and rendering the corresponding views of each segmented object. These observations are then used to train a mesh reconstruction model through photometric supervision. Extensive experiments on several widely used benchmarks demonstrate that MEGA achieves state-of-the-art performance in recovering accurate object-level 3D occupancy. Moreover, MEGA enables complex physical interactions by combining high-quality object-level meshes for geometric occupancy with 3DGS representations for photorealistic rendering.

</details>


### [123] [Rethinking Memorization Mitigation in Diffusion Models: Reinforcing Text Conditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01723)
*Hyungjun Joo,Sehwan Kim,Hyeonggeun Han,Sangwoo Hong,Jungwoo Lee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A training-free method to mitigate memorization in text-to-image diffusion models by redistributing cross-attention with Gaussian smoothing, reinforcing content tokens while attenuating padding tokens, without requiring additional denoiser evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-image diffusion models can exhibit memorization by closely reproducing individual training examples, but effective mitigation must preserve useful prompt information to guide alternative depictions.

Method: The method redistributes cross-attention with Gaussian smoothing before reinforcing content-token contributions and attenuating padding contributions, without additional denoiser evaluations.

Result: On Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.0, all evaluated smoothing widths lie on the empirical Pareto frontiers for training-image similarity versus both prompt alignment and image preference. The method reduces template reproduction in DeepFloyd IF without further tuning.

Conclusion: Jointly controlling conditioning allocation and strength can generate prompt-consistent alternatives while reducing memorization.

Abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress in image synthesis, yet can exhibit memorization by closely reproducing individual training examples. Effective mitigation must preserve useful prompt information to guide alternative depictions. We introduce a training-free method that redistributes cross-attention with Gaussian smoothing before reinforcing content-token contributions and attenuating padding contributions, without additional denoiser evaluations. With this intervention, stronger content conditioning can improve prompt alignment at comparable training-image similarity. A local analysis identifies when reinforcement preserves shared value information while redistribution reduces localized attention mass. On Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.0, all evaluated smoothing widths lie on the empirical Pareto frontiers for training-image similarity versus both prompt alignment and image preference. A configuration selected on Stable Diffusion reduces template reproduction in DeepFloyd IF without further tuning. These findings support jointly controlling conditioning allocation and strength to generate prompt-consistent alternatives.

</details>


### [124] [ATI-VLA: Action-Centric Predictive Vision-Language-Action Models via Actionable Alignment Then Adaptive Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01741)
*Yijie Zhu,Rui Shao,Jie He,Wei Li,Bo Zhao,Yelin Wang,Xiaochen Yuan,Tao Tan,Miao Zhang,Xiaojiang Peng,Zitong Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ATI-VLA introduces an action-centric predictive vision-language-action framework for robotic manipulation that addresses modality misalignment between observations and actions through a two-step approach: shared codebook alignment and adaptive injection of predictive latents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predictive VLA models aim to improve robotic manipulation via future observation forecasting, but existing approaches underperform direct action prediction models due to modality misalignment between observations and actions, and joint optimization conflicts that divert learning from action-centric objectives.

Method: ATI-VLA employs a two-step design: 1) Actionable Representation Alignment via a Shared Codebook - maps predictive observation and action representations into a shared discrete latent space via a unified codebook to mitigate modality misalignment; 2) Action-Centric Adaptive Injection - injects predictive observation latents into action decoding as explicit predictive priors through a lightweight adaptive side-path under a single action-centric objective.

Result: Extensive experiments on both simulation and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that ATI-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance with faster convergence.

Conclusion: The proposed ATI-VLA framework successfully addresses the limitations of predictive VLA models by aligning modalities and enabling adaptive predictive guidance, achieving superior performance in robotic manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Predictive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models aim to improve robotic manipulation via future observation or world dynamics forecasting. However, existing approaches often fail to realize this potential and underperform direct action prediction models. We argue that these limitations stem from modality misalignment between observations and actions, together with joint optimization conflicts that drive learning away from an action-centric objective. To this end, we introduce ATI-VLA, an Action-Centric Predictive Vision-Language-Action framework via Actionable Alignment Then Adaptive Injection. Specifically, it follows a two-step design: 1) Actionable Representation Alignment via a Shared Codebook. It aligns predictive observation and action representations by mapping both modalities into a shared discrete latent space via a unified codebook, making predictive observation latents readily usable for action generation and mitigating modality misalignment. 2) Action-Centric Adaptive Injection of Predictive Latents. Building upon this, it then injects predictive observation latents into action decoding as explicit predictive priors via a lightweight adaptive side-path, enabling adaptive predictive guidance under a single action-centric objective. Extensive experiments on both simulation and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that ATI-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance with faster convergence.

</details>


### [125] [3DROID: A Renderable 3D Gaussian Dataset with Measured Per-Scene Reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01744)
*Wonguen Cho,Junhoo Lee,Nojun Kwak*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the gap between 2D robot perception and 3D manipulation by using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) as 3D supervision. The authors investigate how extrinsic camera reliability and pose conditioning affect feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction, and propose a calibration-aware pipeline to anchor reconstructed scenes to the robot's metric workspace. They also release a dataset with scene-level reliability information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robot manipulation models primarily reason from 2D observations but operate in the 3D physical world. While recent work augments robot data with geometric priors (depth, point clouds, 3D trajectories), 3DGS representations are designed for photometric fidelity and may not preserve real-world metric scale, especially when camera extrinsics are unreliable. This creates a need to understand how extrinsic reliability affects 3DGS reconstruction quality for robot manipulation.

Method: The authors study the effect of extrinsic reliability and pose conditioning on feed-forward 3DGS. They propose a calibration-aware pipeline that anchors reconstructed scenes to the robot's metric workspace. The approach involves evaluating how pose conditioning affects novel-view synthesis and geometric accuracy under different levels of extrinsic camera reliability.

Result: Pose conditioning improves novel-view fidelity. However, the geometric benefit depends on the reliability of the injected extrinsics - when extrinsics are unreliable, the geometric reconstruction suffers. The authors successfully created a renderable, metric-pose-anchored dataset with scene-level reliability information for robot manipulation research.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that pose conditioning is beneficial for novel-view synthesis but requires reliable camera extrinsics for geometric accuracy. The proposed calibration-aware pipeline enables metric-scale 3DGS reconstruction anchored to the robot's workspace. The released dataset (available on HuggingFace) provides valuable resources for robot manipulation research with built-in reliability annotations.

Abstract: Robot manipulation models primarily reason from 2D observations while acting in the 3D physical world. To bridge this gap, recent work has augmented robot data with geometric priors such as depth, point clouds, and 3D trajectories, while renderable 3D Gaussian representations provide another promising form of 3D supervision. However, 3DGS representation is designed mainly for photometric fidelity and may not preserve real-world metric scale, particularly when the supplied camera extrinsics are unreliable. We study the effect of extrinsic reliability and pose conditioning on feed-forward 3DGS, and propose a calibration-aware pipeline that anchors reconstructed scenes to the robot's metric workspace. Our experiments show that pose conditioning improves novel-view fidelity, while its geometric benefit depends on the reliability of the injected extrinsics. Using this pipeline, we present a renderable, metric-pose-anchored dataset with scene-level reliability information for robot manipulation research. Our dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/wonguen/3DROID

</details>


### [126] [FFBL-Coop: Association-Decoupled Cooperative 3D Multi-Object Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01750)
*Haoxin Wu,Xiaokai Bai*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FFBL-Coop is a cooperative 3D tracking framework that separates instance admission from identity management to handle errors from cross-view appearance differences and spatial misalignment. It uses three key components: Confidence-ranked Slot Admission (CSA), Unified Representation Aggregation (URA), and Cooperative-Priority Identity Anchoring (CPIA). A shared codebook enables payload compression while maintaining performance close to the uncompressed variant.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cooperative 3D tracking must integrate complementary observations across agents and time while maintaining consistent identities. However, when evidence integration and identity inheritance share a matching decision, errors from cross-view appearance differences and spatial misalignment can compromise both feature fusion and track continuity.

Method: The proposed FFBL-Coop follows a "fuse first, bind later" approach with three main components: (1) Confidence-ranked Slot Admission (CSA) allocates cooperative queries to available ego slots using confidence and spatial proximity; (2) Unified Representation Aggregation (URA) uses cooperative semantic features and aligned anchors to guide ego-feature retrieval, refining the augmented query bank within a shared transformer decoder; (3) Cooperative-Priority Identity Anchoring (CPIA) combines learned association with persistent mappings to establish accepted identity assignments across frames. A shared codebook is used for payload compression.

Result: FFBL-Coop achieves AMOTA/AP of 0.611/0.548 on V2X-Seq and 0.688/0.653 on Griffin-25M, with performance close to the uncompressed variant.

Conclusion: The fuse-first, bind-later framework effectively separates instance admission from identity management, enabling robust cooperative 3D tracking. The shared codebook enables payload reduction while retaining high tracking accuracy.

Abstract: Cooperative 3D tracking must integrate complementary observations across agents and time while maintaining consistent identities. When evidence integration and identity inheritance share a matching decision, errors arising from cross-view appearance differences and spatial misalignment can compromise both feature fusion and track continuity. We propose FFBL-Coop, a fuse first, bind later framework that separates instance admission from identity management. Confidence-ranked Slot Admission (CSA) allocates cooperative queries to available ego slots using confidence and spatial proximity. Unified Representation Aggregation (URA) uses cooperative semantic features and aligned anchors to guide ego-feature retrieval, refining the augmented query bank within a shared transformer decoder. After refinement, Cooperative-Priority Identity Anchoring (CPIA) combines learned association with persistent mappings to establish accepted identity assignments across frames. A shared codebook reduces transmitted payload while retaining AP and AMOTA close to the uncompressed variant. FFBL-Coop achieves AMOTA/AP of 0.611/0.548 on V2X-Seq and 0.688/0.653 on Griffin-25M. Code will be released.

</details>


### [127] [Cog-VADU: A Training-Free Cognitive Reasoning Framework for Video Anomaly Detection and Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01754)
*Mohd Ubaid Wani,Sara Atito,Josef Kittler,Muhammad Awais*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Cog-VADU is a training-free framework that reformulates video anomaly detection as a sequential cognitive reasoning task using Large Vision-Language Models. It uses Chain-of-Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP) to maintain temporal memory through propagated rationales and a cross-modal re-ranking stage for semantic consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing VAD approaches rely on dataset-specific training and annotations, limiting generalization in open-set scenarios. Zero-shot methods using LVLMs lack temporal continuity and structured reasoning capabilities.

Method: Cog-VADU introduces CoADTP, which unrolls an LVLM into a recurrent reasoning chain across video segments, propagating structured rationales to maintain implicit temporal memory. A cross-modal re-ranking stage aligns textual rationales with visual embeddings for semantic consistency and temporal coherence.

Result: Cog-VADU achieves competitive zero-shot performance on multiple public VAD benchmarks. The CoADTP mechanism consistently enhances reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic manner.

Conclusion: The proposed framework provides interpretable and generalizable anomaly understanding for real-world applications, successfully addressing temporal continuity and structured reasoning limitations in existing zero-shot VAD methods.

Abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to temporally localize abnormal events in videos. Most existing approaches rely on dataset-specific training and curated annotations, limiting generalization in open-set scenarios. Recent zero-shot methods based on Large Vision- Language Models (LVLMs) alleviate this dependency but often lack temporal continuity and structured reasoning. We propose Cog-VADU, a fully training-free framework that reformulates VAD as a sequential cognitive reasoning task. Cog-VADU introduces Chain-of- Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP), which unrolls an LVLM into a recurrent reasoning chain across video segments. By propagating structured rationales over time, the model maintains implicit temporal memory, enabling robust discrimination between com- plex anomalies and high-motion normal activities. To improve reliability, we further design a cross-modal re-ranking stage that aligns textual rationales with visual embeddings, enforcing semantic consistency and temporal coherence for refined and stable predictions. Extensive experiments on multiple public VAD benchmarks demonstrate that Cog-VADU achieves competitive zero-shot performance. Moreover, cross-model evaluations show that CoADTP consistently enhances reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic manner, pro- viding interpretable and generalizable anomaly understanding for real-world applications.

</details>


### [128] [GenCOPE: Syn2Real Generalized Category-Level Object Pose Estimation for Robotic Picking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01758)
*Jian Liu,Wei Sun,Zhenqi Dai,Hui Yang,Jian Xiao,Nicu Sebe,Na Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses synthetic-to-real (Syn2Real) generalization for category-level object pose estimation (COPE). The goal is to train a model on rendered synthetic data only and deploy it directly in real-world scenarios, eliminating the need for labor-intensive real-world data collection. The approach uses 2D and 3D semantic consistency constraints to learn domain-invariant representations, combined with 2D-3D cross consistency learning and dense cross-modality fusion for refined pose estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing COPE methods require labor-intensive real-world training data for novel object categories, limiting scalability. The paper aims to achieve synthetic-to-real generalization where models trained solely on synthetic data can directly generalize to real-world deployments, addressing the significant domain gap between synthetic and real data, particularly in texture appearance.

Method: The method includes: (1) Learning domain-invariant representations that capture semantic commonalities among objects within the same category using 2D and 3D semantic consistency constraints to reduce sensitivity to domain-specific features; (2) An end-to-end pose regression framework with 2D-3D cross consistency learning; (3) Dense cross-modality fusion to refine pose estimation; (4) Operating exclusively on global features for a lightweight and efficient architecture.

Result: Extensive experiments on REAL275 and Wild6D benchmarks, as well as real-world robotic manipulation scenes, demonstrate superior Syn2Real generalization performance.

Conclusion: The proposed paradigm achieves effective synthetic-to-real generalization for COPE, enabling training on synthetic data only while maintaining strong performance on real-world scenarios, with a lightweight architecture suitable for robotic deployment.

Abstract: Category-level object pose estimation (COPE), capable of generalizing to intra-class unknown objects, has become a core technique for robotic 3D scene understanding. However, existing COPE methods still require labor-intensive recollection of real-world training data for novel object categories, which limits their scalability in practical applications. This paper aims to achieve synthetic-to-real (Syn2Real) generalized COPE, where a model is trained solely on rendered synthetic data and directly generalized to real-world deployments. The central challenge lies in the significant domain gap between synthetic and real-world data, particularly in texture appearance. To address this, we aim to enhance domain generalization by learning domain-invariant representations that capture semantic commonalities among objects within the same category. We introduce 2D and 3D semantic consistency constraints to reduce the sensitivity of feature encoders to domain-specific features. In addition, we propose an end-to-end pose regression framework that performs 2D-3D cross consistency learning, leveraging dense cross-modality fusion to further refine pose estimation. Since simplicity and effectiveness are essential for real-world robotic deployment, our model operates exclusively on global features, yielding a highly lightweight and efficient architecture. Extensive experiments on the REAL275 and Wild6D benchmarks, as well as real-world robotic manipulation scenes, show superior Syn2Real generalization performance of our paradigm. Code and demos are released at https://paperreview99.github.io/GenCOPE/.

</details>


### [129] [PhysDEM: Physics-Defined Energy-Matching Diffusion for Spatiotemporal Field Generation under Scarce Measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01759)
*Zhenyu Liang,Yining Huang,Yubo Zhao,Jack C. P. Cheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhysDEM is a physics-defined diffusion framework that generates plausible spatiotemporal physical fields from scarce, spatially sparse measurements by combining governing PDEs with diffusion models, without requiring full-field datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional data-driven diffusion models require full-field datasets, which are often unavailable when observations are insufficient to characterize a distribution over complete fields. This limitation prevents effective field inference from scarce measurements in real-world applications.

Method: The framework employs three key components: (1) A Gibbs target constructed by reweighting a measurement-conditioned Gaussian reference with PDE residual energy; (2) An exact conditional-mean identity that reduces denoising to supervised learning of the standardized energy-induced mean correction; (3) A physics-displacement probability flow that cancels Gaussian reference terms, enabling amortized sampling with changing measurements through Gaussian conditioning without retraining.

Result: Experiments on synthetic PDE systems and real-world-informed applications demonstrate that PhysDEM supports coherent field recovery and efficient sampling while maintaining stable diagnostics under tested noise levels.

Conclusion: PhysDEM is the first physics-defined diffusion model enabling amortized spatiotemporal field inference without preassembled full-field datasets, offering practical value for field assessment.

Abstract: Generating and predicting spatiotemporal physical fields from scarce measurements is challenging, as observations are insufficient to characterize a distribution over complete fields. This limits conventional data-driven diffusion models that rely on full-field datasets. We introduce PhysDEM, a physics-defined diffusion framework that combines governing equations with spatially sparse observations to generate multiple plausible fields. First, we construct a Gibbs target by reweighting a measurement-conditioned Gaussian reference with PDE residual energy. Second, we derive an exact conditional-mean identity that reduces denoising to supervised learning of the standardized energy-induced mean correction. Third, a physics-displacement probability flow cancels Gaussian reference terms and enables amortized sampling with changing measurements through Gaussian conditioning, without retraining. Experiments on synthetic PDE systems and real-world-informed applications demonstrate that PhysDEM supports coherent field recovery and efficient sampling while maintaining stable diagnostics under tested noise levels, illustrating its practical value for field assessment. To our knowledge, PhysDEM is the first physics-defined diffusion model enabling amortized spatiotemporal field inference without preassembled full-field datasets.

</details>


### [130] [OneStreamer: Unifying Perception, Memory, and Proactive Response in Streaming Video Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01762)
*Xiangyu Zeng,Yuandong Yang,Zhiqiu Zhang,Yuhan Zhu,Xinhao Li,Qingyi Si,Dingyu Yao,Changlian Ma,Haoran Chen,Xinyu Chen,Yansong Shi,Junhao Zhou,Yifei Li,Jun Zhang,Chuanyu Qin,Chenxu Yang,Xinlei Yu,Kun Ouyang,Yuchen Shao,Qianshan Wei,Changhai Zhou,Jun Gao,Jiaqi Wang,Limin Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OneStreamer is a streaming video LLM that jointly learns query-independent evidence recording and task response through a shared proactive generation process. It uses Proactive Hierarchical Caption Memory (PHCM) to produce time-grounded captions and summaries, and Proactive State Transition Learning (PSTL) to handle state transitions. The model achieves state-of-the-art results on 8 streaming video understanding benchmarks with a 4B parameter model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Streaming video LLMs face a fundamental challenge: they must retain evidence before knowing its relevance to future tasks, and respond when sufficient evidence becomes available. The key challenge is forming reusable factual memory without compromising real-time perception capabilities.

Method: OneStreamer introduces two key innovations: (1) Proactive Hierarchical Caption Memory (PHCM) - produces time-grounded local-detail captions and summaries of completed events, where streaming caption targets supervise interpretation of observed video prefixes during training, and at inference, model-generated records complement a recent visual window; (2) Proactive State Transition Learning (PSTL) - reduces dominance of repeated waiting states by preserving supervision at all output anchors and selecting representative state-change and state-persistence tokens. The method also includes a streaming data synthesis pipeline creating OneStreamer-1M dataset with over 1 million records.

Result: The 4B parameter OneStreamer model achieves the best results among all compared methods across all eight evaluated streaming video understanding benchmarks. Ablations show that retaining generated captions improves historical QA without degrading real-time perception. PSTL also outperforms dense state supervision while supervising only 27.5% of annotated state tokens.

Conclusion: Proactive generation serves as a shared learning interface connecting perception, memory formation, and timely response in streaming video interaction. The approach demonstrates that combining evidence recording with task response through unified proactive generation effectively addresses the trade-off between real-time perception and factual memory formation.

Abstract: Streaming video LLMs must retain evidence before its relevance to future tasks is known and respond when sufficient evidence becomes available. The challenge is to form reusable factual memory without compromising real-time perception. We introduce OneStreamer, which jointly learns query-independent evidence recording and task response through a shared proactive generation process. Its Proactive Hierarchical Caption Memory (PHCM) produces time-grounded local-detail captions and summaries of completed events. Streaming caption targets supervise the interpretation of observed video prefixes during training. At inference, model-generated records complement a recent visual window, providing reusable factual context without revisiting historical visual features. Proactive State Transition Learning (PSTL) reduces the dominance of repeated waiting states by preserving supervision at all output anchors and selecting representative state-change and state-persistence tokens. We further develop a streaming data synthesis pipeline that aligns output content and timing with available evidence. Combining the resulting streaming captions and QA with cleaned open-source data yields OneStreamer-1M, a broad-coverage streaming video interaction dataset with over one million records spanning diverse tasks. Our 4B model achieves the best results among the compared methods across all eight evaluated streaming video understanding benchmarks. Ablations show that retaining generated captions improves historical QA without degrading real-time perception. PSTL also outperforms dense state supervision while supervising only 27.5% of annotated state tokens. Together, these results support proactive generation as a shared learning interface connecting perception, memory formation, and timely response in streaming video interaction.

</details>


### [131] [GIFTBench: Diagnosing Generalization in Image Forgery Localization and Informing Model Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01778)
*Baoke Dou,Ziye Wang,Hao Wang,Guoqing Cai,Wende Tan,Chenyang Si,Liucheng Guo,Yueming Lyu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces GIFTBench, a comprehensive multi-axis benchmark for image forgery localization (IFL) containing 115,013 manipulated images with pixel-level annotations. It enables axis-specific transfer analysis across manipulation source, semantic target, editing operation, and composition complexity. The benchmark serves both as an evaluation tool and training resource, leading to the development of ForenScope, a detection and localization framework that improves cross-dataset localization while retaining detection capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing IFL benchmarks have limited manipulation conditions and entangle multiple factors in cross-dataset evaluation, providing incomplete views of localization generalization. There is a need for comprehensive evaluation under diverse distribution changes.

Method: GIFTBench is designed with 115,013 manipulated images spanning four axes: manipulation source, semantic target, editing operation, and composition complexity. Evaluation is conducted on 12 external datasets. ForenScope is developed using classification-adapted representations, multi-depth multi-scale spatial features, learned layer fusion, and selective coarse-scale conditioning.

Result: Diagnostic studies reveal asymmetric cross-source transfer, recall-dominated failures, and heterogeneous degradation across semantic, operational, and compositional changes. Training on GIFTBench consistently improves aggregate transfer to external datasets. ForenScope shows improved cross-dataset localization while retaining image-level detection capability.

Conclusion: GIFTBench serves both as a diagnostic evaluation tool and an effective training resource for cross-domain image forgery localization. The benchmark's scale and diversity substantially improve localization generalization, and the ForenScope framework demonstrates the practical application of diagnostic findings to achieve better cross-dataset performance.

Abstract: Reliable evaluation of image forgery localization (IFL) requires assessing models under diverse distribution changes, yet existing benchmarks often cover limited manipulation conditions or entangle multiple factors in cross-dataset evaluation. Consequently, aggregate performance provides an incomplete view of localization generalization. We introduce GIFTBench, a multi-axis benchmark of 115,013 manipulated images with pixel-level annotations spanning manipulation source, semantic target, editing operation, and composition complexity. GIFTBench supports axis-specific transfer analysis and evaluation on twelve external datasets. Its diagnostic studies reveal asymmetric cross-source transfer, recall-dominated failures, and heterogeneous degradation across semantic, operational, and compositional changes. Beyond diagnosis, the scale and diversity of GIFTBench provide a substantially broader training distribution than conventional IFL datasets. Training representative localizers on GIFTBench consistently improves their aggregate transfer to external datasets, showing that the benchmark serves not only as an evaluation tool but also as an effective training resource for cross-domain localization. Guided by the diagnostic findings, we further develop ForenScope, a detection and localization framework combining classification-adapted representations with multi-depth, multi-scale spatial features, learned layer fusion, and selective coarse-scale conditioning. Experiments show improved cross-dataset localization while retaining image-level detection capability. The GIFTBench dataset showcase page is available at https://giftbench-preview.doudoudouya337.chatgpt.site.

</details>


### [132] [VETO: Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01785)
*Gueter Josmy Faure,Hao Ping Wang,Min-Hung Chen,Winston H. Hsu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VETO is a training-optional plug-in for Vision-Language Models that achieves dual-axis compression of video tokens through intra-frame (optimal-transport based semantic merging) and inter-frame (temporal redundancy elimination) compressors, enabling up to 45% faster inference while preserving or improving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Processing long videos with VLMs is bottlenecked by the quadratic cost of visual tokens, making long-form inference prohibitively expensive. Existing single-axis compression methods treat spatial and temporal redundancy independently and hit a hard efficiency floor.

Method: VETO employs hierarchical dual-axis compression: (1) Intra-frame compressor merges semantically similar tokens within each frame via optimal-transport inspired matching; (2) Inter-frame compressor identifies and merges temporally redundant frames. The key insight is compressing spatial dimensions first to drastically reduce the cost of subsequent global temporal matching.

Result: VETO achieves up to 45% faster inference on LLaVA-OneVision-7B while preserving or improving accuracy. Under extreme token starvation (10% budget), VETO outperforms VFlowOpt (54.9%), VisionZip (52.6%), and FastV (47.9%) with 55.7% accuracy. Zero-shot accuracy is preserved or improved across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA.

Conclusion: VETO eliminates the efficiency bottleneck of single-axis compression through hierarchical dual-axis compression, with advantages that grow with modern fully-fused attention infrastructure. It demonstrates universal applicability across multiple VLM architectures while achieving significant inference speedup and superior accuracy under token-constrained conditions.

Abstract: Processing long videos with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is bottlenecked by the quadratic cost of visual tokens, making long-form inference prohibitively expensive. While single-axis compression methods mitigate this, they hit a hard efficiency floor because they treat spatial and temporal redundancy independently. We present VETO (Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision-Language Models), a training-optional plug-in that eliminates this bottleneck through dual-axis compression: (i) an intra-frame compressor that merges semantically similar tokens within each frame via optimal-transport inspired matching, and (ii) an inter-frame compressor that identifies and merges temporally redundant frames. The key design insight is hierarchical ordering: by first compressing spatial dimensions, VETO drastically reduces the cost of subsequent global temporal matching, bypassing the efficiency wall of single-axis approaches, with an advantage that grows with modern fully-fused attention infrastructure. Empirically, VETO achieves up to 45% faster inference (e.g., on LLaVA-OneVision-7B) while preserving or improving accuracy. Under extreme token starvation (10% budget), VETO outperforms VFlowOpt (54.9%), VisionZip (52.6%), and FastV (47.9%) with 55.7% accuracy. We demonstrate universal applicability across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA, with zero-shot accuracy preserved or improved in all cases.

</details>


### [133] [Continuous Conditioning of VLAs with Augmenting EMG and Visual Task Descriptors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01794)
*Edward W. Staley,Connor O. Pyles,Rahul Hingorani,Frank Camargo,Griffin Milsap,Jared Markowitz,Matthew S. Fifer,Michael Wolmetz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes two alternative task-conditioning methods for Vision-Language-Action models: electrophysiology (EMG) conditioning and visual annotation conditioning, demonstrating their superiority over language-only prompting in cluttered scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLAs heavily rely on language for task conditioning, but the authors hypothesize that other modalities could provide supplemental task information, especially in ambiguous or cluttered scenes where language may be insufficient.

Method: Two models were developed: (1) EC-VLA concatenating 8-channel EMG envelopes to the proprioceptive vector, and (2) VA-VLA incorporating visual segmentation annotations to image inputs. Evaluated on a cube-selection task across three participants.

Result: EC-VLA matches the language-prompted baseline in uncluttered in-distribution conditions and substantially outperforms it in cluttered, out-of-distribution scenes. VA-VLA shows modest improvements in in-distribution scenes and substantial improvement in cluttered, out-of-distribution trials.

Conclusion: Task-conditioning beyond language provides significant benefits, particularly in challenging/cluttered environments. This opens avenues for multimodal task conditioning in VLA systems.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely strongly on language for describing task information, despite having multimodal inputs. We hypothesize that other modalities in the state space may present opportunities for supplemental task conditioning, which may be particularly relevant in cluttered or otherwise ambiguous scenes. We introduce two tuned models to test this hypothesis: (1) an electrophysiology-conditioned VLA (EC-VLA) that incorporates 8-channel electromyography envelopes as continuous conditioning input concatenated to the proprioceptive vector, and (2) a visually-annotated VLA (VA-VLA) that incorporates visual segmentation annotations to the image inputs. On a cube-selection task evaluated across three participants, EC-VLA matches a language-prompted baseline in uncluttered, in-distribution conditions and substantially outperforms it in cluttered, out-of-distribution scenes. Similarly, VA-VLA shows modest improvements over a language-prompted baseline in in-distribution scenes with substantial improvement in cluttered, out-of-distribution trials. Together, these results provide strong evidence for the potential benefit of task-conditioning beyond language.

</details>


### [134] [PhaseAT: Fourier Phase Adversarial Training for Medical Image Domain Generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01807)
*Ahmed Sharshar,Asif Hanif,Naveen Kumar Kummari,Mohammad Yaqub,Mohsen Guizan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhaseAT is a phase-aware adversarial training framework for medical domain generalization that creates phase-perturbed training views in the Fourier domain to stress spatial organization while preserving appearance statistics, achieving over 20% improvement in single-source DG.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable clinical deployment of deep medical image models is hindered by distribution shifts across scanners, sites, and acquisition protocols. Existing DG methods focus on style/intensity diversification but can leave networks dependent on domain-specific texture correlations.

Method: PhaseAT forms phase-perturbed training views in the Fourier domain by iteratively updating bounded phase perturbations while keeping amplitude spectrum unchanged. Perturbations are applied only to the luminance channel in YCbCr color space, with a phase-saliency mask concentrating updates on most influential frequencies. The model is trained with weighted combination of losses on clean and phase-perturbed samples, supporting both single-source and multi-source DG.

Result: Validated on two challenging medical datasets, PhaseAT achieves over 20% improvement in single-source domain generalization, outperforming several state-of-the-art DG methods.

Conclusion: The proposed phase-aware adversarial training approach effectively addresses domain shift in medical imaging by manipulating Fourier phase information rather than style/intensity, demonstrating significant improvements over existing domain generalization methods.

Abstract: Reliable clinical deployment of deep medical image models is hindered by distribution shifts across scanners, sites, and acquisition protocols. Existing domain generalization (DG) methods often focus on style or intensity diversification, but they can still leave networks dependent on domain-specific texture correlations. Inspired by evidence that Fourier phase encodes semantic structure, we introduce PhaseAT, a phase-aware adversarial training framework for medical DG. PhaseAT forms phase-perturbed training views in the Fourier domain by iteratively updating a bounded phase perturbation while keeping the amplitude spectrum unchanged, thereby stressing spatial organization under matched appearance statistics. Perturbations are applied only to the luminance channel in YCbCr color space to avoid chromatic artifacts. Additionally, a simple phase-saliency mask concentrates updates on the most influential frequencies. The model is trained with a weighted combination of losses on clean and phase-perturbed samples, supporting both single-source and multi-source DG. We validate our method on two challenging medical datasets and demonstrate that PhaseAT achieves over 20% improvement in single-source domain generalization, outperforming several state-of-the-art DG methods. The code implementation is available at: https://github.com/ahmed-sharshar/PhaseAT.

</details>


### [135] [From Pixels to Policy: A Multi-Agent System for Intervention and Geo-Spatial Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01870)
*Hosam Elgendy,Utkarsh Mall*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces VIDA-Geo, a multi-agent system that discovers urban interventions (e.g., adding trees, benches) from aerial/street-view images to improve target urban indicators like perceived safety and greenery, using a combination of segmentation, diffusion-based inpainting, and indicator scoring models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing geospatial vision methods only monitor urban indicators but don't propose interventions or estimate their effects. Evaluating proposed urban interventions is costly, time-consuming, and impractical. The authors aim to address this gap by creating an implicit digital twin for testing intervention hypotheses.

Method: VIDA-Geo is a multi-agent system that coordinates three components: (1) segmentation model to identify editable areas, (2) diffusion-based inpainting model to generate realistic interventions, and (3) indicator scoring model to evaluate changes. The system uses a black-box indicator model combined with a generative editing model as an implicit digital twin.

Result: The approach outperforms baselines on 8 indicators across aerial and street-view imagery, achieving up to 2X higher perceptual quality and policy alignment scores. The system provides multiple candidate interventions for expert city-planner evaluation.

Conclusion: The proposed VIDA-Geo system demonstrates the feasibility of automatically discovering urban interventions that improve target indicators while maintaining perceptual realism and policy alignment. This supports a city-planner-in-the-loop workflow for urban design decisions.

Abstract: Urban environments are shaped by design choices with long-term implications for health, safety, and quality of life, yet evaluating proposed interventions remains costly, time-consuming, and often impractical. Existing geospatial vision methods largely focus on monitoring urban indicators from aerial and street-view imagery, rather than proposing interventions and estimating their effects on such indicators. Moving beyond recognition, we introduce the problem of discovering interventions that improve target indicators for a given aerial or street-view image. We argue that a black-box indicator model, combined with a generative editing model, can serve as an implicit digital twin for testing intervention hypotheses. We present VIDA-Geo , a multi-agent system that explores this intervention space by coordinating segmentation, diffusion-based inpainting, and indicator scoring models to produce interventions that are both perceptually realistic and aligned with real-world policies. We evaluate our system on 8 indicators across aerial and street-view imagery, measuring changes in factors such as perceived safety and greenery. Our approach outperforms existing baselines in many cases, achieving up to 2X higher perceptual quality and policy alignment scores. Finally, our model provides users with multiple candidate interventions, supporting an expert city-planner-in-the-loop workflow.

</details>


### [136] [EvenSplat: Coupled 2D-3D Decomposition for Gaussian Splatting under Exposure and Illumination Variation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01876)
*Tongyu Wu,Jacob Edwards,Ziteng Cui,Caigui Jiang,Cheng Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EvenSplat is a novel 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates capture-specific illumination artifacts from true scene geometry and color. It couples image-space illumination decomposition with a Gaussian-carried illumination field, plus a camera-response network and local exposure-compensation module. The method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, especially under high-contrast illumination conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multi-view reconstruction methods like 3D Gaussian Splatting incorrectly treat lighting artifacts (exposure changes, illumination variation, shadows) as intrinsic scene properties. This entangles capture-specific illumination with recovered geometry and color, degrading reconstruction quality under uneven lighting conditions.

Method: EvenSplat combines: (1) image-space illumination decomposition, (2) an illumination field carried by Gaussians for shared 2D-3D lighting explanation, (3) a camera-response network to handle global differences, and (4) a local exposure-compensation module for residual differences across training images.

Result: EvenSplat generally outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets, with particularly strong performance under high-contrast illumination. The framework was validated on both real-world captured and simulated benchmarks covering cross-view exposure, spatial illumination variation, and high-contrast lighting scenarios.

Conclusion: EvenSplat successfully separates illumination from geometry and color in 3D Gaussian Splatting, providing more accurate scene reconstruction under challenging uneven lighting conditions. The approach is particularly effective for high-contrast illumination scenarios where traditional methods struggle.

Abstract: A surface photographed under even light presents nearly the same appearance from every angle; the same surface under uneven light does not. Exposure changes between views, illumination varies within a single image, and locally strong light sources leave one region bright and its neighbor in shadow. Multi-view reconstruction methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting treat these lighting artifacts as if they were properties of the scene, entangling capture-specific illumination with the geometry and color they recover. We present EvenSplat, a framework that separates the two. EvenSplat couples an image-space illumination decomposition with an illumination field carried by the Gaussians, so that the same explanation of the lighting is shared between the two-dimensional and three-dimensional views of the scene; a camera-response network and a local exposure-compensation module absorb the global and residual differences that remain across training images. Through extensive experiments across multiple datasets and diverse forms of uneven illumination (cross-view exposure, spatial illumination variation, and high-contrast lighting) on both real-world captured and simulated benchmarks, EvenSplat generally outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly under high-contrast illumination.

</details>


### [137] [Memory-Guided B-Roll Generation from User Video Collections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01884)
*Cusuh Ham,Fabian Caba Heilbron,Josef Sivic,Bryan Russell*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MemComposer is a three-stage system for generating B-roll video sequences that complement user's primary footage (A-roll). It uses a collection memory to plan, retrieve, and generate grounded multi-shot sequences while preserving characters, settings, objects, and style from the user's video collection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The challenge is selecting visual evidence from hours of captured footage to guide generation of each shot in a B-roll sequence that complements the user's A-roll while maintaining consistency with the collection's visual elements.

Method: Three-stage system: (1) Offline entity-centric memory construction from raw video with visual references; (2) Memory-guided planning to create grounded sequence and retrieve conditioning frames; (3) Iterative generation and critique to enforce identity, setting, and sequence-level consistency.

Result: Against ungrounded text-to-video planner: wins 60.0% prompt-adherence and 92.8% visual-alignment. Against retrieval-only sequences: wins 94.5% prompt-adherence, but retrieval-only preferred for visual alignment in 58.2% of cases.

Conclusion: Collection memory and reference retrieval provide significant grounding benefits. Generating missing shots improves prompt adherence, but retrieval-only approaches maintain better visual alignment with original footage.

Abstract: We introduce an approach for collection-grounded B-roll sequence generation. Given a user's video collection, a directive given in natural language, and a target duration, the goal is to produce a multi-shot sequence that complements the user's primary footage (A-roll) while preserving the collection's characters, settings, objects, and style. This task is challenging as one must choose the visual evidence from hours of captured footage that should guide the generation of each shot in the sequence. We address this challenge with MemComposer, a three-stage system that turns raw footage into a structured memory with visual references (characters, settings, objects, and style) and uses it to plan, retrieve, and generate grounded B-roll sequences. First, in a one-time offline stage, MemComposer constructs an entity-centric memory from raw video. Second, it uses the memory and user directive to plan a grounded sequence and retrieve conditioning frames for each shot. Third, it iteratively generates and critiques the sequence to enforce identity, setting, and sequence-level consistency. We evaluate MemComposer in a user preference study along two dimensions: prompt adherence and visual alignment to the user's collection. Against an ungrounded text-to-video planner, MemComposer wins 60.0\% of prompt-adherence and 92.8\% of visual-alignment comparisons, showing the grounding benefit of collection memory and reference retrieval. Against retrieval-only sequences assembled from captured footage, MemComposer wins 94.5\% of prompt-adherence comparisons, showing the value of generating missing shots, while retrieval-only sequences are preferred for visual alignment in 58.2\% of comparisons.

</details>


### [138] [Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Enhanced Radiometer Image Precipitation Estimation using Conditional Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01890)
*Victor Enescu,Assaad Zeghina,Matthieu Meignin,Nicolas Viltard,Cécile Mallet*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel unsupervised domain adaptation method using flow matching models for satellite radiometer images, enabling precise domain alignment without requiring large labeled datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep generative networks require large supervised/annotated datasets, which are scarce for satellite instruments due to limited overlap with labeled data and domain shifts. This creates a significant challenge for satellite image analysis tasks.

Method: The method leverages parts of the deterministic ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in flow matching models, conditioned on different satellite instruments to achieve precise domain alignment. The approach is unsupervised and theoretically bijective to preserve essential information during adaptation.

Result: Experiments on the GPM-Core constellation demonstrate the benefit of conditional domain adaptation, particularly in improving rain precipitation estimation from radiometer imagery.

Conclusion: Flow matching models offer a promising solution for unsupervised domain adaptation in satellite remote sensing, effectively bridging domain gaps while preserving critical information, with demonstrated success in precipitation estimation tasks.

Abstract: Deep generative networks have recently achieved unprecedented performance in precise image and video editing using sophisticated textual prompts. However, the effectiveness of such models heavily depends on access to very large supervised and annotated image datasets, which can be very difficult to obtain. This is particularly true for satellite instruments, which very rarely overlap with labelled data, and suffer from domain shifts in the rare occasions they do. In this paper, we investigate the potential of flow matching models for unsupervised domain adaptation of satellite radiometer images. Our main contribution is a novel unsupervised method that achieves precise domain alignment by leveraging parts of the deterministic ordinary differential equations in flow matching models, conditioned on different satellite instruments. A key strength of our approach is its ability to preserve essential information while adapting across any domains since the perturbations are in theory bijective.
