Extensive experiments conducted on the GPM-Core constellation show the benefit of our conditional domain adaptation, particularly in improving rain precipitation estimation from radiometer imagery.

</details>


### [139] [MapLightning: Online Vectorized HD Map Construction with 1D Map Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01905)
*Shen Zheng,Anurag Ghosh,Mani Ramanagopal,Srinivasa Narasimhan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MapLightning proposes replacing dense BEV grids with compact 1D learnable map tokens for online vectorized HD map construction in autonomous driving. It uses a transformer-based mapper with self-attention to aggregate image and map tokens, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency with 16.7× fewer tokens, 1.73× faster inference, and 53% less memory usage compared to prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior methods for online vectorized HD map construction rely on dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grids as intermediate representation, which limits efficiency and scalability for safe autonomous driving. The authors aim to create a more efficient representation that maintains accuracy while enabling real-time inference.

Method: MapLightning replaces dense BEV grids with a compact set of 1D learnable map tokens. The method uses self-attention (instead of vanilla cross-attention) for constructing map tokens from image features, enabling joint interactions and contextual aggregation. The transformer-based mapper concatenates map and image tokens, applies full self-attention, discards image tokens, and retains updated map tokens for decoding. The map decoder uses full (not deformable) cross-attention for better global context. Importantly, the network does not use camera projection parameters, making it robust to camera-extrinsic perturbations.

Result: MapLightning uses up to 16.7× fewer intermediate tokens than dense BEV-based methods. The lightweight variant surpasses MapTRv2 by +10.1 mAP on nuScenes and +16.2 mAP on Argoverse 2, while delivering 1.73× faster inference (40+ FPS) with 53% less memory. Improvements are also demonstrated on uncertainty-aware map construction and downstream trajectory prediction.

Conclusion: MapLightning successfully demonstrates that replacing dense BEV grids with compact 1D learnable map tokens enables superior efficiency (fewer tokens, less memory, faster inference) while achieving state-of-the-art accuracy. The approach is robust to camera-extrinsic perturbations and shows improvements in downstream tasks like trajectory prediction, making it promising for scalable autonomous driving applications.

Abstract: Online vectorized HD map construction is essential for scaling safe autonomous driving and requires accurate, real-time inference. Prior methods typically rely on dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grids as the intermediate representation. We propose \textit{MapLightning}, which replaces the dense BEV grid with a compact set of 1D learnable map tokens. To construct map tokens from image features, we choose self-attention over vanilla cross-attention because it enables joint interactions and contextual aggregation among image and map tokens. Our transformer-based mapper concatenates map and image tokens, applies full self-attention, discards the image tokens, and retains the updated map tokens for decoding. This design offers three advantages. First, our representation is efficient, using fewer tokens, consuming less memory, and running faster. Second, the lightweight design allows the map decoder to use full rather than deformable cross-attention for better global context. Third, unlike BEV-based methods, our network does not use camera projection parameters, making it robust to camera-extrinsic perturbations. MapLightning uses up to 16.7$\times$ fewer intermediate tokens than dense BEV-based methods and achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on nuScenes and Argoverse~2. Its lightweight variant surpasses MapTRv2 by +10.1 mAP on nuScenes and +16.2 mAP on Argoverse~2, while delivering 1.73$\times$ faster inference (40+ FPS) with 53\% less memory. We further show improvements on uncertainty-aware map construction and downstream trajectory prediction. Code and models will be released.

</details>


### [140] [DecomVoxel: Harnessing 3D-Native Priors with Guided In-situ Denoising Optimization for Decompositional Scene Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01914)
*Junfeng Ni,Zirui Zhou,Yixin Chen,Yu Liu,Nan Jiang,Zhifei Yang,Song-Chun Zhu,Siyuan Huang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DecomVoxel is a novel decompositional scene reconstruction method that formulates object completion as guided in-situ denoising optimization, bridging 3D-native priors with neural scene reconstruction to achieve high-quality textured meshes with clean topology, geometry, and appearance under heavy occlusions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing decompositional scene reconstruction methods struggle with quality under heavy occlusions. While 2D image-based generative priors suffer from multi-view inconsistency due to lack of 3D awareness, 3D-native priors provide stronger structural inductive biases but frequently cause spatial drift and misalignment in complex scenes.

Method: DecomVoxel introduces: (1) A reformulated epsilon-based distillation loss for stable latent refinement; (2) Adaptive spatial guidance utilizing occupied and vacant anchors with temporal annealing to suppress generative hallucinations and mitigate spatial drift. The method bridges 3D-native priors with neural scene reconstruction through guided in-situ denoising optimization.

Result: Experiments on Replica and ScanNet++ datasets show that DecomVoxel significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods while faithfully preserving original spatial layout, structural fidelity, and style-consistent texture. The method delivers high-quality textured meshes with clean topology, geometry, and appearance.

Conclusion: DecomVoxel pushes the boundary of decompositional reconstruction by providing a robust solution for reconstructing complex real-world scenes with high-quality results, successfully addressing the challenges of heavy occlusions, spatial drift, and misalignment in existing approaches.

Abstract: Decompositional scene reconstruction aims to reconstruct high-quality objects and background, yet existing methods still struggle with the level of quality under heavy occlusions. While generative priors offer a potential solution, 2D image-based priors often suffer from multi-view inconsistency due to a lack of 3D awareness. Conversely, 3D-native priors provide stronger structural inductive biases but frequently lead to spatial drift and misalignment within complex scenes. To address these issues, we propose DecomVoxel, formulating object completion as a guided in-situ denoising optimization that bridges 3D-native priors with neural scene reconstruction. Our framework introduces a reformulated epsilon-based distillation loss to ensure stable latent refinement, alongside adaptive spatial guidance that utilizes occupied and vacant anchors with temporal annealing to suppress generative hallucinations and mitigate spatial drift. Experiments on Replica and ScanNet++ show that DecomVoxel significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods while faithfully preserving the original spatial layout, structural fidelity, and style-consistent texture. Our method pushes the boundary of decompositional reconstruction by delivering high-quality textured meshes with clean topology, geometry, and appearance, providing a robust solution for the decompositional reconstruction of complex real-world scenes. Code is available at https://github.com/DecomVoxel/DecomVoxel.

</details>


### [141] [MoLE: Mixture of Latent Experts for Complementary Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01917)
*Yingcheng Liu,Tianyi Jiang,Yujuan Ding,jiangbo Ai,Xun Jiang,Guoqing Wang,Wei Ye,Yi Bin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MoLE (Mixture of Latent Experts) is a framework that improves latent visual reasoning in vision-language models by encouraging different latent tokens to extract complementary visual information rather than redundant representations. It uses dedicated latent visual experts with isolated evidence extraction and summary experts for aggregation, achieving 78.6 average score across five benchmarks (4.9% better than supervised fine-tuning, 3.6% better than the strongest baseline).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing latent visual reasoning methods allow multiple latent tokens to access the same visual evidence through shared value projections, leading to redundant latent representations. Simply increasing the latent budget doesn't help because tokens extract similar information rather than complementary visual details.

Method: MoLE introduces a Mixture of Latent Experts framework with two key components: (1) Isolated latent visual experts that control what visual evidence each expert observes and how it transforms that evidence, and (2) Dedicated latent summary experts to aggregate complementary representations. A two-stage training pipeline first forces visual evidence through the latent pathway, then restores direct visual access - requiring no predefined expert roles or intermediate visual targets.

Result: Across five visual reasoning benchmarks, MoLE achieves an average score of 78.6, outperforming data-matched supervised fine-tuning by 4.9 points and the strongest evaluated latent visual reasoning baseline at the same latent budget by 3.6 points. Representation analyses show lower latent-state similarity and more diverse visual attention. Masking the latent pathway reduces average performance by 9.2 points.

Conclusion: Specializing latent computation (encouraging different latent tokens to extract complementary visual information) is more effective than merely increasing the number of latent tokens. The approach demonstrates that latent visual experts acting as specialized visual experts significantly improves visual reasoning performance.

Abstract: Latent visual reasoning equips vision--language models with continuous intermediate states that can process visual evidence without explicit textual reasoning traces or repeated image operations. However, existing methods often allow multiple latent tokens to access the same visual evidence through shared value projections, providing no mechanism for them to extract complementary visual information; simply increasing the latent budget can therefore yield redundant latent representations. We argue that effective latent reasoning should encourage different latent tokens to extract complementary visual information, and thereby act as specialized visual experts. Based on this insight, we propose MoLE, a Mixture of Latent Experts framework that controls both what visual evidence each latent visual expert observes and how it transforms that evidence. MoLE isolates latent visual experts during evidence extraction and uses dedicated latent summary experts to aggregate the complementary representations of latent visual experts. A two-stage training pipeline first forces visual evidence through this latent pathway and then restores direct visual access, requiring neither predefined expert roles nor intermediate visual targets. Across five visual reasoning benchmarks, MoLE achieves an average score of 78.6, outperforming data-matched supervised fine-tuning by 4.9 and the strongest evaluated latent visual reasoning baseline at the same latent budget by 3.6. Representation analyses show lower latent-state similarity and more diverse visual attention, while masking the latent pathway reduces average performance by 9.2. These results demonstrate that specializing latent computation is more effective than merely increasing the number of latent tokens.

</details>


### [142] [CLoSeR: Closing the Loop for Long-Context Streaming Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01927)
*Moyang Li,Zihan Zhu,Wei Zhang,Marc Pollefeys,Daniel Barath*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses tracking drift in long-context streaming 3D reconstruction using feedforward foundation models. The proposed method (CLoSeR) leverages global descriptor retrieval for loop closure detection and optimizes frame poses on SE(3) manifold to achieve drift-free, kilometer-scale reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing feedforward foundation models for 3D reconstruction suffer from large tracking drift in long-context streaming reconstruction due to error accumulation. This limits their ability to produce accurate, drift-free reconstructions at kilometer scale.

Method: The method detects loop candidates through global descriptor retrieval, constructs loop-conditioned windows to estimate relative poses between looped frames, and optimizes all frame poses on the SE(3) manifold with sequential and loop closure constraints. The approach leverages the globally consistent scale produced by the streaming reconstruction backbone, avoiding pose graph optimization on Sim(3) or higher-dimensional SL(4) manifolds.

Result: The method significantly reduces drift and produces consistent geometry on kilometer-scale sequences, outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

Conclusion: By revisiting loop closure with streaming reconstruction foundation models, the proposed CLoSeR method enables accurate, drift-free, kilometer-scale reconstruction through efficient SE(3) pose optimization with sequential and loop closure constraints.

Abstract: Feedforward foundation models have recently shown remarkable 3D reconstruction capabilities. However, existing models exhibit large tracking drift in long-context streaming reconstruction due to error accumulation. In this paper, we revisit loop closure with streaming reconstruction foundation models to enable accurate, drift-free, kilometer-scale reconstruction. Specifically, our method detects loop candidates through global descriptor retrieval, and constructs loop-conditioned windows to estimate the relative poses between looped frames. Given the observation that our adopted streaming reconstruction backbone produces a globally consistent scale, we optimize all frame poses on the SE(3) manifold with sequential and loop closure constraints, avoiding the pose graph optimization on the Sim(3) or higher-dimensional SL(4) manifolds employed in prior works. Extensive experiments show that our method reduces drift and produces consistent geometry on kilometer-scale sequences, significantly outperforming the state of the art. Code is available at https://github.com/MoyangLi00/CLoSeR.git.

</details>


### [143] [Fewer Tokens, Better Action: GPT-6 Astra Robot Agents with 14% Higher Success Rate but 65% Fewer Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01939)
*Ruiyang Si,Jianxin Bi,Shunyu Yang,Rui Ni,Wenbo Huang,Qiang Wang,Shulong Jiang,Duomin Wang,Xiuyu Li,Haiwen Feng,Zhen Dong,Daquan Zhou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PyRUA-Lean is an interactive code-execution framework for VLM robot agents that reduces token overhead by combining feedback-driven primitive composition with selective observation. It composes classical robot primitives and learned VLA policies into Python cells with conditional checks and local retries, returning only explicitly requested feedback. This approach achieves 71.7% success vs 63.1% baseline, while using 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens on solved instances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision language model (VLM) agents for robot control incur substantial token overhead from repeated model invocations and redundant observations, making efficient feedback handling critical for practical deployment.

Method: PyRUA-Lean couples feedback-driven primitive composition with selective observation. The agent composes classical robot primitives and learned vision-language-action (VLA) policies into Python cells that perform conditional checks and local retries, returning only explicitly requested images and state feedback for replanning.

Result: Under equal LLM-call budgets across 700 simulated tasks from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, PyRUA-Lean increases overall success from 63.1% to 71.7%. On instances solved by both agents, it uses 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens.

Conclusion: The feedback-driven primitive composition with selective observation approach significantly improves efficiency and success rates of VLM robot agents, reducing computational overhead while maintaining or improving task completion.

Abstract: Vision language model (VLM) agents can control robots through visual feedback and action primitives, but repeated model invocations and redundant observations incur substantial token overhead. We introduce PyRUA-Lean, an interactive code-execution framework that couples feedback-driven primitive composition with selective observation: the agent composes classical robot primitives and learned vision-language-action (VLA) policies into Python cells that perform conditional checks and local retries, returning only explicitly requested images and state feedback for replanning. Across 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, we compare PyRUA-Lean with a tool-calling baseline using the same GPT-6 Astra planner and underlying robot primitives. Under equal LLM-call budgets, PyRUA-Lean increases overall success from 63.1% to 71.7%. On instances solved by both agents, it uses 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens.

</details>


### [144] [Latent-Foresight: End-to-End Learning Predictable Representations for Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01942)
*Efstathios Karypidis,Spyros Gidaris,Nikos Komodakis*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Latent-Foresight, an end-to-end framework that jointly learns a latent tokenizer and flow-based generative dynamics model to predict future scene evolution. Unlike prior two-stage approaches that use fixed dimensionality reduction on VFM features, this method explicitly shapes latent representations for temporal predictability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for future scene prediction rely on two-stage pipelines where VFM features are compressed using PCA or autoencoders, and a separate predictor is trained on the frozen latent space. This decoupling between representation learning and temporal prediction provides no guarantee that the latent space is structured for predictable dynamics.

Method: The proposed Latent-Foresight framework jointly learns a latent tokenizer and a flow-based generative dynamics model in an end-to-end manner. Key design choices include preventing latent collapse and aligning reconstruction with generative objectives to enable stable joint optimization.

Result: The approach learns more temporally coherent latent representations and consistently outperforms two-stage baselines across multiple future scene understanding tasks and prediction horizons. It eliminates separate training stages, including during high-resolution adaptation.

Conclusion: End-to-end joint optimization of tokenizer and dynamics model produces better temporally structured representations than decoupled two-stage approaches. This work demonstrates the importance of aligning representation learning with temporal prediction objectives for scene understanding tasks.

Abstract: Predicting the future evolution of a scene is a fundamental capability for world modeling. Recent work has shown that operating in the feature space of Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) yields semantically rich representations that support diverse future scene understanding tasks. However, existing approaches rely on two-stage pipelines, where VFM features are first compressed using fixed dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA) or independently trained autoencoders, and a separate predictor is trained on top of the resulting frozen latent space. This decoupling between representation learning and temporal prediction, as well as approaches that apply predictors directly on raw VFM features, provides no guarantee that the latent space is structured for predictable dynamics. In this work, we propose Latent-Foresight, an end-to-end framework that jointly learns a latent tokenizer and a flow-based generative dynamics model, explicitly shaping the representation to support temporal predictability. To enable stable joint optimization, we introduce several key design choices that prevent latent collapse and align reconstruction with generative objectives. Extensive experiments show that our approach learns more temporally coherent latent representations and consistently outperforms two-stage baselines across multiple future scene understanding tasks and prediction horizons, while eliminating separate training stages, including during high-resolution adaptation. We provide the implementation code and model weights at https://github.com/Sta8is/Latent-Foresight

</details>


### [145] [Anti-Persona: Disrupting Unauthorized Identity Binding and Recognition in Personalized Vision--Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01944)
*Abhishek Basu,Fahad Shamshad,Karthik Nandakumar*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Anti-Persona is a defense method that protects against unauthorized identity binding and recognition in personalized Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) by adding subtle visual perturbations that disrupt identity prototype alignment in the vision-encoder space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Few-shot personalization in LVLMs creates a significant privacy risk: adversaries can use a few reference images to bind a target identity and subsequently detect that identity in new images through natural-language queries. This identity binding attack enables unauthorized subject-aware querying and personalized retrieval, posing serious privacy concerns.

Method: The method exploits the key insight that identity personalization relies on visual features shared across multiple reference images. The approach: 1) Aggregates visual features from multiple reference images into an identity prototype, 2) Optimizes visually subtle perturbations that disrupt prototype alignment in the vision-encoder space, 3) Applies spatial smoothing and low-frequency preservation to maintain visual fidelity and resilience to image compression. The defense is prompt-independent and supports both proactive anti-personalization and reactive image protection.

Result: Experiments on two representative personalized LVLMs demonstrate protection rates of up to 95.0% while preserving visual fidelity. The method remains stable across prompt variations and evaluated identity-query tasks, and improves black-box transfer under encoder mismatch.

Conclusion: Anti-Persona provides an effective image-level defense against identity binding attacks in personalized LVLMs, achieving high protection rates while maintaining visual quality. Its prompt-independence and resilience to compression make it practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: Few-shot personalization enables large vision--language models (LVLMs) to learn user-specific visual concepts for applications such as personalized retrieval and subject-aware querying. However, it also creates a privacy risk: an adversary can bind a target identity from a few reference images and subsequently detect that identity in new images through natural-language queries. We introduce Anti-Persona, an image-level defense against unauthorized identity binding and recognition in personalized LVLMs. Our key insight is that identity personalization relies on visual features shared across multiple reference images. We aggregate these features into an identity prototype and optimize visually subtle perturbations that disrupt prototype alignment in the vision-encoder space. Spatial smoothing and low-frequency preservation further promote visual fidelity and practical resilience to image compression. The resulting protection does not depend on a specific prompt and supports both proactive anti-personalization and reactive image protection. Experiments on two representative personalized LVLMs demonstrate protection rates of up to $95.0\%$ while preserving visual fidelity. The method remains stable across prompt variations and evaluated identity-query tasks, and improves black-box transfer under encoder mismatch.

</details>


### [146] [EndoLive: Real-Time Style Transfer for Endoscopic Endonasal Skull Base Surgical Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01956)
*Griffin Hurt,Calvin Brinkman*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EndoLive is a real-time style transfer framework that transforms cadaveric endoscopic video to simulate living human anatomy, addressing the discrepancy between surgical training on cadavers and actual live surgeries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex endoscopic surgeries require extensive training, but cadaveric specimens differ significantly from living patients in tissue color and bleeding behavior, making the transition from training to live surgery challenging for surgeons to identify critical anatomical structures.

Method: EndoLive combines ConStructS GAN for realistic surgical style transfer with HyPER-GAN for complex real-time translations, trained on unpaired cadaveric and live endoscopic images, and tested on various devices.

Result: The framework achieves cadaveric-to-live translation at speeds well above real-time requirements while maintaining semantic consistency of critical anatomical structures.

Conclusion: EndoLive successfully bridges the gap between cadaveric training and live surgery by providing realistic real-time visual translation of endoscopic footage, potentially improving surgical training and preparation.

Abstract: Complex surgical procedures around critical anatomy, such as the endoscopic endonasal skull base surgery, requires significant practice and training on the part of the surgeon before they are allowed to perform the operation on a live patient. This training in typically done in cadaveric specimens, due to them containing the same critical structures as a living human. However, cadavers are not a perfect 1-to-1 substitute for a living patient. The dead and preserved tissues of a cadaver are colored completely differently than a living human, and -- without complex and expensive pumping systems -- do not bleed in the same way. As a result, identifying the critical pieces of anatomy that make this procedure so complex can be quite different in a live case than in a surgeon's cadaveric practice. This paper presents EndoLive, a framework for real-time style transfer between cadaveric endoscopic video and living human endoscopic video. Our method combines the ConStructS GAN model for realistic style transfer for surgical applications, with the HyPER-GAN model that can learn complex translations and perform them in real-time. We train EndoLive on unpaired cadaveric and live images taken from an endoscope, and test the trained model with cadaveric video, on a variety of devices. Experimental results demonstrate that EndoLive can perform cadaveric-to-live translation at speeds well above the minimum necessary for real-time, while maintaining semantic consistency of critical anatomical structures. Our source code is available at https://github.com/griffhurt/endolive.

</details>


### [147] [RASteer: Retain-Aware Activation Steering for Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01969)
*Yongliang Wu,Haori Lu,Yulun Wu,Jinqi Luo,Xingyu Zhu,Yaoyao Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RASteer is a training-free method for removing target concepts (copyrighted styles, characters, unsafe content) from text-to-image diffusion models while preserving the generation of non-target content. It addresses the problem that existing activation steering methods inadvertently suppress retained concepts due to overlap between target and retained concepts in the model's representation space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing activation steering methods build erasure directions primarily from target concepts, but these directions contain shared components that retained concepts rely on. Steering directly along this direction suppresses retained concepts and harms generation of non-target content. The core problem is the overlap between target and retained concepts in the model's representation space.

Method: The proposed RASteer method consists of two components: (1) Retain-Orthogonal Steering (ROS) builds a retain subspace from concepts to preserve and removes components aligned with this subspace from the erasure direction, making steering more specific to the target. (2) Overlap-Adaptive Calibration (OAC) uses the overlap between the erasure direction and retain subspace at each layer and denoising step to control how much shared components are removed, balancing target erasure and concept preservation.

Result: Experiments on unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure across multiple backbones and benchmarks show that RASteer matches or outperforms activation steering and weight editing baselines, achieving a better balance between erasure and preservation.

Conclusion: RASteer provides an effective training-free solution for concept erasure in diffusion models, successfully addressing the trade-off between removing target concepts and preserving the ability to generate non-target content through retain-aware steering and adaptive calibration.

Abstract: Concept erasure aims to remove a target concept, such as a copyrighted style, a recognizable character, or unsafe content, from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model while preserving its ability to generate other content. Existing activation steering methods build an erasure direction mainly from the target concept and adjust model activations along it at inference time. However, target and retained concepts often overlap in the model's representation space, so this direction also contains shared components that retained concepts rely on. Steering directly along this direction can therefore suppress retained concepts and harm the generation of non-target content. To address this issue, we propose Retain-aware Activation Steering (RASteer), a training-free method. RASteer first builds a retain subspace from the concepts to preserve. Retain-Orthogonal Steering (ROS) then removes components aligned with this subspace from the erasure direction, making steering more specific to the target. Since fully removing the shared components can weaken erasure, we further introduce Overlap-Adaptive Calibration (OAC). At each layer and denoising step, OAC uses the overlap between the erasure direction and the retain subspace to control how much of each shared component is removed, balancing target erasure and concept preservation. Experiments on unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure across multiple backbones and benchmarks show that RASteer matches or outperforms the activation steering and weight editing baselines we evaluate, achieving a better balance between erasure and preservation.

</details>


### [148] [Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01973)
*Yifan Wang,Gordon Guocheng Qian,Yanyu Li,Anil Kag,Yun Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TVRL introduces token-level credit assignment for video generation RL, using a frozen vision-language model's gradients to identify which video tokens affect the reward score, enabling more precise optimization than scalar rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL for video generation assigns one scalar reward to entire videos, which cannot localize errors - this causes optimization to perturb satisfactory tokens while under-targeting tokens that actually need correction.

Method: TVRL derives token-level credit from the reward being optimized by using a frozen vision-language model's answer likelihood. The model's outputs contribute to video-level reward while gradients reveal which video tokens affect the score. Implemented via Group Relative Policy Optimization using prompt-derived question rewards averaged into group-relative advantage and detached question-conditioned token-credit maps to reweight dense denoising-transition log-probabilities in clipped policy ratio.

Result: On VBench-2.0, TVRL achieves Overall score of 57.69, outperforming base model by 3.60 points. Improves matched GRPO baselines across three SDE samplers (SAGE, Flow, Dance) by 2.68-3.15 points and across four reward models (VideoAlign, VideoScore2, UnifiedReward2, Qwen3.5-9B) by 1.33-3.15 points.

Conclusion: Token-level credit assignment in video generation RL significantly improves performance over scalar rewards by enabling precise targeting of tokens that need correction while preserving satisfactory tokens.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for video generation usually assigns one scalar reward to an entire sampled video. Yet a video is not uniformly flawed: some visual tokens may already satisfy the prompt, whereas others require correction. A scalar reward cannot localize errors, causing optimization to perturb satisfactory tokens while under-targeting the tokens that actually need to change. We introduce Token-Level Video Reinforcement Learning, TVRL, a framework that derives token-level credit from the reward being optimized. Our key insight is that the answer likelihood of a frozen vision-language model provides both signals: its outputs contribute to the video-level reward, while magnitudes of its video-input gradients reveal which generated video tokens most affect that score. We instantiate TVRL in Group Relative Policy Optimization by averaging prompt-derived question rewards into one group-relative advantage and using detached, question-conditioned token-credit maps to reweight dense denoising-transition log-probabilities inside the clipped policy ratio. On VBench-2.0, TVRL achieves an Overall score of 57.69, outperforming the base model by 3.60 points. TVRL also improves matched GRPO baselines across three SDE samplers (SAGE, Flow, and Dance) by 2.68--3.15 points and across four reward models (VideoAlign, VideoScore2, UnifiedReward2, and Qwen3.5-9B) by 1.33--3.15 points.

</details>


### [149] [Continual Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models by Suppressing Cross-Edit Interference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01989)
*Yongliang Wu,Haori Lu,Jinqi Luo,Wei Cao,Xingyu Zhu,Yaoyao Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CEASE is a training-free method for continual concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models that uses subspace constraints to prevent interference between multiple erasure operations, addressing the problem of degradation in unrelated generations and collapse of previously erased targets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As erasure requests arrive over time, models must remove new targets without undoing prior erasures. Existing methods do not constrain interference across edits: residual perturbations outside the retain set interact and accumulate, degrading unrelated generations and sometimes collapsing previously erased targets into noise.

Method: CEASE imposes two subspace constraints on a closed-form solver: (1) adds the token representation of the shared replacement to the solver's invariance matrix, and (2) when interference is detected, projects the current update onto the orthogonal complement of dominant output directions extracted from cumulative past updates. A closed-form decomposition attributes accumulated interference to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions.

Result: Across continual erasure of celebrities, artistic styles, and instances, CEASE achieves the most consistent erase-preserve trade-off, while existing methods either degrade general generation or insufficiently erase targets.

Conclusion: CEASE successfully addresses the continual concept erasure problem by using subspace constraints to suppress interference sources, providing better balance between erasing unwanted concepts and preserving general generation capabilities compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Concept erasure removes copyright-protected, privacy-sensitive, or otherwise undesirable concepts from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models to support content governance and compliance. As erasure requests arrive over time, models must remove new targets without undoing prior erasures. Existing methods do not constrain interference across edits: residual perturbations outside the retain set interact and accumulate, degrading unrelated generations and sometimes collapsing previously erased targets into noise. We propose CEASE (Continual Erasure via Adaptive Subspace Editing), a training-free method that imposes two subspace constraints on a closed-form solver. CEASE adds the token representation of the shared replacement to the solver's invariance matrix and, when interference is detected, projects the current update onto the orthogonal complement of dominant output directions extracted from cumulative past updates. A closed-form decomposition attributes the accumulated interference to repeated activation of the shared replacement and overlap between successive update directions, showing that the two constraints suppress these respective sources. Across continual erasure of celebrities, artistic styles, and instances, CEASE achieves the most consistent erase-preserve trade-off, while existing methods either degrade general generation or insufficiently erase targets.

</details>


### [150] [Comparing a gradient boosting algorithm to the GOES FDC for wildfire detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01994)
*Asaf Vanunu,Boaz Nadler,Arnon Karnieli*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This study develops a CatBoost machine learning model for wildfire detection using GOES ABI satellite imagery, which outperforms the operational GOES Fire Detection and Characterization (FDC) product in precision, recall, F1 scores, and earlier detection capabilities, especially during nighttime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wildfires pose severe risks to human life, ecosystems, and property, requiring accurate and early detection methods. The operational GOES FDC product has limitations, particularly low recall during nighttime, necessitating improved detection approaches.

Method: A CatBoost model was trained on a large dataset containing thousands of GOES ABI images matched with over 300,000 VIIRS fire detections. The model was evaluated on a separate dataset across five different regions.

Result: The CatBoost model achieved F1 scores 0.16 to 0.38 higher than GOES FDC across all regions. It detected 26 out of 51 historical fire events before both VIIRS and GOES FDC, compared to only 6 earlier detections by GOES FDC. Notably, the CatBoost model achieved accurate detection during nighttime while GOES FDC had very low recall (~0.03).

Conclusion: Machine learning models, particularly CatBoost, can offer significant improvements over existing geostationary fire products, including higher accuracy, fewer false alarms, and earlier wildfire detection capabilities.

Abstract: Wildfires pose severe risks to human life, ecosystems, and property. This study presents a machine learning approach for wildfire detection from GOES ABI imagery. A CatBoost model was trained on a large dataset with thousands of ABI images and over 300,000 matching VIIRS fire detections. An evaluation on a separate dataset across five regions showed that the learned CatBoost model outperformed the operational GOES Fire Detection and Characterization (FDC) product. It achieved higher precision, recall, and F1 scores both within and outside the training area. The CatBoost model achieved F1 scores that were 0.16 to 0.38 higher than the GOES FDC in all regions. In addition, out of 51 historical fire events, the CatBoost detected 26 fires before both VIIRS and GOES FDC, compared to only six earlier detections by the GOES FDC. Importantly, the CatBoost model achieved accurate wildfire detection also during nighttime, whereas the GOES FDC obtained very low recall values, around 0.03. This study demonstrates that machine learning models may offer significant improvements over existing geostationary fire products, including higher accuracy, fewer false alarms, and earlier detection.

</details>


### [151] [From Reasoning Failures to Composable Video Spatial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01999)
*Pengzhan Sun,Junbin Xiao,Ramanathan Rajaraman,Shiu-hong Kao,Angela Yao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem that spatial reasoning benchmarks for vision-language models provide only task-level scores without revealing which underlying capabilities cause success or failure. The authors diagnose four sources of error and develop CROSS, a training-free library that improves performance on spatial reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spatial reasoning benchmarks evaluate vision-language models across diverse tasks, but task-level scores do not reveal which underlying capabilities account for success or failure. Each task requires recovering spatial evidence, representing geometry, and reasoning over it. The authors wanted to understand and diagnose the specific reasons for failure.

Method: The authors disentangle spatial reasoning capabilities by comparing predicted and ground-truth spatial context under a shared schema and coordinate contract. This reveals four recurring sources of error: (1) inaccurate perception, (2) missing information in the spatial context, (3) selection of wrong measurement, and (4) errors in reference frames or in tracking position and orientation. Based on this diagnosis, they develop CROSS, a training-free library of typed geometric operators and spatial skills that function over available evidence to support reliable video spatial reasoning.

Result: CROSS raises the average score from 55.9% to 60.2% on ReVSI and improves the SpatialClaw result from 62.8% to 66.3% on DSI-Bench.

Conclusion: Explicit handling of spatial conventions can repair systematic reasoning failures without additional training. The approach supplies verified context to non-coding VLMs or callable skills to a SpatialClaw agent.

Abstract: Spatial reasoning benchmarks evaluate vision-language models across diverse tasks, but task-level scores do not reveal which underlying capabilities account for success or failure. Each task requires recovering spatial evidence, representing geometry, and reasoning over it. We disentangle these capabilities by comparing predicted and ground-truth spatial context under a shared schema and coordinate contract. This comparison reveals four recurring sources of error: inaccurate perception, missing information in the spatial context, selection of the wrong measurement, and errors in reference frames or in tracking position and orientation. Guided by this diagnosis, we develop CROSS, a training-free library of typed geometric operators and spatial skills that function over available evidence to support reliable video spatial reasoning. The resulting library supplies verified context to non-coding VLMs or callable skills to a SpatialClaw agent. We evaluate \methodname{} on five benchmarks. \methodname{} raises the average score from 55.9\% to 60.2\% on ReVSI and improves the SpatialClaw result from 62.8\% to 66.3\% on DSI-Bench. These gains demonstrate that explicit handling of spatial conventions can repair systematic reasoning failures without additional training.

</details>


### [152] [Weather-Aware Domain Adaptation for Street-View Weather Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02000)
*Hossein Maghsoumi,George Atia,Yaser P. Fallah*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses multi-class weather recognition from street-view images under domain shift, where training data comes from non-street-view sources. The proposed WA-ADDA method conditions the domain discriminator on predicted weather to learn features that are both domain-invariant and weather-sensitive. A multi-dataset benchmark and standardized evaluation protocol are also introduced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adverse weather conditions (rain, snow, fog, dust) pose significant challenges for camera-based perception in autonomous driving. The key problem is domain shift: most available training data come from non-street-view sources that differ markedly from real driving scenes, making it difficult to deploy weather recognition models in practical autonomous driving applications.

Method: The paper proposes Weather-Aware Adversarial Discriminative Domain Adaptation (WA-ADDA), which conditions the domain discriminator on predicted weather labels. This approach promotes learning features that are both domain-invariant (usable across different data sources) and weather-sensitive (able to distinguish different weather conditions). The method is evaluated across multiple backbone networks: ResNet-50, EfficientNet, VGG, and DenseNet.

Result: WA-ADDA consistently improves street-view performance across all tested backbone architectures. The method yields strong per-class recalls in challenging weather conditions (rain, snow, fog, dust) while preserving accuracy in clear-weather scenarios. The multi-dataset benchmark and standardized evaluation protocol enable consistent comparison.

Conclusion: The findings demonstrate the feasibility of domain-adapted weather recognition for autonomous driving. The proposed WA-ADDA approach effectively bridges the domain gap between non-street-view training data and real street-view target images. The benchmark and evaluation protocol provide valuable resources for advancing robust on-board weather perception systems.

Abstract: Adverse conditions such as rain, snow, fog, and dust remain challenging for camera-based perception in autonomous driving. We study multi-class weather recognition from street-view images under domain shift, where most available training data come from non-street-view sources that differ markedly from real driving scenes. We propose Weather-Aware Adversarial Discriminative Domain Adaptation (WA-ADDA), which conditions the domain discriminator on predicted weather to promote features that are both domain-invariant and weather-sensitive. We also assemble a multi-dataset benchmark by unifying diverse non-street-view weather collections as sources and real street-view images as targets, and define a standardized evaluation protocol with macro accuracy as the primary metric. Across backbones (ResNet-50, EfficientNet, VGG, DenseNet), WA-ADDA consistently improves street-view performance and yields strong per-class recalls in challenging conditions while preserving clear-weather accuracy. These findings highlight the feasibility of domain-adapted weather recognition and the value of our benchmark for advancing robust, on-board perception.

</details>

### [153] [GS-PQM: A Parameter-Domain Quality Metric for Compressed Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00195)
*Pedro Martin,António Rodrigues,João Ascenso,Maria Paula Queluz*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: GS-PQM is a novel full-reference quality metric for Gaussian Splatting compression that operates directly in the GS parameter domain, using Support Vector Regression to estimate perceptual quality from parameter-domain distortion errors, outperforming 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing GS quality assessment relies on rendering predefined viewpoints, making quality estimates dependent on view selection. There was a need for a reliable objective quality assessment method that operates directly in the GS parameter domain to compare compression methods and guide development of more efficient GS codecs.

Method: GS-PQM estimates perceptual quality from a set of parameter-domain distortion errors using a Support Vector Regression model. It is a full-reference quality metric that operates directly in the GS parameter domain rather than requiring rendering.

Result: GS-PQM outperforms 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics in assessing compressed GS content, providing an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to rendering-based quality assessment.

Conclusion: GS-PQM offers an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to rendering-based quality assessment for evaluating GS compression methods, with superior performance compared to 25 existing metrics across image, video, and point-cloud quality assessment approaches.

Abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian Splatting (GS) compression have enabled substantial reductions in GS model size. Reliable objective quality assessment is therefore essential for comparing compression methods and guiding the development of more efficient GS codecs. Existing GS quality assessment typically relies on image and video quality metrics, requiring rendering of predefined viewpoints and making the quality estimate dependent on the selected views. This paper introduces GS-PQM, a novel full-reference quality metric for post-training GS compression that operates directly in the GS parameter domain. GS-PQM estimates perceptual quality from a set of parameter-domain distortion errors using a Support Vector Regression model. Experimental results show that GS-PQM outperforms 25 existing image, video, and point-cloud quality metrics in assessing compressed GS content, providing an accurate and computationally efficient alternative to rendering-based quality assessment.

</details>


### [154] [Diffusion Editing with Soft Mask: Pixel Level Redo of Image and Video with Adjustable Strength](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00359)
*Candi Zheng,Yuan Lan*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: SoftPaint is a zero-shot sampling method that enables fine-grained, pixel-level control in diffusion models using soft masks, allowing continuous spectrum edits from content preservation to full re-synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current diffusion models with prompt and reference image-guided editing are too coarse for pixel-level control. Training fine-grained control requires expensive pixel-wise annotations, while existing zero-shot methods yield unsatisfactory results.

Method: A Langevin-iteration-based sampler that respects per-pixel soft mask strengths, which is gradient-free and memory-efficient. It applies universally to image and video diffusion models.

Result: Achieves smooth, pixel-level edits across multiple image and video backbones, enabling tasks such as video editing.

Conclusion: SoftPaint provides a practical solution for fine-grained diffusion-based editing without requiring expensive pixel-wise annotations, offering universal applicability to image and video models with efficient computation.

Abstract: Diffusion models with prompt and reference image-guided editing have seen rapid progress, yet they remain too coarse for pixel-level control. One promising direction is to incorporate a soft mask that specifies spatially varying edit strengths but training such fine-grained control demands expensive pixel-wise annotations, while existing zero-shot methods often yield unsatisfactory results. We introduce SoftPaint, a new zero-shot sampling method that leverages soft masks to enable a continuous spectrum of edits, from fully preserving the original content to completely re-synthesizing the masked region. Going beyond zero-shot inpainting methods, we design a Langevin-iteration-based sampler that respects per-pixel soft mask strengths, which applies universally to image and video diffusion models, enabling tasks such as video editing. The method is gradient-free, memory-efficient, and achieves smooth, pixel-level edits across multiple image and video backbones.

</details>


### [155] [Smooth Curves from Curvature-Driven Subdivision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00020)
*Hassan Ugail*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: The paper introduces a novel interpolatory subdivision scheme where new points are defined by a curvature-profile model rather than traditional affine combinations. The scheme uses curvature estimation from circumscribed circles, Frenet integration with geodesic shooting, and places new points at half arc length. It works in both planar and spherical settings, exactly reproduces geodesics and circles, and when linearized becomes the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme. The authors resolve a conjecture by Ewald, Reif, and Sabin by proving that the refined polygons converge to a regular limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature (C² in arc length).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from addressing limitations in existing subdivision scheme theory, particularly the straightening condition proposed by Ewald, Reif, and Sabin which fails for this scheme. The authors seek to establish a theoretical framework that correctly characterizes geometric regularity for this curvature-based approach, ultimately confirming a conjecture that regularity is governed solely by the normal companion scheme.

Method: The method involves: (1) Estimating curvatures from circumscribed circles on each edge; (2) Prescribing a curvature profile based on these estimates; (3) Reconstructing the segment via Frenet integration with geodesic shooting; (4) Placing new points at half arc length. The planar linearization is achieved through a unique curvature prefilter, which transforms the scheme into the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme. The analysis focuses on measuring the normal part of relative distortion to repair the failed straightening condition.

Result: The scheme achieves convergence and geometric regularity. The refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature, which is twice continuously differentiable in arc length (C²). The straightening condition of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin fails for this scheme, but measuring only the normal part of the relative distortion successfully characterizes its regularity.

Conclusion: The paper concludes that the curvature-profile subdivision scheme provides a geometrically sound approach to interpolation that works identically in the plane and on the sphere. The key theoretical contribution is proving that regularity is governed by the normal companion scheme alone, confirming the conjecture of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin. This resolves an open problem in subdivision scheme theory by showing that the normal component of distortion is sufficient to characterize convergence and smoothness.

Abstract: We introduce and analyse an interpolatory subdivision scheme in which each inserted point is defined by a curvature-profile model rather than by an affine combination of its neighbours, and we establish its convergence and geometric regularity. On each edge, curvatures estimated from circumscribed circles prescribe a curvature profile, the segment is reconstructed by Frenet integration with geodesic shooting, and the new point is taken at half arc length. The construction works identically in the plane and on the sphere, reproduces geodesics and circles exactly, and a unique curvature prefilter turns its planar linearisation into the six-point Deslauriers-Dubuc scheme. The straightening condition of Ewald, Reif, and Sabin fails for this scheme. Measuring only the normal part of the relative distortion repairs their theory, and we prove that the refined polygons converge to a regular interpolatory limit curve with continuous tangent direction and curvature, twice continuously differentiable in arc length. Regularity is thus governed by the normal companion scheme alone, as these authors conjectured.

</details>


### [156] [Implementation Note 2: Approximating a Smooth Three-Dimensional Function on a Coarse Lattice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00203)
*Dennis Luxen*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: A method for approximating smooth 3D functions using low-resolution lookup tables combined with tetrahedral interpolation, with a specific application to RGB-to-CMYK color conversion. The method uses integer-only arithmetic, requiring no floating-point or division operations, making it suitable for low-power and real-time applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable efficient and accurate 3D function approximation (particularly for color conversion) on resource-constrained devices. Traditional approaches either require significant memory (full 8-bit lookup table needs 64 MiB) or computational resources for floating-point operations, which are unsuitable for low-power embedded systems.

Method: The method involves: (1) Preprocessing: sampling a 3D function once on a coarse grid (n=16 cells per axis yields 17³ nodes); (2) Runtime: for each input, locate the enclosing grid cube, select one of 6 tetrahedra within that cube, and compute weighted sum of the 4 corner values. The key innovation is an integer-only implementation requiring no floating-point or division operations, with all intermediate values fitting in 32 bits.

Result: For RGB-to-CMYK conversion with n=16 table (17³ nodes, 16-bit values): memory requirement is 38 KiB (vs. 64 MiB for full 8-bit table). Mean error is 0.08% ink per channel. The integer implementation differs from exact fractional tetrahedral interpolation by at most 1 unit of 16-bit output, with white and black reproduced exactly.

Conclusion: The proposed lookup table with tetrahedral interpolation and integer arithmetic is highly suitable for low-power devices and real-time applications with limited computational resources. It achieves a good balance between memory efficiency (38 KiB vs. 64 MiB), accuracy (0.08% mean error), and computational simplicity (integer-only, no floating-point/division).

Abstract: A smooth 3D function can be efficiently and accurately approximated by a 3D lookup table of significantly lower resolution combined with tetrahedral interpolation. The function is sampled once on a coarse grid in a preprocessing step. For each input, the enclosing grid cube is located, one of the 6 tetrahedra in this cube is selected, and the values at its 4 corners are combined by a weighted sum.
  For RGB to CMYK color conversion, a particularly frequent application of this, a table with $n = 16$ cells per axis ($17^3$ nodes, 16-bit values) requires 38\,KiB. A full 8-bit table requires 64\,MiB. As shown in an experimental evaluation, the mean error of the $n = 16$ table is 0.08\,\% ink per channel. For 8-bit input, the lookup uses integer arithmetic only (Section~\ref{sec:integer}). It requires no floating point and no division, and all intermediate values fit in 32 bits. Floating point is needed only to build the table, once and offline. The integer result differs from tetrahedral interpolation with exact fractions by at most 1 unit of the 16-bit output, and white and black are reproduced exactly. This makes the approach suitable for low-power devices and real-time applications where computational resources are limited.

</details>


### [157] [Plate-Local River Generation: Deterministic, Terrain-Aware, Downhill-Flowing Rivers for Infinite Procedural Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00301)
*Michael K. Davis*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper presents a deterministic algorithm for generating coherent, downhill-flowing river networks in infinite procedural worlds. The approach uses tectonic plate seeds to define terrain fields and bounded Voronoi-like plate domains, enabling localized river preprocessing. Rivers are traced downhill from highland sources and their heights are monotonically adjusted to guarantee downhill flow. The system uses lazy caching per plate and on-demand evaluation for efficient interactive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing procedural terrain generation methods produce coherent, downhill-flowing river networks only on fixed domains, while approaches for infinite worlds typically sacrifice network coherence or downhill-flow guarantees. There is a need for a method that can generate terrain-aware rivers in infinite procedural worlds while maintaining coherence and downhill-flow properties.

Method: The method uses tectonic plate seeds to define continuous terrain fields and bounded Voronoi-like plate domains. Within each plate, terrain is sampled on a low-resolution grid, and rivers are traced downhill from highland source nodes to coastlines, local minima, or existing confluences. River heights are monotonically adjusted along each path to ensure every segment descends. The river network is generated and cached lazily per plate. During full-resolution terrain sampling, distance to the cached river network is computed exactly, and river height is interpolated along nearby segments and blended with locally evaluated terrain on demand.

Result: The algorithm guarantees downhill flow along every river channel of the final terrain. The bounded warp of plate borders stays below the river border margin, ensuring coherence. The design enables efficient on-demand evaluation for interactive procedural worlds.

Conclusion: The proposed method makes terrain-aware river generation practical for interactive procedural worlds by supporting efficient on-demand evaluation while maintaining network coherence and downhill-flow guarantees. Performance analysis demonstrates the practical viability of the approach.

Abstract: Existing procedural terrain generation methods produce coherent, downhill-flowing river networks only on fixed domains, whereas approaches that extend to infinite worlds typically sacrifice network coherence or downhill-flow guarantees. This work presents a deterministic, terrain-aware, downhill-flowing river algorithm for infinite procedural worlds. Tectonic plate seeds define both continuous terrain fields and corresponding bounded Voronoi-like plate domains, so localized river preprocessing can operate directly on the geometric domain without sampling terrain fields for the purpose of locating plate boundaries. Within each plate, the terrain field is sampled on a low-resolution grid, and rivers are traced downhill from highland source nodes to coastlines, local minima, or existing confluences. River heights are then monotonically adjusted along each path so that every stored segment descends. The resulting river network is generated and cached lazily per plate, so each plate is processed independently of its neighbors. During full-resolution terrain sampling, the distance to the cached river network is computed exactly, and river height is interpolated along nearby segments and blended with the locally evaluated terrain on demand, without caching the blended result itself. Because the warp of the plate borders is bounded below the river border margin, this guarantees downhill flow along every river channel of the final terrain. Together, these design choices make terrain-aware river generation practical for interactive procedural worlds by supporting efficient on-demand evaluation, as demonstrated by the performance analysis presented in this work.

</details>


### [158] [Dirichlet Splatting: Differentiable Rendering for Wave-Based Inverse Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00618)
*Xingyu Chen,Wuqiong Zhao,Xinyu Zhang,Tzu-Mao Li*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: This paper introduces a novel rendering primitive for wave-based coherent imaging (terahertz tomography, synthetic-aperture acoustics, millimeter-wave radar) that replaces Gaussian splatting with the physically exact Dirichlet kernel, paired with a specialized optimizer (DSFW) to handle the challenging optimization landscape. The method achieves 0.018 bin RMSE and 10-50x speedup over waveform-level automatic differentiation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wave-based coherent imaging forms images via Fourier-processing finite-length signals with an exact point spread function that is a Dirichlet kernel (complex-valued, oscillatory, periodic). However, transplanting 3D Gaussian splatting to coherent sensing fails because Gaussian splats discard sidelobe energy (10-20% of total) and phase that governs coherent interference between reflectors.

Method: 1) Replace learned Gaussian footprint with physically exact Dirichlet kernel of finite-window DFT, modulated by a surfel carrying area, normal, and material; 2) Use Dirichlet Sliding Frank-Wolfe (DSFW) solver combining variable projection, residual dual certificates, and certificate-driven hard replacement of low-utility surfels; 3) Add periodic low-resolution coupled Levenberg-Marquardt correction to navigate the rugged loss landscape.

Result: The Dirichlet kernel admits O(1) closed-form evaluation, enabling forward model that matches FFT ground truth to machine precision while remaining differentiable end-to-end. On dense terahertz reconstruction, the method recovers reflector centers to 0.018 bin RMSE, 10-50x faster than waveform-level automatic differentiation, where Gaussian splats fail.

Conclusion: The proposed Dirichlet kernel primitive with DSFW solver successfully bridges the gap between 3D Gaussian splatting and coherent imaging physics, achieving superior accuracy and efficiency compared to both Gaussian splatting and waveform-level automatic differentiation approaches.

Abstract: Wave-based coherent imaging, including terahertz tomography, synthetic-aperture acoustics, and millimeter-wave radar, forms images by Fourier-processing finite-length signals, with an exact point spread function that is not Gaussian but a Dirichlet kernel: complex-valued, oscillatory, and periodic. However, transplanting 3D Gaussian splatting to coherent sensing fails by construction; Gaussian splats discard the sidelobe energy (10-20% of the total) and the phase that governs coherent interference between reflectors. Our key idea is to replace the learned Gaussian footprint with the physically exact Dirichlet kernel of the finite-window DFT, modulated by a surfel that carries area, normal, and material, so that the rendering primitive matches the measurement physics instead of approximating it. We pair this primitive with a specialized solver, Dirichlet Sliding Frank-Wolfe (DSFW), that combines variable projection, residual dual certificates, and certificate-driven hard replacement of low-utility surfels, with periodic low-resolution coupled Levenberg-Marquardt correction, navigating the rugged loss landscape that breaks generic first-order optimizers. The Dirichlet kernel admits an O(1) closed-form evaluation, so the forward model matches FFT ground truth to machine precision while remaining differentiable end-to-end. On dense terahertz reconstruction, our method recovers reflector centers to 0.018 bin RMSE, 10-50x faster than waveform-level automatic differentiation, where Gaussian splats fail.

</details>

### [159] [Frozen Scenes, Shifting Winners: Configuration Fragility in Text-to-3D Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00447)
*Anson Y. Lam,Shuqing Li,Michael R. Lyu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits whether text-to-3D leaderboard rankings can change when generated scenes remain fixed but render/caption settings vary. Using 300 frozen scenes from 6 generators, 8 render/caption factors, and 19 alignment evaluators, the study finds that configuration variance exceeds between-generator variance for 17/19 evaluators, and 18/19 evaluators change their point-estimate winner under some configuration. However, no reversal survives simultaneous inference over the full search.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to investigate the stability and reliability of text-to-3D generation leaderboards, specifically whether the evaluation protocol itself (camera settings, caption wording) can influence rankings. This addresses concerns about measurement protocol dependency in generative AI benchmarking.

Method: The study uses 300 frozen scenes from six generators, varying eight render and caption factors across 19 alignment evaluators plus one perceptual-quality control. They test four targeted scene degradations and analyze ranking stability, decision uncertainty, and targeted sensitivity.

Result: Peak configuration variance exceeds between-generator variance for 17/19 alignment evaluators. Prompt-bootstrap lower bounds exceed 1 for 11/19 evaluators. Rankings are more stable than scores, yet 18/19 evaluators change their point-estimate winner under some configuration. No reversal survives simultaneous inference over the full search. No evaluator exceeds 67% directional discrimination on layout scrambling.

Conclusion: The audit demonstrates that observed winner changes are descriptive, not confirmed changes in generator superiority. The authors recommend reporting (generator, score, card ID) with protocol-dependent comparisons and selection-aware uncertainty to improve leaderboard reliability.

Abstract: Can a text-to-3D leaderboard change when every generated scene stays fixed? We audit this question for rendered-image evaluation, where camera settings and caption wording become part of the measurement protocol. Across 300 frozen scenes from six generators, we vary eight render and caption factors for 19 alignment evaluators plus one perceptual-quality control, then test four targeted scene degradations. Peak configuration variance exceeds between-generator variance for 17/19 alignment evaluators, with prompt-bootstrap lower bounds above 1 for 11/19. Rankings are more stable than scores, yet 18/19 evaluators change their point-estimate winner under some configuration. Pairwise protocol margin envelopes show which comparisons keep their direction across the tested settings. Selected pairs have opposite pointwise intervals, but no reversal survives simultaneous inference over the full search. Thus the observed winner changes are descriptive, not confirmed changes in generator superiority. Sensitivity remains separate: no evaluator, even the prompt-free control, exceeds 67% tie-adjusted directional discrimination on layout scrambling, which is diagnostic rather than human-validated ground truth. The audit separates score stability, decision uncertainty, and targeted sensitivity, and recommends reporting (generator, score, card ID) with protocol-dependent comparisons and selection-aware uncertainty.

</details>


### [160] [Heavy-Tailed Memory Traces in Long-Horizon Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00010)
*Xinyuan Song,Zekun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in evaluating language agent memory systems: beyond task success and token cost, the "shape" of memory use matters. The authors discover that under finite context and repeated retrieval, agent memory concentrates on a small core while leaving rare states in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. They propose Core-Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget using exponent τ while retaining a summarized tail, achieving significant token savings while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory systems for long-horizon language agents are evaluated only by task success or token cost. The authors argue that the missing evaluation metric is the "shape" of memory use - how memory concentrates on certain states while leaving others in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. This observation motivates the need to understand and control the core-tail distribution of memory retrieval.

Method: The authors conduct a "conservative tail audit" to study memory concentration effects. They compare different agent policies (random-walk vs semantic LLM policies) and find that concentration patterns are reproducible but policy-dependent. Based on this audit, they propose Core-Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget with a single exponent τ while retaining a summarized tail.

Result: On Synthetic Graph World: CTWM preserves full state and transition coverage, reduces prompt tokens by 5.9%, and lowers bottom-half tail prediction error by 13.6% relative to graph-memory baseline. On ALFWorld: consistent token savings. On LongMemEval: 24.48% token reduction with aggregate accuracy parity.

Conclusion: Heavy-tailed memory traces are not only a diagnostic of finite retrieval but also a practical control signal for token-efficient agent world models. The core-tail structure provides a new dimension for evaluating and optimizing memory systems in long-horizon language agents.

Abstract: Long-horizon language agents increasingly rely on external memory as a frozen world model, yet current memory systems are usually judged only by task success or token cost. We argue that the missing object is the shape of memory use: under finite context and repeated retrieval, agent memory can concentrate on a small core while leaving rare states in a long tail where prediction errors accumulate. We study this effect through a conservative tail audit and find that concentration is reproducible but policy-dependent. Random-walk agents produce log-normal-compatible retrieval artifacts, whereas semantic LLM policies yield the strongest truncated-power-law-compatible core--tail traces. Motivated by this audit, we propose Core--Tail World Model (CTWM), a rank-based memory controller that allocates prompt budget with a single exponent $τ$ while retaining a summarized tail. On Synthetic Graph World, CTWM preserves full state and transition coverage, reduces prompt tokens by 5.9%, and lowers bottom-half tail prediction error by 13.6% relative to a graph-memory baseline. The same paired comparison gives consistent token savings on ALFWorld and a 24.48% token reduction on LongMemEval with aggregate accuracy parity. These results suggest that heavy-tailed memory traces are not only a diagnostic of finite retrieval, but also a practical control signal for token-efficient agent world models.

</details>


### [161] [When Do Causal World Models Help Modular LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00012)
*Xinyuan Song,Zekun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents that act through interconnected services (order, payment, inventory, shipment). The key insight is that standard observational world models fail to capture causal relationships between modules, leading to irreducible interventional errors. The framework uses local actions as intervention-response evidence to recover cross-module causal interfaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a fundamental gap in LLM agent planning: observational traces show correlations (e.g., payment precedes shipment) but cannot identify causal relationships (whether payment authorizes shipment, inventory mediates the effect, or a hidden trigger explains both). This gap becomes critical when agents need to plan interventions in modular systems where actions in one module affect valid transitions in another.

Method: The authors propose FedCausalCompose, which uses local actions as intervention-response evidence to identify cross-module causal interfaces. They analyze the conditions under which causal world models outperform observational models, specifically examining how intervention-response coverage and local mechanism errors affect prediction accuracy. They test this in diagnostic agent settings with different environment types (structured tool environments vs. dialogue/narrative environments).

Result: Key findings: (1) Observational world models incur irreducible interventional error under unblocked back-door paths; (2) Interface recovery improves with intervention-response coverage; (3) Oracle causal composition beats non-causal lower bounds when coverage and local mechanism errors are controlled; (4) Causal interfaces help most in structured tool environments with explicit API signatures; (5) Dialogue/narrative environments often ignore causal information unless it becomes decision-relevant through attention anchors.

Conclusion: The paper identifies a concrete condition for causal world models in LLM agents: causal structure helps when cross-module interfaces are both statistically identifiable (through intervention-response evidence) and presented in a form the agent can use at action time (e.g., API preconditions/effects). This work bridges causal inference and LLM agent planning, providing a framework for when and how causal world models add value in modular agent systems.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act through modular systems, such as order, payment, inventory, and shipment services, where actions in one module change which transitions are valid in another. Standard world models usually fit observational traces, but this is not the quantity needed for intervention-time planning: a trace may show that payment precedes shipment without identifying whether payment authorizes shipment, inventory mediates the effect, or a hidden trigger explains both. We study this gap through FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents in which local actions provide intervention-response evidence for cross-module interfaces. We first show that observational world models incur an irreducible interventional error under unblocked back-door paths, that interface recovery improves with intervention-response coverage, and that an oracle causal composition can beat the non-causal lower bound when coverage and local mechanism errors are controlled. We then test the resulting prediction in diagnostic agent settings. Causal interfaces help most in structured tool environments, where API signatures expose preconditions and downstream effects. In contrast, dialogue and narrative environments often ignore raw edge lists unless a short attention anchor makes the causal information decision-relevant. These results identify a concrete condition for causal world models in LLM agents: causal structure helps when cross-module interfaces are both statistically identifiable and presented in a form the agent can use at action time.

</details>


### [162] [From Proposal to Verified Effect: Praxa, an Evidence-Bound Harness for Governed AI Agent Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00015)
*Stefan G. Creadore*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Praxa is an agent harness architecture that makes LLM agent state transitions (proposal, authority, dispatch, verified external effect, promotion) explicit through deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion. The paper presents four evidence lanes but notably does not establish superiority in any comparison - all claims are hedged with "does not establish" or "does not support superiority."


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors identify that LLM agents can propose and execute actions, but the different states (proposal, authority, dispatch, verified external effect, promotion) represent different claims that need explicit representation and testing. The motivation is to create an architecture that makes authority-to-effect transitions explicit and testable.

Method: Praxa implements five mechanisms: (1) deterministic admission for proposal handling, (2) brokered execution for authority management, (3) external read-back for verified external effects, (4) reconciliation for state consistency, and (5) reviewed promotion for state transitions.
