Four evidence lanes are reported: unit/workerd testing, Terminal-Bench pilot, coordination-proxy comparison, and deployed evidence analysis.

Result: Four evidence lanes: (1) 1,027/1,027 unit tests, 89/89 Workerd tests, 363 source files instrumented; (2) Terminal-Bench pilot showed no superiority for reliability layer (37.49% more input, 50.73% more output tokens); (3) Coordination-proxy comparison showed 37.11% fewer tokens, 33.84% lower cost but doesn't establish improved quality/latency; (4) Deployed evidence shows bounded reflection etc. but no production outcome lift.

Conclusion: The contribution is an "evidence-bound architecture" making authority-to-effect transitions explicit and testable. Critically, the paper explicitly states that current evidence does NOT establish: adversarial security, production safety, general specialist superiority, autonomous recursive optimization, or user benefit. The paper is notably self-critical and hedged.

Abstract: Large-language-model agents can propose and execute actions, but proposal, authority, dispatch, verified external effect, and serving promotion are different claims. We present Praxa, an agent harness that represents these states explicitly through deterministic admission, brokered execution, external read-back, reconciliation, and reviewed promotion. We report four evidence lanes. First, an author-run repository-local audit at a pinned revision passed 1,027/1,027 unit tests and 89/89 Workerd tests, instrumented all 363 expected source files, and met four coverage floors; raw per-test transcripts and independent reproduction are unavailable. Second, in a provider-backed Terminal-Bench Core 0.1.1 pilot across 12 curated tasks, baseline and reliability-layer arms each passed 17/36 strict trials. The reliability layer used 37.49% more input and 50.73% more output tokens, so the pilot does not support superiority. Third, in a post-debug, two-order coordination-proxy development comparison, baseline and a source-authored candidate each completed 180/180 trials with equal measured accuracy, full hermetic crash recovery, and zero protected violations. The candidate used 37.11% fewer tokens, 33.84% lower estimated endpoint cost, and 11.63% fewer steps; this does not establish improved quality, latency, or production behavior. Fourth, deployed source/configuration evidence shows bounded reflection, recall accounting, memory compilation, and tool-health paths, but no production outcome lift. Praxa's supported contribution is an evidence-bound architecture that makes authority-to-effect transitions explicit and testable. Current evidence does not establish adversarial security, production safety, general specialist superiority, autonomous recursive optimization, or user benefit.

</details>


### [163] [What Do Rationales Communicate? A Message-Intervention Study in Role-Specialized QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00018)
*Jiameng Zhang,Hongqiu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates what rationales passed from reasoner to verifier actually contribute in role-specialized QA pipelines. Using a message-intervention diagnostic that varies only the rationale while fixing evidence and answers, the authors find that faithful rationales add almost no answer accuracy over no rationale, but corrupted rationales strongly alter support judgments (10-22% shift with blind verifier, 34-55% with explicit rationale-checking). This reveals the rationale channel as a failure surface rather than a performance enhancer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to understand what value rationale messages actually provide in reasoner-to-verifier pipelines - whether they improve answers, strengthen support assessment, or introduce new failure modes. The motivation is to diagnose the actual utility of the rationale channel rather than assuming it helps.

Method: The authors introduce a "message-intervention diagnostic" that fixes the evidence and candidate answer while systematically varying only the rationale passed across the reasoner-to-verifier boundary. They test on 400 examples from MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultiHopQA using DeepSeek as both generator and verifier. They compare faithful rationales, corrupted rationales, and harmless paraphrases under both blind verifier and explicit rationale-checking prompts. They also conduct human audits.

Result: Faithful rationales add almost no answer accuracy over no rationale. Corrupted rationales strongly alter support judgments: 10-22% shift with blind verifier, 34-55% with explicit rationale-checking. Final answers move less (2-30%), and only 2.9-35.3% of corrupted support flips co-occur with answer changes. Human audits reveal 16/42 valid corruptions are corruption-overtrust cases, and blind humans reject or mark unclear 9/10 audited corrupted rationales that the model accepts.

Conclusion: The rationale channel is a verification-message mechanism that primarily affects support assessment rather than answer accuracy. It should be evaluated as a potential failure surface, not merely as a route to higher answer accuracy. The channel can be active, amplified, inert, or folded into the task label depending on context.

Abstract: Role-specialized QA pipelines increasingly pass rationales from a reasoner to a verifier, but it is unclear what this message actually buys: better answers, stronger support assessment, or a new failure surface. We introduce a message-intervention diagnostic that fixes the evidence and candidate answer while varying only the rationale passed across the reasoner-to-verifier boundary. On 400 MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultiHopQA examples with DeepSeek as generator and verifier, faithful rationales add almost no answer accuracy over no rationale, while corrupted rationales strongly alter support judgments. Under a blind verifier prompt, harmless paraphrases shift support by only 0--2.5%, whereas corrupted rationales shift support by 10--22%; an explicit rationale-checking prompt amplifies the same pattern to 34--55%. Final answers move less (2--30%), and only 2.9--35.3% of corrupted support flips co-occur with answer changes. Human audits show why this matters: 16/42 valid corruptions are corruption-overtrust cases, and blind humans reject or mark unclear 9/10 audited corrupted rationales that the model accepts. Cross-model and task-boundary checks show when the channel is active, amplified, inert, or folded into the task label. Rationale sharing should be evaluated as a verification-message mechanism, not merely as a route to higher answer accuracy.

</details>


### [164] [Measuring the Microtask Eligibility Gap: When Is an Off-the-Shelf SLM Enough for an Agent Harness?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00025)
*Jundong Hu,Shekar Ramachandran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates whether off-the-shelf small language models (SLMs) can handle microtasks around an LLM planner (auto-approving shell commands, writing memory, selecting tools, ranking past turns) and whether quantization helps. The authors find that 0 out of 16 configurations (4 tasks × 4 Qwen3 models) pass practitioner-defined thresholds, and quantization does not improve eligibility. The gap is attributed to capability deficits rather than decoding threshold issues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether SLMs can handle microtasks around frontier LLMs in agent systems, and whether quantization could make them viable alternatives. They aim to determine if SLMs meet practitioner-defined performance thresholds.

Method: The authors built a benchmark of 4 microtasks with fixed prompts and automatic metrics, each with a pre-specified threshold τ anchored to a cheap non-LLM baseline and a CI-aware eligibility rule. They evaluated Qwen3 models (0.6/1.7/4/8B) at FP16, greedy decoding, with one frozen prompt and no tuning. They used diagnostic tests (T1/T3/T4 via logprob decision-threshold, T2 via context-length/cascade probe) to separate capability deficits from decoding threshold issues. They also tested 4-bit quantization (RTN/GPTQ/AWQ) and replicated on Llama-3.x. Robustness was checked via τ-sweep and prompt paraphrasing.

Result: 0 of 16 configurations passed eligibility. Quantization caused damage dependent on model size and moved no configuration into eligibility. The failures were categorized into 4 regimes: capability deficits vs. decoding threshold issues. The results replicated on Llama-3.x (12/12 ineligible) and were robust to anchor choice and prompt wording (0/112 eligible across original + 3 paraphrases per cell).

Conclusion: Practitioners should place SLMs behind a baseline that meets the CI-backed threshold, using SLMs only where the baseline fails. A 4B reranker over BM25 shortlist beats BM25 (+0.047 [0.020, 0.073]), but does not itself certify eligibility. The gap tracks model size more than precision.

Abstract: Agent harnesses increasingly want to run small language models (SLMs) on the microtasks around a frontier large language model (LLM) planner: auto-approving shell commands, writing memory, selecting tools, ranking past turns. We ask whether off-the-shelf SLMs meet practitioner-defined thresholds and, when they fail, why, and whether quantization changes the answer. We build a benchmark of 4 such microtasks with fixed prompts and automatic metrics, each with a pre-specified threshold $τ$ anchored to a cheap non-LLM baseline and a CI-aware eligibility rule (a configuration passes only if its confidence bound clears $τ$). Sweeping Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B at their best (FP16, greedy, one frozen prompt, no tuning), we find an eligibility gap: 0 of 16 (4 tasks $\times$ 4 models) configurations pass (verified by checking the raw outputs and parser behavior). A logprob decision-threshold diagnostic (T1/T3/T4; T2 via a context-length/cascade probe) separates the failures into capability deficits and failures that can be addressed by changing the decoding threshold (4 regimes). Quantization to 4-bit (RTN/GPTQ/AWQ) does damage that depends on model size and moves no configuration into eligibility (certified on the reconstructable hard-label tasks T1/T3, diagnostic/windowed robustness on T2/T4), so the gap tracks model size more than precision; it replicates on Llama-3.x (12/12 ineligible) and is robust to the anchor choice (a $τ$-sweep) and to prompt wording (0/112 eligible across the original plus 3 neutral paraphrases per cell). The practical implication: place SLMs behind a baseline that meets the CI-backed threshold, and use the SLM only where the baseline fails to meet the threshold; e.g. a 4B re-ranker over a BM25 shortlist beats BM25 ($+0.047$ [0.020, 0.073], without itself certifying eligibility).

</details>


### [165] [Characterizing a Configuration Where Inference-Time PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting Is Inert: Evidence from Three Reasoning LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00047)
*Khawaja Murad ul Hassan,Mehran Ebrahimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG), an inference-time intervention where a high-scoring prefix from a pruned chain-of-thought is grafted as an in-context demonstration into a still-decoding sibling. Through extensive experiments across multiple models, benchmarks, and PRMs, the authors find that PPFG performs statistically identically to independent parallel-CoT baseline. Analysis reveals that only 14% of injection events target genuinely struggling chains, while the rest target already-succeeded, near-completion, or flat-PRM-plateau chains where rescue grafts cannot help.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from observed diversity collapse in parallel chain-of-thought reasoning, which has motivated inference-time interventions. PPFG represents the most cost-minimal operationalization of cross-trajectory step-level transfer. The authors test it at the operating point where prior fragment-grafting work reported gains only under additional compensating ingredients, to isolate and evaluate this mechanism's standalone effectiveness.

Method: The authors tested PPFG on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Math-Shepherd on full MATH500 (n=500, three seeds), examining both stagnation- and random-targeting variants. They conducted a four-bucket classification of 322 stagnation-rule injection events to characterize why the intervention fails. The study replicated findings across three base LMs, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and a compatibility-gate sweep. They used two-one-sided-tests analysis to promote parity to positive equivalence on all twelve Qwen/LLaMA cells, and performed per-event spot-checks and surviving-sibling counterfactual analysis.

Result: PPFG in both stagnation- and random-targeting variants is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel-CoT baseline on every measured axis. Only 14% of injection events targeted genuinely struggling chains; the rest landed on chains that had already succeeded, were near completion, or sat on a flat PRM plateau. A random control matches the same parity at 2.4x the firing rate, indicating the inertness is not heuristic-specific. The finding replicates across three base LMs, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and a compatibility-gate sweep. Injected chains prune at 2.75x the matched-step rate, but no population-level compensation is observed. A hindsight oracle bounds any per-problem gain from choosing PPFG over independent at +0.13 pp.

Conclusion: The study establishes that PPFG provides no measurable benefit over independent parallel-CoT at the tested operating point. The authors contribute an equivalence-testing template for establishing inference-time mechanism nulls, with every claim scoped to its tested operating point. The failure is attributed to poor targeting: the intervention primarily injects fragments into chains that don't need rescue (already succeeded, near completion, or on flat PRM plateau), rather than genuinely struggling chains. This work suggests that future fragment-grafting interventions need better targeting mechanisms to be effective.

Abstract: Diversity collapse in parallel chain-of-thought has motivated inference-time interventions built on a natural design: when a process reward model (PRM) prunes a chain, its high-PRM prefix is extracted and grafted verbatim as an in-context demonstration into a still-decoding sibling. We isolate this mechanism, PRM-Pruned Fragment Grafting (PPFG), as the most cost-minimal operationalization of cross-trajectory step-level transfer, and test it at the operating point where prior fragment-grafting work reports gains only under additional compensating ingredients. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Math-Shepherd on full MATH500 (n=500, three seeds), PPFG in both stagnation- and random-targeting variants is statistically indistinguishable from an independent parallel-CoT baseline on every measured axis. We characterize why: a four-bucket classification of 322 stagnation-rule injection events shows only 14% targeted a genuinely struggling chain; the rest landed on chains that had already succeeded, were near completion, or sat on a flat PRM plateau, states a rescue graft cannot change. No compound-gate refinement jointly achieves well-targeted firing and adequate density, and a random control matches the same parity at 2.4x the firing rate, so the inertness is not heuristic-specific. The finding replicates across three base LMs, six benchmarks, a second PRM, and a compatibility-gate sweep; two-one-sided-tests analysis promotes the parity to positive equivalence on all twelve Qwen/LLaMA cells. A per-event spot-check finds injected chains prune at 2.75x the matched-step rate, but a surviving-sibling counterfactual finds no population-level compensation. A hindsight oracle bounds any per-problem gain from choosing PPFG over independent at +0.13 pp. We contribute an equivalence-testing template for establishing inference-time mechanism nulls, with every claim scoped to its tested operating point.

</details>


### [166] [Gradient-Aligned Pair Selection for Personalized Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00061)
*Ruoming Jin,Xinyu Li,Hao Zhou,Jianfeng Zhu,Ruixin Guo,Feodor Dragan,Lei Xu,Haixun Wang,Yang Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses personalized LLM alignment by proposing GAP-DPO, a geometry-aligned preference optimization method that performs utility-aware pair selection. The key insight is that preference pair selection is a geometric decision affecting optimization outcomes, not just a heuristic preprocessing step.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing DPO approaches for personalized preference learning rely on heuristic pair selection criteria (e.g., likelihood-based extremes) that decouple optimization from explicit user utility, leading to degraded personalization. The authors recognized that pair selection critically affects personalization quality but lacks a principled framework.

Method: The paper formalizes personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by analyzing the first-order interaction between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. Under off-policy sampling, they show DPO transitions from error-corrective to reinforcement-like updates when preference margins align with utility gradients. Based on this, they propose GAP-DPO, which performs utility-aware, geometry-aligned pair selection while controlling distribution shift via epoch-wise regeneration.

Result: Experiments on personalized text generation benchmarks show that GAP-DPO consistently improves stylistic fidelity, preference alignment, and generation quality compared to standard DPO variants.

Conclusion: Gradient alignment serves as a unifying principle for personalized preference optimization. Pair selection is an intrinsic component of optimization geometry rather than a heuristic preprocessing step. This work establishes a principled framework for understanding and improving preference pair selection in personalized LLM alignment.

Abstract: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) requires aligning generation behavior with user-specific preferences rather than aggregate quality. While Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a stable framework for preference learning, its effectiveness in personalized settings critically depends on how preference pairs are selected. Existing approaches typically rely on heuristic criteria, such as likelihood-based extremes, which decouple optimization from explicit user utility and can lead to degraded personalization. We formalize personalized preference learning as a geometry-aligned optimization problem by analyzing the first-order interaction between gradients of expected user utility and DPO update directions. Our analysis reveals that, under off-policy sampling, the DPO update transitions from a purely error-corrective signal to a reinforcement-like update when preference margins are directionally aligned with utility gradients. This perspective exposes pair selection as a geometric decision that governs whether preference optimization advances or hinders personalization. Motivated by this insight, we propose GAP-DPO (Geometry-Aligned Preference DPO), an iterative algorithm that performs utility-aware, geometry-aligned pair selection while controlling distribution shift via epoch-wise regeneration. Experiments on personalized text generation benchmarks show that GAP-DPO consistently improves stylistic fidelity, preference alignment, and generation quality compared to standard DPO variants. Together, our results establish gradient alignment as a unifying principle for personalized preference optimization and demonstrate that pair selection is an intrinsic component of the optimization geometry rather than a heuristic preprocessing step.

</details>


### [167] [K-Dense BYOK: An Open-Source AI Research Assistant That Runs Locally and Keeps a Hash-Chained Lab Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00074)
*Aubrey M. Brueckner,Darshil Patel,Yuhuan He,Timothy Kassis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: K-Dense BYOK is an open-source AI research assistant that runs locally on researchers' computers, providing scientific scaffolding, workflow templates, and comprehensive record-keeping. It distinguishes itself from general AI assistants through its library of scientific procedures, Living Lab Notebook with non-erasable entries, and activity logging that captures agent actions (not just claims). Benchmark tests on 20 interdisciplinary research prompts showed it outperformed two managed platforms on scientific quality and research execution, being the only solution to record software environments and provide reproducible commands.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation addresses two key problems: (1) the need for AI research assistants that keep data on researcher-controlled machines rather than cloud platforms, and (2) the common failure of model overclaiming (where AI agents make claims about what they did that aren't verifiable), identified in the authors' earlier benchmark of nine frontier models.

Method: K-Dense BYOK was evaluated against two managed platforms on 20 interdisciplinary research prompts using a pre-fixed rubric. The system was tested for: scientific quality, research execution, environment record-keeping, and reproducibility (presence of commands to regenerate results). The key innovation is the logging mechanism that observes agent actions rather than accepting agent self-reports.

Result: K-Dense BYOK outperformed both managed platforms on both scientific quality and research execution. It was the only system that recorded the software environment and provided reproducible commands. One competing platform using the same frontier model supplied neither. A limitation noted: environment records were files written by the agent, not captured in the observed log itself.

Conclusion: K-Dense BYOK represents a viable open-source alternative to cloud-based AI research assistants, with superior record-keeping and reproducibility. The key innovation of observation-based logging (rather than agent self-reporting) addresses model overclaiming. Future work is needed to capture software environment information directly in the log rather than relying on agent-written files.

Abstract: K-Dense BYOK (bring your own keys) is a free, open-source AI research assistant for scientists in any field that runs on the researcher's own computer. The researcher supplies access to a model of their choice, hosted or running locally, and the application supplies everything else: a place for the work to run, a layer of scientific scaffolding, and a complete record. Each project is an ordinary folder, so the data, the code, the results, and the record stay on a machine the researcher administers and can be read years later without the application. Three things separate it from a chat assistant or a general-purpose coding agent. It ships a library of written scientific procedures, guided workflow templates, catalogs of where research data can be found, and reviewer and writer roles the agent can hand work to. It keeps a Living Lab Notebook whose entries link into an argument and are added to but never erased. And it records what happened by watching what the agent does rather than by taking the agent's word for it, in a log the agent has no tool that can write to. That choice targets the most common failure, model overclaiming, in our earlier benchmark of nine frontier models, by making claims checkable rather than preventing them. On twenty interdisciplinary research prompts, scored under a rubric fixed in advance, K-Dense BYOK led two managed platforms on both scientific quality and research execution. Its deliverables were the only ones that recorded the software they ran in, and the only ones that usually arrived with a command that regenerates the results. One of the managed platforms ran the same frontier model and supplied neither. Those environment records were files the agent wrote, not part of the observed log, which does not yet capture the software environment itself. The code is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/k-dense-byok.

</details>


### [168] [Scientific Agents: Evaluating Profession-Specific System Prompts on Scientific Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00084)
*Timothy Kassis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Detailed profession-specific system prompts (like the Scientific Agents corpus with 503 AGENTS.md profiles) do not improve accuracy over minimal baselines on science benchmarks, while costing 2.2-4.5x more per response. They actually perform worse on tool-using bioinformatics tasks (46.7% vs 56.7% solve rate).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research investigates whether detailed profession-specific system prompts improve LLM accuracy on scientific tasks, motivated by the widespread use of such prompts despite unknown efficacy and significant token/cost implications.

Method: Evaluated 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles from Scientific Agents using Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter. Tested across nine text-based science benchmarks (4,531 questions, 100 matched profiles) and 60 BioMysteryBench bioinformatics problems. Compared five conditions: full profile, minimal baseline, opening role sentence, generic scientific guide, and unrelated domain profile. Used automated rule-based grading with API-error retries.

Result: No accuracy improvement: average profile-baseline difference is -0.6 percentage points (95% CI [-1.5, +0.2]). Profiles produced 1.5-2.3x more tokens and cost 2.2-4.5x more. On tool-using tasks, profiles achieved 46.7% vs 56.7% at baseline (-10.0 pp). However, longer prompts showed one advantage: 71.6% vs 54.0% first-pass answer retention during API drops.

Conclusion: For the tested model and tasks, loading full profession profiles by default does not improve accuracy and costs considerably more. The observed benefit on API drop recovery comes from prompt length/formatting rather than domain expertise. Further research is needed on selective retrieval of profile sections or open-ended scientific tasks.

Abstract: Detailed profession-specific system prompts raise token use and estimated cost per response without a consistent accuracy gain. We evaluate Scientific Agents, an open-source corpus of 503 profession-specific AGENTS.md profiles, with Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter in the Pi agent harness. We compare matched profiles with four controls: a minimal baseline ("You are a helpful assistant"), the profile's opening role sentence, a generic scientific rigor guide, and a profile from an unrelated domain. Across nine text-based science benchmarks (4,531 sampled questions, 100 matched profiles), 4,488 items completed all five conditions after API-error retries, scored with automated, rule-based grading. The average profile-baseline accuracy difference is -0.6 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [-1.5, +0.2] across fixed tasks), and no benchmark shows a statistically clear improvement. Matched profiles produced 1.5-2.3 times as many output tokens and cost 2.2-4.5 times more per successful call. On 60 tool-using BioMysteryBench bioinformatics problems (three runs each for baseline and profile), mean solve rates were 46.7% with the profile and 56.7% at baseline, a difference of -10.0 percentage points (95% interval [-16.7, -3.3]) driven by more frequent token- and time-limit stops under the profile. Longer prompts had one unexpected operational advantage: on SuperGPQA, frequent provider API drops left the short baseline with a correct first-pass answer on only 54.0% of items, against 71.6% with the profile. Generic and mismatched prompts were about as reliable, so this gain comes from prompt length or formatting rather than domain expertise. For the tested model and tasks, loading full profession profiles by default does not improve accuracy and costs considerably more; whether selective retrieval of profile sections or open-ended scientific tasks would change this remains to be tested.

</details>


### [169] [Not All Experience Belongs in the Weights: Component Routing for Self-Improving GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01787)
*Beining Wu,Zihao Ding,Jun Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the debate between fine-tuning (weights) vs. prompt engineering (context) for self-improving GUI agents by proposing "component routing" - splitting experience into 4 component types (locators, procedures, state facts, lessons) and routing each to its optimal destination. The authors find that locators and lessons perform better in weights while procedures and state facts work better in context, and they develop a predictive rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality that achieves 24/24 accuracy on held-out data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research motivation stems from a disagreement in prior literature about whether self-improving GUI agents should store their experience trajectories in model weights (via fine-tuning) or in context (via retrieval into prompts). The authors hypothesize that this disagreement arises because trajectories bundle items with different properties, so conclusions about the "bundle" depend on its mix of components.

Method: The authors introduce "component routing" - a method that splits experience into four component types: locators, procedures, state facts, and lessons. Each component is sent to either the context or weights based on its properties. They compare this approach across three backbone families, two environments, and three seeds. They also develop a predictive rule based on two properties measured before training: recurrence (how often an item recurs) and state-conditionality (whether an item depends on state).

Result: The key findings are: (1) Locators and lessons perform better when stored in weights, while procedures and state facts perform better in context. (2) The predictive rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality achieves 100% accuracy (24/24) in recovering the destination for held-out backbone families. (3) Routing by this rule beats all whole-trajectory baselines and outperforms the better single destination by +3.5 points on average. (4) Additional insights: note readout decreases after the same component is written to weights (most for frequently recurring items), context gains increase with information gap, and weights gains decrease with policy gap.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that component-specific routing significantly outperforms whole-trajectory approaches. The rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality can accurately predict optimal destinations for different experience components. This suggests that the traditional binary choice between weights vs. context storage is suboptimal - a differentiated approach based on component properties yields substantial improvements. The authors plan to release code and data.

Abstract: Self-improving GUI agents keep the trajectories they produce and return them to the agent, by fine-tuning or by retrieval into the prompt, and studies that compare the two destinations disagree. We attribute this to the unit of experience: a trajectory bundles items with different properties, so a conclusion about the bundle depends on its mix. To address this, (i) we introduce component routing, which splits the experience into locators, procedures, state facts and lessons and sends each component to the context or to the weights, compared on the same items across three backbone families, two environments and three seeds. One pool has two destinations: locators and lessons win in the weights, procedures and state facts in the context. (ii) We fit a rule in two properties measured before any training, recurrence and state-conditionality; it recovers the destination of a held-out backbone family in 24 of 24 cells, two interventions move a component toward the boundary, and routing by the rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline and, by +3.5 points on average, the better single destination of each backbone. (iii) We identify how training and producer-consumer differences change the value of the two destinations: note readout decreases after the same component is written into the weights, most for the items that recur most, context gains increase with the information gap, and weights gains decrease with the policy gap. Code and data will be released.

</details>


### [170] [Comedic Fool's Gold: Reward Exploits and Countermeasures in Conversational Humor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00197)
*Sam Larson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates automated reward design for training language models in conversational humor, identifying reward exploits and developing countermeasures. Two reward approaches (embedding-based surprise and audience laughter prediction) are found vulnerable to shortcuts, and while countermeasures partially work, they fail to fully achieve the preregistered target.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers aim to train language models to generate conversational humor using automated rewards, addressing the challenge that manual human feedback is expensive and slow. They specifically want to capture "understandable surprise" and "predicted audience amusement" as reward signals.

Method: The study employs three main methods: (1) controlled tests to identify reward exploits, (2) countermeasures including a fluency filter and laughter cue normalization, and (3) three sequential reinforcement learning runs evaluating successive reward revisions.

Result: The embedding-based surprise reward accepts word-shuffled replies as readily as witty ones; the fluency filter detects shuffles but rejects some legitimate witty replies. The audience model is vulnerable to laughter cues in either speaker's messages; normalization blocks covered attacks but unmatched expressions remain exploitable. The final run improves combined evaluation score by 0.0903 and reduces zero-score sessions by 40%, but humor-specific improvement remains below the preregistered target.

Conclusion: The findings illustrate a broader challenge in automated reward design: countermeasures must block exploitable shortcuts while preserving the behavior the reward was intended to encourage. This creates a fundamental tension between robustness and sensitivity in reward engineering.

Abstract: We investigate automated rewards for training language models in conversational humor, focusing on reward exploits and countermeasures. Two approaches aim to capture understandable surprise and predicted audience amusement. Controlled tests show that an embedding-based surprise reward accepts word-shuffled replies as readily as witty ones. A fluency filter detects the shuffles, but the combined reward also rejects some witty replies and fails further validation. An audience model's predicted laughter is instead vulnerable to laughter cues in either speaker's messages. Normalizing these cues across speakers blocks the covered attacks, although unmatched expressions remain exploitable. Three reinforcement-learning runs evaluate training with successive reward revisions. The final run improves the combined evaluation score by 0.0903 and reduces zero-score sessions by 40%, but its humor-specific improvement remains below our preregistered target. These findings illustrate a broader challenge for automated reward design: countermeasures must block exploitable shortcuts while preserving the behavior the reward was intended to encourage.

</details>


### [171] [EviGraph: Proof-Carrying Selective Recommendation over Temporal Public-Service Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00212)
*Yixi Zhou,Sikun Wang,Lei Fan,Fan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EviGraph is a system that improves public-service recommendations by distinguishing critical decision requirements from resolvable information gaps, using a temporal knowledge graph and deterministic verification, reducing unnecessary abstention without adding unnecessary verification layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public-service recommendations require evidence matching service, scope, and date. However, treating every missing detail as decisive leads to withholding useful recommendations, while insufficient verification can allow unsupported recommendations.

Method: EviGraph uses a language agent to link decision requirements to evidence in a temporal knowledge graph, coupled with a deterministic checker to verify whether recommendations are supported by evidence.

Result: Evaluation on a bilingual Hong Kong public-service benchmark with executable policy references shows that distinguishing critical requirements from unresolved information reduces unnecessary abstention. However, additional verification can withdraw supported recommendations without improving decision quality.

Conclusion: Reliable evidence-based navigation depends on specifying what must be established for a decision, rather than simply adding more verification. The key is identifying critical decision requirements rather than accumulating more checks.

Abstract: Public-service recommendations require evidence that matches the requested service, scope, and date. Yet treating every missing detail as decisive can withhold useful recommendations. We introduce EviGraph, which distinguishes critical decision requirements from information that can remain unresolved. A language agent links these requirements to evidence in a temporal knowledge graph, while a deterministic checker establishes whether a recommendation is supported. Evaluation on a bilingual Hong Kong public-service benchmark with executable policy references shows that this distinction reduces unnecessary abstention. Additional verification, however, can withdraw supported recommendations without improving decision quality. These findings suggest that reliable evidence-based navigation depends on specifying what must be established for a decision, rather than simply adding more verification.

</details>


### [172] [Build2SPARQL: A Large-Scale Text-to-SPARQL Benchmark Dataset for Building Knowledge Graph Querying](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00224)
*Wooyoung Jung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Build2SPARQL is a large-scale benchmark for translating natural-language questions to SPARQL queries on building automation knowledge graphs (Brick and ASHRAE 223P). It generates 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions through a KG-grounded pipeline where queries are validated by graph-traversal code while LLMs only generate questions. Evaluation shows significant accuracy improvements (0.2-20% to 56-65%) with retrieval-augmented generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs using ontologies like Brick and ASHRAE 223P. A promising application is text-to-SPARQL translation, allowing building operators to query graphs through natural language. However, progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks.

Method: The authors developed a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code (ensuring query correctness independent of model behavior), while large language models generate only the natural-language questions. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families (linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered) and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P).

Result: The benchmark yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. Two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. Retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

Conclusion: The Build2SPARQL benchmark provides a large-scale, validated dataset for text-to-SPARQL research on building automation KGs. The KG-grounded pipeline ensures query correctness, and the significant accuracy improvements with retrieval-augmented generation demonstrate the benchmark's utility for advancing natural-language interfaces to building knowledge graphs.

Abstract: Building automation systems are increasingly represented as semantic knowledge graphs (KGs) using ontologies such as Brick and ASHRAE 223P, creating a machine-readable substrate for artificial-intelligence applications. One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

</details>


### [173] [Robust Is Salient: An Informed Adversary Moves the Optimal Signal onto the Salience Pole](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00233)
*Cris Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: When an informed adversary shares the audience of a constrained signalling channel, the signal that best protects the truth is the signal that best describes it. The adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with salience across 108 confirmatory items, differing on only 2,748 of 200,000 items—exactly where salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. This creates a structural limit: no measurement can distinguish whether language model responses shift toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience because they are identical.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how an informed adversary affects optimal signaling in constrained channels, and whether adversarial robustness aligns with prior salience-based models or requires a different approach.

Method: Introduced an adversary to a forced-choice task (abstracted from Deception: Murder in Hong Kong). The adversary knows the target, observes the signal, and argues for the strongest wrong answer using a persuasion budget β. As β grows, the optimal signal shifts from posterior-maximizing (Bayesian) to margin-maximizing (salience). At β=0, the game reproduces the original oracle model with listener temperature τ=1. Tested two adversary framings on seven language models across 108 items.

Result: On 108 confirmatory items, the adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with the salience pole. Across 200,000 items, the two differ on only 2,748 items—lying exactly where the prior salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. Where defined, robustness is achieved by moving from Bayesian discrimination entirely to salience. 18.2% of the pool has an optimum that shifts under a finite budget. Two adversary framings changed choices of seven language models on 30 to 77 of 108 items.

Conclusion: This is a structural limit, not a null result: where the robust target and salience target coincide, no measurement can determine whether model responses shift toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience. The diagnostic check is cheap: before evaluating adversary-awareness, verify whether the robust target coincides with a heuristic target on the evaluation items.

Abstract: When an informed adversary shares the audience of a constrained signalling channel, the signal that best protects the truth is the signal that best describes it. On 108 confirmatory items, the adversary-robust optimum aligns exactly with the salience pole from prior work. Across a 200,000-item pool, the two differ on only 2,748 items --- lying exactly where the prior salience-to-Bayes coordinate is undefined. Where defined, robustness is achieved by moving from Bayesian discrimination entirely to salience. We show this by introducing an adversary to a forced-choice task (abstracted from Deception: Murder in Hong Kong). The adversary knows the target, observes the signal, and argues for the strongest wrong answer using a persuasion budget, $β$. As $β$ grows, the optimal signal shifts from the posterior-maximizing option to the margin-maximizing one; at $β= 0$, the game reproduces the original oracle model with a listener temperature of $τ= 1$. This effect is real: 18.2 percent of the pool has an optimum that shifts under a finite budget, and each item's critical budget is exact. This coincidence structurally limits empirical evaluation. Two adversary framings change the chosen option of seven language models on 30 to 77 of 108 items against an exact no-effect rate. Yet, no measurement can determine whether this movement is toward the adversary-aware optimum or toward salience, because the two options are identical. This is a structural limit, not a null result. The diagnostic check is cheap: before evaluating adversary-awareness, verify whether the robust target coincides with a heuristic target on the evaluation items.

</details>


### [174] [Conflicting Supervision Moves Commitment, Not Capability: A 12.29σ arrangement effect that is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic score](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00234)
*Wenhui Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how learning rate schedules interact with data ordering to influence what neural networks learn. The authors show that the learning rate schedule acts as an "averaging operator" that determines whether data order affects model behavior. They demonstrate empirically that order effects can be large (12.29-sigma) but invisible to conventional benchmarks, and that marking the convention in prompts can recover performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand what information about data ordering gets encoded into neural network parameters during training, and whether learning rate schedules modulate this effect.

Method: Controlled experiments with ten orderings of one corpus, varying only lr_scheduler_type between constant and cosine decay schedules. Measured allocation shares, contrast floors, and performance across arms.

Result: At constant rate, interior spans 0.2221 in allocation and 11.63 contrast floors. Under cosine decay, the same ten arms occupy two distinguishable states. Acc_A+acc_B remains constant within 9.7% while allocation share runs 0.04 to 0.87. The 12.29-sigma arrangement switch becomes zero under convention-agnostic metrics. Marking convention in prompt collapses the switch and reaches 87.5% of union ceiling.

Conclusion: Learning rate schedules are not neutral background conditions but active "averaging operators" that determine whether data ordering affects model behavior. Order effects are invisible to exact-match benchmarks but can be recovered by marking conventions in prompts. "Order matters" and "order does not matter" are endpoints on a single continuum controlled by the schedule.

Abstract: "Train a model on the same problems written under two incompatible conventions, both correct, and ask what the ordering of that data writes into the parameters. The learning-rate schedule is not a background condition for that question. It is the averaging operator, and it decides the answer. We prove a bound in which the arrangement and the schedule enter the ordering effect as separate multiplied factors: the arrangement only as a block period, the schedule only as how much weight the endpoint can place on any one moment of the run. A decaying schedule cannot put a large step size and an uncontracted remainder at the same moment; a constant one does exactly that at the last step. That decay moderates ordering effects has been reported in pretraining; the mechanism, the separation, and a controlled measurement of both halves are ours. Ten orderings of one corpus, one budget, everything but the path held fixed, run twice under families differing in lr_scheduler_type and nothing else: at a constant rate the interior spans 0.2221 in allocation, 11.63 contrast floors, monotone in how blocked the arrangement is. Under the single cosine every published arm uses, the same ten arms occupy two distinguishable states where their own resolution would allow about ten. "Order matters" and "order does not matter" are the two ends of one knob. What the path writes is which convention the model commits to, and no exact-match benchmark can see it. Across twelve arms acc_A+acc_B is constant to within 9.7% while the allocation share runs 0.04 to 0.87, so the 12.29-sigma arrangement switch this paper measures is exactly zero under a convention-agnostic metric. That conservation is quoted from the decayed family throughout, the constant-rate one being a noisier place to read it. Marking the convention in the prompt collapses the switch and reaches 87.5% of the union ceiling."

</details>


### [175] [Knowing When to Yield: Grounded Arbitration of User Corrections in Text-Based Embodied Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00282)
*Yezhou Cheng,Runjia Du,Zeming Liu,Hang Lyu,Zehua Yang,Bojun Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAVA (Grounded Correction Arbitration) is a system for embodied agents to handle potentially incorrect human corrections by choosing among accepting, rejecting, inspecting the world, or asking the speaker. It uses observation-bounded evidence, legal probes, and expected-loss rules. In ALFWorld experiments, semantic priors reduce interaction costs, but environmental VOI does not show clear advantage over clarification seeking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core question is how an embodied agent should respond when a person's correction may be wrong. This requires deciding whether to accept corrections, reject them, inspect the environment for verification, or ask the speaker for clarification—the agent needs an "evidence contract" rather than simply comparing approaches.

Method: GAVA was implemented with observation-bounded evidence, legal probes, and a one-step expected-loss rule. Experiments were conducted in text-only ALFWorld using 162 checkpoints producing 972 paired true/false interventions. Training used 340 unseen scenarios; testing used 77 non-overlapping seen checkpoints (308 scenarios). Comparisons included always verify, uniform GAVA, perfect speaker, and calibrated no-VOI approaches.

Result: Complete local inspections gave 100% correction accuracy. GAVA reduced interaction cost vs. always verify under perfect speaker. An exploratory training-only object-location prior lowered interaction and joint cost on 340 scenarios by 0.490 and 0.420. These gains replicated on 77 checkpoints (308 scenarios): 0.595 and 0.517, with 95% CIs excluding zero. Semantic GAVA made 4 factual errors per cohort (98.8%/98.7% accuracy). All methods completed every task.

Conclusion: Results support selective information gathering with semantic priors under declared costs, but do not establish a general advantage of environmental value of information over clarification seeking. The study uses normalized claims, complete symbolic observations, and controlled speakers; it does not evaluate human participants, visual input, or physical robots.

Abstract: How should an embodied agent respond when a person's correction may be wrong? We formulate grounded correction arbitration as a choice among accepting, rejecting, inspecting the world, and asking the speaker. GAVA implements this interface with observation-bounded evidence, legal probes, and a one-step expected-loss rule. In text-only ALFWorld, 162 checkpoints produce 972 paired true and false interventions. Complete local inspections give GAVA and always verify 100 percent correction accuracy, establishing the evidence contract rather than a comparative advantage. In same-episode execution, GAVA reduces interaction cost against always verify but ties a cost threshold under a perfect speaker. An exploratory training-only object-location prior lowers interaction and declared joint cost on 340 unseen scenarios by 0.490 and 0.420 relative to uniform GAVA. After freezing the policy, costs, baselines, and multiplicity plan, the gains replicate on 77 non-overlapping seen checkpoints, covering 308 scenarios: 0.595 and 0.517, with both 95 percent checkpoint-bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Joint cost also improves over an identical-prior fixed policy, while the matched calibrated no-VOI comparison remains inconclusive. Semantic GAVA makes four factual errors in each cohort, corresponding to 98.8 percent and 98.7 percent accuracy, and all methods complete every task. Results support selective information gathering with semantic priors under declared costs, but do not establish a general advantage of environmental value of information over clarification. The study uses normalized claims, complete symbolic observations, and controlled speakers; it evaluates neither human participants, visual input, nor physical robots.

</details>


### [176] [Rules to Tools: Executable Checks for LLM Agents in Scientific Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00313)
*Jingjie Ning,Guojiang Zhao,Chen Xu,Shanshan Zhong,Xiaochuan Li,Ji Zeng,Guolin Ke*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A study comparing "Rules to Tools" (R2T) approach versus text-based instructions for scientific coding agents to repair code. The tool approach (prepared executable checks) achieves 29/30 repair success vs 26/30 with text in main cohorts, with task-dependent outcomes and varying agent-side costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific coding agents receive equations, boundary conditions, and output requirements in writing, then must assess the programs they revise. R2T aims to supply prepared executable checks of public scientific requirements to improve repair outcomes compared to text-based instructions.

Method: Matched repair groups share written checks, starting programs, model, and budgets across multiple cohorts: two task-ID cohorts (30 tasks each), an eight-ID cohort (16 tasks), a larger shared-definition cohort (24 tasks), five development-exposed tasks with alternate starting programs, and a matched PDE comparison. The tool group receives callable implementations while text group receives written instructions.

Result: Main task-ID cohorts: 26/30 (text) vs 29/30 (tools), with 3 tasks favoring tools, 1 favoring text, and 11 tying. Eight-ID cohort: 13/16 vs 15/16 (bootstrap 95% CI: [-12.5, 43.75] pp). Larger cohort: 13/24 per group (tie). Development-exposed: 3/10 vs 7/10. Fresh source-through-Python: 15/16. PDE comparison: 23/24 (text) vs 24/24 (tools), with 31.2% lower reported model output for checks. Agent-side output savings vary by cohort; public CPU use rises in both task-ID cohorts.

Conclusion: The tool approach (prepared checks) provides task-dependent repair advantages in most tasks, with specific tasks (17, 77, 11) favoring tools and task 37 favoring text. Results measure the trade-offs between repair outcomes and agent-side costs when using prepared executable checks versus text-based instructions in scientific coding contexts.

Abstract: Scientific coding agents receive equations, boundary conditions, and output requirements in writing, then must assess the programs they revise. Rules to Tools (R2T) supplies prepared executable checks of public scientific requirements. Matched SciCode repair groups share written checks, starting programs, model, and budgets; the tool group receives a callable implementation. Across two task-ID cohorts, complete repair is 26/30 with text and 29/30 with the prepared checks. Three task IDs favor tools, one favors text, and eleven tie. The eight-ID cohort scores 13/16 versus 15/16, with a task-cluster bootstrap 95% interval of [-12.5, 43.75] percentage points for the difference. The larger shared-definition SciCode cohort ties at 13/24 per group. Five development-exposed tasks with alternate starting programs score 3/10 versus 7/10. The tool group favors tasks 17, 77, and 11; initial checks flag task 17 and report no violation for tasks 77 and 11. Task 37 favors text and has no initial reported violation. A fresh source-through-Python arm also reaches 15/16, matching the dedicated command's aggregate. In a matched PDE comparison, detailed text scores 23/24 and checks score 24/24, with 31.2% lower reported model output for checks. Agent-side output savings vary by cohort, while public CPU use rises in both task-ID cohorts. These results measure task-dependent repair outcomes and agent-side costs with prepared checks.

</details>


### [177] [Predictive Credit: Measuring What Scientific Explanations Add to Experimental Forecasts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00314)
*Jingjie Ning,Xueqi Li,Yibo Kong,Dongting Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a benchmark protocol for measuring "predictive credit" - whether explanations from research agents improve forecasting accuracy compared to simple descriptions. Across 336 controlled learning states, 12 Tox21 biological endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks, the authors test whether matched explanations (vs. donor context) improve predictive performance. Results were largely inconclusive: matched explanations failed to demonstrate statistically significant gains over descriptions in most tests, though some secondary analyses showed modest improvements under specific conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a fundamental question in AI-assisted scientific reasoning: does providing mechanistic explanations from research agents actually improve predictive accuracy compared to simply describing what will happen? The motivation is to establish rigorous benchmarks for evaluating research agents in scientific forecasting tasks.

Method: The authors design a paired forecast methodology where forecasts share intervention, forecaster, and outcome while varying description, matched explanation, and donor context. Five validation checks track: (1) commitment (researchers commit to predictions before seeing outcomes), (2) delivery (explanations delivered before outcome resolution), (3) predictive gain (matched vs. description), (4) alignment (explanations align with actual outcomes), and (5) known-signal uptake. Experiments span three domains: controlled learning (336 prospective states), Tox21 (12 biological endpoints), and OpenML (24 ML tasks). The study tests multiple model configurations including DeepSeek V4 Pro, V4 Flash, and a researcher-authored positive control.

Result: Main results were largely null or inconclusive: (1) v5's frozen credit decision was inconclusive; (2) Tox21's preregistered ROC AUC interval-score harm test was unmet (D-M = -.0026, 95% CI [-.0174, .0104]); (3) OpenML's joint formation, point-equivalence, and repeatability rule was unmet; (4) matched point-accuracy gains over description remained unconfirmed; (5) Tox21/OpenML seed-donor intervals spanned zero. Some secondary findings showed modest improvements: under DeepSeek V4 Pro, matched and donor cards reduced secondary Tox21 drift by 64.5% and 59.1%. However, DeepSeek V4 Flash replay raised matched point MAE from .01823 to .02020. OpenML full-card assignment widened nominal 80% intervals by 21%, with 49.3% coverage vs. 51.4% for description. A researcher-authored positive control lowered point MAE by 2.60 percentage points vs. description.

Conclusion: The protocol provides a rigorous framework for measuring predictive credit in research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting. However, natural-explanation credit (whether explanations from AI agents improve predictions) remained unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions. The authors note that the positive control (human-authored mechanism) did show improvement, suggesting the methodology can detect effects when they exist, but that current AI-generated explanations do not provide measurable predictive credit at the resolutions tested.

Abstract: Research agents explain planned experiments. We measure predictive credit with paired forecasts sharing an intervention, forecaster, and outcome while varying description, matched explanation, and donor context. Five checks track commitment, delivery, predictive gain, alignment, and known-signal uptake. Across 336 prospective states in controlled learning, 12 Tox21 endpoints, and 24 OpenML tasks, v5's frozen credit decision was inconclusive. Tox21's preregistered ROC AUC interval-score harm test was unmet ($D-M=-.0026$, 95 percent interval [$-.0174$, .0104]); OpenML's joint formation, point-equivalence, and repeatability rule was unmet. Matched point-accuracy gains over description remained unconfirmed, and Tox21/OpenML seed-donor intervals spanned zero. Under requested DeepSeek V4 Pro, matched and donor cards reduced secondary Tox21 drift by 64.5 and 59.1 percent. A DeepSeek V4 Flash replay raised matched point MAE from .01823 to .02020 and missed matched-donor interval-score equivalence. OpenML full-card assignment widened nominal 80 percent intervals by 21 percent, with 49.3 percent coverage versus 51.4 percent for description and content in 66/144 cards. Direct-text Flash delivered all 144 notes without detectable matched point-accuracy gain. A researcher-authored mechanism positive control lowered point MAE by 2.60 percentage points versus description. The protocol measures predictive credit for research-agent benchmarks and scientific forecasting; natural-explanation credit remained unconfirmed at the tested donor resolutions.

</details>


### [178] [ContractRL: Shielded Group-Relative Policy Optimization for Auditable Tool-Call Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00328)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Yina Sa,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContractRL is a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol for JSON that models verifier-guided repair as a bounded decision process. It uses contract-derived action masks to filter malformed RFC-6902 operations and achieves 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 tokens, outperforming Patch-SFT (0.9076, 44.9 tokens) and full regeneration (0.9148, 137.2 tokens).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or execution contract. Complete object regeneration enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit. A more efficient and auditable approach is needed.

Method: ContractRL models JSON repair as a bounded decision process where the policy observes candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget at each step. A contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. A contract-constrained group-relative objective guides patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze.

Result: Under identical verifier information, ContractRL achieves 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration (192 cases per seed, five seeds). Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 to 0.9375. A three-seed paired evaluation yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI [+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039) against Patch-SFT.

Conclusion: ContractRL demonstrates that contract-constrained sequential repair outperforms full regeneration and supervised patch methods. The gains are attributed to localized correction as shown by feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses. Adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

Abstract: Structured tool calls often fail after only a small number of fields violate a schema or an execution contract. Regenerating the complete object enlarges the action surface and makes repeated repair difficult to audit. We introduce ContractRL, a contract-constrained sequential repair protocol that models verifier-guided JSON repair as a bounded decision process. At each step the policy observes the candidate, typed verifier feedback, JSON Pointer, immutable repair history, and remaining budget; a contract-derived action mask filters malformed or prohibited RFC-6902 operations before a deterministic validator performs the transition. We specify a contract-constrained group-relative objective for patch, retry, and abstention decisions while keeping canonical targets and semantic labels outside the online state until trace freeze. Under identical verifier information, ContractRL attains 0.9362 semantic success with 34.4 generated tokens, compared with 0.9076 and 44.9 tokens for Patch-SFT and 0.9148 and 137.2 tokens for full regeneration over 192 cases per seed and five seeds. Policy optimization improves semantic success from 0.9186 for supervised ContractRL to 0.9375. A separate three-seed paired evaluation against Patch-SFT yields a semantic difference of +0.0396 (95% CI $[+0.0137,+0.0662], p=0.0039$). Feedback, action-mask, budget, and schema-shift analyses connect these gains to localized correction, while adversarial and multi-turn evaluations characterize the remaining failure modes.

</details>


### [179] [Mathematical Transfer in LLMs Follows Reasoning Approach More Than Topic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00331)
*Sajad Goudarzi,Samaneh Zamanifard,Seyed Amin Seyed Haeri,Moloud Nasiri,Hamed Rahimian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether topic or reasoning approach is a better organizing principle for selecting mathematical training data for LLMs. Across two designs with 5 base models and 3 training seeds each, same-approach (SA) training consistently outperforms same-topic (ST) training in all 40 comparisons, with advantages of 10.8% and 14.3% on average across the two designs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The researchers wanted to determine the optimal organizing principle for selecting mathematical training data for LLMs - whether to group by mathematical topic (e.g., probability examples for probability targets) or by reasoning approach (worked solutions sharing a solution method but possibly from different mathematical domains).

Method: Two counterbalanced 2×2 designs were used: (1) probability and combinatorics crossed with invariant reasoning and double counting (2,000 problems), and (2) number theory and geometry crossed with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). Every cell served as the held-out target in turn. Same-approach (SA) sources shared the target's method but changed the topic, while same-topic (ST) sources shared the topic but changed the method. Five base models and three training seeds were tested per design.

Result: SA outperformed ST in all 40 seed-pooled model--target comparisons. In Design 1, model-level advantages ranged from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points (mean: 10.8%). In Design 2, advantages ranged from 12.0 to 16.0 percentage points (mean: 14.3%). All ten model-level 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. Notably, ST sources were more similar to targets under embedding and lexical measures, meaning the SA advantage ran opposite to measured statement-level resemblance.

Conclusion: Reasoning approach is a more effective matching criterion than topic for mathematical transfer across the evaluated topic-approach combinations. This suggests that LLMs benefit more from learning generalizable reasoning methods than from domain-specific mathematical content.

Abstract: When selecting mathematical training data for LLMs, a natural organizing principle is topic: probability examples for probability targets. An alternative is reasoning approach: worked solutions that share a solution method with the target, even when the mathematical domain differs. We ask which relation produces greater transfer after fine-tuning. We evaluate two counterbalanced $2\times2$ designs: probability and combinatorics crossed with invariant reasoning and double counting (2,000 problems), and number theory and geometry crossed with complement and pigeonhole reasoning (800 problems). In each design, every cell serves as the held-out target in turn: same-approach (SA) sources share the target's method but change the topic, while same-topic (ST) sources share the topic but change the method. Every source appears once in each role, so additive source-quality effects cancel from the equally weighted aggregate contrast. Across five base models and three training seeds per design, SA outperforms ST in all 40 seed-pooled model--target comparisons. Model-level advantages range from 8.2 to 16.2 percentage points in the primary design (mean: 10.8) and from 12.0 to 16.0 in the second design (mean: 14.3); all ten model-level 95% confidence intervals exclude zero. In both designs, ST sources are more similar to targets under embedding and lexical measures, so the SA advantage runs opposite to the measured ordering of statement-level resemblance. These findings identify reasoning approach as a more effective matching criterion than topic for mathematical transfer across the evaluated topic--approach combinations.

</details>


### [180] [Fault-Tolerant Budget Conservation in Distributed Multi-Agent Delegation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00349)
*Genliang Zhu,Chu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses resource authorization challenges in distributed multi-agent AI systems where failures (lost replies, timeouts, message duplicates, partitions, DAG joins) can cause budget overspend. The authors propose a fault-tolerant budget conservation mechanism using exclusive escrow credits that move through a delegation DAG, with operation reservations, signed dispatch permits, and quarantine mechanisms. The approach ensures budget bounds are preserved across various failure scenarios including crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resource limits are becoming critical for AI agents delegating work across concurrent and failure-prone workers. Existing mechanisms (parent-child allocation constraints, affine objects, distributed escrow) fail to prevent overspend in specific failure scenarios: lost replies, effects completing after timeout, message repeats, branch partitions, and DAG joins aliasing one lineage. This creates a fundamental authorization boundary problem in distributed multi-agent systems.

Method: The paper formalizes fault-tolerant budget conservation through: (1) Representing budgets as quantized resource vectors using exclusive escrow credits moving through a delegation DAG; (2) Converting credits to operation reservations bound to lineage, epoch, normalized effect, maximum charge, receiver, and idempotency key before dispatch; (3) Persisting signed dispatch permits with quarantine; (4) Gateway verification before first acceptance; (5) Keeping uncertain effects charged until authenticated settlement, fenced authoritative no-effect proof, or permanent retirement. Evaluation uses bounded TLA+ model checking, JavaScript explorer, and crash-injected SQLite experiments.

Result: The mechanism proves ownership partition, ledger and effect conservation, descendant non-amplification, at-most-once settlement, late-completion safety, and partition confinement under explicit assumptions (mediation, durability, authentication, normalization, gateway). An indistinguishability result shows partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation. Experimental validation confirms the mechanism preserves issued budget bounds across crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules, and detects timeout-refund and historical-certificate-validation mutants.

Conclusion: The proposed budget conservation mechanism successfully prevents resource overspend in distributed multi-agent delegation scenarios despite concurrent failures and network partitions. The combination of exclusive escrow credits, operation reservations with comprehensive binding parameters, signed dispatch permits with quarantine, and delayed settlement charging provides a robust solution. The theoretical guarantees (ownership partition, conservation laws, at-most-once settlement) combined with empirical validation through model checking and crash injection experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness within its declared scope.

Abstract: Resource limits are becoming an authorization boundary for AI agents that delegate work across concurrent and failure-prone workers. Parent-child allocation constraints, affine objects, and distributed escrow do not by themselves prevent overspend when replies are lost, effects complete after timeout, messages repeat, branches partition, or DAG joins alias one lineage. We formalize fault-tolerant budget conservation for distributed multi-agent delegation. Budgets are quantized resource vectors represented by exclusive escrow credits that move through a delegation DAG. Before dispatch, a branch converts credit into an operation reservation bound to lineage, epoch, normalized effect, maximum charge, receiver, and idempotency key. It persists a signed dispatch permit with quarantine; the gateway verifies that permit before first acceptance. Uncertain effects remain charged until authenticated settlement, a fenced authoritative no-effect proof, or permanent retirement. We prove ownership partition, ledger and effect conservation, descendant non-amplification, at-most-once settlement, late-completion safety, and partition confinement under explicit mediation, durability, authentication, normalization, and gateway assumptions. An indistinguishability result shows that partition-local availability requires exclusive preallocation. Bounded TLA+ checking, an independent JavaScript explorer, and crash-injected two-process SQLite experiments exercise the declared scope and detect timeout-refund and historical-certificate-validation mutants. The mechanism preserves the issued budget bound across the evaluated crash, retry, duplicate, partition, join, and late-completion schedules.

</details>


### [181] [ActiveSaddler: Automated Curriculum Learning for Agent Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00906)
*Sungho Park,Wonjoong Kim,Jue Zhang,Wook-Shin Han,Pengfei Gao,Chanyoung Park,Yongqiang Yao,Rao Fu,Elsie Nallipogu,Qingwei Lin,Victor Rühle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ActiveSaddler is an automated curriculum learning framework for LLM agent harness optimization that dynamically adapts the training scenario curriculum as the harness evolves, treating failure patterns as bandit arms and balancing exploitation of known weaknesses with exploration for new failure patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing harness optimization methods focus on how to update prompts, tool interfaces, and control logic from execution feedback, but keep the training scenarios fixed. The authors argue that as the harness evolves, the most useful scenarios for optimization change, so the curriculum should co-evolve with the harness - a previously overlooked optimization dimension.

Method: ActiveSaddler models the curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It abstracts recurring failures into reusable "failure-pattern arms," estimates potential learning progress from targeting each pattern, and uses an adaptive balancing mechanism to revisit known weaknesses while exploring unseen scenarios for new failure patterns. The method continually updates both discovered failure patterns and their priorities based on optimization outcomes.

Result: Experiments on GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that ActiveSaddler consistently discovers stronger harnesses, improving test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points respectively over the same harness optimizer using a fixed scenario order. Ablations confirm that these gains depend on three key components: dynamically constructing optimization targets, estimating their evolving utility, and balancing continued optimization with new failure discovery.

Conclusion: Automated curriculum learning is established as a new crucial optimization dimension for harness optimization. The co-evolution of the training curriculum with the harness enables more effective LLM agent improvement than methods that keep the curriculum fixed throughout optimization.

Abstract: Automated harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents by iteratively updating their prompts, tool interfaces, and control logic from execution feedback. However, existing methods primarily optimize how the harness is updated while largely fixing which training scenarios generate the feedback that drives those updates. As the harness evolves, the scenarios most useful for further optimization can change, suggesting that the training curriculum itself should adapt alongside the harness. We formulate this missing dimension of harness optimization as an automated curriculum learning problem and introduce ActiveSaddler. ActiveSaddler models the evolving curriculum as a non-stationary bandit with dynamically instantiated optimization targets. It abstracts recurring failures into reusable failure-pattern arms, estimates the potential learning progress from further targeting each pattern, and adaptively balances revisiting known weaknesses with exploring unseen scenarios for new ones. Optimization outcomes continually update both the set of discovered failure patterns and their priorities, allowing the curriculum to co-evolve with the harness. Experiments on GAIA2 and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that ActiveSaddler consistently discovers stronger harnesses, improving test Pass@1 by 4.4 and 7.5 percentage points over the same harness optimizer using a scenario order fixed before optimization, respectively. Ablations further show that these gains depend on dynamically constructing optimization targets, estimating their evolving utility, and balancing continued optimization with new failure discovery. Together, these results establish automated curriculum learning as a new crucial optimization dimension for harness optimization.

</details>


### [182] [JusticeAxis: Benchmarking Legal Judgment between Rigid Rule Application and Ungrounded Discretion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00353)
*Zhengkai Tu,Mingda Zhang,Zijia Wang,Xiaoying Tang,Jimmy Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper formalizes legal judgment as a reference-anchored task and introduces JusticeAxis (256 criminal cases from 18 countries with multimodal evidence) and JusticeAgent (a multi-agent system with element and judge agents using skills distilled from execution trajectories under Bayesian credible bounds).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
