Motivation: Existing legal judgment methods swing between rigid statute matching and ungrounded discretion, with benchmarks scoring only labels/rubrics and experience remaining unverified.

Method: The authors propose JusticeAxis dataset (256 real-world criminal cases with audio, image, text evidence, 3 lawyer-written judgments per case) and JusticeAgent system (element agents establish facts, judge agent applies law under skills carrying circumstances, skills distilled from execution trajectories and admitted under Bayesian credible bounds).

Result: Failure direction varies with scale: open-weight backbones drift to unsupported grounds, frontier models to statutory default. JusticeAgent as a plugin carries frozen open-weight backbone to commercial level performance.

Conclusion: JusticeAgent effectively bridges the gap between rigid statute matching and ungrounded discretion in legal judgment, serving as a simple yet powerful plugin that elevates open-weight models to commercial-level performance.

Abstract: A sound judgment applies the law to established facts and weighs the circumstances in which they arose. However, existing methods swing between rigid statute matching and ungrounded discretion, benchmarks score a label or a rubric, and the experience that would supply the balance stays unverified. We formalize legal judgment as a reference-anchored task, whose object is a single decision that stays tied to the statute and to the circumstances at once. We introduce JusticeAxis, 256 real-world criminal cases from 18 countries with audio, image, and text evidence, and three lawyer-written judgments for every case: the recorded one and one for each failure. We further propose JusticeAgent, a harness whose element agents establish the facts and whose judge agent applies the law under skills carrying experience of the circumstances. Skills are distilled from execution trajectories and admitted only under Bayesian credible bounds. Experiments show that failure turns direction with scale: open-weight backbones drift to unsupported grounds, frontier models to the statutory default. We further verify that JusticeAgent, as a simple yet effective plugin, carries a frozen open-weight backbone to commercial level. Project resources are available at https://github.com/beita6969/JusticeAxis.

</details>


### [183] [AVSD-Scenes: A Dataset for Audio-Visual Description of Urban Scenes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01861)
*Dhanunjaya Varma Devalraju,Arshdeep Singh,Mark D. Plumbley*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AVSD-Scenes is a new paired audio-visual scene description dataset for urban environments containing 12,291 samples. Audio and visual descriptions are generated separately using Qwen2-Audio-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, then combined using LLMs (Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, Gemma-3-27B-it) to create multimodal descriptions that capture complementary information from both modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing datasets that jointly describe both auditory and visual information for urban scenes are limited. Natural language descriptions can provide rich semantic representations of audio-visual urban scenes, but there was a need for a dataset that captures complementary information from both modalities.

Method: 1) Generate audio-based descriptions using Qwen2-Audio-7B
2) Generate visual-based descriptions using Qwen2.5-VL-7B
3) Combine modality-specific descriptions using LLMs (Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, Gemma-3-27B-it) to produce multimodal descriptions
4) Benchmark using semantic alignment, cross-modal retrieval, scene classification, LLM-as-a-judge, and human assessment

Result: - Multimodal descriptions improve semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval compared to modality-specific descriptions
- Up to 94.5% accuracy in urban scene classification
- Combining audio, visual, and description embeddings improves accuracy to 95.4%
- Descriptions remain highly scene-discriminative even without scene labels in prompting, indicating they capture semantic info from content rather than just label information

Conclusion: The proposed AVSD-Scenes dataset successfully provides rich multimodal scene descriptions. Multimodal descriptions outperform modality-specific ones in semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval while preserving strong scene-discriminative information. The approach demonstrates that combining audio, visual, and description embeddings yields the best classification performance.

Abstract: Natural language descriptions can provide rich semantic representations of audio-visual urban scenes, yet datasets that jointly describe both auditory and visual information remain limited. In this paper, we introduce AVSD-Scenes, a paired audio-visual scene description dataset for urban environments. The dataset contains 12,291 audio-visual scene descriptions generated from the TAU Urban Audio-Visual Scenes dataset. To construct the dataset, we first generate audio- and visual-based descriptions using Qwen2-Audio-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, respectively. These modality-specific descriptions are then combined using large language models, namely Qwen3-14B, Mistral-Small-3.2-24B-Instruct-2506, and Gemma-3-27B-it, to produce multimodal descriptions that capture complementary information from both modalities. We benchmark AVSD-Scenes using semantic alignment, cross-modal retrieval, scene classification, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and human subjective assessment. Results show that multimodal descriptions improve semantic alignment and cross-modal retrieval performance compared with modality-specific descriptions while preserving strong scene-discriminative information. The generated descriptions achieve up to 94.5% accuracy in urban scene classification, while combining audio, visual, and description embeddings further improves accuracy to 95.4%. Furthermore, the descriptions remain highly scene-discriminative even when scene labels are removed from the prompting instructions, indicating that they capture semantic information derived from the audio-visual content rather than merely reflecting label information.

</details>


### [184] [Finding the Right Fit: Model-Harness Interactions across Agent Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00917)
*Yixuan Li,Yiyun Zhou,Yao Long Teng,Fuchao Yang,Yanchen Deng,Zhiyi Lyu,Xuyu Dong,Feng Chen,Bo An*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates 66 agent system configurations (4 harnesses × 5 models + native pairings) across 3 benchmarks, finding that model rankings reverse across harnesses, vendor harnesses are not reliably best, and higher cost doesn't guarantee higher scores. The key insight is that model, harness, and task should be evaluated together.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether a strong model, harness, or pairing stays strong when the setting changes, and to investigate if vendor harnesses are best for their models and if higher cost yields better scores.

Method: Evaluated 66 configurations: four configurable harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness, PI, openJiuwen) paired with five models on TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, and Terminal-Bench 4, plus native Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude pairings. Analyzed 6,204 scored trajectories.

Result: Model rankings reverse across harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails by 30.16 points in PI. For 4/5 models, best harness changes across benchmarks. Some pairings hold: openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks (5.61-11.11 points margin). Higher cost does not reliably buy higher scores; GPT scores higher under PI than DSH at less than 1/4 the cost.

Conclusion: Model, harness, and task should be evaluated together. The harness's failure handling matters significantly—GPT does best with PI's lean scaffold while Kimi (prone to malformed tool calls) does best in openJiuwen. Released harness adapters, evaluation code, and all 6,204 scored trajectories.

Abstract: Choosing an agent system means choosing both a language model and the harness through which it acts. We ask whether a strong model, harness, or pairing stays strong when the setting changes. We evaluate 66 configurations: four configurable harnesses (OpenHands, DeepSeek Harness, PI, and openJiuwen) paired with five models on TUA-Bench, ALE-CLI, and Terminal-Bench 4, plus the native Codex-GPT and Claude Code-Claude pairings. Model rankings reverse across harnesses. On Terminal-Bench 4, Claude leads GPT by 7.94 points in OpenHands but trails it by 30.16 points in PI. For four of the five models, the best harness changes from one benchmark to another, yet some pairings hold: openJiuwen gives Kimi its highest score on all three benchmarks, by 5.61 to 11.11 points. A model's own vendor harness is not reliably its best, and higher cost does not reliably buy a higher score. On Terminal-Bench 4, GPT scores higher under PI than under DSH at less than a quarter of the cost per task. Matched trajectories suggest why fit varies. Models start almost all repairs themselves, so much depends on whether the harness hands failures back in a form the model can use. GPT does best with PI's lean scaffold, while Kimi, which often issues malformed tool calls, does best in openJiuwen. We argue that the model, the harness, and the task should be evaluated together, and we release the harness adapters, evaluation code, and all 6,204 scored trajectories at https://github.com/liyix/finding-the-right-fit and https://huggingface.co/datasets/yixuanli97/finding-the-right-fit.

</details>


### [185] [What Should an Agent Remember? Disentangling Retention from Retrieval in Bounded-Memory Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00366)
*Juli Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses confounds in memory evaluation for persistent agents by separating retention (what information to keep) from selection (what to surface when queried). Through a streaming-recall benchmark with 300 seeded episodes, the study demonstrates that proper evaluation methodology requires holding access fixed when comparing selection methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory evaluations often conflate retention and selection decisions by comparing methods that differ in both aspects simultaneously. This makes it impossible to isolate the true effect of either component, leading to misleading conclusions about what improves memory performance.

Method: Built a streaming-recall benchmark that crosses retention and selection rules. Evaluated every condition on the same 300 seeded episodes. Conducted two types of comparisons: (1) holding access fixed to isolate selection effects, and (2) a mixed comparison changing both access and selection to measure their individual contributions. Also evaluated on SQuAD dataset.

Result: Query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 percentage points (95% CI: 12.8-18.2) when access is held fixed. A mixed comparison shows 68.7-point advantage, with 53.2 points attributable to access changes. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection reach the retention ceiling. All 319 failures in bounded recency are caused by eviction (not ranking errors). Recall drops to 0% as targets recede far into the past. On SQuAD, dense retrieval outperforms lexical retrieval on natural text while preserving the retention ceiling.

Conclusion: Bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately to avoid confounds and accurately assess memory system performance.

Abstract: A persistent agent must decide both what to retain as information arrives and what to surface once a query appears, yet memory evaluations can confound these decisions by comparing methods that differ in both retention and selection. We build a streaming-recall benchmark crossing retention and selection rules and evaluate every condition on the same 300 seeded episodes. Holding access fixed, query-aware selection improves required-fact recall by 15.5 percentage points (95% CI: 12.8 to 18.2), whereas a mixed comparison that also changes history access reports a 68.7-point advantage, of which 53.2 points are attributable to access. Under bounded retention, query-aware, dense, and oracle selection reach the retention ceiling, and all 319 observed failures in the bounded recency condition are caused by eviction rather than ranking errors. Recall falls to 0% as targets recede sufficiently far into the past. Repeating the evaluation on SQuAD preserves the retention ceiling while showing that dense retrieval can outperform lexical retrieval on natural text. These results show that bounded-memory evaluations should hold access fixed and report retention and selection separately.

</details>


### [186] [Trustworthy Data- and ML-Ops for Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01282)
*Antonio Emanuele Cinà,Giovanni Scodeller,Cecilia Caterina Pasquale,Silvia Siri,Davide Anguita,Fabio Roli,Simona Sacone,Luca Oneto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper provides a comprehensive review of Trustworthy DataOps and MLOps in Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics (ITS&L), examining their importance in improving efficiency, reliability, and decision-making precision. It addresses gaps in current literature, explores DataOps and MLOps components, tools, and case studies, and examines methods to strengthen trust in AI systems for real-world ITS&L applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid evolution of ITS&L relies heavily on Data, AI, and ML integration. There is a need to address trustworthiness in AI applications and understand how DataOps and MLOps can improve efficiency and reliability in transportation and logistics services.

Method: Comprehensive literature review identifying gaps in current research, exploring DataOps and MLOps complexities, discussing their necessity, key components, available tools, practical insights, and case studies relevant to ITS&L.

Result: The paper establishes a foundational understanding of DataOps and MLOps in ITS&L, identifies methods and tools for building trust in AI systems, and charts a path for future research in developing efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems.

Conclusion: This work serves as a vital resource for researchers, industry practitioners, and policy makers, highlighting persisting challenges and future prospects in the rapidly advancing field of trustworthy AI in ITS&L.

Abstract: The rapid evolution of Intelligent Transportation Systems and Logistics (ITS\&L) has become a cornerstone of the modern social economy, relying heavily on the integration of Data, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and, more specifically, Machine Learning (ML). This paper provides a comprehensive review of Trustworthy Data and Machine Learning Operations (DataOps and MLOps) in the ITS\&L domain, underscoring their importance in improving efficiency, reliability, and decision-making precision within transportation and logistics services. We begin by identifying gaps in current literature, offering clear context for our contribution. Subsequently, we explore the complexities of DataOps and MLOps, discussing their necessity, key components, available tools, practical insights, and case studies relevant to ITS\&L. Additionally, we address the critical issue of Trustworthiness in AI applications, examining methods and tools designed to strengthen confidence in AI systems - especially in real-world ITS\&L scenarios. The paper concludes with a discussion of persisting challenges and future prospects in this rapidly advancing field, aiming to serve as a vital resource for researchers, industry practitioners, and policy makers. Overall, this work not only establishes a foundational understanding of DataOps and MLOps in ITS\&L but also charts a path for further research and innovation in developing more efficient, sustainable, and trustworthy intelligent transportation and logistics systems.

</details>


### [187] [When Harnesses Lose the Signal: Causal Evaluation of Recovery in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00372)
*Shuyao Xiao,Shengling Wang,Xuan Chen,Ke Chao,Ming Cui,Feifei Qian,Chaoyang Mei,Fanlin Meng,Ziming Yu,Junxi Yin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical limitation in LLM agent evaluation: recovery mechanisms are typically judged only by average task success, which obscures whether recovery operations help or harm individual trajectories. The authors propose framing recovery as a causal decision problem and introduce the Causal Intervention Router (CIR), a lightweight policy that selectively applies recovery based on pre-recovery information. On ALFWorld tasks with Qwen3-14B, CIR improves success from 70.33% to 73.33% while preserving all correct trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key insight is that recovery operations present a fundamental tension: the same operation can either rescue a failing trajectory or disrupt one that would otherwise succeed. Current evaluation metrics (average task success) hide this trade-off, making it impossible to distinguish beneficial from harmful recovery. The authors argue this requires a causal approach to properly evaluate when recovery is worthwhile.

Method: The paper frames recovery as a causal decision problem by comparing trajectories with and without recovery from the same execution state, separating rescue effects from harm effects. The Causal Intervention Router (CIR) is introduced as a lightweight policy that uses information available before recovery to decide whether intervention is worthwhile. The approach was evaluated on long-horizon ALFWorld tasks using Qwen3-14B as the base model.

Result: CIR raises task success from 70.33% to 73.33%, achieving a gain of 3.00 percentage points. Importantly, CIR leaves all evaluated trajectories with correct observations untouched. Control experiments demonstrate that the benefit of recovery cannot be explained solely by the new observation returned by the environment, indicating the causal mechanism is essential.

Conclusion: The work provides a practical framework for evaluating recovery in LLM agents and demonstrates that selective intervention via CIR can improve performance while preserving correct trajectories. The causal framing and the CIR policy offer a principled way to decide when recovery is worthwhile, moving beyond naive average-success metrics.

Abstract: Large language model agents rely on external harnesses to pass information between the model and its environment and to recover from execution errors. Yet recovery is usually judged only by average task success. This hides an important tension. The same operation can rescue a failing trajectory or disrupt one that would otherwise succeed. We frame recovery as a causal decision problem. Starting from the same execution state, we compare what happens with and without recovery, separate rescue from harm, and study how the value of recovery changes over time. We then introduce the Causal Intervention Router (CIR), a lightweight policy that uses information available before recovery to decide when intervention is worthwhile. On long-horizon ALFWorld tasks with Qwen3-14B, CIR raises success from 70.33% to 73.33%, a gain of 3.00 percentage points. It leaves all evaluated trajectories with correct observations untouched. Additional controls show that the benefit of recovery cannot be explained solely by the new observation returned by the environment. These results provide a practical way to evaluate recovery and apply it selectively.

</details>


### [188] [MCRI: A Four-Dimensional Framework for Analyzing and Evaluating Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01506)
*Zongrui Yang,Li Xintong,Runchen Xu,Zhongsheng Wang,Zhedong Lin,Haoyuan Li,Jiamou Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes MCRI Framework, a four-dimensional evaluation method for analyzing AI agent skills based on information gain and behavioral constraint. Operationalized as MCRI-Eval, it uses LLMs to evaluate 63,812 skills and achieves superior skill selection performance across three benchmarks compared to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The transition from single-tool to modular composite architectures in AI agents creates a need for systematic skill evaluation. However, no structured framework exists for analyzing and evaluating skills in this context. The authors aim to fill this gap by proposing a framework that can provide pre-execution signals for prioritizing promising skills.

Method: The MCRI Framework has four dimensions based on information gain and behavioral constraint. It is operationalized as MCRI-Eval, a large language model-based evaluation method. The evaluation uses 63,812 public skills from OpenClaw Skill Hub with 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions across three benchmarks: BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web.

Result: MCRI-Eval scores show positive association with community popularity signals and achieve the highest downstream ranking agreement. Compared to strongest baselines, MCRI-Eval selected skills improve top-1 performance by 17.7 percentile points on BigCodeBench, 22.8 on BFCL-Fundamental, and 19.6 on Mind2Web.

Conclusion: MCRI-Eval provides a useful pre-execution signal for prioritizing promising skills before costly execution-based evaluation, demonstrating its value as a practical tool for skill selection in modular AI agent systems.

Abstract: As agents evolve from single-tool systems into modular, composite architectures, skills are becoming an important mechanism for capability development and distribution. However, the academic community lacks a structured framework for systematically analyzing and evaluating skills. Drawing on information gain and behavioral constraint, we propose the four-dimensional MCRI Framework and operationalize it as MCRI-Eval, a large language model-based evaluation method. We evaluate MCRI-Eval using 63,812 public skills from the OpenClaw skill Hub, with 58,275 skill-conditioned model executions across BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web. MCRI-Eval scores are positively associated with community popularity signals and achieve the highest downstream ranking agreement among the evaluated methods. MCRI-Eval also improves top-1 skill selection across all three benchmarks: compared with the strongest baseline on each benchmark, the skills selected by MCRI-Eval advance by 17.7, 22.8, and 19.6 percentile points in downstream performance rank on BigCodeBench, BFCL-Fundamental, and Mind2Web, respectively. These results indicate that MCRI-Eval provides a useful pre-execution signal for prioritizing promising skills before costly execution-based evaluation.

</details>


### [189] [Benchmarking Prompt Optimization of Large Language Models With Chess](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00416)
*Timothée Lesort,Alejandra López de Aberasturi Gómez,Tristan Karch,Tom Veniat,Philippe Modard,Karl Tuyls,Ludovic Denoyer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a chess benchmark (1,118 Lichess puzzles) for studying Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) with frozen LLMs. The benchmark addresses key challenges in LLM evaluation: benchmark saturation, test set contamination, and expensive grading. It is designed to be challenging (~55% solve rate for best model), discriminative (reveals performance variations), renewable (fresh puzzles, adjustable difficulty), and affordable (~$800 for complete study).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from fundamental challenges in evaluating large language models as their capabilities advance: benchmarks can saturate, public test sets risk contamination, and assessing harder tasks requires expensive infrastructure. These challenges are particularly acute in Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO), where evaluation is repeated throughout the search process. The authors needed a benchmark that is cheap, deterministic, sufficiently challenging, and renewable as models evolve.

Method: The authors built a chess puzzle benchmark from 1,118 Lichess puzzles. They evaluated six APO algorithms on eight target models, measuring: (1) baseline strength, (2) response to optimization, (3) transfer across models, and (4) transfer to game play. The benchmark uses exact-match scoring with engine-based evaluation of alternative moves.

Result: Key findings: (1) Even the strongest model (Gemini 3.5 Flash used as meta-model) solves only ~55% of puzzles, demonstrating the benchmark's challenge level; (2) The benchmark is discriminative - revealing gains, unchanged performance, and regressions across different APO methods and models; (3) The complete study cost approximately $800, demonstrating affordability.

Conclusion: The chess benchmark is well-suited for APO research because it is: (i) challenging - leaving room for improvement even for strongest models; (ii) discriminative - revealing meaningful performance differences; (iii) renewable - with fresh puzzles to reduce contamination and adjustable difficulty; (iv) affordable - enabling comprehensive studies at reasonable cost. The authors release all puzzles, code, and dataset-renewal scripts to support future research.

Abstract: Evaluating large language models becomes increasingly challenging as their capabilities advance: benchmarks can saturate, public test sets risk contamination, and assessing harder tasks can require expensive grading or execution infrastructure. These challenges are amplified in automatic prompt optimization (APO), where evaluation is repeated throughout the search for better prompts. Studying APO therefore requires a benchmark that is cheap and deterministic to score, hard enough to leave room for improvement, and renewable as models evolve. We introduce a chess benchmark built from 1,118 Lichess puzzles to study APO for frozen LLMs: we optimize their prompts without updating their model weights. Chess combines inexpensive exact-match scoring, engine-based evaluation of alternative moves, and a renewable supply of problems with adjustable difficulty. Unlike evaluations that report only success on isolated test items, the benchmark also connects puzzle-solving gains to short game-play rollouts within the same domain. We use it to evaluate six APO algorithms on eight target models, measuring not only baseline strength but also how much each model responds to optimization and whether optimized prompts transfer across models and to game play. Chess is thus a well-suited benchmark for APO: it is (i) challenging, as even the strongest evaluated model, Gemini 3.5 Flash (used as the meta-model), solves only about 55\% of puzzles; (ii) discriminative, revealing gains, unchanged performance, and regressions across methods and models; (iii) renewable, with fresh puzzles to reduce contamination risk and adjustable difficulty to maintain headroom as models improve; and (iv) affordable, as the complete study runs for around \$800. We release the puzzles, optimization and evaluation code, and dataset-renewal scripts (https://github.com/imec-ailabs/Automatic-Prompt-Optimization-with-Chess).

</details>


### [190] [Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01833)
*Ngoc Phuoc An Vo,Aarya Doshi,Vadim Sheinin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A continuous evaluation framework for enterprise AI agents that combines outcome-level and process-level checks to detect behavioral drift that final-output evaluation misses. Applied to 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models, revealing that over 92% of runs passing final numerical checks still contained process-level deviations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, but final-output evaluation alone can miss process-level behavioral drift that affects reliability and accuracy.

Method: The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. It uses dependency attribution to identify root causes of failures.

Result: Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6%) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1%) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced mean failed checks from 6.34 to 2.65 roots per run. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with bootstrap intervals showing significance for all Revenue comparisons and one Productivity comparison.

Conclusion: The framework provides runtime-resolved templates enabling reusable regression coverage across evaluated configurations. Longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

Abstract: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, yet final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift. We present a continuous evaluation framework combining outcome-level and process-level checks, applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6 percent; Wilson 95 percent CI: 87.7-95.6 percent) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.9-95.3 percent) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced a mean of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 roots. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons. Runtime-resolved templates provided reusable regression coverage across the evaluated configurations; longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

</details>


### [191] [JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00437)
*Haoyang Su,Weiran Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JevSpawn is a compositional policy that bridges natural language task specifications with finite probabilistic exploration, addressing the limitations of slow LLM token-by-token generation and the constraint of pre-specified finite fields in Jev-style models. It uses parallel action spawning with feedback-driven branch selection, representation revision, and recovery mechanisms to enable efficient autonomous task solving.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents generate intermediate reasoning and actions token by token, which makes extended interactions slow and computationally expensive. While Jev-style models offer fast probabilistic predictions over finite fields, they require those fields to be specified in advance, limiting autonomous task solving where available actions must be derived from natural language instructions and adapted through interaction.

Method: JevSpawn introduces a compositional policy that: (1) couples parallel action spawning with feedback-driven branch selection; (2) incorporates representation revision; (3) enables recovery from retained alternatives. It uses shared action structure and model prefixes to reduce repeated generation and context computation without additional training.

Result: Evaluations on eight benchmark tasks against seven agent baselines and a TypeSafe Jev variant show that JevSpawn establishes itself as a promising approach to structured agentic inference, with improved task performance and faster navigation.

Conclusion: JevSpawn represents a promising approach to structured agentic inference, combining the fast probabilistic predictions of Jev-style models with the flexibility of natural language task specifications. It achieves improved task performance and faster navigation compared to baseline agents and a TypeSafe Jev variant.

Abstract: LLM agents generate intermediate reasoning and actions token by token, making extended interactions slow and computationally expensive. Jev-style models offer fast probabilistic predictions over finite fields, but require those fields to be specified in advance. This requirement limits autonomous task solving, where the available actions must be derived from natural language instructions and adapted through interaction. We introduce JevSpawn, a compositional policy that connects natural language task specifications to finite probabilistic exploration. Parallel action spawning is coupled with feedback driven branch selection, representation revision, and recovery from retained alternatives. Shared action structure and model prefixes reduce repeated generation and context computation without additional training. Evaluations on eight benchmark tasks against seven agent baselines and a TypeSafe Jev variant establish JevSpawn as a promising approach to structured agentic inference, with improved task performance and faster navigation.

</details>


### [192] [Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00511)
*Yizhi Liu,Balaji Padmanabhan,Siva Viswanathan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "epistemic actions" from cognitive science to LLM-based agents, arguing that agent design must address how decision-ready evidence is produced. It identifies three modes: acquiring missing evidence, transforming available evidence, and probing systems to create revealing responses. The concept of "epistemic scaffolding" is proposed for interfaces and tools that enable these actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based agents can search and explore, but agent design gives less attention to whether available evidence is ready for decision-making. Sometimes evidence is missing, hidden in form, or comparisons don't exist yet.

Method: The paper bridges cognitive science concepts (epistemic actions) with LLM-based agent design, proposing a framework of three modes and introducing "epistemic scaffolding" as a design principle.

Result: The paper establishes a conceptual framework distinguishing three modes of epistemic actions and argues for the importance of epistemic scaffolding in agent design.

Conclusion: Agent design must address how decision-ready evidence is produced, not just how to complete tasks. This requires designing interfaces, tools, and environments that enable epistemic actions and make them auditable.

Abstract: Before a difficult decision, people often act simply to understand the situation better. We turn an object to see another side, place alternatives next to each other, or change one condition and observe what happens. These actions may not complete the task, but they improve the evidence needed for the next choice. LLM-based agents can search and explore, yet agent design gives less attention to an earlier question: is the available evidence ready for the decision? Sometimes necessary evidence is missing. In other cases, the evidence is present but its form hides what matters, or the comparison needed to judge it does not yet exist. Cognitive science calls actions that improve the basis for a later choice epistemic actions. We bring this idea to LLM-based agents and distinguish three modes: acquiring missing evidence, transforming available evidence, and probing a system to create a revealing response. We use the term epistemic scaffolding for the interfaces, tools, and environments that make these actions possible and auditable. This paper argues that agent design must address how decision-ready evidence is produced.

</details>


### [193] [Ontology-Based Contextual AI Evaluations (OB-CAIE) Methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00529)
*Julie Krugler Hollek,Michael Zargham,Mala Kumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: The ontology-based contextual AI evaluation (OB-CAIE) methodology was developed to address a lack of scientific rigor that arises from unclear testing coverage, to balance human expertise and automations, and to address a lack of reproducibility of AI evaluation testing environments. OB-CAIE strengthens the current state of AI evaluations by addressing the first step in the scientific method by clearly defining what will be tested. Two ontologies represent the tractable problem space in the OB-CAIE methodology: the Domain-Specific Ontology (DSO) and the Evaluation Process Ontology (EPO). The DSO is the what; the EPO is the how. An OB-CAIE problem space can be used for one or multiple AI evaluations. The OB-CAIE methodology allows for human judgment at specific points, in scientifically grounded ways, and in complex subject areas where human feedback is genuinely irreducible or machine irreplaceable. A key advantage of the OB-CAIE methodology is that failure points can be traced, visualized and analyzed within the canonical OB-CAIE methodology problem space.

</details>


### [194] [Science or Slop?: Benchmarking and Mitigating Scientific Slop in AI-Generated Papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00531)
*Yerim Oh,Young-Jun Lee,Jaewoo Ahn,Gunhee Kim,Dongyeop Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper presents SciSlopBench, a benchmark of 390 AI-generated scientific papers paired with human-written papers, and proposes measures to detect "scientific slop" - AI-generated papers that appear plausible but have flawed scientific reasoning. It also introduces SciSlopHarness, a framework to reduce AI slop through evidence-based revision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-generated scientific papers (AI slop) are increasingly common and contain complex patterns that bypass existing token-based AI detectors. The scientific reasoning connecting different parts of these papers breaks down, potentially misleading readers. Existing detection methods like Binoculars only achieve 68.7% accuracy on such papers.

Method: The researchers constructed SciSlopBench with 390 AI-generated papers spanning computer science, life sciences, social sciences, and natural sciences, each paired with a human-written paper matched by research problem and contribution type. They developed six measures across Structure, Argument, and Artifacts to identify AI-generated papers. They also proposed SciSlopHarness, a harness-level framework that guides a fixed LLM to revise slop only where experimental records support changes.

Result: The proposed measures achieved 85.9% accuracy in identifying AI papers (vs. 68.7% for Binoculars). Higher scientific slop correlated with lower ICLR ratings and distinguished rejected from accepted papers above chance from 2017-2025. SciSlopHarness reduced the remaining AI-human gap by 63% over the strongest revision baseline without requiring human reference targets.

Conclusion: AI-generated scientific papers leave fundamental traces in their global reasoning. Responsible mitigation requires strict evidentiary grounding rather than mere prose refinement. The framework demonstrates that reducing scientific slop is possible through evidence-based revision.

Abstract: AI-generated content, often called AI slop, is increasingly common everywhere, particularly in academia. Slop in AI-generated scientific papers, however, has more complex patterns that cannot be easily detected by existing token-based AI detectors. Each part of such a paper looks plausible while the scientific reasoning that connects the parts breaks down, which can mislead how readers assess the work. We benchmark these failures as scientific slop through six measures across Structure, Argument, and Artifacts. We construct SciSlopBench with 390 AI-generated papers, mostly in computer science but spanning the life, social, and natural sciences, each paired with a human-written paper matched by research problem and contribution type. Our measures identify the AI paper in each pair with 85.9% accuracy, compared with 68.7% for Binoculars. Higher scientific slop accompanies lower ICLR ratings and distinguishes rejected from accepted papers above chance in every year from 2017 to 2025. Reducing these patterns, however, is not as simple as directly optimizing the measures. We therefore propose SciSlopHarness, a harness-level framework that guides a fixed LLM to revise slop only where the experiment records support the change. While standard revisions leave residual slop and direct slop-aware prompting triggers reward hacking, SciSlopHarness reduces the remaining AI-human gap by 63% over the strongest revision baseline without requiring human reference targets. Overall, we demonstrate that AI-generated scientific papers leave fundamental traces in their global reasoning, and that responsible mitigation demands strict evidentiary grounding rather than mere prose refinement.

</details>


### [195] [Worse Together: How Performance Breaks Down in Multi-User Multi-Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00583)
*Sahan Paliskara,Nattaput Namchittai,Andrew Lampinen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies multi-user, multi-agent coordination across 5 frontier models and 77 scenarios in 4 environments (API key, clinic, personal assistant, merge queue). Teams of agents consistently underperform a single coordinator agent, with coordination failures including stalling, action overriding, and fabricating claims. The paper identifies environment-specific mitigations and releases MAMUBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents increasingly serve multiple users and encounter other agents over shared resources (codebase, calendar, budget), coordination often fails, resulting in worse group outcomes than if a single agent had acted for everyone.

Method: Experimental study comparing a single coordinator agent (serves every user) vs. a team of agents (each serves one user), with and without communication channels, across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: API key sharing (compute budget), clinic sharing (calendar), personal assistant (group order/booking), and merge queue (release cutoff).

Result: Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment. Without a communication channel, teams completely collapse in two environments. Even with a channel, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps (e.g., coordinator fulfills ~2x as many user requests in personal assistant environment). Distinct failure behaviors identified: stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims.

Conclusion: Effective but environment-specific mitigations exist: team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and platform check (reading peers' messages before committing). The authors will release three environments as MAMUBench (74 scenarios) for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination.

Abstract: People are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, and those agents are increasingly encountering other people's agents over shared resources such as a codebase, a calendar, or a budget. When each agent acts for a different user with different goals, coordination often fails, and the group ends up worse off than if a single agent had acted for everyone. We study this multi-user, multi-agent setting across five frontier models and 77 scenarios in four environments: an API key environment in which agents share a compute budget, a clinic in which they share a calendar, a personal assistant environment in which they share a group order or booking, and a merge queue in which they share a release cutoff. In each scenario, we compare a single agent that serves every user (a coordinator) to a team in which each agent serves one user, with and without a communication channel between the agents. Teams deliver worse group outcomes than the coordinator in every environment: without a channel, they completely collapse in two environments, and even with one, coordination overhead creates substantial gaps. For example, in the personal assistant environment, the coordinator fulfills a targeted user request about twice as often as teams. We identify distinct behaviors associated with this poor group-level performance, including stalling as teams grow, overriding each other's actions, and fabricating claims. We find effective but environment-specific mitigations, such as a team lead, explicit procedural instructions, and a platform check that makes an agent read its peers' messages before committing. We will release the API key, clinic, and personal assistant environments as MAMUBench, comprising 74 scenarios for evaluating multi-user, multi-agent coordination.

</details>


### [196] [Legal Research Bench: Measuring End-to-End Reliability in Long-Horizon Legal Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00609)
*Katrina Drozdov,Oliver Chen,Langston Nashold,Rayan Krishnan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Legal Research Bench (LRB) is a benchmark of 413 U.S. legal research questions designed to evaluate language model agents on legal research tasks. The study evaluates 13 frontier models with various tools and finds that even the best model (Claude Opus 4.8) achieves only 42.9% fully correct answers, revealing that LLM agents remain far from reliable for legal research applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Legal research is a core but time-consuming workflow requiring identification of controlling authority, verification of validity, reconciliation of statutes/cases, and synthesis of grounded answers. While language model agents are natural fits for this retrieval-intensive workflow, their reliability is critical - missing authorities, stale citations, or wrong conclusions can make answers unusable. Automating even part of this workflow would be valuable, but requires reliable AI systems.

Method: The researchers created LRB with 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with gold answers, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. They evaluated 13 frontier models using a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. Responses were scored through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied AND its cited authorities verify. The LLM judge was validated against expert attorneys to ensure benchmark scores track attorney judgment.

Result: Among 13 models tested, the strongest performer was Claude Opus 4.8, achieving fully correct answers on only 42.9% of questions. Performance varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Notably, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy across models.

Conclusion: LLM agents remain far from reliable for legal research tasks. The benchmark reveals significant limitations in current frontier models' ability to perform accurate legal research, with even the best models failing on the majority of questions. This highlights the need for continued development before practical deployment in legal workflows. The LRB benchmark provides a rigorous evaluation framework for tracking progress in this domain.

Abstract: Legal research is a core and time-consuming legal workflow. Lawyers must identify controlling authority, verify that it remains valid, reconcile statutes and cases, and synthesize a grounded answer. Language model agents are a natural fit for this retrieval-intensive workflow, and automating even part of it would be valuable. But that value depends on reliability: a single missing authority, stale citation, or wrong legal conclusion can make an otherwise plausible answer unusable. We introduce \textbf{Legal Research Bench} (LRB), a benchmark of 413 open-ended U.S. legal research questions written by experts, each paired with a gold answer, supporting authorities, and a binary grading rubric. We evaluate thirteen frontier models in a harness with web search, case-law search, page parsing, and retrieval tools. We score agent responses through all-pass grading with source verification, where a response is correct only if every required criterion is satisfied and its cited authorities verify. We also validate the LLM judge against expert attorneys ensuring that benchmark scores track attorney judgment. Agents remain far from reliable: among the models we tested, the strongest, Claude Opus 4.8, is fully correct on 42.9\% of questions. Performance also varies substantially by task setting: all-pass rates differ across areas of law and are lower on questions requiring reconciliation of conflicting authorities. Across models, more turns, tool calls, and inference cost do not predict higher accuracy.

</details>


### [197] [Spatial Strategies, Not Actions: Vector-Quantized Geodesics as Tools for LLM-Driven Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00613)
*Gabriel Turinici*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a hybrid architecture for LLM-based agents that combines geometrical tools with a LLM orchestrator to improve spatial understanding in grid-world environments. The approach uses geodesic trajectory extraction and vector quantization for tool discovery, with the LLM handling high-level reasoning and tool selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based agents are criticized for lacking spatial understanding and mainly exploiting statistical text patterns rather than true spatial comprehension.

Method: The architecture combines: (1) Geodesic trajectory collection from the environment, (2) Vector quantization to extract representative trajectory subsets, (3) Offline LLM training to associate natural language descriptions with trajectories (making them tools), (4) Online LLM acts as high-level orchestrator choosing appropriate tools based on current state and goal, (5) Low-level control via primitive actions executing selected trajectories. Testing used Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment with a zoom tool and collision detection tool.

Result: The fast non-reasoning configuration matched the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while reducing decision time from minutes to seconds.

Conclusion: The two-level learning approach (unsupervised trajectory quantization for tool discovery + LLM for reasoning) successfully enables spatial comprehension in LLM agents, achieving comparable performance to complex reasoning methods with significantly reduced computational cost.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) based agents are often criticized for lacking spatial understanding and mainly exploiting statistical text patterns. We investigate their spatial comprehension through an architecture combining geometrical tools with a LLM serving as a high-level orchestrator in grid-world environments. The agent first collects geodesic trajectories, which are then vector-quantized to extract a representative subset. Offline, the LLM associates a natural language description of the underlying behavioral patterns to each selected trajectory, making it a tool. Online, the LLM chooses the appropriate tool conditioned on the current state and goal. Low-level control is handled by primitive actions that execute the trajectory associated with the tool. From an agentic AI perspective, this approach separates learning into two levels: tool discovery is handled through unsupervised quantization of trajectories, while reasoning and decision-making are handled by the LLM. We test the approach in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment with an open vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). Pairing the geometry-derived tool library with an agent-centered zoom tool and a collision detection tool lets a fast, non-reasoning configuration match the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while cutting the cost of a decision from minutes to seconds.

</details>


### [198] [CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00636)
*Chenmu Zhang,Levi Felix,Jun-Jie Zhang,Xingfu Li,Xuelian Jiang,Tao Jiang,Subhendu Mishra,Xixi Qin,Boris Yakobson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CompMat-Bench is a benchmark of 94 computational materials research tasks designed to evaluate AI agents without running expensive simulations. Agents achieve 66.0-90.4% pass rates on single tasks with full guidance, but performance degrades with longer workflows or reduced guidance. Most failures are due to scientific errors rather than software usage errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is impractical due to the time and resources required for expensive simulations. Repeating simulations across agents and trials makes evaluation costly. There was a need for a benchmark that can assess agents on materials research steps without actually running the underlying simulations.

Method: The authors created CompMat-Bench with 94 tasks derived from published computational materials studies. They pre-computed the expensive simulation inputs and results, then assessed agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs. Evaluation uses fixed rules without an LLM judge. Four conditions are supported: single tasks/workflows, each with full or reduced methodological guidance.

Result: Three LLM-based agents achieved pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks with full guidance on single tasks. Longer workflows and reduced guidance both limit performance, but differently: weaker agents degrade under both conditions, while the strongest agent only fails when long workflow combines with reduced guidance. Most failures (attributed via failure analysis) are scientific errors rather than software usage errors.

Conclusion: CompMat-Bench provides a practical basis for comparing AI agents on real materials research steps and analyzing failure modes. The benchmark reveals that current agents can complete individual research steps but struggle with complex workflows and limited guidance, with scientific reasoning being a key challenge.

Abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 66.0-90.4% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the strongest agent falls only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes most failures to scientific errors rather than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.

</details>


### [199] [Incident-Arena: Getting agents to the last nine of reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00648)
*Andre Fu,Malik Drabla,Leon Liu,Meji Abidoye,Marek Suppa,Lata Mishra,Adnan El Assadi,Yiyuan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Incident-Arena, a benchmark for evaluating AI coding agents in production incident response (agentic SRE). The benchmark features 20 realistic tasks deploying actual applications to ephemeral Kubernetes clusters with injected faults and load profiles. Frontier models achieve below 64.3% success rates, with failures stemming from diagnosis errors, incomplete repairs, and unsafe regressions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for AI coding agents suffer from three critical limitations: (1) unrealistic environments using toy repositories, (2) non-standard framework implementations, and (3) simple static verifiers. This gap is significant because AI agents are widely used in engineering workflows, yet their ability to handle real-world production incident response remains under-evaluated.

Method: The authors built Incident-Arena with 20 carefully selected tasks grounded in real-world deployed open-source software. Each task: (1) deploys a production application to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, (2) injects a fault from the config layer through underlying images, (3) applies a sustained load profile based on task requirements. They introduce a novel verification method that goes beyond static checks to functional verifiers, holding system-level metrics stable while ensuring repairs are done safely.

Result: Agent trials average 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, demonstrating long-horizon reasoning capabilities. Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models score below 64.3% success rate. Failures span three categories: diagnosis/localization errors, incomplete repairs, and unsafe regressions.

Conclusion: Current frontier AI models struggle with agentic SRE tasks despite their effectiveness in general coding. The benchmark reveals significant gaps in handling real-world production incidents, particularly in diagnosis accuracy, repair completeness, and safety guarantees. Incident-Arena provides a more realistic and rigorous evaluation framework for agentic SRE systems.

Abstract: AI coding agents are ubiquitous in engineering workflows amongst industry and academia. Yet, despite their use in app coding, relatively less attention has been paid to their ability to execute on production incident response. This emerging field, termed agentic site-reliability-engineering (SRE) contains benchmarks limited by (1) unrealistic environments, typically toy repositories (2) non-standard framework implementations and (3) simple static verifiers. We introduce Incident-Arena, a human-built benchmark of 20 carefully selected tasks grounded in real-world deployed open source software. Each task deploys a production application to an ephemeral Kubernetes cluster, injecting a fault from the config layer through underlying images, and a sustained load profile given the task requirements. We also present a novel verification method, going beyond static checks to functional verifiers, holding systems level metrics stable, while ensuring repairs are done safely. Agent trials run an average of 2.81M tokens and 41 turns, going beyond existing benchmarks, demonstrating agentic long horizon reasoning. Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models score below 64.3%, with failures extending from diagnosis/localization errors, through incomplete repairs and unsafe regressions.

</details>


### [200] [Agent Evaluation Reliability: More Tasks Won't (Always) Fix An Agent Leaderboard](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00651)
*Michael Hardy,Ruhana Azam,Anka Reuel,Mykel Kochenderfer,Sanmi Koyejo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines the reliability of agent evaluations for ranking LLMs. The authors develop a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework and apply it to 22 benchmarks, finding that while fixed model-scaffold systems can be ranked reliably (0.935-0.994), underlying model reliability is much lower (0.148-0.841). They show that scaffold choice significantly impacts conclusions, more tasks have limited value, and pooling diverse benchmarks can improve reliability at lower cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, but rankings may reflect evaluation conditions (scaffolds, tasks) rather than just the model itself. The reliability of such evaluations depends on the intended claim - whether ranking deployed systems or underlying models. This raises questions about what conclusions current agent evaluations can reliably support.

Method: The authors developed a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework specifically designed for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards. They applied this framework to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index. The framework separates signal (performance differences relevant to the intended claim) from noise (irrelevant variation that can change rankings). They measured: (1) fixed model-scaffold system reliability, (2) underlying-model reliability, (3) inter-scaffold reliability (whether scaffolds preserve model rankings), and (4) the effect of pooling diverse benchmarks.

Result: Four key findings emerged: (1) Reliability depends on measurement goal - fixed model-scaffold systems are ranked reliably (0.935-0.994), while underlying-model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). (2) Scaffold choice can change conclusions - inter-scaffold reliability varies substantially across evaluations. (3) More tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty - even infinitely many similarly constructed tasks improve model-ranking reliability by at most 0.097 when uncertainty is dominated by limited scaffold coverage. (4) Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve cross-task rankings at lower cost - pooling raises projected reliability from 0.44 to 0.75 at the same task budget and can reduce projected cost by up to 83%.

Conclusion: Evaluation design should follow the intended claim: identify what a score or ranking should mean, diagnose what limits its reliability, and spend evaluation budget on the sources of uncertainty that matter. The key insight is that reliability claims are claim-dependent - an evaluation that reliably ranks deployed systems may not reliably rank underlying models. Practical recommendations include focusing on the specific source of uncertainty relevant to the intended use case and pooling diverse benchmarks when ranking across diverse agentic tasks.

Abstract: Agent evaluations are increasingly used to compare LLMs and inform deployment decisions, yet ranks can reflect not only the model but also the effects of the evaluation conditions such as the scaffolds or tasks. This makes reliability claim-dependent: an evaluation that reliably ranks deployed systems may not reliably rank underlying models. We ask which conclusions current agent evaluations reliably support and what additional evaluation would improve them. We develop a Bayesian variance-decomposition framework for sparse, imbalanced agent leaderboards and apply it to 22 benchmarks from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard and Harbor Index. The framework separates signal, performance differences relevant to the intended claim, from noise, irrelevant variation that can still change rankings. We find: (1) Reliability depends on the measurement goal. Fixed model-scaffold systems are ranked reliably (0.935-0.994), while underlying-model reliability is substantially lower (0.148-0.841). (2) Scaffold choice can change conclusions. Inter-scaffold reliability measures whether scaffolds preserve model rankings, showing that scaffold effects vary substantially across evaluations. (3) More tasks cannot resolve all uncertainty. Even infinitely many similarly constructed tasks improve model-ranking reliability of a benchmark by at most 0.097 when uncertainty is dominated by limited scaffold coverage. (4) Pooling diverse benchmarks can improve cross-task rankings at lower cost. For rankings across diverse agentic tasks, pooling benchmarks raises projected reliability from 0.44 to 0.75 at the same task budget and can reduce projected cost by up to 83\%. Evaluation design should follow the intended claim: identify what a score or ranking should mean, diagnose what limits its reliability, and spend evaluation budget on the sources of uncertainty that matter.

</details>


### [201] [When More Data Is Not Enough: The Context-Sufficiency Frontier in Generative AI Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00654)
*Merieme Askour,Ayoub Merimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a theory of "context sufficiency" for AI-driven personalization, proposing that the relevance of context to customer intent matters more than volume. Through full-factorial experiments at a home-furnishing retailer, the authors demonstrate that relevant context improves recommendation appropriateness while irrelevant context degrades it and destabilizes retrieval. The framework introduces four context states (insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, interference) and the Context-Sufficiency Frontier to identify minimal relevant context sets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical problem in generative AI personalization: once context becomes easy to supply, more context is not necessarily better. The authors observe that while generative AI allows providers to supply dynamic situational information at the moment of response, there is no theoretical framework for determining how much or what type of context is appropriate. This creates a need to understand the relationship between context volume and personalization effectiveness.

Method: A full-factorial experiment was conducted using a generative recommender system at a large home-furnishing retailer. The experiment tested different combinations of relevant and irrelevant context to measure their effects on recommendation appropriateness and retrieval stability.

Result: The experiments revealed a nuanced relationship between context and personalization quality. Relevant context (information aligned with the customer's current intent) improved recommendation appropriateness. Conversely, irrelevant context reduced appropriateness and destabilized retrieval, demonstrating that context quality matters more than quantity. The research identified four context states: insufficiency (too little), sufficiency (optimal), saturation (diminishing returns), and interference (harmful).

Conclusion: The framework shifts personalization paradigm from supplying more context toward identifying what the current interaction actually requires and enforcing constraints throughout the service process. The Context-Sufficiency Frontier concept provides a theoretical tool for locating the minimal relevant set of context needed for effective personalization.

Abstract: Personalization has long relied on customer data to infer what an individual is likely to value. We call this customer evidence: the customer's historical behavior and preferences. Generative AI extends personalization by allowing providers to supply changing situational information at the moment a response is produced, without encoding every condition in advance. We define this provider-side context as information about what is possible, permitted, or advisable now. This flexibility creates a new problem: once context becomes easy to supply, more is not necessarily better. We develop a theory of context sufficiency in which the relevance of context to the customer's current intent matters more than its volume. The theory identifies four states, insufficiency, sufficiency, saturation, and interference, and introduces the Context-Sufficiency Frontier to locate the minimal relevant set. In a full-factorial experiment with a generative recommender at a large home-furnishing retailer, relevant context improved appropriateness, while irrelevant context reduced it and destabilized retrieval. The framework shifts personalization from supplying more context toward identifying what the current interaction actually requires and enforcing constraints throughout the service process.

</details>


### [202] [Backdoor Containment via Expert Quarantine and Shutdown in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00663)
*Jianwei Li,Min-Seon Kim,Jung-Eun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes a new defense strategy called "learn, but channel" for backdoor attacks in LLMs. Instead of preventing backdoor formation or purifying after training, this approach allows backdoors to form but routes them into a quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. The method, called Quarantined Expert Shutdown (QES), uses routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving normal capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing defenses either suppress backdoor learning or learn then purify. This paper introduces a third strategy: learn but channel - allowing backdoor formation but containing it in a quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment time, avoiding the need for trigger screening or weight updates.

Method: QES augments a Transformer-based language model with: 1) routed expert-specific LoRA branches, 2) lightweight routers, and 3) auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation is simply zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight.

Result: Reduces attack success rate (ASR) from 100% to 0-10% across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected.

Conclusion: The "learn, but channel" strategy represents a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs, offering computationally efficient containment with a single constant-time operation at deployment.

Abstract: Backdoored large language models (LLMs) can behave normally on benign inputs while producing attacker-specified outputs under hidden triggers. Existing defenses span four stages--prior-training, in-training, post-training, and inference-time--and share one of two underlying strategies: either suppress backdoor learning (by filtering poisoned data or interrupting its acquisition during optimization) or learn, then purify (by repairing model weights or gating inputs after a fully backdoored model has formed). We propose a third strategy, learn, but channel: allow backdoor formation during training but route it into a designated, quarantined component that can be disabled at deployment. To this end, we propose Quarantined Expert Shutdown QES, a computationally efficient containment strategy built in a regularization-steered MoE-like setting. Specifically, given a poisoned dataset, QES augments a Transformer-based language model with routed expert-specific LoRA branches and lightweight routers, and uses auxiliary routing objectives to attract trigger-conditioned behavior into a designated expert while preserving benign capability elsewhere. At deployment, mitigation reduces to a single constant-time operation: zeroing the quarantined expert's routing weight, without trigger screening or further updating model weights. Empirically, our methods reduce the attack success rate ASR from 100% to 0-10% on most settings across two tasks, three attacks, and four model families, while downstream utility is often preserved or only modestly affected. These results establish learn, but channel as a previously unexplored regime for backdoor containment in generative LLMs.

</details>


### [203] [A Simple Doxastic Deontic Logic for Norm-Guided Decision Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00668)
*Thorsten Engesser,Agata Ciabattoni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a doxastic deontic logic for autonomous systems to make decisions under conflicting norms and unreliable information. It defines a distinction between subjective and objective optimization for norm compliance, and shows conditions under which these coincide and can be solved via weighted partial MaxSAT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous systems face fundamental challenges when making decisions in environments with conflicting norms, incomplete information, and unreliable data. Existing approaches lack a formal framework for handling norms that depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and other norms.

Method: The authors introduce a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic, extended with explicit conditional norms and combined with multi-agent KD45 (a belief logic). This allows norms to depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and norms. They then define the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem where an agent chooses decisions minimizing weighted norm violations.

Result: The paper provides: (i) conditions under which subjective optimization (relative to agent's beliefs) coincides with objective optimization (relative to actual facts), and (ii) a polynomial-time reduction of optimal decision-making to weighted partial MaxSAT.

Conclusion: The framework enables autonomous systems to reason about norm compliance in a computationally tractable way, even when beliefs are incomplete or unreliable. The reduction to MaxSAT provides a practical approach for solving norm compliance optimization in real-world applications.

Abstract: Making decisions despite conflicting norms and incomplete or unreliable information is a fundamental challenge for autonomous systems. We introduce a simple doxastic deontic logic for this setting: a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic, extended with explicit conditional norms and combined with multi-agent KD45, so that norms can depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and norms. On this logic we define the Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem, where an agent chooses a decision minimizing weighted norm violations. We distinguish subjective optimization (relative to the agent's beliefs) from objective optimization (relative to the actual facts). We give conditions under which (i) the two coincide and (ii) optimal decision-making can be reduced to weighted partial MaxSAT in polynomial time.

</details>


### [204] [Ontology-Grounded, Reasoner-Verified Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Reasoning in Scientific AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00682)
*Nishtha N. Vaidya,Stephan Grimm,Thomas Hubauer,Thomas A. Runkler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A pipeline that automatically generates ontology-grounded multiple-choice question benchmarks from OWL 2 ontologies to evaluate logical reasoning in LLMs. Uses OWL reasoner to verify correct answers and distractors, generating 17,819 MCQs across three ontologies (Pizza, PMDco, DOID).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in scientific AI applications requiring logical reasoning, but they often produce factual inaccuracies. Existing benchmarks have scaling issues and LLM-based generation risks embedding flaws. There is a need for high-quality, grounded benchmarks with verifiable correctness.

Method: The pipeline generates MCQs from OWL 2 ontologies with correct answers grounded by design. Distractors are created by perturbing class expression axioms, and their incorrectness is verified via OWL reasoner entailment checks. Four semantic categories of distractors are used: from class unsatisfiability to weakened subsumptions.

Result: Generated 112 (Pizza), 2,491 (PMDco), and 15,216 (DOID) MCQs. Quality metrics: mean LLM judge scores of 4.02, 4.36, and 3.36 out of 5 for fluency; correct-answer-to-distractor similarity above 0.8. Six LLMs evaluated zero-shot achieve 41.1-76.8% accuracy vs 25% random baseline.

Conclusion: This work provides a step toward more reliable benchmarks for assessing logical reasoning in scientific AI. The benchmarks are challenging and discriminative, enabling diagnostic evaluation of specific reasoning failures across different semantic categories.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly underpin scientific AI applications that reason over structured knowledge, from biomedical question answering to materials informatics. However, their logical reasoning often falls short, producing factual inaccuracies unacceptable in these settings. Reliable evaluation remains challenging: manual dataset construction scales poorly, and LLM-based generation risks embedding the very flaws it aims to measure. High-quality benchmarks must ground both correct and incorrect labelled examples in explicit background knowledge, formally verifiable by a standard reasoner. We propose a pipeline that automatically generates ontology-grounded multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks from any sufficiently axiomatised OWL 2 ontology, with correct answers grounded in the ontology by design. Distractors are generated by perturbing the right-hand-side class expressions of class definition axioms, and their incorrectness is formally verified by an OWL reasoner via entailment checks. We evaluate the pipeline on three ontologies: Pizza (small, academic), PMDco (complex, materials science), and DOID (large, biomedical), generating 112, 2,491, and 15,216 MCQs respectively. Distractors span four semantic categories from class unsatisfiability to weakened subsumptions, enabling diagnostic evaluation of specific reasoning failures. Items meet natural language quality standards: mean LLM judge scores of 4.02, 4.36, and 3.36 out of 5 confirm fluency, and correct-answer-to-distractor similarity above 0.8 shows that wrong options cannot be dismissed on surface form alone. Six LLMs evaluated zero-shot achieve 41.1-76.8% accuracy, well above the 25% random-guessing baseline, indicating the benchmarks are challenging and discriminative. This work is a step towards more reliable benchmarks for assessing logical reasoning in scientific AI.

</details>


### [205] [Backdoor Purification for LoRA-Tuned LLMs via Null-Space Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00685)
*Jianwei Li,Jung-Eun Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel backdoor purification method for LoRA-tuned LLMs that works without prior knowledge of triggers, clean references, or post-hoc retraining. The method constructs orthogonal null spaces in input/output channels to project LoRA updates, reducing attack success rate from ~100% to <10% while preserving model capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
