Motivation: Existing backdoor purification methods rely on strong assumptions (prior knowledge of triggers, clean references, aggressive retraining) that limit practical applicability. The authors aim to purify LoRA-tuned LLMs without these constraints.

Method: The method uses data curation and feature approximation to extract high-fidelity backdoor directions, then constructs orthogonal null spaces in both input and output channels for each layer/head. LoRA updates are projected onto these null spaces. The approach scales from single-layer text classification to full-parameter LLM in generative tasks through ablation studies.

Result: The null-space projection method reduces attack success rate (ASR) from nearly 100% to less than 10%, while preserving the base model's benign performance and the adapter's learned downstream abilities.

Conclusion: The proposed null-space projection approach effectively purifies backdoor attacks in LoRA-tuned LLMs without requiring prior trigger knowledge, clean references, or retraining, making it highly practical for real-world deployment.

Abstract: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, the risk of backdoor attacks has become more severe. Existing backdoor purification methods typically rely on at least one of the strong assumptions, such as prior knowledge of triggers, access to clean references, or aggressive retraining, and they often lack comprehensive evaluations. These constraints substantially limit their practical applicability. To overcome these challenges, our work proposes purifying LoRA-tuned LLMs without these assumptions and even without post-hoc retraining of the suspect parameters. Our objective is to significantly reduce the attack success rates (ASR) while preserving both (i) the base model's general capabilities and (ii) the new downstream skills learned through the adapter. Through a series of ablation studies, we progressively scale our approach from a single layer in a text classification setting to a full-parameter LLM in the generative task. Through careful data curation and feature approximation, we extract high-fidelity backdoor directions and, for each layer or head, construct orthogonal null spaces in both the input and output channels, onto which the LoRA updates are projected. Empirically, our null-space projection method reduces the ASR from nearly 100% to less than 10%, while preserving the base model's benign performance and the adapter's learned abilities during downstream task adaptation.

</details>


### [206] [R-GroundBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for R-Group Groundingin Markush Molecular Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00700)
*Xin Wang,Zichuan Ying,Xinna Lin,Junqi Zhang,Hanyi Xiong,Tianyu Gao,Hairong Zhang,Qixiang Hua,Botian Shi,Zhenhailong Wang,Kaicheng Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: R-GroundBench is a new benchmark for evaluating AI models on R-group grounding in Markush chemical structures (variable placeholders used in pharmaceutical patents). The benchmark reveals a significant performance gap between easy recognition tasks (90%+ accuracy) and hard grounding tasks (56-66% for general models, 25.7-46.2% for chemical-domain VLMs), highlighting that current AI systems lack reliable molecular grounding capabilities for chemical design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current molecule-language benchmarks only evaluate fully specified molecules, leaving the critical task of R-group grounding (connecting variable placeholders to actual molecular structures) largely unevaluated. This gap is problematic because Markush structures are ubiquitous in pharmaceutical patents and require reasoning across molecular, textual, and chemical information.

Method: Built a diagnostic benchmark from real patent Markush structures with two evaluation tracks: (1) Multiple-Choice VQA track with controlled difficulty (Easy/Hard) and modality splits, and (2) open-ended Generation track. The benchmark controls for shortcuts to ensure genuine evaluation of grounding capabilities.

Result: Models achieve >90% accuracy on Easy VQA but only 56-66% on Hard VQA when shortcuts are controlled. Chemical-domain VLMs achieve only 25.7-46.2% on Hard VQA despite domain-specific pretraining. Generation Exact Match remains below 20% for most models and below 8% when visual input is required.

Conclusion: Current AI systems lack reliable grounding and execution for Markush editing. There is a substantial gap between recognition and molecular grounding capabilities, highlighting fundamental challenges for AI-driven scientific discovery in the chemical/pharmaceutical domain.

Abstract: Recent advances in AI for scientific discovery enable molecular understandingand design, yet reasoning over incomplete chemical representations remainsunclear.Markush structures, which encode molecular families through variable R-groupplaceholders (\textit{R\textsubscript{1}}, \textit{R\textsubscript{2}}, \textit{X}, etc.), are ubiquitous in pharmaceutical patents and requiregrounding across molecular, textual, and chemical information.However, existing molecule-language benchmarks focus on fully specifiedmolecules, leaving R-group grounding largely unevaluated.We introduce R-GroundBench:, a diagnostic benchmark built from real patent Markushstructures, featuring a Multiple-Choice (VQA) track with controlled difficultyand modality splits, and an open-ended Generation track.Our results reveal a substantial gap between recognition andmolecular grounding.While models achieve over 90\% accuracy on Easy VQA, performance drops to56--66\% on Hard VQA when shortcuts are controlled.Chemical-domain VLMs also remain unreliable, achieving only 25.7--46.2\% on HardVQA despite domain-specific pretraining.Moreover, Generation Exact Match remains below 20\% for most models and below8\% when visual input is required.These findings reveal that current AI systems lack reliable grounding andexecution for Markush editing, highlighting challenges for AI-drivenscientific discovery.

</details>


### [207] [Meta-Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Fast Adaptation of Interactive Policies with Applications to Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00705)
*Huiwen Yan,Kyriakos G. Vamvoudakis,Mushuang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework that enables fast adaptation of interactive policies across a distribution of Markov games. It addresses the challenge of extending meta-RL from single-agent to multi-agent systems by defining a new solution concept called meta-NE and establishing conditions for its equivalence to stationary points of gradient-play-based algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing meta-RL approaches focus on single-agent systems. Extending these to multi-agent systems is challenging because tasks are characterized by both the environment and agents' strategic interactions, requiring a fundamentally different approach to handle the added complexity of multi-agent dynamics.

Method: The paper models MARL problems as Markov games (MGs) and develops a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. A new concept called "meta-NE" is defined to describe the desired solution concept. The study establishes sufficient conditions for the equivalence between a meta-NE and a stationary point of the gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm.

Result: Evaluation on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrates that the proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed meta-MARL framework is effective for rapid interactive policy adaptation in multi-agent systems, achieving superior adaptation speed compared to existing pretrained MARL baselines.

Abstract: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework to enable fast adaptation of interactive policies in a multi-agent system (MAS). Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to rapidly adapt to new tasks/environments using a bi-level optimization mechanism. However, existing meta-RL generally focuses on single-agent systems. Extending these frameworks and algorithms to multi-agent systems poses additional challenges, as tasks are characterized by not only the environment but also agents' strategic interactions. To address these challenges, we model multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems as Markov games (MGs) and develop a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. A new concept, called meta-NE, is defined to describe the desired solution concept in a meta-MARL problem. Sufficient conditions for the equivalence between a meta-NE and a stationary point of the gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm are established. Our evaluation on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrates that the proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines, validating the effectiveness of our framework.

</details>


### [208] [ReLiveGym: Evaluating Long-Lived Agents over Weeks of Replayed Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00710)
*Xisen Jin,Jingheng Li,Zhenglun Chen,Junyi Du,Xiang Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReLiveGym is a diagnostic evaluation environment for long-lived LLM agents that operate over simulated weeks of real-world data streams (news, market, social media), addressing persistent monitoring and recurring action tasks that existing agent benchmarks miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-horizon agent work assumes static environments, but real-world deployments require agents that operate unattended for days/weeks, act at right timing, and adapt to dynamic environments over time.

Method: Introduced ReLiveGym environment with tasks spanning diverse time sensitivity, reasoning intensity, and recurrence levels. Evaluated 8 base language models, investigating model choice and harness design (especially action timing mechanisms). Also tested continuous learning from hindsight feedback.

Result: Action timing mechanism is a critical harness-design axis for long-lived tasks; optimal design varies across tasks and model choices. Continuous learning from feedback helps address failure modes.

Conclusion: Model choice, action timing mechanism, and use of feedback are important design considerations for long-lived LLM agents. Code publicly available.

Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents become widely adopted, they are increasingly deployed for tasks that require persistent monitoring or recurring actions (e.g., market analysis). These agents are expected to operate unattended for days or weeks, act at the right timing, and adapt to the dynamic environment over time. These challenges are not fully captured in the existing long-horizon agent work, as they often consider a static environment that is not temporally changing. We introduce ReLiveGym, a diagnostic evaluation environment of long-lived tasks in which agents act sparsely over simulated weeks of chronologically replayed real-world news, market, and social-media streams. The tasks span diverse levels of time sensitivity, reasoning intensity, and recurrence. Across eight base language models, we investigate how model choice and harness design affect agent performance on such long-lived tasks. Our results show that how agents determine when to act arises as an important harness-design axis for long-lived tasks; and that the optimal design varies across tasks and sometimes model choices as well. We also evaluate how continuous learning from hindsight feedback affects performance and addresses failure modes observed in these long-lived tasks. These findings indicate model choice, action timing mechanism, and use of feedback as important considerations in the design of long-lived agents. Code: https://github.com/SaharaLabsAI/ReLiveGym

</details>


### [209] [Robust Nash Alignment under Preference Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00715)
*Shihab Ahmed,Debamita Ghosh,David Tang,Yudan Wang,Alvaro Velasquez,Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for aligning language models to uncertain pairwise preferences. It addresses the brittleness of standard preference-based alignment methods by formulating a robust optimization problem that considers worst-case performance against any preference kernel within an ambiguity set around nominal preferences.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preference-based alignment methods typically optimize against a single preference model, making them brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain (noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment). This uncertainty in preferences can lead to suboptimal or failed alignment in real-world applications.

Method: The paper introduces a four-player primal-dual proxy game involving: (1) leader policy, (2) follower policy, (3) adversarial kernel, and (4) dual variable. A single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm is developed to solve this proxy game. The approach provides a certified lower bound on worst-case performance when the ambiguity set captures preference uncertainty.

Result: The proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective. The paper quantifies the proxy-to-hard gap and characterizes an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. The algorithm achieves O(1/√T) average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, implying near-optimal robust policy for the original objective.

Conclusion: Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment with uncertain preference validate the convergence theory and show improved performance over nominal baselines. The framework provides a principled way to handle preference uncertainty in alignment.

Abstract: Preference-based alignment methods typically optimize against a single preference model, and can therefore be brittle when pairwise preferences are uncertain: noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment. To address these issues, we propose Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework for alignment to uncertain pairwise preferences. Our formulation has a major learner seeking a policy with a large worst-case win rate against both an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel lying in an ambiguity set around a nominal preference. When the ambiguity set captures the uncertainty in preferences, the resulting robust objective of the game directly yields a certified lower bound on worst-case performance. However, we note this problem is computationally challenging to optimize, and to address this, we introduce a four-player primal-dual proxy game involving the leader policy, follower policy, adversarial kernel, and dual variable, and develop a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm for it. We show that the proxy always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective, quantify the proxy-to-hard gap, and characterize an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. We then prove an \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})\) average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap, which implies a near-optimal robust policy for the original robust objective. Experiments on controlled tabular games and LLM alignment with uncertain preference further validate the convergence theory and show improved performance over nominal baselines.

</details>


### [210] [Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS): Reducing Representational Complexity for Enterprise AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00791)
*Terry Dorsey,Kevin Huggins*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as a method to reduce unnecessary complexity in enterprise information artifacts while preserving essential information. It proposes Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model with four dimensions (Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, Supporting Sources) for comparing complexity across different representation states. The paper explores two key consequences: lifecycle obligations with an economic cost model, and improved AI reasoning performance when representational complexity is reduced.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise information systems accumulate complex representational structures over time due to applications, projects, technologies, organizational boundaries, and local requirements. This complexity creates challenges for maintenance, governance, and interpretation by both human consumers and AI systems. The motivation is to provide a systematic approach to simplify enterprise representations while preserving necessary information.

Method: The paper develops ERC as a representation-neutral model with four dimensions: Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, and Supporting Sources. Objects, Interactions, and Behaviors form dependent categories, while Supporting Sources characterizes representation exposure. ERC is defined at both representation and task levels, enabling comparison between architectural simplification and retrieval optimization. An economic model is proposed to distinguish recurring global costs, recurring task-level costs, and one-time transformation costs over a defined time horizon.

Result: The paper establishes that ERC provides measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance. Evidence from text-to-SQL research demonstrates that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy. The model distinguishes between representation-level and task-level ERC, enabling nuanced analysis of simplification efforts.

Conclusion: ERS offers a systematic approach to enterprise representation simplification. ERC serves as a measurement framework (not a universal metric) for comparing complexity across representation states. The framework enables evaluation of lifecycle costs, economic outcomes, and AI system performance. The key insight is that reducing task-level ERC decreases the representational extent that AI systems must identify, relate, and interpret, thereby improving reasoning accuracy.

Abstract: Enterprise information is represented through artifacts shaped by applications, projects, technologies, organizational boundaries, and local requirements. These structures accumulate over time, creating representational complexity that must be maintained by the enterprise and interpreted by information consumers and AI systems. This paper introduces Enterprise Representation Simplification (ERS) as reducing unnecessary representational complexity while preserving required information within a defined scope, and Enterprise Representation Complexity (ERC), a representation-neutral model for comparing complexity across representation states.
  ERC characterizes representational extent through four dimensions: Representation Objects, Interactions, Behaviors, and Supporting Sources. Objects, Interactions, and Behaviors form dependent categories, while Supporting Sources characterize representation exposure. ERC is defined at representation and task levels, enabling comparison and distinguishing architectural simplification from retrieval optimization.
  The paper develops two consequences of ERS. First, representational structures create lifecycle obligations for maintenance, governance, dependencies, change, enhancement, and operation. An economic model distinguishes recurring global representation cost, recurring task-level cost, and one-time transformation cost, enabling evaluation over a defined time horizon. Second, reductions in task-level ERC reduce the representational extent an AI system must identify, relate, and interpret. Text-to-SQL research provides evidence that reduced schema and reasoning complexity can improve reasoning accuracy.
  ERC is not a universal complexity, performance, or cost metric. It provides measurable architectural variables for comparing representational alternatives, transformation effects, economic outcomes, and AI reasoning performance.

</details>


### [211] [Sapien: A Stateful Policy Engine for Autonomous AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00797)
*Corinn Tiffany,Wen Zhang,Eugene Bagdasarian,Lillian Tsai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Sapien is a policy engine for AI agents that enforces stateful contextual policies using extended regular expressions with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks to prevent rogue actions in multi-step tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contextual security defenses can prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing task-specific policies, but in multi-step tasks, determining valid actions often depends on the agent's prior actions and learned information. Existing approaches fail to capture this stateful nature of security policies.

Method: Sapien uses a policy specification language that extends regular expressions with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks to specify permitted tool-call sequences.

Result: Sapien achieves minimal utility loss (within a few percent of unconstrained agent). When the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies block 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon, which is twice as many attacks as tool allowlists block on long-horizon tasks.

Conclusion: The approach effectively balances security with utility preservation, significantly outperforming baseline tool allowlists in blocking attacks on long-horizon tasks while maintaining high agent performance.

Abstract: Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from taking rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and enforcing it on the agent's tool calls. In multi-step tasks, however, which actions are valid often depends on what the agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, deferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an unconstrained agent's utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked, Sapien's policies rule out 93-95% of attacks on AgentDojo and 62-85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists on long-horizon tasks).

</details>


### [212] [Kepler: Auditable World Models for ARC-AGI-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00834)
*Wensen Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Kepler is an open-source evaluation harness for ARC-AGI-3 that represents agent hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through transition and prediction checks. Under a frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, it achieved 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games, with 181/183 levels using no more actions than human baselines. The paper also reports three evaluation failures and discusses limitations of score-only metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments where rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. The motivation appears to be developing a robust evaluation framework (Kepler) that can properly assess agent reasoning capabilities through executable world models and validation checks, while addressing evaluation failures that can occur in such complex environments.

Method: Kepler represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through: (1) retrospective transition checks - verifying state transitions match predictions, and (2) conditional prediction checks - testing predictions under specific conditions. The evaluation uses a single frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration across all games without per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns.

Result: Achieved 100.00 RHAE (server-verified) on all 25 public games. On 181 of 183 completed levels, the final Opus attempt used no more actions than median-human baseline. Retained board runs used 8,256 environment actions (7,292 in scored levels). Generated 858.0 million tokens with 97.37% cache reads at $777.72 cost. Three evaluation failures were identified: source-code leakage, agents reconstructing removed harness, and autonomous repair masking broken planner. Animation frames contained task-relevant information absent from settled text grids. Across final Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol boards, 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100%.

Conclusion: Public-set score alone has limited discriminative value. This motivates the need for first-attempt reporting, cost-conditioned evaluation, and verification-aware metrics. The results indicate that comprehensive evaluation frameworks are needed beyond simple score-based assessments.

Abstract: ARC-AGI-3 evaluates agents in interactive environments whose rules and objectives must be inferred from observation. We present Kepler, an open-source harness that represents hypotheses as executable world models and validates them through retrospective transition checks and conditional prediction checks. Under one frozen Claude Opus 5 configuration, Kepler obtained a server-verified 100.00 RHAE on all 25 public games, with no per-game model selection or score-conditioned reruns. On 181 of 183 completed levels, the final Opus attempt used no more actions than the corresponding median-human baseline. The retained board runs used 8,256 environment actions, of which 7,292 occurred in scored levels. Retained local provider-session records yield 858.0 million tokens, 97.37% cache reads, and a \$777.72 cost at September 1, 2026 API list-equivalent rates. We also report three evaluation failures: source-code leakage that produced an invalid perfect run, agents reconstructing a removed harness in a control condition, and autonomous repair masking a broken planner. A single-game observation case study showed that animation frames contained task-relevant information absent from settled text grids. Across the final Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol boards, 48 of 50 game-model cells reached 100. These results indicate that public-set score alone has limited discriminative value and motivate first-attempt, cost-conditioned, and verification-aware reporting.

</details>


### [213] [Learning Multiple Timescales for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00849)
*Pedro Robles Dutenhefner,Dikshant Shehmar,Wagner Meira,Marlos C. Machado*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GITA introduces a novel approach to offline goal-conditioned RL by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple temporal abstraction levels (k values), outperforming fixed-k methods and baselines on long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing offline GCRL approaches struggle with long-horizon tasks because discounting shrinks value differences between distant states below the function approximation error, eliminating the signal for ranking states. While temporal abstraction (treating k steps as one transition) can restore this signal, no single fixed k is optimal for all state-goal distances—large k preserves long-range differences but collapses nearby distinctions, and vice versa.

Method: GITA conditions a single value function on k and trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values. This allows larger positive advantages for state-goal pairs to contribute more strongly to updates, retaining both local resolution and long-range signal without committing to a single k.

Result: On OGBench, GITA raises average success rate by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL and by 7 percentage points (14% relative) over the strongest fixed-k method OTA, achieving state-of-the-art performance across all tasks.

Conclusion: GITA effectively addresses the trade-off between local resolution and long-range signal in temporal abstraction by leveraging multiple k values simultaneously, providing a superior solution for offline goal-conditioned RL in long-horizon scenarios.

Abstract: Existing approaches to offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) struggle with long-horizon tasks. Discounting shrinks value differences between distant states until they fall below the function approximation error, leaving the agent with no signal for ranking states. Temporal abstraction, which treats k environment steps as a single transition, restores this signal at long range, but no single fixed k suits all state-goal distances: large k preserves value differences across long temporal distances while collapsing distinctions between nearby states, and small k does the reverse. We make this trade-off explicit and introduce Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA), which conditions a single value function on k. GITA trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, so scales assigning larger positive advantages to a state-goal pair contribute more strongly to its update. GITA does not need to choose between local resolution and long-range signal; it retains both without committing to a single k. On OGBench, GITA outperforms a broad range of offline GCRL baselines, raising average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL. It also improves over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA, by 7 percentage points (14% relative).

</details>


### [214] [An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870)
*Sara Riazi,Pedram Rooshenas*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an LLM-based pedagogical agent that provides scaffolded feedback for database design (ERD) education, using a four-stage workflow with hidden diagnosis that progressively discloses feedback to students. In deployment across 383 episodes, 71.1% of student revisions incorporated the diagnostic feedback, with positive reception regarding delayed disclosure and student agency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be addressing challenges in teaching conceptual database design, particularly the need to provide effective, scaffolded feedback that supports student learning without simply giving away answers. The system aims to balance feedback specificity with student agency, grounded in multiple sources (student artifacts, assignment requirements, rubrics, instructional resources).

Method: The system uses an architecture that separates hidden artifact-grounded diagnosis from the student-facing feedback workflow. It implements a four-stage progressive disclosure workflow: (1) concept checks, (2) guided application, (3) low-detail feedback, and (4) localized clarification. Each feedback request creates a stateful episode linked to versioned ERD states. The system was deployed across three ERD environments.

Result: 71.1% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after Stages 1-2. Qualitative analysis showed staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, and allowed later recovery, though some errors still shaped revisions. Survey responses (self-selected sample) favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted indirectness and repetition.

Conclusion: The four-stage disclosure model appears effective for LLM-based pedagogical feedback in domain-specific design tasks. The separation of hidden diagnosis from disclosure workflow enables controlled feedback granularity. However, limitations include: some LLM errors still influenced revisions, and students perceived indirectness and repetition. Future work likely involves addressing error propagation and reducing redundancy.

Abstract: We present an educator-guided LLM pedagogical agent for scaffolded feedback in conceptual database design. Integrated into an entity--relationship diagram (ERD) editor, the system grounds feedback in the student artifact, assignment requirements, educator-authored rubrics, and instructional resources. Its architecture separates hidden, artifact-grounded diagnosis from the workflow that controls the form and disclosure level of student-facing support.
  We instantiate the architecture as a four-stage workflow progressing from concept checks and guided application to low-detail feedback and localized clarification. Each feedback request creates a stateful episode linked to versioned ERD states. In a deployment spanning three ERD environments and 383 feedback episodes, 71.1\% of observed target-level changes fully or partially incorporated the hidden diagnostic target, including many after Stages~1--2. Qualitative analysis showed that staged disclosure sometimes withheld inaccurate details, supported selective uptake, or allowed later recovery, though some errors still shaped revisions. Survey responses from a self-selected sample favored delayed disclosure and student agency but noted indirectness and repetition.

</details>


### [215] [MemFit: Efficient Long-Term Agentic Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00872)
*Mitchell Piehl,Muchao Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemFit is a long-term memory system for conversational agents that reduces cost and latency by using LLM-free insertion (appending turns verbatim), segment summary indexing, and multi-path retrieval with cross-encoder reranking. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmarks while significantly reducing memory construction time and cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory systems for LLMs rely on expensive LLM agents to organize and consolidate memory, resulting in costly and inefficient write operations. Existing approaches either require costly LLM calls for memory construction or discard surface-level details through compression, limiting their scalability and efficiency for persistent agentic memory.

Method: MemFit stores each conversation turn verbatim in an append-only store with near-instantaneous, LLM-free insertion, indexing turns with segment summaries rather than replacing them. It uses an LLM-free, multi-path retrieval strategy combining lexical and semantic signals with cross-encoder reranking over caption-augmented episodes, applicable in both textual and multimodal settings.

Result: MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance on three widely used benchmarks (LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S) while reducing memory construction time and cost several-fold.

Conclusion: MemFit provides a scalable and efficient solution for persistent agentic memory by eliminating LLM dependencies for memory operations while maintaining high retrieval quality through sophisticated multi-path retrieval and reranking strategies.

Abstract: Long-term memory systems for large language models (LLMs) have gained popularity for extending reasoning capabilities across applications. Current memory systems rely on LLM agents to organize and consolidate memory, resulting in costly, inefficient write operations. To address this limitation, we propose MemFit, a long-term memory system for conversational agents that reduces the cost and latency of memory operations. Unlike existing systems that rely on expensive LLM calls for memory construction or discard surface-level details through compression, MemFit stores each turn verbatim in an append-only store with near-instantaneous, LLM-free insertion, indexing turns with segment summaries rather than replacing them. Additionally, MemFit uses an LLM-free, multi-path retrieval strategy that combines lexical and semantic signals with cross-encoder reranking over caption- augmented episodes in both textual and multimodal settings. Empirical results on three widely used benchmarks, LoCoMo, MemGallery, and LongMemEval-S, show that MemFit achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing memory construction time and cost several-fold, providing a scalable and efficient solution for persistent agentic memory.

</details>


### [216] [OR for AI That Does OR: Routing LLMs up the Escalator inside the OSCAR Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00912)
*Jinzhi Bu,Haixin Tang,Huanan Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OSCAR is an LLM-based optimization modeling framework that uses a certified offline Simulator to verify improvements beyond feasibility. It achieves 95-100% accuracy with small open-weight LLMs at 3.1-5.8x lower cost than commercial LLMs like Codex and Claude Code, while supporting local deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that LLMs translating business descriptions into optimization models may produce executable code that misrepresents constraints or objectives, leading to optimal solutions for the wrong problem. Even when solutions satisfy intended operating rules, better plans may exist. Organizations need a framework that produces accurate formulations at low cost, ideally running locally, while effectively allocating attempts across LLMs of varying price and capability.

Method: OSCAR uses a three-component architecture: (1) Simulator - certified against labeled decision examples to compare optimization candidates; (2) Coder - LLM generates optimization models; (3) Reviewer - evaluates model quality. The search process is modeled as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty, deciding which LLMs to call and when to stop. Two approaches are developed: (1) cost-ordered escalation under known-prior conditions, and (2) prior-free competitive guarantees for general menus.

Result: On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieves 95-100% accuracy using two small open-weight LLMs (each deployable locally on a single GPU). Their single-attempt accuracies average 29% and 48%. In five runs per problem, Codex and Claude Code incur average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times OSCAR's, respectively. The framework supports both local deployment and cloud usage depending on budget and confidentiality requirements.

Conclusion: OSCAR provides a cost-effective, accurate framework for LLM-based optimization modeling that achieves 95-100% accuracy while reducing costs by 3.1-5.8x compared to commercial LLMs. The key insight is using certified simulators to verify improvements beyond mere feasibility, combined with strategic LLM selection and stopping rules. Organizations should maintain labeled decision examples and can adapt the framework as LLM capabilities evolve.

Abstract: Large language models can translate business descriptions into optimization models, but executable code may misrepresent constraints or objectives. A solver can then return an optimal solution to the wrong problem. Even when the solution satisfies the intended operating rules, a better plan may exist. For organizations that repeatedly use optimization modeling, an LLM-based framework should produce accurate formulations at low cost and, ideally, run locally. We study how to verify improvements and allocate attempts across LLMs that differ in price and capability. We develop OSCAR (Optimization modeling by Simulator, Coder, And Reviewer), which uses an offline Simulator certified against labeled decision examples to compare candidates and continues searching beyond feasibility. We model the search for the next certified improvement as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty: which LLMs to call and when to stop. In a simplified known-prior setting, we give conditions under which cost-ordered escalation is optimal. For general menus, we derive a prior-free competitive guarantee. On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieves 95% to 100% accuracy at the reported settings using two small open-weight LLMs, each deployable locally on a single GPU. Their single-attempt accuracies average 29% and 48%. In five runs per problem, Codex and Claude Code incur average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times OSCAR's, respectively. OSCAR supports open-weight models locally or in the cloud, depending on budget and confidentiality requirements. Firms should maintain labeled decision examples of feasible and infeasible decisions to clarify plain-language operating rules. OSCAR follows these labels when an LLM's interpretation conflicts with them. As LLM capabilities and prices change, OSCAR's simple operating rules and adjustable settings help firms adapt their model choices and benefit from these advances.

</details>


### [217] [ABDA-NL: A Natural-Language Scenario Explorer for Argument-Based Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00947)
*Shawn Bowers,Martin Caminada,Haoyang Liu,Bertram Ludäscher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ABDA-NL is a natural-language interface for argument-based discussion systems, combining large language models with a deterministic ASPIC+ reasoning engine under grounded semantics. It allows users to explore argument conclusions, ask questions from documents, and author new knowledge in plain English, with LLM proposals validated by users before taking effect.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation addresses a key usability barrier in formal argumentation systems: the need for users to understand and interact with complex formal representations (arguments, attacks, acceptance labels) without requiring technical expertise. The system aims to make argument-based reasoning accessible through natural language while maintaining the rigor and determinism of formal argumentation.

Method: The method combines: (1) ASPIC+ knowledge bases with grounded semantics as the core reasoning engine; (2) A large language model as an intermediary layer for natural language understanding and generation; (3) User validation workflow where every LLM-generated proposal must be confirmed before execution; (4) Interactive discussion game visualization for explaining why conclusions are reached.

Result: The system provides: (1) Acceptance/rejection/undecided status for conclusions; (2) Interactive explanations via grounded discussion game; (3) What-if analysis through suspending assumptions/rules or changing preferences; (4) Document-based Q&A capabilities; (5) Plain-English authoring of new facts, assumptions, and rules. The LLM translates between natural language and formal representation while the ABDA engine remains the sole source of computational truth.

Conclusion: ABDA-NL successfully bridges formal argumentation systems and natural language interaction. The architecture leverages LLMs for language tasks while preserving the deterministic, interpretable nature of ASPIC+ reasoning. The human-in-the-loop validation ensures system reliability. This represents a practical step toward making argument-based reasoning tools accessible to non-technical users.

Abstract: ABDA-NL adds a natural-language interface to ABDA, a system for argument-based discussion using ASPIC- knowledge bases under grounded semantics. Users see which conclusions are accepted, rejected, or undecided, open an interactive rendering of the grounded discussion game to learn why, explore what-if alternatives by suspending assumptions and rules or changing preferences, ask questions that are answered from a scenario's reference documents, and author new facts, assumptions, and rules in plain English. A large language model provides the bridge between language and formalism: it answers questions from the documents and the current state of the scenario, and it translates plain-English edits into candidate formal statements. The deterministic ABDA engine remains the sole source of arguments, attacks, and acceptance labels, and every proposal of the model is validated and confirmed by the user before it takes effect.

</details>


### [218] [PG-SFT: Balancing Capability Acquisition and Retention in Offline Agent Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00949)
*Ronghua Li,Zi Liang,Zhishan Li,Shinan Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses a critical challenge in training specialized tool-using agents via supervised fine-tuning (SFT): standard SFT on agent trajectories improves target benchmarks but degrades other capabilities of the base model (reasoning, tool calling, code generation). The authors propose Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT), which uses turn-level information gain of agent trajectories to adjust supervision strength, achieving a better trade-off between acquiring new capabilities and preserving existing ones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard SFT on offline agent trajectories forces models to imitate reasoning and actions token-by-token, which harms other capabilities of the base model. The authors aim to balance the trade-off between acquiring new capabilities (target task performance) and preserving existing ones (general reasoning, tool calling, code generation) during agent trace SFT.

Method: The authors propose Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT), which leverages turn-level information gain of agent trajectories as an indicator to adjust supervision strength. They compare several baselines including standard SFT, KL penalty constraining distributional drift, and limiting update magnitude.

Result: PG-SFT yields a more favorable trade-off on evaluated benchmarks compared to baselines. It substantially reduces distributional drift and broad capability degradation, though at the cost of slight degradation in target-task performance. Standard SFT improves target benchmarks while lowering non-target benchmark scores. Simply using KL penalty or limiting update magnitude did not avoid the regression trend.

Conclusion: Balancing the acquisition-retention trade-off depends not only on whether the model is anchored to its base behavior, but also on where and how strongly supervision should depart from that behavior. PG-SFT provides a promising approach by using turn-level information gain to adaptively adjust supervision strength.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on offline agent trajectories is the standard approach for training specialized tool-using agents, but forcing models to imitate reasoning and actions token by token may harm other capabilities (e.g., general reasoning, tool calling, code generation) of the base model. In this work, we focus on studying \emph{how to better balance the trade-off between acquiring new capabilities and preserving existing ones during agent trace SFT}. By comparing several baselines in our setup, standard SFT improves the target benchmark while lowering several non-target benchmark scores; meanwhile, simply constraining distributional drift using KL penalty or limiting the update magnitude did not avoid this regression trend. Motivated by recent token-wise adaptive learning objectives, this work proposes \textbf{Privilege-Guided SFT (PG-SFT)} to leverage turn-level information gain of agent trajectories as an indicator to adjust supervision strength. PG-SFT yields a more favorable observed trade-off on the evaluated benchmarks, substantially reducing distributional drift and broad capability degradation at the cost of slight degradation in target-task performance. Our findings suggest that balancing the acquisition--retention trade-off depends not only on whether the model is anchored to its base behavior, but also on where and how strongly supervision should depart from that behavior.}

</details>


### [219] [Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00961)
*Jérémie Lumbroso*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in AI supervision: the conflation of "cybernetic" language (directing action) with "epistemic" language (representing truth). The authors argue that current AI oversight relies on explanation-shaped outputs calibrated for approval rather than truth, leading to "rubber-stamping." They propose a governance criterion requiring every consequential AI decision to carry its counterfactual condition (what would have happened differently) in a testable form, accompanied by a two-part reconstruction test and a deliberation-recording convention (ORRCF).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The bottleneck in AI-assisted code generation is shifting from writing code to supervising AI systems. However, the field lacks a working distinction between cybernetic language (coordinating action) and epistemic language (coordinating understanding). Current oversight mechanisms fail because they check only whether output was approved, not whether the reasoning is retrievable and checkable. This creates a "rubber-stamping" problem where explanations are shaped for approval rather than truth.

Method: The authors present three delegation episodes (illustrations, not controlled evidence), one public record case where a recommendation was withdrawn on its own stated terms, and one failure case illustrating oversight requiring no reasons. They propose: (1) a governance criterion requiring every consequential choice to carry its counterfactual condition in a testable form, (2) a two-part reconstruction test scoring delegation records by whether a second reader can predict agent behavior under perturbation, and (3) a deliberation-recording convention (ORRCF) making the counterfactual condition a required component of recorded choices.

Result: The paper provides conceptual and practical frameworks for distinguishing genuine oversight from rubber-stamping. The proposed criterion and reconstruction test offer operational mechanisms for making AI decision-making auditable. The failure case demonstrates the problem of oversight without accountability, while the successful episodes show epistemic engagement is practicable while remaining auditable.

Conclusion: Without a counterfactual condition attached to consequential choices, third parties cannot distinguish genuine decisions from rubber stamps. The proposed governance criterion, reconstruction test, and ORRCF convention provide actionable mechanisms for ensuring AI systems are genuinely accountable rather than merely producing approval-shaped explanations. This represents a fundamental shift from checking approval to requiring verifiable reasoning behind AI decisions.

Abstract: As code generation is increasingly delegated to AI systems, the bottleneck is shifting from writing code to supervising the systems that write it --- a shift CS-education researchers have begun to name. This shift exposes a vocabulary gap: the field asks for "human oversight" without a working distinction between the two things language does in a delegation channel --- coordinate action (cybernetic: words succeed when the world comes to match them) and coordinate understanding (epistemic: they succeed when they answer to the world and a hearer can check that they do). The failure this names is not cybernetic language but epistemic-form language doing cybernetic work: explanation-shaped output calibrated for approval rather than truth. Oversight that checks only whether an output was approved is satisfiable by rubber-stamping; oversight that holds an agent accountable requires the reasoning behind its work be retrievable and checkable. We present three delegation episodes --- illustrations, not controlled evidence --- in which epistemic engagement proved practicable while remaining auditable, one public record where a recommendation was withdrawn on its own stated terms, and one failure case illustrating oversight that requires no reasons for its discretionary choices. We propose a criterion for agentic-system governance, alongside existing technical trust properties: every consequential choice should carry the condition under which it would have gone otherwise, in a form a third party can test. Without such a condition, a third party cannot distinguish a decision from a rubber stamp. We give the criterion an operational form --- a two-part reconstruction test scoring a delegation record by whether a second reader can predict what the agent does under a perturbation --- and a deliberation-recording convention, ORRCF, that makes the condition a required component of every recorded choice.

</details>


### [220] [VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00972)
*Caiqi Zhang,Rujun Han,Zifeng Wang,Zoey CuiZhu,Nigel Collier,Tomas Pfister,Chen-Yu Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriHarness is an agentic verification framework that enables LLM agents to verify their own outputs in long-horizon tasks without reference answers. It uses disagreement resolution and consensus challenging mechanisms, along with evidence tools and reusable skills, to select and revise outputs. The method achieves up to 6.4 points improvement over single rollouts and can self-improve from failure feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents tackle increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks, verifying outputs becomes extremely challenging since reference answers and grading rubrics are unavailable at test time. The key insight is that repeated sampling yields multiple rollouts with complementary correct claims, but a reliable verification mechanism is needed to determine which claims to trust.

Method: VeriHarness transforms the underlying LLM into an agentic verifier by providing it with a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. It employs two key mechanisms: (1) Disagreement Resolver - checks competing claims against environmental evidence to identify correct alternatives, and (2) Consensus Challenger - tests shared claims and searches for omitted requirements that consensus may have concealed. These findings guide selection and revision of the final artifact.

Result: Evaluated on five long-horizon workspace benchmarks with two frontier models (Gemini 3.5 Flash and Claude Opus 4.8), VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among baselines. Evidence-backed revision further improves performance, bringing gains over single rollout of 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 points with Claude Opus 4.8. Verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback.

Conclusion: VeriHarness represents a novel approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. The key insight that "disagreement exposes correct alternatives while consensus conceals errors" provides a new paradigm for self-verification. The release of ~26,000 rollouts across benchmarks supports future research in this direction.

Abstract: As LLM agents undertake increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks, verifying their outputs becomes increasingly challenging. We study how verification capability can be strengthened with a fixed base model, without access to reference answers or grading rubrics at test time. Repeated sampling yields multiple rollouts that can contain complementary correct claims, but we need a reliable verification mechanism to determine which claims to trust. We first find that disagreement often exposes correct alternatives, while consensus can conceal errors. These observations motivate VeriHarness, which turns the underlying LLM a generator uses into an agentic verifier by giving it a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. A disagreement resolver checks competing claims against environmental evidence, while a consensus challenger tests shared claims and searches for omitted requirements. Their findings guide the selection and revision of the final artifact. Across five long-horizon workspace benchmarks and two frontier models, VeriHarness achieves the highest selection scores among the evaluated baselines. Evidence-backed revision further improves average performance, bringing gains over a single rollout to 6.2 points with Gemini 3.5 Flash and 6.4 points with Claude Opus 4.8. We further show that verification skills can self-improve from failure feedback, demonstrating VeriHarness as a novel and critical approach for scaling long-horizon agentic verification. We release the full pool of approximately 26,000 rollouts across all five benchmarks and both models, produced at a cost of over $100,000, to support future research on agentic verification.

</details>


### [221] [RISED: RubrIcs for agentic multi-environment Selection and sElf-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00979)
*Jingtan Wang,Sirajul Salekin,Young mok Jung,Javier Movellan,Bryan Kian Hsiang Low,Manjot Bilkhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RISED is a method for training a single LLM agent across diverse interactive environments by using rubric-based textual feedback to guide both online data selection and policy supervision, addressing limitations of scalar rewards in multi-environment RL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies in multi-environment RL: (1) allocate training at environment level without considering cross-environment relationships, (2) rely on scalar rewards that provide limited information about relationships between environments, and (3) fail to provide within-group reward contrast when all rollouts succeed or fail. This motivates using richer textual feedback (rubrics) to guide learning.

Method: RISED uses an LLM judge to tag each rollout with predefined rubrics shared across environments. Rubrics serve two purposes: (1) Guide online data selection by selecting data aligned with the overall behavioral composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data. (2) Provide policy supervision: positive rubrics (desired behaviors) supply token-level supervision via on-policy self-distillation teacher; negative rubrics (undesired behaviors) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes.

Result: RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment, across different model backbones. Rubric-based analysis can characterize behavioral changes accompanying these gains.

Conclusion: Rubric-based feedback effectively addresses limitations of scalar rewards in multi-environment RL by providing cross-environment relationship information and within-group reward contrast. The approach demonstrates that using textual rubrics for both data selection and policy supervision leads to generalist agents that perform well across diverse environments.

Abstract: Training a single LLM agent jointly across diverse interactive environments has attracted increasing attention as a route to generalist agents. Existing curriculum and data-selection strategies often allocate training at the environment level or prioritize local reward-based signals, without explicitly considering relationships between current rollouts across environments for prompt-group selection. Meanwhile, as environments are learned at different rates, all-failure and all-success rollout groups can coexist within a batch, leaving those data without group-relative reward signals. Both challenges highlight limitations of relying solely on scalar rewards in multi-environment RL: they provide limited information about cross-environment relationships and no within-group reward contrast when rewards are identical. This motivates richer textual feedback, such as rubrics describing rollout behaviours, to guide learning. Beyond rubrics' usage as reward, we repurpose rubrics to guide both online data selection and policy supervision. An LLM judge tags each rollout using a predefined rubric vocabulary shared across environments. The resulting profiles guide the selection of data that aligns with the overall behavioural composition of the mixed-environment batch while limiting overlap with already-selected data. Available positive rubrics (describing desired behaviours) provide privileged context for an on-policy self-distillation teacher, supplying additional token-level supervision, while negative rubrics (describing undesired behaviours) guide subsequent rollout generation away from recurring failure modes. Together, these components form RISED. Across model backbones, RISED achieves the highest mean pass rate across environments and ranks first or second in every individual environment. Rubric-based analysis of RISED can further characterize the behavioural changes accompanying these gains.

</details>


### [222] [Evaluating LLM-Generated Preference Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01000)
*Fan Huang,Minsuk Kim,C. Tyler Diggans,Filippo Radicchi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether Large Language Models can serve as reliable probabilistic generators for simulating human preferences across three domains (air travel, restaurants, consumer products). The study finds that while LLMs exhibit self-coherence (stable most probable outcomes), there is substantial discordance across model families and scales, with outcomes influenced more by model choice than prompt wording.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as probabilistic generators for simulation, synthetic data generation, and decision support where real-world data are unavailable. However, the structure and reliability of the distributions they produce remain understudied, creating a need to systematically evaluate their suitability as human preference stand-ins.

Method: The researchers systematically analyzed LLM-generated preference distributions across nine open-weight models, three choice domains (air travel, restaurants, consumer products), and tested robustness under temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering.

Result: All models exhibited self-coherence with most probable outcomes stabilizing rapidly under repeated sampling. However, substantial discordance was observed across both model families and scales, with little consensus even among their most probable outcomes. These patterns proved robust across all conditions tested.

Conclusion: The findings challenge the common assumption that sufficiently capable LLMs produce similar preference distributions when used as survey respondent stand-ins. Outcomes are influenced more by the choice of model than by prompt wording, raising concerns about using LLMs as proxies for human preferences in simulation and decision support contexts.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as probabilistic generators for simulation, synthetic data generation, and decision support in settings where real-world data are unavailable. Yet, the structure and reliability of the distributions they produce remain understudied. Here, we systematically analyze LLM-generated distributions of preferences for air travel, restaurants, and consumer products. Encouragingly, all models considered in our analysis exhibit self-coherence, with the most probable outcomes stabilizing rapidly under repeated sampling. At the same time, we observe substantial discordance across both model families and scales, with little consensus even among their most probable outcomes. These patterns hold across nine open-weight models, three choice domains, and show robustness under temperature changes, greedy decoding, and perturbations of prompt and ordering. Our findings indicate that outcomes are influenced more by the choice of model than by the wording of the prompt, challenging the common assumption that sufficiently capable LLMs produce similar preference distributions when used as stand-ins for survey respondents.

</details>


### [223] [Calibration-risk routing for controlled world-model adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01001)
*Yifan Zhang,Liang Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MC-WM is a model-based reinforcement learning approach that addresses the simulator-to-target distribution shift problem by separating target data into fit, selection, and calibration partitions, using a learned confidence signal to weight policy updates without modifying physical rewards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In MBRL, there's often a gap between the simulator (source) and target environment. When limited target data is available, both correcting the simulator and directly fitting the target can fail. This creates a model-selection problem where it's unclear which approach will generalize better.

Method: The Model-Corrected World Model (MC-WM) separates initial target data into three disjoint partitions: (1) fit partition for training, (2) selection partition for model selection, and (3) calibration partition for calibration assessment. The system then deploys the model family with lower standardized calibration risk. A learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates are used to weight one-step imagined policy updates while preserving original physical rewards.

Result: Evaluated on 540 unique reported run cells across three controlled Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) shifts. One exact-routing cell was repeated after a pre-deployment artifact gate, resulting in 541 completed executions.

Conclusion: The proposed MC-WM framework provides a systematic approach to handling simulator-to-target shifts in MBRL by combining data partitioning, calibration-based model selection, and confidence-weighted policy updates.

Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) can exploit simulated experience, but a simulator-to-target shift creates a model-selection problem: correcting the simulator and fitting the target directly can each fail under limited target data. We introduce the Model-Corrected World Model (MC-WM), which separates initial target data into disjoint fit, selection, and calibration partitions and deploys the family with lower standardized calibration risk. A learned confidence signal and deterministic validity predicates weight one-step imagined policy updates without rewriting physical rewards. We evaluate 540 unique reported run cells across three controlled Multi-Joint dynamics with Contact (MuJoCo) shifts; one exact-routing cell was repeated after a pre-deployment artifact gate, giving 541 completed executions.

</details>


### [224] [What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01002)
*Keith J. Holyoak,Martin M. Monti*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper develops a causal framework for evaluating whether non-human entities (animals or AI) possess consciousness, based on analogical reasoning. The key insight is distinguishing between similarities in causal factors (mechanisms that generate consciousness) versus similarities in behavioral/cognitive effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address the philosophical and practical challenge of determining consciousness in entities other than humans. With advances in AI, this question has become pressing: traditional behavioral approaches provide limited evidence because they don't establish the causal mechanisms underlying consciousness.

Method: The proposed framework weighs source-target similarity by causal relevance while accounting for: (1) unknown causes, (2) disabling differences, and (3) alternative routes to consciousness. It distinguishes between two types of similarity: causal factors vs. downstream behavioral effects.

Result: Applied to biological systems, the framework explains why analogical support for consciousness weakens with increasing evolutionary distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, behavioral similarity alone provides only limited evidence for consciousness because the relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established.

Conclusion: The framework clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness: evidence about causal mechanisms (not just behavioral outputs) would be needed. This provides a systematic approach for evaluating consciousness in AI and other non-human entities.

Abstract: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. Historically, such inferences have focused on nonhuman animals, but advances in artificial intelligence have raised the possibility of conscious AI. Here we develop a causal framework for evaluating such evidential analogies. The key distinction is between similarities in factors plausibly involved in generating consciousness and similarities in downstream behavioural or cognitive effects. Our framework weights source-target similarity by causal relevance while allowing for unknown causes, disabling differences and alternative routes to consciousness. Applied to biological systems, it explains why analogical support generally weakens with increasing causal distance from humans. Applied to contemporary AI, it suggests that behavioural similarity provides only limited evidence for consciousness because relevant causal correspondences remain poorly established. The framework also clarifies what evidence would strengthen claims of artificial consciousness.

</details>


### [225] [Beyond Answer Confidence: A Controlled Audit of Self-Knowledge in a Black-Box Decision Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01006)
*Sharath M Shankaranarayana,Davor Runje,Jan Jannink*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits whether a decision model's confidence reliably indicates missing knowledge vs. random uncertainty. Using Jev model across 15+ datasets and 6 generated task families, they find confidence is calibrated on familiar tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge—assigning high confidence (up to 0.80) even with no relevant information, and exceeding accuracy by 0.21-0.33 on out-of-knowledge-boundary news. Targeted yes/no questions (e.g., "is outcome settled?") provide sharper readouts than confidence scores. Knowledge audits need explicit controls for surface cues.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While calibration makes probabilities useful on average, it does not establish whether low confidence reflects chance or missing knowledge, nor whether confidence appropriately falls when a model moves beyond its knowledge boundary. This distinction is critical for routing, abstention, and automated action.

Method: Audited Jev decision model using over 15 public datasets and 6 generated task families with paired interventions that vary information supplied for a fixed item—allowing controlled comparison of what the model knows vs. doesn't know.

Result: Jev's confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: (1) with no answer-relevant information, it assigns up to 0.80 to a salient option; (2) on news beyond observed knowledge boundary, confidence exceeds accuracy by 0.21-0.33; (3) recalibration on earlier months does not close this gap. Targeted yes/no questions perform better: whether outcome is settled (AUROC 1.00), whether evidence suffices (0.95 vs 0.85 for confidence). Asking "does Jev know the answer?" flags fabricated entities and post-boundary news (0.91) but shows no advantage with realistic names or dates removed.

Conclusion: Black-box knowledge audits need explicit controls for surface cues. Standard confidence metrics can be misleading outside the training distribution, and explicit knowledge-checking questions may be necessary for reliable uncertainty estimation.

Abstract: Decision models return probabilities intended for routing, abstention and automated action. Calibration makes those probabilities useful on average, but does not establish whether low confidence reflects chance or missing knowledge, nor whether confidence falls when a model moves beyond what it knows. We audit this distinction in Jev, a decision model, with over 15 public datasets and 6 generated task families, with paired interventions that vary the information supplied for a fixed item. Jev's confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: with no answer-relevant information it assigns up to 0.80 to a salient option, and on news beyond an observed knowledge boundary it exceeds accuracy by 0.21--0.33, a gap that recalibration on earlier months does not close. Targeted yes/no questions give sharper readouts of the case: whether an outcome is settled (AUROC 1.00) and whether the evidence suffices (0.95, against 0.85 for confidence on the same items). Asking whether Jev knows the answer appears to flag fabricated entities and post-boundary news (0.91), but with realistic names or with dates removed it shows no advantage over answer uncertainty. Black-box knowledge audits therefore need explicit controls for surface cues. Code: https://github.com/Syntheme/beyond-answer-confidence.

</details>


### [226] [From Discovery to Decision: Finite-Budget Recoverability in LLM Voting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01014)
*Shaoang Li,Jian Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the "discovery-to-decision gap" in voting over multiple LLM responses during test-time scaling. Under fixed call budgets, discovered correct answers must accumulate enough votes to win, creating a fundamental tension. The authors derive recoverability thresholds, show candidate set expansion with endpoint winner contraction, and provide exact finite-horizon endpoint probabilities. Key findings include: merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness but cannot improve plurality accuracy, and singleton reachability yields an exact locking certificate. Empirical results show 21.1 point improvement with input permutation and 28-30% call savings with exact locking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To characterize the discovery-to-decision gap in LLM ensemble inference - the tension between discovering correct answers and accumulating enough votes to win under fixed call budgets. Current approaches expand candidate pools but fail to ensure discovered answers win, creating a fundamental limitation in test-time scaling.

Method: Theoretical analysis using realized vote state and remaining call budget. Derivation of sharp recoverability threshold. Analysis of candidate set expansion and endpoint winner contraction. Exact finite-horizon endpoint probability computation under iid response law. Empirical validation on Word16 benchmark.

Result: Key findings: (1) Candidate set can only expand while reachable endpoint winners can only contract during sampling; (2) Merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness but cannot improve plurality accuracy; (3) Singleton reachability yields a gold-free exact locking certificate; (4) Most discovered-but-unselected correct answers lose reachability only after discovery; (5) Input permutation improves raw-plurality accuracy by 21.1 points with unchanged single-call correctness; (6) Exact locking saves 28-30% of calls at 16-call budget while preserving every fixed-budget output.

Conclusion: The discovery-to-decision gap is characterized by a fundamental tension between candidate expansion and endpoint winner contraction. The recoverability threshold and exact locking mechanism provide practical tools for optimizing LLM ensemble inference under fixed budgets. Input permutation and exact locking offer significant accuracy improvements and computational savings without sacrificing correctness.

Abstract: Voting over multiple LLM responses is a common primitive in test-time scaling and ensemble inference. Collecting more responses can expand the candidate pool and increase the chance that a correct answer is discovered. Under a fixed call budget, a discovered answer still needs to accumulate enough support within the remaining calls to become the final plurality winner, creating a discovery-to-decision gap. In this work, we characterize this gap through the realized vote state and remaining call budget. We derive a sharp recoverability threshold and show that, as sampling proceeds, the observed candidate set can only expand while the set of reachable endpoint winners can only contract, inducing a candidate-level conversion window. Under a specified iid response law, the same state yields exact finite-horizon endpoint probabilities. We further show that merging wrong-answer identities preserves single-call correctness and cannot improve plurality accuracy, and that the effect of redistributing wrong-answer probability depends on the realized vote state. Singleton reachability yields a gold-free exact locking certificate. For a known answer universe, its first trigger is the earliest prefix at which all admissible continuations yield the same fixed-budget output. Empirically, most discovered-but-unselected correct answers lose reachability only after discovery. In a controlled Word16 study, input permutation improves raw-plurality accuracy by 21.1 points with essentially unchanged single-call correctness. Exact locking saves 28-30% of calls at a 16-call budget while preserving every fixed-budget output.

</details>


### [227] [Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01017)
*Xuehang Guo,Haoyu Wang,Shengyu Chen,Zach Chen,Wei Cheng,Qingyun Wang,Haifeng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InFlowOp is a multi-agent workflow optimization system that uses a label-free cost model to determine task decomposition granularity and agent assignment before execution, and corrects faults during execution using the same cost metric. It also introduces Braid, a benchmark for multi-agent coordination tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building multi-agent LLM workflows is challenging because: 1) determining task decomposition granularity, 2) selecting appropriate agents for subtasks, and 3) deciding when to create new specialists are difficult upfront decisions. Additionally, improving workflows is costly as it requires reference answers, graded outcomes, or trained assessors, with fixes applied through re-execution, re-search, or retraining.

Method: InFlowOp proposes a label-free cost model that prices each decision by weighing agent competence against task demands versus the agent's computational cost. It uses bidirectional optimization before execution to determine decomposition and assignment, and during execution, corrects faults with the cheapest move using the same cost metric. Braid benchmark is introduced to evaluate multi-agent coordination requiring capabilities beyond single agents.

Result: InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to +11.97%, and achieves +9.64% improvement with in-flow optimization across various domains and backbone models.

Conclusion: InFlowOp successfully provides a unified cost-based framework for both building and running multi-agent workflows, demonstrating significant performance improvements over baselines through its label-free cost optimization approach.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining.
