We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.

</details>


### [228] [Beyond Final Accuracy: Auditing Communication in LLM Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01042)
*Shixuan Li,Wei Yang,Peiyu Zhang,Anzhe Cheng,Heng Ping,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICR is a controlled framework that isolates communication effects from reasoning by evaluating answer revision following independent reasoning. It reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can hide substantially different revision behaviors, and that communication quality should be evaluated as a joint product of message content and receiver policies rather than an intrinsic channel property.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-agent communication evaluation is confounded: improvements could stem from effective communication, favorable agent architecture, or additional reasoning. Final accuracy merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication changes decisions. There lacks a controlled framework to disentangle these factors.

Method: Independent--Communicate--Revise (ICR) framework: (1) Fixes initial reasoning trajectories to isolate communication effects; (2) Measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents' initial correctness; (3) Uses no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. Tested across four reasoning benchmarks (MedQA, GPQA-D, and two others) comparing textual and latent communication channels.

Result: Four key findings: (1) Similar aggregate accuracy conceals substantially different revision behaviors; (2) Full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation compared to answer-only transmission across all four benchmarks; (3) Richer messages amplify both beneficial and harmful influence; (4) Structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, with varying effects on selectivity across channels and tasks.

Conclusion: Communication quality should not be treated as an intrinsic property of a channel. Evaluation should focus on selective revision, examining how message content and receiver policies jointly produce benefits and harms. ICR provides a unified framework for this analysis.

Abstract: Multi-agent communication aims to help agents benefit from one another's information. Yet improvements in system performance leave a fundamental ambiguity: do they reflect effective communication, a favorable agent architecture, or simply additional reasoning? Because communication methods are commonly evaluated within the systems they were designed for, these factors are difficult to disentangle. Final accuracy further merges corrected errors and corrupted answers into a single outcome, obscuring how communication changes decisions. We introduce Independent--Communicate--Revise (ICR), a controlled framework that evaluates communication as answer revision following independent reasoning. ICR fixes initial reasoning trajectories, measures correction and preservation conditional on both agents' initial correctness, and uses a no-message revision control to quantify gains beyond additional reasoning. Across four reasoning benchmarks, our audit of textual and latent communication reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can conceal substantially different revision behaviors. Compared with transmitting answers alone, full reasoning increases correction while reducing preservation on all four benchmarks, so richer messages amplify beneficial and harmful influence alike. Receiver-policy comparisons on MedQA and GPQA-D further show that a structured verification policy shifts every channel toward greater preservation and lower correction, while its effect on selectivity varies across channels and tasks. These findings challenge treating communication quality as an intrinsic property of a channel. ICR therefore recenters evaluation on selective revision, providing a unified framework for examining how message content and receiver policies jointly produce benefits and harms.

</details>


### [229] [Empty Commitments: When Agents Promise What Their Runtime Cannot Deliver](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01045)
*Jiaqi Tang,Lan Wei,Bingyu Shen,Boyang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses "empty commitments" in chatbots—promises about future actions that agents cannot fulfill due to their technical configuration, not due to execution failures. The authors formalize this concept within commitment semantics, identify three failure types, propose an anchoring condition for viable promises, and describe a measurement protocol with five experimental setups testing persistence affordances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chatbots frequently make promises about future actions (e.g., "I will remind you tomorrow") that they cannot actually fulfill because they lack the necessary persistence tools or runtime capabilities. This creates a transparency issue where users receive false expectations.

Method: The authors define empty commitments on top of commitment semantics, establish three failure types and an anchoring condition for promises that tools could make real, and propose a response-level outcome taxonomy. They then describe a measurement protocol involving follow-up requests across five setups that incrementally add persistence affordances, testing with both implicit and explicit environments.

Result: The paper provides a formal framework for identifying and measuring empty commitments in conversational agents, with a systematic methodology for testing how different persistence affordances affect an agent's ability to fulfill promised future actions.

Conclusion: The work establishes that empty commitments represent a fundamental design and transparency issue in chatbot development, where agents should not make promises about future actions unless they have the technical infrastructure to fulfill them. The proposed framework enables systematic identification and measurement of this problem.

Abstract: A chatbot that says "I will remind you tomorrow" will not run again until the user writes. We call such a promise an empty commitment: a promise of an action after the current turn that nothing in the agent's tools or runtime can carry out. Unlike a broken promise, its emptiness follows from the agent's configuration alone; no later trajectory is needed. We define empty commitments on top of commitment semantics, with three failure types, an anchoring condition for promises that a tool could make real, and a response-level outcome taxonomy. We then describe a measurement protocol: follow-up requests run in five setups that add one persistence affordance at a time, with the environment either left implicit or stated.

</details>


### [230] [Network World Models as Environments for Algorithm Design on Complex Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01048)
*Rishab Alagharu,Hongji Pu,Zeeshan Memon,Xinyuan Song,Yuntong Hu,Liang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns to predict network diffusion dynamics under interventions, serving as a fast simulator to accelerate algorithm design for network optimization tasks. The approach enables a coding agent to iteratively design and refine algorithms using feedback from rollouts, achieving comparable or superior results to baselines in 138/141 settings while providing up to 14.5x speedup over Monte Carlo simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Complex systems like networks require evaluating actions whose effects unfold over time (e.g., seeding nodes for campaigns, immunizing against epidemics). Current approaches rely on expensive simulation to score candidate actions, creating a computational bottleneck when evaluating many candidates across multiple trajectories.

Method: The paper proposes an action-conditioned Network World Model that: (1) Learns network diffusion dynamics under interventions over time, (2) Applies each action to the network, and (3) Predicts the resulting outcome. This model serves as a fast evaluator inside an algorithm design loop where a coding agent designs and refines executable algorithms using feedback from full rollouts, action-level credit, and counterfactual probes over alternative interventions.

Result: Across eight network tasks and five diffusion models, the designed algorithms match or exceed the strongest reported baseline in 138 of 141 settings while enabling up to 14.5 times faster rollouts than Monte Carlo simulation.

Conclusion: The action-conditioned Network World Model successfully bridges the gap between expensive simulation and efficient algorithm design for network interventions. By learning to predict diffusion dynamics under interventions, it enables rapid evaluation of candidate actions, allowing automated algorithm design to find effective solutions with significant computational savings.

Abstract: World models, which simulate an environment and predict how it changes under actions, are increasingly used in real-world applications such as robotics. Complex systems call for the same tool because the effect of an action is not immediate. Seeding nodes for a campaign, or immunizing nodes against an epidemic, changes little on its own; what matters is the outcome that unfolds over the steps that follow. Designing an algorithm that selects such actions to maximize expected performance on a task is inherently iterative, and every candidate must be scored by the outcome it produces. Obtaining that outcome has relied on simulation, whose cost becomes a bottleneck when candidates are evaluated over many sampled trajectories. We propose an action-conditioned Network World Model that learns a network's diffusion dynamics under interventions over time, applies each action to the network, and predicts the outcome that follows. It serves as a fast evaluator inside an algorithm design loop in which a coding agent designs and refines executable algorithms using feedback from full rollouts, action-level credit, and counterfactual probes over alternative interventions. Across eight network tasks and five diffusion models, the designed algorithms match or exceed the strongest reported baseline in 138 of 141 settings while enabling up to 14.5 times faster rollouts than Monte Carlo simulation. Code will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [231] [Improving Math Reasoning through Value-guided Informative Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01080)
*Shaohuai Liu,Yuning Wu,Haoran Liu,Enzo Jia,Devin Chen,Kai Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: APIVIS is a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning in RLVR. It combines direct and searched responses within rollouts, applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens, and uses exact value-guided selection to improve expected verifier reward at each searched state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RLVR methods introduce search into rollouts to increase trajectory diversity, but diversity alone does not guarantee that the search-induced rollout policy improves upon the current policy. There is a gap in ensuring search actually leads to policy improvement.

Method: APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens to preserve learning signals when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. The method uses exact value-guided selection to improve expected verifier reward at each searched state, with approximate guarantees under bounded value-estimation error.

Result: Experiments on widely recognized mathematical reasoning benchmarks and different model scales demonstrate substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods.

Conclusion: APIVIS effectively validates the combination of Gumbel search with selective supervision and value-guided selection for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models through RLVR.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Recent work introduces search into RLVR rollouts to increase trajectory diversity, but diversity alone does not ensure that the search-induced rollout policy improves upon the current policy. To address this gap, we propose APIVIS, a training-time framework that adapts finite-budget Gumbel search to chunk-level mathematical reasoning. APIVIS combines direct and searched responses within each rollout group, allowing improvements found by search to produce informative relative rewards. It further applies selective supervision to search-improved tokens, preserving a learning signal when uniform group rewards render GRPO ineffective. We show that exact value-guided selection improves the expected verifier reward at each searched state and that this guarantee extends to the complete rollout policy, with a corresponding approximate guarantee under bounded value-estimation error. Experiments on widely recognized mathematical reasoning benchmarks and different model scales demonstrate substantial improvements over competitive search-based methods, validating the effectiveness of APIVIS.

</details>


### [232] [YouRA: A Persistent-State Architecture for Evidence-Traceable Autonomous Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01097)
*Yoonkyu Woo,Woojin Lee,Jin-Xia Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: YouRA addresses the critical gap between manuscript claims and executed experiments in end-to-end research agents by introducing a stateful, evidence-traceable architecture. It preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across research trajectories through three integrated components: Verification State Architecture (VSA), Independent Controller, and Stateful Reflection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, but manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This structural gap exists because research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines.

Method: YouRA integrates three components: (1) Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; (2) Independent Controller that converts state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; (3) Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset.

Result: On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablation study confirms separable contributions of all four components (VSA, Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery); removing either core-state component drops performance below the full system.

Conclusion: YouRA successfully bridges the claim-evidence gap in autonomous research agents by maintaining persistent, verifiable state across research pipelines. The architecture's three core components work synergistically to improve traceability, reduce hallucinations, and enable effective recovery from failures. The ablation study validates that each component provides separable and essential contributions to the system's performance.

Abstract: End-to-end research agents can now produce complete scientific papers, yet manuscript claims often diverge from executed experiments. This gap is structural: research state, failure histories, and claim-evidence alignment are not maintained as persistent, verifiable state across long-horizon pipelines. We present YouRA (Your Research Agent), an architecture for stateful, evidence-traceable autonomous research. YouRA preserves research state, execution evidence, and failure history across the research trajectory by integrating three components: a Verification State Architecture (VSA) that tracks hypotheses, gates, and evidence pointers; an Independent Controller that turns state and reflection records into lifecycle, recovery, and debate/review control while separating control from execution; and Stateful Reflection that logs failures as structured lessons and routes recovery through bounded repair, redesign, or reset. On MLR-Bench's predefined ten-task end-to-end subset, YouRA improves over both MLR-Agent and AI Scientist V2 on scalar Overall across all three matched backbones. An automated diagnostic using MLR-Bench's hallucination taxonomy reports intersection/union counts for four fact-based failure types, and data-provenance diagnostic shows more real-data-based outputs. Ablating each of the four components (the VSA, the Independent Controller, MCP tool access, and reflection-guided recovery) supports their separable contributions. Removing either core-state component drops YouRA below the full system. Code: https://github.com/PrayPrey/Your-Research-Agent.

</details>


### [233] [Beyond State-of-the-Art: Standardising Environmental Impact Metrics for AI Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01116)
*Lachlan McGinness,Dan Pagendam,Robert Offner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the environmental impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) by analyzing sustainability reporting in NeurIPS 2025 papers, proposing standardized carbon accounting metrics, and introducing the SMAJ (Smallest Model that Achieves the Job) framework to promote sustainable AI practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The environmental footprint of LLMs is growing as their capabilities and ubiquity increase, yet the machine learning community lacks standardized practices for carbon accounting, and environmental impact reporting is nearly non-existent in academic literature.

Method: The authors conducted an automated literature review of 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025, defined standardized sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, created heuristics for estimating carbon cost of LLM inference, and implemented these metrics in a software tool called carbonbenchmark.

Result: The review revealed that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent in ML papers. The authors developed standardized sustainability metrics, inference carbon cost estimation heuristics, and a drop-in software solution (carbonbenchmark) for tracking and reporting emissions.

Conclusion: To address the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, the authors formalize the SMAJ framework, which challenges the field to prioritize computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional State-of-the-Art accuracy metrics.

Abstract: As the capabilities and ubiquity of Large Language Models (LLMs) grow, so does their environmental footprint. Despite calls for responsible AI, the machine learning community lacks standardised practices for carbon accounting. Our automated literature review of the 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 reveals that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent. To catalyse a shift toward sustainable AI, we define standardised sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, accompanied by simple heuristics to estimate the carbon cost of LLM inference. We implement these metrics in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution for tracking and reporting emissions.
  Finally, to combat the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, we formalise the `Smallest Model that Achieves the Job' (SMAJ), a framework which challenges the field to prioritise computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional `State-of-the-Art' (SotA) accuracy.

</details>


### [234] [AbsorbEvo: An Agentic Framework for Autonomous Inverse Design of Microwave Absorbers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01119)
*Zhicheng Feng,Yubo Zhao,Xuefeng Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AbsorbEvo is an agentic framework that uses large language models combined with physics-based prediction and historical feedback to autonomously design high-performance microwave absorbers from natural-language specifications, validated through full-wave simulations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing microwave absorbers requires specialized expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science, and simulation programming, with time-consuming optimization processes. There is a need for automated systems that can translate natural-language performance objectives into verified designs without extensive human expertise.

Method: The framework integrates: (1) LLM for proposing parameter adjustment directions and magnitudes based on task objectives and computational history; (2) Directed increments combined with global sampling for candidate generation; (3) Low-cost predictive model as physics prior for ranking candidates; (4) Full-wave simulation for high-ranking designs only; (5) Physical validity checks for performance evaluation; (6) Experience distillation into textual skills with independent validation.

Result: On AbsorbBench-36 tasks with identical proposal budgets, AbsorbEvo achieved 79.17% task success rate, compared to 25.00% for generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Mean best coverage was 0.7816 vs 0.6434 and 0.6448 respectively.

Conclusion: AbsorbEvo demonstrates that integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback enables effective natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers, significantly outperforming generic agents and random search methods.

Abstract: Designing high-performance microwave absorbers requires specialized expertise in electromagnetic theory, materials science and simulation programming, and entails time-consuming optimization. Here, we present AbsorbEvo, an agentic framework for autonomous inverse design that translates natural-language performance objectives into designs verified by full-wave simulations. Its candidate evolution strategy integrates language reasoning, physics-based prediction and historical feedback. A large language model proposes the directions and magnitudes of parameter adjustments based on task objectives and computational history. The system combines directed increments with global sampling to generate candidates and uses a low-cost predictive model as a physics prior to rank them. Only high-ranking designs undergo full-wave simulation. Results passing physical validity checks are used to evaluate performance and guide subsequent search. Experience from training tasks is further distilled into textual skills, which are independently validated before use in new tasks. Under identical proposal budgets on held-out AbsorbBench-36 tasks, AbsorbEvo achieved a task success rate of 79.17%, versus 25.00% for a generic agent and 12.50% for random search. Its mean best coverage was 0.7816, compared with 0.6434 and 0.6448, respectively. By integrating language reasoning and physics-based feedback into design decisions, AbsorbEvo provides a methodological foundation for natural-language-driven autonomous inverse design of microwave absorbers.

</details>


### [235] [CortexBridge: Cortical Alignment of EEG Montages for Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01124)
*Jiazhen Hong,Xiaotian Zhou,Zihao Ding,Kailong Wang,Yu Wu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CortexBridge is a lightweight adapter that enables EEG foundation models pretrained with fixed electrode layouts to work with arbitrary montages by mapping them into a shared cortical latent space using electrode and atlas coordinates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG foundation models are typically pretrained with fixed channel vocabularies or limited montages, making transfer difficult when electrode layouts change. This limits the practical applicability of pretrained models to new or different EEG recording setups.

Method: CortexBridge combines EEG features with electrode coordinates and atlas coordinates to map arbitrary montages into a shared cortical latent space. The approach was evaluated using three frozen foundation models (EEGPT, LaBraM, CBraMod) on five BCI datasets from the MOABB benchmark.

Result: CortexBridge improved performance in 13 of 15 evaluations. Average balanced accuracy gains were 0.80% for EEGPT, 0.70% for LaBraM, and 3.26% for CBraMod, with a maximum gain of 13.02% on 12-class SSVEP classification. Visualizations showed task-dependent spatial patterns, with SSVEP showing more concentrated representation in the Yeo Visual network compared to auditory P300.

Conclusion: Cortical alignment serves as a learnable and anatomically grounded routing mechanism that enables heterogeneous EEG montages to interface with pretrained foundation models, addressing the portability challenge of EEG foundation models across different electrode configurations.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models are often pretrained with a fixed channel vocabulary or a limited set of montages, making transfer difficult when electrode layouts change. We propose CortexBridge, a lightweight adapter that combines EEG features with electrode and atlas coordinates to map arbitrary montages into a shared cortical latent space. Evaluated with three frozen foundation models on five brain-computer interface (BCI) datasets from the Mother of All BCI Benchmarks (MOABB), CortexBridge improves performance in 13 of 15 evaluations. The gains in balanced accuracy average 0.80% for EEGPT, 0.70% for LaBraM, and 3.26% for CBraMod, with a maximum gain of 13.02% on 12-class steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) classification. Visualizations of the learned atlas representations reveal task-dependent spatial patterns, with SSVEP showing a more concentrated representation in the Yeo Visual network than auditory P300. These results establish cortical alignment as a learnable and anatomically grounded routing mechanism from heterogeneous EEG montages to pretrained foundation models.

</details>


### [236] [Grounding Large Language Models in DSGE Simulators for Policy Generation and Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01128)
*Aditya Dubey,Namah Gupta,Vinti Agarwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper tests whether large language models can produce economically consistent policy responses by embedding an instruction-tuned LLM within six DSGE (Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium) simulators. The study addresses the long-horizon credit assignment problem where policy effects may be delayed by several quarters, comparing PPO (which has a learned value function) against GRPO (a critic-free baseline).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to move beyond evaluating LLM policy responses based on linguistic plausibility alone, and instead test whether LLM-generated policies actually produce consistent and economically sound outcomes when placed within realistic economic simulations.

Method: The researchers implemented a Python interface for DSGE simulators supporting repeated rollouts, persistent shocks, state cloning, and rolling-horizon simulation. They placed the LLM in a sequential decision-making loop where it observes the economy, receives discourse changes, selects bounded policy actions, and receives rewards. PPO was used as the primary method (with generalized advantage estimation for delayed reward propagation), while GRPO served as a matched critic-free baseline. Experiments tested directional semantic signals, reward horizon, trajectory warm starts, cross-simulator transfer, and historically anchored pandemic and monetary policy shocks.

Result: The abstract does not present specific quantitative results, but describes the experimental framework and comparison between PPO and GRPO for handling the credit assignment problem in long-horizon economic policy simulation.

Conclusion: The objective is to judge policy actions by their simulated economic consequences rather than by plausible language alone, addressing whether LLM policy recommendations are actually consistent with economic dynamics.

Abstract: Large language models can produce economic policy responses that sound reasonable, but this does not show that their actions are consistent with economic dynamics. We test this by placing an instruction-tuned language model inside six Snowdrop-backed dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) simulators. At each turn, the model observes the economy and a change in economic discourse, selects a bounded policy action, and receives the next simulated state and an economic reward. We implement a common Python interface for repeated rollouts, persistent shocks, state cloning, and rolling-horizon simulation.
  This setting creates a long-horizon credit-assignment problem. Policy effects may appear several quarters after an action is taken. PPO has a learned value function that can propagate delayed reward to earlier tokens through generalized advantage estimation. GRPO has no learned value function and instead assigns a group-relative advantage from complete rollout returns. It therefore cannot distinguish which earlier turn caused the outcome; if every rollout receives the same return, the normalized advantage is zero. We use PPO as the primary method and GRPO as a matched critic-free baseline. The experiments also test directional semantic signals, reward horizon, trajectory warm starts, cross-simulator transfer, and historically anchored pandemic and monetary-policy shocks. The objective is to judge policy actions by their simulated economic consequences rather than by plausible language alone.

</details>


### [237] [Auditing Action Settlement in LLM Agent Environments: Order, Progress, and Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01138)
*Haotian Chen,Bowen Ye,Yuning Zhang,Jingkun Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses concurrent action arbitration in LLM agent environments through a typed snapshot-settlement contract mechanism, testing five policies across exhaustive trials and evaluating order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Concurrent actions in LLM agent environments require arbitration even when each proposal is individually valid. The researchers aim to implement a settlement contract that can handle multiple valid proposals and audit three key properties: order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency.

Method: The researchers implemented a typed snapshot-settlement contract and tested five settlement policies through: (1) 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials, (2) 2,160 scripted multistep episodes, and (3) a separate full-state journal audit with 156 checkpoints and 1,332 constructed corruptions.

Result: Key findings: (1) Joint policies are spatially order-invariant conditional on fixed priorities; (2) Conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents in a six-agent doorway task versus 90.28% for random tickets (59.03 percentage point improvement, 95% CI: 50.00-68.06); (3) All policies preserve tested spatial constraints; (4) Priority arbitration still misses the independent small-instance optimum; (5) Full-state journal audit exactly replays 156 checkpoints and rejects 1,332 corruptions with retained terminal anchor.

Conclusion: The evidence demonstrates that typed snapshot-settlement contracts can effectively arbitrate concurrent actions in LLM agent environments while preserving spatial constraints and enabling replay consistency. The study focuses on execution semantics rather than human realism or long-run fairness.

Abstract: Concurrent actions in large language model (LLM) agent environments require arbitration even when each proposal is individually valid. We implement a typed snapshot-settlement contract and audit three distinct properties: order sensitivity, useful progress, and replay consistency. Five settlement policies are tested in 28,800 exhaustive permutation trials and 2,160 scripted multistep episodes. Joint policies are spatially order-invariant conditional on fixed priorities, yet conservative rejection completes only 31.25% of agents in a six-agent doorway task versus 90.28% for random tickets; the paired improvement is 59.03 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval: 50.00-68.06). All policies preserve the tested spatial constraints, and priority arbitration still misses the independent small-instance optimum. A separate full-state journal audit exactly replays 156 checkpoints and rejects 1,332 constructed corruptions with a retained terminal anchor. The evidence concerns execution semantics, not human realism or long-run fairness.

</details>


### [238] [ReSolve: Reusing Candidate Reasoning through Selective Generative Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01140)
*Bangji Yang,Jiajun Fan,Hongba Ma,Xi Zhu,Weizhi Zhang,Minghao Guo,Ye Li,Hamid Palangi,Jiaxuan You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReSolve is a training-free inference procedure that reuses intermediate reasoning from multiple sampled solutions to improve answer accuracy in competition-mathematics problems, using selective generative moderation to examine derivations when candidates disagree or lack parseable answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is that sampling multiple solutions wastes computation on intermediate deductions and unfinished arguments—current approaches only use final answers, discarding valuable reasoning work. The authors propose reusing this candidate reasoning rather than treating it as disposable.

Method: ReSolve uses an answer-distribution controller that invokes a model to examine existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack a parseable answer. The generated solution is incorporated into a bounded loop. Evaluated using Hybrid scoring on 130 competition-mathematics problems with two independently sampled candidate pools.

Result: ReSolve obtains 100 and 99 correct answers (vs. 91 and 92 for voting over 4 candidates). It uses 46.3-47.2% fewer tokens than 8-sample self-consistency (94-96 correct). Ablation study shows visible derivations are crucial—removing them drops accuracy from 100 to 93. Selective moderation reduces moderation tokens by ~54% and total tokens by 6.2% while achieving similar accuracy to always-on moderation.

Conclusion: Results support candidate reasoning as reusable inference computation. However, the method does not establish an accuracy advantage over additional sampling or a distinct benefit from specialized route instructions. The key contribution is demonstrating that intermediate reasoning can be productively reused rather than discarded.

Abstract: Sampling multiple solutions spends computation on intermediate deductions and unfinished arguments as well as final answers. We introduce ReSolve, a training-free inference procedure that reuses this candidate reasoning through selective generative moderation. An answer-distribution controller invokes a model to examine existing derivations when candidates disagree or lack a parseable answer, then incorporates the generated solution into a bounded loop. Under Hybrid scoring on 130 competition-mathematics problems evaluated with two independently sampled candidate pools, ReSolve obtains 100 and 99 correct answers, compared with 91 and 92 for voting over the same four candidates, with no correct-to-incorrect changes relative to that vote in either pool. Eight-sample self-consistency obtains 94 and 96 correct answers while consuming substantially more tokens; ReSolve uses 46.3% and 47.2% fewer tokens in the two evaluations. A controlled ablation removes visible derivations while retaining answer keys, vote counts, and the per-state output-cap rule, reducing accuracy from 100 to 93 correct despite increasing computation. Selective and always-on Uniform moderation both solve 97 problems, while selectivity reduces moderation tokens by approximately 54% and total pipeline tokens by 6.2%. These results support candidate reasoning as reusable inference computation. They do not establish an accuracy advantage over additional sampling or a distinct benefit from specialized route instructions.

</details>


### [239] [When Does Exercise-Specific Joint Selection Help? An Audit of Evaluation and Control Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01188)
*Haotian Chen,Jingkun Yu,Yuning Zhang,Bowen Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper audits a previous finding about exercise-specific joint selection improving skeleton-based movement correctness classification. Through a rigorous analysis of 1,057 repetitions from 10 subjects, the authors find that the apparent gains are highly sensitive to the choice of estimand and control conditions, concluding that previous joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation appears to be investigating whether the claimed benefits of exercise-specific joint selection for skeleton-based movement correctness classification are robust across different evaluation methods, or whether they might be artifacts of particular analytical choices.

Method: The authors conducted an exploratory audit using: (1) separation of evaluation aggregation methods (pooled vs. within-person AUROC), subset structure (manual selection vs. random/structure-matched controls), and temporal representation; (2) dimension-matched random maps (n=1,000) as controls; (3) additional controls for bilateral structure and trunk inclusion; (4) comparisons across multiple algorithms (kNN, RBF-SVM, logistic regression, random-convolution); (5) sequence-order and paired-seed controls.

Result: The key findings include: (1) manual-subset kNN gain drops from 0.055 (pooled out-of-fold AUROC) to 0.020 (equal-weight within-person AUROC), with both confidence intervals including zero; (2) 14 out of 1,000 random maps match or exceed the manual pooled result, but 145 do when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion are matched; (3) RBF-SVM retains a positive within-person gain, while logistic regression and random-convolution show negative point gains; (4) results are highly sensitive to the estimand and control structure used.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls. This audit does not establish a new algorithm or clinical benefit—it primarily serves as a methodological cautionary tale about the importance of rigorous evaluation in movement correctness classification research.

Abstract: Exercise-specific joint selection can improve skeleton-based correctness classification, but what does that gain establish? We audit 1,057 repetitions from ten REHAB24-6 subjects, separating evaluation aggregation, subset structure, and temporal representation. The manual-subset kNN gain changes from 0.055 for pooled out-of-fold AUROC to 0.020 for equal-weight within-person AUROC; both paired intervals include zero. Among 1,000 dimension-matched random maps, 14 match or exceed the manual pooled result, versus 145 when bilateral structure and trunk inclusion are also matched. RBF-SVM retains a positive within-person gain, whereas logistic regression and a random-convolution comparator have negative point gains under that estimand. Sequence-order and paired-seed controls further qualify the interpretation. This exploratory audit shows why joint-selection claims require explicit estimands and structurally appropriate controls; it does not establish a new algorithm or clinical benefit.

</details>


### [240] [Federated Agent Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01195)
*Qiang Yang,Zhiqiang Kou,Xueyi Zhang,Dong-Dong Wu,Hanlin Gu,Jing Guo,Yang Liu,Di Jiang,Qian Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Federated Agent Optimization (FAO), a new framework for distributed LLM agents to collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while preserving privacy. It extends conventional federated learning beyond model parameters to include memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience from task execution, tool use, feedback, and local knowledge. However, this experience cannot be directly shared due to privacy and proprietary constraints, and conventional federated learning is insufficient as agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters.

Method: The paper formulates FAO as a multi-objective optimization problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost. It organizes the optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge/skills. The framework characterizes how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities.

Result: A unified view of how distributed agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing is provided, with key challenges identified and promising research directions outlined for trustworthy federated agent systems.

Conclusion: FAO represents a novel research direction that addresses the limitations of conventional federated learning for LLM agents. The framework enables collaborative improvement while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local, paving the way for future research in federated agent systems.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in private environments and accumulate valuable experience from task execution, tool use, feedback, and local knowledge. Yet such experience is distributed across organizations and cannot be directly shared because of privacy and proprietary constraints. Conventional federated learning is insufficient for this setting, as agent capabilities extend beyond model parameters to memory, tools, rewards, skills, and structured knowledge. In this paper, we formulate \textbf{Federated Agent Optimization (FAO)}, which studies how distributed agents can collaboratively improve through controlled information exchange while keeping raw data, complete trajectories, and private knowledge local. We define FAO as a multi-objective problem balancing agent utility, privacy leakage, and communication cost, and organize its optimization space across policy, memory, tool use, reward, and structured knowledge and skills. We further characterize how private experience can be abstracted, protected, aggregated, and adapted into transferable capabilities, providing a unified view of how agents can benefit from one another without direct experience sharing. Finally, we identify the key challenges of FAO and outline several promising directions for future research toward trustworthy federated agent systems.

</details>


### [241] [Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207)
*Ziyi Chen,Yan Zhang,Jianhui Wei,Daoan Zhang,Zuozhu Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DARS addresses the credit assignment problem in RL for LLM training by using a dependency graph of predicates to assign step-level rewards. It tracks which steps verify, invalidate, or repair predicates, with verified predicates discounted by graph distance from broken prerequisites. Independent work remains valid while work built on mistakes is penalized.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Terminal rewards in RL for LLMs provide poor guidance about which individual steps contribute to success. Existing credit assignment methods fail to account for the fact that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted, while independent work remains valid. Every step in a failed episode has zero total future reward even when progress was made.

Method: DARS represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations. An annotator marks which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs. Verified predicates are discounted according to graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite. Independent predicates are unaffected. Repairs update weights based on remaining errors. Invalidated predicates need re-verification to regain credit. A fixed potential converts annotations into signed per-step rewards. Integrates with GiGPO, ARPO/AEPO without changing rollout strategies or optimizers.

Result: Improves success by up to 10 points over GiGPO on ALFWorld, raises WebShop task score and Search-R1 QA accuracy, complements AEPO on AIME24/25 with Python interpreter, exceeds OmniOPD in tool-free reasoning at 1.7B and 4B. Ablations show step-level credit, dependency attenuation, and graph topology each contribute. A distilled 8B annotator matches API performance.

Conclusion: DARS provides effective step-level credit assignment for LLM RL training by modeling task progress as a dependency graph. The method works across multiple task families and model sizes (1.5B-8B), integrates with existing training methods, and can be run efficiently with a distilled annotator without requiring a frontier judge.

Abstract: When training large language models with reinforcement learning, terminal rewards provide little guidance about which steps matter. Common methods for assigning step credit overlook that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted while independent work remains valid. With only a final success/failure reward, every step in a failed episode has zero total future reward, even when it made progress. We propose Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS), which represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations and assigns step-level credit over the dependency graph. An annotator marks which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs. Verified predicates are discounted according to graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite, while independent predicates are unaffected. Repairs update these weights based on any errors that remain; invalidated predicates need re-verification to regain credit. A fixed potential converts these annotations into signed per-step rewards. A common reward and annotation interface allows DARS to integrate with a range of reasoning and agentic training methods, such as GiGPO and ARPO/AEPO, without changing their rollout strategies or optimizers. Across five task families and models from 1.5B to 8B, DARS improves success by up to 10 points over GiGPO trained with the same budget and harness (ALFWorld), raises the WebShop task score and Search-R1 QA accuracy, complements AEPO's entropy-based training on AIME24/25 with a Python interpreter, and exceeds OmniOPD in controlled tool-free reasoning comparisons at 1.7B and 4B. Ablations show that step-level credit, dependency attenuation, and graph topology each contribute. On ALFWorld, a distilled 8B annotator matches the API annotator, enabling DARS to run efficiently without a frontier judge. Code is available at https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/DARS.

</details>


### [242] [Reputation, Strategy, and Emotion Effects on Generative AI Cooperation: A Comparison Across Reasoning and Non-Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01222)
*Celso de Melo,Zishan Feng,James Hale,Kazunori Terada,Giorgio Coricelli,Jonathan Gratch*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper examines cooperative behavior in frontier generative AI models using the iterated prisoner's dilemma, testing how reputation, strategy, and emotional signaling affect AI cooperation. Two studies compare non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o) with reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2), revealing that reasoning models show more sophisticated and hierarchical cue-weighting strategies, reduced "fake cooperation" (Potemkin effect), but heterogeneous end-game behaviors with different exploitability profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As Gen AI systems take on increasingly autonomous roles in socially consequential interactions, understanding their cooperative behavior and the signals that shape it becomes essential for responsible deployment.

Method: Experimental study using the iterated prisoner's dilemma paradigm, manipulating three factors: (1) counterpart reputation (positive, unknown, negative), (2) strategy (extortion vs. generosity), and (3) non-verbal emotional signaling (facial expressions conveying competitive or cooperative appraisals. Study 1 tested non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o); Study 2 tested reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2). A diagnostic "harmony game" was used to detect the Potemkin effect (superficial cooperation without genuine social sensitivity).

Result: Non-reasoning models: cooperation systematically shaped by all three factors, but models varied substantially in weighting each factor. Reasoning models: more concentrated reliance on strategy and reputation, near-elimination of Potemkin effect, and more conditional role for emotion consistent with hierarchical cue-weighting. Reasoning models showed heterogeneous end-game behavior ranging from sustained cooperation to systematic last-round defection, revealing model-specific exploitability profiles.

Conclusion: Gen AI models are increasingly sophisticated, though heterogeneous, social actors. The findings underscore the practical value of developing standardized cooperation benchmarks to inform responsible deployment of Gen AI in interactive, socially consequential settings (e.g., negotiation).

Abstract: As generative AI (Gen AI) systems take on increasingly autonomous roles in economically and socially consequential interactions, understanding their propensity to cooperate -- and the signals that shape this propensity -- has become essential. We examine cooperative behavior in frontier Gen AI models using the iterated prisoner's dilemma, manipulating counterpart reputation (positive, unknown, negative), strategy (extortion vs. generosity), and non-verbal emotional signaling (facial expressions conveying competitive or cooperative appraisals). In a first study with non-reasoning models (Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o), cooperation was systematically shaped by all three factors, paralleling patterns long documented in human behavioral research, though models varied substantially in how heavily each factor was weighted. A second study with reasoning models (Claude 4.6, Gemini 3, GPT-5.2) revealed a more concentrated reliance on strategy and reputation, a near-elimination of the Potemkin effect observed in non-reasoning models (evidenced by near-uniform cooperation in a diagnostic harmony game), and a more conditional role for emotion consistent with a hierarchical cue-weighting strategy rather than a simple loss of social sensitivity. Reasoning models also showed heterogeneous end-game behavior, ranging from sustained cooperation to systematic last-round defection effect, revealing model-specific exploitability profiles with direct practical relevance for deployment in negotiation and other multi-round interactions. Together, these findings characterize Gen AI models as increasingly sophisticated, though heterogeneous, social actors, and underscore the practical value of developing standardized cooperation benchmarks to inform the responsible deployment of Gen AI in interactive, socially consequential settings.

</details>


### [243] [HHR: Hierarchical Hash Retrieval for Efficient LLM Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01230)
*Lianjun Liu,Tiantian Zheng,You Huang,Weiqi Yan,Mingte Qiu,Huazhong Liu,Xiaofeng Zhu,Yunshan Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Hierarchical Hash Retrieval (HHR), a coarse-to-fine framework to address the mismatch between Hamming distance and attention relevance in hash-based sparse attention for efficient long-context LLM inference. HHR combines Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR) and Learned Hash Projection (LHP) to suppress false positives and recover false negatives, achieving 1.10-point improvement on LongBench and up to 3.30x decoding speedup at 128K context length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hash-based retrieval for efficient long-context LLM inference suffers from a critical mismatch: Hamming distance poorly correlates with attention relevance because hash binarization discards feature magnitude information, leading to false-positive retrieval of low-logit keys and false-negative omission of high-logit keys.

Method: The proposed HHR framework uses two components: (1) Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR) learns head-wise orthogonal transformations to redistribute feature magnitudes and derive discriminative page-level logit bounds for pruning low-logit keys while preserving important candidates. (2) Learned Hash Projection (LHP) learns head-wise projection spaces that align Hamming distance with true Query-Key relevance ranking for fine-grained retrieval. This coarse-to-fine approach progressively improves retrieval accuracy.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate superior performance. On LongBench, HHR improves average score by 1.10 points. At 128K context length, it achieves up to 3.30x decoding speedup and 2.83x end-to-end speedup for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

Conclusion: HHR effectively addresses the hash binarization limitation by combining coarse-grained pruning (GKR) with fine-grained learned projection (LHP), substantially improving hash-based sparse attention fidelity and enabling efficient long-context inference with significant speedups while maintaining accuracy.

Abstract: Efficient long-context inference is essential for large language models (LLMs), yet it poses a severe computational bottleneck. Hash-based retrieval offers an efficient alternative by encoding queries and keys into binary codes and using Hamming distance for key selection. However, this leads to a critical mismatch between Hamming distance and attention relevance. Query-Key logits depend jointly on directional similarity and feature magnitudes, whereas hash binarization discards magnitude information, causing both false-positive retrieval of low-logit keys and false-negative omission of high-logit keys. To address these failures, we propose Hierarchical Hash Retrieval (HHR), a coarse-to-fine framework that progressively improves retrieval accuracy through Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR) and Learned Hash Projection (LHP). GKR learns a head-wise orthogonal transformation to redistribute feature magnitudes and derive more discriminative page-level logit bounds, enabling effective pruning of low-logit keys while preserving important candidates. LHP then learns a head-wise projection space that aligns Hamming distance with the true Query-Key relevance ranking for fine-grained retrieval. By combining GKR and LHP, HHR suppresses false positives and recovers false negatives, substantially improving the fidelity of hash-based sparse attention. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that HHR achieves superior performance over existing methods. For example, on LongBench, HHR improves the average score by 1.10 points and, at a context length of 128K, achieves up to a 3.30x decoding speedup and a 2.83x end-to-end speedup for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianjunl13-sudo/HHR.

</details>


### [244] [Learning to Ask: Information Acquisition for SLM-LLM Collaboration, under a budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01236)
*Yongjun Kim,Xiaoxiao Li,Jaeho Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a three-stage RLVR framework for efficient collaboration between a small language model (SLM) and a black-box large language model (LLM) advisor under API budget constraints. Instead of delegating reasoning, the SLM selectively queries the LLM as needed, learning when to call the advisor, how to formulate useful queries, and how to integrate the received information into reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SLM-LLM collaboration approaches treat it as a computation allocation problem, which is inefficient in black-box API settings due to coarse-grained delegation and repeated context transmission. The authors propose reframing this as an information acquisition problem where the SLM remains the primary reasoner.

Method: Three-stage RLVR framework that jointly learns: (1) when to invoke the LLM advisor, (2) how to formulate targeted queries, and (3) how to integrate advisor information into the reasoning process. The approach uses reinforcement learning to optimize advisor invocation and information use.

Result: The approach improves the performance-cost tradeoff over existing collaboration baselines on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, and in some settings matches or exceeds oracle problem-level routing. The strategy also transfers to other advisor model families without further training.

Conclusion: The information acquisition paradigm is more effective than computation allocation for SLM-LLM collaboration in API-constrained settings. The three-stage RLVR framework successfully enables selective, targeted LLM queries that maintain efficiency while leveraging strong reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Collaboration between a small language model (SLM) and a large language model (LLM) offers an opportunity to combine the efficiency of smaller models with the strong reasoning capabilities of larger ones. Existing approaches primarily frame such collaboration as a computation allocation problem, determining which model should handle each portion of the reasoning process. In black-box API-based settings, however, this paradigm can be inefficient due to coarse-grained delegation or repeated transmission of context across model switches. In this work, we instead formulate SLM-LLM collaboration as an information acquisition problem, under an API budget constraint. The SLM remains the primary reasoner and selectively queries a black-box LLM advisor only when needed, issuing targeted queries rather than delegating the reasoning process itself. To realize this strategy, we develop a three-stage RLVR framework that learns whether to call the advisor, how to formulate useful queries, and how to integrate the collaboration into the reasoning process by jointly refining advisor invocation and information use. Across mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, our approach improves the performance--cost tradeoff over existing collaboration baselines and, in some settings, matches or exceeds oracle problem-level routing. Finally, we show that our strategy can transfer to other advisor model families, without further training.

</details>


### [245] [Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graphs for Dynamic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01249)
*Yan Luo,Selim-Antoine Lali,Jeremy Moebel,Iliass Khoutaibi,Ahmadou Aidara,Mengyu Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces dynamic task routing, where event streams revise task bindings and systems must select the correct document version at query time. The authors repurpose six benchmarks into 31,119 dynamic episodes with 373,428 queries, and propose RIAG, a bounded multi-agent policy that achieves 54.24% accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, significantly outperforming the baseline method (32.22% at 18.00 calls/query).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional reasoning protocols use fixed, preselected tasks and cannot test whether an agent propagates relevant updates, preserves unaffected work, or reconstructs historical task bindings. This limitation necessitates studying dynamic task routing where event streams revise task bindings.

Method: The authors repurpose six benchmarks (MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA, MATH, GPQA, HumanEval) into dynamic episodes. They introduce RIAG (Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graph), a bounded multi-agent policy that: separates deterministic temporal resolution from task reasoning, caches solutions by immutable document identity, starts each fresh task with two unexposed attempts, and conditionally invokes audit and repair (max four calls per document version).

Result: Homogeneous RIAG achieves 54.24% joint routing-and-answer accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, compared with 32.22% at 18.00 calls/query for the strongest comparison method. Heterogeneous RIAG reaches 49.78% at 0.63 calls/query.

Conclusion: RIAG successfully addresses the dynamic task routing problem with significantly better efficiency (30x fewer calls) while achieving higher accuracy than baseline methods. The approach demonstrates a central trade-off between recomputing after every event (wasting work) and unguarded reuse (returning stale conclusions).

Abstract: Conventional reasoning protocols present a fixed, preselected task, so they cannot test whether an agent propagates relevant updates, preserves unaffected work, or reconstructs a historical task binding. We therefore study \emph{dynamic task routing}, in which an event stream revises task bindings and a system must select the document version valid at each query time before solving it. To study this problem, we repurpose six widely used benchmarks: MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MedMCQA, MATH, GPQA, and HumanEval into 31{,}119 dynamic episodes comprising 373{,}428 temporally categorized queries. This setting exposes a central trade-off: recomputing after every event wastes work, whereas unguarded reuse returns stale conclusions. We introduce the Revision-Aware Independent Agent Graph (RIAG), a bounded multi-agent policy that separates deterministic temporal resolution from task reasoning. RIAG caches solutions by immutable document identity, starts each fresh task with two unexposed attempts, and conditionally invokes audit and repair, using at most four calls per document version. On this collection, homogeneous RIAG achieves 54.24\% joint routing-and-answer accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, compared with 32.22\% at 18.00 calls/query for the strongest comparison method; heterogeneous RIAG reaches 49.78\% at 0.63 calls/query.

</details>


### [246] [DeFA: Dependency-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01256)
*Bo Deng,Xinlei Zheng,Yi Wei,Kang Zhou,Chongyang Tao,Renzhao Liang,Xuanren Chen,Lifan Guo,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DeFA is a dependency-guided framework for identifying and attributing failures in LLM agent executions. It uses event dependency graphs and failure propagation graphs to trace errors across long trajectories, partitioning executions into segments to handle complexity. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks and can improve downstream task accuracy by 6-15 percentage points when used for agent skill evolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge is that errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated by many steps, making decisive-error localization difficult. Understanding both step content and step dependencies is crucial for accurate failure attribution.

Method: DeFA combines protocol relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory. It identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. For handling long trajectories, DeFA partitions executions into segments, combining detailed content of the current segment with summaries of other segments. Finally, it uses step evidence and the steps' roles in failure propagation to identify the decisive error, responsible agent, and error category.

Result: DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accuracy across all evaluated backbones on Who and When and the Who and When Pro text subset. It also achieves the highest failure-mode accuracy among taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. The method demonstrates applicability to multimodal failure attribution on image and video trajectories. Ablations confirm the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph.

Conclusion: DeFA provides effective failure attribution for LLM agents across text, image, and video modalities. When used for skill evolution in Trace2Skill, it improves downstream task accuracy by 6-15 percentage points over the native pipeline, demonstrating that diagnostic feedback can support agent improvement on subsequent tasks.

Abstract: Errors in LLM agent executions and their visible consequences can be separated by many steps, making decisive-error localization a matter of understanding both step content and step dependencies. We introduce DeFA, a dependency-guided framework for agent failure attribution. DeFA first combines protocol relations and semantic dependencies into an event dependency graph spanning the trajectory. It then identifies events that may violate task requirements and traces their sources and subsequent effects to construct a failure propagation graph. Finally, DeFA uses step evidence and the steps' roles in failure propagation to identify the decisive error, responsible agent, and error category. To support long trajectories, DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment's detailed content with summaries of the other segments, giving local diagnosis access to global execution context. Across Who and When and the Who and When Pro text subset, DeFA achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accuracy with all evaluated backbones, and the highest failure-mode accuracy among taxonomy-aligned methods on Pro. Further experiments on image and video trajectories demonstrate its applicability to multimodal failure attribution. Ablations support the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph. Using DeFA's diagnostic feedback for skill evolution in Trace2Skill improves downstream task accuracy by 6-15 percentage points over the native pipeline, showing that the diagnoses can also support agent improvement on subsequent tasks.

</details>


### [247] [Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01262)
*Lili Chen,Gavin Buskes,Yuxin Ren,Chin Tong Leong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A pilot study designing a GenAI-powered practice platform to provide immediate, scaffolded feedback in large electrical engineering classes, moving human oversight from real-time grading to upfront solution verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large electrical engineering classes face high student-to-demonstrator ratios, causing feedback delays of days. While GenAI could scale conversational feedback, using it for grading raises trust and accountability concerns, yet keeping humans in the loop reintroduces delays that diminish feedback value.

Method: Designed and piloted a GenAI practice platform that delivers immediate, scaffolded feedback during self-directed practice. Human oversight was relocated from real-time grading to upfront verification of solutions. Studied student engagement, perception of feedback value and reliability, and transferability to other engineering subjects.

Result: The study aimed to understand student engagement patterns, perceived value and reliability of AI-generated feedback, and identify lessons applicable to other engineering subjects.

Conclusion: The approach resolves the tension between immediacy and trustworthiness by separating real-time feedback delivery from human oversight. Lessons learned from the pilot inform transferability to other engineering disciplines.

Abstract: Timely and specific feedback is one of the strongest influences on student learning, yet it is difficult to sustain in large electrical engineering classes where the ratio of students to demonstrators is high and a learner who is stuck may wait days to find out why an approach was wrong. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers a way to scale conversational feedback, but using it to grade assessed work raises trust and accountability concerns, and keeping a human in the loop to assure its judgements reintroduces the very delay that erodes the value of feedback. The result is a tension between the immediacy that makes feedback so impactful and the human oversight that makes it trustworthy. In this work, we set out to resolve that tension in practice by designing and piloting a GenAI practice platform that delivers immediate, scaffolded feedback during self-directed practice. This relocates human oversight from real-time grading to the upfront verification of solutions. Our goal was to understand how students engaged with the tool, how they perceived the value and reliability of its feedback, and what lessons transfer to other engineering subjects.

</details>


### [248] [SCOPE-AD: Sequential cost-aware ordinal-belief planning with energy-based models for diagnostic agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01278)
*Ziwen Yu,Ivan Koychev,Elizabeth Coulthard,Ting Zhou,Bolin Chen,Dian Hong,Zinuo You,Yujiao Wang,Anthony Mulholland,Qiang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE-AD is a cost-aware diagnostic agent for Alzheimer's disease that sequentially decides which tests to acquire and when diagnosis is sufficient, using an ordinal-belief planning framework with energy-based models to achieve 77.70% Macro-F1 at $50.46 average cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Alzheimer's disease diagnosis requires sequential evidence acquisition with heterogeneous test costs and patient burden. Existing fixed-modality predictors cannot jointly decide which test to acquire next or when sufficient evidence is available for diagnosis.

Method: SCOPE-AD uses a mask-aware ordinal model to represent uncertainty along the CN-MCI-AD continuum. Retrospective training provides sampled Bellman targets for an energy-based teacher, whose action distributions are distilled into a Qwen policy. At deployment, the agent selects acquisition or diagnosis actions under availability and budget constraints, updating evidence and ordinal belief after each acquisition.

Result: On ADNI dataset, SCOPE-AD achieves 77.70% Macro-F1 at an average acquisition cost of $50.46, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.34 percentage points. Full-modality evaluation only improves Macro-F1 by 1.89 points while increasing acquisition cost by 116.7 times.

Conclusion: Selective acquisition is highly cost-effective for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis, as full-modality evaluation provides minimal accuracy improvement at dramatically higher cost.

Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) diagnosis requires sequential evidence acquisition under heterogeneous test costs and patient burden. Fixed-modality predictors do not jointly decide which test to acquire or when the available evidence is sufficient for diagnosis. We propose SCOPE-AD (Sequential Cost-Aware Ordinal-Belief Planning with Energy-Based Models for Diagnostic Agents) for cost-aware classification of cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD cases. A mask-aware ordinal model represents uncertainty along the ordered CN--MCI--AD continuum. Retrospective training records provide sampled Bellman targets for an energy-based teacher, whose action distributions are distilled into a Qwen policy. At deployment, the agent selects acquisition or diagnosis actions under availability and budget constraints without access to unacquired values. After each acquisition, the evidence and ordinal belief are updated before the next decision. On ADNI, SCOPE-AD achieves 77.70\% Macro-F1 at an average acquisition cost of \$50.46, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.34 percentage points. Full-modality evaluation raises Macro-F1 by only 1.89 points while increasing acquisition cost by 116.7 times. These results support selective acquisition for cost-effective diagnosis.

</details>


### [249] [ITC-MoE: Importance-guided Token-aware Compression for MoE Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01296)
*Lianjun Liu,Shipeng Li,You Huang,Weiqi Yan,Mingte Qiu,Huazhong Liu,Xiaofeng Zhu,Yunshan Zhong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ITC-MoE is a compression framework for Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Language Models that addresses cross-mode non-uniform redundancy and token-wise utilization variation through two components: Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) and Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR). It achieves 96.33% accuracy retention on MultiArith with 30% compression budget and up to 7.22x speedup.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE DLMs offer flexible parallel decoding and increased model capacity but suffer from substantial computation and storage costs due to large expert parameters. Existing low-rank MoE compression methods use static factorization and fixed rank allocation, which fail to capture the distinctive properties of MoE DLMs: cross-mode non-uniform redundancy (varying parameter redundancy and sensitivity across input, output, and expert modes) and token-wise utilization variation (hot and cold tokens have different spectral characteristics and expert activation patterns).

Method: ITC-MoE consists of two complementary components: (1) Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) incorporates activation and gradient importance into expert weight transformation, jointly factorizes expert weights across multiple modes, and adaptively allocates ranks under a fixed parameter budget. (2) Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR) applies lightweight low-rank compensation to compression-sensitive hot tokens and restricts the candidate expert set for cold tokens with concentrated routing patterns.

Result: On SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32, ITC-MoE maintains 96.33% accuracy on MultiArith under a 30% compression budget while achieving up to 7.22x end-to-end speedup.

Conclusion: ITC-MoE successfully reduces computation and storage costs of MoE DLMs while preserving generation quality by jointly adapting compression capacity and inference execution to parameter redundancy and token-wise variation. The code is publicly available.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer flexible parallel decoding and increased model capacity, but their large number of expert parameters incurs substantial computation and storage costs. Existing low-rank MoE compression methods largely rely on static factorization and fixed rank allocation, which overlook the distinctive properties of MoE DLMs. Specifically, we identify two properties: cross-mode non-uniform redundancy, where parameter redundancy and sensitivity to rank truncation vary across the input, output, and expert modes, and token-wise utilization variation, where hot and cold tokens exhibit distinct spectral characteristics and expert activation patterns. To address these challenges, we propose ITC-MoE, an Importance-guided Token-aware Compression framework for MoE DLMs. ITC-MoE consists of two complementary components. First, Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) incorporates activation and gradient importance into expert weight transformation, jointly factorizes expert weights across multiple modes, and adaptively allocates ranks under a fixed parameter budget. Second, Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR) applies lightweight low-rank compensation to compression-sensitive hot tokens and restricts the candidate expert set for cold tokens with concentrated routing patterns. By jointly adapting compression capacity and inference execution to both parameter redundancy and token-wise variation, ITC-MoE substantially reduces the computation and storage costs of MoE DLMs while preserving their generation quality. For example, on SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32, ITC-MoE maintains an accuracy of 96.33% on MultiArith under a 30% compression budget, while achieving up to a 7.22x end-to-end speedup. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianjunl13-sudo/ITC-MoE.

</details>


### [250] [Questionnaire-Guided Disaggregation of Energy Appliance Use for Domestic Smart Meter Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01297)
*Achal Nanjundamurthy,Rupam Misra,Suzanne Little,Alan F. Smeaton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a label-free energy disaggregation system for Ireland's smart metering data (30-minute resolution), combining event detection with questionnaire-guided estimation to identify usage from 9 appliance categories. The method was evaluated on four datasets and achieved superior performance compared to two existing disaggregation systems, with statistically significant improvements (p<0.001).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a practical limitation: Ireland's smart meters record electricity at 30-minute intervals, which is sufficient for billing time-of-use tariffs but inadequate for identifying individual appliance usage. This prevents households from understanding their consumption patterns and making informed decisions to reduce energy costs.

Method: The proposed hybrid method combines two approaches: (1) event detection for identifying high-power loads, and (2) questionnaire-guided estimation for estimating usage of other appliances. The system is label-free, meaning it doesn't require pre-trained models or appliance signatures from the target household.

Result: The hybrid method achieved the lowest whole-decomposition error across all buildings in all four datasets compared to two independently developed disaggregation systems. It demonstrated better month-level performance over 54 paired months with statistical significance (p<0.001, Holm-corrected).

Conclusion: The method provides practical value by offering households actionable advice on their energy consumption patterns and recommendations for reducing or shifting usage to lower costs. The large-scale validation using real-world data from nearly 3,000 Irish consumers over 4,800 years strengthens the credibility of the findings.

Abstract: Ireland's smart metering programme records electricity use at 30-minute resolution, with smart meters installed in over 80\% of households as of late 2025. While this is useful for billing of smart, time-of-use tariffs, it is too coarse to capture use of domestic appliances.
