We present a label-free disaggregation system that breaks usage data into 9 appliance categories by combining event detection for high-power loads with questionnaire-guided estimation. Our evaluation draws on four datasets: a calibration household with a commercial comparator, two public benchmarks (UK-DALE and REFIT) with per-appliance sub-metering, and a smart meter dataset of more than 4,800 years of use from 2,968 Irish consumers. Compared against two independently developed disaggregation systems our hybrid method combining analysis of usage data with questionnaire results, achieves the lowest whole-decomposition error on all buildings across the datasets, with better month-level performance over 54 paired months ($p<0.001$, Holm-corrected). Our method provides useful advice on a household's energy consumption patterns and advice on how to reduce or shift usage on some appliances in order to reduce costs.

</details>


### [251] [DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01306)
*Stephanie Finley,Liudas Panavas,Thomas Mikkelson,Cam Hinton,Stacey Ganss,Bradley Monton,Emily Kendall,Michelle Spradlin,Lydia Bye,Michael O'Brien,Lauren Ylvisaker,Derek Ray,Suhaas Garre,Sushant Mehta,Edwin Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DAYJOB is a benchmark of 130 professional tasks in healthcare and finance designed to evaluate AI agents on realistic, ambiguous work requests. Each task is a containerized environment with binary criteria that an agentic judge uses to evaluate outputs. The best model (Claude Opus 5.5) passes only ~24% of tasks, revealing that agents often accept contradictory premises and carry errors through otherwise consistent analyses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Professional work frequently begins with brief, ambiguous requests that require professionals to determine what's needed, which documents are relevant, and whether the request's premise is valid. Current benchmarks don't capture this reality of professional work.

Method: The authors built DAYJOB with 130 tasks (50 healthcare, 80 finance) created by professionals. Each task is a containerized Harbor environment with an expert rubric of binary criteria (median 47.5-57.5 per task). An agentic judge evaluates attempts against all criteria; passing requires meeting every criterion. They tested 30 model configurations from 13 developers.

Result: The strongest model, Claude Opus 5.5, passes 24.7% of healthcare and 23.9% of finance attempts. The median configuration passes only 0.6% (healthcare) and 2.5% (finance). Case studies reveal agents accept premises that records contradict and carry wrong inputs through otherwise consistent analyses.

Conclusion: Current AI agents perform poorly on realistic professional tasks, even the best models. The benchmark reveals critical failures: agents accept contradictory information and propagate errors. The authors release healthcare tasks, 50 finance tasks, the evaluation harness, and the leaderboard to advance research.

Abstract: Professional work often starts with a brief request that leaves the professional to work out what is needed, which documents matter, and whether the request's premise holds. We introduce DAYJOB, a benchmark of 130 tasks built by professionals in healthcare (50) and finance (80). The tasks are estimated to take a professional 13.6 hours on average in healthcare and 16.6 in finance. Each task is a containerized Harbor environment with an expert rubric of binary criteria (median 47.5 and 57.5 per task) that an agentic judge applies to the delivered files, and an attempt passes only if it meets every criterion. Across 30 model configurations from 13 developers, the strongest, Claude Opus 5.5, passes 24.7% of healthcare and 23.9% of finance attempts, and the median configuration passes 0.6% and 2.5%. In case studies, agents accept premises that the record contradicts and carry wrong inputs through otherwise consistent analyses. We release all healthcare tasks, 50 of the 80 finance tasks, the evaluation harness, and the leaderboard.

</details>


### [252] [ProtoFlow: Prototype-Guided Flow Matching for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01320)
*Shibo Feng,Wanjin Feng,Yang Qiu,Deheng Ye,Peilin Zhao,Chunyan Miao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ProtoFlow is a novel multivariate time series forecasting framework that combines vector-quantized autoencoding with prototype-prior flow matching. It maps multivariate sequences into discrete latent space using VQ, constructs a structured prior from the learned codebook, and uses a DiT-based rectified flow to transport samples from this prototype prior to future latent representations, avoiding the issues of autoregressive token generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods have limitations: diffusion-based methods require many sampling steps; VAE-based methods use autoregressive token generation suffering from exposure bias and training-inference mismatch; flow matching typically uses generic Gaussian prior. The key insight is that the VQ codebook already captures representative latent prototypes and can serve as a more informative prior for flow matching.

Method: 1) Map multivariate sequences into discrete latent space using vector quantization (VQ); 2) Construct a structured prior from the learned codebook (prototype prior); 3) Learn a DiT-based rectified flow to transport samples from this prototype prior to future latent representations conditioned on historical observations; 4) Replace generic noise initialization with learned prototype prior.

Result: ProtoFlow avoids the rollout mismatch of AR token prediction and promotes faster training convergence. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show superior forecasting performance with efficient inference.

Conclusion: By combining VQ autoencoding with prototype-prior flow matching, ProtoFlow achieves efficient non-autoregressive forecasting with better performance than existing approaches, offering a promising direction for multivariate time series forecasting.

Abstract: Generative modeling has shown strong promise for multivariate time mseries (MTS) forecasting, especially scale to high-dimensional settings. Diffusion-based methods achieve competitive performance but typically require many sampling steps at inference. VAE-based non-iterative forecasting frameworks have therefore emerged as an efficient alternative. Within this line of work, vector quantization (VQ) enables controllable latent space modeling by mapping multivariate series into compact discrete representations. Existing VQ-based forecasting methods, however, typically rely on autoregressive (AR) token generation, which suffers from exposure bias and training-inference mismatch. Flow matching provides an efficient non-autoregressive alternative for latent forecasting, but existing formulations usually initialize transport from a generic Gaussian prior. We instead observe that the trained VQ codebook already captures representative latent prototypes and can thus serve as a more informative prior for flow matching. Based on this insight, we propose ProtoFlow, a forecasting framework that combines vector-quantized autoencoding with Prototype-prior Flow matching. Our method first maps multivariate sequences into a discrete latent space, then constructs a structured prior from the learned codebook, and finally learns a DiT-based rectified flow to transport samples from this prior to future latent representations conditioned on historical observations. By replacing generic noise initialization with a learned prototype prior, ProtoFlow avoids the rollout mismatch of AR token prediction and promotes faster training convergence. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show that it consistently achieves superior forecasting performance with efficient inference.

</details>


### [253] [TRACE: Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure for Multi-Turn Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01323)
*Fengpeng Li,Kemou Li,Qizhou Wang,Haiwei Wu,Jiantao Zhou,Di Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRACE is a token-level training objective for safety-aligned LLMs that prevents multi-turn attack bypass by weighting tokens based on refusal-attributable advantage. It achieves the lowest attack success rate across all 35 model-attack pairs tested while maintaining utility within 1.23 points of baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs can be compromised when harmful requests are spread across multiple turns, even though they refuse single-turn harmful prompts. Current preference objectives only evaluate single responses, making multi-turn risk control ineffective.

Method: TRACE uses a token-level objective where each token on safe responses is weighted by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage. This advantage compares a frozen reference model with its refusal-ablated copy, allowing earlier tokens to receive credit from later refusal signals. At high-gap positions, it combines observed tokens with policy-selected alternatives in erasure targets and uses a gradient-norm penalty for the retain set.

Result: TRACE achieves the lowest attack success rate (ASR) across all 35 model-attack pairs (5 open-weight models × 7 multi-turn attacks), while limiting utility drop to at most 1.23 points on MMLU and HellaSwag benchmarks.

Conclusion: Theoretical analysis provides sufficient conditions for bounding multi-turn trajectory risk from single-turn suppression. TRACE successfully prevents multi-turn jailbreak attacks while preserving model utility, outperforming existing safety alignment methods.

Abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) often refuse a harmful request but comply once the same goal is spread over several turns. Preference objectives score whole responses to single prompts, so their training loss alone cannot control risk on unseen histories. Our analysis gives sufficient conditions under which suppression at supervised single-turn contexts yields a bound on multi-turn trajectory risk. The bound accounts for coverage, transfer slack, and leakage, and characterizes contraction relative to a base-policy risk budget evaluated on the trained policy's contexts. TRACE (Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure) turns this principle into a token-level objective. On the safe response, each token is weighted by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage. The advantage compares a frozen reference model with its refusal-ablated copy, allowing earlier response tokens to receive credit from later refusal-related evidence. At high-gap positions on rejected responses, TRACE combines the observed token with policy-selected alternatives in the erasure target. A gradient-norm penalty replaces the retain set. Across five open-weight models and seven multi-turn attacks, TRACE gives the lowest attack success rate (ASR) in all 35 model and attack pairs, while the model utility evaluated on MMLU and HellaSwag drop by at most 1\.23 points. Source code can be found in the supplemental material.

</details>


### [254] [PPO-HRAP: Proximal Policy Optimization with a Hybrid Regime-Aware Policy for Risk-Controlled Trading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01325)
*Duong Hien Chi Kien,Thanh Trung Huynh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PPO-HRAP is a hybrid regime-aware reinforcement learning trading policy that combines Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with an interpretable volatility-aware regime prior. It balances upside participation with drawdown control by blending learned PPO actions with regime-derived target exposure, using a reward function incorporating log returns, VIX-conditioned drawdown penalties, exposure deviation, and turnover costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning for trading struggles to balance upside participation with drawdown control. Profit-only policies can collapse toward passive long exposure, while aggressively risk-penalized rewards become too defensive during volatile periods. There is a need for a method that can adapt to different market regimes while maintaining risk-adjusted returns.

Method: PPO-HRAP combines PPO with an interpretable regime prior. The agent observes market features and portfolio-state variables, receives a composite reward (portfolio log return + VIX-conditioned drawdown-increase penalty + target-exposure deviation + turnover cost), and executes a blended action between the PPO actor output and a regime-derived target exposure. The regime prior is volatility-aware using VIX conditioning.

Result: On the held-out 2020-2022 SPY test window, PPO-HRAP achieves 27.62% total return, 8.48% annualized return, 0.6447 Sharpe ratio, 0.8588 Sortino ratio, and 0.4592 Calmar ratio, while reducing maximum drawdown from 34.10% (Buy and Hold) to 18.47%. Across five SPY seeds, mean total return is 0.2725 ± 0.0109 and mean Sharpe ratio is 0.6219 ± 0.0565. Single-run cross-asset tests on QQQ and DIA show first-place ranking on total return and Sharpe ratio for all three assets.

Conclusion: Blending learned actions with a volatility-aware regime prior is a practical approach to improve risk-adjusted trading behavior. However, the current policy still incurs high turnover and cross-asset robustness beyond SPY remains limited to single-run evidence, indicating areas for further improvement.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning for trading often struggles to balance upside participation with drawdown control. Profit-only policies can collapse toward passive long exposure on upward-drifting assets, while aggressively risk-penalized rewards can become too defensive during volatile periods. This paper proposes PPO-HRAP, a hybrid regime-aware policy that combines Proximal Policy Optimization with an interpretable regime prior. The agent observes both market features and portfolio-state variables, receives a reward combining portfolio log return, VIX-conditioned drawdown-increase penalty, target-exposure deviation, and turnover cost, and executes a blended action between the PPO actor output and a regime-derived target exposure. On the held-out 2020-2022 SPY test window, PPO-HRAP achieves 27.62% total return, 8.48% annualized return, 0.6447 Sharpe ratio, 0.8588 Sortino ratio, and 0.4592 Calmar ratio, while reducing maximum drawdown from 34.10% for Buy and Hold to 18.47%. Across five SPY seeds, PPO-HRAP remains stable with mean total return $0.2725 \pm 0.0109$ and mean Sharpe ratio $0.6219 \pm 0.0565$. Single-run cross-asset tests on QQQ and DIA further show that the proposed method ranks first on total return and Sharpe ratio for all three reported assets. These results suggest that blending learned actions with a volatility-aware regime prior is a practical way to improve risk-adjusted trading behavior, although the current policy still incurs high turnover and cross-asset robustness beyond SPY remains limited to single-run evidence.

</details>


### [255] [An ontology for cross-sectoral crisis management: core and public health modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01326)
*Aldo Gangemi,Rita T. Sousa,Luigi Asprino,Giorgia Lodi,Andrea G. Nuzzolese,Valentina Presutti,Johannes Gysen,Diana F. Sousa,Luigi Spagnolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ECMO is a modular OWL-based ontology for disaster risk reduction and response, designed as a network of ontological modules with a public health module aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for a cross-sectoral reference framework to enable consistent and unified knowledge representation and integration across disaster risk reduction and response domains.

Method: ECMO is structured as a network of ontological modules, with ECMO-CORE capturing fundamental crisis management concepts (hazard, event, exposure, impact, response measure) using ontology design patterns and OWL2 punning technique. Domain-specific modules are defined, including a public health module aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11. The utility is demonstrated by representing data from the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources system to generate an end-to-end pipeline populating an ECMO-compliant knowledge graph from unstructured epidemiological news.

Result: Initial results demonstrate that ECMO provides the formal guardrails necessary for consistent and unified knowledge representation and integration.

Conclusion: ECMO successfully serves as a cross-sectoral reference ontology for disaster risk reduction and response, with the ontology publicly available under CC BY 4.0 license.

Abstract: This paper presents the European Crisis Management Ontology (ECMO), a modular OWL-based ontology intended as a cross-sectoral reference for disaster risk reduction and response. ECMO is designed to be organised as a network of ontological modules. Among the modules, ECMO-CORE captures fundamental crisis management concepts such as hazard, event, exposure, impact, and response measure and uses ontology design patterns and the OWL2 punning technique to resolve ambiguities between hazard types and event manifestations. In addition, domain-specific modules are defined as in the case of the public health module aligned with SNOMED CT and ICD-11. To demonstrate the resource's utility, we used ECMO to represent the data of the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources system of the Joint Research Centre to generate an end-to-end pipeline that populates an ECMO-compliant knowledge graph from unstructured epidemiological news. Initial results demonstrate that ECMO provides the formal guardrails necessary for consistent and unified knowledge representation and integration. The ontology is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20070268 and is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license.

</details>


### [256] [Verify Claims, Not Scores: Evidence-Based Verification of Modular Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01348)
*Ali Atiah Alzahrani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a claim-specific verification audit framework for modular agents that plan, act, check, and refine. Instead of using aggregate task scores, the audit scores evidence by recording conclusions with supporting evidence, verdicts (supported, unsupported, unresolved, not evaluated), and boundaries of validity. Three tools provide evidence: oracle policies to measure attainable improvement, component replacement to locate lost value, and tests to verify if the verifier's score correctly identifies what it claims to bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent evaluation relies on aggregate task scores, which cannot reveal whether improvement was actually attainable, which specific component lost value, or what the agent's own verification checks actually certify. This lack of transparency makes it difficult to diagnose and improve modular agent systems.

Method: The proposed verification audit framework uses three complementary tools: (1) Oracle policies measure attainable improvement under explicitly stated action sets, allowing low values to be traced to evaluation rather than environment; (2) Component replacement with perfect counterparts identifies lost value, with null results read as unresolved when downstream components could mask them; (3) Separate tests verify whether the verifier's score correctly identifies the quantity it claims to bound. The framework was applied to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes.

Result: The empirical findings revealed: (1) The value of perfect regime information depends on the action set used to measure it; (2) The scenario generator discards most of the regime signal while better local fidelity does not improve decisions; (3) The runtime verifier can be bypassed with no visible change in outcomes.

Conclusion: The contribution is the verification audit protocol itself and the evidential distinctions it enforces, which provide systematic transparency into agent component performance. The empirical findings are specific to the portfolio-allocation agent and synthetic environment studied, but demonstrate the framework's ability to diagnose where value is lost and whether verification checks are meaningful.

Abstract: When developers change one component of an agent, such as its controller, a learned model or its verifier, they usually judge the change by an aggregate task score. That score cannot tell whether improvement was attainable, which component lost value, or what the agent's own checks certify. We introduce a claim-specific verification audit for modular agents that plan, act, check and refine. Instead of scoring the agent, the audit scores the evidence: each conclusion is recorded with the evidence behind it, one of four verdicts (supported, unsupported, unresolved or not evaluated) and the boundary within which it holds. Three tools supply that evidence. Oracle policies measure attainable improvement under an explicitly stated action set, so that a low value can be traced to the evaluation rather than to the environment. Replacing one component at a time with a perfect counterpart locates lost value, with null results read as unresolved whenever a downstream component could mask them. A separate test asks whether the verifier's score identifies the quantity it is read as bounding. Applied to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes, the audit shows that the value of perfect regime information depends on the action set used to measure it, that the scenario generator discards most of the regime signal while better local fidelity does not improve decisions, and that the runtime verifier can be bypassed with no visible change in outcomes. The contribution is the protocol and the evidential distinctions it enforces; the empirical findings are specific to the agent and environment studied.

</details>


### [257] [Generation Provenance Before Behavior Attribution: Auditing Synthetic Speech Research Objects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01378)
*Sidi Chang,Peiying Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of attributing machine learning model behavior to synthetic training data by proposing a "generation-provenance substrate" - a framework that tracks the complete lineage of synthetic data items from source specification through generation to final training data. The authors demonstrate this in a Japanese care-handoff pipeline with 113 synthetic speech assets, but find that even with comprehensive provenance, full causal attribution remains elusive.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ML training pipelines lose critical information about how synthetic training data was generated. Waveform-label pairs don't preserve the knowledge of what produced each training item, making it impossible to understand what caused specific model behaviors. This creates a fundamental attribution problem in synthetic data pipelines.

Method: The authors propose a generation-provenance substrate that binds together: source specification, generated content, waveform, target, fact requirements, quality signals, review lineage, and immutable manifest identity. They audit this framework in a private Japanese care-handoff pipeline containing 113 assets (1.552 hours of synthetic speech across six scenario families) with linked audio, transcripts, candidate notes, and fact checklists.

Result: The case study reveals that while two faithful-only manifests are scenario-seed-disjoint and immutably versioned, exact upstream attribution remains blocked by floating generator aliases, missing per-clip TTS and code stamps, and an unversioned checking prompt. The authors conclude that generation provenance is necessary but not sufficient for behavior attribution - it defines the candidate causal graph and audit units, but contributive attribution still requires frozen training runs and intervention/influence evidence.

Conclusion: The paper contributes: (1) a compact provenance contract for synthetic data, (2) an audit protocol for implementation, and (3) a bounded case study demonstrating the practical challenges. However, the authors explicitly note limitations: no causal training-data attribution is claimed, no clinical validity is asserted, and unrestricted public release is not offered. The work establishes that provenance tracking is a necessary first step but alone insufficient for understanding how specific training data influences model behavior.

Abstract: Attributing model behavior to synthetic training data requires knowing what produced each training item before estimating what that item caused. A waveform-label pair does not preserve this knowledge. We propose a generation-provenance substrate in which a synthetic research object binds source specification, generated content, waveform, target, fact requirements, quality signals, review lineage, and immutable manifest identity. Producer and selection mechanism determine evidentiary meaning; storage location and variable name do not. We audit this substrate in a private Japanese care-handoff pipeline. A 113-asset review population contains 1.552 hours of synthetic speech across six scenario families; all items have linked audio, transcripts, candidate notes, and fact checklists, but human evidence is selective and source-specific. Two faithful-only manifests are scenario-seed-disjoint and immutably versioned, while exact upstream attribution remains blocked by floating generator aliases, missing per-clip TTS and code stamps, and an unversioned checking prompt. We argue that generation provenance is necessary but not sufficient for behavior attribution: it defines the candidate causal graph and audit units, whereas contributive attribution still requires frozen training runs and intervention or influence evidence. The paper contributes a compact provenance contract, an audit protocol, and a bounded case study for synthetic-data attribution; controlled research access may be offered, but we do not claim causal training-data attribution, clinical validity, or unrestricted public release.

</details>


### [258] [Gacha Decoding: Eliciting Diverse Generations Through Instruction Following](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01382)
*Scott Geng,Yufei Zhang,Joseph Lee,Jerry Li,Marjan Ghazvininejad,Pang Wei Koh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Gacha Decoding is an inference-time method that treats generation diversity as an instruction-following problem, combining the LM's instruction-following capability with external randomness to scalably identify distinct response modes. It outperforms prior approaches by up to 2.4x in Vendi score and achieves 11x efficiency in finding high-quality modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the long-observed tension between diversity and model capability in language model generation. Prior approaches rely on token entropy, which declines as models become better instruction followers. The authors seek a method that inverts this relationship.

Method: Treat diversity as an instruction-following problem by combining the LM's instruction-following capability with randomness from an external RNG (Random Number Generator) tool. This "planning with dice" approach enables scalable identification and realization of distinct response modes.

Result: Across four open-ended domains (in-the-wild chat, creative writing, planning for image generation, and protein design), Gacha Decoding significantly outperforms existing diversity approaches at equal quality: up to 2.4x Vendi score improvement over the next-best prior approach, and reaches the same number of high-quality modes with over 11x fewer samples. It also discovers novel modes that no other approach surfaces.

Conclusion: Instruction following, rather than token entropy alone, can drive generation diversity. As the underlying LM becomes a better instruction follower, diversity under Gacha Decoding consistently improves—even as token entropy declines. This inverts the traditional diversity-capability trade-off.

Abstract: We introduce Gacha Decoding, an inference-time method for eliciting diverse language model generations that scales with model capability. Across open-ended domains (in-the-wild chat, creative writing, planning for image generation, and protein design), Gacha Decoding significantly outperforms existing generation diversity approaches at equal quality (up to 2.4x Vendi over the next-best prior approach), reaching the same number of high-quality modes with over an order of magnitude fewer samples (11.0x) and discovering novel modes that no other approach surfaces. Our key insight is to treat diversity as an instruction-following problem: rather than relying on the LM's token entropy, we combine its instruction-following capability with randomness from an external RNG tool to scalably identify and realize distinct modes of the response space. This approach of "planning with dice" enables Gacha to invert the long-observed tension between diversity and model capability. As the underlying LM becomes a better instruction follower, diversity under Gacha Decoding consistently improves--even as its token entropy and diversity under prior approaches decline. Together, our results highlight that instruction following, rather than token entropy alone, can drive generation diversity.

</details>


### [259] [PRISM: A Category-Theoretic Framework for Measuring and Refining Multimodal Analogies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01383)
*Mirella Zeisler,Ojas Shirekar,Mircea Licǎ,Chirag Raman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PRISM is a modality-agnostic framework that measures and improves relational alignment in multimodal analogies using category theory and VLMs, featuring a pullback score for quantification and an iterative refinement loop for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI approaches to multimodal analogy generation lack an interpretable measure of whether relational structure is understood and maintained in generated outputs.

Method: PRISM represents analogies as explicit relational mappings using category theory concepts, instantiates these structures across modalities via VLMs, and quantifies alignment using a pullback score. It includes an iterative refinement loop that uses the pullback score as in-context feedback to revise generated images toward greater relational depth.

Result: On AnaloBench, pullback score alone achieves 82.5% accuracy in selecting correct analogies. Human evaluation shows 57.65% preference for refined outputs. VLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations confirm improved metaphor consistency and analogy appropriateness over zero-shot generation.

Conclusion: PRISM effectively captures meaningful relational information and improves analogy quality, though refinement may favor visually crowded compositions over genuinely deeper relational correspondences.

Abstract: Analogical reasoning involves identifying and preserving relational structures across domains. However, existing approaches to AI-driven multimodal analogy generation lack an interpretable measure of whether this structure is understood and maintained in the generated output. We address this gap with Pullback Refinement via Interpretable Structural Mapping (PRISM), a modality-agnostic framework for measuring and improving relational alignment in multimodal analogies, evaluated on visual metaphor generation. PRISM represents analogies as explicit relational mappings grounded in category theory and uses VLMs to instantiate these structures across modalities. Its first component, the pullback score, quantifies relational alignment from the resulting graph representation. On the AnaloBench benchmark, selecting the correct analogy purely by pullback score achieves 82.5% accuracy, demonstrating that the score captures meaningful relational information. PRISM's second component is an iterative refinement loop that uses the pullback score as an in-context feedback signal to iteratively revise the generated image towards greater relational depth. VLM-as-a-judge and human evaluations show that PRISM consistently improves metaphor consistency and analogy appropriateness over zero- shot generation, with human participants preferring the refined output in 57.65% of pairwise comparisons. However, a qualitative analysis reveals that refinement can favour visually crowded compositions rather than genuinely deeper relational correspondences.

</details>


### [260] [AiSearch: Interactive Multi-Modal Search with VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01389)
*Ali Koksal,Mei Chee Leong,Vicky Sintunata,Ching Ling Chin,Wee Teck Fong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AiSearch is a flexible multimodal retrieval framework that leverages Vision Language Models (VLMs) for natural language search over images and videos, featuring interactive search refinement through user feedback and visual benchmarking across multiple VLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern retrieval systems need to be both automated and interactive, enabling users to search and refine results in real time to better match user intent.

Method: AiSearch utilizes the zero-shot capabilities of Vision Language Models (VLMs) to enable natural language search over visual content (images and videos), with interactive refinement through user feedback and cross-model benchmarking.

Result: A flexible multimodal retrieval framework that supports natural language search over images/videos, interactive search refinement via user feedback, and visual benchmarking across multiple VLMs for task-specific model selection.

Conclusion: AiSearch provides a comprehensive solution for multimodal retrieval that balances automation with interactivity, while enabling users to evaluate and select the most suitable VLM for their specific tasks.

Abstract: Modern retrieval systems must both be automated and interactive, allowing users to search and refine results in real time. We present AiSearch, a flexible multimodal retrieval framework that leverages the zero shot capabilities of Vision Language Models (VLMs) for natural language search over images and videos. AiSearch supports interactive search refinement through user feedback to tailor results to the user's intent, and allows visual benchmarking across multiple VLMs, enabling users to select the most suitable model for their task.

</details>


### [261] [Contrastive Attention Mitigates Spectral Bias in Spiking Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01403)
*Xiaoli Liu,Malu Zhang,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Spiking Transformers combine energy-efficient spiking neural networks with self-attention, but suffer from a performance gap versus ANNs. This paper reveals that both spiking neurons and spiking self-attention act as low-pass filters, dissipating high-frequency components. The proposed Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA) addresses this by extracting contrast prototypes via global contrastive aggregation and applying local differential refinement, inspired by biological visual system's edge-detection properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The performance gap between Spiking Transformers and ANNs persists, with prior works attributing it to binary activations. This paper identifies the root cause: both spiking neurons and spiking self-attention (SSA) act as low-pass filters through multiscale spectral analysis, leading to dissipation of high-frequency information.

Method: The proposed Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA) draws inspiration from the edge-detection and differential sensing properties of biological visual systems. It consists of two key components: (1) Global contrastive aggregation to extract contrast prototypes, and (2) Local differential refinement to enhance high-frequency information.

Result: SCA is a general module that consistently boosts Spiking Transformers across image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking. It achieves lower complexity while offering superior efficiency over original SSA.

Conclusion: SCA establishes itself as a fundamental building block for energy-efficient Spiking Transformers, effectively addressing the high-frequency information loss issue and bridging the performance gap with ANNs while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: Spiking Transformers merge the energy-efficiency of spiking neural networks (SNNs) with the representational power of self-attention, creating a promising architecture for high-performance, energy-efficient computation. However, a performance gap persists versus its counterparts in artificial neural networks (ANNs). Unlike prior works attributing this to binary activations, we reveal that both spiking neurons and spiking self-attention (SSA) act as low-pass filters through multiscale spectral analysis. This characteristic leads to the dissipation of high-frequency components. To address this issue, we propose the Spiking Contrastive Attention (SCA) paradigm, which draw inspiration from the edge-detection and differential sensing properties of biological visual system. By extracting contrast prototypes via global contrastive aggregation and applying local differential refinement, SCA effectively enhances high-frequency information. Extensive experiments show that SCA is a general module that consistently boosts Spiking Transformers across image classification, semantic segmentation, and event-based tracking. Furthermore, it achieves lower complexity, offering superior efficiency over original SSA. These results establish its potential as a fundamental building block for energy-efficient Spiking Transformers.

</details>


### [262] [Beyond Memory: Harnessing Long-Horizon Agents with Explicit Belief States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01415)
*Yu Luo,Jiamin Jiang,Yimin Zuo,Xidao Wen,Rongchen Gao,Yongqian Sun,Shenglin Zhang,Guiyang Liu,Cheng Zhang,Fang Situ,Qi Zhou,Dan Pei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PoS is an inference-time framework that constructs and maintains explicit belief states for LLM agents, combining estimates of current world state with unresolved task requirements. It validates belief consistency and monitors task progress to detect "Belief Trapping" (when agents act without meaningful progress). Experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM backbones show state-of-the-art performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents undertaking complex tasks do not ensure coherent understanding of the current world through their memory organization of interaction history. Current approaches focus on history retention and compression, but fail to maintain explicit, actionable beliefs about the world state and remaining task requirements.

Method: PoS constructs explicit belief states at inference time that combine: (1) estimates of current world state, and (2) unresolved task requirements. The framework includes: (1) consistency validation to keep beliefs reliable, (2) task progress monitoring to detect "Belief Trapping" where the agent continues acting without meaningful progress, and (3) tailored recovery mechanisms based on trapping pattern and type of unresolved requirement.

Result: PoS achieves the highest overall performance on every benchmark across all three LLM backbones. Ablations demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and recovery mechanisms. Context-scaling experiments show resilience to context growth.

Conclusion: Belief construction and continual maintenance should serve as a foundation for long-horizon context management in LLM agents, beyond simple history retention and compression. The explicit representation of world state and unresolved requirements, combined with consistency validation and progress monitoring, enables more reliable and effective agent behavior.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now undertake increasingly complex tasks, but the way they organize interaction history into memory does not ensure a coherent understanding of the current world. We introduce PoS, an inference-time framework that constructs and continually maintains explicit belief states as the agent's decision context. Each belief combines an estimate of the current world state with unresolved task requirements, making explicit what the agent still needs to learn and accomplish. To keep this belief reliable and actionable, PoS validates its consistency and monitors task progress to detect Belief Trapping, where the agent continues to act without making meaningful progress toward the goal. Recovery is then tailored to both the trapping pattern and the type of unresolved task requirement. Experiments on four benchmarks spanning execution and diagnosis show that PoS achieves the highest overall performance on every benchmark with all three LLM backbones. Ablations demonstrate the importance of consistency validation and recovery, while context-scaling experiments show resilience to context growth. Together, these results support belief construction and continual maintenance as a foundation for long-horizon context management beyond history retention and compression.

</details>


### [263] [SpikeMoE: Brain-Inspired Competitive Routing for Flexible Spiking Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01418)
*Xiaoli Liu,Yujie Liang,Jialin Li,Malu Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpikeMoE integrates Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) using a biologically inspired k-WTA router based on hippocampal CA1 competition-inhibition dynamics. It achieves state-of-the-art SNN performance while maintaining energy efficiency, with a two-stage module for handling missing modalities in multimodal tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The challenge lies in designing an expert selection mechanism based on spiking activity to integrate neuronal-scale spiking dynamics with model-scale expert selection, while also addressing incomplete multisensory inputs in multimodal tasks.

Method: 1) Spike-based k-WTA Router: Uses lateral inhibition and refractory period inspired by hippocampal CA1 region to select Top-K experts based on discrete spike counts. 2) Two-stage missing-modality modeling: Combines empirical prototypes from observed-modality pool with modality-specific learnable embeddings to construct missing-modality representations.

Result: SpikeMoE achieves state-of-the-art performance among SNN baselines, matches or exceeds ANN counterparts, maintains robustness across diverse missing-modality conditions, and demonstrates favorable trade-off between performance and energy efficiency.

Conclusion: The integration of spiking dynamics with sparse expert computation is validated. SpikeMoE represents a promising approach to energy-efficient brain-inspired computing, successfully combining the benefits of SNNs (event-driven computation) and MoE (conditional computation).

Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) enable event-driven computation through biologically inspired dynamics at the neuronal scale, while Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) perform conditional computation through expert selection at the model scale. Integrating their strengths offers potential for flexible neural architectures. A key challenge, however, lies in designing an expert selection mechanism based on spiking activity. To address this, we introduce a spike-based k-WTA Router inspired by competition-inhibition observed in the hippocampal CA1 region. The router incorporates lateral inhibition and refractory period to select Top-K experts according to discrete spike counts. Building on this, we present SpikeMoE, a framework that integrates neuronal-scale spiking dynamics with model-scale expert selection. To address incomplete multisensory inputs in multimodal tasks, we further equip SpikeMoE with a two-stage missing-modality modeling module that combines empirical prototypes from an observed-modality pool with modality-specific learnable embeddings to construct missing-modality representations. Experiments on vision, language, and multimodal benchmarks demonstrate that SpikeMoE achieves state-of-the-art performance among the SNN baselines, matches or exceeds the performance of ANN counterparts, and maintains robustness across diverse missing-modality conditions. These results demonstrate a favorable trade-off between performance and energy efficiency, validating the integration of spiking dynamics with sparse expert computation and highlighting SpikeMoE as a promising approach to energy-efficient brain-inspired computing.

</details>


### [264] [A Deterministic and Auditable AI Security Risk Assessment Framework with ATLAS Aligned Executable Rules and Formal Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01436)
*Yixuan Huang,Basel Halak,Boojoong Kang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an evidence-driven AI security assessment framework that operationalizes security assessment as a deterministic decision function. It normalizes heterogeneous artifacts into a project-independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a four-level ordinal scale, maps MITRE ATLAS techniques to controls, and outputs technique-indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable evidence links. The framework is formally verified for correctness and evaluated on five open-source AI projects, demonstrating consistent downward shifts in feasibility profiles under strengthened controls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the increasing deployment of AI systems in high-impact and safety-critical settings, where security assessment remains difficult to reproduce and defend under audit. Existing approaches rely on narrative checklists or assessor-driven scoring and lack explicit, machine-evaluable mapping from observable engineering artifacts to stable technique-level outcomes. This creates a gap in reproducible, auditable, and automated security assessments for AI systems.

Method: The framework uses several key methods: (1) Normalizing heterogeneous artifacts into a project-independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a bounded four-level ordinal scale; (2) Compiling technique-level predicates from a pinned MITRE ATLAS snapshot via an explicit mitigation-to-control mapping; (3) Outputting technique-indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable links back to triggering evidence; (4) Packaging normative choices as a versioned assessment policy object for repeatable reassessment; (5) Formally verifying boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity of the compiled evaluator over the full declared score domain.

Result: The evaluation on five public open-source AI projects showed consistent downward shifts in feasibility profiles under strengthened observable controls. However, worst-case residual feasibility persists when technique-specific core controls remain absent from the evidence scope. The framework demonstrated responsiveness to real engineering changes through fork-based implementations of SBOM generation and CI security scanning gates.

Conclusion: The framework successfully addresses the reproducibility and auditability challenges in AI security assessment by providing a deterministic, machine-evaluable approach. The formal verification ensures semantic correctness, while the evaluation demonstrates practical applicability. The persistence of residual feasibility when core controls are absent highlights the importance of comprehensive control implementation. Future work could explore extending the framework to additional AI security domains and refining the control taxonomy based on broader empirical studies.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in high impact and safety critical settings, yet security assessment remains difficult to reproduce and defend under audit. Existing approaches often rely on narrative checklists or assessor driven scoring, and they lack an explicit, machine evaluable mapping from observable engineering artefacts to stable technique level outcomes. We present an evidence driven AI security assessment framework that operationalises assessment as a deterministic decision function. The framework normalises heterogeneous artefacts into a project independent Control ID taxonomy scored on a bounded four level ordinal scale, compiles technique level predicates from a pinned MITRE ATLAS snapshot via an explicit mitigation to control mapping, and outputs technique indexed feasibility and impact levels with traceable links back to the triggering evidence. We package all normative choices as a versioned assessment policy object to support repeatable reassessment across snapshots. To ensure semantic correctness, we formally verify boundedness, totality, ordered semantic consistency, and monotonicity of the compiled evaluator over the full declared score domain. We evaluate the framework on five public open source AI projects pinned to explicit repository snapshots, quantify before and after changes under a unified hardening intervention, and validate responsiveness to real engineering changes through fork based implementations of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation and Continuous integration (CI) security scanning gates. Results show consistent downward shifts in feasibility profiles under strengthened observable controls, while worst case residual feasibility persists when technique specific core controls remain absent from the evidence scope.

</details>


### [265] [DRelay: Global Draft Context for Prefix-Aware Parallel Speculative Decoding Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01439)
*Zhuoyu Wang,Junnan Huang,Xinyu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DRelay is a novel speculative decoding method that improves parallel drafting in LLMs by using global information from the entire draft block to repair early selection errors. It employs a global reader to extract predictive information across positions and a causal selector to determine whether to retain or replace tokens, extending the accepted prefix length.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Parallel drafting in speculative decoding suffers from limited gains due to early selection errors. Even when the correct token exists in the candidate pool, a single early error prevents subsequent predictions from being used, restricting the efficiency of speculative decoding for LLMs.

Method: DRelay uses two key components: (1) A global reader that extracts predictive information across positions for each candidate from the entire draft block; (2) A causal selector that combines candidate-level information with tokens selected at preceding positions to determine token retention or replacement. The method involves joint training of the draft backbone and selector, combining candidate-support learning with a repair objective, where repair loss is weighted according to each block position's potential contribution to the consecutive accepted prefix.

Result: Across eight diverse benchmarks on an H800 GPU, DRelay consistently improves both average acceptance length and end-to-end decoding performance over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark. Under SGLang serving, DRelay achieves 14.7%-16.8% improvement over DFlash, 8.7%-9.3% over Domino, and 8.1%-9.3% over DSpark in average end-to-end speedup.

Conclusion: DRelay successfully addresses the early selection error problem in parallel drafting through prefix-aware selective repair using global information, achieving significant improvements in acceptance length and decoding speedup across multiple benchmarks and serving scenarios.

Abstract: Parallel drafting reduces the drafting overhead of speculative decoding for large language models (LLMs), but its gains remain limited by the accepted prefix length. Even when the correct token is present in the candidate pool, a single early selection error prevents subsequent predictions from being used. We propose DRelay, which uses global information from the entire draft block to perform prefix-aware selective repair of candidate selections before target-model verification. DRelay bases its decisions on candidate correlations and the selected path: a global reader extracts predictive information across positions for each candidate. While a causal selector combines candidate-level information extracted by the global read with the tokens selected at preceding positions to determine whether the native choice at the current position is consistent with the global evidence and the selected prefix. It then decides whether to retain or replace the token, thereby repairing early errors and extending the accepted prefix. We further jointly train the draft backbone and the selector, combining candidate-support learning with a repair objective, while weighting the repair loss according to each block position's potential contribution to the consecutive accepted prefix. Across eight diverse benchmarks on an H800 GPU, DRelay consistently improves both average acceptance length and end-to-end decoding performance over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark. Under SGLang serving, DRelay improves average end-to-end speedup over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark by 14.7%-16.8%, 8.7%-9.3%, and 8.1%-9.3%, respectively.

</details>


### [266] [A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Personalized Health Checkup Interpretation and Guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01451)
*HyungJun Kim,Taehan Lee,Soojin Cheon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a multi-agent LLM system for personalized health checkup result interpretation, which identifies multiple intents, maps them to task-specific agents, executes them in parallel, and synthesizes outputs. The multi-agent approach showed statistically significant improvements over single-agent baseline across multiple evaluation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized interpretation of health checkup results requires reasoning across longitudinal records, medical knowledge, lifestyle guidance, and healthcare navigation - a complex task that single-agent LLM systems may struggle to handle adequately.

Method: The researchers developed a multi-agent LLM system that identifies multiple intents, maps each to a task-specific agent, executes them in parallel, and synthesizes their outputs. They compared answers generated in Single Agent and Multi Agent settings on 120 Korean compound queries combining 2-4 requirements, using synthetic health checkup records. Evaluation used multiple LLM judges and two human evaluators.

Result: The Multi Agent improved the weighted LLM-judge score from 1.695 to 1.797 (p = 0.027), with consistent improvements across three additional LLM judges (Δ = +0.111 to +0.186, all p < 0.05). Improvements were seen in usefulness, consistency, and handling of every requirement in compound queries. Numerical accuracy and grounding improved significantly under only one judge, medical safety showed no difference, and critical failures were similar (15.0% vs 13.3%). Two human evaluators preferred Multi Agent in 66.7% and 68.3% of pairwise comparisons. However, Multi Agent increased latency by 1.31× and cost by 2.02×. Subgroup analysis showed improvement concentrated in queries involving personal-record lookup.

Conclusion: The multi-agent LLM system significantly improves health checkup result interpretation compared to single-agent approach, with gains in usefulness, consistency, and compound query handling, while maintaining similar medical safety and critical failure rates. The trade-offs include increased latency and cost. The improvement is most pronounced for queries involving personal-record lookup.

Abstract: Personalized interpretation of health checkup results requires reasoning across longitudinal records, medical knowledge, lifestyle guidance, and healthcare navigation. We present a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system that identifies multiple intents, maps each to a task-specific agent, executes them in parallel, and synthesizes their outputs. We compared answers generated in Single Agent and Multi Agent settings on 120 Korean compound queries combining two to four requirements, using synthetic health checkup records. The Multi Agent improved the weighted LLM-judge score from 1.695 to 1.797 (p = 0.027), and three additional LLM judges showed consistent improvements ($Δ$ = +0.111 to +0.186, all p < 0.05). The gains came from usefulness, consistency, and the handling of every requirement in compound queries, whereas numerical accuracy and grounding improved significantly under only one of the four judges and medical safety did not differ, and critical failures occurred at similar rates (Single Agent 15.0% vs. Multi Agent 13.3%). Two human evaluators preferred Multi Agent in 66.7% and 68.3% of pairwise comparisons. Multi Agent execution increased latency and cost by 1.31$\times$ and 2.02$\times$, respectively. In exploratory subgroup analyses, the improvement was concentrated in queries involving personal-record lookup.

</details>


### [267] [Rethinking Probability-Based Reinforcement Learning From Posterior Concentration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458)
*Shiu-Hong Kao,Yubo Zhao,Zhenyu Tian,Pengzhan Sun,Yicong Li,Angela Yao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses reliability issues in verifier-free reinforcement learning for training LLMs on reasoning tasks. The authors identify a "Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP)" where probability rewards collapse to low-variance intervals in long reasoning traces, causing optimization instability. They propose RLCPR, which uses uncertainty-aware data sampling and concentration-aware regularization to mitigate this issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verifier-free RL with probability-based rewards lacks reliability in long-horizon reasoning tasks. The authors aim to address the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP) where probability rewards become indistinguishable as reasoning traces lengthen, leading to unstable and inefficient optimization.

Method: The proposed RLCPR framework has two components: (1) Uncertainty-aware data sampling to reduce concentration-prone rollouts before generation, and (2) Concentration-aware regularization to penalize unnecessarily long traces when posterior rewards collapse.

Result: RLCPR outperforms the state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baseline by up to 4.0% on six of seven benchmarks, including general-domain and mathematical reasoning challenges, while achieving higher token efficiency.

Conclusion: The Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP) is a critical failure mode in verifier-free RL with probability-based rewards. By explicitly accounting for PCP through uncertainty-aware sampling and concentration-aware regularization, RLCPR achieves better optimization stability and token efficiency compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Verifier-free reinforcement learning with probability-based rewards offers a promising way to train LLMs on general reasoning tasks where external verifiers are unavailable. Yet the reliability of these rewards, especially in long-horizon reasoning, remains underexplored. This work identifies a length-dependent failure mode of probability rewards, which we call the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP). We show that the probability of a reference answer conditioned on a reasoning trace often collapses to a low-variance interval as the trace becomes lengthy. This phenomenon results in nearly indistinguishable rewards, which, under GRPO-based settings, makes probability-based policy optimization unstable and inefficient. Motivated by this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Concentration-aware Posterior Rewards (RLCPR), a verifier-free RL framework to explicitly account for PCP for better optimization stability and token efficiency. It has two components: uncertainty-aware data sampling, which reduces concentration-prone rollouts before generation, and concentration-aware regularization, which penalizes unnecessarily long traces when posterior rewards collapse. Extensive experiments show that, alongside higher token efficiency, RLCPR outperforms the state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baseline by up to 4.0% on six of seven benchmarks, including general-domain and mathematical reasoning challenges.

</details>


### [268] [NextMe-800: Anticipating Personal Behavior from Months of Egocentric Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01461)
*Zhaoxu Meng,Yiming Sun,Mingyuan Gao,Jiachang Zhang,Zhuhan Dai,Yipeng Du,Zheng Lian,Jian-Qiao Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces NextMe-800 (~800-hour egocentric dataset from one volunteer over 126 days with images, gaze, audio) and NextAct (1,500-point benchmark) to study personalized action anticipation as open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction, using hierarchical annotations and embedding-based soft edit distance for evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: People often plan ambitiously but act habitually, wishing they could have simulated hindsight at the moment of choosing. The authors aim to help people formulate more realistic plans by generating plausible trajectories from personal history, enabling better-informed decisions.

Method: The authors collected NextMe-800: an approximately 800-hour first-person dataset from one volunteer over 126 days with 1 Hz images, gaze, and audio, captioned at five hierarchical abstraction levels from atomic actions to major activities. They formulate personalized action anticipation as open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction and construct NextAct, a 1,500-point benchmark combining NextMe-800 with the multi-person EgoLife dataset. Evaluation uses an embedding-based soft edit distance metric to assess how well models anticipate personal behavior across abstraction levels and prediction horizons.

Result: The paper evaluates different models' ability to anticipate personal behavior across abstraction levels and prediction horizons using the proposed benchmark.

Conclusion: NextMe-800 and NextAct provide a months-long resource and evaluation framework for studying how far ahead personal behavior can be anticipated from egocentric observation, enabling research into personalized action anticipation at various temporal horizons.

Abstract: We often plan ambitiously yet act habitually and wonder, in retrospect, whether we would have planned differently had we known what we would actually do. Hindsight offers a valuable perspective on past decisions, although we often wish we could have simulated hindsight at the moment of choosing. If a system could generate plausible trajectories from one's personal history, such previews might help people formulate more realistic plans and make better informed decisions. We introduce NextMe-800, an approximately 800-hour first-person dataset from one volunteer over 126 days with 1 Hz images, gaze, and audio, captioned at five hierarchical abstraction levels from atomic actions to major activities. We formulate personalized action anticipation as open-vocabulary K-step sequence prediction and construct NextAct, a 1,500-point benchmark combining NextMe-800 with the multi-person EgoLife dataset. Using an embedding-based soft edit distance as the metric, we evaluate how well different models can anticipate personal behavior across abstraction levels and prediction horizons. NextMe-800 and NextAct provide a months-long resource and evaluation framework for studying how far ahead personal behavior can be anticipated from egocentric observation.

</details>


### [269] [Auditing Routing Entropy as an Uncertainty Signal in Attention-Residual Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01495)
*Wenhao Liang,Lin Yue,Wei Emma Zhang,Mingyu Guo,Olaf Maennel,Weitong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether routing entropy in dynamic architectures (Attention-Residual variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small) carries information about prediction correctness beyond the model's own confidence. The authors perform rigorous statistical tests across multiple training seeds and find no reliable incremental information: routing signals don't survive multiplicity correction, don't replicate across seeds, and don't improve over confidence-only predictors. However, they note this establishes control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery, not the absence of conditional routing information.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to audit whether the routing trace (a per-example routing signature in dynamic architectures) provides additional information about prediction reliability beyond what the model's confidence score already reveals. This is important for interpretability and uncertainty quantification in neural networks.

Method: The authors train AR variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small on CIFAR-10/100 with a soft-binned calibration auxiliary loss. They perform three checks: (1) whether routing signal appears at fixed confidence, (2) whether it replicates across training seeds, and (3) whether a held-out predictor can exploit routing information against output-only and shuffled-trace controls. They also conduct a sensitivity audit by injecting effects of known size and measuring recovery fraction.

Result: The main findings are: (1) No test in the fixed 30-test binned family survives multiplicity correction, (2) Results don't recur across sibling seeds, (3) Scalar routing probe yields no pooled improvement in routing-stratified calibration, (4) Entropy-profile probe predicts correctness better than shuffled profiles but worse than confidence-only predictor, (5) Sensitivity audit shows profile probe recovers 24-59% of oracle gain at 0.010 nats injected effect, and correction probe recovers 8% and 23% in CIFAR-100 settings.

Conclusion: The results establish control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery, rather than demonstrating the absence of conditional routing information. The authors bound how far non-detections can be interpreted, noting that the routing trace does not provide reliable additional information beyond confidence scores for predicting correctness.

Abstract: Dynamic architectures leave a per-example routing trace beside each prediction, and diffuse routing is easy to read as a sign that the prediction is unreliable. We audit that reading for routing entropy in Attention-Residual (AR) variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small, trained from scratch on CIFAR-10/100 with a soft-binned calibration auxiliary loss, asking whether the trace carries information about correctness beyond what the model's own confidence already reveals. Three checks probe this increment: does a routing signal appear at fixed confidence, does it replicate across training seeds, and can a held-out predictor exploit it against output-only and shuffled-trace controls? A sensitivity audit then injects effects of known size and measures the fraction of each that the probes recover. No test in the fixed 30-test binned family survives multiplicity correction, and neither the nominal hit nor a borderline result recurs in its sibling seeds. Across 24 paired runs a scalar routing probe yields no pooled improvement in routing-stratified calibration, and an entropy-profile probe predicts correctness better than the same probe given shuffled profiles yet worse than a confidence-only predictor in both binary log-loss and Brier score: a gain over shuffled traces does not become a gain over the output. Conditioning on the complete logit vector leaves the corresponding comparison unresolved. The audit bounds how far these non-detections can be read: at an injected effect of 0.010 nats the profile probe recovers 24-59% of the oracle gain, and a reference-preserving correction probe recovers 8% and 23% in the two CIFAR-100 settings, below the threshold we fixed for applying it to real labels. The results establish control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery, not the absence of conditional routing information.

</details>


### [270] [OpenMTB-Audit: Exposing Over-Refusal and Clinical Expert Perspectives in LLM-Based Molecular Tumor Board Safety Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01497)
*Negin Ashrafi,Jia Luo,Stacey M. Frumm,Roxana Daneshjou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces OpenMTB-Audit, a benchmark for evaluating AI safety in molecular tumor boards, revealing that LLMs suffer from over-refusal (failing to retain "Partially Supported" labels in 83.3-100% of cases). The authors propose MTB-AuditAgent, a seven-module framework that reduces over-refusal to 6.7% and achieves 91.2% accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI integrates into molecular tumor board workflows, there's a critical safety challenge: distinguishing truly unsupported recommendations from evidence-supported options that still require oncologist review due to incomplete information, poor performance status, or other clinical caveats. Current LLMs exhibit over-refusal, achieving high safety scores through label collapse rather than clinically calibrated reasoning.

Method: The authors created OpenMTB-Audit, an open-source benchmark of 500 synthetic non-small cell lung cancer cases spanning five adversarial error categories with four safety labels. They evaluated eight LLM configurations and conducted a two-oncologist annotation study. They developed MTB-AuditAgent, a deterministic seven-module framework separating evidence verification, missing-information detection, safety classification, and abstention.

Result: All LLM configurations failed to retain the Partially Supported label in 83.3-100% of true Partially Supported cases, achieving high aggregate safety scores through label collapse. MTB-AuditAgent reduces over-refusal to 6.7% and achieves 91.2% accuracy (95% CI: 88.6-93.6%). The annotation study found disagreement concentrated at the boundary between information sufficiency and treatment optimization.

Conclusion: Over-refusal in MTB AI systems is a significant safety issue that can be addressed through structured frameworks like MTB-AuditAgent. The boundary between information sufficiency and treatment optimization represents a critical area requiring careful clinical delineation. Preserving clinically meaningful distinctions between safety labels is essential for practical clinical deployment.

Abstract: Molecular tumor boards integrate genomic findings, clinical context, and therapeutic evidence to support precision oncology. As AI enters this workflow, a key safety challenge is distinguishing truly unsupported recommendations from evidence-supported options that still require oncologist review because of incomplete information, poor ECOG performance status, or other clinical caveats. We introduce OpenMTB-Audit, an open-source benchmark of 500 synthetic non-small cell lung cancer cases spanning five adversarial error categories and four safety labels: Supported, Partially Supported, Unsupported, and Insufficient Information. Across eight large language model configurations, we identify pervasive over-refusal: all LLM configurations failed to retain the Partially Supported label in 83.3-100% of true Partially Supported cases, achieving high aggregate safety scores through label collapse rather than clinically calibrated reasoning. To address this limitation, we developed MTB-AuditAgent, a deterministic seven-module framework separating evidence verification, missing-information detection, safety classification, and abstention. It reduces over-refusal to 6.7% and achieves 91.2% accuracy (95% CI: 88.6-93.6%). A two-oncologist annotation study found disagreement concentrated at the boundary between information sufficiency and treatment optimization, underscoring the need to preserve clinically meaningful distinctions.

</details>


### [271] [Sharpening Tax in Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01509)
*Changdae Oh,Qi Zeng,Qi Qi,Andrey Zhmoginov,Deren Lei,Yun He,Hoang Phan,Hangoo Kang,Azalia Mirhoseini,Sharon Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL post-training of LLMs improves single-shot accuracy but reduces solution coverage (pass@K) under repeated sampling, creating a "sharpening tax." Pre-trained models with inference harness can outperform post-trained models in coverage despite lower accuracy. A new metric (Sharpening Tax) and solution (PTGS) are proposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: An emerging hypothesis suggests RL post-training merely sharpens existing behaviors rather than acquiring new capabilities, improving pass@1 at the cost of solution coverage. This trade-off has been observed in math/coding but was unclear for agentic tasks requiring multi-turn tool use.

Method: 1) Comparing pre-trained vs post-trained LLM agents across 14 model pairs from 4 families on 3 agentic benchmarks (42 cases total). 2) Analyzing how post-training affects task difficulty distribution. 3) Proposing Sharpening Tax metric to quantify loss in test-time scalability. 4) Developing Posterior-Tempered Group Sampling (PTGS) - a Bayesian sampler that adapts temperature per prompt based on estimated difficulty.

Result: Pre-trained LLMs with inference harness often surpass post-trained counterparts in pass@K given sufficient test-time budget despite lower pass@1. Post-training pushes tasks toward extremes (always solved/never solved), improving sampling efficiency at the cost of coverage. Sharpening Tax is prevalent in most settings, can be estimated from few rollouts, and correlates with other metrics. PTGS pays smaller tax than fixed-temperature baseline, solving more tasks under repeated sampling while improving single-shot accuracy.

Conclusion: The sharpening tax is a general phenomenon in RL post-training for agentic tasks. Pre-trained models should not be dismissed as agents. Simple interventions like PTGS can mitigate the coverage-accuracy trade-off. Future work should explore how to acquire new capabilities without sacrificing coverage.

Abstract: An emerging hypothesis about reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models (LLMs) is that it merely sharpens existing behaviors of a base model, improving single-shot accuracy at the cost of solution coverage. Although this trade-off has been observed in math and coding tasks, it need not extend to agentic tasks, where multi-turn tool use and interaction may require capabilities newly acquired during post-training. Our surprising finding is that pre-trained LLMs, equipped with a light inference harness, can serve as capable agents. Despite far lower accuracy (pass@1), they often surpass their post-trained counterparts in solution coverage (pass@K) given a sufficient test-time budget. We further analyze the underlying mechanism and show that post-training pushes tasks toward two extremes, always solved or never solved, and thereby improves sampling efficiency and consistency at the cost of solution coverage. To measure this cost, we propose Sharpening Tax, a diagnostic metric that quantifies the loss in test-time scalability after post-training. Across 14 base/post-trained model pairs from four families and three agentic benchmarks (42 cases in total), the tax is prevalent in most settings, can be estimated from a few rollouts, and correlates well with other metrics. Finally, we present posterior-tempered group sampling (PTGS), a simple plug-and-play Bayesian sampler that adapts the sampling temperature per prompt to its estimated difficulty. Applied during RL training in two agentic environments, PTGS pays a smaller tax than the fixed-temperature baseline, solving more tasks under repeated sampling while also improving single-shot accuracy.

</details>


### [272] [Decision Titan: Test-Time Training for Long-Term Memory in Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01513)
*Jude Waide,Robert Lieck*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces Decision Titan, which augments a Decision Transformer with Test-Time Training (TTT) layers to address long-term dependency challenges in offline Reinforcement Learning. Tested on the X-Maze environment, the model can learn dependencies 20x longer than the context window and generalize to lengths 1.7x training data, with performance dependent on time embeddings and information encoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sequential decision-making in AI faces challenges with long-term dependencies: RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients and limited expressivity, while Transformers have quadratic attention scaling. TTT has shown success in NLP but hasn't been applied to RL or studied for how memory functions in practice.

Method: The authors augment a Decision Transformer with TTT layers (Decision Titan), storing episodic memories in neural network parameters via gradient descent at both train and test time. They evaluate on X-Maze (extension of T-Maze) designed to test sequential memory, and visualize gate values over time to understand the memory mechanism.

Result: Decision Titan can learn long-term dependencies with ranges 20x longer than the context window and generalizes to lengths 1.7x the training data. However, temporal generalization depends on the time embeddings used, and the ability to learn long-term dependencies depends on how relevant information is encoded.

Conclusion: The TTT framework shows promise for RL applications requiring long-term memory, but its effectiveness is contingent on proper time embedding design and information encoding strategies. This work bridges TTT from NLP to RL and provides insights into how the memory mechanism functions.

Abstract: Long-term dependencies remain a major challenge for sequential decision-making in the field of AI: RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients and the limited expressivity of vector-based hidden states, whilst Transformer-based models are limited by the quadratic scaling of attention. Recent work has proposed tackling this problem with the Test-Time Training (TTT) framework, which stores episodic memories in the parameters of a neural network through gradient descent at both train and test-time. This approach has seen success in the domain of Natural Language Processing, however, to the best of our knowledge it has not yet been applied to the domain of Reinforcement Learning (RL), nor has there been a study analysing how this memory practically functions. In this paper, we study the potential of the TTT framework for offline RL by augmenting a Decision Transformer with TTT layers, dubbed the Decision Titan. We analyse performance and properties of the model in the X-Maze environment, an extension of T-Maze designed to test sequential memory, and investigate how the memory mechanism learns by visualising gate values over time. Our key findings are that Decision Titan can learn long-term dependencies with ranges 20x longer than the context window, generalises to lengths 1.7x the training data, but crucially temporal generalisation depends on the time embeddings used, and the ability to learn long-term dependencies depends on how the relevant information is encoded.

</details>


### [273] [Towards Reliable Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01531)
*Manasa Mariam Mammen,Priyanka Mary Mammen,Zafer Kayatas,Stefan Wagner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates five Vision-Language models on driving-related QA tasks under degraded visual conditions, finding that visual corruption effects vary significantly across models, datasets, and input settings. The Visual Evidence Augmentation (VEA) method shows mixed improvements in reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
