Motivation: The increasing use of Vision-Language models (VLMs) in autonomous driving for safety-critical tasks requires robust and reliable performance. However, real-world visual inputs can be degraded by sensor imperfections and environmental conditions, potentially affecting both predictions and confidence calibration. This is particularly concerning for autonomous driving where accurate predictions and reliable uncertainty estimation are essential for safety.

Method: Evaluated five VLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-E4B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, DriveFusion/DriveFusionQA-4B, and NVIDIA Alpamayo-1.5-10B) across four driving-related QA datasets with different visual input settings including single-frame, multi-view, multi-frame, and monocular inputs. Applied Visual Evidence Augmentation (VEA), an inference-time method, to examine whether it can improve model reliability under degraded visual conditions.

Result: The effects of visual corruption vary across models, datasets, and input settings, with changes in both accuracy and confidence reliability differing across conditions. VEA improves performance for some models and datasets, but the gains are not consistent across all settings.

Conclusion: Visual corruption impacts VLM performance and reliability differently depending on the model, dataset, and input configuration. While VEA provides some benefits in certain settings, it does not consistently improve performance across all conditions, highlighting the ongoing challenge of ensuring VLM reliability in real-world autonomous driving scenarios with degraded visual inputs.

Abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) are increasingly being explored in autonomous driving for tasks such as scene understanding, driving reasoning, decision-making, and end-to-end driving. As their role becomes more prominent, ensuring their robustness and reliability is increasingly important. In real-world conditions, visual inputs may be degraded by sensor imperfections and environmental conditions, potentially affecting both model predictions and their associated confidence. Such degradation is especially concerning in autonomous driving, where safety-critical decisions require models to make accurate predictions and recognize when their predictions may be unreliable. In this work, we evaluate five VLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma4-E4B, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, DriveFusion/DriveFusionQA-4B, and NVIDIA Alpamayo-1.5-10B) across four driving-related QA datasets with different visual input settings, including single-frame, multi-view, multi-frame, and monocular inputs. Our results show that the effects of visual corruption vary across models, datasets, and input settings, with changes in accuracy and confidence reliability and also differing across conditions. We then apply Visual Evidence Augmentation ($\mathrm{V}{\scriptstyle \mathrm{EA}}$), a recent inference-time method to examine whether it can improve model reliability under degraded visual conditions. We find that $\mathrm{V}{\scriptstyle \mathrm{EA}}$ improves performance for some models and datasets, although the gains are not consistent across all settings.

</details>


### [274] [Neither Black nor White: Balancing Semantic and Collaborative Signals with Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01533)
*Aleksei Medvedev,Alejandro Ariza-Casabona,Steven Derby,Gonzalo Fiz Pontiveros,Xinyang Shao,Florian Spiess*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS), a unified framework that reframes Semantic ID (SID) construction for generative recommendation from representation learning to recursive clustering on graphs. The framework subsumes prior approaches (RQ-VAE, RQ-KMeans) as special cases with empty graphs, and introduces two instantiations: RecDMoN (differentiable graph pooling) and RQ-GAE (graph-aware extensions). Experiments show up to +52% Hit@10 improvement over CF-aware state-of-the-art methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors argue that existing SID work treats SID construction as representation learning (encoding items into quantised latent space), which is incidental. They propose that SID construction is fundamentally a recursive clustering problem, where the natural object to cluster is a graph with nodes carrying semantic content and edges carrying collaborative signal. This reframing enables a unified framework that exposes content-only quantisation as one corner of a larger design space along two previously collapsed axes: graph construction and recursive partition algorithm.

Method: The proposed GrIS framework treats SID assignment as hierarchical graph partition. The authors explore two contrasting instantiations: (1) RecDMoN, which performs hierarchical assignment via differentiable graph pooling, and (2) RQ-GAE, which extends RQ-VAE with graph-aware item representations and a graph reconstruction objective. Both approaches treat graph construction and partition as explicit, separately configurable components.

Result: On multiple real-world datasets, GrIS consistently improves over CF-aware state-of-the-art methods, with gains of up to +52% Hit@10. The framework demonstrates that treating SID construction as recursive clustering on graphs yields significant improvements over prior approaches that treat it as pure representation learning.

Conclusion: The paper establishes that SID construction is fundamentally a recursive clustering problem on graphs, not merely representation learning. The GrIS framework provides a unified view that subsumes prior approaches and enables systematic evaluation of improvements along both graph construction and partition algorithm axes. The significant performance gains (+52% Hit@10) validate the proposed reframing and demonstrate the value of incorporating collaborative signal through graph structures.

Abstract: Existing work on Semantic IDs (SIDs) for generative recommendation treats SID construction as a representation learning problem: encode items into a quantised latent space and read off codes. We argue this view is incidental. SID construction is, at heart, a recursive clustering problem, and once stated this way the natural object to cluster is a graph whose nodes carry semantic content and whose edges carry collaborative signal; SID assignment becomes a hierarchical graph partition. This reframing yields a unified framework, Graph-Informed Semantic IDs (GrIS), that subsumes prior approaches rather than displacing them. RQ-VAE and RQ-KMeans are recovered as the special case where the graph is empty, exposing content-only quantisation as one corner of a larger design space along two so-far-collapsed axes: graph construction and recursive partition algorithm. We explore two contrasting instantiations: RecDMoN, which performs hierarchical assignment via differentiable graph pooling, and RQ-GAE, which extends RQ-VAE with graph-aware item representations and a graph reconstruction objective. On multiple real-world datasets, GrIS consistently improves over CF-aware SOTA, with gains of up to +52\% Hit@10. Because graph construction and partition are explicit, separately configurable components, improvements on either axis can be combined and evaluated systematically.

</details>


### [275] [The AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator: A Framework to Support Technical Assessment in AI Regulatory Sandboxes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01539)
*Alessio Buscemi,German Castignani,Daniele Pagani,Maxime Cordy,Jordi Cabot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses the infrastructure challenges of operationalizing technical testing within EU AI Regulatory Sandboxes (AIRS), proposing an open-source framework called AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator to harmonize fragmented testing tools and enable scalable, structured testing required by the EU AI Act.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The EU AI Act mandates all Member States to establish AIRS by August 2027. However, the tooling ecosystem for technical testing is structurally fragmented, with heterogeneous tools producing outputs that are difficult to compare, trace, and reuse. Running structured technical testing at scale demands dedicated infrastructure that currently lacks standardization.

Method: The authors derive 11 architectural and governance requirements from: (1) the procedural conditions of AIRS engagements, and (2) the AI Act obligations for high-risk systems. Based on these requirements, they develop the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator - an open-source framework featuring: a curated Catalogue of tests and controls with a stable plug-in API, a shared data model for harmonizing heterogeneous outputs, role-specific dashboards for multi-disciplinary interpretation, and audience-segmented reporting. An early-stage pilot was conducted within a live AIRS engagement.

Result: The pilot exercised the harmonisation and reporting layers within a live AIRS engagement and contributed to an official Exit Report, demonstrating the framework's practical applicability.

Conclusion: The AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator provides a foundation for standardized technical testing infrastructure across EU Member States. The paper discusses the governance questions raised by the Catalogue's tiered contribution model and institutional pathways for an open-source assessment ecosystem to emerge across Member States.

Abstract: The EU's Artificial Intelligence Act requires all Member States to establish AI Regulatory Sandboxes (AIRS) by August 2027: supervised environments bringing together national Competent Authorities, technical experts, and the organisations under assessment. When AIRS engagements include structured technical testing, running such testing at scale demands dedicated infrastructure, yet the tooling ecosystem remains structurally fragmented, with heterogeneous tools producing outputs that are difficult to compare, trace, and reuse. From the procedural conditions of AIRS engagements and the AI Act obligations for high-risk systems, we derive 11 architectural and governance requirements for the infrastructure that operationalises technical testing within an AIRS. In response to these requirements, we introduce the AI Assessment Sandbox Configurator, an open-source framework combining a curated Catalogue of tests and controls accessed through a stable plug-in API, a shared data model that harmonises heterogeneous outputs, role-specific dashboards for multi-disciplinary interpretation, and audience-segmented reporting. We describe the architecture and current release, and report an early-stage pilot that exercised the harmonisation and reporting layers within a live AIRS engagement and contributed to an official Exit Report. We discuss the roadmap, the governance questions raised by the Catalogue's tiered contribution model, and the institutional pathways through which an open-source assessment ecosystem could emerge across Member States.

</details>


### [276] [Evaluating Physical Consistency and Plausibility in Generative Scenario Models for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01581)
*Manasa Mariam Mammen,Zafer Kayatas,Stefan Wagner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces a five-layer evaluation protocol for assessing generative AI models used in autonomous driving scenario generation. The protocol addresses the lack of transparency in AI-generated scenarios by evaluating internal representations (kinematic alignment, statistical baselines, latent controllability, activation analysis) and output consistency with vehicle dynamics constraints (e.g., lateral jerk thresholds). The method is demonstrated on VAE-based and other generative models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI models are increasingly used for scenario generation in autonomous driving, but they lack transparency into learned representations and consistency with real-world vehicle dynamics. This limits their use in safety-critical validation and certification workflows, requiring formal assurance mechanisms.

Method: A layered evaluation protocol with five layers: (1) kinematic alignment inspection, (2) statistical baseline comparison, (3) latent controllability assessment, (4) activation analysis of network layers, and (5) evaluation of model outputs against vehicle dynamics constraints (lateral jerk thresholds). Applied to VAE-based scenario generator and other generative models.

Result: While standard output-level metrics and visualizations suggest realistic scenarios, the protocol reveals deeper insights: it exposes the extent of latent space alignment with kinematic features and identifies cases where visually plausible trajectories violate vehicle-dynamics constraints.

Conclusion: The five-layer evaluation protocol provides meaningful transparency into generative AI models for autonomous driving, applicable beyond VAE architecture. It complements existing methods by assessing internal representations and output consistency, supporting safety-critical validation and certification workflows.

Abstract: Generative AI models are increasingly used for scenario generation in autonomous driving. While they can generate realistic-looking scenarios, they often provide limited transparency into learned representations and consistency with real-world vehicle dynamics. This lack of formal assurance limits their use in safety-critical validation and certification workflows. To address this aspect, we introduce a layered evaluation protocol that complements existing methods by assessing models across five layers. The first four layers inspect internal representations and network layers through kinematic alignment, statistical baseline comparison, latent controllability, and activation analysis. The fifth layer evaluates model outputs against vehicle dynamics constraints such as lateral jerk thresholds. We demonstrate the protocol on a Variational Autoencoder (VAE)-based scenario generator. Although standard output-level metrics and visualizations suggest that the generated scenarios are realistic, our protocol provides deeper insight into the extent to which the model's latent space aligns with kinematic features and whether visually plausible trajectories satisfy vehicle-dynamics constraints. We further apply the protocol to additional generative models, demonstrating its applicability beyond the VAE architecture.

</details>


### [277] [Agents Are Systems, Not Models: Rethinking Agentic Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01618)
*Luis Wiedmann,Leander Girrbach,Cordelia Schmid,Zeynep Akata*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper evaluates coding agents as configurable systems rather than fixed entities, examining how choices in task information, reasoning, self-verification, time budget, and backbone model affect performance on a new benchmark of four scientific tasks. The study reveals substantial run-to-run variability (54% of outcome variance), with task information having the largest effect, and demonstrates that system-level implementations (like dedicated verification tools) are more effective than prompting for desired behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent evaluations treat agents as fixed systems and report single metrics like success rate. However, in practice, agents are configurable systems where users make choices about what to tell the agent, how long to let it run, and which model to use. These configuration choices can significantly impact performance, cost, consistency, and robustness, but are underexplored.

Method: The authors created a new benchmark of four scientific tasks where a coding agent must find and correctly operate a published specialist model. They investigated five parts of agent configuration: task information, reasoning, self-verification, time budget, and backbone model. They ran over 18,000 agent trajectories and used a trajectory-based taxonomy to analyze agent behavior.

Result: The study found substantial run-to-run variability, with approximately 54% of outcome variance coming from repeating the same configuration rather than changing it. Task information provided to the agent had the largest effect, exceeding both time budget and model size, while also reducing cost and improving calibration. Configuration choices interact: additional time helps only when the agent has sufficient information or a capable enough model. Additionally, prompting for verification has little effect, whereas providing a dedicated verification tool substantially changes verification behavior.

Conclusion: Agents should be evaluated as configurable systems rather than fixed entities. Some desired behaviors (like verification) are more effectively implemented in the system than requested through prompting. The benchmark and over 18,000 agent trajectories are released for further research.

Abstract: Agent evaluations increasingly go beyond a single success rate, reporting metrics such as cost, consistency, and robustness. Yet they typically treat the agent itself as fixed. In practice, an agent is a configurable system: users decide what to tell it, how long to let it run, and which model to use, and each of these choices can change how well and how consistently it performs. We study these choices on a new benchmark of four scientific tasks, where a coding agent must find and correctly operate a published specialist model. We investigate five parts of the agent's configuration: task information, reasoning, self-verification, time budget, and backbone model. We find substantial run-to-run variability, with approximately 54% of the outcome variance coming from repeating the same configuration rather than changing it. Across configurations, the information provided to the agent has the largest effect, exceeding both time budget and model size, while also reducing cost and improving calibration. Configuration choices also interact: additional time helps only when the agent has sufficient information or a capable enough model to use it. Finally, a trajectory-based taxonomy of agent behavior reveals that prompting an agent to verify its answer has little effect on its verification behavior, whereas providing a dedicated verification tool changes that behavior substantially. These results suggest that agents should be evaluated as configurable systems themselves, and that some desired behaviors are more effectively implemented in the system than requested through prompting. We release the benchmark and more than 18,000 agent trajectories.

</details>


### [278] [FedLore: Communication and Memory Efficient Federated Learning via Shared Gradient Low-Rank Projection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01620)
*Junkang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FedLore addresses federated training of foundation models by sharing a low-rank optimization basis within each round and refreshing it across rounds, enabling exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates while eliminating projection bias caused by subspace fragmentation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated training of foundation models is constrained by client memory and communication costs. Existing LoRA-based methods reduce these costs through low-rank adapters but have fixed rank budgets that limit adaptation. Gradient low-rank optimization offers flexibility but suffers from subspace fragmentation, where independently chosen client subspaces interact with data heterogeneity to bias aggregated directions.

Method: FedLore shares a low-rank optimization basis within each round and refreshes it across rounds. This enables exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates and eliminates projection bias. The subspace refresh mechanism allows the accumulated model update to exceed the per-round rank budget. The analysis establishes an O(T^{-1/2}) stationarity bound for the projected-SGD variant under a global-gradient coverage condition with standard smoothness and variance assumptions.

Result: Experiments on vision and language tasks, including federated pre-training, show that FedLore outperforms evaluated low-rank adapter baselines and matches or exceeds full-parameter training, while reducing communication and optimizer-state memory.

Conclusion: FedLore provides an effective solution for federated training of foundation models, addressing the subspace fragmentation problem through shared low-rank bases. It achieves comparable or better performance than full-parameter training while significantly reducing communication and memory costs, making it practical for resource-constrained federated settings.

Abstract: Federated training of foundation models is constrained by client memory and communication costs. LoRA-based methods reduce these costs through low-rank adapters, but their fixed rank budget can limit adaptation. Gradient low-rank optimization offers greater flexibility, yet independently chosen client subspaces create a problem we term \emph{subspace fragmentation}: local projections interact with data heterogeneity to bias aggregated directions, while aggregation can increase update rank and communication cost. Thus, accurate local gradient compression need not preserve global descent. We propose \texttt{FedLore}, which shares a low-rank optimization basis within each round and refreshes it across rounds. The shared basis enables exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates and eliminates the identified projection bias. Subspace refresh allows the accumulated model update to exceed the per-round rank budget. We characterize the aggregation bias and establish an $O(T^{-1/2})$ stationarity bound for the projected-SGD variant under a global-gradient coverage condition and standard smoothness and variance assumptions, with bounded gradient heterogeneity. Experiments on vision and language tasks, including federated pre-training, show that \texttt{FedLore} outperforms the evaluated low-rank adapter baselines and matches or exceeds full-parameter training, while reducing communication and optimizer-state memory.

</details>


### [279] [Measuring the Stability Assumption Behind Action Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01626)
*Aryan Goyal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper investigates why action chunking improves behavioural cloning by studying how action errors propagate through a policy. Using experiments across 12 manipulation tasks, the authors inject small errors and measure their growth/shrinkage under open-loop and closed-loop execution regimes. They find that error amplification is common, stable states are rare, and closed-loop reactivity does not reliably emerge from standard imitation learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors challenge the prevailing explanations for why action chunking works in behavioural cloning (temporal consistency, horizon reduction, representation learning, reduced error compounding). Instead, they seek to understand what actually happens to action errors once they enter the system by empirically measuring error propagation rates.

Method: The authors inject small action errors at each state and measure how fast they grow or shrink under two execution regimes: open-loop (replaying chunk without replanning) and closed-loop (policy replans after perturbation). They fit propagation rates to label states as contracting, expanding, or unresolved. They also train predictors to see if propagation behavior can be predicted from camera frames and proprioception.

Result: Confidently stable states are rare, while error amplification is common. The propagation rate depends strongly on fitting horizon - amplification is typically front-loaded, so short windows overestimate longer-horizon propagation. A state's open-loop regime can be recovered from camera frames and proprioception, but closed-loop propagation is only partially recoverable because it depends on post-perturbation policy actions.

Conclusion: Error-compounding arguments alone do not fully explain action chunking. Neither passive open-loop dynamics nor policy replanning consistently contracts injected errors, and replanning rarely turns open-loop amplification into confident contraction. The authors suggest that closed-loop reactivity should be trained explicitly using perturbation- and tree-coverage-oriented training, rather than expected to emerge from standard imitation learning.

Abstract: Action chunking improves the performance of policies learned by behavioural cloning, and several mechanisms have been proposed to explain why, including temporal consistency, horizon reduction, representation learning, and reduced error compounding. We instead study what happens to an action error once it enters the system. At each state, we inject a small action error and measure how fast it grows or shrinks under two execution regimes: open-loop, where the rest of the chunk is replayed without replanning, and closed-loop, where the policy replans after the perturbation. The fitted rate labels each state as contracting, expanding, or unresolved. Across twelve manipulation tasks from three benchmark suites, we find that confidently stable states are rare, while error amplification is common among states whose propagation rate can be resolved. We further find that the measured propagation rate depends strongly on the fitting horizon: amplification is typically front-loaded, so short windows can overestimate longer-horizon propagation. Finally, we train predictors on these labels and find that a state's open-loop regime can be recovered from camera frames and proprioception alone, while its closed-loop propagation is only partially recoverable because it also depends on how the policy acts after the perturbation. These results suggest that error-compounding arguments alone do not provide a complete account of action chunking: neither passive open-loop dynamics nor policy replanning consistently contracts an injected error, and replanning rarely turns open-loop amplification into confident contraction. This suggests that closed-loop reactivity should be trained explicitly, using perturbation- and tree-coverage-oriented training to expose policies to deviations they must recover from, rather than expected to emerge reliably from standard imitation learning.

</details>


### [280] [CoEvolve: Construct-to-Edit Visual Grounding with Bidirectional State Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01710)
*Dongwei Sun,Yujie Zhang,Bowen Yao,Pei Liu,Jing Yao,Xiangyong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoEvolve introduces a construct-to-edit visual grounding framework that separates grounding into explicit state construction and state editing, using Region-Evolution Reinforcement (RER) for progressive semantic-spatial reasoning and Bidirectional Denoising Refiner (BDR) for coordinate refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multimodal grounding models compress multiple complex tasks (target identification, spatial reasoning, boundary estimation) into a single prediction, making intermediate localization errors difficult to diagnose and correct. Free-form rationales lack measurable, editable spatial states.

Method: CoEvolve uses two main components: (1) Region-Evolution Reinforcement (RER) that organizes grounding into a progressive semantic-spatial trajectory with explicit candidate regions at each step; (2) Bidirectional Denoising Refiner (BDR) that treats reasoning text as fixed semantic context and refines coordinate fields through bidirectional same-position reconstruction. Geometry- and behavior-level objectives provide target geometry and edit-preference signals.

Result: With a 9B backbone, CoEvolve rivals models up to 241B parameters in grounding accuracy. A single BDR pass improves mean box overlap by over 27 percentage points under controlled corruption, demonstrating strong error recovery.

Conclusion: The explicit state construction and source-matched editing are complementary, enabling effective diagnosis and correction of localization errors. The framework shows strong performance on both natural-image and remote-sensing grounding tasks.

Abstract: Visual grounding localizes an object described by language with a bounding box. Most multimodal grounding models compress target identification, spatial reasoning, and boundary estimation into one terminal prediction. Free-form rationales make reasoning linguistically explicit but do not necessarily expose measurable, editable spatial states. Intermediate localization errors are therefore difficult to diagnose and correct, allowing incorrect region choices and imprecise boundaries to persist in the final box. We introduce CoEvolve, a construct-to-edit framework that separates grounding into explicit state construction and state editing. Region-Evolution Reinforcement (RER) organizes grounding analysis into a progressive semantic--spatial trajectory, with each reasoning step committing to an explicit candidate region. Bidirectional Denoising Refiner (BDR) treats the reasoning text as fixed semantic context and refines the trajectory's coordinate fields through bidirectional same-position reconstruction. Geometry- and behavior-level objectives provide target geometry and edit-preference signals for consolidating reliable candidates, preserving accurate inputs, or correcting toward annotations. Evaluations cover natural-image and remote-sensing grounding. With a 9B backbone, CoEvolve rivals models up to 241B parameters in grounding accuracy. Under controlled corruption, a single BDR pass improves mean box overlap by over 27 percentage points, demonstrating strong recovery from substantial localization errors. State-source comparisons further support the complementarity of explicit state construction and source-matched editing. The project is at https://sundongwei.github.io/CoEvolve_Project/.

</details>


### [281] [vFedProtoQNAS: Prototype-Guided Personalized Quantum Neural Architecture Search for Virtual Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01718)
*Seok Bin Son,Samuel Yen-Chi Chen,Soohyun Park,Joongheon Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes vFedProtoQNAS, a prototype-guided personalized quantum neural architecture search method for federated learning that enables collaboration through class-wise prototype sharing instead of parameter aggregation, addressing device heterogeneity and structural diversity challenges in quantum federated learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation addresses two key challenges in quantum federated learning: 1) Device heterogeneity - different clients have varying computational capabilities, making a single shared QNN architecture unsuitable; 2) Parameter mixing problem - when using personalized QNAS, averaging parameters across structurally different QNNs mixes semantically inconsistent circuit operations, harming model quality.

Method: vFedProtoQNAS employs a prototype-guided approach where: 1) Each client independently performs quantum neural architecture search (QNAS) to find a device-specific QNN; 2) Clients compute class-wise local prototypes from latent representations of their private data; 3) The server aggregates and refines global prototypes as federated semantic anchors; 4) Clients use global prototypes to refine local prototypes, enabling semantic collaboration without sharing model parameters. This eliminates the need for direct parameter aggregation across structurally different QNN architectures.

Result: vFedProtoQNAS improves accuracy by 3.70% over the baseline FedAvg method and enhances class-consistent representation alignment across clients. This demonstrates that prototype-based collaboration is more effective than direct parameter aggregation for heterogeneous quantum neural architectures in federated settings.

Conclusion: The proposed vFedProtoQNAS successfully addresses the challenge of heterogeneous QNN architectures in federated quantum learning by replacing parameter aggregation with prototype-based collaboration. This approach enables clients with different device capabilities to benefit from federated learning without requiring identical model architectures. The method achieves 3.70% accuracy improvement over FedAvg and enhances class-consistent representation alignment, demonstrating the effectiveness of semantic prototype sharing in quantum federated learning scenarios.

Abstract: Quantum federated learning (QFL) has emerged as a promising approach for collaboratively training compact quantum neural networks (QNNs) over distributed private data on resource-constrained devices. However, differences in device capabilities make a single shared QNN architecture unsuitable for all clients. While personalized quantum neural architecture search (QNAS) allows each client to select a device-specific QNN, averaging parameters across structurally different QNN architectures mixes semantically inconsistent circuit operations. To address this, prototype-guided personalized QNAS for virtual FL (vFedProtoQNAS) is proposed, where model parameters are never aggregated across clients and federated collaboration is achieved through class-wise prototype sharing. Each client independently searches and trains a client-specific QNN, computes class-wise local prototypes from latent representations, and refines them using global prototypes from the server as federated semantic anchors. Experiments demonstrate that vFedProtoQNAS improves accuracy by 3.70\% over FedAvg and enhances class-consistent representation alignment.

</details>


### [282] [TopK-Guided: Adaptive, Budget-Aware Activation Sparsity for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01763)
*Mukund Agarwalla,Chih-Jen Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TopK-Guided is a training-free method that improves activation sparsity in LLM inference by combining bounded token-level sparsity adaptation with sensitivity-aware block-level budget allocation, outperforming existing methods like TEAL and WINA on Llama-2 and Llama-3 models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing training-free sparsity methods (threshold-based like TEAL and TopK-based like WINA) have limitations: TEAL doesn't tightly control realized sparsity, while WINA uses the same sparsity budget for every token and every transformer block despite varying token importance and block sensitivity.

Method: TopK-Guided combines two components: (1) bounded token-level sparsity adaptation to allow flexibility while maintaining control, and (2) sensitivity-aware block-level budget allocation that allocates different sparsity budgets to different transformer blocks based on their sensitivity.

Result: TopK-Guided consistently improves perplexity and downstream accuracy over TEAL and WINA across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models while preserving the same sparsity-dependent projection compute as WINA. The largest gains are achieved at high sparsity levels.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully addresses the limitations of both threshold-based and TopK-based approaches by providing both token-level adaptability and block-level sensitivity awareness, with ablations confirming both components provide complementary improvements.

Abstract: Activation sparsity speeds up large language model (LLM) inference by setting unimportant activations to zero so that the corresponding computations can be skipped. Existing training-free methods, however, make different trade-offs: threshold-based methods such as TEAL adapt the sparsity level to each token but do not tightly control the realised sparsity, while TopK-based methods such as WINA enforce a fixed sparsity level but use the same sparsity budget for every token. Both also apply the same budget across transformer blocks, despite large differences in block sensitivity. We introduce TopK-Guided, a training-free method that addresses both limitations by combining bounded token-level sparsity adaptation with sensitivity-aware block-level budget allocation. Across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, TopK-Guided consistently improves perplexity and downstream accuracy over TEAL and WINA while preserving essentially the same sparsitydependent projection compute as WINA, with the largest gains at high sparsity. Ablations show that both components provide complementary improvements.

</details>


### [283] [VideoEvolve: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Video Temporal Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01766)
*Bingjun Luo,Yuhuan Fan,Jialin Guo,Siqi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VideoEvolve is a framework that automatically evolves agent harnesses for video temporal grounding (localizing events in videos from natural language queries), using a Cloze-Structured Harness Representation and Branch-Guided Harness Evolution to improve grounding performance across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual refinement of agent harnesses for video temporal grounding requires diagnosing grounding failures and coordinating changes to both agent workflows and instructions, which is labor-intensive and complex. This paper aims to automate the harness evolution process.

Method: The framework uses: (1) Cloze-Structured Harness Representation that preserves stage interfaces while leaving agent workflows and instructions open to evolution; (2) Branch-Guided Harness Evolution that preserves promising code branches for continued refinement, using execution feedback to guide local edits and validation to determine which improvements are carried forward.

Result: Experiments demonstrate improved grounding performance across multiple benchmarks. Component analyses identify instruction refinement as a consistent source of gains, while benefits of evolved code vary across evaluation settings.

Conclusion: Automated harness evolution is an effective approach to improving video temporal grounding, with instruction refinement being a consistent source of performance gains.

Abstract: Video temporal grounding aims to localize events in videos from natural-language queries. For agents built around frozen video-language models, the harness determines how queries guide temporal predictions and how those predictions are refined. Manually refining these harnesses requires diagnosing grounding failures and coordinating changes to both agent workflows and instructions. We introduce VideoEvolve, a framework that automatically evolves agent harnesses for video temporal grounding. VideoEvolve uses a Cloze-Structured Harness Representation that preserves stage interfaces while leaving agent workflows and instructions open to evolution. Branch-Guided Harness Evolution preserves promising code branches for continued refinement, using execution feedback to guide local edits and validation to determine which improvements are carried forward. Experiments demonstrate improved grounding performance across multiple benchmarks. Component analyses identify instruction refinement as a consistent source of gains, while the benefits of evolved code vary across evaluation settings. Together, these results support automated harness evolution as an effective approach to improving video temporal grounding. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/VideoEvolve .

</details>


### [284] [RealCompanion: Benchmarking Human Understanding from Reasoning over Longitudinal Real-World Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01780)
*Arman Behnam,Sunglyoung Kim,Liangwei Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces \bench, a benchmark dataset of 27,218 messages across 10 real human-AI companion relationships lasting up to 120 days, with derived annotations (profile, persona, chat ground truth, question set) to test long-term memory and understanding in AI companions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks use artificial data and cannot test whether an AI companion truly understands a person over time. Real conversation records are private, necessitating a benchmark with real relationships and pre-determined evaluation criteria.

Method: The authors released ten real conversations with four derived files, each citing supporting messages. They tested recency windows for memory retrieval, attempted detectors for memory needs, and compared three agent systems for persona reconstruction.

Result: Three findings: (1) A recency window finds 95.9% of probes and only 2.2% require actual memory retrieval; 96% of gains come from non-memory messages. (2) No detector can identify when memory is needed; authored questions leak cues, and labeling messages as memories increases their use by 10-14 points. (3) Three agent systems achieve the same F1 for persona reconstruction but differ 31-fold in cost.

Conclusion: Long-term memory in AI companions is rarely needed in practice, making detection of memory needs challenging. The same performance can be achieved at vastly different cost points, suggesting significant optimization opportunities in AI companion design.

Abstract: A companion that talks with a person for months should come to understand them. It should remember what they said, infer who they are, and know when the past bears on the message in front of it. Testing this requires a real person's record, and such records are private, so benchmarks generate the person and the questions and settle in advance what matters. We release \bench, ten real relationships with an AI companion: 27,218 messages over up to 120 days, released as the conversation and four files derived from it, a profile, a persona, a chat ground truth and a question set, each citing the messages it rests on. Every chat label carries the reasoning trace that produced it, checked stage by stage against the conversation. Three findings follow. First, the past is rarely needed and far away. Pooled measures mislead: a recency window finds the required message for 95.9\% of probes and 2.2\% of those that need memory, and at the natural rate 96\% of the gain from supplying recorded evidence comes from messages that need none. Second, no detector we tried can tell when memory is needed on real messages, authored questions over the same histories leak the cue, and labeling the same messages as memories raises their use by ten to fourteen points. Third, three agent systems reconstruct the persona with the same F1 at a 31-fold difference in cost.

</details>


### [285] [Q-Learning for Reachability in MEC-Free MDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01781)
*Lu-Chin Chang,Suguman Bansal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Quasar is the first model-free reinforcement learning algorithm with asymptotic guarantees for reachability on MDPs without non-terminal maximal end components (MECs). It uses Q-learning with temporal-difference updates, reducing memory complexity from O(|S|²|A|) to O(|S||A|) and achieving orders of magnitude better sample efficiency than model-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior model-based RL methods for reachability specifications require explicit estimation of transition probabilities, creating high memory overhead. There was a need for a model-free approach that could match asymptotic guarantees while being more practical for deployment.

Method: The algorithm follows the classical Q-learning approach, using temporal-difference updates to converge to an optimal policy without learning transition probabilities. It operates on the fragment of MDPs free of non-terminal MECs, which is the building block every MDP reduces to via the standard MEC quotient.

Result: The algorithm reduces memory footprint from O(|S|²|A|) to O(|S||A|). On the Quantitative Verification Benchmark Set, it converges to the optimal policy with orders of magnitude fewer samples than the previous model-based state-of-the-art.

Conclusion: This work represents a concrete step toward practical deployment of reachability learning and specification-guided RL, providing a memory-efficient, sample-efficient model-free alternative to previous model-based approaches while maintaining asymptotic convergence guarantees.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for reachability specifications is fundamental to sequential decision-making. Prior work establishes asymptotic convergence to optimal policies, but only through model-based methods that must explicitly estimate the transition probabilities of the underlying Markov Decision Process (MDP). We present Quasar, the first model-free algorithm with asymptotic guarantees for reachability on the fragment of MDPs free of non-terminal maximal end components (MECs), a building block to which every MDP reduces by the standard MEC quotient. Our algorithm follows the classical Q-learning approach, using temporal-difference updates to converge to an optimal policy without ever learning the transition probabilities. The resulting learner reduces the memory footprint from the O(|S|^2|A|) that model-based methods require to O(|S||A|). On the standardized Quantitative Verification Benchmark Set, our algorithm converges to the optimal policy with orders of magnitude fewer samples than the previous model-based state-of-the-art. Together these results are a concrete step toward the practical deployment of reachability learning and, with it, of specification-guided RL.

</details>


### [286] [LineupRL: Verifiable Reinforcement Learning for Time Series Captioning via Caption-to-Series Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01800)
*Haochen Zhang,Laura Yao,Zachary Plotkin,Gengwei Zhang,Tianlong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LineupRL is a reinforcement learning pipeline for time series captioning that uses caption-to-series identification as a verifiable reward. A frozen LLM verifier must identify the correct time series from distractors given only raw values and the generated caption, enabling a 3B VLM to outperform a 72B VLM baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for time series captioning is limited by the quality of larger model captions it distilled from, and cannot exceed that quality. Existing reinforcement learning rewards were designed for other modalities and tasks, transferring poorly to open-ended time series generation.

Method: The proposed LineupRL uses an RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) approach where the reward is caption-to-series identification. A frozen LLM verifier reads the generated caption and candidate time series as raw values (not charts) and must pick the described time series from multiple distractors. This matching task is lighter than writing questions or judging caption quality, allowing off-the-shelf LLMs to serve as verifiers.

Result: LineupRL outperforms SFT and RL baselines on every metric across two captioning benchmarks. It also works for forecasting and reconstruction tasks where the predictor sees only the caption. The 3B VLM trained by LineupRL outperforms a 72B VLM (with 1/24 of the parameters) that provided the SFT baseline's captions.

Conclusion: LineupRL demonstrates that RLVR with caption-to-series identification is effective for time series captioning. The approach resists reward hacking and produces captions that both trace trends and name values at key points. This method enables smaller models to surpass much larger ones through proper reward design.

Abstract: Time series captioning is a fundamental step in time series understanding and can also serve as the bridge between signal and natural language. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) relies on a larger model's captions and cannot exceed their quality. Reinforcement learning (RL) can, but its rewards were designed for other modalities and other tasks, and they transfer poorly to open-ended generation in the time series domain. We address this by proposing LineupRL, a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) pipeline whose reward is caption-to-series identification. The reward model is a frozen large language model (LLM) verifier that reads the generated caption and the candidate time series as raw values, never the chart, and must pick the described time series from multiple distractors. Matching is a far lighter demand on the verifier than writing questions or judging a caption, so an off-the-shelf LLM can supply the reward. Across two captioning benchmarks, and on forecasting and reconstruction where the predictor sees only the caption, LineupRL outperforms SFT and RL baselines on every metric. The 3B vision language model (VLM) trained by LineupRL also outperforms, at 1/24 of the parameters, the 72B VLM whose captions the SFT baseline is distilled from. Our case study shows that LineupRL resists reward hacking, and that the captioner it trains both traces the trend and names the values at key points.

</details>


### [287] [AI-assisted mitotic counting improves reproducibility and efficiency across multiple tumour types](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01813)
*Simon Graham,Mostafa Jahanifar,Quoc Dang Vu,Vygante Maskoliunaite,Donatas Petroska,Ruta Barbora Valkiuniene,Ayat Gamal Lashen,Jen Hong Ong,Amede Ogechi Nnorom,Sinclair Couper,Natasha Kardasz,Reshma Agrawal,Brinder Singh Chohan,Jose Luis Solorzano Rendon,Shonali Natu,Arvydas Laurinavicius,Nasir Rajpoot,David Snead*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MitPro is an AI tool that directs pathologists to regions with highest mitotic activity and highlights mitotic figures for review. A retrospective study with 385 whole-slide images from 3 centers, 7 tumor types, and 13 pathologists showed AI assistance increased intraclass correlation coefficient from 0.589 to 0.949 and reduced mean assessment time from 286.4 to 127.8 seconds per slide.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitotic counting is crucial for tumor grading, diagnosis, and prognosis but manual assessment is time-consuming and subject to inter-pathologist variability. This study aimed to address these challenges by developing an AI-assisted tool to improve consistency and efficiency.

Method: Retrospective, non-interventional, paired reader study with 385 whole-slide images from 3 centers in 3 countries, 7 tumor types, and 3 different scanners. 13 pathologists independently assessed each slide without AI assistance, then with AI assistance after a minimum 2-week washout period. Additional validation performed using HALO AP and Sectra image management systems with 2 additional tumor types.

Result: AI-assisted counting increased intraclass correlation coefficient from 0.589 to 0.949. Mean assessment time decreased from 286.4 to 127.8 seconds (average saving of 151.8 seconds per assessment). Improvements were consistent across different systems and tumor types. A subtle shift towards higher mitotic counts and scores was observed, with score change frequency comparable to inter-pathologist variation.

Conclusion: MitPro demonstrates significant potential as an assistive tool for more consistent and efficient mitotic assessment in routine pathological practice, with substantial improvements in reproducibility and efficiency while maintaining pathologist control over final counts.

Abstract: Mitotic counting is an important component of tumour grading, diagnosis and prognostic assessment across several tumour types, but manual assessment is time-consuming and subject to inter-pathologist variability. To help address these challenges, we developed MitPro, an AI tool designed to improve consistency and efficiency by directing pathologists towards regions with the highest predicted mitotic activity and highlighting mitotic figures for review, while retaining pathologist control over region selection and the final count. We evaluated its effect on the reproducibility and efficiency of mitotic counting in a retrospective, non-interventional, paired reader study comprising 385 whole-slide images from 3 centres in 3 countries and 7 tumour types using 3 different scanners. 13 pathologists participated, with each slide assessed independently by 3 pathologists without AI assistance and again with AI assistance after a minimum 2 week washout period. Across all slides, AI-assisted counting increased the intraclass correlation coefficient from 0.589 to 0.949. Mean pathologist-level median assessment time decreased from 286.4 to 127.8 seconds, corresponding to an average saving of 151.8 seconds per assessment. Improvements in agreement and efficiency were also observed in supporting analyses using HALO AP and Sectra image management systems and in 2 additional tumour types outside the main study population. AI-assisted assessment was associated with a subtle shift towards higher mitotic counts and scores, consistent with identification of more active mitotic hotspots and fewer missed mitotic figures. The frequency of score change between unassisted and AI-assisted assessment was comparable with inter-pathologist variation during routine counting. These findings support the use of MitPro as an assistive tool for more consistent and efficient mitotic assessment in routine practice.

</details>


### [288] [Code Owns the Simulation, Jev Owns the Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01834)
*Yaodong Yang,Hongyao Tang,Yi Ma,Xingyu Fan,Weixun Wang,Jinpeng Li,Tianpei Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Judgment models (like \jev{}) succeed at evaluating options directly described in input but fail when required to simulate/predict outcomes. They solve 99% of Cognitive Reflection Test questions (evaluation tasks) but fail on games requiring opponent prediction or multi-step planning. When code provides predictions (e.g., lookahead, physics simulation), \jev{} becomes an expert controller.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine what decisions judgment models can be trusted with, since they return probabilities without reasoning text, making them attractive as agent action-selection layers.

Method: Tested \jev{} on four domains: Cognitive Reflection Test (counterintuitive questions), one-shot matrix games (strategic interactions), ALFWorld (text-based household tasks), and robot control. Compared performance on evaluation tasks (right option judgeable from input) versus simulation tasks (requires predicting something not in input).

Result: Sharp boundary found: \jev{} achieves 99% on CRT (evaluation) but fails on simulation tasks. In matrix games, it plays suboptimally as if rational opponent acted randomly. In ALFWorld, it takes捷径 (e.g., puts unwashed knife directly in drawer instead of washing first). Failures stem from inability to perform simulation within single call—though when asked separately, it correctly predicts opponent actions. When code supplies predictions (lookahead in ALFWorld, physics simulation in robot control), \jev{} becomes expert controller.

Conclusion: Judgment models excel at evaluation but not simulation. Practical implication: let code handle prediction/simulation; use judgment models purely for evaluation when given necessary information. This enables reliable deployment as action-selection layer when paired with appropriate simulation infrastructure.

Abstract: Judgment models such as \jev{} return, in a single call and without reasoning text, a probability for each described option. This makes them attractive as an agent's action-selection layer, but it is unclear which decisions they can be trusted with. We test \jev{} on reflection tests, one-shot matrix games, the text game ALFWorld and robot control, and find a sharp boundary. \jev{} succeeds when the right option can be judged from what the input describes, which we call \emph{evaluation}. Specifically, it solves 99\% of the counterintuitive Cognitive Reflection Test questions. However, it fails when the right option depends on \emph{simulation} (i.e., predicting something not in the input), such as the opponent's action or the subgoal that must come first. In games, \jev{} plays suboptimally as if its rational opponent acted at random, because the opponent's action is not given. In ALFWorld, \jev{} favors commands that mention an object or place named in the task description. For example, given the task ``put a clean knife in the drawer'', \jev{} carries an unwashed knife straight to the drawer instead of first washing it at the sink. Surprisingly, many of these failures are not due to a lack of knowledge. Asked separately what the opponent will do, \jev{} usually answers correctly, and it responds well given the opponent's action. It fails when one call must both perform the simulation and evaluate based on it. This suggests letting code make the prediction or simulation. When code supplies it, such as a lookahead in ALFWorld and physics simulation in robot control, \jev{} becomes an expert controller through its general evaluation ability.

</details>


### [289] [On the Divergence of Accuracy and Mechanism Consistency in Time Series World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01842)
*Haochen Zhang,Jiaheng Guo,Zhen Xu,Zachary Plotkin,Nicholas Konz,Zhen Tan,Tianlong Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical gap in Time Series World Models (TSWM): while current approaches are trained and evaluated on prediction error under executed plans, they fail to properly respond to changed (unexecuted) plans. The authors introduce a formalization separating state, actions, and exogenous inputs, along with a new metric called "mechanism consistency" that checks whether shifting an action moves the forecast in the declared direction. Through benchmarks on 8 public datasets, they find that prediction error and mechanism consistency actually diverge, and propose "directional supervision" as a solution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current TSWM approaches are trained and evaluated on prediction error under executed plans, but world models need to compare unexecuted plans. The key problem is that how these models respond to changed plans remains completely untested. The authors wanted to identify which design choices matter and whether accurate forecasters respond to changed plans as real systems do.

Method: The authors developed a formalization that separates state, actions, and exogenous inputs, distinguishes continuous, mode, and event actions, and introduces "mechanism consistency" - a metric built on declared action-state relations with known directions (e.g., vasopressor raising blood pressure). They consolidated eight public datasets with real actions from engineered infrastructure and clinical care, varying prediction space, plan fusion, and plan encoding across seven backbones and five seeds. They also proposed "directional supervision" - a loss that penalizes the wrong-signed part of the response to a shifted action.

Result: Key findings: (1) Frozen latent prediction space lowers MAE by 9.9% over observation space; (2) Gated output fusion lowers MAE by 12.7% over input concatenation on average, with both improving all eight datasets; (3) Temporal plan encoding changes average MAE by at most 2.2%; (4) Prediction error and mechanism consistency diverge - the lowest-error configuration is at or below chance in consistency on four of five datasets with declared mechanisms, and no design choice avoids this; (5) Directional supervision significantly raises consistency on penalized mechanisms with no change in MAE.

Conclusion: The paper provides a recipe for building TSWMs: (1) Use a frozen latent space and output-side fusion for accuracy; (2) Add a training objective (directional supervision) for mechanism consistency. This addresses the fundamental issue that standard training on prediction error does not guarantee that models will respond correctly to changed plans - a critical requirement for real-world deployment of world models.

Abstract: A time series world model (TSWM) predicts a controlled system's state from its observed history and planned actions and exogenous inputs. Current approaches build forecasters with actions as covariates, trained and evaluated on prediction error under the executed plan. Yet world models compare unexecuted plans, but their responses to changed plans remain untested. We ask which design choices matter and whether accurate forecasters respond to changed plans as real systems do. We address both with a formalization and benchmark. The formalization separates state, actions and exogenous inputs, distinguishes continuous, mode and event actions, and introduces mechanism consistency, a metric built on declared action-state relations with known directions, such as a vasopressor raising blood pressure: it checks whether shifting an action moves the forecast in the declared direction. The benchmark consolidates eight public datasets with real actions from engineered infrastructure and clinical care, varying prediction space, plan fusion and plan encoding across seven backbones and five seeds. First, a frozen latent prediction space lowers MAE by 9.9% over observation space and gated output fusion lowers it by 12.7% over input concatenation on average, with both improving all eight datasets; temporal plan encoding changes average MAE by at most 2.2%. Second, prediction error and mechanism consistency diverge: the lowest-error configuration is at or below chance in consistency on four of five datasets with declared mechanisms, and no design choice avoids this. Finally, directional supervision, a loss penalizing the wrong-signed part of the response to a shifted action, significantly raises consistency on penalized mechanisms with no change in MAE. Together they give TSWMs a recipe: a frozen latent space and output-side fusion for accuracy, and a training objective for mechanism consistency.

</details>


### [290] [Temporal-Difference Learning for Dragonchess](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01845)
*Jim O'Connor,Annika Hoag,Sarah Goyette,Gary B. Parker*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates two adaptive AI methods (evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda)) in the 3D chess game Dragonchess. The researchers re-implemented the game engine from PyGame to C++ to enable large-scale testing (10,000 games). Both adaptive methods outperformed all other agents in a round-robin tournament, with no significant performance difference between them, demonstrating the efficacy of adaptive methods in structurally complex, novel game domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dragonchess presents a challenging environment due to its unique three-dimensional board structure and high computational demands. The research aims to study how adaptive methods can update evaluation heuristics in novel environments, specifically whether evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda) can effectively learn in this structurally complex game domain.

Method: The researchers re-implemented the Dragonchess engine from PyGame to C++ for improved performance. They conducted a large-scale experiment with 10,000 games, using confidence intervals and significance tests for statistical rigor. The study employed a round-robin tournament format comparing the two adaptive methods against other agents.

Result: Both evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda) outperformed all other agents in the round-robin tournament. However, there was no statistically significant difference in performance between the evolved (evolutionary transfer learning) and learned (TD(lambda)) evaluation functions.

Conclusion: Adaptive methods (both evolutionary and reinforcement learning approaches) are effective in structurally complex, novel game domains like Dragonchess. The equivalence in performance suggests that both methods can successfully update evaluation heuristics, though neither offers a clear advantage over the other in this context.

Abstract: Our research investigates how two adaptive AI methods, evolutionary transfer learning and TD(lambda), perform in the three-dimensional chess environment Dragonchess. The game challenges players with its unique board structure and computational load, making it an ideal setting to study how adaptive methods can update evaluation heuristics in novel environments. In this work we re-implement the Dragonchess engine, changing it from a PyGame engine to C++. This enables faster gameplay, allowing us to run 10,000 games with confidence intervals and significance tests, rather than a single small tournament. Both adaptive methods outperform all other agents in the round-robin tournament. Our results showed that there is no significant difference in the performance between the evolved and learned evaluations. This research establishes the efficacy of adaptive methods in structurally complex, novel game domains.

</details>


### [291] [Mapping the RAG Landscape: A Four Axis Taxonomy of Efficiency, Defense, Interactivity, and Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01936)
*Meghana Sunil,Shravya V,Shravan Venkatraman,Joe Dhanith PR*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey examines contemporary Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) developments, organizing research into a four-axis taxonomy: retrieval efficiency, robustness/security, interactive workflows, and complex reasoning. It reviews retrieval methods, evaluation practices, and architectural variants while identifying persistent challenges in quality, reliability, and explainability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Language Models suffer from static, bounded knowledge and hallucination problems. While RAG addresses these issues by incorporating external retrieval, prior surveys focused mainly on core architectures. This paper fills the gap by examining broader challenges and capabilities beyond foundational designs.

Method: The survey organizes the field into a four-axis taxonomy: (1) improving retrieval efficiency, (2) strengthening robustness and security, (3) supporting user-driven and interactive workflows, and (4) enabling multi-step or complex reasoning. It reviews methods spanning dense and sparse retrieval, fusion strategies, embedding optimizations, and reinforcement learning-based retrieval policies.

Result: The survey synthesizes evaluation practices, domain-specific applications, and architectural variants (Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG). It formalizes key RAG components and highlights how advances influence practical deployment and system design.

Conclusion: Persistent challenges remain in retrieval quality, reliability, domain adaptation, scalability, and explainability. Opportunities exist for building RAG systems that are more reliable, adaptable, and transparent.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency across many tasks but remain limited by their static, parameter bound knowledge and their susceptibility to hallucinating information. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these issues by incorporating external retrieval into the generation process, grounding model outputs in verifiable and up to date sources. While prior surveys primarily focus on core RAG architectures and standard pipelines, recent research explores broader challenges and capabilities that extend beyond these foundational designs. This survey provides a consolidated and structured examination of contemporary RAG developments, organizing the field into a four axis taxonomy: improving retrieval efficiency, strengthening robustness and security, supporting user driven and interactive workflows, and enabling multi step or complex reasoning. We formalize key components of the RAG framework and review methods spanning dense and sparse retrieval, fusion strategies, embedding optimizations, and reinforcement learning based retrieval policies, highlighting how these advances influence practical deployment and system design. We also synthesize evaluation practices, domain specific applications, and architectural variants such as Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG. Finally, we outline persistent challenges related to retrieval quality, reliability, domain adaptation, scalability, and explainability, and identify opportunities for building RAG systems that are more reliable, adaptable, and transparent.

</details>


### [292] [Counterfactual Auditing of Bias in Open-Source Large Language Models for Clinical Triage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01963)
*Manar Aljohani,Brandon Ho,Kenneth McKinley,Dennis Ren,Xuan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a comparative counterfactual audit of 10 open-source LLMs for pediatric Emergency Severity Index (ESI) prediction, examining how demographic, socioeconomic, and system-context variables improperly influence acuity assignment. The study finds substantial variation in counterfactual sensitivity across models, with fine-tuned models performing best and larger model size not necessarily reducing bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Emergency department triage is a high-stakes task where demographic, socioeconomic, and system-context information may improperly influence acuity assignment. With increasing interest in using open-source LLMs for clinical decision support, it is critical to understand how counterfactual bias varies across different model families, sizes, and domain adaptations before clinical deployment.

Method: The researchers constructed paired counterfactual variants from real and handbook-style clinical vignettes, changing only one injected demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare-access, behavioral, social, or system-context variable while holding clinical presentation fixed. They tested 10 models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, a QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, MedGemma variants, MedLLaMA2-7B, GPT-OSS-20B, and GPT-OSS-120B. They measured counterfactual shift, undertriage, overtriage, shifts greater than one ESI level, mean shift, and mean absolute shift.

Result: Counterfactual sensitivity varied substantially across models and did not consistently decrease with larger model size or medical-domain pretraining. The fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B showed the lowest overall sensitivity (5.27% any-shift rate, 0.0534 mean absolute shift) compared to 16.02% and 0.1706 for the base model. Several larger or medical-domain models showed more significant shifts. Stratified and correlation analyses revealed clinically important directionality and shared failure patterns hidden by aggregate rates.

Conclusion: Counterfactual auditing represents a lightweight, clinically interpretable framework for comparing fairness risks in open-source LLMs before clinical deployment. The findings highlight that larger model size or medical-domain pretraining does not guarantee reduced bias, and fine-tuned models may offer better fairness performance.

Abstract: Emergency department (ED) triage is a high-stakes prioritization task in which demographic, socioeconomic, and system-context information may improperly influence acuity assignment. Although open-source large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for local and privacy-preserving clinical decision support, it remains unclear how counterfactual bias varies across model families, sizes, medical-domain models, and domain-adapted models. We present a comparative counterfactual audit of ten open-source LLMs for pediatric Emergency Severity Index (ESI) prediction. Starting from real and handbook-style clinical vignettes, we construct paired counterfactual variants that change only one injected demographic, socioeconomic, healthcare-access, behavioral, social, or system-context variable while holding the clinical presentation fixed. Models include Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, a QLoRA fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, MedGemma variants, MedLLaMA2-7B, GPT-OSS-20B, and GPT-OSS-120B. We measure any counterfactual shift, undertriage, overtriage, shifts greater than one ESI level, mean shift, and mean absolute shift. Counterfactual sensitivity varied substantially and did not consistently decrease with larger model size or medical-domain pretraining. The fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B showed the lowest overall sensitivity, with a 5.27% any-shift rate and mean absolute shift of 0.0534, versus 16.02% and 0.1706 for the base model. Several larger or medical-domain models showed more significant shifts. Stratified and correlation analyses further revealed clinically important directionality and shared failure patterns hidden by aggregate rates. These findings support counterfactual auditing as a lightweight, clinically interpretable framework for comparing fairness risks in open-source LLMs before clinical deployment.

</details>


### [293] [Can AI Oversight Be Zero Knowledge?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01995)
*Alessandro Chiesa,Ziyi Guan,Burcu Yildiz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether interactive zero-knowledge proofs can verify AI outputs on confidential data (like medical records or drug structures) without revealing the underlying data. The authors prove that zero-knowledge proofs for general oracle-aided computation are impossible in the random oracle model, even with unbounded computational resources. However, they show a positive result: if the oracle signs its answers, then zero-knowledge verification becomes possible assuming only collision-resistant hash functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI systems increasingly process confidential data (medical records, drug structures) and produce sensitive outputs. The key challenge is verifying output correctness without revealing the confidential input data. While prior work focused on efficient verification (verifier faster than computation), this paper addresses the privacy dimension: can the verifier confirm correctness while learning nothing about the confidential data?

Method: The paper uses theoretical computer science methods, particularly in the random oracle model. It proves impossibility results via contradiction, showing that if zero-knowledge proofs existed for all oracle-aided computations, it would lead to computational assumptions being violated. For the positive result, it constructs protocols using cryptographic signatures and collision-resistant hash functions.

Result: Negative result: In the random oracle model, there are no zero-knowledge proofs for all oracle-aided computations, even when both prover and verifier run much longer than the computation itself. This impossibility extends to the "debate" model for scalable oversight. Positive result: If the oracle attaches a cryptographic signature to each answer, every oracle-aided computation can be verified in zero knowledge with efficient prover and verifier, assuming only collision-resistant hash functions.

Conclusion: The paper establishes a fundamental limitation: privacy-preserving verification of general oracle-aided computation is impossible without additional assumptions. However, it provides a practical solution: requiring oracle-signed answers enables zero-knowledge verification with standard cryptographic assumptions. This offers an alternative approach to scalable AI oversight that doesn't rely on honest opponents or computation robustness, potentially useful for verifying AI outputs on sensitive data like medical assessments or proprietary drug candidates.

Abstract: AI systems increasingly produce outputs from confidential data, such as a fitness-for-duty assessment from medical records or the predicted properties of a drug candidate from its secret structure. It is important to verify that such outputs are correct without revealing the underlying data. A recent line of work studies verification of AI outputs via interactive proofs and debate for oracle-aided computation, where correctness may depend on an oracle such as human judgment, a physical experiment, or the web. These works focus on verification by a verifier that runs much faster than the computation. However, such efficient verification is impossible for general oracle-aided computation, and these works therefore rely on additional assumptions. We focus instead on privacy: allowing the verifier to run in time polynomial in the computation, we ask whether interactive arguments for oracle-aided computation can be zero knowledge, so that the verifier learns nothing about the confidential data beyond the correctness of the output.
  We prove that, in general, they cannot. In the random oracle model, there are no zero-knowledge proofs for all oracle-aided computations, even if both the prover and the verifier are allowed to run much longer than the computation itself. The impossibility extends to debate, a canonical model for scalable oversight.
  On the positive side, we show that if the oracle attaches a cryptographic signature to each of its answers, then every oracle-aided computation can be verified in zero knowledge with an efficient prover and verifier, assuming only collision-resistant hash functions. Beyond privacy, this also gives an alternative approach to scalable oversight that relies neither on an honest opponent, as in debate, nor on the robustness of the computation, as in prior single-prover protocols.

</details>


### [294] [Mingbird: A Local-First Agent Harness Enabling Small Open Models to Complete Real Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02001)
*Hao Wang,Ting Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mingbird is a local-first agent harness designed to address failure modes of small open-weight models (2-9B) under cloud-scale agent harnesses. It introduces 10 compensation mechanisms and achieves significantly higher task completion rates (0.886 on LRAB) compared to existing harnesses (0.405-0.631), with evidence suggesting harness design rather than model capability is the primary failure source.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Small open-weight models (2-9B) running on ordinary laptops fail to complete real tasks under cloud-scale agent harnesses due to tool prefill overflow, self-correction divergence, tool demonstration loops, and silent task abandonment. The authors hypothesized that a substantial share of these failures is attributable to the harness rather than the model itself.

Method: Controlled single-machine comparison on a self-built benchmark (LRAB) with 4 harnesses × 4 open models (2B-35B) × 18 real tasks, plus evaluation on τ²-bench (278 tasks). Three representative mechanisms were introduced: (1) byte-level net-zero prefill budget, (2) finish gate that re-reads task before accepting completion, and (3) signature-level loop detection. A leave-one-mechanism-out ablation was conducted, though noted as directional only due to high variance.

Result: On LRAB (controlled comparison), Mingbird achieved 0.886 overall vs 0.631 (goose), 0.479 (opencode), and 0.405 (agent-mini). On τ²-bench (278 tasks), Mingbird scored 0.856 vs 0.791 and 0.737. A frontier-model probe on the same 18 tasks showed 0.997 to 0.478 across harnesses. The batch-matched comparison (full stack vs text re-read alone) showed executable completion guards provided +0.10 paired improvement across three replications.

Conclusion: Harness design significantly impacts small model performance in agent tasks. Mingbird's ten mechanisms compensate for small-model failure forms, substantially outperforming existing harnesses. Limitations include self-built benchmark, single-machine testing, and single-trial scoring, with same-night replications showing mean shifts up to 0.069.

Abstract: Small open-weight models (2-9B) run on ordinary laptops, but under cloud-scale agent harnesses they rarely complete real tasks: tool prefill overflows the context, self-correction diverges, tool demonstrations loop, and tasks are silently abandoned. We present evidence, from a controlled single-machine comparison and one third-party benchmark, that a substantial share of these failures is attributable to the harness rather than the model.
