We introduce Mingbird, a local-first agent harness for Windows and Ollama whose ten mechanisms compensate point-by-point for small-model failure forms, three of them representative: a byte-level net-zero prefill budget, a finish gate that re-reads the task before accepting completion, and signature-level loop detection. On LRAB, a controlled comparison holding machine, models, budgets, and scoring fixed (4 harnesses $\times$ 4 open models (2B-35B) $\times$ 18 real tasks, deterministic artifact scoring), Mingbird reaches 0.886 overall against 0.631 (goose), 0.479 (opencode), and 0.405 (agent-mini), with all 288 cells published; on $τ^2$-bench (278 tasks, three arms, one protocol) it totals 0.856 against 0.791 and 0.737; and a frontier-model probe on the same 18 tasks spans 0.997 to 0.478 across harnesses, with well-formed scaffolds staying within 0.072 of each other. A leave-one-mechanism-out ablation is reported as directional only: same-night replications of the same arm move its mean by up to 0.069, the size of every nominal single-trial delta, and the one batch-matched comparison (full mechanism stack versus text re-read alone) gives the executable completion guards a paired +0.10 across three replications. The evidence carries stated limits: a self-built benchmark, a single machine, and single-trial scoring.

</details>


### [295] [Counting Moves, Weighing Voices: Bayesian Dialectical Argumentation for Calibrated Multi-LLM Councils under Persistent Adversaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02005)
*Ionel Eduard Stan,Paolo Napoletano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BDA introduces a method to calibrate confidence estimates in multi-LLM councils by treating deliberation moves (proposals, challenges, concessions) as observations of agent reliability. It infers per-agent reliability under adversarial behavior and yields calibrated posterior probabilities while identifying and discounting persistently unreliable agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing council aggregation methods fail in two key ways: (1) their confidence estimates measure decisiveness rather than actual probability of correctness, and (2) they cannot identify or discount persistently unreliable agents. As LLMs are increasingly used for reasoning, calibrated confidence and robustness against unreliable agents are critical.

Method: Bayesian Dialectical Argumentation (BDA) treats the council's typed moves—who proposed, challenged, or conceded which answer—as observations of a classical annotator model with per-agent reliabilities. This formulation recasts multi-agent deliberation as a reliability estimation problem, using the deliberation trace to infer agent reliability under persistent adversarial behavior. Evidence is weighted according to inferred agent reliability.

Result: Across binary and multi-class benchmarks, BDA achieves the best calibration among zero-cost council aggregation methods (requiring no additional LLM calls), improves robustness under persistent adversarial coalitions, and remains competitive in clean settings.

Conclusion: BDA successfully yields calibrated posterior probabilities over candidate answers while allowing persistently unreliable agents to be inverted rather than merely outvoted, solving both the calibration and robustness problems of existing council aggregation methods.

Abstract: A multi-LLM \emph{council} lets several large language models (LLMs) deliberate on a question and return an answer together with a confidence estimate. As these systems become increasingly used for reasoning, that confidence should represent a calibrated \emph{probability of being correct}, and the decision should remain robust when some agents are persistently unreliable. Existing \emph{council aggregation} methods fail on both fronts: their confidence estimates measure decisiveness rather than correctness, and they cannot identify or discount persistently unreliable agents. We introduce Bayesian Dialectical Argumentation (BDA), which treats the council's \emph{typed} moves---who proposed, challenged, or conceded which answer---as observations of a classical annotator model with \emph{per-agent} reliabilities. This formulation recasts multi-agent deliberation as a reliability estimation problem, using the deliberation trace to infer agent reliability under persistent adversarial behavior. By weighting evidence according to inferred agent reliability, BDA yields calibrated posterior probabilities over candidate answers while allowing persistently unreliable agents to be inverted rather than merely outvoted. Across binary and multi-class benchmarks, BDA achieves the best calibration among zero-cost council aggregation methods, requiring no additional LLM calls, and improves robustness under persistent adversarial coalitions while remaining competitive in clean settings.

</details>


### [296] [Atoms to Processes: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Chemical Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02014)
*Michael Baldea,Linda J. Broadbelt,Marianthi G. Ierapetritou,Akhilesh Jain,Ankur Kumar,Thomas A. Kwan,Fèlix Llovell,Andrew J. Medford,Ilias Mitrai,Joel Paulson,Junyi Qiao,Matthew P. Rivera,Kirti C. Sahu,Lev Sarkisov,Zachary P. Smith,Calvin Tsay,Ching-Mei Wen,Victor M. Zavala,Huacheng Zhang,Dan Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This perspective article reviews how AI and machine learning are transforming chemical engineering across multiple domains—from atomic-scale simulations to industrial operations. The paper emphasizes the shift from black-box approaches toward hybrid physics-informed frameworks that integrate AI/ML with first-principles models, arguing that AI amplifies rather than replaces core chemical engineering principles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The rapid advancement of AI/ML has created new opportunities to address long-standing challenges in chemical engineering, including predictive accuracy, data scarcity, extrapolation limitations, interpretability, and model lifecycle management. The authors aim to provide a unifying perspective on how these tools can be effectively integrated with domain knowledge.

Method: This is a perspective/review paper that surveys recent methodological developments and representative applications of AI/ML in chemical engineering, emphasizing hybrid and physics-informed approaches that respect conservation laws, thermodynamic consistency, and structural constraints.

Result: The paper identifies a unifying trend across domains: the move toward hybrid frameworks that combine AI/ML with first-principles models. These approaches improve robustness, reliability, and enable meaningful human-AI collaboration by providing interpretable information at appropriate abstraction levels.

Conclusion: AI and ML are not replacing but amplifying core chemical engineering principles. Realizing their full potential requires thoughtful integration of AI/ML with first-principles understanding and domain expertise, particularly as the field moves toward autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable systems.

Abstract: The rapid maturation of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has catalyzed a profound shift in how chemical engineering problems are formulated, analyzed, and solved. Advances in computing, data availability, and learning algorithms have enabled AI/ML methods to impact applications spanning atomic-scale simulations, materials and catalyst discovery, transport and thermodynamics, separations, process systems engineering, and industrial operations. This article provides a perspective on recent methodological developments and representative applications, emphasizing how AI/ML tools are being integrated with first-principles models to address challenges of predictive accuracy, data scarcity, extrapolation, interpretability, and model lifecycle management. Across domains, a unifying trend is the move away from purely black-box approaches toward hybrid and physics-informed frameworks that explicitly respect conservation laws, thermodynamic consistency, and known structural constraints. These approaches not only improve robustness and reliability, but also enable meaningful human-AI collaboration by providing information at an appropriate level of abstraction for the task and decision context. We conclude that AI and ML are not replacing the core principles of chemical engineering; rather, they are amplifying them. As the field advances toward increasingly autonomous, adaptive, and sustainable systems, the thoughtful integration of AI/ML with first-principles understanding and domain expertise will be essential to realizing their full potential across both research and industrial practice.

</details>


### [297] [SPHERE: Adaptive VR Indoor Scene Generation via LLM-Enhanced Spatial Preference Learning and Human-in-the-Loop RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02023)
*Hyeonmin Lee,Zheng Wei,Kyungmin Kwon,Jumin Seo,Jiwon Park,Hayoung Oh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SPHERE is an adaptive VR framework that enables continuous human-AI co-creation in 3D indoor scene synthesis by extracting persistent spatial preferences from multimodal interactions (speech and controller edits), using hierarchical constraints for geometric resilience, and employing human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning for dynamic retrieval policy updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based 3D indoor scene synthesis pipelines fail to retain user-specific preferences across sessions, making immersive authoring repetitive and physically fatiguing due to the need for repeated corrective edits.

Method: SPHERE extracts spatial preferences from natural multimodal interactions (speech and controller edits), abstracts raw edits into hierarchical constraints modeling both local functional and global topological contexts, and uses a human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning mechanism to dynamically update retrieval policies based on user's final edited scenes.

Result: User study (N=42) and offline ablation demonstrate SPHERE significantly reduces corrective edits and physical demand, prevents bias toward shallow object-level traits, and yields geometrically resilient, profile-aligned layouts.

Conclusion: Capturing demonstrated spatial logic enables controlled spatial adaptation, establishing a reliable governed human-AI collaboration framework for immersive VR authoring.

Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) advance 3D indoor scene synthesis, current pipelines fail to retain user-specific preferences across sessions, making immersive authoring a repetitive and physically fatiguing process. We present SPHERE, an adaptive VR generation framework that transforms isolated synthesis into continuous human-AI co-creation. SPHERE extracts persistent spatial preferences from natural multimodal interactions (speech and controller edits). To ensure geometric resilience against spatial distortions, it abstracts these raw edits into hierarchical constraints modeling both local functional and global topological contexts. Furthermore, a human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning mechanism dynamically updates retrieval policies based on the user's final edited scenes. A mixed-design user study ($N=42$) and an offline ablation demonstrate that SPHERE significantly reduces corrective edits and physical demand, preventing bias toward shallow object-level traits to yield geometrically resilient, profile-aligned layouts. Ultimately, SPHERE demonstrates how capturing demonstrated spatial logic enables controlled spatial adaptation, establishing a reliable, governed human-AI collaboration framework for immersive authoring. Project page and source code will be available at: https://github.com/hyeonmin11/SPHERE

</details>


### [298] [Global Coherence: When Every Agent Is Right and the Team Is Still Wrong - A Local-to-Global Semantic Foundation for Multi-Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02036)
*Xin Heng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the "global coherence problem" in AI agents—where individually valid decisions can collectively produce invalid outcomes due to missing shared state. The authors prove the Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem, which defines the exact boundary for when a policy can guarantee valid actions. They propose a runtime semantics framework (X = H, C, G, F; D) and validate it through nine empirical studies on benchmarks like TeamBench and tau2-bench Telecom, demonstrating that local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a fundamental limitation in multi-agent AI systems: even capable models can fail when they cannot distinguish between worlds that produce the same observation but require different actions. This "observation-aliasing" problem causes locally valid decisions to jointly produce invalid global results—a failure of shared state, not model intelligence.

Method: The paper combines theoretical analysis (Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem) with empirical validation. The theorem establishes that a policy can guarantee valid actions only when all worlds producing the same observation share an admissible action. The runtime semantics framework X = (H, C, G, F; D) is proposed, where: H = topology of overlapping scopes, C = category for state-changing actions, G = groupoid for reversible translations, F = sheaf for testing local view consistency, and D = minimal history preserving only action-altering distinctions. Nine studies test this on benchmarks including TeamBench and tau2-bench Telecom.

Result: The empirical studies confirm the theory: on a controlled revision benchmark, the same model scores 40/40 when the deciding event is visible but only 12-17/40 (near chance at 1/3) when hidden; restoring one authoritative fact returns 40/40. On TeamBench, ordinary teams exceed shared budget in 5/5 runs, a visible live count leaves 4/5 violations, and commit enforcement leaves 0/5. In tau2-bench Telecom, current-state checks score 0.07 after silent reverts while the harness scores 1.00. Where a conventional solver owns complete relevant state, it ties the harness.

Conclusion: The counterintuitive conclusion is that local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state. More reasoning, roles, messages, or samples cannot recover the missing distinction when observation-aliasing occurs. A stronger model can reason better within its context but cannot see beyond it. The harness (which owns shared state and governs commit) is essential for ensuring global coherence.

Abstract: AI agents can each make locally valid decisions yet jointly produce an invalid result. We call this the global coherence problem: a failure of shared state, not merely of model intelligence.
  Our Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem gives the exact boundary. A policy can guarantee a valid action exactly when all worlds producing the same observation share an admissible action. If k indistinguishable worlds require pairwise-disjoint actions, the best randomized worst-case success is 1/k; more reasoning, roles, messages, or samples cannot recover the missing distinction. A stronger model can reason better within its context, but it cannot see beyond it.
  We then give local-to-global runtime semantics X = (H, C, G, F; D): topology H records overlapping scopes; category C governs state-changing actions; groupoid G retains reversible translations; sheaf F tests whether local views glue into one world; and minimal history D keeps only distinctions that alter legal futures. Models propose; the harness owns shared state and governs commit.
  Nine studies test both the failure and its boundary. On a controlled revision benchmark, the same frontier model scores 40/40 when the deciding event is visible; when it is hidden, tested arms score 12--17/40, consistent with chance (1/3); restoring one authoritative fact returns 40/40. On TeamBench, ordinary teams exceed a shared budget in 5/5 runs, a visible live count leaves 4/5 violations, and commit enforcement leaves 0/5. In tau2-bench Telecom, current-state checks score 0.07 after silent reverts, while the harness scores 1.00. Where a conventional solver already owns the complete relevant state, it ties the harness as predicted. The counterintuitive conclusion is that local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state.

</details>


### [299] [Mimir: Physics-Grounded LLM Agents for Long-Horizon Irrigation Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02038)
*Yimeng Liu,Mi Zhang,Younsuk Dong,Zhichao Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mimir is a physics-grounded LLM agent for long-running physical control tasks (irrigation management), using two repair timescales: fast (numerical verification and bounded action selection) and slow (persistent contextual principles from failure patterns). It achieves 51% less irrigation than historical schedules while maintaining lowest control cost among evaluated methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents are mostly evaluated on episodic tasks with immediate feedback, but long-running physical control operates in a fundamentally different regime where actions alter future states, errors compound, and agents must improve without rewriting physical rules. Irrigation was chosen as a test case because daily decisions interact with soil-water dynamics over entire growing seasons.

Method: Mimir uses a two-timescale architecture: (1) Fast timescale - a structured physical interface and deterministic simulator converts LLM output into numerically checked, revised proposals before bounded deterministic action selection; (2) Slow timescale - recurrent failure patterns are consolidated into persistent contextual principles that condition future proposals, while the physical model, evaluator, and execution constraints remain immutable.

Result: Under a common retrospective evaluator across multiple sites, crops, and years, Mimir achieves the lowest reported aggregate control cost among evaluated references and uses about 51% less irrigation than the historical schedule replay. Ablation studies show higher control cost when forward simulation, verified revision, or persistent context is removed. Model-scale and model-family studies show no monotonic gain from increasing LLM size.

Conclusion: Persistent physical agents can combine semantic reasoning with bounded, evidence-driven self-improvement while reserving physical truth and actuator authority for explicit numerical mechanisms. The key insight is that separating semantic reasoning (LLM) from numerical execution (deterministic verification) enables safe and effective long-running control.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly combine reasoning, tool use, and action, but most evidence comes from episodic tasks with relatively immediate feedback and reset failures. Long-running physical control operates in a different regime: actions alter future states, errors compound across decisions, and an agent must improve from experience without being allowed to rewrite the physical rules that make execution safe. We study this regime through irrigation, where daily decisions interact with soil-water dynamics over entire growing seasons. We present Mimir, a physics-grounded LLM agent organized around two repair timescales. At the fast timescale, a structured physical interface and deterministic simulator turn an LLM output into a proposal that we numerically check, revise, and subject to bounded deterministic action selection before execution. At the slow timescale, recurrent failure patterns are consolidated into persistent contextual principles that condition future proposals, while the physical model, evaluator, and execution constraints remain immutable. Under a common retrospective evaluator across multiple sites, crops, and years, Mimir attains the lowest reported aggregate control cost among the evaluated references and uses about 51% less irrigation than the historical schedule replay. The ablation study show higher control cost when forward simulation, verified revision, or persistent context is removed; model-scale and model-family studies show no monotonic gain from increasing LLM size. The resulting lesson show that persistent physical agents can combine semantic reasoning with bounded, evidence-driven self-improvement while reserving physical truth and actuator authority for explicit numerical mechanisms.

</details>


### [300] [HydroJEV: A one-second, training-free screen for cyber-attack and fault attribution in water distribution networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02048)
*Tianwei Mu,Shengyan Jiang,Mingzhe Yuan,Qing Luo,Min Xiao,Wenhong Wang,Jun Li,Manhong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Jev, a training-free model that returns class probabilities in ~1 second, can serve as a fast first-tier triage for SCADA alarms in water distribution networks. It matches rule tree performance (macro-F1 0.62-0.64), outperforms supervised classifiers with limited labeled data, and is 20-40x faster than frontier LLMs. This approach can reduce LLM reviewer workload by 35-38% while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When SCADA alarms are raised in water distribution networks, operators must quickly determine whether they indicate a cyberattack, physical fault, normal transient, or faulty sensor. Current solutions have limitations: supervised classifiers require scarce labeled incident data, and frontier LLMs are too slow (tens of seconds per decision). There is a need for a fast, training-free first-tier screening method.

Method: Jev was compared against a hand-written rule tree, a supervised classifier, and seven cloud LLMs on a four-class cause-attribution benchmark (C-Town network in EPANET). Experiments were conducted in four sealed, pre-registered rounds using identical evidence. Only a label-free prior correction was applied. The gated cascade approach (accepting only benign Jev verdicts confirmed by the rule tree) was tested on two additional networks.

Result: Jev matched the rule tree (macro-F1 0.62-0.64 vs 0.56-0.61) and exceeded the supervised classifier by 0.36-0.42 on event subtypes absent from its training labels. It outperformed the classifier when fewer than ~4 labeled events per class were available. Jev was 20-40x faster than frontier LLMs. The gated cascade spared an LLM reviewer 35-38% of windows without loss of macro-F1, and remained within non-inferiority margins when transferred to two other networks.

Conclusion: A fast, training-free screen can take over about one-third of the review load in SCADA anomaly triage while preserving the accuracy of deliberate review. This approach offers a practical solution for water utility operators to quickly filter alarms before involving more resource-intensive methods like LLMs.

Abstract: When a SCADA alarm is raised in a water distribution network, operators must decide quickly whether it reflects a cyberattack, a physical fault, a normal transient or a faulty sensor. Supervised classifiers need labelled incidents that utilities rarely have, and frontier large language models (LLMs) take tens of seconds per decision. We tested whether Jev, a training-free model that returns class probabilities in about one second, can serve as the first tier of this triage. On a four-class cause-attribution benchmark built on the C-Town network in EPANET, Jev was compared with a hand-written rule tree, a supervised classifier and seven cloud LLMs on identical evidence in four sealed, pre-registered rounds. With only a label-free prior correction, Jev matched the rule tree (macro-F1 0.62-0.64 against 0.56-0.61 in distribution) and exceeded the supervised classifier by 0.36-0.42 on event subtypes absent from its labels, in all four rounds, and it outperformed the classifier whenever fewer than about four labelled events per class were available. Jev also decided 20-40 times faster than frontier LLMs. Accepting only benign Jev verdicts confirmed by the rule tree spared an LLM reviewer 35-38% of windows on fresh sealed sets without loss of macro-F1. Transferred unchanged to two further networks, this gated cascade stayed within the non-inferiority margin of its reviewer on all four sets. A fast, training-free screen can therefore take over about a third of the review load in SCADA anomaly triage while preserving the accuracy of deliberate review.

</details>


### [301] [External Observers May See More Clearly: Cross-Model Span-Level Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models via Hidden State Probing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02066)
*Kingshuk Gupta,Davide Buscaldi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces an internal hidden state framework for fine-grained, span-level hallucination detection in Large Language Models (LLMs), moving beyond token-wise binary classification to capture the sequential boundaries of semantic drift. The approach inspects layer-wise activation patterns to detect hallucination onset and continuation tokens, and additionally proposes a novel cross-model detection framework where one model observes another's internal representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly serve as foundational reasoning engines, but their tendency to hallucinate remains a critical vulnerability. Existing internal state probes reduce hallucination detection to token-wise binary classification, which fails to capture the structured, sequential boundaries of semantic drift - meaning current methods cannot precisely identify when hallucination begins and how it propagates through generated text.

Method: The paper proposes two key methods: (1) A fine-grained span-level hallucination detection framework that inspects layer-wise activation patterns to identify exact hallucination onset and continuation tokens in LLM generation; (2) A novel cross-model detection framework where one model (observer) monitors the internal representations elicited by another model's generation, enabling external detection of hallucinations.

Result: The approach successfully isolates hallucination onsets and achieves substantial improvements in Precision-Recall AUC over random baselines, despite extreme class imbalance (hallucination tokens are rare). In the cross-model framework, an external observer can match or exceed a generator's self-detection of hallucination onsets, including when the observer is a smaller model, demonstrating that self-detection is not the ceiling for onset localization.

Conclusion: Internal hidden state analysis enables precise span-level hallucination detection beyond binary token classification. The novel cross-model detection paradigm shows that external observers can match or outperform self-detection, even with smaller models, suggesting that self-detection is not the upper bound for hallucination onset localization. This opens avenues for more effective hallucination mitigation strategies.

Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as foundational reasoning engines, their tendency to hallucinate remains a critical vulnerability. While recent internal state probes offer a promising alternative to slow external retrieval systems, they largely reduce hallucination detection to a token-wise binary classification task, failing to capture the structured, sequential boundaries of semantic drift. Here, we introduce an internal hidden state framework for fine-grained, span-level hallucination detection. By inspecting layer-wise activation patterns, we attempt to detect the exact hallucination onset and continuation tokens in an LLM generation. Our experiments show that this approach successfully isolates hallucination onsets, achieving substantial improvements in Precision-Recall AUC over random baselines despite extreme class imbalance. Ultimately, we propose a novel cross-model detection framework in which one model observes the internal representations elicited by another model's generation. We find that an external observer can match or exceed a generator's self-detection of its own hallucination onsets, including when the observer is the smaller model, suggesting that self-detection is not the ceiling for onset localisation.

</details>


### [302] [Causal Memory Policy: Making Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02070)
*Arman Behnam,Binghui Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical identification problem in memory-augmented LLMs: when memories are never retrieved, their utility cannot be estimated using standard methods. The authors propose Causal Memory Policy (CMP), which intervenes on retrieval itself to identify memory utility through causal inference techniques, though they also find that identified utility alone is insufficient for retention decisions on unseen queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current memory-augmented LLM systems estimate memory utility based only on retrieved memories. However, when a memory is never retrieved, its utility remains unidentified—this is a "retrieval-level positivity violation" that existing diagnostics cannot detect since they only examine memory operations rather than retrieval processes.

Method: CMP introduces a causal framework that intervenes on retrieval by reserving fixed context slots for memories sampled with known propensities. Memory utility is estimated using self-normalized inverse propensity weighting under a balanced assignment design. The theoretical analysis proves: (1) causal factorization of memory utility through retrieval, (2) unbiasedness and exact variance of the estimator, and (3) optimal decision rule under irreversible operations.

Result: Empirically, identification fails for 54% of required memories on LongMemEval and 67% on LoCoMo datasets. This failure persists even in deployed memory systems. CMP improves discrimination between required and non-required memories from 0.54 to 0.66 AUC. Notably, per-query utility achieves 0.78 AUC on the query it was estimated for, yet no aggregation method can predict a memory's value on unseen queries.

Conclusion: The paper reveals a fundamental identification problem in memory-augmented LLMs and provides CMP as a solution. However, a key limitation emerges: even with correct identification of memory utility, no aggregation method can reliably predict a memory's usefulness for future unseen queries, suggesting that retention decisions may require approaches beyond utility estimation.

Abstract: Memory-augmented large language models must decide which memories to retain, and recent systems do so by estimating each memory's effect on task performance. However, these estimates rely entirely on retrieved memories. When a memory is never retrieved, store-level interventions produce identical outcomes, leaving its utility unidentified. This is a retrieval-level positivity violation, invisible to diagnostics that examine only memory operations. We introduce Causal Memory Policy (CMP), a causal framework that restores identification by intervening on retrieval itself, reserving a fixed number of context slots for memories sampled with known propensities. CMP estimates memory utility by self-normalized inverse propensity weighting under a balanced assignment design. We prove the causal factorization of memory utility through retrieval, the unbiasedness and exact variance of the estimator, and the optimal decision rule under irreversible operations. Empirically, identification fails for 54% of required memories on LongMemEval and 67% on LoCoMo, and the failure persists in a deployed memory system. CMP improves discrimination between required and non-required memories from 0.54 to 0.66 AUC. Finally, we show that identified memory utility alone is insufficient for retention decisions: per-query utility reaches 0.78 AUC on the query for which it is estimated, yet no aggregation available to a retention policy predicts a memory's value on unseen queries. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/cmp-release-D0C3/.

</details>


### [303] [PyPottery: an AI-powered end-to-end suite for pottery processing and publication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02072)
*Lorenzo Cardarelli*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PyPottery is an open-source AI-powered suite with four modules (PyPotteryScan, PyPotteryInk, PyPotteryTrace, PyPotteryLayout) that semi-automates ceramic documentation workflows, achieving a median 40x speedup over traditional methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ceramic materials study is fundamental to archaeological research, but the post-production workflow for pottery documentation remains labor-intensive and creates significant publication bottlenecks. There was a need for AI-assisted tools to streamline this traditionally manual process.

Method: The framework was evaluated on 50 hand-drawn sheets containing 240 pottery drawings from the Terramara di Montale (Italy). The four integrated modules perform: automated image extraction and handwriting recognition (PyPotteryScan), automatic inking of pencil drawings (PyPotteryInk), semantically-aware vectorization (PyPotteryTrace), and automated layout generation (PyPotteryLayout). Usability studies were conducted with participants to assess the time savings.

Result: The framework achieved substantial time savings. Usability study participants reported a median perceived speedup of 40x over traditional workflows, with a range of 17.5x to 120x.

Conclusion: AI-assisted tools like PyPottery have significant potential in archaeological documentation. The paper addresses the strategic redistribution of cognitive labor toward augmentation rather than full automation, suggesting a human-AI collaboration model rather than complete replacement.

Abstract: The study of ceramic materials constitutes a cornerstone of archaeological research, yet the post-production workflow for pottery documentation remains labor-intensive and creates significant publication bottlenecks. This paper presents PyPottery, an open-source, AI-powered suite designed to semi-automate the complete ceramic documentation pipeline. The suite comprises four integrated modules: PyPotteryScan for automated image extraction and handwriting recognition; PyPotteryInk for automatic inking of pencil drawings; PyPotteryTrace for semantically-aware vectorization; and PyPotteryLayout for automated layout generation. Evaluated on 50 hand-drawn sheets containing 240 pottery drawings from the Terramara di Montale (Italy), the framework achieved substantial time savings confirmed by usability study participants, who reported a median perceived speedup of 40$\times$ over traditional workflows (range: 17.5$\times$--120$\times$). These results highlight the potential of AI-assisted tools in archaeological documentation, while the paper addresses the strategic redistribution of cognitive labor toward augmentation rather than automation.

</details>


### [304] [Homomorphic Advantage Operator: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning Under Fully Homomorphic Encryption Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02074)
*Abid Mohamed Nadhir,Ahmad Al Hanbali,Beggas Mounir*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces HAO (Homomorphic Advantage Operator), a stabilization framework for applying Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to deep reinforcement learning. HAO prevents polynomial approximation divergence caused by the Bellman drift by adapting zero-mean centering projection from advantage-based value estimation to TD targets, requiring no additional non-linear multiplicative depth or expensive ciphertext bootstrapping.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying privacy-preserving machine learning on cloud for intelligent systems with confidential data faces significant challenges. While FHE offers a solution for secure computation, applying it to reinforcement learning requires replacing non-linear operations with polynomial approximations that diverge catastrophically due to a unique recursive error phenomenon called the Bellman drift.

Method: HAO adapts the zero-mean centering projection from advantage-based value estimation directly to temporal-difference (TD) targets. This linear projection annihilates the uniform state-value baseline that drives the Bellman drift, maintaining per-state action rankings while requiring zero additional non-linear multiplicative depth and avoiding expensive ciphertext bootstrapping. Evaluation used three-tier methodology: tabular MDP, encrypted CartPole with real CKKS operations, and 20-node logistics routing benchmark.

Result: HAO strictly bounds network pre-activations within the safe polynomial approximation domain. HAO RL agents achieved 0% boundary breaches across all random seeds, while regularization alone (L2 weight decay and gradient clipping) breached on 3 of 5 seeds and unstabilized baseline did so in 83.8% of episodes. HAO agents improve optimal policy accuracy by 18.0 percentage points in tabular domains and remain stable when DP-SGD-style Gaussian noise is added to clipped gradients.

Conclusion: HAO provides an effective stabilization framework for FHE-based deep reinforcement learning, successfully preventing polynomial approximation divergence through zero-mean centering projection. The framework achieves 0% boundary breaches, significant improvement in policy accuracy, and compatibility with differential privacy techniques, making it practical for privacy-preserving cloud-based RL applications.

Abstract: Privacy-preserving machine learning presents significant deployment challenges on the cloud for intelligent systems with confidential data. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) offers a compelling solution for secure computation, preserving data confidentiality of cloud computations. However, applying FHE to reinforcement learning (RL) requires replacing non-linear operations with polynomial approximations, which diverge catastrophically due to a unique recursive error phenomenon known as the Bellman drift. This article introduces the Homomorphic Advantage Operator (HAO), a stabilization framework designed to prevent polynomial approximation divergence in FHE-based deep RL. HAO adapts the zero-mean centering projection from advantage-based value estimation directly to temporal-difference (TD) targets. This linear projection annihilates the uniform state-value baseline that drives the Bellman drift, maintaining per-state action rankings while requiring zero additional non-linear multiplicative depth and avoiding expensive ciphertext bootstrapping. The proposed HAO framework was evaluated using a three-tier experimental methodology, including a tabular Markov Decision Process (MDP), an encrypted CartPole environment using real CKKS cryptographic operations, and a 20-node logistics routing benchmark with dense continuous features. The results demonstrate that the proposed HAO strictly bounds network pre-activations within the safe polynomial approximation domain. The proposed HAO RL agents achieved 0% boundary breaches across all random seeds used, whereas regularization alone (L2 weight decay and gradient clipping) breached the bound on 3 of 5 seeds and the unstabilized baseline did so in 83.8% of episodes. Finally, HAO agents improve optimal policy accuracy by 18.0 percentage points in tabular domains and remain stable when DP-SGD-style Gaussian noise is added to the clipped gradients.

</details>


### [305] [A Comparative Explainability Framework for DeBERTa-v3 in Zero-Shot Medical Abstract Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02116)
*Javier Diaz Esteban-Herreros,David Muñoz-Valero,Raquel Martínez-España,Jose M. Juarez,Juan Moreno-Garcia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a comparative explainability framework to audit DeBERTa-v3 for zero-shot medical abstract classification, addressing the "disagreement problem" where different attribution methods produce divergent explanations. The study compares five explanation methods (SHAP, LIME, Occlusion, Input x Gradient, Attention x Gradient) using Jaccard index to quantify pairwise agreement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the disagreement problem in Explainable AI, where different attribution methods produce conflicting explanations for the same input and prediction, specifically in the context of medical text classification using transformer models.

Method: Implemented an NLI engine over the Medical Abstracts corpus with five enriched hypotheses per diagnostic category and 1,000 balanced samples per class. Compared five explanation methods: SHAP and LIME (model-agnostic), Occlusion and Input x Gradient (deep-learning-specific), and Attention x Gradient (transformer-specific). Standardized explanations through top-token attribution and quantified pairwise agreement using Jaccard index.

Result: High predictive accuracy achieved across well-defined clinical domains, but performance degrades under high semantic ambiguity. Explanatory stability directly mirrors predictive certainty—strong convergence in univalent categories, marked drop under diagnostic uncertainty. Three systemic failure mechanisms identified: lexical hypersensitivity, semantic overlap, and loss of attribution coherence.

Conclusion: The combined use of multiple explanation methods and quantitative agreement metrics is recommended for auditing transformer-based models in medical text classification. Specific clinical ontologies should be prioritized over broad diagnostic labels to improve reliability.

Abstract: A comparative explainability framework is presented to audit DeBERTa-v3 under zero-shot classification of medical abstracts. The work addresses the disagreement problem in Explainable Artificial Intelligence, where different attribution methods produce divergent explanations for the same input and prediction. A natural language inference engine is implemented over the Medical Abstracts corpus with five enriched hypotheses per diagnostic category and a balanced sample of one thousand texts per class. Five explanation methods are compared: SHAP and LIME as model-agnostic approaches, occlusion and Input x Gradient as deep-learning-specific approaches, and Attention x Gradient as a transformer-specific approach. Explanations are standardized through top-token attribution, and pairwise agreement is quantified using the Jaccard index. High predictive accuracy is achieved across well-defined clinical domains, whereas performance degrades under high semantic ambiguity. Explanatory stability directly mirrors predictive certainty, exhibiting strong convergence in univalent categories and a marked drop under diagnostic uncertainty. Furthermore, qualitative error auditing uncovers three systemic failure mechanisms: lexical hypersensitivity, semantic overlap, and loss of attribution coherence. The results support the combined use of several explanation methods and quantitative agreement metrics when auditing transformer-based models in medical text classification, and suggest prioritizing specific clinical ontologies over broad diagnostic labels.

</details>


### [306] [VISTA: A Visual Harness for Reasoning in an Interactive World](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02200)
*Qiushi Han,Keya Hu,Linlu Qiu,Cathy Wu,Kaiming He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: We show that multimodal models possess strong reasoning abilities and that an appropriate harness can unlock their potential to solve tasks across diverse interactive environments. We introduce VISTA, a visual harness that gives a general-purpose multimodal model long-horizon vision. VISTA allows the model to directly perceive the environment through visual observations and maintains a lossless visual memory that preserves past observations in their original form. The model can actively retrieve these observations and reorganize its visual input as it reasons. On ARC-AGI-3, VISTA improves Claude Opus 5.0's Relative Human Action Efficiency score from 40.68 to a perfect 100.00, with the model completing all 25 public games using 57.4% fewer actions than first-time human participants. VISTA's simple design also allows it to extend naturally to diverse visual environments with minimal adaptation. Across three additional benchmarks covering a diverse range of visual games and puzzles, it substantially outperforms baselines using the same underlying model with minimal harnesses. Our results highlight VISTA's potential as a general-purpose visual harness for advancing multimodal agents in complex visual environments.

</details>


### [307] [ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02202)
*Sohyeon Kim,Yoonho Lee,Bo Liu,Dayoon Ko,Rulin Shao,Seungone Kim,Graham Neubig,Pang Wei Koh,Aakanksha Chowdhery,Akari Asai,Omar Khattab,Yejin Choi,Gunhee Kim,Chelsea Finn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper studies how scientists identify relevant prior work for their research projects, and whether AI systems can replicate this skill. The authors built ScholarCatalyst, a dataset with 184 lead authors labeling which prior papers advanced their projects. They found that AI agents (0.42 R@20) underperform embedding retrieval (0.48 R@20), with even advanced models like Claude Fable 5.1 only reaching 0.51 R@20, highlighting the need for new training methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding what makes great scientists effective at identifying relevant prior work from an ever-growing research archive, and whether current AI systems can replicate this skill in scientific discovery.

Method: Built ScholarCatalyst using an automated pipeline where 184 lead authors of 207 recent CS papers labeled which prior papers did or could have advanced their project, each with detailed rationale. Created a retrieval task where given an initial research question, the goal is to retrieve relevant papers from literature available when the project began. Tested agentic search and embedding retrieval approaches.

Result: Agentic search (0.42 R@20) performed worse than embedding retrieval (0.48 R@20) despite using the same retriever as a tool. Even Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, only reached 0.51 R@20.

Conclusion: Current AI systems struggle with the expert intuition required for scientific literature search. New training recipes are needed to equip models with this skill. ScholarCatalyst represents a step toward building scientific agents that can take half-formed ideas and identify the prior research they need.

Abstract: What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. Using our automated pipeline that makes author annotation scalable, we build ScholarCatalyst by having 184 lead authors of 207 recent computer science papers label which candidates did or could have advanced their project, each with a detailed rationale. We introduce a retrieval task with author-provided judgments: given an initial research question, retrieve these papers from only the literature available when the project began. Agentic search does no better than embedding retrieval (0.42 vs. 0.48 Recall@20) despite calling that same retriever as a tool. Even an agent built on Claude Fable 5.1, which may have seen the completed papers during training, reaches only 0.51 R@20. These results highlight the need for new training recipes that equip models with expert intuition for searching broad corpora. We envision ScholarCatalyst as a step toward scientific agents that can take a half-formed idea and point to the prior research it needs.

</details>

### [308] [Software Project Management with LLM-Based Automation: Coordination, Validation, and Governance in Practice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00027)
*Ronnie de Souza Santos,Cleyton Magalhaes,Italo Santos*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates how software project managers perceive changes in their work and learning demands when LLM-based automation is integrated into software development. Using an exploratory case study in a large multi-project organization, the research finds that LLMs influence planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities, but do not introduce new formal management practices. Key effects include uneven productivity impacts, increased review/validation needs, reduced visibility into task execution, and greater reliance on managerial judgment. Learning demands are experiential and focus on understanding LLM capabilities, critically assessing outputs, and guiding responsible use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a gap in software engineering research: while LLMs have been extensively studied for task-level and developer-centered uses, there is limited understanding of how automation affects software project managers' work and learning demands. This study addresses that gap by capturing managerial perspectives on LLM-based automation in practice.

Method: The research adopted an exploratory case study approach, collecting data from software project managers working in a large, multi-project software organization. This qualitative method allows for in-depth understanding of managerial perspectives on automation in real-world practice.

Result: The analysis reveals that LLM-based automation influences planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities rather than introducing new formal management practices. LLMs become embedded in everyday project work, producing uneven effects on productivity, increasing the need for review and validation, and reducing visibility into task execution. These effects lead to greater reliance on managerial judgment and coordination. Learning demands were perceived as experiential and incremental, centered on understanding LLM capabilities and limitations, critically assessing generated artifacts, and guiding responsible use within teams.

Conclusion: The findings provide empirical evidence on how software project management work is adapted when LLM-based automation is integrated into ongoing software development practice. The study highlights that automation reshapes managerial activities rather than replacing them, emphasizing the continued importance of human judgment, coordination skills, and ongoing learning in managing LLM-integrated software projects.

Abstract: As software engineering has evolved, development environments have increasingly integrated automated support for tasks such as testing, analysis, and code generation, requiring project management to coordinate both human work and automated workflows. In this paper, we investigate how software project managers perceive changes in their work and learning demands associated with LLM-based automation. Motivated by a gap in software engineering research, which has largely focused on task-level and developer-centered uses of LLMs, we adopted an exploratory case study approach to capture managerial perspectives on automation in practice. Based on the experience of software project managers working in a large, multi-project software organization, our analysis indicates that LLM-based automation influences planning, estimation, coordination, monitoring, and governance activities rather than introducing new formal management practices. Participants described LLMs as becoming embedded in everyday project work, producing uneven effects on productivity, increasing the need for review and validation, and reducing visibility into task execution. These effects contribute to greater reliance on managerial judgment and coordination. Learning demands were perceived as experiential and incremental, centered on understanding LLM capabilities and limitations, critically assessing generated artifacts, and guiding responsible use within teams. The findings provide empirical evidence on how software project management work is adapted in contexts where LLM-based automation is integrated into ongoing software development practice.

</details>


### [309] [Localizing Post-Wire Semantic Changes in MCP Agent Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00182)
*Aditi Patodiya*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper presents a differential testing method for validating Model Context Protocol (MCP) message handling across four agent frameworks. Testing 18 designed fixtures revealed 13 unique divergences involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Only Google ADK fully satisfied all primary contracts, while others showed interface-specific changes or failures. The study emphasizes that post-wire regression tests must specify both information requirements and how consumers read them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent frameworks implementing MCP may not preserve critical distinctions needed by downstream software. The lack of systematic testing across framework interfaces creates potential compatibility issues that aren't caught by standard testing approaches.

Method: Differential testing method that traces a fixed tool result through each framework's public interfaces and checks explicit consumer requirements. Applied to 18 designed fixtures across four pinned Python integrations.

Result: 13 unique fixture-task divergences identified involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfied all primary contracts; other integrations showed interface-specific changes or execution failures. Most failures in OpenAI's strict rich-content handling stemmed from treating absent optional fields as equivalent to null. Exploratory replay showed JSON parsing recovers more structured values but also introduces incorrect values and values for fields absent at source.

Conclusion: Post-wire regression tests need to specify both the information required and how the consumer reads it. The study provides reproducible, interface-specific evidence from controlled cases rather than production failure rates or model-behavior measurements.

Abstract: Valid Model Context Protocol (MCP) messages do not guarantee that an agent framework preserves the distinctions downstream software needs. We present a differential testing method that follows a fixed tool result through each framework's public interfaces and checks explicit consumer requirements. Applied to 18 designed fixtures in four pinned Python integrations, the method identifies 13 unique fixture-task divergences involving structured values, declared errors, and rich content. Google ADK satisfies every primary contract in its observed path; the other integrations show interface-specific changes or an execution failure. Whether a change matters depends on the consumer: treating absent optional fields as equivalent to null explains most of OpenAI's strict rich-content failures. In an exploratory replay, parsing JSON text recovers more structured values but also returns incorrect values and values for fields absent at the source. Documented settings help in conflicting-output stress cases without restoring a separate structured slot. Fault challenges expose an oracle weakness and test its repair on fresh cases. The study provides reproducible, interface-specific evidence from controlled cases, not production failure rates or model-behavior measurements. Its practical implication is that post-wire regression tests need to specify both the information required and how the consumer reads it.

</details>


### [310] [Testing and Verification of Quantum Compilers through Assurance Contracts and Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00255)
*Furqan Nasir,Muhammad Arif Shah,Iftikhar Alam*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This is a comparative survey paper analyzing methods for ensuring correctness of quantum compilers, including verified transformations, equivalence checking, and various testing approaches. The paper provides a source catalogue, extraction matrix, and worked examples to demonstrate why circuit validation may miss interface-level errors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantum compiler assurance requires semantic relations matching intended use and observations that can expose violations at the delivered interface. This integrative survey addresses the need to compare different verification methods for quantum compilers.

Method: The paper compares verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential and metamorphic testing, and property-based testing. It uses a source catalogue and extraction matrix to distinguish formal guarantees, empirical findings, analytical deductions, and proposed practice. Includes worked examples involving layout metadata, parameter bindings, and ancillary qubits.

Result: Four documented failure cases connect conditional applicability, parameter association, termination, and phase conventions to method selection. Validating circuits under reconstructed interpretation can leave delivered interface unchecked. Published bug counts, mutation results, and processing benchmarks support different claims but don't establish common effectiveness ranking. The proposed regression architecture remains unevaluated as a complete system.

Conclusion: The resulting guidance specifies applicability, complementary observations, and treatment of inconclusive outcomes. Practical value requires controlled comparisons on independently adjudicated compiler-change events. The proposed regression architecture needs evaluation on actual compiler changes.

Abstract: Quantum compiler assurance requires a semantic relation that matches the intended use and observations that can expose violations at the delivered interface. This critical integrative survey compares verified transformations, equivalence checking, differential and metamorphic testing, property-based testing, and evidence for assurance across revisions. A source catalogue and focused extraction matrix distinguish formal guarantees, reported empirical findings, analytical deductions, and proposed practice. A recorded coverage update and source-level selection decisions make the review auditable within its declared scope. Four documented failure cases connect conditional applicability, parameter association, termination, and phase conventions to method selection. A worked example involving layout metadata, parameter bindings, and ancillary qubits demonstrates why validating a circuit under a reconstructed interpretation can leave the delivered interface unchecked. An illustrative revision scenario then separates fault detection from change attribution. The resulting guidance specifies applicability, complementary observations, and treatment of inconclusive outcomes. Published bug counts, mutation results, and processing benchmarks support different claims and do not establish a common effectiveness ranking. The proposed regression architecture remains unevaluated as a complete system; its practical value requires controlled comparisons on independently adjudicated compiler-change events.

</details>


### [311] [Code That Works, Environments That Don't: Measuring Environment Reproducibility in AI-Generated Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00425)
*Bhanu Prakash Vangala,Tanu Malik*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper introduces a framework for evaluating environment specification in code generation - a critical but overlooked dimension of code quality. The authors propose a three-layer framework (declared, runtime-installed, and necessary-and-sufficient dependencies) and find that current coding agents systematically fail at this task, with dependency agreement as low as 7% across agents for identical tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Functional correctness of generated code is commonly used as the primary quality metric, but environment specification - accurately identifying dependencies required to execute the code - is equally critical but ignored. The authors identify this gap and aim to establish environment specification as a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality.

Method: The authors developed an agent protocol for environment specification and a three-layer framework comprising: (1) declared dependencies (explicitly listed), (2) runtime-installed dependencies (actually needed at execution), and (3) necessary-and-sufficient dependencies (minimal complete set). They evaluated three agents across four languages and fifty programming tasks to assess how agents misspecify software environment dependencies.

Result: Current coding agents exhibit systematic generalization failures in environment specification. Key findings: (1) dependency specifications are inconsistent, redundant, or incomplete; (2) functional tests do not detect these issues; (3) dependency set agreement is as low as 7% for identical tasks across agents; (4) newer agents show no meaningful improvement over older ones; (5) the largest divergence occurs between declared and runtime dependency layers; (6) environment priors learned from training distributions are the primary driver of these failures.

Conclusion: Environment specification is a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality that current benchmarks fail to capture. The systematic failures suggest this is not resolved by model scale or recency. The authors motivate the need for training objectives and evaluation protocols that jointly optimize for functional correctness and environmental portability.

Abstract: Code generation has emerged as a central capability of large language models, with coding agents now able to produce functionally correct software projects from natural language prompts. However, functional correctness alone does not capture a critical dimension of generation quality: environment specification, defined as the accurate identification of the dependencies required to execute generated code, is equally critical. We develop an agent protocol for environment specification and introduce a three-layer framework comprising declared, runtime-installed, and necessary-and-sufficient dependencies to systematically assess coding agents for environment specification. Using this protocol, we evaluate the extent to which coding agents systematically misspecify software environment dependencies and how this misspecification varies across three agents, four languages, and fifty programming tasks. Our results show that current coding agents exhibit systematic generalization failures along this dimension, producing dependency specifications that are inconsistent, redundant, or incomplete in ways that functional tests do not detect. Across agents, dependency set agreement is as low as 7% for identical tasks, and newer agents show no meaningful improvement, suggesting the failure is not resolved by scale or recency. The largest divergence occurs between the declared and runtime dependency layers, implicating environment priors learned from the models' training distributions as the primary driver. Our findings establish environment specification as a distinct, measurable axis of code generation quality that current benchmarks do not capture, and motivate training objectives and evaluation protocols that jointly optimize for functional correctness and environmental portability.

</details>


### [312] [Extending LLM-based support for software engineers with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00555)
*Aarsh Shah,Ronnie de Souza Santos,Italo Santos,Cleyton Magalhaes,Kiev Gama*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Tether 2.0 is an LLM-based assistant designed to support software engineers with ADHD through structured workflow-oriented interaction across planning, coding, debugging, and review phases. It combines structured interaction modes, activity-aware context, and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software engineering workflows are not designed for developers with ADHD, despite known challenges with task initiation, sustained attention, and completion. Existing LLM-integrated programming tools do not account for neurodiversity or support structured progression across development tasks.

Method: The approach combines structured interaction modes, activity-aware context, and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity. The system was evaluated through expert feedback and hands-on use with a software engineer with ADHD.

Result: Tether 2.0 supports requirement clarification, task decomposition, incremental implementation, debugging, and completion. It enables users to maintain progress and resume work after interruptions.

Conclusion: LLM-based assistants can support direction, sustained progress, and learning in software development when designed with workflow structure and context-aware interaction, specifically for neurodiverse users.

Abstract: Software engineering workflows are often not designed to accommodate the needs of developers with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), despite known challenges related to task initiation, sustained attention, and completion. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into programming tools, but existing systems do not account for neurodiversity or support structured progression across development tasks. In this work, we present Tether 2.0, an LLM based assistant designed to support software engineers with ADHD through workflow oriented interaction across planning, coding, debugging, and review. The tool was named Tether 2.0 because it builds upon the open source code and foundations of the original Tether system. Our approach combines structured interaction modes, activity aware context, and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity. We evaluate the system through expert feedback and hands on use with a software engineer with ADHD. Our results indicate that Tether 2.0 supports requirement clarification, task decomposition, incremental implementation, debugging, and completion, while enabling users to maintain progress and resume work after interruptions. These findings suggest that LLM based assistants can support direction, sustained progress, and learning in software development when designed with workflow structure and context aware interaction.

</details>


### [313] [Understanding and Mitigating Library-Related Issues in LLM-Generated Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00622)
*Yacine Majdoub,Rinad Hamid,Eya Ben Charrada,Ahmad Abdellatif,Haifa Touati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses library-related errors in LLM-generated code (e.g., invalid imports, outdated APIs, hallucinated dependencies) by proposing an agentic approach that integrates task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation. The study analyzes 100 LLM-generated files (84% contain errors) and evaluates the approach on 300 tasks across 5 LLMs, achieving 38.1%-54.6% error reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs increasingly assist software practitioners in code generation, but often produce incorrect library usage leading to compilation/runtime failures. This undermines reliability of AI-assisted software development, especially for rapidly evolving Python frameworks where APIs change frequently.

Method: The researchers conducted: (1) An exploratory study analyzing 100 LLM-generated code files to characterize library-related issues; (2) Design of an agentic approach with four components - task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation; (3) Evaluation on 300 code generation tasks from LangChain and AutoGen across five LLMs (GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Mistral, Llama 3).

Result: 84% of generated files contain at least one library-related error. Common patterns include incorrect import paths, missing imports, hallucinated libraries, deprecated usage, and unused imports. The proposed approach reduced library-related errors by 38.1%-54.6% and increased code correctness by up to 16% across all evaluated models.

Conclusion: The agentic approach effectively mitigates library-related errors in LLM-generated code. The combination of task analysis, documentation grounding, and automated validation provides a promising solution for improving reliability of AI-assisted software development, with consistent improvements across different LLM models.

Abstract: Software practitioners increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate code that integrates external libraries. However, LLMs often produce incorrect library usage, such as invalid imports, outdated API calls, and hallucinated dependencies, leading to compilation or runtime failures that reduce the reliability of AI-assisted software development. In this paper, we propose an agentic approach to mitigate libraryrelated errors in LLM-generated code. More specifically, we first conduct an exploratory study to characterize the library-related issues produced by LLMs. Our analysis of 100 LLM-generated code files reveals that 84% of generated files contain at least one library-related error, with recurring patterns including incorrect import paths, missing imports, hallucinated libraries, deprecated library usage, and unused imports. Based on these findings, we design an agentic approach that integrates task analysis, documentation grounding, code generation, and automated validation to improve library usage during code synthesis. We evaluate our approach on 300 code generation tasks derived from realworld implementations of rapidly evolving Python frameworks, including LangChain and AutoGen, across five LLMs: GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3, Mistral, and Llama 3. The results show that our approach consistently improves code generation quality across all evaluated models, reducing library-related errors by 38.1% - 54.6% and increasing code correctness by up to 16%.

</details>


### [314] [ASAD: Adaptive Software Agents for Debugging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00629)
*Yacine Majdoub,Eya Ben Charrada,Haifa Touati*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ASAD is an adaptive multi-agent debugging system that dynamically configures agent teams based on bug complexity, using a central coordinator for iterative planning, reflection, and execution. It outperforms static approaches by 12-20% in fix rates and 4-9% in precision while reducing agent usage by 32%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM-based multi-agent debugging frameworks rely on rigid, predefined architectures where the number of agents, roles, and interaction patterns are fixed before bug analysis. This one-size-fits-all approach is mismatched to the heterogeneous nature of software defects—simple bugs waste resources on unnecessary coordination, while complex bugs suffer from insufficient or poorly aligned expertise.

Method: ASAD initiates debugging by analyzing the faulty code and dynamically determines: (1) the number of agents to deploy, (2) the specialized roles they should have, and (3) the collaboration strategy they should follow. A central coordinator orchestrates the process through iterative planning, reflection, and execution—applying fast single-pass repairs for simple issues while assembling purpose-built teams for complex failures.

Result: Evaluated on Defects4J, DebugBench, and CodeFlaws using DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3, and GPT-5: (1) Improves bug-fix rates by 12-20% over chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, (2) Outperforms static multi-agent systems by 4-9% in fix precision, (3) Reduces average agent usage by 32%. The system dynamically adjusts agent count and roles—resolving simple bugs with minimal coordination and scaling involvement only for complex cases.

Conclusion: ASAD demonstrates that adaptive agent configuration based on bug nature and complexity significantly improves debugging performance. The key innovation is the dynamic, on-demand allocation of agents and roles rather than static, predefined teams, leading to better resource efficiency and higher fix rates across diverse software defects.

Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into multi-agent systems has shown great potential for automated debugging. Yet nearly all current frameworks rely on rigid, predefined architectures: the number of agents, their roles, and their interaction patterns are fixed before any analysis of the bug occurs. This one-size-fits-all approach is fundamentally mismatched to the heterogeneous nature of software defects. Simple bugs waste resources on unnecessary coordination, while complex ones suffer from insufficient or poorly aligned expertise. This paper introduces ASAD, an adaptive agentic system for debugging that configures its team according to the nature and complexity of each bug. ASAD initiates the debugging process by analyzing the faulty code and dynamically determines the number of agents to deploy, the specialized roles they should have, and the collaboration strategy they should follow. A central coordinator orchestrates this process through iterative planning, reflection, and execution; applying fast single-pass repairs for simple issues while assembling purpose-built teams to tackle more complex failures. We evaluate ASAD on three established benchmarks: Defects4J, DebugBench, and CodeFlaws, using multiple LLMs, such as DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3 and GPT-5. ASAD consistently improves bug-fix rates by 12--20% over chain-of-thought(CoT) prompting and consistently outperforms static multi-agent systems by 4--9% in fix precision while reducing average agent usage by 32%. Crucially, our system dynamically adjusts the number and roles of agents: it resolves simple bugs with minimal coordination and scales agent involvement only for more complex cases.

</details>


### [315] [FORALL-LEAN-AGENT for Auditable Reasoning in Formal Mathematics and Software Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00885)
*Naing Oo Lwin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Coding agents increasingly automate Lean proof development, but successful compilation alone does not establish that a candidate proves the intended statement under acceptable assumptions. We present FORALL-LEAN-AGENT, a frontend-agnostic framework for auditable reasoning in formal mathematics and software verification. The framework combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, and fresh review with statement comparison, axiom audits, and independent proof checking where supported. Verification evidence and reviewer decisions are bound to the same candidate artifact, making acceptance traceable. We evaluate the framework on VeriSoftBench, PutnamBench, and both problems in the Lean Eval softwareverification track. On the 100-task VeriSoftBench subset, integration with FORALLLEAN-AGENT raises benchmark-rule success from 93 to 100 for GPT-5.6 Sol at low effort while reducing cost from $69 to $62. The PutnamBench evaluation accepts all 672 problems at an average of $4.72 each. These results show that agent harness design can improve correctness and efficiency while providing evidence beyond aggregate solve counts.
