### [316] [Understanding Issues, Causes and Solutions in Open-Source LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00905)
*Asad Ur Rehman,Syed Mohammad Kashif,Ruiyin Li,Peng Liang,Zengyang Li,Arif Ali Khan*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An empirical study analyzing 944 issues from 21 open-source LLM-based multi-agent systems to identify challenges, causes, and solutions. Findings show Orchestration & Execution Issues are most common, with Workflow/Tool Integration/Memory Problems as primary causes, and Workflow Optimization as the main solution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the growing adoption of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) in open-source projects, there is limited understanding of the practical challenges practitioners face, their root causes, and potential solutions. This study addresses this gap by systematically analyzing real-world issues from open-source LLM-based MAS projects.

Method: Collected 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-based MAS projects. Applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to identify 944 issues specifically related to LLM-based MAS. These issues were then analyzed to identify frequent problems, underlying causes, and potential solutions.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners; (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are the most frequent causes of issues; (3) Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution approach.

Conclusion: The study provides empirically grounded implications for practitioners and researchers to improve orchestration, tool integration, and memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS. The findings suggest these three areas are critical for enhancing the reliability and performance of multi-agent systems.

Abstract: With the advancement of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), an increasing number of opensource projects are adopting multi-agent architectures as the foundation of their core functionality. Although research and practice on MAS have attracted considerable attention, limited studies have explored the challenges faced by practitioners of open-source LLM-based MAS, the causes of these challenges, and potential solutions. To address this gap,we conducted an empirical study to understand the issues that practitioners encounter when developing and using open-source LLM-based MAS, the possible causes of these issues, and potential solutions. We collected 22,848 closed issues from 21 open-source LLM-basedMASand applied a mixed automated and manual filtering approach to reduce the dataset to 944 issues related to LLM-based MAS.We then analyzed these issues to understand the frequent issues encountered by practitioners, their underlying causes, and potential solutions. Our study results show that (1) Orchestration & Execution Issue is the most common issue faced by practitioners, (2) Workflow Problem, Tool Integration Problem, and Memory Problem are identified as the most frequent causes of the issues, and (3) Optimize Workflow is the predominant solution to the issues. Based on the study results, we derive empirically grounded implications for practitioners and researchers aimed at improving orchestration, tool integration, and memory mechanisms in LLM-based MAS.

</details>


### [317] [Groundability, Not Scale Alone: When Weak Reviewers Can Audit Strong Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01023)
*Junyu Guo,Shangding Gu,Ming Jin,Javad Lavaei*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably determine whether a code patch solves its issue, addressing the challenge of reviewing plausible but incomplete patches from coding agents. The study analyzes 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents and 101 controlled cases, finding that structured but unchecked evidence improves defect detection but also increases over-rejection. A frozen cascade approach using patch-caused static errors and generated tests achieves 0.89 coverage and 0.76 catch rate on GPT-5.4 traces, with the main bottleneck being producing reliable checks without official tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can return plausible patches that omit required behavior, making review difficult because long traces and confident summaries often hide what was missed. This research aims to determine when a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably decide whether a patch solves its issue.

Method: The study analyzed 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents and 101 controlled cases. They evaluated structured but unchecked evidence on 154 GPT-5.4 traces, then provided official execution evidence as an upper-bound diagnostic. They tested five of six reviewers on 122 held-out traces after freezing one of two formats per reviewer. They also evaluated a frozen cascade with patch-caused static errors and generated tests that first fail on the unpatched repository.

Result: On 154 GPT-5.4 traces, structured but unchecked evidence raised both defect catch and over-rejection. With official execution evidence, five of six reviewers improved both rates on 122 held-out traces; two classified every trace correctly. Reviewer size was not a consistent predictor of quality. The frozen cascade achieved: on 121 GPT-5.4 traces - coverage 0.89, risk 0.33, catch 0.76, over-rejection 0.66; on 59 Gemini traces - coverage 0.86, risk 0.26, catch 0.80, over-rejection 0.67. Most false rejections occurred when unresolved cases reached the reviewer.

Conclusion: Official execution evidence shows the potential of weak review when decisive checks are available. However, producing equally reliable checks without official tests remains the main bottleneck. The frozen cascade approach provides a promising alternative but still has significant over-rejection rates.

Abstract: Coding agents can return plausible patches that omit required behavior. These failures are hard to review because long traces and confident summaries often hide what was missed. We ask when a nominally weaker reviewer can reliably decide whether a patch solves its issue. We study 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents and 101 controlled cases. On 154 GPT-5.4 traces, structured but unchecked evidence raises both defect catch and over-rejection. We then provide official execution evidence as an upper-bound diagnostic. After choosing and freezing one of two formats per reviewer, five of six reviewers improve both rates on 122 held-out traces; two classify every trace correctly. Reviewer size is not a consistent predictor of quality. Because official tests are unavailable in deployment, we also evaluate a frozen cascade with patch-caused static errors and generated tests that first fail on the unpatched repository. On 121 scored held-out GPT-5.4 traces and 59 Gemini traces, its coverage is 0.89 and 0.86, risk is 0.33 and 0.26, catch is 0.76 and 0.80, and over-rejection is 0.66 and 0.67. Most false rejections occur when unresolved cases reach the reviewer. Official execution evidence shows the potential of weak review when decisive checks are available. Producing equally reliable checks without official tests remains the main bottleneck.

</details>


### [318] [Safety Must Survive Self-Improvement: Why Failures Persist and How Agents Recover](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01073)
*Yunbei Zhang,Janet Wang,Saiyue Lyu,Yingqiang Ge,Kaiqu Liang,Zijian Jin,Chandan K Reddy,Jihun Hamm*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper studies safety challenges in recursive self-improvement (RSI) systems where AI agents optimize themselves across generations. Using a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks with LLM editors, the authors show that unsafe programs can persist across generations (22/48 cases) due to historical scores preserving incorrect solutions. They propose interventions including score refreshing, editing initial implementations, and validated rollback to maintain safety while preserving 43% deployment savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address safety concerns in recursive self-improvement systems, where agents pass useful changes across generations. The key challenge is preventing unsafe behavior from persisting while enabling recovery when failures occur. The authors identify a critical problem: when authorization dependencies change, historical scores can incorrectly preserve unsafe programs that were previously validated but are no longer safe under current conditions.

Method: The authors use a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks with fixed LLM editors that optimize executable agent components. Independent traces record the effects of revisions. They implement paired interventions that separate: (1) which revisions pass validation, (2) which program continues running, and (3) which program the editor revises next. They study scenarios including authorization dependency changes, unchanged contracts with rejected proposals, and recovery by editing initial vs. failed implementations.

Result: Key findings include: (1) Historical scores preserve unsafe programs in 22/48 framework histories despite correct alternatives existing in every affected archive; (2) Refreshing scores restores correctness on original suite but residual failures remain on independently composed tests; (3) Failures persist under unchanged contracts when all proposals are rejected and failed incumbent remains active; (4) Editing initial implementation instead of failed one improves recovery, though advantage varies across editors; (5) Full validation and validated rollback achieve fully correct programs in core trajectory while retaining over 43% deployment savings.

Conclusion: The conclusion emphasizes that preserving agent safety in RSI systems requires two critical practices: (1) checking what will run under current conditions (not relying on historical validation), and (2) carefully choosing which implementation to edit next. The authors demonstrate that combining full validation with validated rollback can maintain safety while achieving significant deployment savings, suggesting practical approaches for safer RSI systems.

Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) allows agents to carry useful changes across generations. Maintaining safety across these generations involves both preventing unsafe behavior from persisting and enabling recovery when failures occur. We study these challenges through a controlled testbed of stateful authorization tasks, where fixed LLM editors optimize executable agent components and independent traces record their effects. Paired interventions separate which revisions pass validation, which program continues running, and which program the editor revises next. After a new authorization dependency invalidates previously tested optimizations, historical scores preserve the same unsafe programs in 22 of 48 framework histories despite a correct alternative in every affected archive. Refreshing scores restores correctness on the original suite, with residual failures on independently composed tests. Failures also persist under an unchanged contract when all proposals are rejected and the failed incumbent remains active. Starting from shared failures, editing the initial implementation instead of the failed one improves recovery, although the advantage varies across editors. Full validation and validated rollback end with fully correct programs in the core trajectory study while retaining over 43% deployment savings. Preserving agent safety requires checking what will run under current conditions and choosing which implementation to edit next.

</details>


### [319] [CompProv Produces Machine Readable Graphs Encoding Microscopic Algebraic Provenance for Reproducible Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01203)
*Minas Abramyan,Mohammed Alaa Ala'anzy,Nasir Saeed*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CompProv is a Java-based audit-oriented provenance framework that captures lineage at the atomic level of individual algebraic operations by encapsulating numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects, producing a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) for deterministic replay and sensitivity analysis without exposing proprietary source code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing provenance systems operate at coarse granularity (files, datasets, pipeline stages), leaving internal algebraic transformations unrecorded. Rounding errors, undocumented substitutions, or missing intermediate values can propagate to final results without recoverable trace, compromising reliability in scientific research and financial modeling.

Method: CompProv encapsulates numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects to capture operation-level lineage, producing a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) that persists as a self-contained artifact rather than a discarded byproduct. Three heterogeneous case studies (DeFi NAV calculation, interferometric gauge-block calibration in metrology, and hydrological model performance evaluation) were used for evaluation.

Result: Deterministic replay reproduced each result exactly in a fresh environment. CPG-based input substitution supported sensitivity analysis without exposing underlying source code. The framework enables numerical integrity auditing without disclosing proprietary business logic and supports temporal auditability once an execution environment has become deprecated.

Conclusion: CompProv establishes an operation-level foundation for auditable-by-design computational systems. Provided the CompProv runtime and wrapper classes are available in the replay environment, a CPG allows numerical integrity to be audited without disclosing proprietary business logic. Scaling to high-throughput computing is identified as future work.

Abstract: The reliability of computational results in scientific research and financial modeling increasingly depends on verifiable traceability, not merely on trust in a reported output. Existing provenance systems operate at the granularity of files, datasets, or pipeline stages, leaving the internal sequence of algebraic transformations connecting an algorithm's inputs to its outputs unrecorded; a rounding error, an undocumented substitution, or a missing intermediate value can propagate to a final result with no recoverable trace. This work presents CompProv, a Java-based, audit-oriented provenance framework that captures lineage at the atomic level of individual algebraic operations by encapsulating numerical values in high-precision wrapper objects, producing a serializable Calculation Provenance Graph (CPG) that persists as a self-contained artifact rather than a discarded byproduct. The framework is evaluated through three heterogeneous case studies: a decentralized-finance NAV calculation, a reconstruction of an interferometric gauge-block calibration in metrology under explicitly documented input assumptions, and a hydrological model performance evaluation. Deterministic replay reproduced each result exactly in a fresh environment, and CPG-based input substitution supported sensitivity analysis without exposing the underlying source code. These results indicate that, provided the CompProv runtime and wrapper classes are available in the replay environment, a CPG allows numerical integrity to be audited without disclosing proprietary business logic, and that its self-contained structure supports temporal auditability once an execution environment has become deprecated. This framework establishes an operation-level foundation for auditable-by-design computational systems, with scaling to high-throughput computing identified as a direction for future work.

</details>


### [320] [A Design Theory for AI-Assisted Software Development Derived from Christopher Alexander's Theory of Form](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01372)
*Chien-Tsun Chen,Yu Chin Cheng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper proposes Misfit-Governed Development (MGD), a methodology for ensuring LLM-generated code meets specified requirements by applying Christopher Alexander's theory of form. The approach uses explicit representations of problems (Jackson's problem frames) and traditions (a four-form pattern language), with deterministic misfit detectors and a dual-loop process separating autonomous LLM iteration from human judgment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-generated code cannot be assumed to meet requirements; traditional verification methods (reviews, testing, static analysis) are insufficient. The authors address Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge regarding the "generativity dimension" - ensuring code fits its context. The core problem is that LLMs act as "non-native vernacular builders" trained on many codebases but native to none, tending to drift toward mainstream conventions rather than local organizational traditions.

Method: The authors developed a design theory based on Alexander's form theory, where fit between form and context is perceived negatively through absence of misfits. They engineered four components: (1) explicit representations of problems using Jackson's problem frames and of tradition using a four-form pattern language; (2) deterministic misfit detectors; (3) a fix loop; and (4) a human-gated legislative circuit. The resulting MGD methodology uses a dual-loop process: an autonomous inner loop where the LLM iterates against gates, and a human outer loop where specifications are judged against the world, forming the S = P = T = W assurance model.

Result: The methodology was validated by building and rebuilding a Scrum system with four event-sourced aggregates from 64 problem-frame specifications, verified by approximately 1,300 generated tests and 28 blocking gates, with one gate applying 188 rules. This demonstrates the approach can effectively govern LLM-generated code quality through systematic misfit detection.

Conclusion: MGD addresses the generativity dimension of Alexander's challenge by providing a systematic framework for ensuring LLM-generated code fits organizational traditions. The moral dimension (whether specifications fit the world) requires human judgment and belongs to the outer loop. The dual-loop architecture separates autonomous LLM iteration from human oversight, providing a practical approach to LLM code quality assurance.

Abstract: Code generated by large language models (LLMs) cannot be assumed to meet specified requirements. Reviews, testing, and static analysis still apply, but which of them a sufficient harness needs, and in what role, is open. We propose a design theory derived from Christopher Alexander's theory of form, and a methodology for applying it. In Alexander's account, fit between a form and its context can be perceived only negatively, through the absence of identified misfits. We make the organization's tradition explicit and derive the misfits from it and from the problem's classification. The theory models the LLM as a non-native vernacular builder, trained on many codebases but native to none, whose output tends to drift toward mainstream conventions rather than the local tradition. We engineer four pieces of machinery: explicit representations of the problem (Jackson's problem frames) and of the tradition (a four-form pattern language); deterministic misfit detectors; a fix loop; and a human-gated legislative circuit governing the representations and detectors. We call the resulting methodology, a practice of harness engineering, Misfit-Governed Development (MGD). Its dual-loop process separates an autonomous inner loop, where the LLM iterates against the gates, from a human outer loop, where specifications are judged against the world. Together they form the S = P = T = W assurance model (specification, program, tests, world), whose equals signs name relations, not identity. We report evidence from building and rebuilding a Scrum system of four event-sourced aggregates from 64 problem-frame specifications, verified by about 1,300 generated tests and 28 blocking gates, one applying 188 rules. This addresses the generativity dimension of Alexander's 1996 OOPSLA challenge. The moral dimension, whether the specification still fits the world, requires human judgment and belongs to the outer loop.

</details>


### [321] [Refactoring React Component Hierarchies to Eliminate Prop Drilling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01376)
*Vangelis Gkinis,Vassilis E. Zafeiris*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper addresses Prop Drilling in React applications - a code smell where data is passed through multiple component hierarchy levels via props. The authors propose a static analysis tool (ReactRefactor) that identifies Prop Drilling instances and automatically refactors them using Context API or Component Composition. Empirical evaluation on open-source React projects reveals that 76.3% of prop drillings can be automatically eliminated.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prop Drilling is discouraged by React documentation and characterized as a code smell, yet there is limited research on its prevalence, complexity, and potential for automated refactoring. This work aims to fill this gap by providing empirical evidence and automated solutions.

Method: The authors develop a static analysis method implemented as a Node.js command-line tool called ReactRefactor. It identifies Prop Drilling instances and applies two automated refactoring strategies: Context API and Component Composition. The tool is evaluated on a benchmark dataset of open-source React applications.

Result: The empirical evaluation reveals: (a) Prop Drilling occurs frequently across benchmark projects regardless of size; (b) complexity is generally low to moderate in terms of data propagation depth, but more prevalent complexity arises from simultaneously forwarding multiple properties along the same path; (c) 76.3% of prop drillings can be automatically eliminated, primarily through refactoring to Context API.

Conclusion: Prop Drilling is a common issue in React applications, but the majority (76.3%) can be automatically refactored using the proposed tool. The Context API approach is more frequently applicable than Component Composition. This demonstrates the feasibility of automated refactoring for this code smell.

Abstract: In React front-end development, Prop Drilling is the practice of propagating data through component properties across multiple levels of the component hierarchy. Despite being discouraged by React documentation and characterized as a code smell by recent research, little is known about its prevalence, complexity, and potential for automated refactoring. In this work, we propose a static analysis method for identifying Prop Drilling instances in a React codebase and eliminating them using two automated refactoring strategies based on Context API and Component Composition. The proposed method is implemented as a Node.js command line tool, ReactRefactor, and empirically evaluated on a benchmark dataset of open-source React applications. The main findings of the empirical evaluation indicate (a) the frequent occurrence of prop drillings across benchmark projects, irrespective of project size; (b) their generally low to moderate complexity in terms of data propagation depth, contrasted with the more prevalent complexity arising from the simultaneous forwarding of multiple properties along the same path; and, (c) the potential for automated elimination of a substantial share (76.3%) of prop drillings, primarily through refactoring to the Context API.

</details>


### [322] [Architectural Degradation: How to Measure and to Remediate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01611)
*Noman Ahmad,Ruoyu Su,Matteo Esposito,Andrea Janes,Valentina Lenarduzzi,Davide Taibi*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A Multivocal Literature Review of 284 studies consolidates research on architectural software degradation, identifying 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation strategies. The field shows strong concentration on static/structural analysis and detection tools, but lacks integration between diagnosis and remediation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality, but existing research remains fragmented across measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies, limiting understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle.

Method: Conducted a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies using an LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication for screening and data extraction, followed by analysis of taxonomies and cross-dimensional relationships.

Result: Identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. Remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions with substantially less consolidation.

Conclusion: The field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. The diagnosis-remediation gap is identified as a key direction for future research.

Abstract: Context. Architectural degradation undermines software maintainability, evolvability, and quality. However, existing research remains fragmented across measurement approaches, metrics, tools, and remediation strategies, limiting our understanding of how these elements relate across the degradation lifecycle. Aim. We consolidate the state of the art on architectural degradation by examining how researchers measure it, which metrics and tools support its assessment, and how existing approaches address remediation. Method. We conducted a Multivocal Literature Review of 284 peer-reviewed and grey-literature studies. We supported screening, data extraction, and classification with a locally executed LLM-assisted pipeline combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation, multi-model validation, and human adjudication. We then analyzed the resulting taxonomies and their cross-dimensional relationships. Results and Conclusions. We identified 277 measurement approaches, 357 metrics, 238 tools, and 395 remediation approaches. Research strongly concentrates on static and structural analysis, structural metrics, and detection-oriented tools. In contrast, remediation spans heterogeneous code-level, architectural, and organizational interventions and shows substantially less consolidation. Overall, the field has developed a mature diagnostic apparatus but has made less progress in connecting degradation detection with effective remediation. Our results provide a structured view of the available techniques and identify the diagnosis-remediation gap as a key direction for future research.

</details>


### [323] [Code Detectors Have a Half-Life: Obsolescence and Metric Illusions in LLM-Generated Code Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01664)
*Alberick Euraste Djire*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates the "detector half-life" problem—where code detectors become obsolete as code-generating models evolve. The study evaluates 8 general-purpose LLM judges and 3 dedicated detectors on human-written code and code from 7 generators across C++, Java, and Python. Results show that: (1) performance varies significantly across generators and prompting strategies, indicating some detectors rely on generator-specific patterns rather than general provenance evidence; (2) accuracy can mask severe prediction bias, as demonstrated by DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieving 0.50 accuracy but 0.00 F1 by classifying almost all samples as AI-generated. Overall, general-purpose LLM judges outperform dedicated detectors but their reliability depends on the judge model, code generator, and prompting strategy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Code detectors validated on one generation of models may not transfer to the next as code-generating models evolve. This limited useful life is termed "detector half-life." The motivation is to understand how well current detectors, including both dedicated tools and general-purpose LLM judges, perform across different code generators and to identify the factors affecting their reliability.

Method: The researchers evaluated eight general-purpose LLM judges and three dedicated detectors (DetectCodeGPT, GPT-Sniffer, and one unnamed) on human-written code and code produced by seven generators across three programming languages (C++, Java, and Python). They assessed performance across different generators and prompting strategies.

Result: Two key problems were identified: (1) Significant performance variation across generators and prompting strategies, suggesting some detectors rely on generator-specific patterns rather than general evidence of code provenance; (2) Accuracy can conceal severe prediction bias—DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieved 0.50 accuracy but 0.00 F1 score by classifying almost every sample as AI-generated. Despite this, general-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F1 scores overall, though their reliability depends on the judge model, code generator, and prompting strategy.

Conclusion: General-purpose LLM judges are promising training-free judges of code provenance and can outperform dedicated detectors. However, their reliability is contingent on the judge model, code generator, and prompting strategy. The authors recommend evaluating LLM judges across multiple generators and reporting macro-F1 alongside class-specific precision and recall to ensure comprehensive performance assessment.

Abstract: Code detectors can become obsolete as code-generating models evolve: a detector validated on one generation of models may not transfer to the next. We call this limited useful life a detector half-life. We evaluate eight general-purpose LLM judges and three dedicated detectors on human-written code and code produced by seven generators across C++, Java, and Python. Our results reveal two problems. First, performance varies considerably across generators and prompting strategies, suggesting that some detectors rely on generator-specific patterns rather than general evidence of code provenance. Second, accuracy can conceal severe prediction bias. DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieved an accuracy of 0.50 but an F1 score of 0.00 across all generators because they classified almost every sample as AI-generated. However, general-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F1 scores. Our results show that general-purpose LLMs are promising training-free judges of code provenance and can outperform dedicated detectors. However, their reliability depends on the judge model, the code generator, and the prompting strategy. We therefore recommend evaluating LLM judges across multiple generators and reporting macro-F1 alongside class-specific precision and recall.

</details>


### [324] [CONTRA: Discovering and Qualifying Behavior-Changing Questions for Selective Clarification in LLM Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01769)
*Zheng Fang,Yongmin Li,Yichang Zhang,Dongming Jin,Haoyu Wang,Shuai Wang,Zhi Jin,Ge Li*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CONTRA is a training-free method that helps coding agents identify key clarification questions to prevent behavioral mismatches between user intentions and generated code. It combines broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based qualification to avoid unnecessary interruptions while ensuring critical ambiguities are addressed early.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents can generate code that appears correct but implements unintended behavior due to silent resolution of underspecified requirements. These assumptions become embedded in subsequent development, making corrections increasingly costly. While early clarification can prevent mismatches, unnecessary questions interrupt developers and slow development. Existing methods struggle to balance identifying key questions while avoiding unnecessary ones.

Method: CONTRA uses a three-stage approach: 1) Generate candidate clarification questions from requirements; 2) Filter out questions unrelated to required behavior or already resolved; 3) For each remaining question, generate programs conditioned on two plausible answers and check for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs. The interaction history is then used to select qualified questions or determine when to stop asking.

Result: CONTRA achieves the highest F1 with all four coding agents on ClarifyCodeBench, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. It also outperforms coding harnesses Claude Code and OpenHands in clarification recall and F1 using the same LLM and evaluation protocol. A Claude Code plugin implementation demonstrates practical utility.

Conclusion: CONTRA successfully addresses the problem of identifying essential clarification questions in coding agents through a training-free approach that combines semantic filtering and execution-based behavioral verification. The method significantly improves over existing baselines and can be integrated into practical development workflows via a Claude Code plugin.

Abstract: Coding agents can generate code that appears correct but implements behavior the user never intended. This mismatch can arise when an agent silently resolves underspecified requirements through its own assumptions. As subsequent development builds on these assumptions, correcting the resulting behavior can become increasingly costly. Early clarification can help prevent such mismatches, but unnecessary questions can interrupt developers and slow down development. Existing methods struggle to identify key clarification questions while avoiding unnecessary ones. Therefore, we propose CONTRA, a training-free method that combines broad question discovery with semantic and execution-based question qualification. CONTRA first generates candidate questions and filters out those unrelated to required behavior or already resolved by the requirement. For each remaining question, it generates programs conditioned on two plausible answers and checks for stable behavioral differences on shared inputs. It then uses the interaction history to select among qualified questions or stop asking. Experiments on ClarifyCodeBench show that CONTRA achieves the highest F1 with all four coding agents, exceeding the best baseline macro-average F1 by 13.88 percentage points. With the same LLM and evaluation protocol, CONTRA also achieves higher clarification recall and F1 than the coding harnesses Claude Code and OpenHands. To support practical use, we also implement CONTRA as a Claude Code plugin that integrates selective clarification into everyday development.

</details>


### [325] [Detecting Inconsistencies in Model Specifications with LLM-as-Verifier Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01847)
*Zichen Xie,Mrigank Pawagi,Lize Shao,Yang Hu,Wenxi Wang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: VeriSpec is the first method to directly detect inconsistencies in LLM model specifications by auditing the specification text itself, using an LLM as a verifier to identify conflicting rules while preserving natural language nuances.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model specifications defining LLM behavior may contain defects where two reasonable principles prescribe incompatible behavior when applied to the same situation. Existing approaches (formalization or behavior-based testing) cannot reliably detect such specification-level inconsistencies.

Method: VeriSpec uses LLM-as-verifier reasoning: (1) Extracts structured, context-aware rules from natural language specifications, (2) Constructs a topic-guided graph to cluster behaviorally related rules at the same authority level, (3) Applies LLM reasoning to detect inconsistencies between rules.

Result: Applied to OpenAI Model Spec: extracted 405 rules, manually validated 5 inconsistencies (all reported to developers who responded positively). Compared with 5 baselines, VeriSpec achieved highest precision (38.5%) and lowest cost per validated inconsistency ($11.12).

Conclusion: Direct specification auditing is a practical complement to behavioral alignment evaluation, catching specification defects at the source before they shape any model. This establishes a new paradigm for quality assurance in LLM specification design.

Abstract: Model specifications define how large language models (LLMs) should behave, guiding alignment training, inference-time behavior, and evaluation. Yet these specifications may themselves contain defects: two individually reasonable principles may prescribe incompatible behavior when applied to the same situation, leaving no response that satisfies both. Detecting such inconsistencies is challenging. Formalizing natural-language specifications risks losing subtle distinctions, while behavior-based testing cannot reliably distinguish specification defects from differences in model behavior. We introduce VeriSpec, the first approach to directly detect inconsistencies in model specifications by auditing the specification text itself. Our key insight is to preserve the specification in natural language while using an LLM as a verifier. VeriSpec extracts structured, context-aware rules, constructs a topic-guided graph to cluster behaviorally related rules at the same authority level, and applies LLM-as-verifier reasoning to detect inconsistencies. Applying VeriSpec to the OpenAI Model Spec, we extract 405 rules and manually validate five inconsistencies, all reported to its developers, who responded positively and have initiated internal discussions. Compared with five baselines, VeriSpec identifies the most validated inconsistencies, achieves the highest precision (38.5%), and incurs the lowest cost per validated inconsistency ($11.12). These results establish direct specification auditing as a practical complement to behavioral alignment evaluation, catching defects at the source before they shape any model. The code is available at https://github.com/HIPREL-Group/VeriSpec.

</details>

### [326] [Supporting Perspective Acquisition and Opinion Formation on Societal Issues Through AI-Generated Japanese Rap Battle Debates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01179)
*Ryota Mibayashi,Toru Urakawa,Dai Takanashi,Tomoya Morohoshi,Kanata Yamagishi,Ryuho Sekikawa,Yasuhiko Nishimura,Yuta Takeuchi,Hideaki Tamori,Takehiro Yamamoto,Hidenari Kiyomitsu,Hiroaki Ohshima*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: This study explores whether AI-generated rap battle-style debates can help people acquire diverse perspectives and form informed opinions on societal issues. Using GPT-5.4-mini to generate brief (1.5 minute) rap battles, researchers found that participants identified nearly twice as many opinions and discussion points, and reconsidered or changed their stances in over half of the cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional debates require substantial time and human resources, limiting their accessibility for learning. The researchers sought to investigate whether a more engaging, AI-generated format (rap battles) could make perspective acquisition more accessible while preserving argumentative structure through rhymed verses.

Method: The researchers automatically generated rap battle-style debates using GPT-5.4-mini and presented them to participants with synthesized audio through a web-based interface. A user study was conducted with 6 participants who viewed 40 debates on societal issues from the All Japan Junior and Senior High School Debate Championships.

Result: Watching approximately 1.5 minute rap battle-style debates nearly doubled the number of opinions and discussion points identified by participants. Additionally, participants reconsidered or changed their stances in 52.5% of the evaluated cases.

Conclusion: Even brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can effectively support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues, demonstrating potential for accessible educational tools in critical thinking development.

Abstract: Acquiring diverse perspectives and forming informed opinions on societal issues are essential for critical thinking and informed decision-making. Although observing debates between opposing viewpoints can promote perspective acquisition, conventional debates require substantial time and human resources, limiting their accessibility. This study investigates whether brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues. Rap battles are debate-style performances in which opposing viewpoints are expressed through rhymed verses, making them engaging while preserving the structure of argumentative dialogue. To conduct this investigation, we automatically generated rap battle-style debates using GPT-5.4-mini and presented them to participants with synthesized audio through a web-based viewing interface. We evaluated the educational effectiveness of this approach through a user study involving six participants who viewed 40 debates generated from topics on societal issues used in the All Japan Junior and Senior High School Debate Championships. The results showed that watching approximately 1.5 minute rap battle-style debates nearly doubled the number of opinions and discussion points identified by participants. Furthermore, participants reconsidered or changed their stances in 52.5% of the evaluated cases. These findings demonstrate that even brief AI-generated rap battle-style debates can effectively support perspective acquisition and opinion formation on societal issues.

</details>

### [327] [Reverse Item Response Theory for Sparsity-Robust Ranking in Fragmented Cancer Drug-Response Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00002)
*Jung Min Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "reverse Item Response Theory (IRT)" as a novel method for pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis, treating cancer types as latent subjects with resistance ability and drugs as items with evasion difficulty. Applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from GDSC2, the method outperforms simple averaging in recovering latent rankings under various missingness regimes and achieves the best Brier score in held-out predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to develop a more robust methodological approach for analyzing drug sensitivity data across cancer types. Traditional methods like simple averaging may not adequately handle missing data and fragmented evaluations in pharmacogenomic studies. The authors aim to create a unified latent scale that can estimate both cancer-type resistance and drug activity simultaneously.

Method: The study applies reverse IRT to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from the GDSC2 database. This approach treats cancer types as latent "subjects" with resistance ability and drugs as "items" with evasion difficulty, estimating both on a shared latent scale. The method was validated across four missingness regimes (MCAR, cancer-biased, and drug-biased sparsity) and compared against four other methods using Brier score for held-out predictions. Bootstrap confidence intervals were used to assess stability of classifications, and cross-platform validation was performed using PRISM data.

Result: Reverse IRT demonstrates superior performance with Delta-rho advantages of +0.089 to +0.095 at 60% missingness across MCAR, cancer-biased, and drug-biased sparsity regimes. It achieves the best Brier score among five evaluated methods in held-out predictions. Bootstrap analysis shows 19 of 28 cancer types have stable resistant/sensitive classifications. Cross-platform PRISM replication shows 82% directional agreement but weak rank-order correlation (rho = 0.25).

Conclusion: The contribution lies in methodological robustness rather than providing a universal clinical resistance leaderboard. The method effectively handles fragmented evaluation scenarios common in pharmacogenomic studies, though cross-platform validation reveals limitations in generalizability (weak rank-order correlation with PRISM data). This suggests the method is valuable for handling missing data and heterogeneous data sources but should not be interpreted as identifying definitive clinical resistance rankings across cancer types.

Abstract: We introduce reverse Item Response Theory (IRT) to pharmacogenomic drug-response analysis by treating cancer types as latent "subjects" with resistance ability and drugs as "items" with evasion difficulty. Applied to 242,036 drug sensitivity measurements from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC2) database, the model estimates cancer-type-level in-vitro resistance and drug-level broad activity on a shared latent scale. Validation across four missingness regimes demonstrates that reverse IRT better recovers the full-data latent ranking than simple averaging, with advantages of Delta-rho = +0.089 to +0.095 at 60% missingness under MCAR, cancer-biased, and drug-biased sparsity. Held-out prediction confirms IRT achieves the best Brier score among five evaluated methods. Bootstrap confidence intervals show 19 of 28 cancer types have stable resistant/sensitive classifications. Cross-platform PRISM replication shows 82% directional agreement but weak rank-order correlation (rho = 0.25), indicating the contribution is methodological robustness under fragmented evaluation, not a universal clinical resistance leaderboard.

</details>


### [328] [How Far is Adam from Natural Gradient Descent?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00004)
*Vihaan Paka-Hegde*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper analyzes Adam optimizer's geometric relationship to natural gradient descent (NGD) across four loss landscapes, finding that Adam's geometric deviation from NGD varies from low in well-conditioned settings to ~10^3 in neural networks, but this deviation doesn't degrade final optimization outcomes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Adam is the standard deep learning optimizer yet its geometric relationship to natural gradient descent contains unresolved questions. The study aims to understand why Adam performs well despite potentially deviating from NGD's natural gradient path.

Method: The study analyzes Adam's full update rule (including momentum) as a diagonal empirical Fisher approximation subject to diagonal truncation, empirical label substitution, and temporal lag. Using the scale-invariant γ(Δθ) metric, they measure Adam's geometric deviation from true NGD across four loss landscapes: well-conditioned linear regression, ill-conditioned linear regression, logistic regression, and a non-convex small neural network.

Result: Adam's geometric trajectory is context-dependent. Deviation remains low in well-conditioned settings but rises significantly under ill-conditioning, reaching misalignments of ~10^3 in the neural network. Higher geometric drift correlates with slower initial optimization but does not degrade final objective minimization; Adam consistently reaches low loss. The improved empirical Fisher (iEF) tracks more stable paths than standard empirical Fisher (EF), which frequently oscillates or diverges.

Conclusion: Adam's practical optimization power may stem from a balance of structural approximation errors and momentum smoothing rather than close tracking of the natural gradient path. This challenges the assumption that NGD-like behavior is necessary for effective optimization.

Abstract: Adam is the standard optimizer in deep learning, yet its geometric relationship to natural gradient descent (NGD) contains unresolved questions. We study Adam's full update rule, including momentum, as a diagonal empirical Fisher approximation subject to diagonal truncation, empirical label substitution, and temporal lag. Using the scale-invariant $γ(Δθ)$ metric, we measure Adam's geometric deviation from true NGD across four loss landscapes: well-conditioned linear regression, ill-conditioned linear regression, logistic regression, and a non-convex small neural network. Adam's geometric trajectory is context-dependent. Deviation remains low in well-conditioned settings but rises significantly under ill-conditioning, reaching misalignments of $\approx 10^3$ in the neural network. Higher geometric drift correlates with slower initial optimization but does not degrade final objective minimization; Adam consistently reaches low loss. Furthermore, the improved empirical Fisher (iEF) tracks more stable paths than the standard empirical Fisher (EF), which frequently oscillates or diverges. Our results suggest Adam's practical optimization power may stem from a balance of structural approximation errors and momentum smoothing rather than close tracking of the natural gradient path.

</details>


### [329] [FourierQK: Filter Shape, Admissibility and the Leakage-Coverage Law](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00009)
*Athanasios Zeris*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates optimal filter shapes for frequency-collapse attention (FourierQK), which replaces standard Q/K dot product with a bandpass-filtered inner product at learned frequencies. Through controlled ablation on character-level language modeling (TinyShakespeare, 6-layer GPT), five filter properties are tested: DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand which filter shape works best for frequency-collapse attention and why. Since FourierQK has shown improvements over standard dot-product attention, the follow-up question is to identify the optimal filter design principles.

Method: Controlled ablation study on character-level language modeling (TinyShakespeare dataset with 6-layer GPT architecture). Five hypotheses were tested: DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage. The study compared various filter types including admissible filters (zero-mean, Mexican Hat DOG m=2), non-admissible Gaussians, and causal time-domain Morlet filters.

Result: Key findings: (1) DC and Nyquist components are actively harmful (val ~2.0, equivalent to phase randomization), confirming oscillatory bandpass structure is essential; (2) optimal single-scale bandwidth is sigma ~2 bins centered at paragraph scale (~70 tokens), giving Delta = +1.15 nats over BASE-DOT; (3) admissible filters (zero-mean, Mexican Hat DOG m=2) outperform non-admissible Gaussians and provide partial protection against bilateral FFT leakage; (4) bilateral FFT leakage scales monotonically with spectral coverage - narrowband filters (gap > +4) are clean, wideband filters (gap < +2) are leaky; (5) causal time-domain Morlet at character scale cannot beat BASE-DOT (K=128 taps covers 50% of T=256 context).

Conclusion: FourierQK is effective in bidirectional attention settings (encoder-style, e.g. BERT) where full-sequence context is available at both training and inference time. Autoregressive generation requires a causal spectral variant such as MorletQK (decoder-style, e.g. GPT). The optimal filter requires zero-mean bandpass structure with specific bandwidth centered at paragraph scale (~70 tokens).

Abstract: Frequency-collapse attention [Zeris, 2026e] achieves large gains over standard dot-product attention by replacing the Q/K dot product with a bandpass-filtered inner product at a learned frequency. A natural follow-up question is: which filter shape works best, and why? We test five hypotheses about filter properties -- DC suppression, Nyquist suppression, bandwidth, centre frequency, and multi-scale coverage -- using a controlled ablation on character-level language modelling (TinyShakespeare, 6-layer GPT). Our main findings are: (1) DC and Nyquist components are actively harmful (val ~= 2.0, equivalent to phase randomisation), confirming that oscillatory bandpass structure is essential, not just any low-dimensional spectral summary; (2) the optimal single-scale bandwidth is sigma ~= 2 bins centred at paragraph scale (~70 tokens), giving a clean gain of Delta = +1.15 nats over BASE-DOT; (3) admissible filters (zero-mean, Mexican Hat DOG m = 2) outperform non-admissible Gaussians at the same scale and provide partial protection against bilateral FFT leakage; (4) bilateral FFT leakage scales monotonically with spectral coverage -- narrowband filters (gap > +4) are clean, wideband filters (gap < +2) are leaky; and (5) causal time-domain Morlet at character scale cannot beat BASE-DOT (K=128 taps covers 50% of T=256 context), motivating word-level experiments in the companion MorletQK paper [Zeris, 2026f]. Together, findings (1)-(5) characterise FourierQK as effective in bidirectional attention settings (encoder-style, e.g. BERT), where full-sequence context is available at both training and inference time; autoregressive generation requires a causal spectral variant such as MorletQK [Zeris, 2026f] (decoder-style, e.g. GPT). Code available at: https://github.com/AthanasiosZeris/energy-gated-attention

</details>


### [330] [Integrating Fairness and Explainability in a Multiple Instance Reinforcement Learning System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00035)
*Bente Hinkenhuis,Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari,Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a multi-objective framework combining RL-MIL, adversarial debiasing, and preference-conditioned hypernetworks for fair student-at-risk prediction. While the RL-MIL baseline achieves strong classification performance, both hypernetwork variants fail to provide controllable trade-offs between predictive performance and Equalized Odds fairness due to mode collapse. The study concludes that explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing, objective separation, and stability analysis are necessary for robust fair RL-MIL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting student performance requires both accuracy and transparency for intervention support, while demographic information poses fairness risks. The study aims to develop a framework that balances predictive performance with fairness (Equalized Odds) through user-defined preference control.

Method: The study employs: (1) RL-MIL to represent students as bags of weakly labeled interactions with an RL agent selecting informative instances; (2) Adversarial debiasing for fairness; (3) Preference-conditioned hypernetworks to control the trade-off between performance and fairness via a user-defined preference scalar. Two hypernetwork variants are evaluated.

Result: The RL-MIL baseline achieves strong classification performance. However, both hypernetwork extensions exhibit mode collapse: changing the preference weight produces little systematic movement along the intended fairness-performance frontier. The failure is attributed to objective dominance, weak gradient propagation through the conditioning mechanism, and interactions between dynamically generated parameters.

Conclusion: Fairness objectives can be incorporated into an interpretable RL-MIL pipeline, but preference conditioning alone does not guarantee controllable multi-objective behavior. Robust fair RL-MIL requires explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing, objective separation, and stability analysis.

Abstract: Predicting student performance from educational interaction data requires models that are both accurate and sufficiently transparent to support meaningful intervention, while demographic information introduces an additional risk of unfair predictions. This study investigates a multi-objective framework that combines reinforcement learning-based multiple instance learning (RL-MIL), adversarial debiasing, and preference-conditioned hypernetworks for student-at-risk prediction. MIL represents each student as a bag of weakly labeled interactions, while an RL agent selects informative instances for downstream classification. Two hypernetwork variants are evaluated to determine whether a user-defined preference scalar can continuously control the trade-off between predictive performance and Equalized Odds. The underlying RL-MIL baseline achieves strong classification performance, but both hypernetwork extensions exhibit mode collapse: changing the preference weight produces little systematic movement along the intended fairness-performance frontier. The failure is associated with objective dominance, weak gradient propagation through the conditioning mechanism, and interactions between dynamically generated parameters. The results show that fairness objectives can be incorporated into an interpretable RL-MIL pipeline, but preference conditioning alone does not guarantee controllable multi-objective behavior. Robust fair RL-MIL therefore requires explicit mechanisms for gradient balancing, objective separation, and stability analysis.

</details>


### [331] [Fast Polynomial Transcendentals for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00049)
*Robert Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that polynomial approximations can accelerate special function operations in LLMs on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, achieving 1.19-2.19x speedups in isolated benchmarks and 0.3-8.0% throughput gains in integrated training tasks, with minimal impact on training loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPU generations scale matrix, special-function, and memory pipelines at different rates, causing kernel bottlenecks to shift as hardware evolves. FlashAttention-4 exposed this imbalance in attention on NVIDIA Blackwell. The authors investigate whether short polynomial programs can accelerate other SFU operations (sigmoid, tanh, SiLU) in LLMs.

Method: The authors compared native PyTorch evaluation with packed fused multiply-add (FMA) programs in IEEE binary16 (FP16), testing L2-resident and HBM-resident working sets. They replaced native sigmoid, tanh, and SiLU with degree-3 or degree-4 bfloat16 (BF16) programs in four GB200 integration tasks: dense SiLU, tanh-softcapped attention, sigmoid attention, and routed-expert SwiGLU. The programs combined analytical symmetry, target-format rounding, and packed arithmetic inside consuming kernels.

Result: Isolated path improvements: 1.19-2.19x in L2 and 1.00-1.70x in HBM. Training-step throughput: dense-SiLU +2.7%, tanh-softcapped-attention +2.9%, routed-expert +8.0%. Sigmoid-attention: +7.4% forward, +0.3% GPU step. At ~100B tokens, training loss differences (polynomial minus native) ranged from -0.107 to +0.079.

Conclusion: Short polynomial programs can effectively accelerate SFU operations in LLMs, with the routed-expert SwiGLU task showing the largest improvement (8.0%). The training loss differences are negligible at common horizons (~100B tokens), indicating that the polynomial approximations maintain model quality while improving performance. The approach is most effective for L2-resident working sets and scales with the complexity of the operation being replaced.

Abstract: Graphics processing unit (GPU) generations scale matrix, special-function, and memory pipelines at different rates, so kernel bottlenecks move as hardware evolves. FlashAttention-4 exposed this imbalance inside attention on NVIDIA Blackwell. We test whether short polynomial programs can accelerate other special-function-unit (SFU) operations in large language models (LLMs). We first compare native PyTorch evaluation with packed fused multiply--add (FMA) programs in an isolated IEEE binary16 (FP16) sweep spanning L2-resident and high-bandwidth-memory (HBM)-resident working sets. We then replace native sigmoid, tanh, and sigmoid linear unit (SiLU) with degree-3 or degree-4 bfloat16 (BF16) programs in four GB200 integration tasks: dense SiLU, tanh-softcapped attention, sigmoid attention, and routed-expert Swish-gated linear unit (SwiGLU). The programs combine analytical symmetry, target-format rounding, and packed arithmetic inside consuming kernels. The isolated paths improve by 1.19--2.19x in L2 and 1.00--1.70x in HBM. The dense-SiLU, tanh-softcapped-attention, and routed-expert substitutions improve complete training-step throughput by 2.7\%, 2.9\%, and 8.0\%, respectively. The sigmoid-attention substitution improves complete-attention forward by 7.4\% and the complete GPU step by 0.3\%. Same-checkpoint open-weight ablations and one paired pre-training comparison per task extend the evaluation to model behavior. At common horizons near 100 billion tokens, the final smoothed training-loss differences (polynomial minus native) range from $-0.107$ to $+0.079$ across the four tasks.

</details>


### [332] [SW-KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Stieltjes-Wigert q-Orthogonal Polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00050)
*Amirhosein Azarpour,Seyyed Moein Kazemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SW-KAN introduces Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials for KANs, addressing the domain mismatch problem in polynomial-based KAN variants by using semi-infinite domain (0, ∞) polynomials with a smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs in image classification and function approximation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Polynomial-based KAN variants face a fundamental challenge: domain mismatch between unbounded real-valued inputs and bounded/semi-infinite support of orthogonal polynomial bases. Existing approaches lack a proper solution for this limitation.

Method: 1) Employ Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials defined on semi-infinite domain (0, ∞)
2) Introduce smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping to bridge domain gap while preserving well-conditioned gradients
3) Leverage numerically stable three-term recurrence for O(N) polynomial evaluation without special-function calls
4) Utilize log-normal weight structure and learnable q-parameter for distinct inductive bias

Result: SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across diverse tasks (image classification, continuous function approximation). It outperforms polynomial KAN baselines on standard benchmarks, with robust performance under resource-constrained conditions (reduced feature dimensionality, limited training data), and strong representational capacity for multivariate functions with remarkably few parameters.

Conclusion: SW-KAN is a compelling alternative for efficient function approximation and classification in resource-constrained settings, offering better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than existing polynomial KAN variants.

Abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) represent a paradigmatic shift in deep learning by replacing fixed node activations with learnable univariate functions on edges, offering enhanced interpretability and parameter efficiency. While recent polynomial-based KAN variants have addressed the computational overhead of original B-spline implementations, they introduce a fundamental yet underexplored challenge: the domain mismatch between unbounded real-valued inputs and the bounded or semi-infinite support of orthogonal polynomial bases. To address this limitation, we propose the Stieltjes-Wigert Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (SW-KAN), a novel architecture that employs Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials defined on the semi-infinite domain (0, infinity). We introduce a smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping that stably bridges the domain gap while preserving well-conditioned gradients, and leverage a numerically stable three-term recurrence that evaluates polynomial expansions in O(N) operations without special-function calls. Through comprehensive experiments spanning image classification and continuous function approximation, we demonstrate that SW-KAN achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across diverse tasks. The log-normal weight structure and learnable q-parameter of Stieltjes-Wigert polynomials provide a distinct inductive bias that enables robust performance under resource-constrained conditions, including reduced feature dimensionality and limited training data. The proposed architecture not only outperforms established polynomial KAN baselines on standard benchmarks but also exhibits strong representational capacity for approximating complex multivariate functions with remarkably few parameters, making it a compelling alternative for efficient function approximation and classification in resource-constrained settings.

</details>


### [333] [Uncertainty-Aware RL-Controlled Adaptive 3D Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00188)
*Alpay Ozkan,Tunc Ozan Aydin,Marc Pollefeys,Jelena Trisovic,Daniel Barath*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an adaptive voxel-based volumetric mapping framework for 3D reconstruction that uses semantic entropy, geometric curvature, and texture richness as complexity cues, combined with a reinforcement learning agent to learn voxel subdivision policies under user-specified memory budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed-resolution voxel grids in 3D reconstruction are inefficient - wasting memory in uniform regions while losing detail in complex ones. Existing adaptive methods like MAP-ADAPT rely on heuristics requiring expert tuning, lack generalization, and provide no explicit memory control mechanism.

Method: The method introduces: (1) Semantic entropy capturing label uncertainty together with geometric curvature and texture richness as scene complexity cues for principled resolution allocation without semantic taxonomies; (2) A reinforcement learning agent that learns voxel subdivision policies under user-specified target memory budget, replacing hand-tuned thresholds with a single intuitive control parameter.

Result: The multi-resolution TSDF achieves higher geometric accuracy, better semantic consistency, and improved memory-accuracy trade-offs compared to MAP-ADAPT and fixed-resolution baselines on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses the limitations of existing adaptive voxel methods by using principled complexity cues (semantic entropy, curvature, texture) and RL-based memory control, yielding superior accuracy-memory trade-offs without relying on semantic taxonomies or expert-tuned parameters.

Abstract: Voxel-based volumetric mapping is fundamental to 3D reconstruction, yet fixed-resolution grids remain inherently inefficient - wasting memory in uniform regions and losing detail in complex ones. Existing adaptive methods, such as MAP-ADAPT, partially address this by varying resolution based on geometry and user-defined semantic class lists, but these heuristics require expert tuning, lack generalization to unseen objects, and provide no explicit mechanism to control memory usage. We propose an adaptive framework that refines voxels based on semantic entropy, which captures label uncertainty, together with geometric curvature and texture richness as scene complexity cues, yielding principled resolution allocation without reliance on semantic taxonomies. To make the accuracy-memory trade-off explicit and user-controlled, we further introduce a reinforcement learning agent that learns voxel subdivision policies under a user-specified target memory budget, replacing hand-tuned thresholds with a single intuitive control parameter. The resulting multi-resolution TSDF achieves higher geometric accuracy, better semantic consistency, and improved memory-accuracy trade-offs compared to MAP-ADAPT and fixed-resolution baselines on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/alpayozkan/UnRL.

</details>


### [334] [Format-Aware Fusion for Fast FP4 Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00053)
*Robert Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents "format-aware fusion" to optimize 4-bit floating-point (FP4) Tensor Core acceleration by co-designing quantization producers with scale domains and consumer layouts. The approach achieves up to 37.9K tokens/s/GPU (vs 18.8K for bfloat16) in Llama-3 8B pretraining, with MXFP variants reaching 86.3% model FLOP utilization while maintaining competitive training loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FP4 Tensor Cores can accelerate matrix multiplication, but the overhead from scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and saved backward state can erase these performance gains. This overhead represents a significant bottleneck that needs to be addressed.

Method: The authors propose "format-aware fusion" which co-designs each quantization producer with its scale domain and consumer layout for native MXFP, global NVFP, and CTA-local NVFP. They evaluate on Llama-3-family 8B pretraining through 160 billion tokens using bfloat16 output projections and compiled cross entropy, with techniques including row-gradient stochastic rounding and fixed-sign 32-value Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning.

Result: In matched same-accelerator probes: bfloat16 achieves 18.8K tokens/s/GPU, Transformer Engine NVFP reaches 27.6K tokens/s/GPU, and the fastest custom route achieves 37.9K tokens/s/GPU. MXFP with row-gradient stochastic rounding achieves 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3% bfloat16 model FLOP utilization) and ends 2.11% above raw bfloat16 training loss. A Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks ends 0.87% above bfloat16 at 27.1K tokens/s/GPU.

Conclusion: FP4 outcomes depend jointly on scale contract, operand, and execution path. Downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings, demonstrating that the choice of FP4 format, quantization strategy, and execution path significantly impacts both performance and model quality. The approach successfully reduces overhead while maintaining reasonable accuracy trade-offs.

Abstract: Four-bit floating-point (FP4) Tensor Cores accelerate matrix multiplication, but scale computation, operand packing, layout construction, and saved backward state can erase the gain. We present \emph{format-aware fusion}, which co-designs each quantization producer with its scale domain and consumer layout for native \mxfp{}, global \nvfp{}, and cooperative-thread-array-local \nvfp{}. We evaluate Llama-3-family 8B pretraining through 160 billion tokens using bfloat16 output projections and compiled cross entropy. In matched same-accelerator probes, bfloat16 and Transformer Engine \nvfp{} reach 18.8K and 27.6K tokens/s/GPU, while our fastest custom route reaches 37.9K. \mxfp{} with row-gradient stochastic rounding and fixed-sign 32-value Hadamard weight-gradient preconditioning reaches 37.2K tokens/s/GPU (86.3\% bfloat16 model FLOP utilization) and ends 2.11\% above the raw bfloat16 training-loss endpoint. A Transformer Engine recipe with four final bfloat16 blocks ends 0.87\% above bfloat16 at 27.1K tokens/s/GPU. Downstream rankings differ from training-loss rankings, showing that FP4 outcomes depend jointly on scale contract, operand, and execution path.

</details>


### [335] ["very likely" Means "uncertain"? How LLMs Diverge from Humans in Linguistic Uncertainty Quantification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00083)
*Jinhao Duan,Zicheng Liu,Zijie Liu,Kaidi Xu,Tianlong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the discrepancy between human verbal uncertainty markers (e.g., "possible," "likely") and how LLMs encode uncertainty. The authors find that LLMs assign different numerical probability levels to verbal markers compared to humans, and propose METHODNAME, an optimization-based algorithm that learns optimal uncertainty profiles from LLM outputs to enable direct comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humans naturally express uncertainty through verbal markers reflecting metacognitive monitoring, yet current LLM uncertainty quantification relies on numerical signals (likelihood, consistency) rather than verbal expressions. This creates a fundamental disconnect between human and machine uncertainty communication, necessitating investigation into whether verbal markers can reliably quantify LLM uncertainty.

Method: The authors curated a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature, then benchmarked LLMs against this human baseline. They developed METHODNAME, an optimization-based algorithm that learns optimal uncertainty profiles over verbal markers directly from LLM outputs by fitting a marker-uncertainty mapping to maximize empirical correctness, rather than using repeated sampling approaches.

Result: LLMs encode verbal uncertainty with numerical probability levels that differ substantially from human conventions. The METHODNAME approach enables direct marker-level comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs, revealing systematic confidence disparities in verbal expressions.

Conclusion: Verbal uncertainty markers cannot be directly used to quantify LLM uncertainty without calibration against human semantics. The proposed METHODNAME provides a framework for disentangling human-LLM confidence mismatches and enables more interpretable uncertainty communication by learning how much probability mass each verbal marker should convey from LLM outputs.

Abstract: Humans express uncertainty verbally via markers (e.g., "possible," "likely"), yet most LLM uncertainty quantification (UQ) relies on costing likelihood- or consistency-based signals. From a cognitive perspective, accurate verbal uncertainty reflects metacognitive monitoring, representing knowledge boundaries ("knowing that you don't know") to support regulation and information seeking. In this paper, we investigate how LLMs diverge from humans in verbal uncertainty quantification and whether verbal markers can reliably quantify LLM uncertainty. We curate a corpus of human uncertainty markers from psychology and decision-science literature and benchmark LLMs against it. We observe that LLMs encode verbal uncertainty with numerical levels that differ substantially from those of humans. We then introduce METHODNAME, a novel optimization-based algorithm that learns an optimal uncertainty profile over uncertainty markers directly from LLM outputs. By fitting a marker-uncertainty mapping to best explain empirical correctness, METHODNAME discovers how much probability mass each verbal marker should convey, rather than estimating uncertainty via repeated sampling. METHODNAME enables a direct, marker-level comparison of confidence semantics between humans and LLMs, disentangling mismatch and revealing systematic confidence disparities in verbal expressions.

</details>


### [336] [Nous: Learning and Certifying Memory Decisions Before Source Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00094)
*Pranav Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that learning and certifying useful memory decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration (Θ(l⁻²) vs Θ(l⁻⁴)), establishing when belief-based agent memory can improve decisions without first calibrating source reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Belief-based agent memory needs reliable decisions about current state, but evidence may be noisy, copied, or stale. The key question is whether memory must calibrate its sources before improving decisions.

Method: Analysis of four-model hidden Markov families, complexity bounds for learning vs. calibration, characterization of identified intervals for policy improvement under unknown identity-plus-background report channels, finite-sample certificates using observable witness regions, and empirical testing in MiniGrid environments.

Result: The new certificate achieves 9/9 improvements over constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins in MiniGrid environments, versus none for the earlier certificate. Learning unknown Bayes decisions requires Θ(l⁻²) records while fixed-precision source estimation requires Θ(l⁻⁴) as persistence l vanishes.

Conclusion: This provides a statistical account of when memory decisions can be learned and justified without recovering source reliability—not a universally superior memory algorithm, but a characterization of when source calibration is unnecessary for decision improvement.

Abstract: Belief-based agent memory needs reliable decisions about current state, yet its evidence may be noisy, copied, or stale. Must a memory calibrate its sources before it can improve its decisions? We separate learning, calibration, and revision certification. On one four-model hidden Markov family, learning an unknown Bayes decision requires Theta(l^-2) records and certifying its improvement over an informative incumbent takes O(l^-2) fresh records from the same observation law, while fixed-precision source estimation requires Theta(l^-4) as persistence l vanishes. Thus learning and certifying useful decisions can require quadratically fewer records than source calibration. A broader model class retains the decision rate and source lower bound. Under an unknown identity-plus-background report channel, we characterize the sharp identified interval for policy improvement and derive a finite-sample certificate using observable witness regions, without pure-class anchors. A robustness extension tolerates bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying; split-trained witnesses apply to arbitrary history spaces with explicit power conditions. We integrate policy-bound receipts with Nous Dimensions and test 45,000 held-out mutable-state histories and 9,000 episodes in three external MiniGrid memory environments with an introduced noisy-report interface. The new certificate accepts 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins, versus none for the earlier certificate in MiniGrid. Strong established inference baselines remain competitive or better. The result is a statistical account of when memory decisions can be learned and justified without recovering source reliability, not a universally superior memory algorithm.

</details>


### [337] [One Mastery Threshold Does Not Fit All Knowledge Tracing Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00095)
*Xianghui Meng,Yujing Zhang,Jionghao Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how mastery thresholds in tutoring systems behave differently across six knowledge tracing (KT) models (including BKT and neural models) when evaluated on four educational datasets. The key finding is that the same numerical threshold produces vastly different outcomes depending on the underlying KT model, because BKT estimates mastery probability while neural models estimate response correctness probability. The study tests 12 thresholds and identifies optimal thresholds under 30 instructional settings, revealing that thresholds should be recalibrated when models or priorities change.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tutoring systems rely on mastery thresholds to decide when students can advance, but there's an implicit assumption that a threshold (e.g., 0.80) means the same thing regardless of which knowledge tracing model is used. This paper challenges that assumption by examining whether different KT models require different thresholds to achieve comparable outcomes.

Method: The researchers evaluated six KT models (including Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and neural models) across four public educational datasets.
