They tested 12 thresholds ranging from 0.50 to 0.99, measuring four outcomes: post-advancement performance, advancement coverage, practice burden, and disparities across prior-performance groups. They also identified balanced thresholds under 30 predefined instructional settings with varying priorities.

Result: BKT was relatively insensitive to threshold changes, while neural models became much more selective as thresholds increased. In half the settings, neural models and BKT differed by more than 0.10 in their optimal thresholds. Stricter thresholds did not reliably reduce performance gaps and could disproportionately restrict advancement—stronger-prior students advanced up to 3.26 times more often than weaker-prior students.

Conclusion: Mastery thresholds should be recalibrated when switching KT models or changing instructional priorities. Thresholds must be evaluated holistically by their effects on performance, practice, advancement, and equitable access—not just by numerical cutoff values. The same threshold does not represent equivalent mastery across different model types.

Abstract: Tutoring systems use mastery thresholds to decide when students can stop practicing and advance, but the same numerical threshold can lead to very different decisions when the underlying knowledge tracing (KT) model changes. We examine six KT models across four public educational datasets and evaluate 12 thresholds from 0.50 to 0.99 using post-advancement performance, advancement coverage, practice burden, and disparities across prior-performance groups. We also identify thresholds that balance performance, extra practice, and advancement under 30 predefined instructional settings. Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) is relatively insensitive to threshold changes, while neural models become much more selective as thresholds increase. This partly reflects different model outputs: BKT estimates latent mastery probability, whereas neural models estimate the probability of a correct next response, so the same cutoff does not represent the same level of mastery. The best-balanced threshold varied substantially across models and settings. In half of the tested settings, neural models and BKT differed by more than 0.10 in their selected thresholds, although this gap became smaller when greater priority was placed on reducing extra practice and allowing more students to advance. Stricter thresholds also did not reliably reduce performance gaps and could disproportionately restrict advancement, with stronger-prior students advancing up to 3.26 times as often as weaker-prior students. These results show that mastery thresholds should be recalibrated when the KT model or instructional priorities change and evaluated by their effects on performance, practice, advancement, and access.

</details>


### [338] [Uncertainty-Aware Learning from Multi-Expert Interval Targets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00102)
*Samira Alkaee Taleghan,Younghyun Koo,Andrew P. Barrett,Farnoush Banaei-Kashani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a machine learning approach to handle expert labels with two sources of uncertainty: within-label imprecision (interval values) and between-expert variation. The method preserves individual expert intervals, separates these uncertainty types, and validates predictive uncertainty components through decomposition matching. Applied to sea-ice concentration prediction, it achieves 31% MAE reduction over hard labels and outperforms baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods treat label uncertainty separately: multi-expert approaches collapse labels to consensus, interval-target methods yield single predictions, and predictive-uncertainty methods rarely validate against observed expert disagreement. This creates a gap in handling both within-label imprecision and between-expert variation simultaneously while validating uncertainty estimates.

Method: Three key components: (1) Harmonize heterogeneous label vocabularies into common probabilistic label space to separate encoding differences from expert judgment; (2) Retain and model individual label intervals with mixture of Beta distributions trained using proper Cramér-distance objective; (3) Decompose predictive uncertainty into within-component, between-component, and model uncertainty, then apply decomposition matching to align predictive components to their intended label-side sources.

Result: On sea-ice concentration prediction, the model reduces MAE by 31% compared to hard labels and outperforms aggregation, interval-distribution, and interval-regression baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully preserves individual expert intervals while separating within-label imprecision from between-expert variation. Decomposition matching enables proper alignment between predictive uncertainty components and label-side uncertainty sources, leading to improved prediction accuracy and better uncertainty quantification.

Abstract: Many machine learning (ML) applications rely on expert labels, and qualified experts may provide different but plausible interpretations of the same observation. Such variation across expert labels may reflect genuine disagreement or ambiguity rather than annotation error. When individual experts additionally report intervals rather than exact values, the supervision contains two distinct sources of label uncertainty: within-label imprecision and between-expert variation. Existing methods treat these forms separately: multi-expert approaches collapse labels to a consensus, interval-target methods often yield a single prediction, and predictive-uncertainty methods rarely validate their uncertainty estimates against observed expert disagreement. To address this problem, we propose an approach that preserves individual expert intervals, separates within-label imprecision from between-expert variation, and validates the corresponding predictive uncertainty components. First, heterogeneous label vocabularies are harmonized into a common probabilistic label space, separating encoding differences from expert judgement. Second, individual label intervals are retained and modeled with a mixture of Beta distributions trained using a proper Cramér-distance objective, preserving distinct expert-reported labels. Third, we decompose predictive uncertainty into within-component, between-component, and model uncertainty, and evaluate whether these components correspond to within-label uncertainty, between-label uncertainty, and model error, respectively. Because this correspondence is not guaranteed, we introduce decomposition matching, which aligns the predictive components to their intended label-side sources. On sea-ice concentration the model reduces MAE by 31\% over hard labels and outperforms aggregation, interval-distribution, and interval-regression baselines.

</details>


### [339] [The Hidden Costs of 99% Accuracy: A Trustworthiness Audit of the Telco Customer Churn Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00118)
*Soumyadeep Roy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper audits the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark for four trustworthiness failures: (1) pre-split SMOTE inflates F1 by 13.1 pp due to test set leakage into synthetic samples, (2) TotalCharges is nearly determined by tenure × MonthlyCharges (R2=0.999) corrupting SHAP interpretations, (3) temperature scaling fails on class-weighted tree ensembles requiring isotonic regression, and (4) cost-optimal thresholds are 5-10× lower than F1-optimal thresholds, saving ~$77K per 1,000 customers. The authors propose a four-component reporting checklist and release reproducible code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark routinely reports >95% accuracy with the most cited study claiming 99.01%, yet the literature lacks scrutiny of these optimistic results. The authors aim to audit this benchmark for trustworthiness failures invisible to accuracy- and F1-centered reporting.

Method: The authors conducted four audits: (1) SMOTE analysis across 10 classifiers and 15 seeds measuring synthetic point contamination, (2) redundancy analysis using R2 diagnostic on TotalCharges, (3) calibration audit comparing isotonic regression and temperature scaling across 15 seeds, and (4) cost-sensitive threshold optimization using a $50 retention offer and 24-month CLV proxy. They also replicated F1 and F2 on Iranian Telecom Churn and Bank Customer Churn datasets.

Result: Pre-split SMOTE inflates churn-class F1 by 13.1 percentage points (Wilcoxon p < 10^-4); ~36% of synthetic training points are nearest-neighbor interpolations of test-set instances. TotalCharges is nearly determined by tenure × MonthlyCharges (R2 = 0.999) yet ranks 9th in SHAP attribution. Isotonic regression outperforms temperature scaling for calibration. Cost-optimal threshold is 5-10× lower than F1-optimal, saving ~$77,000 per 1,000 customers. F1 generalizes across datasets; F2 generalizes only within telecom.

Conclusion: The IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark suffers from multiple trustworthiness failures that inflate performance metrics and corrupt interpretations. The authors propose a four-component reporting checklist (pipeline disclosure, redundancy diagnostic, calibration audit, and cost-sensitive thresholds) and release reproducible implementation to improve benchmarking practices in churn prediction and beyond.

Abstract: Customer churn prediction on the IBM Telco Customer Churn benchmark (n = 7,043) routinely reports test accuracies above 95%, with the most cited published study reporting 99.01%. We audit this benchmark for four trustworthiness failures invisible to the accuracy- and F1-centred reporting that dominates the literature. First, pre-split SMOTE inflates churn-class F1 by 13.1 percentage points across ten classifiers and fifteen seeds (Wilcoxon p < 10^-4 per classifier); the same leaky pipeline ordering paired with class weighting yields no inflation, isolating the effect to SMOTE's geometric construction. We measure the mechanism directly: approximately 36% of synthetic training points are nearest-neighbour interpolations of test-set instances. Second, the TotalCharges field is approximately determined by tenure multiplied by MonthlyCharges (R2 = 0.999); removing it changes accuracy by less than 0.2 percentage points, yet TreeSHAP ranks it ninth in mean absolute attribution - a pattern that materially corrupts SHAP-based interpretation. We propose an R2 > 0.95 pre-modelling diagnostic. Third, in a 15-seed calibration audit, isotonic regression is the strongest default; temperature scaling fails on class-weighted tree ensembles whose predicted-probability distribution is bimodal. Fourth, the cost-optimal decision threshold (under a 50 USD retention offer and 24-month CLV proxy) is approximately 5-10 times lower than the F1-optimal threshold, saving approximately 77,000 USD per 1,000 customers. We replicate F1 and F2 on Iranian Telecom Churn (within domain) and Bank Customer Churn (across domain): F1 generalises; F2 generalises only within telecom. We synthesise these findings into a four-component reporting checklist - pipeline disclosure, redundancy diagnostic, calibration audit, and cost-sensitive thresholds - and release a reproducible implementation.

</details>


### [340] [Generalized Biomedicine Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00120)
*Luyao Tang,Yingkai Yang,Hanqi Chen,Jiewei Zheng,Chaoqi Chen,Cheng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses open-world challenges in medical imaging by introducing Generalized Biomedicine Discovery (GBD) - a unified benchmark and framework for long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware discovery. The proposed SCAN method mimics expert diagnosis by suppressing expected patterns, highlighting unexpected deviations, and integrating these into global representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world medical images face open-world shifts including long-tailed rare diseases, subtle lesions masked by normal anatomy, and hierarchical taxonomies. Existing open-world paradigms assume flat, balanced label spaces, failing to address these biomedical challenges. The key insight is that dominant known patterns form a visual manifold that masks subtle novelty.

Method: SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN) follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression: (1) Predictive suppression to filter expected norms, (2) Surprise-evoked salience to highlight unexpected deviations, and (3) Complementary accommodation to integrate these shifts into global representations.

Result: SCAN improves novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge, and can be plugged into existing architectures to better navigate the known-unknown trade-off in medical imaging.

Conclusion: The proposed GBD benchmark and SCAN method provide a unified framework for addressing multiple open-world challenges in biomedical imaging, successfully balancing known class preservation with novel discovery capabilities.

Abstract: In real-world clinical practice, medical images face open-world shifts: (i) long-tailed rare diseases, (ii) subtle lesions dominated by normal anatomy, and (iii) hierarchical taxonomies. Yet most open-world paradigms assume flat, balanced label spaces, leaving these biomedical demands unresolved. We introduce Generalized Biomedicine Discovery (GBD) and a unified benchmark spanning long-tail, anomaly, and taxonomy-aware discovery. Our key insight is that dominant known patterns form a visual manifold that masks subtle novelty. Inspired by expert diagnosis, we propose SCAN (Surprise-evoked Complementary AccommodatioN), which follows a cognition-inspired perceptual progression: it applies predictive suppression to filter expected norms, triggers surprise-evoked salience to highlight unexpected deviations, and performs complementary accommodation to integrate these shifts into global representations. Extensive experiments show that SCAN improves novel concept discovery while generally preserving established clinical knowledge, and it plugs into existing architectures to better navigate the known-unknown trade-off in medical imaging. Code is available at https://github.com/lytang63/generalized-biomedicine-discovery.

</details>


### [341] [Classification Based on Association Rules Algorithm for Breast Cancer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00174)
*Ali Alsalama,Ahmed Kubba,Ghaith Jamjoum,Zaher Al Aghbari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel association rule-based data mining technique for breast cancer classification using a weighted classification approach. The method consists of three core algorithms: Rule Generation, Rule Pruning, and Rule Prediction, aiming to improve early breast cancer detection through interpretable classification rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Breast cancer is a leading cause of female mortality worldwide with high occurrence rates. Early detection is critical, and association rule-based classification offers the advantage of producing results that are easily understandable for medical professionals, making it a favored approach for breast cancer detection.

Method: The proposed approach employs three core algorithms: (1) Rule Generation - identifies frequent itemsets and creates association rules; (2) Rule Pruning - eliminates rules using specific criteria and separates them into major and minor groups based on their influence on training data; (3) Rule Prediction - applies the pruned rules to classify test data.

Result: The final prediction algorithm was tested on several testing samples to demonstrate the feasibility and performance of the approach.

Conclusion: The proposed weighted association rule-based classification method shows promise for breast cancer classification, offering interpretable results suitable for medical professionals. The three-algorithm pipeline (Rule Generation, Rule Pruning, Rule Prediction) provides a systematic approach to classification, though the abstract does not provide specific performance metrics.

Abstract: Breast cancer is a significant contributor to female mortality across the world, displaying one of the highest oc currence rates among the various cancer types. In response to the need for early breast cancer detection, researchers have increasingly turned to association rule-based classification as a favored method. Association Rule mining is a data mining approach which offers the benefit of yielding results that are readily understandable for medical professionals. This paper introduces a novel association rule-based data mining technique for breast cancer classification based on a weighted classification approach. This implementation employs three core algorithms: Rule Generation, Rule Pruning, and Rule Prediction. Rule Generation identifies frequent itemsets and creates association rules. Rule Pruning eliminates rules using specific criteria and separates them into major and minor groups based on their influence on training data. Rule Prediction applies the pruned rules to classify test data. The final prediction algorithm was tested on several testing samples to show the feasibility and performance of the approach.

</details>


### [342] [Four Ways to Grow a Classifier and Why One of Them Cannot Learn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00180)
*Cagri Temel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates four growth decisions in constructive classifiers (tree-structured and neural network models) and measures what each decision actually achieves. The key finding is that deepening a soft decision tree by turning leaves into gates buys nothing due to zero gradients, while the other three decisions each provide measurable benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to understand the actual value added by different growth decisions in constructive classifiers, since these models add structure during training (tree levels, hidden units, leaf splits) but it's unclear what each decision contributes.

Method: The study uses one fixed protocol to measure four growth decisions: (1) deepening a soft decision tree by converting leaves to gates, (2) fitting new hidden units to residual error, (3) splitting the leaf with largest expected error, and (4) requiring statistical significance before split. Experiments run over three seeds of five-fold cross-validation on Iris, Wine, and Digits datasets.

Result: The main finding is that deepening soft decision trees (Decision 1) causes a 19.6 point accuracy drop on Iris, 19.1 on Wine, and 55.6 on Digits compared to training the same depth from scratch. The diagnosis reveals that new gates have identically zero gradients, making learning impossible. Decision 2 (new hidden units) yields smaller networks but not better accuracy; Decision 3 (largest expected error split) achieves 0.885 accuracy with only 3.7 splits vs 63 for complete depth-six tree; Decision 4 (statistical significance) provides no benefit and makes the tree larger and less accurate.

Conclusion: Three of four growth decisions buy something: fitting new hidden units to residuals buys smaller networks, splitting the leaf with largest expected error buys sparsity, and requiring statistical significance buys nothing negative (actually worse). The key contribution is diagnosing why deepening soft decision trees fails (zero gradients) and providing a simple fix: random perturbation of children after adding parameters, with a one-line test to verify nonzero gradients.

Abstract: Constructive classifiers add structure while they train: a level to a tree, a unit to a hidden layer, a split at a leaf. This paper asks what each of four such growth decisions actually buys, measured under one fixed protocol in tree-structured and constructive models, and gives an exact diagnosis and a fix for the one that buys nothing.
  The diagnosis concerns the most natural way to deepen a soft decision tree: turn every leaf into a gate whose two children inherit the parent's class distribution, so that the function is unchanged. I prove that this leaves the gradient of every new gate identically zero and, with the gate at 1/2, gives the two children identical gradients, so the added level can never learn. Unlike the symmetry that Net2Net breaks with noise or the saddle point that splitting steepest descent escapes with second-order information, first-order information here is not weak but absent. Over three seeds of five-fold cross-validation the construction loses 19.6 accuracy points on Iris, 19.1 on Wine and 55.6 on Digits against the same depth trained from scratch. The fix is a small random perturbation of the children, whose size barely matters. The practical rule is one line in a test: after adding parameters, assert that their gradient is nonzero.
  The other three decisions each buy one thing. Fitting a new hidden unit to the residual error before installing it buys a smaller network on every dataset, though not a more accurate one, and on Digits it costs accuracy significantly. Splitting the leaf with the largest expected error buys sparsity, reaching 0.885 with 3.7 splits where a complete depth-six tree uses 63, but loses 4.3 points on a harder problem. Requiring statistical significance before a node receives a more expressive split buys nothing: the tree gets larger and less accurate.
  Every number in the paper is inserted from the measurement script.

</details>


### [343] [Energy Time-Series Imputation with Differentially Private Diffusion Models via Clipping-Aware Objective Conditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00209)
*Huizhen Huang,Yu Li,Tao Huang,Chen Hou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses privacy-sensitive energy time-series imputation using diffusion models trained with differentially private SGD (DP-SGD). The key innovation is identifying and solving the gradient clipping problem at late timesteps of cosine diffusion schedules, where low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) causes large pre-clipping gradients that get clipped, reducing optimization signal. The proposed solution combines v-prediction, static loss weighting, and diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting to improve imputation utility while maintaining differential privacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable recovery of missing measurements is critical for monitoring and analysis in energy time-series systems. Fine-grained measurements may contain sensitive temporal information, requiring privacy protection. Standard diffusion models with ε-prediction suffer from gradient clipping issues at late timesteps due to low SNR conditions, which degrades imputation performance.

Method: The method introduces clipping-aware objective conditioning for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation: (1) v-prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, (2) static loss weighting as uniform-scaling control, and (3) diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. Evaluation across five real-world energy datasets under various missingness scenarios (random point, contiguous block, persistent outages, multiple severities).

Result: The proposed method consistently improves imputation utility over the ε-prediction baseline under matched DP-SGD settings. Gradient diagnostics confirm: lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps.

Conclusion: Clipping-aware objective conditioning effectively addresses the gradient clipping problem in DP-SGD training for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation. The combination of v-prediction and schedule-aware dynamic weighting provides a practical solution for privacy-preserving energy data analysis.

Abstract: Reliable recovery of missing measurements is important for monitoring and analysis in energy time-series systems, where fine-grained measurements may contain sensitive temporal information. Diffusion models trained with differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) provide a promising framework for privacy-sensitive energy time-series imputation. Under cosine diffusion schedules, late timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard $\varepsilon$-prediction can induce large pre-clipping gradients. Such gradients are more likely to be clipped, reducing the retained optimization signal. The artificial intelligence (AI) contribution lies in formulating this objective--clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under fixed-threshold DP-SGD and developing timestep-aware objective conditioning for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation. The method adopts $v$-prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, uses static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and introduces diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. For the engineering application, we evaluate the method on five real-world energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. Under matched DP-SGD settings, the proposed method consistently improves imputation utility over the $\varepsilon$-prediction baseline. Gradient diagnostics reveal lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps, supporting the effectiveness of clipping-aware objective conditioning for energy time-series imputation.

</details>


### [344] [Useful to Whom? Sample Value Is Defined Only Relative to the Learner](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00221)
*Yangze Liu,Xiao-Long Yin,Zhongyi Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates whether the optimal training data subset (coreset) depends on the target learner, not just the data itself. Through controlled experiments, the authors find that the "crossover boundary" (where different sample selection strategies perform equally well) shifts based on the learner's architecture - changing model width moves this boundary from 57 to 85 samples per class on ImageNet-100. The key finding is that the same selected subset has different value for different learners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core question is: does a selection strategy's effectiveness depend on the target learner? Prior work showed easy-first and geometric coverage criteria win in different budget regimes, but it was unclear if this boundary is fixed by the data or changes with the learner. This matters practically because choosing wrong criterion wastes compute.

Method: Controlled experiments freezing selected subsets while manipulating only the training learner. Techniques include: (1) varying ResNet-18 width, (2) manipulating input grid size (stride controls), (3) testing on native-224px ImageNet-1k, and (4) swapping CNN for ViT architecture.

Result: Key findings: (1) Doubling ResNet-18 width moves crossover from 57→85 samples/class; (2) Input grid size affects the boundary - enlarging grid shifts boundary left, weakening with width; (3) Last downsampling stride removal recovers leftward shift; (4) On ImageNet-1k, width effects smaller - LFrac flat, EL2N shifts modestly; (5) ViT makes coverage win throughout measured range even with CNN-selected subsets.

Conclusion: The crossover boundary is learner-dependent, not data-fixed. No universal scaling law exists. Practical implication: selection strategy must be evaluated with respect to the specific target learner, not just the dataset. Network structure (width, stride, architecture type) can shift which samples are most valuable.

Abstract: What kind of data does a model need in order to learn? Coreset selection makes this question concrete: under a budget, keep the samples most useful for training. Easy-first and geometric coverage criteria can win in different budget regimes, separated by a crossover boundary. We ask whether this boundary is fixed by the data or changes with the target learner. Controlled experiments freeze the selected subsets and manipulate only the training learner. On low-resolution ImageNet-100, doubling ResNet-18's width moves the crossover from 57 to 85 samples per class: the learner changes the relative value of the same samples. A wider sweep reveals an interaction between input grid and capacity. Enlarging the grid while retaining the same image information shifts the boundary left, and this shift weakens as width increases. Stride controls reproduce and reverse the grid effect without changing the input grid; removing only the last downsampling stride is sufficient to recover the leftward shift. Under the native-224px ImageNet-1k protocol, width effects are smaller and depend on the probe: LFrac remains nearly flat, while EL2N shifts modestly right. Swapping the convolutional learning system for a ViT makes coverage win throughout the measured range, even when the easy subsets come from the convolutional proxy. These results establish learner dependence through frozen-subset interventions and identify network structure that can move the boundary. They do not yield a universal scaling law. Their practical implication is direct: a selection strategy's preferred budget regime must be evaluated with respect to the target learner.

</details>


### [345] [Constant-Memory Recall: Learned Associations in a Fixed Matrix State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00232)
*Samuel Larson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates a small DeltaNet variant with fixed-size recurrent memory for remembering 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. The model achieves 99.95% mean accuracy with 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state, maintaining near-perfect recall even with extended context (1,798 tokens). However, parameter-matched Transformer and vector baselines fail to solve the task, preventing fair memory-efficiency comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed-size recurrent memory limits storage growth during inference, but successful recall depends on task and training. The authors aim to understand whether a small DeltaNet variant can effectively memorize new key-value pairings and compare its performance with baseline models.

Method: The study uses a small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases, trained to remember 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. The model has 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state. Experiments include testing recall with extended filler context (1,798 tokens), ablating the first memory block, and conducting an exploratory 48-pair test. Parameter-matched vector and Transformer baselines are used for comparison.

Result: The DeltaNet achieves 99.95% mean accuracy across three training seeds when choosing among the sequence's values. Recall remains near perfect when filler extends the pre-query context to 1,798 tokens without adding pairings. Zeroing the first memory block completely removes recall ability. An exploratory 48-pair test remains near chance after one quarter of the primary training budget and does not locate a capacity limit. All baseline models (vector and Transformer) remain near chance even after additional training searches.

Conclusion: The DeltaNet with fixed-size recurrent memory can successfully memorize and recall 32 key-value pairings with high accuracy, even with extended context. However, the failure of baseline models to solve the task prevents a fair memory-efficiency comparison. The capacity limit remains unresolved, and the first memory block is critical for recall.

Abstract: Fixed-size recurrent memory limits storage growth during inference, but successful recall depends on the task and training. We study a small DeltaNet variant with fixed token-specific key biases, trained to remember 32 new key-value pairings per sequence. With 32 KiB of recurrent matrix state, it achieves 99.95% mean accuracy across three training seeds when choosing among the sequence's values. Recall remains near perfect when filler extends the pre-query context to 1,798 tokens without adding pairings. Zeroing the first memory block removes this recall. An exploratory 48-pair test remains near chance after one quarter of the primary training budget and does not locate a capacity limit. Parameter-matched vector and Transformer baselines remain near chance, including the Transformer after additional training searches. This unresolved baseline failure prevents a memory-efficiency comparison.

</details>


### [346] [Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RL on Agentic Coding Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00890)
*Sushant Mehta,Logan Ritchie,Edwin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether reinforcement learning (RL) on expert-built agentic coding tasks can help coding agents overcome "last mile" failures (dropping requirements, insufficient testing, breaking existing behavior, unchecked assumptions). The researchers post-trained Kimi K2.7 Code (a 1T-parameter MoE model) using RL on 1,700 tasks and evaluated on six external benchmarks across three agent harnesses. Results show significant improvements across all benchmarks, with transfer learning demonstrated on tasks released after training data collection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents often fail in the final stages of tasks: they drop requirements, test only cases their implementation already handles, break existing functionality, or validate against unchecked assumptions. This "last mile" problem limits the practical utility of coding agents. The researchers wanted to investigate whether RL training on expert-built agentic coding tasks could close this gap and whether the learned behaviors would transfer beyond the training distribution.

Method: The study used Kimi K2.7 Code, a 1T-parameter (32B active) open-weight mixture-of-experts model. They applied one epoch of GSPO (Group Sampling Policy Optimization) on a rank-32 LoRA adapter for post-training. The training dataset consisted of 1,700 tasks: 1,000 repository tasks graded by hidden fail-to-pass tests and pass-to-pass tests of existing behavior, and 700 terminal tasks graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. The reward function was the fraction of target checks passed, dropping to zero if any pass-to-pass test failed. Evaluation was conducted on six external benchmarks across three agent harnesses: SWE-Bench Pro, DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench 2.1, Terminal-Bench 3, Terminal-Bench 4, and SWE-Marathon.

Result: One epoch of RL training improved pass@1 on all six external benchmarks. SWE-Bench Pro improved from 60.1 to 64.8, DeepSWE from 31.0 to 43.4, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 67.4 to 82.0, Terminal-Bench 3 from 1.4 to 12.1, Terminal-Bench 4 from 0.0 to 7.6, and SWE-Marathon from 5.0 to 25.0. The pooled improvement over five independent task sets was statistically significant (p < 0.001), and remained significant on the three sets released after training data was collected (p = 0.004). Improvements were also observed on both harnesses never used in training. Median trajectories on DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 3 were 24-35% shorter in agent steps. Analysis showed the base model's failed DeepSWE runs were mostly near-misses, and on newly solved tasks, the trained model avoided all four failure modes.

Conclusion: Reinforcement learning on expert-built agentic coding tasks effectively closes the "last mile" gap in coding agents. The trained model shows significant improvements across multiple benchmarks and demonstrates transfer learning to tasks released after training data collection, as well as to harnesses never used in training. The model not only solves more tasks but also uses fewer agent steps, suggesting more efficient problem-solving. The key insight is that the base model's failures were often near-misses that could be corrected through proper RL training, and the trained model learns to avoid specific failure modes (dropping requirements, insufficient testing, breaking existing behavior, and unchecked assumptions).

Abstract: Coding agents often fail in the last mile: they build most of a feature but drop a requirement, test only the cases their implementation already handles, break behavior that was supposed to stay intact, or validate against an unchecked assumption. We ask whether reinforcement learning (RL) on expert-built agentic coding tasks closes this gap, and whether what the agent learns transfers beyond the training distribution. We post-train Kimi K2.7 Code, a 1T-parameter (32B active) open-weight mixture-of-experts model, with RL alone on 1,700 tasks: 1,000 repository tasks graded by hidden fail-to-pass tests and by pass-to-pass tests of existing behavior, and 700 terminal tasks graded by expert-written hidden verifiers. The reward is the fraction of target checks passed and drops to zero if any pass-to-pass test fails. One epoch of GSPO on a rank-32 LoRA adapter improves pass@1 on each of the six external benchmarks we evaluated, across three agent harnesses: SWE-Bench Pro (60.1 to 64.8), DeepSWE (31.0 to 43.4), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (67.4 to 82.0), Terminal-Bench 3 (1.4 to 12.1), Terminal-Bench 4 (0.0 to 7.6), and SWE-Marathon (5.0 to 25.0). Pooled over the five independent task sets (Terminal-Bench 4 revises Terminal-Bench 3), the improvement is significant (p < 0.001), and it remains significant on the three sets released after the training data was collected (p = 0.004); the model also improves under both harnesses never used in training. Median trajectories on DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 3 are 24-35% shorter in agent steps. The base model's failed DeepSWE runs are mostly near-misses, and on the tasks the trained model newly solves, paired trajectories show it avoiding each of the four failure modes above.

</details>


### [347] [How Many Categories Are Enough? Distribution-Free Certification Limits for Few-Shot Anomaly Thresholds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00236)
*Gia Huy Thai,Nguyen Thai Anh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Few-shot anomaly detectors are judged by ranking metrics, yet deployment requires an alarm threshold with a controlled false-alarm rate (FAR). We ask how much normal evidence, in images or category units, is needed to certify such a threshold for an unseen category. Using a frozen DINOv2 principal component analysis (PCA) residual ranker on 15 MVTec and 12 VisA categories under four corruption types, we show that target-only leave-one-image-out (LOIO) calibration is resolution-limited and shift-fragile: rank values cannot fall below $1/(k+1)$, and at the attainable level $α=0.20$, empirical FAR reaches 0.341 on Gaussian-corrupted MVTec at $k=4$, 1.7 times the nominal level. A category-count feasibility calculus is then derived: even with all-zero category losses and no multiplicity charged, any deterministic, uniformly valid, distribution-free 95% upper confidence bound (UCB) requires at least 14, 29, and 59 independent and identically distributed (iid) category draws at $α=0.20$, $0.10$, and $0.05$; these counts are necessary but not sufficient. The Cross-category Reliability Estimation with Source Support (CRESS) protocol splits source categories into disjoint reference, proposal, and certification roles. With only three or four certification categories, all 960 frozen configurations return the fail-closed threshold $τ^\star=0$, and the smallest category-level UCB is 0.950. Image-unit analyses of the same archive select positive thresholds in 36.7% to 60.3% of target cells; these bounds hold for the selected source mixture, not for the marginal risk of a new-category draw. The contribution is a quantitative feasibility boundary and an estimand-aware protocol specifying when source evidence can, and cannot, support a transferable reliability claim.

</details>


### [348] [Exposing the Cost of Deep Learning Audio Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01619)
*Constance Douwes,Paul Magron,Romain Serizel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a methodology to estimate the energy consumption of the development phase in deep learning projects, using activity logs from the Grid5000 platform. Through a case study of audio projects, the research reveals that development-phase energy costs are 3-256 times greater than training the best-performing model alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing studies on deep learning's environmental impact focus mainly on training and inference, while neglecting the development phase (architecture prototyping and intensive experiments), which is highly energy-demanding. There was a need for methodology to estimate these overlooked costs.

Method: The researchers developed a methodology to estimate energy costs based on activity logs from the Grid5000 shared computing platform used by the LORIA laboratory. They conducted a case study focusing on audio projects developed in the Multispeech research team, evaluating four projects and comparing development-phase energy costs to training costs.

Result: The energy required for the development phase is 3 to 256 times greater than that required to train the best-performing model alone, across the four audio projects studied.

Conclusion: The findings advocate for more systematic reporting of energy consumption across the entire life cycle of deep learning-based audio projects, not just during training/inference phases.

Abstract: The environmental impact of deep learning has attracted increasing attention over the past decade. Existing studies mainly focus on the energy and carbon emissions of model training and inference, while the whole development phase is often overlooked. Yet, architecture prototyping and intensive experiments are conducted during this stage, which is highly energy-demanding. In this article, we propose a methodology to estimate these costs, based on activity logs from the Grid5000 shared computing platform used by the LORIA laboratory. As a case-study, we focus on audio projects developed in the Multispeech research team. We evaluate the overall energy cost of four projects, and we compare them to those of training the reported models. Our results show that the energy required for the development phase is 3 to 256 times greater than that required to train the best-performing model alone. These results advocate for a more systematic reporting of energy consumption across the entire life cycle of deep learning-based audio projects.

</details>


### [349] [Contingent Exposure Routing for Financial AI: Outage Risk and the Cost of Indivisible Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00239)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a stress test methodology for routing financial decisions through backup endpoints during model outages, analyzing how different failover strategies affect concentration of decision errors across institutions. The study evaluates randomized routing, conditional-expectation rounding, and swap procedures across synthetic portfolios and real API replay data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When primary model endpoints fail, financial institutions must route decisions to backup systems, which changes which institutions share decision errors. The authors aim to understand and quantify the risk concentration that arises from failover patterns, particularly whether shared backups create concentrated exposure versus diversified risk.

Method: The authors formulate outage-contingent routing through a local market-impact response matrix and study expected squared price displacement. They use symmetric constructions to analyze concentration floors, derive exact second moments for independent randomized routing, and develop conditional-exposure rounding with a swap procedure. Validation uses 60 synthetic portfolio networks (11,340 scenarios) and 1,024 recorded API responses on rebalancing tasks.

Result: The swap procedure reduces risk by 6.57% for single endpoint removal and 10.53% for double endpoint removal at the central feedback setting. Real API replay shows 3.30% held-out reduction (paired bootstrap interval 2.07-4.57%). Shared backups can create order-one concentration floors as primary endpoints grow, while balanced fallback risk decreases inversely with surviving endpoint count. Strongly aligned errors, inferior endpoints, and indivisibility limit diversification benefits.

Conclusion: The contribution is an auditable routing stress test framework and implementation analysis, not an estimate of real-market crash probabilities. The methodology provides a systematic way to evaluate failover routing strategies, though it has limitations under strongly correlated errors, poor backup quality, and indivisible decision constraints.

Abstract: Model failover restores availability, but changes which financial institutions share decision errors. We formulate outage-contingent routing through a local market-impact response matrix and study expected squared price displacement. A symmetric construction shows that a shared backup can leave an order-one concentration floor as the number of primary endpoints grows, while balanced fallback risk decreases inversely with the surviving endpoint count. For indivisible decisions, we derive the exact second moment of independent randomized routing and an effective-exposure granularity that determines its gap from fractional allocation. Conditional-expectation rounding gives a finite-agent bound without coupled quotas; a separate swap procedure preserves endpoint counts and is assessed against dual lower bounds. Across 60 synthetic portfolio networks and 11,340 scenario evaluations, the latter reduces risk by 6.57% and 10.53% for single and double endpoint removals at the central feedback setting with independent errors. A replay of 1,024 recorded API responses on constructed rebalancing tasks gives a smaller held-out reduction of 3.30% (paired bootstrap interval 2.07--4.57%). Strongly aligned errors, inferior endpoints, and indivisibility limit diversification. The contribution is an auditable routing stress test and implementation analysis, not an estimate of real-market crash probabilities.

</details>


### [350] [The Null Is the Hard Part: Exact Tests for Memorization in Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00251)
*Sushovan Majhi,Pramita Bagchi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses critical flaws in memorization audits of generative models: current methods lack proper null distributions and use arbitrary thresholds, leading to false conclusions. The authors propose two null hypotheses (for whole-model and single-image analysis) and demonstrate that when properly calibrated, most detected "memorization" disappears under statistical controls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memorization audits of generative models currently use similarity scores against arbitrary thresholds without null distributions, making conclusions unreliable. The field needs proper statistical calibration to distinguish true memorization from random chance.

Method: The authors propose: (1) For whole-model analysis: a permutation test treating training and held-out images as exchangeable given model samples; (2) For single-image analysis: ranking images among random controls and resampling independent generations. They apply false-discovery rate (FDR) control and test the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile (IECP).

Result: Under proper null calibration: (1) Nearest-neighbor preference still fires on 7/24 generators, but count restricted to near-duplicate scale on none (McNemar p=0.016); (2) Ranking yields 596 false discoveries among 2,365 controls; (3) Resampling makes null 3× too narrow; (4) 36 of 61 MemBench images certified at 5% FDR vs. 46 with calibrated maximum; (5) MemBench mitigations halve SD memorization; (6) 10/24 generators reproduce nothing under their own null test.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that null distribution specification is the critical challenge in memorization detection. They recommend the scale-restricted statistic (small-scale mass of IECP) for counting distinct copied images and testing whether two models copy the same images. Proper calibration shows most detected memorization vanishes under statistical controls.

Abstract: Memorization audits of generative models read similarity scores against thresholds, with no null distribution, and the conclusions they support can be wrong. By MemBench's rule, the benchmark's mitigations roughly halve Stable Diffusion's memorization; audited with false-discovery control, two thirds of the certified images are no longer detected under random prompt perturbations, five sixths under attention rescaling, and all of them under embedding optimization. The field's data-copying test, read against its own null, flags ten of twenty-four generators that reproduce nothing. We argue that for memorization the null is the hard part, and supply two. For a whole model, training and held-out images are exchangeable given its samples, and relabelling them is a permutation test, exact for any statistic when the held-out images are a random split; under it, a nearest-neighbour preference still fires on seven of those twenty-four, and a count restricted to the near-duplicate scale on none (McNemar p=0.016). For single images, the natural nulls fail twice, measurably: ranking an image among random images yields 596 false discoveries among 2,365 controls, and resampling independent generations makes the null three times too narrow. Calibrated against matched controls, the audit certifies 36 of 61 MemBench images at 5% false-discovery rate, held-out controls are certified in 0.01% of calibration splits, and on this benchmark two generations per image recover that count. A calibrated maximum, which reads occasional rather than typical copying, certifies 46. As the scale-restricted statistic we recommend the small-scale mass of the Intersection Euler Characteristic Profile, which also counts distinct images copied and tests whether two models copy the same ones.

</details>


### [351] [Sharp Oracle-Regret Tradeoffs for Projection-Free Online Convex Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00254)
*Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies online convex optimization where the learner can only access the feasible set through a linear optimization oracle. The main result establishes a dimension-free minimax expected regret of Θ(GD max{√T, T/(1+min{Q,BT})^{1/4}}) for convex G-Lipschitz losses with diameter D, Q total oracle calls, and B calls per round. The lower bound holds for arbitrary randomized learners, and a counted approximate-gradient method achieves the matching rate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand the fundamental limits of online convex optimization when the learner has restricted access to the feasible set (only via a linear optimization oracle), rather than full convex set access. This models scenarios where querying the feasible set is expensive or constrained.

Method: The paper uses several key technical constructions: (1) Universal feasibility forcing actions into the hull of the supplied ball and preceding oracle replies; (2) A fixed-body construction coupling fresh phase directions to a shared simplex to make useful replies costly repeatedly; (3) A counted approximate-gradient method with interleaved blocks to achieve the matching upper bound.

Result: The dimension-free minimax expected regret is Θ(GD max{√T, T/(1+min{Q,BT})^{1/4}}). Special cases include: T^{3/4} rate with one call per round (B=1), and quadratic total budget needed for √T regret. For prescribed smoothness β, a curvature-dependent lower bound is derived.

Conclusion: The characterization is sharp for convex Lipschitz losses. The threshold above which the general characterization remains sharp is identified for prescribed smoothness β. Total-budget and strict per-round guarantees are provided as special cases.

Abstract: We characterize the regret attainable in online convex optimization when access to the feasible set is limited to an exact linear optimization oracle. The learner is given an inscribed ball and a diameter bound and must remain feasible on every consistent instance. For convex $G$-Lipschitz losses, diameter at most $D$, a total allowance of $Q$ oracle calls, and a strict limit of $B$ calls per round, the dimension-free minimax expected regret is $Θ(GD\max\{\sqrt T,T/(1+\min\{Q,BT\})^{1/4}\})$. The lower bound applies to arbitrary randomized learners. Universal feasibility first forces each action into the hull of the supplied ball and the preceding oracle replies. A fixed-body construction then couples fresh phase directions to a shared simplex, making useful replies costly repeatedly even though all losses have a common minimizer. A counted approximate-gradient method with interleaved blocks attains the matching rate. Total-budget and strict per-round guarantees follow as special cases, including the $T^{3/4}$ rate with one call per round and the quadratic total budget needed for $\sqrt T$ regret. For prescribed smoothness $β$, an analytic construction yields a curvature-dependent lower bound and identifies the threshold above which the general characterization remains sharp.

</details>


### [352] [Verification Pulses and the Cost of Escaping Wrong Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00256)
*Shivam Gupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies how external verification with a limited budget can recover a population from wrong consensus in an asynchronous binary register system. It derives analytical results for minimum verification effort needed, validates them with exact birth-death calculations, and tests the framework on language model responses, finding that modest mean prediction errors can hide significant underestimate of terminal consensus.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem addresses a critical limitation: external verification can correct individual outputs but may fail to shift the entire population from a wrong consensus basin. The research aims to determine the minimum verification budget needed to escape wrong consensus and understand how timing and targeting of verification affect recovery success.

Method: The study employs three approaches: (1) Analytical derivation of minimum fuel required to cross basin boundary under peak verification constraint for general nonlinear response; (2) Exact birth-death calculation for finite populations to obtain probability of wrong consensus after verification pulses; (3) Empirical validation using 13,392 language model responses including calibration and 108 held-out trajectories, with distributional auditing.

Result: The key finding identifies a critical budget window with leading term Nlog(x₀/b) and √N correction. With 16 majority-updated slots and 14 initially wrong, 9 random checks exceed the mean-field threshold, but 23 are needed for 95% eventual recovery in the exact model. The experiment reveals calibration produces different fitted response regimes, but all adjusted schedule-comparison intervals include zero. A distributional audit shows modest mean-prediction error can conceal large underestimate of terminal consensus occupancy.

Conclusion: The results support risk-calibrated reset scheduling under a specified update contract, while explicitly separating it from distinct-target checking and unrestricted evidence broadcast. The substantial gap between mean-field predictions and exact calculations highlights the importance of accounting for variance from repeated verification targets and autonomous amplification after verification stops.

Abstract: External verification can correct individual outputs while leaving a self-reinforcing population in the basin of a wrong consensus. We study how the timing and addressing of a fixed verification budget affect recovery in an asynchronous binary register. For a general nonlinear response, we derive the minimum fuel required to cross a basin boundary under a peak verification constraint. For a finite population, an exact birth--death calculation gives the probability of subsequent wrong consensus after a pulse. Our main asymptotic result identifies the critical budget window: a leading term $N\log(x_0/b)$ and a correction of order $\sqrt N$, with separate variance contributions from repeated verification targets and autonomous amplification after verification stops. The distinction is substantial: with 16 majority-updated slots and 14 initially wrong, 9 random checks cross the mean-field budget threshold, whereas 23 are required for 95% eventual recovery in the exact model. A prospectively specified experiment records 13,392 language-model responses, including calibration and 108 held-out trajectories. Calibration produces different fitted response regimes, but all four adjusted schedule-comparison intervals include zero. A distributional audit also finds that modest mean-prediction error can conceal a large underestimate of terminal consensus occupancy. The results support risk-calibrated reset scheduling under a specified update contract, while explicitly separating it from distinct-target checking and unrestricted evidence broadcast.

</details>


### [353] [Attention Manifolds: Steering or Blocking Language Models by Editing Learned B-Spline Surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00257)
*Naveen Mysore*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "attention manifolds" - learned 2D B-spline surfaces that modulate value vectors in transformer attention based on query-key interactions, rather than just determining attention weights. The method preserves pretrained behavior while adding only 0.3% parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In standard transformer attention, the query determines how much to attend but not what to extract - the same value vector is sent to every receiver regardless of the query's content. This limits the expressive power of attention mechanisms.

Method: Attention manifolds are learned tensor-product cubic B-spline surfaces S_d(q_d, k_d) that modulate each value dimension based on query-key interaction. Initialized to zero to preserve pretrained behavior, they add only 0.3% parameter overhead. The method can also create "attention walls" by setting coefficients to -1.

Result: Applied to LLaMA 3.2-1B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct: (1) WikiText-2 validation perplexity reduced by 2-2.5 points; (2) 69-83% of 112 diverse prompts see changed greedy-decoded output; (3) 94-100% change rate on ambiguous/polysemous inputs; (4) improves output quality by correcting factual errors, increasing precision, and adding specificity; (5) inverting layer coefficients changes output for 9/10 prompts; (6) attention walls can redirect harmful content to educational content.

Conclusion: Attention manifolds provide a geometric mechanism for model steering with minimal parameter overhead. They enable precise control over information flow through specific dimensions, offer mechanical editability for model behavior, and show promise for safety applications through attention walls that can redirect problematic prompts.

Abstract: In standard transformer attention, a source token sends the same value vector to every receiver. The query determines \emph{how much} to attend but not \emph{what} to extract. This work introduces \textbf{attention manifolds}: learned 2D B-spline surfaces $S_d(q_d, k_d)$ that modulate each value dimension based on the query-key interaction. Each surface is a tensor-product cubic B-spline initialized to zero, preserving pretrained behavior. Applied to LLaMA 3.2-1B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct, attention manifolds reduce WikiText-2 validation perplexity by 2--2.5 points with 0.3\% parameter overhead. Across 112 diverse prompts, surfaces change greedy-decoded output for 69\% (1B) to 83\% (3B) of cases, with the strongest effects on ambiguous and polysemous inputs (94--100\% change rate). The surfaces improve output quality: correcting factual errors (\emph{``the CAP theorem has three main components''} $\to$ \emph{``it is impossible to guarantee all three''}), increasing precision (\emph{``impossible to know certain properties''} $\to$ \emph{``impossible to know both position and momentum''}), and adding specificity (a generic quote $\to$ an attributed Saint Augustine citation, consistently at both scales). The learned surfaces are also mechanically editable: inverting a layer's coefficients changes greedy output for 9/10 prompts (KL~0.010), providing a geometric mechanism for model steering. Setting surface coefficients to $-1$ creates ``attention walls'' that block value flow through specific dimensions. In a preliminary experiment, a layer-wide wall redirects an explosive-device prompt from specific instructions to general educational content, suggesting a path toward safety-oriented manifold shaping.

</details>


### [354] [FastCI: Efficient GPU-Intensive CI for LLM Training Frameworks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01967)
*Tianshuo Qiao,Naiqian Zheng,Xiaopeng Liu,Shuguang Wang,Diandian Gu,Xuanzhe Liu,Xin Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FastCI is a framework that improves continuous integration (CI) efficiency for large language model (LLM) training frameworks by selecting affected tests using runtime evidence, pruning equivalent tests, prioritizing high-risk tests, and optimizing test workloads. It reduces CI latency by 77.5% and GPU resource usage by 63.9%, while improving code coverage retention by 3.2%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM training frameworks are growing in size and complexity, requiring GPU-intensive tests for CI. Traditional CI becomes a bottleneck because these tests involve complete model training or evaluation, which is time-consuming and resource-heavy, hindering fast-paced development.

Method: FastCI uses four key strategies: (1) runtime evidence to select affected tests, (2) pruning tests that execute changed code in equivalent contexts, (3) prioritizing high-risk tests to expose failures earlier, and (4) optimizing test workloads along dimensions outside the intended validation scope.

Result: FastCI reduces CI latency by 77.5% and GPU resource usage by 63.9%, while improving modified code coverage retention by 3.2%, compared to currently deployed CI pipelines.

Conclusion: FastCI has been integrated into ByteDance's LLM training framework CI pipelines, demonstrating practical effectiveness in real-world deployment.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) keep growing in size and complexity, their training frameworks evolve at a rapid pace as well. Therefore, continuous integration (CI) is critical for maintaining the quality and stability of these frameworks. However, unlike traditional software, CI for LLM training frameworks relies on GPU-intensive tests, which usually involve complete model training or evaluation. This leads CI itself to become a new bottleneck for fast-paced development. In this paper, we introduce FastCI, a framework that improves the efficiency of CI for LLM training frameworks. FastCI leverages runtime evidence to select affected tests and prune tests that execute changed code in equivalent contexts. Then FastCI prioritizes high-risk tests to expose potential failures earlier, and optimizes test workloads along dimensions outside the intended validation scope of each test. Evaluated on the CI workload of our LLM training framework, FastCI reduces the CI latency by 77.5% and the GPU resource usage by 63.9%, while improving the modified code coverage retention by 3.2%, compared with the currently deployed CI pipelines. FastCI has now been integrated into the CI pipelines of our LLM training framework at ByteDance.

</details>


### [355] [Large Language Bayes Is Not Reparameterisation-Invariant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00265)
*Jian Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Large Language Bayes (LLB) weights depend on how probabilistic programs are written (parameterized), not just their mathematical content. The same measure can produce weights differing by up to 31.9× depending on centered vs non-centered parameterization, even though log marginal likelihood is invariant to reparameterization. This affects Bayes factors and posterior estimates, with errors controlled by the spread Δ of bound shortfalls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Informal modelling with LLB:LLB approximates Bayesian inference by sampling candidate probabilistic programs from a language model, running approximate inference on each, and averaging them with weights proportional to an exponentiated evidence bound. A key question is whether this weighting is well-defined—that is, invariant to how a model is written.

Method: Empirical investigation across: (1) eight schools problem comparing centered vs non-centered parameterizations, (2) importance weighting to reduce discrepancy, (3) full-covariance Gaussian matched to posterior moments, (4) experiments across likelihood families, dimensions and funnel severities, (5) 360 programs from six language models to assess parameterization tendencies

Result: Log marginal likelihood is invariant to reparameterization (to 5.7×10⁻¹⁴ on eight schools), but evidence bound weights differ by 6.1×. Importance weighting reduces this to 2.2×; full-covariance Gaussian matching leaves 1.9× on eight schools and 8.9× in 64 dimensions. Discrepancy reaches 31.9× and reverses sign across settings, so no single writing is uniformly preferable. It inverts Bayes factors against eight natural competitors. The induced error is controlled by spread Δ of bound shortfalls through a sharp Hilbert-distance bound. Across 360 programs, parameterization ranges from 0% to 100% centered and is stable within each model. Detecting equivalent programs statistically can falsely merge different models; verifying reparameterizations closes this window.

Conclusion: LLB's weighting scheme depends on parameterization, not just the underlying mathematical model. This is a fundamental issue that affects Bayes factors and posterior inference. The error can be controlled by the spread Δ, but no single parameterization is universally best. Statistical detection of equivalent programs risks false mergers; verifying reparameterizations resolves this.

Abstract: Large Language Bayes (LLB) answers an informal modelling question by sampling candidate probabilistic programs from a language model, running approximate inference on each, and averaging them with weights proportional to an exponentiated evidence bound. We show that this weighting depends on how a model is written. The log marginal likelihood is invariant to reparameterisation; the evidence bound is not. On eight schools the centered and non-centered programs are the same measure to $5.7\times10^{-14}$, yet their weights differ by $6.1\times$; importance weighting reduces this only to $2.2\times$, and reproducing the inference LLB actually runs, a full-covariance Gaussian matched to the posterior moments, still leaves $1.9\times$ on eight schools and $8.9\times$ in $64$ dimensions. Across likelihood families, dimensions and funnel severities the discrepancy reaches $31.9\times$ and reverses sign, so no single writing is uniformly preferable. It inverts Bayes factors against eight natural competitors, and the induced error in the model posterior, and in any downstream target, is controlled by the spread $Δ$ of the bound shortfalls through a known sharp Hilbert-distance bound. Across $360$ programs from six language models the parameterisation written ranges from $0\%$ to $100\%$ centered and is stable within a model. Detecting equivalent programs statistically can falsely merge genuinely different models at practical sample budgets; verifying reparameterisations we generate ourselves cannot, and closes the window.

</details>


### [356] [MOVE: Multimodal Open-world Verification and Expansion for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00268)
*Zekai Chen,Jiayang Xing,Xun Wu,Miao Zhang,Xunkai Li,Kairui Yang,Zhengyu Wu,Xu Wang,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MOVE addresses the open-world problem in multimodal graph learning where new classes may emerge after deployment. It identifies unknown nodes using multimodal evidence, leverages multimodal LLMs to generate candidate classes, and selectively expands the class space only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing redundancy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multimodal graph learning, models are trained with a fixed label space but new classes may emerge after deployment. Existing approaches detect unknown nodes and use LLMs to generate candidate class descriptions, but fail to determine whether existing classes are insufficient or whether generated classes are reliable enough. Three key challenges were identified: 1) multimodal information beyond individual modalities is required for unknown-node identification, 2) LLM-generated class descriptions may not fully capture multimodal class characteristics, and 3) directly adding candidate classes can introduce redundant categories.

Method: MOVE proposes a three-stage framework: 1) Unknown node identification - jointly considers visual tokens, textual attributes, and graph context to identify nodes that cannot be assigned to existing classes; 2) Candidate class generation - leverages a multimodal LLM to generate candidate classes; 3) Selective class expansion - expands the class space only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing unnecessary categories.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that MOVE achieves an average improvement of 11.87% across unknown recognition, open-domain annotation, and downstream graph learning tasks.

Conclusion: MOVE successfully addresses the open-world class expansion problem in multimodal graph learning by combining multimodal information for unknown detection, LLM-based candidate generation, and evidence-based selective expansion, achieving significant improvements across multiple evaluation tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal graph learning faces a fundamental challenge: new classes may emerge after deployment, while models are trained with a fixed label space. Existing approaches typically detect unknown nodes and use LLMs to generate candidate class descriptions, but they do not determine whether existing classes are insufficient to cover these nodes or whether a generated class is reliable enough to expand the class space. Our empirical study reveals three challenges: multimodal information beyond individual modalities is required for unknown-node identification, LLM-generated class descriptions may not fully capture multimodal class characteristics, and directly adding candidate classes can introduce redundant categories. Based on these observations, we propose MOVE, a multimodal open-world class verification and expansion framework. MOVE identifies nodes that cannot be assigned to existing classes by jointly considering visual tokens, textual attributes, and graph context, leverages a multimodal LLM to generate candidate classes, and selectively expands the class space only when candidates are consistently supported by multimodal evidence without introducing unnecessary categories. Experiments demonstrate that MOVE achieves an average improvement of 11.87\% across unknown recognition, open-domain annotation, and downstream graph learning tasks.

</details>


### [357] [Coupling Perception and Reasoning in Federated Multimodal Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00277)
*Zekai Chen,Xun Wu,Hailin Zhang,Xunkai Li,Yu Liu,Kairui Yang,Muyan Huang,Xuaner Chen,Rong-Hua Li,Guoren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedCORE is a federated adaptation framework for multimodal graph foundation models (GFMs) that addresses the limitation of existing methods by jointly optimizing Encoder and GNN updates through a shared low-dimensional latent state, reducing the Encoder-GNN pairing gap by 80.7%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing federated GFM adaptation methods freeze the multimodal Encoder while only updating GNN modules, limiting adaptation to how information is propagated without adapting what information is extracted. Empirical studies reveal that Encoder and GNN adaptations are not independent - they exhibit pairing sensitivity when modules are swapped across clients.

Method: FedCORE represents both Encoder and GNN updates through a shared low-dimensional latent state ("core"). This core is jointly optimized from multimodal and structural signals, with federated evolution performed directly in the shared state space, preserving compatibility between perception (Encoder) and reasoning (GNN) adaptations.

Result: FedCORE reduces the Encoder-GNN pairing gap from 30.6 to 5.9, representing an 80.7% reduction over independent joint adaptation methods.

Conclusion: By jointly optimizing Encoder and GNN updates through a shared latent space, FedCORE successfully addresses the pairing sensitivity issue in federated GFM adaptation, enabling more effective and compatible multimodal graph reasoning across decentralized clients.

Abstract: Federated multimodal graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to adapt pretrained multimodal models to decentralized graph data, where each client owns a private multimodal graph and cannot share raw information. These models typically combine a multimodal Encoder that extracts semantic evidence from heterogeneous modalities and a graph neural network (GNN) that performs relational reasoning over graph structures. However, existing federated GFM adaptation methods mainly update graph-side modules while keeping the multimodal Encoder frozen, limiting adaptation to \emph{how information is propagated} while fixing \emph{what information is extracted}. Through empirical studies, we reveal that Encoder and GNN adaptations are not independent: Encoder adaptation is affected by graph relations, while cross-client module swapping reveals substantial pairing sensitivity between separately parameterized Encoder and GNN updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{FedCORE}, a federated adaptation framework that represents Encoder and GNN updates through a shared low-dimensional latent state. FedCORE jointly optimizes this core from multimodal and structural signals and performs federated evolution directly in the shared state space, preserving compatibility between perception and reasoning adaptations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedCORE reduces the Encoder--GNN pairing gap from $30.6$ to $5.9$, corresponding to an $80.7\%$ reduction over independent joint adaptation.

</details>


### [358] [Stable and Counterfactually Robust Physical World Models from Imposed Structure and Learned Physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00280)
*Yufeng Wang,Parivesh Priye,Lu Wei,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses fundamental limitations of world models in physics simulation—specifically energy creation, drift, and inability to handle parameter changes. The authors propose a framework where general physical structure (reversible dynamics from energy gradients, confining energy, one-way energy ports) is hard-coded while system-specific physics (energy functional, constitutive relations, dissipation) is learned from data. The model achieves second-law compatible dissipation, correct intervention responses, 100× training horizon stability, and robustness across electromagnetic, particle, and fluid systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models imitating physical systems face critical failures: energy creation, trajectory drift/divergence, and inability to adapt when physical laws change. The authors question how much physical structure must be hard-coded versus learned from data to achieve four simultaneous properties: second-law compatible dissipation, correct intervention responses, long-term stability (100× training horizon), and robustness to disturbances.

Method: The proposed framework imposes general physical structure: (1) dynamics generated from gradient of learned energy through fixed reversible operator, (2) energy restricted to confining class, (3) one-way port can remove but never inject energy, (4) drive channel is known, (5) intervened parameter enters through separable map. The model learns energy functional, constitutive relations, dissipation rate, and couplings from data. Three physical systems are tested: electromagnetic cavity, particle-in-cell grid, and shallow-water fluid, with ~9000 parameters.

Result: Models with ~9000 parameters successfully recover constitutive functions with unit slope, distinguish conserving from dissipating worlds by four orders of magnitude using a single set of weights, and transfer changes in sign, magnitude, rate, and gravity to unseen values. Equal-capacity models without the imposed structure perform at chance or worse. A nonlinear constitutive law is recovered with preserved curvature and predicts held-out interventions 2-17× better than converged linear models.

Conclusion: Hard-coding general physical structure (energy-based dynamics, confining energy, one-way ports, known drive channels, separable intervention maps) enables learning system-specific physics from data while satisfying second-law dissipation, intervention correctness, long-term stability, and robustness. This approach significantly outperforms unstructured models of equal capacity, demonstrating that imposing physical priors is essential for reliable world models.

Abstract: A world model learns to forecast how a physical system evolves from recorded trajectories, yet the systems it imitates obey physical laws that are neither fully supplied nor reliably respected. The model may create energy, drift or diverge over long rollouts, and answer a changed law query using the law observed during training. We ask how much general physical structure must be hard coded into a world model, and how much system-specific physics can then be learned from data, for four properties to hold simultaneously: second law compatible dissipation, correct responses to interventions on physical parameters, stability out to one hundred times the training horizon, and robustness to disturbances. The imposed structure is general: dynamics are generated from the gradient of a learned energy through a fixed reversible operator, the energy is restricted to a confining class, a one way port can remove energy but never inject it, the drive channel is known, and the intervened parameter enters through a separable map. The model learns the energy functional, constitutive relations, dissipation rate, and couplings. Across an electromagnetic cavity, a particle in cell grid, and a shallow-water fluid, models with roughly nine thousand parameters recover constitutive functions with unit slope, separate conserving from dissipating worlds by four orders of magnitude using a single set of weights, and transfer changes in sign, magnitude, rate, and gravity to unseen values, where equal-capacity models without the same structure perform at chance or worse.
