A nonlinear constitutive law is recovered with its curvature preserved and predicts a held-out intervention $2$-$17\times$ better than a converged linear model.

</details>


### [359] [Partial AUC Maximization from Positive-unlabeled Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00284)
*Atsutoshi Kumagai,Tomoharu Iwata,Taishi Nishiyama,Hiroshi Takahashi,Kazuki Adachi,Yasuhiro Fujiwara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel method for maximizing partial AUC (pAUC) from positive and unlabeled (PU) data only, without requiring labeled negative data. The approach represents pAUC using positive and marginal densities within an empirical risk minimization framework and trains a classifier by maximizing a smoothed empirical pAUC estimator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many real-world applications like cybersecurity, medical care, and advertising, high pAUC is desirable but labeled negative data are difficult to collect due to privacy concerns or annotation expertise requirements. Existing pAUC maximization methods require both labeled positive and negative data, limiting their practical applicability.

Method: The authors employ an empirical risk minimization framework and show that pAUC (including its FPR-dependent thresholds) can be represented using only positive and marginal densities. From this theoretical foundation, they derive an empirical estimator from PU data and train a classifier by maximizing this smoothed empirical pAUC estimator.

Result: The proposed method was experimentally validated on ten real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness for pAUC maximization from PU data.

Conclusion: The paper presents a viable solution for maximizing partial AUC when only positive and unlabeled data are available, bridging a practical gap in binary classification where negative labels are scarce or unavailable. This enables pAUC optimization in real-world scenarios with limited labeled data.

Abstract: The partial area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (pAUC) is an important performance metric for binary classification that summarizes true positive rates within a specific range of false positive rates (FPRs). Classifiers that achieve high pAUC need to be obtained in many real-world applications such as cybersecurity, medical care, and advertising. Although many methods for maximizing the pAUC have been proposed, they typically require both labeled positive and negative data for training. However, in practice, labeled negative data are often difficult to collect due to privacy concerns or the need for high expertise to annotate them. In this paper, we propose a method for maximizing the pAUC from positive and unlabeled (PU) data without negative data. Within an empirical risk minimization framework, we show that the pAUC, including its FPR-dependent thresholds, can be represented using only the positive and marginal densities, and derive an empirical estimator from PU data. A classifier is then trained by maximizing the derived smoothed empirical pAUC estimator. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method with ten real-world datasets.

</details>


### [360] [Bellman-Certified Rounding for Sparse Policy Deployment in MDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00325)
*Zhaojun Peng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the loss in discounted return when continuous policy optimization solutions are rounded to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. The authors develop reusable envelopes from 2d+2 Bellman solves to provide pre-rounding guarantees, and introduce rank-two rational representations for weighted curvature integration along trajectories. They prove linear dimension dependence is unavoidable and that exact global curvature thresholding is hard, with empirical results showing significant improvements in certification coverage and bound-to-loss ratios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that continuous policy optimization may spread updates across many states, but deployment often permits only a few complete state-level changes. This creates a tension between the continuous policy improvement and the need for sparse, deployable policies. The authors aim to understand and bound the performance loss from rounding continuous policies to sparse binary ones.

Method: The authors derive reusable envelopes from 2d+2 Bellman solves that support both uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. They use a rank-two rational representation for each exchange to enable weighted curvature integration along the realized trajectory. The approach involves curvature bounds and integration techniques to provide post-rounding performance guarantees.

Result: Theoretical results: (1) Linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, (2) Exact global curvature thresholding is hard. Empirical results: (1) Candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from 48.2% to 74.1% on structured suite, (2) At γ=0.95, local integration lowers median bound-to-loss ratio from 402.3 to 2.08 on coupled instances.

Conclusion: The paper provides practical methods for certifying policy rounding quality in finite MDPs, with the candidate-specific bounds and local integration techniques offering significant improvements over baseline approaches. The theoretical lower bounds establish fundamental limits on what can be achieved.

Abstract: Continuous policy optimization may spread an update across many states, even when deployment permits only a few complete state-level changes. We study how much discounted return can be retained when continuous row mixtures are rounded to sparse binary policies in finite MDPs. Policy-dependent visitation couples the row edits, while long horizons make global curvature bounds conservative. From $2d+2$ Bellman solves, we derive reusable envelopes that support uniform and candidate-specific guarantees before rounding. A rank-two rational representation of each exchange further permits weighted curvature integration along the realized trajectory. We prove that linear dimension dependence is unavoidable when the budget scales, and that exact global curvature thresholding is hard. Candidate-specific bounds raise pre-rounding certification coverage from $48.2\%$ to $74.1\%$ on the structured suite. At $γ=0.95$, local integration lowers the median bound-to-loss ratio from $402.3$ to $2.08$ on coupled instances.

</details>


### [361] [Beyond Diagonal State Space Models: Exact Non-Abelian Group Tracking, Solvability Barriers, and Geometric Physical Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00329)
*Zeyu Jia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Non-Commutative State Space Models (NC-SSM) to address limitations of existing SSMs (Mamba, S4D, LRU) that are bounded by transition matrix commutativity and solvable affine transformation groups. The proposed method lifts state transitions to compact Lie groups (SU(2), SO(3), SO(N)) using Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms, achieving exact norm-preserving isometry and significantly better performance on non-solvable groups and sequence modeling tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing selective state space models (SSMs) like Mamba, S4D, and LRU are constrained by transition matrix commutativity and solvable affine transformation groups. When stacked in multi-layer diagonal networks, they suffer severe optimization degradation on non-solvable simple groups (e.g., A_5) because simulating non-abelian commutators requires exponential circuit emulation depth. This limits their ability to model complex non-commutative structures and long-range dependencies.

Method: The authors propose Non-Commutative State Space Models (NC-SSM) by lifting state transitions to compact Lie groups (SU(2), SO(3), SO(N)). Key techniques include: (1) Closed-form Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms for exact norm-preserving isometry (||U_t|| = 1); (2) Pure Hopf-filiation Bloch projective readouts to eliminate sign ambiguity; (3) True quaternion parallel prefix scans for 9.06x speedup at T=2048; (4) Identity-Gated Lie SSMs to eliminate sparse syntax phase drift.

Result: Extensive benchmarks across 14 experimental regimes show: (1) NC-SSM achieves 100% tracking on S_3, D_4, Q_8 and simple group A_5, vs 6.60% for 3-layer diagonal baseline (p=8.81e-4); (2) Cayley-SO(5)-SSM breaks Klein's 1884 ceiling on S_5 (50.92% vs 5.25%, p=0.0015, 7.8x variance reduction over SO(3)); (3) SO(3)-SSM preserves Riemannian manifolds across 300 steps (<3.12e-6 drift, >580,000x advantage), achieving 0.04° dead-reckoning error; (4) NC-SSM achieves 74.36% on Dyck-2 and 30.26% on deep AST scope tracking (p=0.0081); (5) Ablation confirms strict isometry is mathematically necessary for lossless long-range associative memory.

Conclusion: The proposed NC-SSM successfully addresses the commutativity and solvability limitations of existing SSMs by operating on compact Lie groups. This enables effective modeling of non-abelian structures and achieves state-of-the-art performance across group theory benchmarks, sequence modeling tasks, and manifold preservation, while strict isometry is confirmed as mathematically necessary for lossless long-range associative memory.

Abstract: Selective state space models (SSMs), such as Mamba, S4D, and LRU, are bounded by transition matrix commutativity (A_t A_t' = A_t' A_t) and solvable affine transformation groups (Aff_D of derived length <= 2). Consequently, stacked multi-layer diagonal networks face severe optimization degradation on non-solvable simple groups such as A_5 due to the exponential circuit emulation depth required to simulate non-abelian commutators. We propose Non-Commutative State Space Models (NC-SSM), their real-orthogonal counterpart SO(3)-SSM, and arbitrary-dimension Cayley-SSM, lifting state transitions to compact Lie groups SU(2), SO(3), and SO(N). Via closed-form Euler-Rodrigues maps and rational Cayley transforms, NC-SSM achieves exact norm-preserving isometry (||U_t|| = 1). We introduce pure Hopf-fibration Bloch projective readouts (S^3/{+-1} =~ S^2 =~ SO(3)) to eliminate sign ambiguity, true quaternion parallel prefix scans (9.06x speedup at T=2048), and Identity-Gated Lie SSMs to eliminate sparse syntax phase drift. Extensive benchmarks across 14 experimental regimes show: (1) NC-SSM achieves 100% tracking on S_3, D_4, Q_8 and simple group A_5, where a 3-layer deep diagonal baseline collapses to 6.60% (p = 8.81e-4); (2) Cayley-SO(5)-SSM breaks Klein's 1884 ceiling on symmetric group S_5 (50.92% vs diagonal 5.25%, p = 0.0015, delivering 7.8x variance reduction over SO(3)); (3) SO(3)-SSM preserves Riemannian manifolds across 300 steps (< 3.12e-6 drift, > 580,000x advantage), achieving 0.04 deg dead-reckoning error and active tangent denoising; (4) NC-SSM achieves 74.36% on Dyck-2 and 30.26% on deep AST scope tracking (p = 0.0081); and (5) ablation confirms strict isometry is mathematically necessary for lossless long-range associative memory.

</details>


### [362] [The Weakest Link: Distilling LLM Reasoning with Worst-Case Constrained Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00332)
*Matthieu Zimmer,Xiaotong Ji,Tu Nguyen,Haitham Bou-Ammar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses a fundamental challenge in distilling reasoning capabilities from large language models into smaller students. Current methods either suffer from reward hacking (correct answers via flawed reasoning) or diluted performance due to KL-based regularization. The key insight is that reasoning quality depends on the weakest link in the chain, not average quality. The authors propose a constrained RL formulation with worst-case constraints on teacher log-likelihood at every trajectory prefix, and derive an unaugmented constrained MDP that preserves hard constraints while enabling low-variance policy gradients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core tension in reasoning distillation is that optimizing purely for task rewards (via GRPO) leads to reward hacking where students produce correct answers through flawed reasoning, while KL-based regularization dilutes task performance and allows compensation - students can make severe logical errors at one step but compensate with high teacher agreement elsewhere. This averaging approach is fundamentally misaligned with reasoning, which depends on the weakest link in the chain.

Method: The authors formulate reasoning distillation as a constrained reinforcement learning problem where task reward is maximized subject to a worst-case constraint on teacher log-likelihood along every prefix of the trajectory. They derive an unaugmented constrained MDP that: (1) preserves hard-constraint semantics through reward transformation, (2) admits a low-variance policy gradient decomposition into single-step and long-term terms, and (3) provably satisfies the worst-case constraint almost surely in the penalty limit. This avoids the prohibitive cost of dual Lagrangian solvers and test-time teacher dependence of state-augmented methods like Saute.

Result: The method significantly expands the accuracy-fidelity Pareto front. By matching the high Final Answer Correctness of pure RL while drastically reducing teacher constraint violations, it achieves the highest rigorous Reasoning Success Rate across all evaluated settings on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed constrained RL approach with worst-case constraints on every trajectory prefix provides a principled solution to reasoning distillation that preserves the validity of the entire reasoning chain rather than allowing averaging of quality. This yields a better trade-off between task accuracy and reasoning fidelity compared to existing approaches.

Abstract: Distilling the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) into smaller students is a central challenge for efficient deployment. Current approaches face a fundamental tension: optimizing purely for verifiable task rewards (e.g., via GRPO) leads to reward hacking, where students arrive at correct final answers through flawed intermediate logic, while regularizing with soft divergence penalties against a teacher (e.g., KL-based distillation) dilutes task performance and, critically, allows the student to compensate for severe logical violations at one step with high teacher agreement at others. We argue that this averaging is fundamentally misaligned with the nature of reasoning: a chain-of-thought is only as valid as its weakest link. Motivated by this observation, we formulate reasoning distillation as a constrained reinforcement learning problem in which the task reward is maximized subject to a worst-case constraint on the teacher log-likelihood along every prefix of the trajectory. To avoid the prohibitive cost of dual Lagrangian solvers and the test-time teacher dependence of state-augmented methods such as Saute, we derive an unaugmented constrained MDP whose reward transformation preserves the hard-constraint semantics, admits a low-variance policy gradient decomposition into single-step and long-term terms, and provably satisfies the worst-case constraint almost surely in the penalty limit. Through extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, we demonstrate that our method significantly expands the accuracy-fidelity Pareto front. By matching the high Final Answer Correctness of pure RL and drastically reducing teacher constraint violations, we ultimately achieve the highest rigorous Reasoning Success Rate across all evaluated settings.

</details>


### [363] [Benchmarking System One decision models against trained classifiers and language models for automated decision gates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00346)
*Amir Rafe,Subasish Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares different machine learning approaches for automated decision-making in software: typed decision models (System One), supervised classifiers, and generative language models. Under various conditions, small trained classifiers excel on intents, decision models outperform zero-shot classifiers without labels, and fine-tuned checkpoints improve over backbones. The study provides condition-dependent design rules for implementing automated decision gates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop design rules for automated decision gates in software by systematically comparing three model classes (decision models, supervised classifiers, generative language models) under matched conditions on workflow, intent, and social-science tasks.

Method: Experimental comparison using eight decision-model checkpoints from six families (including hosted model Jev) and two generative comparators, tested on workflow, intent, and social-science items under various conditions (with/without labels, different thresholds, temperature settings).

Result: - Small trained classifiers are most accurate on intents with task labels
- Decision models exceed zero-shot classifiers on workflows/intents without labels
- Larger generative models match Jev on workflows/intents
- Fine-tuned decision checkpoints gain intent accuracy over untuned backbones
- Temperature calibration degrades with more options
- Jev accepts 0.310 of out-of-scope requests at 5% threshold
- Swapping yes/no flips 50.5 answers per hundred for Jev
- Intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev achieves 43% of full cost

Conclusion: The results yield condition-dependent design rules for implementing automated decision gates in software systems, showing that optimal model choice depends on available labels, task type, and cost constraints.

Abstract: Software that hands branching decisions to a model needs a declared option and a probability it can threshold. Typed decision models, also called System One models, return such probabilities without generating text, while supervised classifiers and generative language models are the established alternatives. Under matched conditions, one harness sends eight decision-model checkpoints from six families, including the hosted model Jev, and two generative comparators the same semantic requests, and scores supervised and zero-shot classifiers on the same workflow, intent and social-science items. The ranking of the model classes depends on the conditions. With the task's own labels, small trained classifiers are the most accurate on intents and not significantly different from the best decision models on workflows. Without labels, every decision model except the encoder-based checkpoints exceeds a zero-shot entailment classifier on workflows and intents. Read through option-key likelihoods, a larger generative model is level with Jev on workflows and intents and accepts more workflow decisions at five percent risk, and fine-tuned decision checkpoints gain intent accuracy over their untuned backbones. Stored temperatures fitted on few options raise calibration error with many options, and a held-out threshold for five percent in-scope risk still lets Jev accept 0.310 of out-of-scope requests. Swapping yes and no flips 50.5 answers per hundred for Jev, while fine-tuned checkpoints cut their backbones' social-science flips. An intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev matches its accuracy at 0.43 of its cost at full graphics-processor utilization. The results yield condition-dependent design rules for automated decision gates.

</details>


### [364] [Deep Learning for Anomaly Detection in Railway Systems: A Structured Survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00363)
*Ammar Bouketta,Smail Niar,Hamza Ouarnoughi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper is a structured survey of deep learning-based anomaly detection approaches for railway systems. It organizes existing methods into a unified taxonomy covering anomaly location, data representation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics. The survey covers architectures including CNNs, RNNs, attention mechanisms, autoencoders, GANs, and transformers, classified into four learning paradigms: classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid. It also addresses data challenges, evaluation metrics, and deployment considerations including edge-cloud architectures and computational constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the increasing need for safe and reliable operation of modern railway systems, which increasingly relies on data-driven monitoring and intelligent fault detection. The growing availability of heterogeneous sensor data from rolling stock and infrastructure has made deep learning an effective paradigm for railway anomaly detection, but there was a need for a structured survey to organize and categorize the diverse approaches in this field.

Method: The method employed is a systematic literature survey. The researchers organized the surveyed methods using a unified taxonomy covering multiple dimensions: anomaly location, data representation and manifestation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics. They categorized existing approaches into four learning paradigms: classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid learning. The survey also examined data-centric challenges, evaluation practices, performance metrics, and practical deployment aspects.

Result: The paper presents a comprehensive structured reference organizing deep learning-based anomaly detection methods for railway systems. It provides a decision-oriented framework that links anomaly characteristics, data properties, and operational constraints to suitable detection paradigms and deployment configurations. The survey covers various deep learning architectures including convolutional, recurrent and attention-based architectures, autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and transformers.

Conclusion: The conclusion highlights that this work provides a structured reference for selecting and deploying deep learning solutions for railway anomaly detection. It also identifies open challenges toward reliable and scalable intelligent monitoring systems, suggesting areas for future research in this domain.

Abstract: Ensuring safe and reliable operation of modern railway systems increasingly relies on data-driven monitoring and intelligent fault detection. Deep learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for railway anomaly detection, driven by the growing availability of heterogeneous sensor data from rolling stock and infrastructure. This paper presents a structured survey of deep learning-based anomaly detection approaches for railway systems. The surveyed methods are organized using a unified taxonomy covering anomaly location, data representation and manifestation, sensing modality, and temporal characteristics. Existing approaches, including convolutional, recurrent and attention-based architectures, autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and transformers, are structured into classification-based, prediction-based, reconstruction-based, and hybrid learning paradigms. The survey also examines data-centric challenges, evaluation practices, performance metrics, and practical deployment aspects, including edge-cloud architectures, computational constraints, and hardware-aware optimization. Finally, a decision-oriented framework links anomaly characteristics, data properties, and operational constraints to suitable detection paradigms and deployment configurations. This work provides a structured reference for selecting and deploying deep learning solutions for railway anomaly detection and highlights open challenges toward reliable and scalable intelligent monitoring systems.

</details>


### [365] [Manifold-Constrained Initial Noise Optimization for Efficient Generative Model Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00365)
*Jinho Chang,Jong Chul Ye*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ZeNOVA is a gradient-free initial noise alignment method for black-box reward optimization in generative models. It uses annealed soft-value guidance, manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics, and Metropolis-Hastings jumping to stably and efficiently optimize initial noise toward higher rewards, outperforming zeroth-order baselines on image and video generation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing initial-noise optimization methods rely on first-order gradient information, which is either inapplicable or suffers from instability and inefficiency in black-box reward scenarios. This limits their practical applicability for reward alignment in modern generative models.

Method: ZeNOVA introduces three key techniques: (1) annealed soft-value guidance for stable reward optimization, (2) manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics to exploit the geometry of the Gaussian prior, and (3) Metropolis-Hastings jumping for improved exploration. It operates in a gradient-free (zeroth-order) manner suitable for black-box scenarios.

Result: ZeNOVA outperforms all evaluated zeroth-order baselines by optimizing initial noise toward higher rewards substantially more stably while exploiting the geometry of the Gaussian prior.

Conclusion: ZeNOVA demonstrates practical applicability to various black-box reward alignment tasks, providing a stable and efficient approach for reward optimization in image and video generative models.

Abstract: Recent advances in distillation and flow-map models have enabled deterministic one- or few-step generation for high-quality data, facilitating a new branch of reward alignment approaches that directly optimize the initial noise from a Gaussian distribution. However, most existing initial-noise optimization methods rely on first-order gradient information, which is either inapplicable or suffers from instability and inefficiency in black-box reward scenarios. Here, we introduce ZeNOVA, a stable and efficient initial noise alignment method in a gradient-free manner. Specifically, we address existing algorithms' major challenge in black-box scenarios through annealed soft-value guidance, manifold-constrained hyperspherical Langevin dynamics, and Metropolis-Hastings jumping. Extensive experiments on image and video generative models show that ZeNOVA outperforms all evaluated zeroth-order baselines by optimizing the initial noise toward higher rewards substantially more stably while exploiting the geometry of the Gaussian prior, demonstrating its practical applicability to various black-box reward alignment.

</details>


### [366] [MoRA: MoE Pruning via Router Bias Learning and Expert Approximation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00367)
*Yushuai Sun,Zikun Zhou,Lin Gao,Jun Yu,Wenjie Pei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MoRA proposes a structured MoE expert pruning framework that combines router bias learning with expert approximation to reduce memory usage while maintaining model performance. It introduces learnable router biases optimized with a language-modeling loss and routing-diversity regularizer, plus an expert approximation mechanism to recover performance after pruning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MoE models suffer from high memory requirements due to needing to load all experts, even though only a subset is active per token. Existing pruning methods have limitations: expert ranking criteria are poorly aligned with model performance, searching for optimal expert subsets is computationally expensive, and routing-behavior redundancy among retained experts is overlooked.

Method: MoRA uses two key components: (1) Router bias learning - learnable bias terms for each expert optimized by minimizing language-modeling loss + routing-diversity regularizer to sharpen routing probabilities and identify critical experts while encouraging diverse routing preferences. (2) Expert approximation - post-pruning enhancement using remaining experts to approximate pruned expert outputs via affine transformation.

Result: Evaluated on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and Moonlight-16B-A3B, removing 25% and 50% of routed experts. MoRA outperforms state-of-the-art pruning algorithms across nine zero-shot benchmarks.

Conclusion: MoRA effectively reduces MoE memory usage through structured expert pruning while maintaining or improving performance compared to existing methods, with the router bias learning and expert approximation mechanisms working synergistically.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable parameter scaling with limited per-token computation by activating only a small subset of experts for each token, but deploying them still requires loading the complete expert pool into memory. Structured expert pruning can effectively reduce the memory usage by removing experts. However, existing pruning methods either use expert ranking criteria that are not well aligned with model performance or rely on effective expert subset searching that is computationally expensive. Moreover, these methods typically overlook the routing-behavior redundancy among the retained experts. In this paper, we propose MoE Pruning via Router Bias Learning and Expert Approximation (MoRA), a framework for structured MoE expert pruning. We introduce a learnable router bias for each expert and optimize these biases by minimizing the language-modeling loss and a routing-diversity regularizer. The learned router biases sharpen the routing probability distributions to identify experts critical to model performance while encouraging the selection of experts with diverse routing preferences. In addition, we introduce an expert approximation mechanism as a post-pruning enhancement. It leverages the remaining experts to approximate the outputs of pruned experts by affine transformation, further improving the performance of the pruned model. We evaluate MoRA on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and Moonlight-16B-A3B, removing 25\% and 50\% of the routed experts in each MoE layer. Extensive experiments on nine zero-shot benchmarks show that MoRA outperforms state-of-the-art pruning algorithms. Our code will be released.

</details>


### [367] [M$^2$Weather: A Benchmark for Joint Multi-Station and Multi-Variable Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00370)
*Rongwen Li,Xiao Wang,Mingyang Wang,Hongwu Liu,Changjian Chen,Zhuo Tang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M^2Weather is a benchmark for joint multi-station and multi-variable weather forecasting, addressing the gap in existing studies that consider spatial dependencies and physical coupling separately. The benchmark includes 2,809 high-quality stations across three spatial scales (France, Europe, Global) with 5 physically coupled weather variables. A lightweight adapter is introduced to examine station-variable relationships without retraining. Evaluation of 16 models shows that joint modeling and completing missing relationships consistently improves forecasting accuracy (reduces MSE).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing weather forecasting studies treat spatial dependencies across stations and physical coupling among weather variables as separate problems, using different datasets and experimental settings. This makes it difficult to systematically assess their individual and joint contributions to forecasting performance. There is a need for a unified benchmark that enables fair comparison of different station-variable modeling approaches.

Method: The paper introduces M^2Weather benchmark with: (1) Multi-criteria quality control and station stratification to collect 2,809 high-quality stations; (2) Three spatial scales (France, Europe, Global) to examine whether conclusions persist across scales; (3) Unified training and evaluation protocols for fair comparison; (4) A lightweight, plug-and-play adapter that can introduce missing station or variable relationships without retraining the base model. Systematic evaluation of 16 representative models was conducted.

Result: Joint modeling of station and variable relationships provides benefits for weather forecasting. Completing missing relationships further reduces MSE for all adapted models on all three datasets (France, Europe, Global). The results demonstrate that complementary information across stations and variables is an important resource for improving station weather forecasting.

Conclusion: The complementary information across stations and variables represents a valuable resource for improving station weather forecasting. The M^2Weather benchmark provides a standardized framework for systematic investigation of station-variable relationships, and the proposed adapter enables efficient exploration of these relationships without model retraining.

Abstract: Station weather forecasting is fundamentally shaped by both complex spatial dependencies across stations and strong physical coupling among weather variables. However, existing studies often consider these relationships separately and use different datasets and experimental settings, hindering systematic assessment of their individual and joint contributions. In this paper, we introduce $M^2$Weather, a benchmark for joint multi-station and multi-variable weather forecasting. Through multi-criteria quality control and station stratification, we collect 2,809 high-quality stations with 5 physically coupled weather variables across three spatial scales: France, Europe, and Global. This multi-scale design lets us examine whether conclusions persist from national to global station networks. We also introduce unified training and evaluation protocols to enable fair comparison of different station-variable modeling paradigms. To further examine the benefits of modeling station-variable relationships, we design a lightweight, plug-and-play adapter. With a trained weather forecasting model, this adapter can introduce missing station or variable relationships without retraining the model. This enables fair and efficient investigation of station-variable relationships. Systematic evaluation of 16 representative models shows the benefits of jointly modeling station and variable relationships. Completing missing relationships further reduces MSE for all adapted models on all three datasets. Together, these results identify the complementary information across stations and variables as an important resource for improving station weather forecasting. Our code can be obtained at https://github.com/hnu-vis/M2-Weather.

</details>


### [368] [When Do Attention-Head Ablations Support Causal Claims? Projection-Level Confounds, Floor Effects, and Matched Controls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00373)
*Juli Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that attention-head ablation - a common method for interpreting language models - can produce misleading results if not carefully implemented. Using GPT-2 small, the authors show that different implementation choices (post-projection vs pre-projection ablation) select completely different important heads (r = 0.057), and that metric choice (binary accuracy vs log-probability) significantly affects conclusions. With proper controls and metrics, the ranking is stable, but task specificity claims are not robust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate the reliability of attention-head ablation as a method for causal attribution in language models. They observe that this widely-used technique may produce fragile inferences due to inconsistent implementation choices.

Method: The authors compare post-projection vs pre-projection ablation implementations, binary accuracy vs log-probability metrics, and use discovery/held-out splits with 1,000 matched random-head and layer-matched-head control draws. Experiments were conducted on GPT-2 small and replicated on DistilGPT2.

Result: Post-projection ablation is nearly uncorrelated with pre-projection ablation (Pearson r = 0.057) and selects a completely disjoint top-5 set of heads. Binary accuracy hides effects at floors and ceilings while log-probability remains graded. With corrected per-head effects, ranking is highly stable across splits (Spearman rho = 0.974) and top-5 heads significantly exceed control distributions (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). However, task specificity is not robust on GPT-2. Findings replicate on DistilGPT2.

Conclusion: Single-head ablation does not by itself justify causal claims. Defensible interpretation requires: (1) correct intervention placement (pre-projection), (2) non-saturated continuous metric (log-probability), and (3) matched held-out controls. The method can work with proper validation but requires careful implementation.

Abstract: Attention-head ablation, zeroing a head and measuring the resulting change in task performance, is a common method for inferring which components of a language model are causally responsible for a behavior. We show using GPT-2 small that this inference can be fragile unless the intervention semantics, evaluation metric, and controls are carefully validated. A natural post-projection implementation of "zeroing a head" is nearly uncorrelated with a corrected pre-projection ablation (Pearson r = 0.057) and selects a completely disjoint top-5 set of important heads. We also show that binary accuracy can hide effects at behavioral floors and near ceilings, whereas gold-token log-probability remains graded. Using a discovery/held-out split and 1,000 matched random-head and layer-matched-head control draws, the corrected per-head effect ranking is highly stable across splits (Spearman rho = 0.974), and the top-5 selected heads significantly exceed both control distributions (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). However, evidence for task specificity is not robust on GPT-2. Replication on DistilGPT2 preserves the intervention-semantic and matched-control findings. These results show that single-head ablation does not by itself justify a causal claim; defensible interpretation requires correct intervention placement, a non-saturated continuous metric, and matched held-out controls.

</details>


### [369] [A First Glance at Jev for Network Traffic Classification: Accuracy, Processing Time, and Cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00376)
*Shenghe Xu,Lifan Mei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates Jev, a general-purpose decision model, for application classification of network flows using only the first ten packets' metadata (sizes, directions, inter-packet times). Experiments on CESNET-QUICEXT-25 show that while labeled examples substantially improve Jev's accuracy (from 9.80% to 28.42% with 40 examples), traditional tree ensembles (Random Forest: 69.95%, Extra Trees: 66.80%) significantly outperform Jev. Comparative tests against GPT-5.6 Sol show Jev is faster but less accurate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: This is the first empirical study of general-purpose decision models (represented by Jev) for application classification of network flows. The authors aim to evaluate whether such models can effectively classify network applications using minimal initial packet information.

Method: The study uses CESNET-QUICEXT-25 dataset with 52,000 records across 26 collection weeks. Features include first ten packets' sizes, directions, and inter-packet times. Jev is tested with varying numbers of labeled examples (40 and 150). Comparison made against Random Forest, Extra Trees, and OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol.

Result: Jev with 40 labeled examples improves from 9.80% to 28.42% accuracy. With 150 examples, accuracy reaches 34.50%. Random Forest (8,000 records training) achieves 69.95% and Extra Trees 66.80%, outperforming Jev in every week. In paired tests, Jev (29%, 0.750s) vs GPT-5.6 Sol (37%, 6.036s) - Jev is faster but less accurate.

Conclusion: Labeled examples substantially improve Jev's performance, but Jev configurations remain less accurate than trained tree ensembles. The study cannot attribute the accuracy gap to a single cause due to unequal supervision budgets and fixed configurations. The paired subset does not establish a clear accuracy advantage for either Jev or GPT-5.6 Sol.

Abstract: We evaluate Jev on ten dataset-defined application labels in CESNET-QUICEXT-25 using only the first ten packets' sizes, directions, and inter-packet times. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first empirical study of general-purpose decision models, represented here by Jev, for application classification of network flows. Across 52,000 records from 26 collection weeks following the training period, 40 fixed labeled examples raise Jev's accuracy from 9.80% to 28.42%. Random Forest and Extra Trees trained on 8,000 records achieve 69.95% and 66.80% and outperform Jev in every week. Increasing Jev's context to 150 examples yields 34.50% on the first test week. On a paired 100-record subset, Jev with 40 examples achieves 29% accuracy at a median request time of 0.750 s, versus 37% and 6.036 s for the generative language model OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol with high reasoning effort through Azure; Jev also incurs lower API charges. The paired subset does not establish an accuracy advantage for either service, and the timing reflects different service configurations. Thus, labeled examples substantially improve Jev, but the tested Jev configurations remain less accurate than trained tree ensembles; unequal supervision budgets and fixed configurations prevent attributing the gap to a single cause.

</details>


### [370] [STCFormer: Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Modeling with Dynamic Cluster Transformer for Station-based Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00377)
*Rongwen Li,Haixin Xie,Mingyang Wang,Hongwu Liu,Kun Fang,Changjian Chen,Zhuo Tang,Kenli Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: STCFormer is an adaptive spatio-temporal Transformer for station-based weather forecasting that dynamically groups stations within each temporal patch based on local evolution patterns. It combines fine-grained local attention within clusters with global attention over regional state summaries, and includes a theoretical Lipschitz bound analysis to explain its robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Station-based weather forecasting faces challenges in modeling complex spatial dependencies. Existing clustering-based selective modeling approaches have limitations: (1) a static grouping across observation windows may obscure local changes in station relationships, and (2) intra-cluster interactions alone may miss important global context. Additionally, the theoretical advantages of selective interactions over dense connectivity remained poorly understood.

Method: STCFormer employs an adaptive spatio-temporal Transformer architecture with three key components: (1) Dynamic station grouping within each temporal patch based on local evolution patterns; (2) Cluster-Guided Attention Block combining fine-grained local attention within clusters and global attention over regional state summaries, allowing each station to access information beyond its own cluster; (3) InfoLoss mechanism motivated by theoretical analysis showing that the Lipschitz upper bound for cluster-conditioned local attention is no larger than its fully connected counterpart.

Result: Experiments on three real-world weather datasets across eight temperature and wind forecasting tasks show that STCFormer achieves the lowest 24-hour mean squared error on all eight tasks and ranks first or second in 47 of 48 comparisons across metrics and forecasting horizons.

Conclusion: STCFormer demonstrates the effectiveness of locally adaptive grouping and complementary local-global interactions for weather forecasting. The theoretical Lipschitz bound analysis provides insight into the robustness benefits of selective interactions. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse forecasting tasks and datasets.

Abstract: Station-based weather forecasting supports daily life and economic activity, yet accurate forecasts require modeling complex spatial dependencies among stations. Recent clustering-based selective modeling offers a promising alternative to dense inter-station interactions. However, a grouping shared across an observation window may obscure local changes in station relationships, while intra-cluster interactions alone may miss important global context. The theoretical advantages of selective interactions over dense connectivity also remain insufficiently understood. We therefore propose STCFormer, an adaptive spatio-temporal Transformer that dynamically groups stations according to their local evolution within each temporal patch. Its Cluster-Guided Attention Block combines fine-grained local attention within clusters and global attention over regional state summaries, allowing each station to access information beyond its own cluster. We further show that a derived Lipschitz upper bound for cluster-conditioned local attention is no larger than its fully connected counterpart, explaining a potential robustness benefit and motivating the design of InfoLoss. Experiments on three real-world weather datasets spanning eight temperature and wind forecasting tasks show that STCFormer achieves the lowest 24-hour mean squared error on all eight tasks and ranks first or second in 47 of 48 comparisons across metrics and forecasting horizons. Ablations and case studies further confirm the benefits of locally adaptive grouping and complementary local-global interactions. Our code can be obtained at https://github.com/hnu-vis/STCFormer.

</details>


### [371] [Fusion techniques of time frequency-based images to predict the outcome of rTMS depression therapy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00380)
*Wael Korani,Md Fahimul Kabir Chowdhury,Mohammed Aledhari,Reza Rostami,Reza Kazemi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using EEG-derived Time-Frequency images with fusion techniques (montage and blending) and a lightweight CNN to predict repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) treatment response in depression patients. The study reveals a critical finding: when using proper subject-disjoint cross-validation (no data leakage), model performance drops to near-chance levels (AUC 0.31-0.54), highlighting the importance of rigorous validation in medical ML applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting rTMS treatment response for depression is clinically challenging due to high inter-subject variability and limited features from single-domain EEG analysis. The authors aim to develop a more robust prediction method using fused Time-Frequency representations from EEG data.

Method: The study introduces two fusion techniques (montage and blending) to extract richer features from EEG-derived Time-Frequency (TF) images. A lightweight custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is trained on fused TF representations. Two datasets were used: primary (15 patients) and secondary (46 patients). Two experimental setups were conducted: (1) segment-level 10-fold cross-validation (with data leakage), and (2) strict subject-disjoint cross-validation. Four time-frequency methods, six fusion mechanisms, and fourteen model architectures were tested.

Result: In the segment-level 10-fold cross-validation (with data leakage), Montage CWT_ST fusion achieved 99.90% accuracy on the primary dataset and 91.90% on the secondary dataset. However, in strict subject-disjoint cross-validation, performance collapsed significantly: almost all configurations yielded AUC between 0.31 and 0.54, with 95% confidence intervals containing 0.5 (chance level). The best subject-level result was Montage CWT_ST on the primary cohort (AUC 0.874 ± 0.183, 82.7% accuracy), but a patient-level permutation test returned p = 0.703, indicating the result is not statistically significant.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates a critical methodological issue in medical ML: when proper subject-disjoint cross-validation is used (ensuring no patient appears in both training and testing), the model's predictive performance collapses to near-chance levels. This highlights the importance of rigorous validation strategies in healthcare ML applications and suggests that EEG-based rTMS response prediction remains a challenging task that requires further research.

Abstract: Depression is a mental condition that can lead to suicide and self-harm. Predicting the outcome of depression treatment is one of the most difficult tasks for clinicians. Among various treatment options, repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is a widely used non-invasive method. Predicting rTMS response using Electroencephalogram (EEG) data is difficult because of high inter-subject variability and limited features from single-domain analysis. We introduce two fusion techniques, montage and blending, to overcome these limitations and extract richer features from EEG-derived Time-Frequency (TF) images. We then propose a lightweight custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on fused TF representations. \textcolor{black}{We use a primary dataset of 15 patients and a secondary dataset of 46 patients. We run two sets of experiments. The first set uses segment-level 10-fold cross-validation. In this setup segments from the same patient can appear in both training and testing. The Montage CWT\_ST fusion reaches 99.90\% accuracy on the primary dataset and 91.90\% on the secondary dataset. The second set uses strict subject-disjoint cross-validation. All segments of a patient stay in one fold and no patient appears in both training and testing. Performance collapses. We test four time-frequency methods, six fusion mechanisms, and fourteen model architectures. With one exception, every configuration on both cohorts falls between AUC 0.31 and 0.54 and every 95\% confidence interval contains 0.5. A patient-level permutation test on the best standalone method returns $p = 0.703$. The best subject-level result is Montage CWT\_ST on the primary cohort, which reaches AUC $0.874 \pm 0.183$ and 82.7\% accuracy.

</details>


### [372] [OmniMed-Jev: Calibrating LVLM Confidence for Trustworthy Medical Multimodal Decisions via System One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00381)
*Luyao Tang,Cheng Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces OmniMed-Jev, a decision-native interface for medical AI that represents medical decisions as explicit Choice, Noul (binary), or Score distributions over candidate sets, rather than generating text. This approach produces calibrated probabilities that more accurately reflect actual accuracy compared to traditional generative medical models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical models require reported confidence to match actual accuracy. Current multimodal medical models express decisions as generated text, where probabilities reflect next-token predictions rather than the actual decision confidence. The authors seek to make confidence scores meaningful by adopting a decision-native interface approach.

Method: OmniMed-Jev represents each medical decision as a Choice (mutually exclusive classes), Noul (binary presence of a finding), or Score (bounded ordered value) over a runtime-supplied candidate set. The model returns a full distribution over that set, making heterogeneous outputs comparable probabilities. This was compared against a generative baseline trained on the same backbone, data, and schedule.

Result: OmniMed-Jev's reported probabilities track observed correctness more closely than the generative baseline, reducing calibration error by up to an order of magnitude and reliability error by up to two. Point-prediction performance remains comparable. The counting task is the one area where the generative baseline maintains an advantage.

Conclusion: Explicit decision modeling through decision-native interfaces can make reported confidence meaningful within evaluated medical tasks. The results are not evidence of clinical readiness, and the comparison cannot fully separate interface effects from associated training differences.

Abstract: Medical models are judged not only on correctness, but on whether reported confidence matches actual accuracy. Generalist multimodal medical models have expanded what a single model can perceive, yet they still express bounded decisions such as diagnoses, findings or cell counts as generated text, so the reported probability reflects the next token rather than the decision itself. Motivated by decision-native interfaces such as Jev, we introduce OmniMed-Jev, which represents each medical decision as a Choice, Noul or Score decision over a runtime-supplied candidate set and returns a full distribution over that set: mutually exclusive classes, binary presence of a finding, or a bounded ordered value. The design is omni in three respects: it accepts diverse imaging modalities, covers different prediction tasks, and expresses them through one candidate-conditioned probability model, so heterogeneous outputs become comparable probabilities rather than task-specific strings. In an interface-controlled comparison against a generative baseline trained on the same backbone, data and schedule, OmniMed-Jev's reported probabilities track observed correctness far more closely, reducing calibration error by up to an order of magnitude and reliability error by up to two, while point-prediction performance remains comparable; counting is the one family where the generative baseline stays ahead. Making the decision distribution the model's output is not a format change but what turns reported numbers into probabilities that mean what they say. These results support explicit decision modeling as a way to make reported confidence meaningful within the evaluated tasks, and they are not evidence of clinical readiness: the comparison cannot separate the interface from associated training differences, which we state alongside the results. Code is available at github.com/lytang63/OmniMed-Jev.

</details>


### [373] [EvoGen-Harness: Learning Where and How to Evolve Image-Generation Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00383)
*Jiabin Luo,Yinan Liu,Chunlei Meng,Yufei Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoGen-Harness is a generator-agnostic framework that improves frozen text-to-image systems by evolving multiple generator-external responsibilities simultaneously, using Trace (Trajectory-Relative Attribution and Coordinated Evolution) to attribute failures and guide the evolution process across responsibilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing T2I improvement approaches only optimize a single dimension (prompts, routing, or workflows), restricting the space for correcting generation failures. The authors aim to enable multi-responsibility evolution for broader adaptation space, but face the challenge that visual feedback reveals failures without indicating where evolution should occur or how to explore efficiently.

Method: The authors propose Trace, which: (1) aggregates evidence across stochastic executions, (2) uses failure attribution as a search prior to focus candidate updates, (3) progressively re-attributes residual failures to coordinate evolution across responsibilities. Additionally, No-Patch and held-out validation prevent unnecessary or harmful updates.

Result: EvoGen-Harness improves over strongest baselines by +0.2633 on GenEval2, +0.0720 on T2I-CompBench++, and +0.0752 on WISE. It achieves 87.9-91.4% attribution recall, 94.8% No-Patch accuracy, and only 1.9% regression.

Conclusion: Attribution-guided multi-responsibility evolution can substantially enhance frozen T2I systems beyond single-dimension adaptation, demonstrating the effectiveness of coordinating evolution across multiple generator-external responsibilities.

Abstract: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems can be improved without modifying generator parameters by adapting the external system around frozen generators. However, existing approaches typically optimize a predefined dimension, such as prompts, routing, or workflows, restricting the space in which generation failures can be corrected. Allowing multiple generator-external responsibilities to evolve provides a broader adaptation space, but introduces a new challenge: visual feedback reveals what failed, but not where persistent evolution should occur or how this space should be explored efficiently. We introduce EvoGen-Harness, a generator-agnostic framework for multi-responsibility image-generation harness evolution, together with Trace (Trajectory-Relative Attribution and Coordinated Evolution). Trace aggregates evidence across stochastic executions, uses failure attribution as a search prior to focus candidate updates, and progressively re-attributes residual failures to coordinate evolution across responsibilities, while No-Patch and held-out validation prevent unnecessary or harmful updates. Across GenEval2, T2I-CompBench++, and WISE, EvoGen-Harness improves over the strongest evaluated baselines by +0.2633, +0.0720, and +0.0752, respectively, while achieving 87.9-91.4% attribution recall, 94.8% No-Patch accuracy, and only 1.9% regression. These results demonstrate that attribution-guided multi-responsibility evolution can substantially enhance frozen T2I systems beyond single-dimension adaptation.

</details>


### [374] [FAER: Auditable Utility-Aligned Trajectory Replay for Language Model Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00385)
*Miaobo Hu,Shuhao Hu,Xiaobo Guo,Xin Wang,Bokun Wang,Tianshu Fu,Daren Zha,Jun Xiao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FAER is an auditable full-trajectory replay framework that addresses the selection-to-learning gap in replay systems, where format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length metrics don't align with downstream learner utility. It introduces a training-free fixed selector as baseline and FAER-UTILITY as a learner-aware selector fitted on calibration blocks. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, FAER-UTILITY achieves quality 0.6624, outperforming fixed selector (0.6329), uniform (0.5482), and format-feedback (0.6037).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Replay selectors often rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length, but cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives. This selection-to-learning gap needed formalization and a solution.

Method: FAER framework includes: (1) training-free fixed selector as protocol baseline; (2) FAER-UTILITY as learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks; (3) normalized gradient alignment as baseline metric; (4) disposable optimizer-aware virtual update for magnitude-aware utility surface; (5) audit contract that freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined.

Result: On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: Fixed selector achieves quality 0.6329 vs uniform 0.5482 and format-feedback 0.6037 under 128 updates. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches 0.6476 ± 0.0139 at 63,276 tokens (189,642 total tokens, 3.48 GPU-hours). FAER-UTILITY achieves 0.6624 at 62,844 tokens (4.26 GPU-hours). Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953 vs 0.3594 for fixed selector, despite different downstream ranking.

Conclusion: FAER provides an auditable framework that closes the selection-to-learning gap by using learner-aware selectors fitted on calibration blocks. The approach outperforms fixed, uniform, and format-feedback selectors, demonstrating that metadata-only cross-fitted calibration can improve downstream learner utility. The audit contract ensures reproducibility by freezing observed fields before evaluation labels are joined.

Abstract: Replay selectors often rank cached trajectories by format feedback, confidence, freshness, or response length, although cache-level correctness and downstream learner utility are distinct objectives. We formalize this selection-to-learning gap and introduce FAER as an auditable full-trajectory replay framework. Its training-free fixed selector is a protocol baseline; FAER-UTILITY is the learner-aware selector fitted on disjoint calibration blocks. The normalized gradient alignment is reported as a baseline, while a disposable optimizer-aware virtual update supplies a magnitude-aware utility surface. The audit contract freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, the matched learner study reports quality 0.6329 for the fixed selector, compared with 0.5482 for uniform and 0.6037 for format-feedback under 128 updates. Metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches $0.6476\!\pm\!0.0139$ over eight seeds (median 0.6481; paired 95% interval $[+0.079,+0.122]$) at 63,276 target-run tokens; its recorded full cost is 189,642 tokens and 3.48 GPU-hours including calibration. The completed FAER-UTILITY row reaches 0.6624 at 62,844 target-run tokens and 4.26 GPU-hours. Format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953, compared with 0.3594 for the fixed selector, despite the different downstream ranking. The completed comparison surfaces report the learner-aware ablation, same-seed gap, policy-optimization rows, and strict zero-shot transfer.

</details>


### [375] [T2SPO: Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00388)
*Bo-Wen Zhang,Junwei He,Maoqi Liu,Feiran Li,Song-Lin Lv,Wentao Ma,Rongyi Lin,Shuhan Zhong,Lan-Zhe Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: T2SPO addresses the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning for LLM agents by using past successful trajectories to provide step-level feedback. It uses a pretrained TabPFN regressor to estimate remaining distance to success at each state, and the changes in this estimate across consecutive states serve as auxiliary credit for agent steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multi-step interactive tasks, rewards typically reflect only final outcomes, providing limited guidance on which intermediate decisions advance the task. This sparse reward problem makes it difficult for LLM agents to learn effective policies through standard RL methods.

Method: T2SPO derives remaining-distance targets from successful trajectories and pairs them with state representations. A pretrained TabPFN regressor estimates remaining distance to success at each state of new rollouts. Changes in this distance estimate across consecutive states yield auxiliary credit for agent steps alongside task-level supervision. Newly completed trajectories refresh the estimator's context without updating its parameters (in-context learning).

Result: Experiments with 1.5B and 7B language models on ALFWorld and WebShop show that T2SPO consistently improves overall task success over GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).

Conclusion: T2SPO provides an effective solution for step-level credit assignment in LLM agent training by leveraging successful trajectories to create a distance-to-success estimator. The method achieves consistent improvements over baseline approaches without requiring parameter updates to the estimator.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning enables large language model (LLM) agents to learn multi-step behaviors through interaction with their environments. However, rewards in many interactive tasks reflect only the final outcome, providing limited guidance on which intermediate decisions advance the task. Successful training trajectories contain intermediate states that can provide supervision for subsequent interactions. We introduce Trajectory-to-Step Policy Optimization (T2SPO), a method that uses past interaction trajectories to provide step-level feedback for policy learning. T2SPO derives remaining-distance targets from successful trajectories and pairs them with representations of the states visited along the way. Conditioned on these examples, a pretrained TabPFN regressor estimates the remaining distance to success at each state of a new rollout. Changes in this distance estimate across consecutive states yield auxiliary credit for agent steps alongside task-level supervision. As training proceeds, newly completed trajectories refresh the estimator's context, incorporating new experience without updating its parameters. Experiments with 1.5B and 7B language models on ALFWorld and WebShop show that T2SPO consistently improves overall task success over GRPO.

</details>


### [376] [MatrixReward: Reward from Rubric Matrix for Open-Ended Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00389)
*Zihan Shen,Qi Liu,Zixuan Yang,Yiqun Chen,Chenglong Zhao,Xiaozhao Wang,Lei He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MatrixReward proposes a novel reward mechanism for open-ended query generation that constructs rewards from a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix. It uses column spread to measure rubric discrimination ability, correlations to detect rubric repetition, and relative-closeness to ideal profiles for final reward calculation. Achieves 63.02 average score on Qwen3-8B, outperforming baseline by ~2.0%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-ended query generation lacks standard answers, necessitating effective reward mechanisms. Existing pointwise scoring rubrics provide limited information about relative quality of sample answers; merging multiple rubric judgments into a single score may mask differences between answers.

Method: MatrixReward constructs rewards from a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix obtained by comparing every pair of sampled responses under each rubric. The spread of each matrix column captures rubric discrimination strength, while correlations between columns reveal rubric repetition. These statistics yield data-dependent rubric weights combined with prior weights. After column normalization and weighting, per-rubric maxima and minima define positive and negative ideal profiles. Each rollout's distances to these ideals determine its relative-closeness quality reward.

Result: Evaluated using Qwen3-8B on four open-ended query-answering benchmarks, MatrixReward achieves an average score of 63.02, outperforming the strongest baseline by approximately 2.0%.

Conclusion: Matrices derived from relative comparisons can be used to construct rewards more reasonably for open-ended generative reinforcement learning. The approach successfully addresses limitations of pointwise scoring by leveraging pairwise comparisons and ideal profile-based distance metrics.

Abstract: Open-ended query generation lacks standard answers, thus necessitating an effective reward mechanism. Pointwise scoring rubrics provide limited information about the relative quality of sample answers under the same prompt; merging multiple rubric judgments into a single score may also mask the differences between these answers. We propose MatrixReward, which constructs rewards from a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix obtained by comparing every pair of sampled responses under each rubric. The spread of each matrix column captures how strongly that rubric distinguishes the current rollouts, while correlations between columns reveal rubric repetition; together, these statistics yield data-dependent rubric weights. We combine these weights with the prior weights of rubrics. After column normalization and weighting, the observed per-rubric maxima and minima define positive and negative ideal profiles. Each rollout's distances to these two ideals determine its relative-closeness quality reward. Evaluated using Qwen3-8B on four open-ended query-answering benchmarks, MatrixReward achieves an average score of 63.02, outperforming the strongest baseline by approximately 2.0%. These results support the idea that matrices derived from relative comparisons can be used to construct rewards more reasonably for open-ended generative reinforcement learning.

</details>


### [377] [Interpretable Synthetic Medical Tabular Data Generation for Clinical Decision Support Using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00391)
*Michael Vasilakakis,Dimitris K. Iakovidis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel framework using Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) for generating synthetic medical tabular data. The approach encodes clinical features as linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets and captures inter-feature dependencies through FCM edge weights derived from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce numerical values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing probabilistic and deep generative models for synthetic medical data lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies. This limits their suitability for safety-critical healthcare applications where trust and transparency are essential. Additionally, privacy concerns restrict access to real clinical data, making synthetic data generation critical for developing and validating Computer-Based Medical Systems (CBMSs).

Method: The proposed method uses Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) where: (1) Clinical features are represented as linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets; (2) Inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections; (3) Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence; (4) Defuzzification produces clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types and domain constraints common in health records.

Result: Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets using a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol shows: Accuracy up to 0.81 and AUROC up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines; KS Complement up to 0.91 and Correlation Similarity up to 0.95 (strong statistical coherence); DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE (adequate privacy guarantees). The method runs exclusively on CPU.

Conclusion: Causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs. The FCM-based approach achieves competitive performance with better interpretability, privacy guarantees, and CPU efficiency compared to state-of-the-art deep generative models like TVAE.

Abstract: Synthetic medical tabular data generation has become essential for developing and validating computer-based medical systems (CBMSs) when real clinical data is restricted due to privacy, ethical, or data availability limitations. Existing probabilistic and deep generative models often lack interpretability and fail to preserve clinically meaningful dependencies, limiting their suitability for safety-critical applications. This paper proposes a novel application of Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) in a framework for synthetic medical tabular data generation with explicit causality and privacy preservation. Clinical features are described using linguistically interpretable fuzzy sets, and inter-feature dependencies are encoded as FCM edge weights computed from fuzzy set intersections. Synthetic patient records are generated by propagating randomly initialized linguistic activation vectors through the FCM until convergence, followed by defuzzification to produce clinically coherent numerical values. The approach natively handles mixed data types, and domain constraints common in health records. Experimental evaluation on UCI medical benchmark datasets demonstrates competitive performance under a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) protocol. The proposed method achieves accuracy of up to 0.81 and AUROC of up to 0.90 on the Heart Disease dataset, matching or exceeding TVAE and Gaussian Copula baselines while running exclusively on CPU. Fidelity metrics including KS Complement (up to 0.91) and Correlation Similarity (up to 0.95) confirm strong statistical coherence, and DCR Baseline Protection scores consistently exceed those of TVAE, confirming adequate privacy guarantees. These results demonstrate that causally grounded, interpretable fuzzy modeling offers a computationally efficient and transparent alternative to deep generative models for trustworthy synthetic data generation in CBMSs.

</details>


### [378] [Forking: Sudden Overfitting Under Replay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00394)
*Shanbin Yu,Shaoyang Guo,Haoran Zhao,Danni Yu,Ziming Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies "forking," a generalization failure in NanoGPT where models with over-encoding n-gram memory branches show sharp separation between training and validation loss at epoch boundaries under data replay. The phenomenon is reproduced in DeepSeek-style models, with low-frequency contexts contributing most to the gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate forking, a generalization failure discovered in NanoGPT autoresearch, to understand its mechanism and implications for model training.

Method: The study reproduces forking in a controlled vanilla NanoGPT setting and in a DeepSeek-style model with Engram. It analyzes how repeated updates affect continuation probabilities and how n-gram modules create context-specific subspaces.

Result: Repeated updates sharpen observed continuations while suppressing unseen ones, whose loss grows with each pass. The n-gram module amplifies this effect. Low-frequency contexts contribute most to the gap, while larger training budgets and crowded tables suppress forking. The phenomenon also appears in short-budget, heavily repeated SFT and RL-like regimes.

Conclusion: Forking represents a new curious phenomenon in deep learning (adding to grokking and double descent). It serves as a cautionary example of unexpected side effects from autoresearch agent-proposed tricks, highlighting the need for careful evaluation of such results.

Abstract: This paper studies forking, a generalization failure discovered in NanoGPT autoresearch. Under data replay, models with an over-encoding n-gram memory branch show a sharp separation of training and validation loss at epoch boundaries, resembling the shape of forks. We study this phenomenon in a controlled vanilla NanoGPT setting and reproduce it in a DeepSeek-style model with Engram. Mechanistically, repeated updates sharpen the continuations observed in training while suppressing the probability of unseen continuations, whose loss grows with each pass. The n-gram module creates weakly interacting context-specific subspaces, amplifying this effect. Low-frequency contexts contribute most of the gap, whereas larger training budgets and heavily crowded tables suppress it. We also observe forking in short-budget, heavily repeated SFT and RL-like regimes. The contributions of this paper are twofold: (1) Forking reveals yet another curious phenomenon in deep learning, in addition to grokking and double descent. (2) Forking is an unexpected and unpleasant by-product of tricks proposed by autoresearch agents. While these agents produce an enormous number of results that seem useful, we should always be careful with their results.

</details>


### [379] [Specificity-Aware Diffusion Steering via Variance-Reduced Sequential Monte Carlo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00395)
*Luran Wang,Linrui Ma,Hannes Stärk,Regina Barzilay*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces specificity-aware steering for diffusion models, addressing the challenge of suppressing negative reference distributions while preserving positive ones in overlapping regions. The method derives a target distribution from an overlap-based objective and uses Sequential Monte Carlo sampling with variance-minimized proposals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current negative guidance methods for diffusion models suffer from eroding positive distributions when negative and positive distributions overlap. The key challenge is suppressing negative mass while minimally distorting the positive distribution—this requires specificity-aware generation that distinguishes regions where positive is preferred over negative.

Method: The paper formulates specificity-aware steering as a target-design problem, deriving a target distribution from an overlap-based objective that retains the desired reference distribution only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired distribution. A Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler with variance-minimized local proposal is developed for sampling from the time-dependent target path. A practical fixed-noise optimization procedure using Jacobian-vector products with desired and undesired score fields is also introduced.

Result: Experiments on synthetic tasks, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image, and peptide-MHC binder show: (1) more effective suppression of undesired regions, (2) reduced mode shift, and (3) improved sampling stability via decreased SMC weight collapse compared to negative-guidance baselines.

Conclusion: The proposed specificity-aware diffusion steering method successfully suppresses undesired regions while preserving positive distributions in overlapping areas, outperforming negative-guidance baselines in effectiveness, mode preservation, and sampling stability.

Abstract: Inference-time steering enables pretrained diffusion models to satisfy new constraints without full retraining. However, specificity-aware generation is difficult: repelling samples from a negative reference distribution can also erode the positive distribution where the two overlap. The key challenge is to suppress negative mass while minimally distorting the positive distribution. We address this problem by formulating specificity-aware steering as a target-design problem and deriving a target distribution from an overlap-based objective. The resulting target keeps the desired reference distribution only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired reference distribution, giving a likelihood-ratio interpretation of specificity. To sample from the corresponding time-dependent target path, we develop a Sequential Monte Carlo sampler with a variance-minimized local proposal. We further introduce a practical fixed-noise optimization procedure with the Jacobian--vector products with the desired and undesired score fields. Experiments on synthetic task, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image tasks and peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder show that the proposed method suppresses undesired regions more effectively, reduces mode shift, and improves sampling stability by decreasing the SMC weight collapse compared with negative-guidance baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/WangLuran/Specificity-Aware-Diffusion-Steering

</details>


### [380] [NEUROTOKEN: Joint Source and Directional AAD with Envelope Decoding via Conditional Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00397)
*Ali Alavi,Donald S. Williamson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the cocktail-party problem by proposing NEUROTOKEN, a neural network with three heads that share an EEG front-end. The key innovation is using conditional likelihood (via ATTUNEFLOW) rather than single statistics like Pearson correlation for auditory attention decoding. The method achieves 9-16% improvement over baselines and reveals that canonical direction-AAD numbers are inflated by 17-45% under strict trial-disjoint protocols.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
