Motivation: Current auditory attention decoding (AAD) methods are fragmented: directional-AAD only classifies side without mapping to specific speech streams, regression-based approaches use noisy Pearson correlation at real-world 1-5 second windows, and envelope reconstruction lacks a native AAD rule. The authors argue the correct approach is to model the conditional likelihood of the attended envelope given EEG, rather than relying on any single statistic.

Method: The authors propose NEUROTOKEN, a single network with three heads sharing one EEG front-end. The core innovation is ATTUNEFLOW, a conditional flow-matching head that scores candidate streams using an integrated velocity-residual likelihood ratio. Two inference-time ensembles are introduced: QUADTRACK (four complementary statistics) and ENV-FLOW (z-normalized QUADTRACK+ATTUNEFLOW) to absorb per-statistic failure modes.

Result: At 5-second windows on KU Leuven, DTU, and NJU datasets, ATTUNEFLOW improves per-segment source-AAD by 9-16% over the strongest non-generative baseline and reduces across-subject variance by ~3x. Trial-level fusion exceeds 93% accuracy on two of three datasets. Additionally, canonical 95-97% direction-AAD accuracy collapses by 17-45% under strict trial-disjoint protocols, revealing inflated baseline numbers.

Conclusion: The likelihood-based formulation is necessary for practical AAD applications. The study demonstrates that conditional flow-matching provides superior performance and reveals that previous high accuracy numbers were inflated due to non-disjoint evaluation protocols. This work provides a more realistic ceiling for AAD and a path toward practical hearing aids and brain-computer interfaces.

Abstract: Identifying which speaker a listener is attending to in a noisy room -- the cocktail-party problem -- is the missing ingredient for next-generation hearing aids and brain-computer interfaces: it tells the device whose voice to amplify. Auditory attention decoding (AAD) reads this answer from EEG, but the literature splits into disconnected pieces: directional-AAD classifies side but does not map side to stream; regression-based source-AAD ranks candidate streams by a single Pearson correlation that is intrinsically noisy at the 1-5 s windows real devices need; and envelope reconstruction has no native AAD rule. We argue the right object is not any single statistic but the conditional likelihood of the attended envelope given EEG, and we make this practical with NEUROTOKEN: a single network whose three heads share one EEG front-end, with a conditional flow-matching head (ATTUNEFLOW) that scores candidates by an integrated velocity-residual likelihood ratio. Two inference-time ensembles -- QUADTRACK (four complementary statistics) and ENV-FLOW (z-normalised QUADTRACK+ATTUNEFLOW) -- absorb per-statistic failure modes for free. On KU Leuven, DTU, and NJU at 5 s, ATTUNEFLOW lifts per-segment source-AAD by 9%-16% over the strongest non-generative baseline and shrinks across-subject variance by ~3x; trial-level fusion exceeds 93% on two of three datasets. In parallel reproductions we show that canonical 95-97% direction-AAD numbers collapse by 17%-45% under a strict trial-disjoint protocol, clarifying both the true ceiling and why a likelihood-based formulation is needed.

</details>


### [381] [WIPSNet: Deep Learning for Paediatric Wheeze Detection from Overnight Impedance Pneumography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00398)
*Felix Oury,Harley Day,Karina Mayoral,Ville-Pekka Seppä,Sejal Saglani,Reiko J. Tanaka*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WIPSNet is a novel deep learning approach using 3D ResNet on continuous wavelet transform scalograms of overnight impedance pneumography signals, achieving AUC of 0.783 vs 0.633 for the current clinical method (EVI) in detecting nocturnal wheeze in pediatric patients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current clinical readout (Expiratory Variability Index - EVI) for overnight impedance pneumography in pediatric respiratory monitoring compresses each recording into a single scalar, achieving low AUC of 0.633 for night-level wheeze classification, indicating need for improved analytical approaches.

Method: Wheeze Impedance Pneumography Scalogram Network (WIPSNet) uses a 3D ResNet architecture operating on stacked continuous wavelet transform scalograms of overnight IP signals. Evaluated on 15-patient cohort (60 nights, 281 hours) and compared against EVI, state-space model (Mamba), and two modern sleep-staging architectures.

Result: WIPSNet achieves AUC of 0.783 ± 0.026, significantly outperforming EVI (0.633), Mamba, and sleep-staging architectures. Performance peaks at volumetric depth corresponding to 32 minutes of temporal context, suggesting multi-scale temporal aggregation is important for modelling nocturnal respiratory dynamics.

Conclusion: Structured time-frequency representations (wavelet transform scalograms) combined with 3D convolutional architectures provide an effective approach for learning from long, irregular physiological time series, improving wheeze detection in pediatric patients.

Abstract: Overnight impedance pneumography (IP) is used to monitor paediatric respiratory health. Its current clinical readout, the Expiratory Variability Index (EVI), compresses each IP recording into a single scalar and achieves an AUC of 0.633 for night-level wheeze classification. We introduce Wheeze Impedance Pneumography Scalogram Network (WIPSNet), a 3D ResNet operating on stacked continuous wavelet transform scalograms of overnight IP signals. On a 15-patient cohort (60 nights, 281 hours), WIPSNet achieves an AUC of $0.783 \pm 0.026$, outperforming EVI, a state-space model (Mamba), and two modern sleep-staging architectures. Performance peaks at a volumetric depth corresponding to 32 minutes of temporal context, suggesting that multi-scale temporal aggregation is important for modelling nocturnal respiratory dynamics. Overall, these results indicate that structured time-frequency representations combined with 3D convolutional architectures provide an effective approach for learning from long, irregular physiological time series.

</details>


### [382] [Metacognitive Reasoning in Energy Based Models using Instance Based Learning Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00399)
*Tailia Malloy,Prateek Kumar Rajput,Serge Lionel Nikiema,Cleotilde Gonzalez,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces MERITED, a framework combining Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) with Energy-Based Models (EBMs) to enable metacognitive reasoning in AI systems. The framework allows AI systems to estimate uncertainty and dynamically allocate computational resources based on that uncertainty, similar to human metacognitive processes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI systems using LLMs cannot estimate uncertainty about outputs before responding, nor can they dynamically allocate resources to producing outputs. This limits their ability to implement metacognitive processes like humans do—where we decide how much effort to put into a task based on our confidence. The authors aim to address this limitation by combining EBMs (which allow uncertainty modeling and dynamic compute allocation) with IBLT (which models human-like decision-making from experience).

Method: The authors propose the MERITED framework, which integrates Instance-Based Learning Theory with Energy-Based Models. They trained a 191M parameter reasoning EBM and implemented the MERITED framework for dynamic compute allocation using an IBL model. The IBL model determines how much computational effort to allocate based on uncertainty estimates from the EBM.

Result: The paper presents two main contributions: (1) the training and open weight sharing of a 191M parameter reasoning EBM, and (2) an implementation of the MERITED framework for dynamic compute allocation using an IBL model.

Conclusion: The MERITED framework enables metacognitive control over reasoning effort in AI systems based on uncertainty, while remaining computationally efficient. This represents a step toward more human-like AI systems that can monitor their own reasoning processes and allocate resources adaptively.

Abstract: Metacognition involves reasoning about cognitive processes themselves. An example is in resource allocation where we choose how much time and effort to put into a reasoning task before we begin based on our confidence. Current Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems that rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot estimate their uncertainty about an output without first responding, and cannot dynamically allocate resources to producing an output, making this type of metacognitive process difficult. A recently proposed alternative to classic transformer architectures that addresses these two concerns is the Energy Based Model (EBM) which allows for interpretable uncertainty modeling and dynamic allocation of compute resources. While EBMs can allow for control of these two processes, the actual metacognitive task of determining compute allocation based on uncertainty is not directly addressed. Instance-Based Learning Theory (IBLT) provides an approach to modeling human-like decisions from experience that has previously been applied to predicting human metacognitive reasoning. In this paper we introduce a framework for MEtacognitive Reasoning with Instance-based Learning Theory and Energy Dynamics (MERITED). Grounded in IBLT, this framework allows for control of the computational effort allocated in an EBM to allow for metacognitive control over reasoning effort based on uncertainty while remaining computationally efficient. This work has two main contributions, the training and open weight sharing of a 191M parameter reasoning EBM, and an implementation of the MERITED framework for dynamic compute allocation using an IBL model.

</details>


### [383] [Representation Transitions Reveal Emerging Safety Risks in Multi-Turn LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00400)
*Haoyu Wang,Wei Zhao,Yedi Zhang,Christopher M. Poskitt,Jun Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents DART, a runtime defense framework that detects multi-turn attacks on agentic systems by monitoring accumulated representation transitions in the model's internal states. It introduces a denoising technique to distinguish harmful attacks from benign representation drift, achieving significant reductions in attack success rates across multiple benchmarks and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-turn attacks on agentic systems can compose individually permissible actions into harmful outcomes, posing a significant challenge. Existing defenses that assess actions or states in isolation fail to detect these attacks. The key insight is that such attacks leave detectable signatures in the agent's internal representations through accumulated representation transitions across context updates.

Method: The paper proposes DART, a runtime framework that: (1) Detects harmful behavior by identifying accumulated representation transitions across context updates, (2) Addresses benign representation drift through a denoising technique that anchors benign traffic at zero and removes leading variation directions, (3) Attributes detected attacks and intervenes with targeted reminders. The approach requires no auxiliary model and adds minimal overhead (0.14-0.56s per monitored step).

Result: Across six models and two multi-turn benchmarks: (1) On MT-AgentRisk: reduces attack success from 84% to 25%, catching every attack with 12% false-alarm rate, outperforming ToolShield (55% attack success), (2) On ASEval: reduces attack success from 97% to 52%, with 8% benign non-refusal cost, (3) Denoising is critical -undenoised monitor catches only 7%-40% of attacks vs 60%-85% for denoised version, (4) Also covers single-turn indirect injection without modification.

Conclusion: DART provides an effective lightweight defense against multi-turn attacks on agentic systems by detecting accumulated representation transitions. The denoising technique is essential for distinguishing harmful attacks from benign drift. The framework achieves significant attack success reduction with low overhead and no need for auxiliary models, making it a practical complement to more computationally intensive speculative defenses.

Abstract: Multi-turn attacks on agentic systems can compose individually permissible actions into harmful outcomes, challenging defenses that assess actions or states in isolation. We show that such attacks leave a detectable signature in the agent's internal representations: harmful behavior emerges as an accumulated representation transition across context updates, whose triggering context can be identified from the same signal. We further find that naive aggregation is confounded by benign representation drift, as a contrastive safety direction need not assign zero to benign transitions. We address this by denoising the direction, anchoring benign traffic at zero and removing its leading variation directions, with no runtime cost.
  These findings motivate DART, a runtime framework that detects and attributes representation shifts and intervenes with targeted reminders. Across six models and two multi-turn benchmarks, DART reduces attack success from 84% to 25% on MT-AgentRisk, catching every attack at a mean false-alarm rate of 12%, and from 97% to 52% on ASEval, at costs in benign non-refusal of 8% and 0%, respectively. On MT-AgentRisk, it outperforms ToolShield, the state-of-the-art multi-turn defense, on all six models: under the same protocol, ToolShield reaches only 55%. Denoising is critical: on ASEval, the undenoised monitor catches only 7%-40% of attacks, while the denoised monitor catches 60%-85%. The same monitor covers single-turn indirect injection without modification and adds only 0.14-0.56 s overhead per monitored step without requiring an auxiliary model, making it a lightweight complement to computation-heavy speculative defenses.

</details>


### [384] [The Conflict Between Logic and Memory: Learning Higher-Order Interactions in Shallow MLPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00403)
*Gongyue Zhang,Honghai Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the phenomenon where neural networks can achieve high training accuracy while failing to learn the true underlying rule that generated the labels. The study focuses on single-hidden-layer MLPs using synthetic tasks with controlled interaction order and nuisance inputs. The authors examine how different optimizers (SGD, Adam, Muon) perform on tasks of varying complexity, and how nuisance inputs affect learning outcomes beyond their immediate predictive effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand why neural networks sometimes learn spurious correlations or fail to capture higher-order interactions in data, even when they achieve perfect training accuracy. This addresses a fundamental gap between memorization and genuine rule learning in deep learning.

Method: The authors use synthetic tasks with controlled properties: pure parity tasks (which contain no predictive lower-order marginals), matched order-2 to 4 sweeps, mixed-order tasks, and compact signal-only regimes. They test different optimizers (SGD, Adam, Muon) and interventions including freezing first-layer weights connected to nuisance inputs and removing inputs at test time.

Result: Key results show: (1) At order 2, all optimizers reach 100% test accuracy; at order 3, SGD achieves 96.25%, Adam 50.87%, and Muon 76.82%; at order 4, Muon reaches 99.21%. (2) Freezing nuisance-input weights raises AdamW's accuracy from 44.73% to 95.07% at epoch 10. (3) Removing nuisance inputs only at test time raises accuracy to 48.38%. (4) In compact signal-only regime, both SGD and Muon learn orders 5-8, with SGD performing better at orders 9-11.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that optimization dynamics and nuisance learning significantly constrain the higher-order rules that shallow networks can realize. The study reveals a connection between target symmetry and shallow ReLU representations, and shows that optimizer choice, task complexity, and nuisance inputs all play crucial roles in whether networks learn genuine underlying rules versus spurious patterns.

Abstract: A network can fit its training examples while failing to recover the rule that generated their labels. We examine this separation in single-hidden-layer multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), using synthetic tasks that control interaction order and the presence of nuisance inputs. We establish elementary benchmark properties: pure parity contains no predictive lower-order marginals, admits an exact Bayes posterior, and can be represented on clean latent inputs by a width-$k$ ReLU network. Experiments then identify distinct optimization outcomes. In a matched order-2--4 sweep, SGD, Adam, and Muon all reach 100\% peak test accuracy at order two; at order three they reach 96.25\%, 50.87\%, and 76.82\%, respectively, while Muon reaches 99.21\% at order four. In a separate mixed-order task, freezing only the first-layer weights connected to independent nuisance inputs raises AdamW's epoch-10 accuracy from 44.73\% to 95.07\%. Removing the same inputs only at test time raises it to 48.38\%. Thus, nuisance-weight learning changes the training outcome beyond its immediate effect on prediction. Bias interventions expose a connection between target symmetry and shallow ReLU representations. In a compact signal-only regime, both SGD and Muon learn orders five through eight, with higher SGD peak accuracy at orders nine through eleven. Together, the results show how optimization and nuisance learning constrain the higher-order rules realized by a shallow network.

</details>


### [385] [RACE: Residual-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Neighbor-Rich Time-Series Foundation Model Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00405)
*Hao-Nan Shi,Tong Wu,Chen-Cong Sun,Yuan Jiang,Han-Jia Ye,De-Chuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RACE is a two-stage framework that corrects time-series foundation model forecasts using query-compatible neighbors without modifying the backbone. It addresses neighbor-rich forecasting scenarios like CGM and Web/cloud workloads where related historical series share useful but unevenly relevant structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing TSFMs perform per-series inference which is ill-suited to neighbor-rich forecasting settings. Current methods either fine-tune for each target domain (costly, limited transferability) or append retrieved series without verification. The key challenges are conflicting residual evidence from neighbors and residual patterns that vary across TSFMs and forecasting tasks.

Method: RACE uses a two-stage approach: (1) RACE-TF retrieves query-compatible neighbors, aligns their residuals to query scale, and aggregates coherent evidence into training-free correction; (2) Full RACE adds a lightweight domain-specific Gate to determine when correction is beneficial. The training workflow is reusable across TSFM backbones.

Result: Across four TSFMs, RACE improves all three domain-aggregate metrics on both primary domains (CGM and Web/cloud workloads), with largest gains on high-error queries. Within each domain, a Gate trained on one TSFM transfers to other backbones without adaptation, improving all 72 cross-backbone metric comparisons over matched frozen targets.

Conclusion: RACE demonstrates that test-time neighborhood scaling can effectively use same-domain neighbor evidence without modifying the backbone. The method achieves strong cross-backbone transferability, suggesting that learned correction strategies can generalize across different forecasting architectures, with particular benefits for challenging queries with high errors.

Abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) perform strongly across forecasting tasks, but their per-series inference is ill-suited to neighbor-rich forecasting, where each query has access to related but nonidentical historical series. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and Web/cloud workloads exemplify this setting: CGM trajectories share physiological patterns but vary across individuals, devices, and conditions, while Web/cloud workloads combine common operating regimes with non-stationarity, heavy tails, and bursts. These histories share useful structure, yet neighbors are not equally relevant. Existing methods either fine-tune TSFMs for each target domain, incurring additional costs and offering limited transferability across backbones, or append retrieved series without verifying whether they support the current forecast. The key challenges are conflicting residual evidence from neighboring series and residual patterns that vary across TSFMs and forecasting tasks. We formulate test-time neighborhood scaling: using same-domain neighbor evidence without modifying the backbone. We propose RACE (Residual-Aware Correction of Forecasting Errors), a two-stage framework for using historical neighbors. We first retrieve query-compatible neighbors, align their residuals to the query scale, and aggregate coherent evidence into the training-free RACE-TF correction. Full RACE then uses a lightweight, domain-specific Gate to determine when applying the correction is beneficial, with a reusable training workflow across TSFM backbones. Across four TSFMs, RACE improves all three domain-aggregate metrics on both primary domains, with the largest gains on high-error queries. Within each domain, a Gate trained on one TSFM transfers to other backbones without adaptation, and the resulting pipeline improves all 72 cross-backbone metric comparisons over the matched frozen targets.

</details>


### [386] [VANDAM: Viewing a nucleotide sequence with DNA molecular priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00411)
*Jeremy Levy,Ariel Larey,Yury Nahshan,Raizy Kellerman,Elay Dahan,Amit Bleiweiss,Guy Leib,Omri Nayshool,Dan Ofer,Tal Zinger,Dan Dominissini,Gideon Rechavi,Marissa Wirth,Simon Lee,Dung Hoang,Noam D. Beckmann,Shane O'Connell,Nicole Bussola,Alexander W. Charney,Yoli Shavit,Nati Daniel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VANDAM is a framework that extends Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs) training with DNA molecular priors, moving beyond the DNA-as-a-string paradigm to explicitly incorporate biochemical, structural, and physical properties. The method improves downstream performance across four architecture families and nine genomic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current GFMs rely on a DNA-as-a-string paradigm with masked token prediction objectives, which does not explicitly model biochemical, structural, and physical properties essential to biological function. The authors argue that molecular properties estimated from sequence using biophysical models can serve as useful priors that training objectives can explicitly exploit.

Method: VANDAM extends GFM training through two mechanisms: (1) In self-supervised training, it predicts regional molecular properties from pooled representations; (2) When functional labels are available, local features are additionally injected at the input to retain molecular priors.

Result: VANDAM consistently improves downstream performance across four architecture families and nine held-out genomic tasks by complementing token-based objectives. Probing experiments further demonstrate that molecular priors generalize to other unseen molecular properties.

Conclusion: The integration of molecular priors into GFM training is beneficial and generalizable. VANDAM provides a general framework for incorporating biophysical domain knowledge into foundation models for genomics, with potential applications beyond the specific tasks evaluated.

Abstract: Contemporary Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs) rely on a DNA-as-a-string paradigm that employs masked token prediction objectives for pretraining. However, this abstraction does not explicitly model the biochemical, structural, and physical properties essential to biological function. Many molecular properties can be estimated from sequence using established biophysical models, so their utility lies not in providing an independent modality, but in introducing priors that training objectives can explicitly exploit. We introduce VANDAM, a framework that extends the training of GFMs with DNA molecular priors. In self-supervised training, VANDAM predicts regional molecular properties from pooled representations. When functional labels are available and can reward retaining molecular priors, local features are additionally injected at the input. VANDAM consistently improves downstream performance across four architecture families and nine held-out genomic tasks by complementing token-based objectives. Probing experiments further demonstrate that the use of molecular priors generalizes to other unseen molecular properties.

</details>


### [387] [EchoPress: Query-Agnostic KV Cache Pruning via Virtual Context Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00412)
*Jiawei Lin,Saibo Geng,Thomas Bourgeat*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EchoPress is a training-free KV cache pruning method that approximates reconstruction-based importance scores using standard prefill attention, matching KVzip's accuracy while reducing compression overhead by 1.7-19.6x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV cache pruning reduces memory in long-context inference but existing methods either rely on costly reconstruction (KVzip) requiring extra forward passes or need model-specific training (learned approximations). The authors seek a training-free method that can identify important KV pairs without reconstruction overhead.

Method: The authors analyze how KVzip's reconstruction scores work and discover they can be approximated using information already computed during standard prefill. EchoPress reconstructs only the first chunk to calibrate importance scores for remaining context, using queries and keys from standard prefill to compute reconstruction attention.

Result: EchoPress matches KVzip's task accuracy across 50%-90% eviction ratios on LongBench and RULER with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, while reducing compression overhead by 1.7-19.6x and total prefill time by up to 2.9x.

Conclusion: Reconstruction-based importance can be approximated without additional model forward passes by leveraging prefill attention computations. This enables efficient training-free KV cache pruning that achieves state-of-the-art quality-efficiency tradeoffs.

Abstract: KV cache pruning reduces long-context inference memory usage by evicting less important key-value pairs. KVzip estimates importance through context reconstruction: prompting a model to repeat the context chunk by chunk. This achieves strong compression quality at the cost of additional forward passes. Learned approximations reduce this cost but require model-specific training. We analyze how KVzip identifies important cached information and show how to approximate its reconstruction scores using information already computed during prefill. These findings motivate EchoPress, a training-free method that approximates reconstruction attention using queries and keys from standard prefill. For each request, it reconstructs only the first chunk to calibrate importance scores for the remaining context. Experiments on LongBench and RULER with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show that EchoPress matches KVzip in task accuracy across eviction ratios from 50% to 90%, while reducing compression overhead by a factor of 1.7-19.6 and total prefill time by a factor of up to 2.9. Code is available at https://github.com/ljwljwljwljw/kvpress/tree/echo-press.

</details>


### [388] [Do Better Scores Mean Better Physics? Physics-Grounded Explanations for Sim2Real Neural Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00415)
*Somyajit Chakraborty,Xizhong Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether lower prediction error in machine learning surrogates for physical simulations correlates with lower error in physically relevant flow statistics. Using flow around a NACA4418 airfoil with paired CFD and PIV data, the authors find that standard error metrics often fail to capture important physical quantities, advocating for complementary physical diagnostics alongside aggregate prediction scores.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors aim to address a critical gap in machine learning for physical simulations: the assumption that lower prediction error automatically translates to better physical accuracy. They question whether conventional error metrics adequately capture physically meaningful flow statistics.

Method: The study uses paired CFD simulations and experimental PIV measurements for flow around a NACA4418 airfoil. Two main approaches: (1) mean-preserving input intervention removing velocity fluctuations from selected regions, tested across four neural operators; (2) output attenuation stress test comparing benchmark errors against domain-summed fluctuation energy.

Result: Removing fluctuations from the most energetic 10% of cells causes larger forecast changes than equal-area random removal. A CNO (Convolutional Neural Operator) shows lower velocity-field error but substantially higher two-component fluctuation-energy error than the reference. The output attenuation test demonstrates disagreement between benchmark errors and physically relevant fluctuation energy.

Conclusion: Single-benchmark error metrics are insufficient for evaluating ML surrogates in physical applications. The authors recommend reporting complementary physical diagnostics alongside aggregate prediction scores, while noting this does not establish counterfactual physical correctness.

Abstract: Machine-learning surrogates accelerate physical simulation, but lower prediction error need not coincide with lower error in physically relevant flow statistics. We examine this question for flow around a NACA4418 airfoil using paired computational-fluid-dynamics simulations and experimental particle-image-velocimetry measurements. A mean-preserving input intervention removes velocity fluctuations from selected regions of observed flow histories. Across four neural operators, removing fluctuations from the most energetic 10% of valid observed cells changes forecasts more than equal-area random removal. Because the masks are not matched for removed fluctuation energy, this contrast measures sensitivity, not independent evidence of physical importance. Separately, a CNO has lower velocity-field error but substantially higher two-component fluctuation-energy error than the reference on both analysis subsets. An output attenuation stress test also demonstrates disagreement between benchmark errors and domain-summed fluctuation energy. These single-benchmark results motivate reporting complementary physical diagnostics alongside aggregate prediction scores; they do not establish counterfactual physical correctness.

</details>


### [389] [Source Identification Is Not Fitness Testing: Measuring the Limits of Synthetic-Data Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00417)
*Joss Armstrong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether provenance (knowing the source of generated data) can help identify better training data when repeatedly training on model-generated examples. Experiments on financial-risk text show that while generator attribution achieves 98.7% accuracy on original passages, it degrades significantly after paraphrasing (53.1%) and style rewriting (29.0%). Two selection methods (source-based vs. reference model score-based) yield different examples but show no stable difference in preventing model degradation. The study concludes that identifying data source and identifying useful training data are separate problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical challenge in AI: when models are repeatedly trained on data they or other models generated, performance can degrade ("model collapse"). The authors investigate whether knowing the provenance (source) of generated data can help select higher-quality examples for training, potentially mitigating this degradation problem.

Method: The study used financial-risk text as the dataset. It conducted two types of experiments: (1) Generator attribution accuracy tests on original passages, paraphrased passages, and style-rewritten passages, plus generated-vs-human detection; (2) A longitudinal comparison over three rounds of generation and retraining, comparing two selection methods—one using source information and one using a reference model score—to evaluate their impact on model degradation.

Result: Generator attribution achieves 98.7% accuracy on original passages but drops to 53.1% after paraphrasing and 29.0% after style rewriting. Generated-versus-human detection remains near-perfect against the human comparison set. The two selection methods (provenance-based vs. reference model score-based) select different examples, but no stable difference in model degradation was detected between them across three training rounds.

Conclusion: Source identity and training utility are separate problems. Neither provenance scores nor the tested criterion-facing proxy (reference model score) is sufficient to predict or prevent degradation in recursive training scenarios. This suggests that identifying which generated data will be beneficial for training requires different approaches than simply identifying where the data came from.

Abstract: Repeated training on model-generated data can degrade later models. One possible response is to use provenance when deciding which generated examples to reuse. We test both how reliably that provenance can be recovered and whether it helps identify better training data. Using financial-risk text, we first identify the source of generated passages and then repeat the test after rewriting them. Generator attribution is 98.7% accurate on the original passages but falls to 53.1% after paraphrasing and 29.0% after style rewriting. Generated-versus-human detection remains close to perfect against the tested human comparison set. We then compare two ways of selecting generated examples over three rounds of generation and retraining. One uses source information. The other uses a score from a separate reference model. The two rules select different examples, but the planned comparison does not detect a stable difference in the degradation of the resulting models. The results show that identifying where data came from and identifying which data are useful for training are separate problems. The experiment therefore separates source identity, criterion-facing selection, and recursive training outcome: neither the provenance score nor the tested criterion-facing proxy is established as sufficient for future recursive behaviour.

</details>


### [390] [CommunityKV: Efficient Long-Context Decoding via Graph Partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00418)
*Joe McKenna,Anastasios Alexandridis,Nathan Susanj,Jing Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CommunityKV is a framework that addresses the computational and memory constraints of scaling Transformers to long contexts by reformulating sparse attention as a community detection problem. It constructs token graphs from QK^T scores during prefill, partitions them into semantically coherent communities, and uses a constant-time local update rule for newly generated tokens during decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The quadratic cost of self-attention and linear growth of key-value cache memory transfer constrain scaling Transformers to long contexts. Existing sparse attention approaches either require large-scale training or rely on semantically coarse heuristics or expensive clustering that cannot be efficiently updated during decoding.

Method: CommunityKV constructs a token graph from QK^T scores already computed during standard prefill, then partitions this graph into communities to enable retrieval of semantically coherent token groups. It uses a local update rule to assign newly generated tokens to communities in constant time, enabling sparse retrieval throughout streaming decoding without global re-partitioning.

Result: With one graph per query head, CommunityKV delivers up to 1.25x the end-to-end generation throughput of dense attention. With query-group graph aggregation, it yields up to 1.71x throughput with comparable accuracy. Evaluated on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 models across three long-context benchmarks.

Conclusion: CommunityKV successfully formulates sparse attention as a community detection problem, enabling efficient constant-time updates during decoding without global re-partitioning. The approach achieves significant throughput improvements (1.25x-1.71x) over dense attention while maintaining comparable accuracy on long-context benchmarks.

Abstract: Scaling Transformers to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of self-attention and the linear growth of key-value cache memory transfer. Sparse attention mitigates this by retrieving only relevant tokens, but current approaches either require large-scale training or, within the training-free regime, rely on semantically coarse heuristics or expensive clustering that is difficult to update efficiently during decoding. We introduce CommunityKV, a framework that formulates sparse attention as a community detection problem. CommunityKV constructs a token graph from the $QK^T$ scores already computed during standard prefill, and partitions the graph into communities to enable retrieval of semantically coherent token groups. A local update rule assigns newly generated tokens to communities in constant time, enabling sparse retrieval throughout streaming decoding without global re-partitioning. We evaluate CommunityKV on Qwen3 and Llama-3.1 models across three long-context benchmarks. With one graph per query head, CommunityKV delivers up to $1.25\times$ the end-to-end generation throughput of dense attention, while query-group graph aggregation yields up to $1.71\times$ with comparable accuracy.

</details>


### [391] [The Life Cycle of a Massive Activation: Stochastic Birth, Weight-Decay-Driven Growth, and Competitive Consolidation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00423)
*S. Aaron McClendon,Jorge Gallego-Feliciano,Antonios Saravanos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how massive activations (residual-stream coordinates with unusually large magnitudes associated with attention sinks) are regulated during transformer training. Through training-trajectory analyses and controlled interventions, the authors discover that weight decay causally controls the turnover of global activation scale, with AdamW-preconditioned growth opposing weight decay to create a balance model explaining peak timing and magnitude.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand how the scale of massive activations associated with attention sinks is regulated during transformer training, which remains incompletely understood despite their importance.

Method: The authors combine training-trajectory analyses with controlled interventions, including ablation studies and controlled continuations with varying weight decay coefficients.

Result: Key findings: (1) Sink-carrying channels vary across random seeds but stabilize early; (2) Over longer training, surrounding channels erode and sink concentrates onto few redundant carriers; (3) Gradient attenuation follows the sink token's collective RMS magnitude; (4) Weight decay causally controls activation scale turnover - removing decay near peak allows scale to keep rising, retaining it produces decline; (5) Peak timing scales approximately log-linearly with decay coefficient λ; (6) Peak magnitudes scale approximately as λ^(-1/2); (7) AdamW preconditioning sustains large-channel cohort against decay.

Conclusion: Weight decay serves as a training-time lever on activation magnitude, with the balance between AdamW-preconditioned growth and weight decay explaining the lifecycle of massive activations. This connects observed life cycles to scale-regulating training dynamics.

Abstract: Massive activations, residual-stream coordinates with magnitudes far larger than typical activations, are associated with attention sinks in transformers, but how their scale is regulated during training remains incompletely understood. Combining training-trajectory analyses and controlled interventions, we trace their emergence, growth, and consolidation. Sink-carrying channels vary across random seeds but stabilize early within each run. Over longer training, surrounding channels erode and the sink concentrates onto a few redundant carriers. Across ablations, gradient attenuation follows the sink token's collective root-mean-square magnitude rather than any single channel, making collective scale central to understanding their effects. Our central result is that weight decay causally controls the turnover of global activation scale. In controlled continuations, removing decay near the peak allows this scale to keep rising, whereas retaining it produces decline even at constant learning rate. We develop a balance model for the rise and peak of massive-activation magnitude, in which AdamW-preconditioned growth opposes weight decay. Sweeping the decay coefficient $λ$ shifts peak timing approximately log-linearly and yields peak magnitudes scaling approximately as $λ^{-1/2}$, consistent with this balance. Optimizer measurements further show that preconditioning sustains the large-channel cohort against decay even when raw maintaining forces are too small to do so. Together, these findings connect the observed life cycle to scale-regulating training dynamics and establish weight decay as a training-time lever on activation magnitude.

</details>


### [392] [IrekoGPT: Turning Structured Pruning into Post-Hoc Slimmable LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00426)
*Pietro Moriello,Pietro Buzzega,Angelo Porrello,Simone Calderara*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IrekoGPT is a post-hoc method for converting pretrained LLMs into slimmable models whose width can be adjusted at inference time. Building on SliceGPT, it retains projection matrices without pruning, allowing a single model to expose nested subnetworks at different widths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable pretrained LLMs to be slimmable at inference time with adjustable width, improving upon existing methods like SliceGPT and PCA-based slimming that lack robustness across different compression ratios.

Method: 1) Retain projection matrices without pruning (unlike SliceGPT); 2) Calibrate each layer across multiple compression ratios for improved robustness; 3) Correct downstream linear layers through gradient-free ridge regression.

Result: Preliminary results on Llama and Qwen models show improvements over naive PCA-based slimming, with the largest gains at high compression ratios.

Conclusion: IrekoGPT provides an effective approach for creating slimmable LLMs with better performance than existing methods, particularly at high compression levels.

Abstract: We introduce IrekoGPT, a post-hoc method for converting pretrained LLMs into slimmable models whose width can be adjusted at inference time. Building on SliceGPT, we retain its projection matrices without pruning them, allowing a single model to expose nested subnetworks at different widths. We improve robustness by calibrating each layer across multiple compression ratios, and correct downstream linear layers through gradient-free ridge regression. Across Llama and Qwen models, preliminary results show improvements over naive PCA-based slimming, with the largest gains at high compression. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/IrekoGPT

</details>


### [393] [XOR-Trellis: Ultra-Low-Complexity Dequantization and Curvature-Aware Hadamard-Free LLM Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00432)
*Xiaofan Que,Nir Elkayam,Spandan Pyakurel,Shuokai Pan,Dibakar Gope*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents techniques for ultra-low-bit quantization of large language model (LLM) weights using trellis-coded quantization without requiring exponentially large codebooks. The authors address two key deployment challenges: achieving high parallel throughput during dequantization and maintaining quantization accuracy without expensive incoherence transformations. They propose a hardware-efficient trellis dequantizer with structured state-to-value mapping and a curvature-aware optimization objective for discrete trellis path selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable practical deployment of high-dimensional LLM weight compression at ultra-low bit widths. Conventional vector quantization requires exponentially large codebooks at low bit widths, making it impractical. Additionally, existing approaches face challenges with reconstruction throughput and accuracy without costly incoherence transformations like Hadamard transforms.

Method: The paper introduces two complementary techniques: (1) An ultra-low-complexity trellis dequantizer that uses a structured, hardware-efficient state-to-value mapping while preserving diverse reconstruction choices for trellis search; (2) A reformulation of discrete trellis path optimization with a curvature-aware objective that reflects model sensitivity directly in the original coordinate space.

Result: The combined techniques enable high-quality ultra-low-bit trellis quantization with inexpensive, highly parallel runtime reconstruction, while eliminating the need for Hadamard-based incoherence processing.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses the practical deployment challenges of trellis-coded quantization for LLM weights, achieving a balance between quantization quality, computational efficiency, and hardware parallelism.

Abstract: Trellis-coded quantization enables high-dimensional compression of large language model (LLM) weights at ultra-low bit widths without the exponentially large codebooks required by conventional vector quantization. Practical deployment, however, presents two challenges: reconstructing compressed weights at sufficient parallel throughput to avoid making dequantization an inference bottleneck, and maintaining quantization accuracy without costly incoherence transformations. We address these challenges with two complementary techniques. First, we introduce an ultra-low-complexity trellis dequantizer that uses a structured, hardware-efficient state-to-value mapping while preserving diverse reconstruction choices for trellis search. Second, we reformulate discrete trellis path optimization with a curvature-aware objective that reflects model sensitivity directly in the original coordinate space. Together, these techniques enable high-quality ultra-low-bit trellis quantization with inexpensive, highly parallel runtime reconstruction and without relying on Hadamard-based incoherence processing.

</details>


### [394] [Every Batch Is Its Own Validation Set: Leave-One-Out Gradient Matching for Online Data Selection in LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00436)
*Hongyu Chen,Xinyi Luo,Ming Zhao,Lin Tang,Zihan Xu,Jing Li,Yuxuan Wang,Haoran Deng,Wei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LOOM fixes in-sample gradient matching for batch selection by removing the diagonal from the gradient Gram matrix, creating an unbiased estimate of update error that weights examples by their gradient SNR, achieving 2.3-2.4 point improvements over full-batch training across multiple fine-tuning tasks and model sizes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In-sample gradient matching selectors are attractive because they need no held-out data, yet they rarely beat training on the whole batch. The authors wanted to understand why this happens and develop a fix.

Method: The authors identify that the diagonal of the gradient Gram matrix causes a covariance penalty that makes training error optimistic and steers selection toward the noisiest examples. The fix: for each example, use other candidates as an independent sample of the data distribution, removing the diagonal to turn the matching objective into an unbiased estimate of the update's error. LOOM computes the Gram matrix in the Adam preconditioner metric during backward pass, selects a weighted subset greedily with a (1-e^{-γ}) guarantee, and uses no held-out data.

Result: Across four fine-tuning tasks and seven backbones (1.5B to 8B parameters), LOOM improves on full-batch training by 2.3 and 2.4 points on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, exceeds every in-sample gradient matcher by 2.4 points and validation-guided methods (GREATS and OPUS) by 1.6-2.0 points, and selects injected label noise at under a fifth of its base rate.

Conclusion: The diagonal of the gradient Gram matrix causes the covariance penalty problem that makes in-sample gradient matching fail. Removing the diagonal transforms the objective into an unbiased estimate of update error, where the minimizer weights examples by their gradient signal-to-noise ratio. When per-example SNR is heterogeneous enough, half of a batch yields a lower-error update than the whole batch.

Abstract: Online batch selection fine-tunes a language model on the most useful part of each candidate batch. Selectors that match the gradient of the candidate batch are attractive because they need no held-out data, yet they rarely beat training on the whole batch. We show why. In-sample gradient matching uses every example as part of its own target, so its objective credits each example with its own gradient noise. This is the covariance penalty that makes training error optimistic, now sitting on the diagonal of the gradient Gram matrix: it steers selection toward the noisiest examples and makes the full batch the best solution the objective can reach. The fix costs nothing. For each example, the other candidates form an independent sample of the data distribution, so removing the diagonal turns the matching objective into an unbiased estimate of the update's error with respect to the population gradient. The minimizer of this leave-one-out objective weights examples by their gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and whenever per-example SNR is heterogeneous enough, half of a batch yields a lower-error update than the whole batch; we give the exact condition. We build \method{} on this principle. It computes the Gram matrix in the metric of the Adam preconditioner during the ordinary backward pass, selects a weighted subset greedily with a $(1-e^{-γ})$ guarantee, and uses no held-out data. Across four fine-tuning tasks and seven backbones from 1.5B to 8B parameters, LOOM improves on full-batch training by 2.3 and 2.4 points on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, exceeds every in-sample gradient matcher by 2.4 points and the validation-guided GREATS and OPUS by 1.6--2.0, and selects injected label noise at under a fifth of its base rate.

</details>


### [395] [One pool, many targets: a conservation layer and what archival data can identify](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00445)
*Zahra Khodagholi,Niloofar Yousefi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental limitation in CRISPR guide RNA design: existing pairwise guide-transcript scoring methods fail to account for conservation of a finite guide-loaded RISC pool when interpreted as independent occupancies. The authors develop a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer with exact implicit gradients, deriving theoretical results including a redistribution theorem and conditional rank-invariance. Experimental validation on archival off-target data reveals weak predictive value for the coupling approach, with heterogeneous dose fits that violate model constraints. The main contribution is a reusable conservation operator and experimental framework for testing thermodynamic models in CRISPR guide design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that current pairwise guide-transcript scoring methods treat each guide-target interaction independently, ignoring the fundamental constraint that there is a finite pool of guide-loaded RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex). When interpreted as independent occupancies, these scores don't enforce conservation - meaning the total probability of all possible guide-RISC complexes must sum to 1. This leads to inaccurate predictions of off-target effects and guide efficacy.

Method: The authors develop a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer formulated as one conservation equation with a unique positive root and exact implicit gradients. This mathematical framework allows them to derive several theoretical results: (1) a redistribution theorem, (2) a qualified high-resource limit, (3) an analysis of the retrieval approximation, and (4) a conditional rank-invariance result showing that within one construct at one dose, rankings by fractional occupancy cannot distinguish equilibrium from independent scoring. They then validate this framework experimentally using archival off-target data, employing paired permutation tests and construct-cluster bootstrap methods to assess predictive value.

Result: The experimental validation yields mixed results: (1) Corrected thermodynamic affinities show weak positive association with measured repression in the direction required for a working predictor, but this association is weak; (2) Neither paired permutation tests nor construct-cluster bootstrap methods establish added predictive value from the coupling approach; (3) GapNet (a descriptive method measuring equilibrium association's cluster standard error) survives differing permutation-null baselines; (4) Dose fits are heterogeneous and frequently violate the model-implied superlinear exponent constraint, preventing identification of the competition parameter; (5) A saturable compression of the competitor set maintains accuracy targets on held-out guide families but doesn't improve computational speed.

Conclusion: The paper provides two main contributions: (1) a reusable conservation operator (the differentiable scalar equilibrium layer) that enforces proper thermodynamic modeling of finite RISC pool competition, and (2) the experimental information needed to test this model. The authors acknowledge that their data does not definitively identify the competition parameter, suggesting that further experimental work with appropriate dose-response measurements is needed. The code is available at https://github.com/shadi97kh/One-Pool-Many-Targets for reproducibility and reuse.

Abstract: Pairwise guide--transcript scores do not enforce conservation of a finite guide-loaded RISC pool when they are interpreted independently as occupancies. We formulate a differentiable scalar equilibrium layer: one conservation equation with a unique positive root and exact implicit gradients. It yields a redistribution theorem, a qualified high-resource limit, an analysis of the retrieval approximation, and a conditional rank-invariance result: within one construct at one dose, rankings by fractional occupancy cannot distinguish equilibrium from independent scoring. We therefore audit the two experiments that proposition leaves open, dose and cross-context, on archival off-target data. Corrected thermodynamic affinities associate weakly with measured repression in the direction a working predictor requires, but a paired permutation test and a construct-cluster bootstrap do not establish added predictive value from the coupling: what survives their differing permutation-null baselines is \GapNet{}, a descriptive \GapNetOverSE{} of the equilibrium association's cluster standard error. The dose fits are heterogeneous and frequently violate the model-implied exponent constraint, which is superlinear rather than sublinear, so these data do not identify the competition parameter. A saturable compression of the competitor set holds both accuracy targets on held-out guide families but is not faster at the size measured. The contribution is a reusable conservation operator and the experimental information needed to test it. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/shadi97kh/One-Pool-Many-Targets.

</details>


### [396] [Exact information accounting for SGD methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00446)
*Akshay Balsubramani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents an exact, information-theoretic framework for analyzing stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants. It shows that preconditioned SGD corresponds to the posterior-mean update of a Gaussian Bayes model, with the one-step regret splitting into intrinsic-time cost and change in comparator information. This identity explains various SGD behaviors including convex convergence, saddle-point escape, generalization-flatness links, and adaptive optimizer dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard geometric analyses of SGD are limited. This paper seeks an information-theoretic alternative that can provide exact, principled understanding of SGD dynamics, including generalization, adaptive optimization, and various SGD variants.

Method: The authors develop an information-theoretic framework treating SGD as posterior-mean updates in a Gaussian Bayes model. They derive an identity for the one-step regret that splits into intrinsic-time cost and change in comparator information, then extend this to an identity for the objective itself.

Result: The framework successfully explains: (1) convex convergence and strict-saddle-point escape as special cases; (2) the flatness-generalization link; (3) standard learning-rate schedules and adaptive optimizers; (4) noisy, momentum, heavy-tailed, and gradient-free SGD variants. Empirical validation on synthetic and real networks shows the identity attributes classical convergence bound slack to dropped terms, separates optimizers by step consistency, and reveals optimizer-dependent generalization patterns.

Conclusion: The information-theoretic identity provides a unifying framework for understanding SGD. For gradient-free SGD, it determines how curvature preconditioners should enter. The sharpness-based generalization certificate requires nearly flat curvature spectrum across all parameters to be non-vacuous at network scale.

Abstract: As an alternative to the standard geometric analyses, we give an exact, information-theoretic analysis of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants. We show that a preconditioned SGD step is the posterior-mean update of a Gaussian Bayes model, and that its one-step regret splits into an intrinsic-time cost and a change in comparator information. The split extends to an identity for the objective itself. Convex convergence, strict-saddle-point escape, the link between flatness and generalization, the standard learning-rate schedules, adaptive optimizers, and the noisy, momentum, heavy-tailed, and gradient-free variants of SGD each correspond to a term or a special case of this identity. We measure its terms on synthetic and real training runs. On real networks it attributes the slack of classical convergence bounds to the terms their derivations drop and separates optimizers that reach the same training loss. That separation follows the number and consistency of their steps. Its relation to which of them generalizes better differs between networks. For gradient-free SGD the identity determines how a curvature preconditioner should enter the update. The sharpness-based generalization certificate it yields, with a data-independent isotropic prior, is vacuous at network scale unless the curvature spectrum is nearly flat across all parameters.

</details>


### [397] [Score the Update, Not the Token: Descent-Aligned Routing for Combinatorial LoRA Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00493)
*Priya Nair,Lukas Brenner,Maya Lindqvist,Daniel Whitmore,Wen-Hsuan Liu,Tom Saliencro,Amara Okonkwo,Rohan Desai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VANE introduces a novel routing mechanism for Mixture-of-LoRA-experts that scores the predicted usefulness of expert updates rather than routing tokens to experts. It decomposes experts into reader-writer pairs, uses a "low-rank compass" to predict descent direction, and scores reader-writer pairs by alignment. This method achieves state-of-the-art results on commonsense reasoning and multi-task benchmarks with fewer parameters than comparable MoE-LoRA approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MoE-LoRA methods have two key limitations: (1) routers score tokens without seeing what any expert would write, and (2) token-level routers only see token mean information (first-order) and miss output factors. The authors argue the router should score the update itself, as the usefulness of adding an expert's update is the inner product between that update and the negative loss gradient at the layer output.

Method: VANE uses a reader-writer decomposition where each expert is split into a down-projection (reader) and up-projection (writer). This transforms the usefulness of each reader-writer pair into an inner product in a shared rank-r space, enabling all N_A × N_B pairs to be scored from just N_A + N_B vectors. The method: (1) uses a low-rank compass to predict the descent direction for each token, (2) scores every reader-writer pair by alignment between its update and the compass without forming any update, (3) activates top-k pairs with additive gates, and (4) provides exact first-order router gradient.

Result: On single-domain commonsense reasoning and a four-domain multi-task mixture with Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, VANE achieves the best average performance among twelve PEFT and MoE-LoRA baselines, improving by 0.9--1.1 points on commonsense reasoning and 1.3--1.5 points on multi-task. This is achieved with less than half the trainable parameters of an 8-expert MoE-LoRA. The router scores also track measured usefulness of experts more closely than token routers.

Conclusion: VANE demonstrates that scoring the update (rather than the token) is a more effective routing mechanism for MoE-LoRA. The reader-writer decomposition enables efficient scoring of all expert pairs, and the low-rank compass provides meaningful descent direction predictions. This approach achieves superior performance with improved parameter efficiency, validating the theoretical argument that update-based routing captures information that token-based routing misses.

Abstract: Mixture-of-LoRA-experts methods raise the capacity of low-rank adaptation by routing each token to a few low-rank experts. Nearly all of them tie one input-side factor to one output-side factor per expert, and nearly all of them route by scoring the token: the router picks experts without seeing what any of them would write. We argue that the router should score the update. To first order, adding an expert's update to a layer output lowers the loss by the inner product between that update and the negative loss gradient at the output. This usefulness is quadratic in the token, so a router that is linear in the token sees only the part of it that runs through the token mean, and routers that rank experts by the norm of their own activations never see the output factor. If each expert is split into a reader (down-projection) and a writer (up-projection), the usefulness of every reader--writer pair becomes an inner product in the shared rank-$r$ space, and all $N_AN_B$ pairs can be scored from $N_A+N_B$ vectors. We build VANE on this identity. A low-rank compass predicts the descent direction of each token. VANE scores every pair by the alignment between its update and the compass without forming any update, activates the top-$k$ pairs with additive gates, and gives every pair its exact first-order router gradient. On single-domain commonsense reasoning and a four-domain multi-task mixture with Llama-3.2-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, VANE attains the best average among twelve PEFT and MoE-LoRA baselines, by 0.9--1.1 and 1.3--1.5 points respectively, with less than half the trainable parameters of an 8-expert MoE-LoRA. Its router scores also track the measured usefulness of experts far more closely than token routers do.

</details>


### [398] [Gumbel Straight Flow: Distilling Autoregressive Models into One-step Flow Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00497)
*Yeongmin Kim,Arnaud Doucet,Andrew Campbell,Valentin De Bortoli,Thomas Mensink,David Ruhe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF) is a continuous flow map language model that leverages noise-data coupling from pretrained autoregressive models, using a flow map semigroup objective with AR teacher guidance for high-quality few-step generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve few-step language generation by leveraging the coupling between Gumbel noise and one-hot token sequences induced by autoregressive models, which yields non-intersecting linear paths connecting noise to sequence representations.

Method: GSF employs a continuous flow map framework that utilizes the noise-data coupling of a pretrained autoregressive language model. The approach uses a flow map semigroup objective where the tangent (velocity) condition is directly guided by the AR teacher to enhance high-quality few-step path sampling.

Result: GSF outperforms current few-step language generation baselines across various benchmarks, including both pretraining and downstream tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed GSF approach successfully demonstrates superior performance in few-shot language generation by effectively coupling Gumbel noise with autoregressive model representations, offering a promising direction for efficient high-quality text generation.

Abstract: We present Gumbel Straight Flow (GSF), a continuous flow map language model that leverages the noise-data coupling of a pretrained autoregressive language (AR) model. We theoretically demonstrate that the coupling between Gumbel noise and one-hot token sequences induced by an autoregressive model yields non-intersecting linear paths connecting the noise to the sequence representations. To further enhance high-quality few-step path sampling, we use a flow map semigroup objective where the tangent (velocity) condition is guided directly by the AR teacher. Across various benchmarks, including pretraining and downstream tasks, GSF can outperform current few-step language generation baselines.

</details>


### [399] [Denoising Surface: Modeling and Predicting Inference Cost for Diffusion LLM Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00499)
*Haoyu Zheng,Fangcheng Fu,Binhang Yuan,Yongqiang Zhang,Liang Deng,Hao Wang,Yuanyuan Zhu,Xiao Yan,Jiawei Jiang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses cost estimation for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) in real-world serving systems. Existing cost proxies (output length, denoising-step count) fail because they ignore the two-dimensional execution structure of block-autoregressive generation and heterogeneous per-step costs. The authors propose Denoising Workload Surface (DWS) to preserve the block-step structure as a probability surface, enabling accurate cost prediction through a lightweight CPU-based predictor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As dLLMs transition from research to real-world serving, accurate per-request inference cost estimation becomes critical for request management (scheduling, resource allocation). However, common cost proxies fall short: output length ignores multi-token unmasking per forward pass, and denoising-step count ignores heterogeneous per-step costs. The core issue is that these proxies collapse a two-dimensional execution structure (output blocks × denoising steps) into a scalar, losing essential cost information.

Method: The authors propose Denoising Workload Surface (DWS) that preserves the two-dimensional block-step structure as a probability surface to weight heterogeneous per-step costs. They design a coarse-to-fine training scheme enabling a lightweight prompt-only predictor to accurately predict the complex DWS. This predictor runs efficiently on a single CPU core, avoiding GPU contention with the serving model. Since DWS decouples request-dependent execution behavior from deployment-specific cost factors, the predictor transfers across hardware configurations without retraining.

Result: In real-world serving experiments, DWS reduces cost-prediction error by up to 2.50× over scalar-based predictors. The DWS-guided shortest-job-first scheduler reduces end-to-end latency by up to 1.92× for online chatbots.

Conclusion: DWS provides a novel two-dimensional cost representation that accurately captures the execution behavior of dLLMs. The lightweight CPU-based predictor achieves high accuracy while avoiding GPU contention, and the transferability across hardware configurations makes it practical for real-world deployment. The DWS-guided scheduler significantly improves serving performance, demonstrating the practical value of accurate cost estimation for dLLM serving systems.

Abstract: As diffusion large language models (dLLMs) become more capable, they are moving from research settings to real-world \textit{serving}, where request management (such as scheduling and resource allocation) relies on accurate estimation of per-request inference cost. However, common cost proxies fall short for dLLMs: output length ignores that one forward pass can unmask multiple tokens, and denoising-step count ignores the \textit{heterogeneous} per-step costs. We observe that the block-autoregressive generation mechanism induces a two-dimensional execution structure over output blocks and within-block denoising steps, whereas these proxies collapse it into a scalar, discarding information essential for characterizing the cost. Motivated by this insight, we propose the Denoising Workload Surface (DWS), which preserves this two-dimensional block-step structure as a probability surface to weight the heterogeneous per-step costs. We then design a coarse-to-fine training scheme that enables a lightweight prompt-only predictor to accurately predict the complex DWS. This predictor runs efficiently even on a single CPU core, avoiding GPU contention with the serving model. Since DWS decouples request-dependent execution behavior from deployment-specific cost factors, the predictor transfers across hardware configurations without retraining. In \textit{real-world} serving experiments, DWS reduces cost-prediction error by up to $2.50\times$ over scalar-based predictors, while the DWS-guided shortest-job-first scheduler reduces end-to-end latency by up to $1.92\times$ for online chatbots.

</details>


### [400] [One-Step Generative Modeling via Training Dynamics Action](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00518)
*Zhangyong Liang,Ying Huang,Haibin Ling*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Training Dynamics Action (TDAction), a method for one-step generative models that selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining distributional progress. It formulates the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derives a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value. The method achieves FID below 1.1 on ImageNet 256×256 without distillation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing transport objectives for one-step generative models primarily assess distributional motion, but neural generators need to realize requested sample displacements jointly through shared parameter updates. The key question is whether to optimize the next distributional move or the route by which the finite generator learns the final map.

Method: The paper proposes TDAction, which selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining prescribed distributional progress. The cost is formulated as a soft-terminal control problem, deriving a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value that accounts for parameter effort and terminal mismatch. This criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs. Under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings. Randomized tangent probes provide a low-rank implementation constructing shared detached targets without adding inference-time trajectory.

Result: On ImageNet 256×256, TDAction attains an FID below 1.1 without distillation. Controlled studies examine the relationship between generator geometry, transport selection, and realized local action.

Conclusion: The proposed criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs. Under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings, demonstrating the method's theoretical consistency while achieving state-of-the-art results on ImageNet.

Abstract: One-step generative models construct a static generator through iterative training-time transport. Existing transport objectives primarily assess distributional motion, although a neural generator needs to realize the requested sample displacements jointly through shared parameter updates. The training-time construction raises the question: \emph{once training becomes the iterative process that constructs the final one-step map, what to optimize: the next distributional move, or the route by which the finite generator learns the final map?} To address the question, we introduce \textbf{T}raining \textbf{D}ynamics \textbf{A}ction (\textbf{TDAction}), which selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining a prescribed level of distributional progress. We formulate the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derive a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value that accounts for parameter effort and terminal mismatch. The criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs; under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings. Randomized tangent probes provide a low-rank implementation that constructs shared detached targets without adding an inference-time trajectory. Controlled studies examine the relationship between generator geometry, transport selection, and realized local action. On ImageNet $256\times256$, TDAction attains an FID below $1.1$ without distillation.

</details>


### [401] [SimplexUQ: An Evaluation Framework and Benchmark for Conformal Uncertainty on Simplex-Valued Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00523)
*Liang You,Hengyu Shi,Dongwen Ou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SimplexUQ is a benchmark for evaluating conformal prediction methods on simplex-valued predictions, revealing that marginal coverage guarantees can mask uneven coverage distribution across different data subgroups. The study compares existing conformal wrappers across 12 tasks and finds no single method dominates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conformal prediction provides marginal coverage guarantees but may spread coverage unevenly across different data subgroups - over-covering easy regions while under-covering hard ones. This allocation problem is not well-understood, especially for simplex-valued predictions (probability distributions).

Method: SimplexUQ benchmark compares existing conformal wrappers (not proposing new ones) using SimplexTasks-12: 6 controlled synthetic regimes + 6 real tasks (class probabilities, topic mixtures, spectral abundances, cell-type fractions, age distributions, emotion mixtures). Evaluation metrics: marginal coverage, worst-stratum coverage, max disparity, radius, and compute.

Result: Global calibration can appear valid while failing badly (CIFAR-10: 0.900 marginal coverage but only 0.542 in worst entropy stratum). Mondrian calibration raises worst stratum to 0.886 and reduces max disparity from 0.358 to 0.022. No wrapper dominates. Mondrian has lower disparity on single target partition for all 12 tasks; BatchMVP has lower disparity over overlapping groups on 5 tasks. Removing predictor bias only partly reduces global-threshold disparity.

Conclusion: Rankings of conformal wrappers depend on evaluation groups and protocol; wrapper selection should be treated as diagnostic comparison rather than universal ranking. The benchmark provides task cards, result provenance, and rebuild instructions for reproducibility.

Abstract: Conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage, but a single calibration threshold can still spread that coverage unevenly, over-covering easy regions and under-covering hard ones. SimplexUQ is, to our knowledge, the first benchmark and reproducible protocol for measuring this allocation problem on simplex-valued predictions; it compares existing conformal wrappers rather than proposing a new one. Its task suite, SimplexTasks-12, combines six controlled synthetic regimes with six frozen-predictor real tasks spanning class probabilities, topic mixtures, spectral abundances, cell-type fractions, age distributions, and emotion mixtures. Each comparison fixes the predictor, score, and response-free stratification map, varies only the wrapper, and reports marginal coverage, worst-stratum coverage, max disparity, and within-task radius and compute. Global calibration can look valid while failing badly: on CIFAR-10 it attains 0.900 marginal coverage but only 0.542 in the worst entropy stratum, and Mondrian calibration raises that stratum to 0.886 while reducing max disparity from 0.358 to 0.022. No wrapper dominates, however. Under smooth synthetic heterogeneity, several repairs are competitive; fixed-map analyses show that rankings depend on the evaluation groups and protocol; and in a 12-task comparison, Mondrian has lower disparity on its single target partition for all 12 tasks, whereas BatchMVP has lower disparity over overlapping groups on five. These are empirical comparisons, not new coverage guarantees. A controlled predictor-bias sweep shows that removing predictor bias only partly reduces global-threshold disparity. We release task cards, result provenance, permitted derived arrays, and rebuild instructions, and treat wrapper selection as a diagnostic comparison rather than a universal ranking.

</details>


### [402] [Random Recursive Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00541)
*Jama Hussein Mohamud,Mirco Ravanelli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The Random Recursive Model (RRM) introduces a parameter-efficient recursive architecture that maintains a pool of L learned layers and performs T recursive steps by randomly sampling one layer per step with replacement. This enables flexible layer reuse beyond fixed layer orders while using significantly fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current recursive models restrict computation to a fixed layer order by repeatedly applying one transformation or a prescribed sequence. The authors seek to enable flexible layer reuse while maintaining parameter efficiency of recurrence.

Method: RRM maintains a pool of L learned layers. For each example and recursive step, one layer is sampled independently with replacement. This allows flexible layer combinations at inference without requiring additional parameters.

Result: RRM matches or exceeds baseline performance on challenging reasoning tasks, often with 50-75% fewer parameters.
