It can vary depth at inference beyond training levels without retraining, and supports Monte Carlo inference and probabilistic test-time scaling that improve performance without retraining.

Conclusion: RRM demonstrates that random layer sampling provides an effective approach to neural network architecture design, offering flexible depth control, computational efficiency, and improved reasoning capabilities through probabilistic inference techniques.

Abstract: Recursive models create computational depth through parameter reuse, offering a parameter-efficient alternative to increasing model size. However, most recursive models repeatedly apply one learned transformation or a prescribed sequence of transformations, restricting computation to a fixed layer order. We introduce the Random Recursive Model (RRM), which maintains a pool of $L$ learned layers and performs $T$ recursive steps by sampling one layer independently with replacement for each example and step. This enables flexible layer reuse while retaining the parameter efficiency of recurrence. We evaluate RRM on challenging reasoning tasks, where it matches or exceeds the baselines, often with 50-75 % fewer parameters. RRM can vary its depth at inference, including beyond that seen during training, without retraining or adding parameters, improving tasks that benefit from deeper iterative computation. RRM also supports Monte Carlo inference and probabilistic test-time scaling, both of which improve performance without retraining. These insights may open new directions in neural network architecture design.

</details>


### [403] [Geometry-Dependent Bounds for Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00545)
*Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions. The authors prove a comparator-uniform first-order inequality achieving coefficient 4/9 (improving prior 0.401 benchmark) with O(√T) expected regret, using one gradient query and projection per round. They provide matching upper and lower bounds at 1/2 for ζ≥1/2, with optimal deficit Θ((1/2-ζ)²) as ζ↑1/2, and show offline approximation guarantees without requiring positive lower bounds on the optimum.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to improve the benchmark for adversarial online maximization of DR-submodular functions. The existing online 0.401 benchmark needed improvement, and the goal was to achieve a better comparator-uniform first-order inequality with efficient query complexity (one gradient query and one projection per round) while maintaining O(√T) regret.

Method: The proof uses a direct ordered-coordinate argument with an objective-independent rational action. The authors employ a three-group symmetry-gap construction for the offline oracle upper bound, and develop parameterized extensions with exact finite-instance bounds. They also provide nonanticipating adaptive-adversary and value-feedback guarantees, including O(T^{3/4}) regret with one noisy value per round.

Result: Key results include: (1) Comparator-uniform first-order inequality with coefficient 4/9, improving the online 0.401 benchmark; (2) Improved coefficient formula underlineα(ζ) = 1/2 - (1-2ζ)_+²/[2(3-2ζ)²] under ζ1 ∈ K ⊆ [0,1]^d; (3) Offline oracle upper bound β_* = 0.470438681380894... at ζ=0; (4) Matching lower and upper bounds at 1/2 for ζ≥1/2; (5) Optimal deficit from 1/2 is Θ((1/2-ζ)²) as ζ↑1/2; (6) For coefficient-revealed polynomials: 1/2 for quadratics, geometry-dependent cubic coefficient starting at 8/17, including 0.49 at ζ=1/5; (7) Offline (4/9 - ε) approximation with polynomially many first-order queries on the cube without requiring supplied positive lower bound on optimum.

Conclusion: The paper establishes improved bounds for adversarial online DR-submodular maximization, with the 4/9 coefficient being a key achievement. The techniques provide matching bounds at 1/2 for certain ζ values, characterize the optimal deficit as quadratic, and give both adaptive-adversary and value-feedback guarantees. The results advance the understanding of online submodular optimization with first-order queries.

Abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets. A learner commits each action before observing its objective and competes with the best fixed action in hindsight. We prove a comparator-uniform first-order inequality that gives coefficient $4/9$, improving the online $0.401$ benchmark, with one gradient query and one projection per round and $O(\sqrt T)$ expected approximate regret. If $ζ{\bf 1} \in K\subseteq[0,1]^d$, the coefficient improves to $\underlineα(ζ)=\tfrac12-(1-2ζ)_+^2/[2(3-2ζ)^2]$. The proof is a direct ordered-coordinate argument with an objective-independent rational action. Conversely, a three-group symmetry-gap construction yields an offline oracle upper bound $β_*=0.470438681380894\ldots$ at $ζ=0$, even with exact value and full-gradient responses. A parameterized extension and exact finite-instance bounds define an upper function for every $ζ$. The lower and upper bounds match at $1/2$ for $ζ\ge1/2$, and show that the optimal deficit from $1/2$ is $Θ((1/2-ζ)^2)$ as $ζ\uparrow1/2$. For coefficient-revealed polynomials we obtain $1/2$ for quadratics and a geometry-dependent cubic coefficient starting at $8/17$, including $0.49$ at $ζ=1/5$. A constant objective sequence yields an offline $(4/9-\varepsilon)$ approximation with polynomially many first-order queries on the cube and projections, without requiring a supplied positive lower bound on the optimum. We also give nonanticipating adaptive-adversary and value-feedback guarantees, including $O(T^{3/4})$ regret with one noisy value per round.

</details>


### [404] [Evaluating Hybrid Quantum-Classical Models for Reduced-Order Brain Deformation Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00554)
*Tao Liu,Ge He,Dongyu Liang,Wujie Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks hybrid quantum-classical ML against classical baselines for reduced-order prediction of brain deformation fields using POD. Classical approaches (POD-MLP, POD-LSTM) outperform all quantum variants in both static regression and temporal forecasting tasks, though enhanced VQC shows improvement over minimal VQC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To mitigate computational intractability of high-dimensional displacement fields in brain deformation prediction by employing Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) and systematically benchmarking quantum vs classical approaches.

Method: POD for dimensionality reduction; two learning objectives: static temporal-to-latent regression and autoregressive latent state forecasting; comparison of classical baselines (POD-MLP, POD-LSTM) against minimal and enhanced hybrid quantum architectures (VQC, QLSTM).

Result: Classical networks provide strongest baselines. POD-MLP outperforms all quantum variants for static regression; enhanced VQC substantially improves upon minimal VQC. POD-LSTM delivers superior predictive accuracy and statistical robustness compared to enhanced QLSTM for temporal forecasting.

Conclusion: Classical architectures retain definitive advantage in both fidelity and stability. While hybrid enhancements successfully recover expressivity in weak quantum circuits, reduced-order physical field learning serves as a rigorous testbed for near-term QML, highlighting current limitations of quantum approaches.

Abstract: We evaluate hybrid quantum-classical machine learning for the reduced-order prediction of spatiotemporal brain deformation fields. To mitigate the computational intractability of high-dimensional displacement fields, we employ Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) to project the data into a compact latent space. Within this framework, we formulate two distinct learning objectives: static temporal-to-latent regression and autoregressive latent state forecasting. We systematically benchmark compact classical baselines against both minimal and enhanced hybrid quantum architectures. Our results demonstrate that classical networks provide the strongest baselines in the present setting. For static regression, a classical POD-MLP outperforms all evaluated quantum variants, although an enhanced Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC) substantially improves upon a minimal VQC baseline. For temporal forecasting, a classical POD-LSTM delivers superior predictive accuracy and statistical robustness compared to an enhanced Quantum LSTM (QLSTM) across varying history windows and random initializations. Overall, this study establishes reduced-order physical field learning as a rigorous testbed for near-term QML, highlighting that while hybrid enhancements successfully recover expressivity in weak quantum circuits, classical architectures retain a definitive advantage in both fidelity and stability.

</details>


### [405] [Redundancy Meets Synergy: Dependency-aware Expert Selection for MoE via Submodular Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00558)
*Zheng Lin,Shaoke Fang,Yuxin Zhang,Jinfeng Xu,Zihan Fang,Zhe Chen,Wei Ni,Jun Luo,Symeon Chatzinotas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DS-MoE proposes a novel expert selection framework for Mixture-of-Experts models that uses difference-of-submodular (DS) optimization to address the limitations of traditional Top-k ranking methods. It mathematically decouples redundancy reduction from synergy maximization to preserve essential expert combinations while reducing memory requirements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mixture-of-Experts models effectively scale model capacity through sparse activation but suffer from prohibitive memory requirements during deployment. Existing expert selection heuristics rely on Top-k ranking, which evaluates experts individually and ignores intricate inter-expert dependencies introduced by the gating network.

Method: The paper analyzes the second-order Taylor expansion of loss degradation to reveal functional duality in expert combinations (redundancy and synergy). It formulates expert selection as a DS function to decouple redundancy reduction from synergy maximization. A tailored majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm with provable monotonicity guarantees is developed to efficiently identify the optimal expert subset.

Result: DS-MoE effectively preserves indispensable expert combinations and achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines in experiments.

Conclusion: The proposed DS-MoE framework provides a theoretically grounded approach to expert selection that captures inter-expert dependencies, offering a promising solution for deploying compact yet capable MoE models.

Abstract: While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models effectively scale model capacity through sparse activation, their deployment is often bottlenecked by prohibitive memory requirements. Extracting a compact subset of experts presents a promising solution. However, existing expert selection heuristics predominantly rely on Top-k ranking, which isolates the evaluation of individual experts and ignores the intricate inter-expert dependencies introduced by the MoE gating network. In this paper, we propose DS-MoE, a theoretically grounded framework that redefines expert selection via difference-of-submodular (DS) optimization. By analyzing the second-order Taylor expansion of the loss degradation, we reveal functional duality within expert combinations: redundancy (where experts encode overlapping representations) and synergy (where experts provide complementary error cancellation). To navigate this duality, we mathematically decouple redundancy reduction from synergy maximization by formulating the selection objective as a DS function. Furthermore, we devise a tailored majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm with provable monotonicity guarantees to efficiently identify the optimal expert subset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DS-MoE effectively preserves indispensable expert combinations, achieving superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [406] [Beyond Affine Transformations: A Soft Dominance Layer for Coordinate-Wise Neural Computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00563)
*Mariano Rivera*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a Soft Dominance Layer as an alternative to conventional affine transformation in neural networks. Each output unit compares input coordinates with learnable reference vectors using sigmoid relaxation, with a sharpness parameter controlling the transition toward hard threshold decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To examine the trainability and direct threshold interpretation of the Soft Dominance Layer as an alternative to affine transformation, not to claim it as a replacement.

Method: Soft Dominance Layer: output units compare input coordinates with learnable reference vectors and aggregate smooth inequality responses. Sigmoid relaxation makes comparisons differentiable, with sharpness parameter α controlling transition toward hard threshold decisions. Tested on MNIST with and without annealing.

Result: On MNIST single-run experiments: Soft Dominance accuracy of 0.9061 without annealing and 0.9173 with annealing, compared to 0.9827 for MLP baseline. Learned reference vectors exhibit spatial structure, providing qualitative evidence of structured learning.

Conclusion: Preliminary proof-of-concept results. Descriptive results do not establish reliable configuration rankings or statistically supported annealing benefit. Repeated-seed experiments and broader datasets are required to assess robustness and practical relevance.

Abstract: This paper presents a preliminary study of an alternative to the affine transformation underlying conventional neural-network layers. In the proposed Soft Dominance Layer, each output unit compares input coordinates with a learnable reference vector and aggregates smooth inequality responses. A sigmoid relaxation makes the comparisons differentiable, while a sharpness parameter $α$ controls their transition toward hard threshold decisions. The aim is to examine the trainability and direct threshold interpretation of this primitive, not to claim a replacement for affine layers. In single-run MNIST experiments, the highest observed Soft Dominance accuracy is $0.9061$ without annealing and $0.9173$ with annealing, compared with $0.9827$ for the MLP baseline. These descriptive results do not establish reliable configuration rankings or a statistically supported annealing benefit. Learned reference vectors exhibit spatial structure, providing qualitative evidence of structured learning. Repeated-seed experiments and broader datasets are required to assess robustness and practical relevance beyond this proof of concept.

</details>


### [407] [Attention Kernels for Learning Maps Between Heavy-Tailed Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00564)
*Kailen Hargenrader,Edoardo Calvello,Bohan Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses operator learning on probability measures using transformers. The authors identify that softmax attention can diverge when dealing with heavy-tailed distributions due to exponential weighting, and propose using slower-growing attention kernels as a solution. They construct two benchmarks with closed-form targets and demonstrate that slower-growing kernels avoid the ensemble collapse observed with softmax on heavy-tailed data, while all kernels perform similarly on Gaussian data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The exponential weighting in softmax attention can cause divergence when learning operators on probability measures with polynomial (heavy) tails. This is a fundamental limitation that needs to be addressed for transformer-based operator learning on such distributions.

Method: The authors construct two benchmarks with closed-form target operators for testing operator learning on measures. They compare softmax against three slower-growing attention kernels (possibly polynomial or other sub-exponential functions) in post-norm transformers, with and without symlog preprocessing. They evaluate using empirical energy and Wasserstein distances.

Result: Without data transformation, softmax models exhibit ensemble collapse on both heavy-tailed benchmarks, while the three slower-growing kernels avoid collapse. Symlog preprocessing enables softmax to avoid collapse on the matrix inverse task but not on the sheared swap task. On Gaussian control, all four kernels perform similarly. Sample size affects sensitivity of empirical metrics to tail differences.

Conclusion: Slower-growing attention kernels are an effective design choice for post-norm transformers learning from heavy-tailed ensembles, as they avoid the ensemble collapse problem observed with softmax while maintaining comparable performance on light-tailed (Gaussian) data.

Abstract: Operator learning on probability measures can be accomplished with transformers. For measures with polynomial tails, the exponential weighting in softmax can make the corresponding measure-level attention integrals diverge. This motivates replacing the exponential with slower-growing functions. We construct two benchmarks for operator learning on measures with closed-form targets. We use these benchmarks to study attention kernel growth and data transformation in post-norm transformers. Without data transformation, the softmax models exhibit ensemble collapse on both heavy-tailed benchmarks, while the three slower-growing kernels avoid collapse. Symlog preprocessing allows softmax to avoid collapse on the matrix inverse task but not on the sheared swap task. On the Gaussian control, all four kernels perform similarly. We also examine how sample size affects the sensitivity of empirical energy and Wasserstein distances to tail differences. These results support slower-growing attention kernels as an effective design choice for post-norm transformers learning from heavy-tailed ensembles.

</details>


### [408] [Make Sparse Rewards Count: Density-Aware Reward Aggregation for Multi-Reward RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00574)
*Tong Zheng,Skylar Zhai,Zhan Cheng,TianMing Sha,Youling Huang,Shuo Zhou,Shaotong Qi,Jingcheng Liang,Xuwei Ding,Pengcheng Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Density-Aware Reward Aggregation (DARA), a method to balance learning progress across multiple reward objectives in RL training of language models. The key insight is that advantage energy (sum of squared advantages) correlates with "active-group density" - the frequency at which each reward provides nonzero relative advantages within rollout batches. DARA applies inverse-square-root density correction to give more weight to less frequently active rewards, achieving faster convergence in tool calling (26% fewer steps) and mathematical reasoning (65% fewer steps) tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multi-reward reinforcement learning trains LLMs to satisfy multiple behavioral objectives simultaneously. However, different objectives exhibit uneven learning progress because reward-wise normalization (as in GDPO) preserves reward-specific relative information within rollout groups, but doesn't account for batch-level signal imbalance where some rewards are frequently inactive while others are consistently active.

Method: The authors analyze the problem through "advantage energy" - the sum of a reward's squared advantages over a batch. Under idealized GDPO normalization, they prove that advantage energy is proportional to active-group density (the fraction of rollout groups where a reward provides nonzero relative advantages). Based on this relationship, they propose DARA with an inverse-square-root density correction that gives greater weight to less frequently active rewards. DARA computes weights from each rollout batch adaptively without modifying the underlying policy optimization objective.

Result: Experiments on tool calling and mathematical reasoning show that DARA learns targeted behaviors faster than GDPO: reaching high format compliance in up to 26% fewer training steps on tool calling, and near-saturated length compliance in up to 65% fewer steps on mathematical reasoning, while remaining competitive in final performance.

Conclusion: The work reveals a previously overlooked batch-level signal imbalance in multi-reward RL and provides a simple yet effective calibration method. DARA's adaptive density weighting successfully balances learning across objectives, leading to faster convergence without changing the core optimization objective. The code is available on GitHub.

Abstract: Multi-reward reinforcement learning trains large language models to satisfy multiple behavioral objectives simultaneously. Reward-wise normalization, as used in GDPO, preserves reward-specific relative information within rollout groups, but different objectives can still exhibit uneven learning progress. We study this behavior through advantage energy, the sum of a reward's squared advantages over a batch. Under idealized GDPO normalization, we show that this energy is proportional to active-group density: the fraction of rollout groups in which the reward provides nonzero relative advantages. This reveals a residual batch-level signal imbalance and provides a basis for calibrating reward contributions. Based on this relation, we propose Density-Aware Reward Aggregation (DARA). We derive an inverse-square-root density correction that gives greater weight to signals from less frequently active rewards. DARA computes its weights from each rollout batch, adapting to changes in reward activity throughout training without modifying the underlying policy optimization objective. Experiments on tool calling and mathematical reasoning show that DARA learns the targeted behaviors faster than GDPO, reaching high format compliance in up to 26% fewer training steps on tool calling and near-saturated length compliance in up to 65% fewer steps on mathematical reasoning, while remaining competitive in final performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhaihaotian/DARA.

</details>


### [409] [From Task Mixtures to Specialized Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00580)
*Hojat Allah Salehi,Mehrdad Mahdavi,Andrew Arash Mahyari,M. Hadi Amini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses "compound heterogeneity" in federated learning, where data is heterogeneous both across and within clients (each client may have a mixture of different task distributions). The authors show that when tasks share the same feature geometry, optimal models for mixed tasks are convex combinations of task-specific optimal models. They propose FedSEE, which uses task-aligned routing to specialized experts and a convex program to recover task experts from small public samples. Experiments show FedSEE improves performance by 2.9 points overall and 3.7 points for the worst-served quartile, avoiding negative transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional federated learning addresses heterogeneity across clients but fails to handle latent task mixtures within each client. In real-world scenarios, clients rarely have homogeneous data—they often possess unknown mixtures of distinct data distributions or tasks. This compound heterogeneity (heterogeneous both across and within clients) is the key problem being addressed.

Method: The authors study adaptation over a common frozen representation and analyze the optimal model structure for clients with mixed task distributions. They show that when tasks share the same feature geometry, the optimal model for a client's task mixture under squared loss is a convex combination of the optimal models for underlying tasks. They propose task-aligned routing to specialized experts, and with access to a small set of task-labeled public samples, derive a convex program to recover task experts and match them to corresponding tasks. The proposed method FedSEE implements this approach.

Result: When task optima form a simplex, task-aligned routing achieves lower risk than any single adapted model for genuinely mixed clients. FedSEE avoids the negative transfer observed in baseline methods and improves performance by 2.9 points overall and 3.7 points for the worst-served quartile.

Conclusion: Effective specialization in federated learning with compound heterogeneity requires input-dependent expert selection aligned with each client's task mixture. FedSEE successfully addresses compound heterogeneity by routing inputs to task-specialized experts, outperforming baselines that fail to handle mixed task distributions within clients.

Abstract: In collaborative foundation model fine-tuning, client data is rarely homogeneous. Instead, clients typically possess unknown mixtures of distinct data distributions, or tasks. Conventional federated learning primarily addresses heterogeneity across clients without explicitly resolving latent task mixtures within each client. We study this setting as compound heterogeneity, where data is heterogeneous both across and within clients. We study adaptation over a common frozen representation and show that, when tasks share the same feature geometry, the optimal model for a client's task mixture under squared loss is a convex combination of the optimal models for its underlying tasks. Thus, a single locally trained model represents the client's overall task mixture, while individual inputs may be drawn from different underlying task distributions. This motivates routing inputs to specialized experts, and we show that, when the task optima form a simplex, task-aligned routing achieves lower risk than any single adapted model for genuinely mixed clients. With access to a small set of task-labeled public samples, we derive a convex program to recover task experts and match them to their corresponding tasks. Our routing analysis shows that effective specialization requires input-dependent expert selection aligned with each client's task mixture. Motivated by this analysis, we propose FedSEE. Across our experiments, FedSEE avoids the negative transfer observed in the evaluated baselines and improves performance by 2.9 points overall and 3.7 points for the worst-served quartile.

</details>


### [410] [Right In-Place (RiP) Convolution: A Simple, General, and Near-Optimal Strategy for Memory-Efficient CNN Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00586)
*Opegbemi Matthias Busoye,Tolulope Matthew Busoye,Eghonghon-aye Eigbe*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents Right In-Place (RiP) convolution, a memory optimization technique for CNN inference on microcontroller-constrained hardware. It corrects errors in prior memory-optimal in-place convolution methods and generalizes to arbitrary convolution parameters, achieving 12.5-33.3% memory reduction on MCUNet models deployed to Raspberry Pi Pico.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation memory, not compute, limits CNN inference on constrained hardware like microcontrollers. Existing in-place convolution methods have restrictive assumptions and contain errors causing either silent corruption or massive memory overestimation. The authors seek to correct these issues and generalize the approach.

Method: The authors identified two failure regimes in prior work: (1) under-allocation causing silent input corruption; (2) unbounded memory overestimation. They corrected both and generalized to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels. They proposed RiP convolution where each layer reads input right-aligned in a shared workspace and writes output left-aligned from index zero. The memory debt is piecewise affine in output pixel index, allowing O(1) breakpoint evaluation to find minimum safe gap without enumerating the output grid.

Result: Across 10,000 random layers, RiP produced no corruption. Across 84 convolutional layers from 25 architectures, it matched the herringbone workspace exactly on 58 and within 5% on 81 layers, using 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average. Deployed to Raspberry Pi Pico 1 and Pico 2, it reduced peak activation memory by 12.5-33.3% at unchanged cycle counts with bit-identical outputs, raising the number of MCUNet models fitting the Pico 1's 256 KB SRAM from six to nine.

Conclusion: Right In-Place convolution is a practical, generalizable solution for memory-efficient CNN inference on microcontrollers. It eliminates the dual-buffer overhead while preserving row-major access patterns and bit-exact outputs, enabling more deep learning models to run on resource-constrained devices.

Abstract: Activation memory, not compute, limits CNN inference on constrained hardware such as microcontrollers. Direct in-place convolution removes the dual-buffer cost, but the memory-optimal formulation of Gural and Murmann assumes valid padding, unit stride, unit dilation, and odd square kernels, and needs a non-sequential traversal costing $2\times$ inference time in transposes. We identify two regimes in which their published closed form does not hold: (1) an under-allocation of exactly $(k-1)C_{in} \bmod (C_{out}-C_{in})$ scalars, active on every convolutional layer of their own deployed network and manifesting as a silent corruption of still-live input; (2) an unbounded overestimate, up to $2{,}432\times$, once the critical leg leaves the output grid. We correct both and generalize to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels. We then propose Right In-Place (RiP) convolution, a bit-identical operation in which every layer reads its input right-aligned in a shared workspace and writes its output left-aligned from index zero. The debt is piecewise affine in the output pixel index, so evaluating its breakpoints in $O(1)$ yields the minimum safe gap without enumerating the output grid, with row-major access preserved. Across $10{,}000$ random layers RiP produced no corruption, and across 84 convolutional layers from 25 architectures it matches the herringbone workspace exactly on 58 and within 5% on 81, using 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average. Written into TinyEngine's kernels and deployed to a Raspberry Pi Pico 1 and Pico 2, it cuts peak activation memory across eleven MCUNet models by 12.5 to 33.3% at unchanged cycle counts and bit-identical outputs, raising the number of models that fit the Pico 1's 256 KB SRAM from six to nine.

</details>


### [411] [ALER: Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting for Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00592)
*Oleg Shchendrigin,Egor Cherepanov,Aleksandr I. Panov,Alexey K. Kovalev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses partially observable reinforcement learning by identifying two overlooked memory requirements: rewriting (overwriting decision-relevant content) and experience fusion (transforming old content based on later observations). The authors propose ALER, an agent combining LSTM with slot memory using Gumbel-Softmax writes and learned gates, which outperforms seven baselines across multiple memory-augmented RL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory architectures and benchmarks in RL primarily focus on retention (keeping information unchanged). However, real-world partially observable scenarios require the ability to actively modify stored information based on new observations - either by overwriting it with new values or fusing old content with transformation rules specified by later observations. This gap motivated the formalization of rewriting and experience fusion as additional memory requirements.

Method: The authors introduce ALER (Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting), which combines an LSTM with a slot-based memory. Key components include: (1) an independently addressed Gumbel-Softmax write mechanism that concentrates weight on one slot for overwriting, and (2) a learned gate that fuses retrieved content with the recurrent state before policy and value heads. They also introduce Rune-Mazes - three environments where rune observations can invert, cancel, reset, or repeat updates to hidden cues, tested under both vector and pixel observations.

Result: ALER achieves at least 0.82 success rate on all sixteen Endless T-Maze configurations and at least 0.99 on all five Rune T-Maze compositions. It obtains the highest mean success rate on four-branch Rune Multi-Corridor with Invert rune. On pixel-based Rune MiniGrid Memory, ALER outperforms PPO-LSTM in eight of ten configurations.

Conclusion: The paper successfully formalizes rewriting and experience fusion as key requirements for memory in partially observable RL, beyond just retention. ALER demonstrates that combining slot-based memory with LSTM and learned fusion mechanisms effectively handles these requirements, outperforming seven baselines across diverse memory benchmarks. The introduced Rune-Mazes environments provide valuable testbeds for evaluating memory rewriting and fusion capabilities in RL agents.

Abstract: In partially observable reinforcement learning (RL), a later observation can make stored information obsolete or change what it implies for the next decision. Memory architectures and benchmarks for RL mostly test retention, the ability to keep information unchanged until it is needed. We formalize two further requirements. Rewriting sets the decision-relevant content to a value independent of the old one, and experience fusion transforms the old content by a rule that a later observation specifies. For tasks built from such updates, we count the memory states that a solution needs, and several baselines reach their lowest success rates on compositions that need more states. We introduce ALER (Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting), an agent that pairs an LSTM with a slot memory. An independently addressed Gumbel-Softmax write that concentrates its weight on one slot overwrites that slot, and a learned gate fuses the retrieved content with the recurrent state before the policy and value heads. We also introduce Rune-Mazes, three environments in which rune observations invert, cancel, reset, or repeat updates of a hidden cue under vector and pixel observations. Against seven baselines, ALER reaches a success rate of at least $0.82$ in all sixteen Endless T-Maze configurations and at least $0.99$ on all five Rune T-Maze compositions, and it has the highest mean success rate on four-branch Rune Multi-Corridor with an Invert rune. On pixel-based Rune MiniGrid Memory, it has a higher mean success rate than PPO-LSTM in eight of ten configurations. Project page: https://quartz-admirer.github.io/ALER-Adaptive-Learnable-Experience-Rewriting/.

</details>


### [412] [MIKASA-Robo-VLA: Benchmarking Memory in VLA Models for Long-Horizon Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00604)
*Egor Cherepanov,Nikita Kachaev,Aleksandr I. Panov,Alexey K. Kovalev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MIKASA-Robo-VLA is a benchmark with 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks designed to evaluate vision-language-action (VLA) policies on memory-dependent tasks where key information disappears during task execution. The benchmark includes 80 memory-dependent tasks (where cues are hidden) and 10 reactive controls, with 28 tasks having information gaps exceeding the 16-frame window of existing VLAs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLA policies only see limited frames (typically 1-16), making it difficult to complete tasks where relevant information disappears before the action is taken. There was no benchmark specifically designed to evaluate how VLAs handle memory-dependent tasks where cues become unavailable.

Method: The authors created MIKASA-Robo-VLA with 90 tasks, 70 of which have environment phase timings specifying an information gap. They released 22,500 oracle trajectories across 10 memory types in RLDS and LeRobotDataset v3 formats. A reference π₀.₅ baseline (using only current images and proprioception, no observation history) was fine-tuned on 14 tasks.

Result: The π₀.₅ baseline achieves 0.211 ± 0.044 mean task success. Performance is lower on Long-split tasks, which is attributed to open-loop chunking and the memory types in that subset.

Conclusion: The benchmark successfully identifies a gap in current VLA capabilities—existing policies cannot handle tasks where information disappears before action execution. The low baseline success rate (21.1%) highlights the need for improved memory mechanisms in VLAs. The 28 tasks with gaps exceeding 16 frames specifically challenge current fixed-context VLA limitations.

Abstract: Vision-language-action policies often see only one or a few recent frames, which makes it difficult to evaluate how they use information that disappears during a task. We introduce MIKASA-Robo-VLA, a benchmark of 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks. All but 10 hide the cue an action depends on. Those 10 are reactive controls. MIKASA-Robo, the suite it rebuilds, has 32 tasks and uses language only in a representative VLA subset. Here every task provides an instruction, while memory-dependent tasks hide a task-relevant cue and reactive controls keep it available. For 70 tasks, environment phase timings specify an information gap, and for 28 of them the gap exceeds the 16-frame window of the widest fixed-context VLA we survey. The gap counts only the interval the cue is provably absent, not the full duration a policy must retain it, so every memory-dependent task still requires memory by construction, including the ones whose measured gap is short. We release 22,500 oracle trajectories across 10 memory types in RLDS and LeRobotDataset v3. A reference $π_{0.5}$ baseline with current images and proprioception, but no observation history or explicit memory module, is fine-tuned on 14 tasks and achieves 0.211 $\pm$ 0.044 mean task success. Its lower success on the evaluated Long-split tasks is confounded by open-loop chunking and the memory types represented in that subset. Project page: https://mikasarobo.github.io/

</details>


### [413] [Learning the identity: a case study of how SGD selects among functional decompositions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00615)
*Andy Arditi,Weian Xie,David Bau,Liu Ziyin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates why stochastic gradient descent (SGD) favors specific solutions when learning the identity function with deep linear residual networks, despite the existence of a manifold of equivalent minimizers. The authors explain this phenomenon through the lens of entropic loss, which measures the expected squared norm of minibatch gradients.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand why SGD reproducibly favors particular solutions among many equivalent ones when training neural networks. Specifically, the authors investigate the identity learning task in deep linear residual networks, where the zero-weight solution is not the only minimizer of the population loss.

Method: The authors use analytical characterization of entropic loss minimizers and empirical validation with SGD. They study how different factors (label noise, weight decay, weight matrix factorization) affect the solutions favored by SGD, and compare these to theoretical predictions derived from entropic loss analysis.

Result: The authors find that on the identity manifold, the population loss is constant while the entropic term distinguishes among different decompositions. Under anisotropic label noise, learned layers exhibit a noise-dependent spectrum. Even with weight decay, SGD does not generally recover the zero-weight solution. Factoring weight matrices as products causes weights to collapse to zero without explicit weight decay. Networks trained with SGD closely match predictions derived from entropic loss minimizers.

Conclusion: The identity learning task serves as a clean case study demonstrating how entropic loss can clarify why SGD favors particular decompositions of the same input-output function. This provides a framework for understanding SGD's implicit bias in more general settings.

Abstract: One might think that learning the identity function with a deep linear residual network is trivial - the path along residual connections already implements the identity, and so the network need only drive its weights to zero. However, this zero-weight solution is just one point on an entire manifold of population-loss minimizers, each corresponding to a different decomposition of the identity across the network's layers. Although the population loss does not distinguish among these solutions, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) reproducibly favors particular ones. For instance, under anisotropic label noise, the learned layers exhibit a noise-dependent spectrum; even with weight decay, SGD does not generally recover the zero-weight solution. Changing only the parametrization, while leaving the set of realizable functions unchanged, yields different behavior: factoring each weight matrix as a product of two matrices causes the weights to collapse to zero, even without explicit weight decay.
  While perhaps mysterious and unintuitive at first, these phenomena can be understood through the lens of entropic loss, which augments the population loss with a term proportional to the expected squared norm of the minibatch gradient (Ziyin et al., 2025). On the identity manifold, the population loss is constant, while the entropic term distinguishes among these decompositions. We characterize its minimizers analytically and use them to derive predictions for the structure of solutions favored by SGD. Networks trained with SGD closely match these predictions.
  Overall, the identity learning task studied here serves as a clean and simple case study of how the lens of entropic loss can clarify why SGD favors particular decompositions of the same input-output function.

</details>


### [414] [Misalignment of Low-Loss Regions Causes Grokking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00620)
*Yongding Tian,Zaid Al-Ars,Maksim Kitsak,Peter Hofstee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Grokking is the delayed emergence of validation-set generalization after a model has already overfit the training set. This work develops an analysis framework based on mode connectivity and low-loss region geometry, which predicts that the standard modular-arithmetic setting does not always produce grokking. Under symmetry-preserving train/validation splits, an "anti-grokking" case is observed where validation performance never recovers, challenging existing explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The mechanism underlying grokking (delayed validation generalization after overfitting) remains unsettled despite being first observed in small algorithmic tasks with transformers. The authors seek to develop a framework to predict and explain when grokking occurs.

Method: The authors develop an analysis framework based on mode connectivity and the geometry of low-loss regions. They use the standard modular-arithmetic setting and test it with a symmetry-preserving train/validation split.

Result: The standard modular-arithmetic setting does not always produce grokking. Under symmetry-preserving train/validation split, a stable anti-grokking case emerges where validation performance does not recover. Grokking arises when low-loss regions induced by training and validation partitions are misaligned; when well-aligned, training hyperparameters alone cannot produce grokking.

Conclusion: Grokking arises from misalignment between low-loss regions induced by training and validation partitions, not from training hyperparameters alone. Once these regions become well-aligned, training dynamics collapse to either trainable or non-trainable behavior, challenging existing correlational explanations of grokking.

Abstract: Grokking refers to the delayed emergence of validation-set generalization after a model has already overfit the training set. Although first observed in small algorithmic tasks trained with transformers, its underlying mechanism remains unsettled. In this work, we develop an analysis framework based on mode connectivity and the geometry of low-loss regions. The framework predicts that the standard modular-arithmetic setting does not always produce grokking: under a symmetry-preserving train/validation split, we observe a stable anti-grokking case in which validation performance does not recover. This counterexample challenges several existing correlational explanations of grokking. More broadly, our analysis framework and results further suggest that grokking arises when the low-loss regions induced by the training and validation partitions are misaligned. Once these regions become well aligned, training hyperparameters alone cannot produce grokking and the observed dynamics collapse to either trainable or non-trainable behavior.

</details>


### [415] [Learning Linear Systems under Heavy-Tailed Noise: A Non-Asymptotic Analysis from A Single Trajectory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00637)
*Xiaomian Yang,Sungho Shin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for least-squares estimation of vector autoregressive (VAR) models with heavy-tailed noise. Under assumptions of i.i.d. noise, bounded noise covariance, and persistent excitation, the estimation error achieves Õ(r^{1/2}T^{-1/2+1/p}) for p > 2, where T is the sample size and r is the noise dimension. The analysis extends to sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian noise distributions, and for ARX models, the dimension factor is independent of the model order.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses the lack of non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantees for VAR model estimation under heavy-tailed noise assumptions, which are common in practical applications but less studied compared to asymptotic results.

Method: The authors employ least-squares estimation on a single observed trajectory, assuming i.i.d. noise with bounded p-th moment (p > 2), bounded noise covariance, and persistent excitation conditions. They develop a unifying framework applicable to broad noise distributions including sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian cases.

Result: The estimation error is bounded by Õ(r^{1/2}T^{-1/2+1/p}), where the Õ notation hides logarithmic terms. The analysis shows that for ARX models, the dimension factor in the error bound is independent of the model order, which is particularly beneficial for high-dimensional models.

Conclusion: The paper provides finite-sample guarantees for VAR model estimation under heavy-tailed noise, offering explicit dependence on sample size, noise dimension, and moment bounds. The independence of the dimension factor from model order in ARX models is a key advantage for practical applications.

Abstract: We establish non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for the least-squares estimation of vector autoregressive models for exponentially stable systems with heavy-tailed noise based on a single observed trajectory. By assuming i.i.d. noise, bounded noise covariance, and persistent excitation, we show that the estimation error is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(r^{1/2}T^{-1/2+1/p})$ under bounded $p$th moment for $p > 2$, where $T$ is the number of samples, $r$ is the noise dimension, and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic terms. We also introduce a unifying approach to sample complexity analysis applicable to broad classes of noise distributions and showcase this by deriving error bounds for sub-exponential and sub-Gaussian noise distributions. Finally, we specialize our analysis to autoregressive models with exogenous inputs and show that the dimension factor of the error bound is independent of the model order.

</details>


### [416] [Group-Invariant Statistics Determine Embedding Geometry: Harmonic Analysis of Representations from Bach to the Night Sky](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00647)
*Liam Storan,Andreas Tolias,Nina Miolane*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper demonstrates that geometric structures (circles, saddles, spheres) observed in language model embeddings arise from symmetry properties in word co-occurrence statistics. The authors prove that when co-occurrence statistics are invariant under a group G, the learned embeddings consist of irreducible representation matrix elements of G.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work showed that translation symmetry in word co-occurrence leads to Fourier geometry (circles and Pringle manifolds). This paper generalizes this to arbitrary symmetry groups to explain more diverse geometric structures observed in learned representations.

Method: Theoretical proof: The authors prove that group invariance in co-occurrence statistics leads to embeddings as irreducible representation (irrep) matrix elements. Three experimental验证: (1) Cyclic group Z12 for months, (2) Dihedral group for musical triads (T/I group), (3) Spherical harmonics for celestial objects.

Result: The theory successfully explains: (i) Circular geometry of months via Z12 Fourier modes, (ii) Circle of fifths emergence in chord embeddings via dihedral group irreps, (iii) Spherical representation of celestial objects via spherical harmonics. All three settings confirm the predicted irrep structure.

Conclusion: The geometry of learned representations in language models is fundamentally a consequence of the statistical symmetry present in the underlying data. Different symmetry groups produce different geometric structures (circles, saddles, spheres) through their irreducible representations.

Abstract: The representations that language models learn for concepts such as months, weekdays, and places display consistent geometric structure: circles and saddle-shaped "Pringle" manifolds. Recent work traced these structures to $\textit{translation symmetry}$ in word co-occurrence statistics, deriving the observed Fourier geometry when co-occurrence depends only on distance on an abelian lattice of concepts. We demonstrate that more general notions of symmetry lead to equally structured predictions. Considering symmetries defined by arbitrary finite groups, compact groups, and homogeneous spaces, we prove that whenever the co-occurrence statistics of a word family are invariant under a group $G$, the learned word embeddings consist of matrix elements of the irreducible representations (irreps) of $G$. Circles and Pringles arise when $G$ is cyclic, in which case the irreps are Fourier modes. We verify the irrep structure in three experimental settings. (i) The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$: for the months of the year we recover the known circular geometry. (ii) A dihedral group acting on the major and minor triads: we unify two classical observations -- that transposition and chord inversion form a group ($T/I$) acting on chords (music theory), which $\textit{implies}$ that the well-known "circle of fifths" emerges in learned chord embeddings (machine learning). (iii) We explain and reproduce a recently discovered spherical representation of celestial objects in large language models (LLMs) as a spherical-harmonic embedding derived from our theory. Our results demonstrate that the geometry of learned representations is often a consequence of the statistical symmetry of underlying data.

</details>


### [417] [Exploring More, Reasoning Better: Stepwise Risk-Sensitive GRPO for Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00661)
*Yue YU,Bowen Zuo,David Crandall,Yinglun Zhu,Dongruo Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: StepRS-GRPO introduces a risk coefficient that varies across denoising states in diffusion LLMs, improving pass@1 accuracy, pass@k coverage, and answer diversity over centered GRPO while maintaining the underlying trainer architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In diffusion large language models (dLLMs), text generation occurs through denoising where multiple tokens can be revealed in parallel. However, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) reuses terminal feedback across these decisions even as the conditioning context changes, creating a mismatch in how rewards are applied across different denoising states.

Method: StepRS-GRPO varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while retaining the underlying trainer. For binary rewards, this transformation is equivalent to a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages. A capability-based calibration suggests a coefficient scale, while endpoint and interpolation ablations guide schedule selection.

Result: Across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, StepRS-GRPO improves both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, while increasing answer diversity. Ablation studies with mass-matched controls support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and gains persist after matching the RMS of advantages to centered GRPO. Reasoning-trace diagnostics show diversity gains extend beyond final-answer strings.

Conclusion: StepRS-GRPO provides a theoretically grounded and empirically validated approach to risk-sensitive optimization in dLLM training, achieving superior performance in accuracy, coverage, and answer diversity compared to centered GRPO, with the benefits validated through rigorous ablation studies.

Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by denoising a sequence or successive blocks, allowing several tokens to be revealed in parallel. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) reuses terminal feedback across these decisions, even as their conditioning context changes. We propose stepwise risk-sensitive GRPO (StepRS-GRPO), which varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while retaining the underlying trainer. For binary rewards, we show that this transformation is exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages. A capability-based calibration suggests a coefficient scale, while endpoint and interpolation ablations guide schedule selection. Across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, StepRS-GRPO improves both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, while increasing answer diversity. In our ablation studies, mass-matched controls support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and the gains persist after matching the root mean square (RMS) of the advantages to that of centered GRPO. Reasoning-trace diagnostics further show that the diversity gains from StepRS-GRPO extend beyond final-answer strings.

</details>


### [418] [Analysis of Quantized and Efficiently Adapted Protein Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00665)
*Ilan Yaniv Zeisler,Sebastian Clancy,Pouriya Bayat,Saaim Raad,Ivan Kraskov,Matthew Xie,Vivian White,Spencer Perkins,Serena Singh,Sepehr Bayat,Keith Pardee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper evaluates 4-bit quantization and QLoRA (low-rank adapter fine-tuning) across multiple protein language models (PLMs) to assess their computational efficiency and performance retention. The study covers 7 PLMs for prediction tasks and 5 generative models, finding that GPU memory can be reduced by up to 90% while maintaining >90% performance in many cases. The authors recommend QLoRA as a first-pass strategy and emphasize the need for distributional analysis in generative tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protein language models are powerful but computationally expensive, limiting their accessibility. This study addresses the gap in understanding how quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning affect PLM performance, representations, and generation capabilities.

Method: Evaluated 4-bit quantization and QLoRA across 7 PLMs (ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3, Profluent-E1) for prediction tasks and 5 generative models (ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM, ESM3) for unconditional generation. Assessed performance, GPU memory usage, training speed, power effects, and representational changes across layers.

Result: Many model-task pairs retained >90% of full fine-tuning performance. Peak GPU memory savings reached ~90% for largest models. QLoRA preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle/late layers. For generative models, 4-bit quantization largely preserved structural/sequence properties but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions.

Conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization effectively reduce PLM computational requirements, especially GPU memory. QLoRA is recommended as a first-pass strategy for memory-limited adaptation, with full fine-tuning reserved for challenging tasks, unstable architectures, or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented with distributional analysis to detect quantization-induced shifts.

Abstract: Background: Protein language models (PLMs) are increasingly used for sequence generation and property prediction, but their size makes fine-tuning and deployment expensive. The effects of quantization and parameter efficient fine-tuning on performance, representations and generation remain insufficiently characterized. Results: We evaluated 4-bit quantization and low-rank adapter fine-tuning (QLoRA) across ESM-2, ESMC, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3 and Profluent-E1. Across protein prediction tasks, many model-task pairs retained more than 90% of full fine-tuning performance. Peak GPU memory savings approached 90% for the largest models, although performance and efficiency varied by model, dataset and training configuration. QLoRA often preserved early-layer representations while inducing task-specific adaptations in middle and late layers, resembling full fine-tuning with smaller representational changes. Training speed and power effects were more varied. For unconditional generation with ProLLaMA, ProtGPT2, ProGen2, ProteinGLM and ESM3, 4-bit quantization largely preserved predicted structural and sequence-level properties, but token-level analysis revealed model-dependent shifts in autoregressive output distributions. Conclusion: QLoRA and 4-bit quantization reduce PLM computational requirements, particularly GPU memory usage. Our results support QLoRA as a first-pass strategy for memory limited adaptation, reserving full fine-tuning for challenging tasks, unstable architectures or low validation recovery. For generative PLMs, sequence-level and structural metrics should be complemented with distributional analysis, since downstream predictions alone may miss quantization-induced shifts. These approaches can broaden access to large-scale protein modelling while requiring model- and task-specific validation.

</details>


### [419] [ORBIT-FMIB: Tracking Order-Resolved Epistatic Information Through ESM-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00672)
*Maryam Rahimimovassagh,Ivan Garibay,Niloofar Yousefi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework to test whether ESM-2 (a protein foundation model) retains higher-order epistatic information as well as lower-order information. Initial results suggested higher-order information was retained less well, but replication substantially reduced this effect and its sign was unstable across different evaluation methods, leaving the directional question unresolved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protein foundation models support mutation-effect and structural prediction, but it's unclear whether they retain higher-order epistatic information as strongly as first- and second-order information across their representation hierarchy. The authors sought to diagnose this capability.

Method: ORBIT-FMIB combines Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. Validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure, then applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations.

Result: Initial run showed Δ_HO-LO = -0.107 (higher-order retained less well). Replication reduced this to Δ_HO-LO = -0.017, with sign unstable across evaluation-pairing choices (-0.011 to +0.015). No robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information.

Conclusion: The directional question remains open - neither selective loss nor equal retention can be confirmed. The study illustrates the importance of adequately-powered reproducibility checks when probing interaction structure in protein foundation models.

Abstract: Protein foundation models support mutation-effect and structural prediction, but predictive performance alone does not reveal which forms of biological interaction information remain accessible through model depth. We ask whether ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information as strongly as first- and second-order information across its representation hierarchy, introducing ORBIT-FMIB, a diagnostic framework combining Walsh-based interaction decomposition with subset-conditioned neural dependence estimation. The method is validated on synthetic landscapes with known interaction structure before being applied to the dense four-site GB1 fitness landscape using frozen ESM-2 representations.
  An initial production run suggested ESM-2 retains higher-order epistatic information less well than lower-order information ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.107$). An independent replication of the complete measurement grid, under matched GPU hardware and identical critic seeds, substantially reduced this contrast ($Δ_{\mathrm{HO-LO}}=-0.017$), and its sign was unstable across otherwise-defensible evaluation-pairing choices applied to the same trained critics ($-0.011$ to $+0.015$). We therefore do not currently have robust evidence that ESM-2 selectively loses higher-order epistatic information, nor that retention is equal across orders; the directional question remains open. The measurement protocol itself, including its documented removal of a positional-subset shortcut in pooled critics, remains validated and is unaffected by this finding. ORBIT-FMIB is offered as a diagnostic framework for probing interaction structure in protein foundation models; this study's own replication result illustrates why such probing requires adequately-powered reproducibility checks before its output is treated as a biological finding.

</details>


### [420] [LabBook: Harnessing Experimental History for Efficient LLM-Driven Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00675)
*Bo Yuan,Wenqian Ye,Zelin Zhao,Lama Moukheiber,Henry Kautz,Aidong Zhang,Yongxin Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LabBook is a single-agent discovery harness that uses an agent-maintained memory to separate complete experimental history retention from selective context construction, improving quality-cost trade-off in LLM-driven discovery without requiring explicit population or branching search structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evolutionary approaches to LLM-driven discovery face a trade-off: using only selected ancestors keeps contexts manageable but omits useful evidence, while including full experimental history produces long, redundant contexts that are inefficient.

Method: A single-agent discovery harness built around LabBook, an agent-maintained memory serving two complementary roles: (1) guiding retrieval of relevant evidence from a complete experimental log, and (2) informing generation of new solutions. At each iteration, the same agent combines its memory with retrieved evidence to jointly produce the next program and an updated LabBook.

Result: On 49 Frontier-CS problems, LabBook improves the observed quality-cost trade-off over evaluated evolutionary baselines with two backbones, while remaining competitive across nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks.

Conclusion: LabBook successfully separates complete history retention from selective context construction without requiring an explicit population or branching search structure, achieving better quality-cost trade-off while maintaining broad applicability across diverse task domains.

Abstract: Evolutionary approaches to LLM-driven discovery often generate new programs from a small set of selected ancestors. This keeps contexts manageable but can omit useful evidence from other experiments, whereas including the full experimental history produces long, redundant contexts. We introduce a simple, single-agent discovery harness built around LabBook, an agent-maintained memory that serves two complementary roles: guiding retrieval of relevant evidence from a complete experimental log and informing the generation of new solutions. At each iteration, the same agent combines its memory with retrieved evidence and jointly produces the next program and an updated LabBook. This separates complete history retention from selective context construction, without requiring an explicit population or branching search structure. On 49 Frontier-CS problems, LabBook improves the observed quality-cost trade-off over the evaluated evolutionary baselines with two backbones, while remaining competitive across nine additional mathematical, systems, and heuristic-design tasks. Code will be released at https://github.com/BoYuanVisionary/LabBook.

</details>


### [421] [Learning Transferable Skills using Goal-Conditioned Bisimulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00676)
*Mohammad Amin Abbasfar,Farbod Azimmohseni,Mohammad Hossein Rohban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses generalization in unsupervised skill discovery by learning action-aware temporal representations with functional equivariance, combined with bisimulation-based skill learning that focuses on execution-critical state features. This enables skills trained in one layout to transfer to unseen environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current unsupervised skill discovery methods either require expert data or fail to transfer to previously unseen layouts. The core challenge is learning representations that capture temporal structure while remaining robust to environmental variations across different layouts.

Method: Two-part approach: (1) Learning action-aware temporal representations that satisfy functional equivariance while preserving local temporal structure; (2) Unsupervised skill discovery using bisimulation that conditions skills only on state features directly affecting execution, enforcing invariant behavior across layouts.

Result: Skills learned in a given environment can effectively solve downstream tasks in various unseen layouts, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization.

Conclusion: The proposed method successfully enables transferable skills across different environment configurations by focusing on execution-critical state features and leveraging functional equivariance properties in temporal representations.

Abstract: Unsupervised skill discovery has emerged as a promising approach for leveraging reward-free datasets to pretrain general-purpose policies. However, current skill discovery methods either require access to expert data or exhibit limited generalization, failing to transfer effectively to previously unseen layouts. A key challenge is to learn representations that capture the temporal structure of the environment while remaining robust to variations across layouts. To address this issue, we present an objective for learning action-aware temporal representations that satisfy the functional equivariance property while preserving the local temporal structure of the environment. Building upon this embedding, we further propose unsupervised skill discovery using bisimulation, which learns transferable skills by conditioning the behavior of skills exclusively on the subset of state features that directly affect their execution. This enforces invariant behavior across different layouts, enabling skills to transfer effectively to other configurations. Finally, through comprehensive empirical evaluations, we show that skills learned in a given environment can be effectively applied to solve downstream tasks in various environment layouts, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization.

</details>


### [422] [Curvature Under Attack in hZACH-ViT: Gauge Symmetry, Boundary Saturation, and Adversarial Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00680)
*Athanasios Angelakis,Marta Gomez-Barrero*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates how curvature interacts with coordinate scale, logit temperature, and numerical safeguards in Vision Transformers (hZACH-ViT). Using Euclidean, Poincare, and spherical prototype heads across MedMNIST datasets, the authors find that while Poincare embeddings at c=1 show good adversarial robustness, they suffer from lower clean performance and hard boundary clipping. Reducing curvature to c=0.1 improves clean performance but significantly hurts robustness. The study concludes that hyperbolic robustness is not intrinsic but depends on implementation-sensitive factors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Curvature is often treated as an intrinsic property of representation learning, but the authors argue that its empirical effects depend on coordinate scale, learned logit temperature, and numerical safeguards. They aim to disentangle these factors to understand whether hyperbolic (Poincare) embeddings provide inherent robustness advantages.

Method: The authors used hZACH-ViT, a compact Vision Transformer with three prototype heads (Euclidean, Poincare, and spherical). They matched backbone architecture, seed-specific initialization, 50-per-class training subset, and optimization protocol across three MedMNIST datasets and five seeds. They conducted PGD and CE+DLR multi-restart attacks, analyzed hard boundary clipping, radial Jacobian, and dimensionless attack trajectories.

Result: At c=1, Poincare had the lowest PGD attack-success rate in all 12 dataset-budget cells and under stronger CE+DLR attacks, but also the lowest clean MacroF1. Reducing Poincare curvature to c=0.1 improved clean MacroF1 in all 15 paired comparisons but increased attack success on OrganAMNIST from 89.7% to 99.3% (paired difference +9.57 points; 95% CI [+5.52, +14.03]). At c=1, 40-47% of clean Poincare features were hard-clipped, radial Jacobian was nearly zero, and attack trajectories were inefficient. The spherical head served as a control and showed much smaller attack differences.

Conclusion: The results do not establish intrinsic hyperbolic robustness. Instead, they identify an implementation-sensitive regime where curvature, scale, and proximity to the Poincare boundary jointly influence clean recognition and adversarial representation motion. The interplay between these factors is crucial for understanding hyperbolic representation performance.

Abstract: Curvature is often treated as an intrinsic property of a representation, although its empirical effect also depends on coordinate scale, learned logit temperature, and numerical safeguards. We study this interaction in hZACH-ViT, a compact Vision Transformer with Euclidean, Poincare, and spherical prototype heads. The backbone architecture, seed-specific initialization, 50-per-class training subset, and optimization protocol are matched across three MedMNIST datasets and five seeds. At the fixed comparison curvature $c=1$, Poincare has the lowest class-macro PGD attack-success rate in all 12 dataset-budget cells and under a stronger CE+DLR multi-restart attack on all three datasets, but it also has the lowest clean MacroF1. An end-to-end curvature intervention changes the interpretation. Reducing Poincare curvature to $c=0.1$ improves clean MacroF1 in every one of the 15 paired seed-dataset comparisons and removes hard boundary clipping, yet on OrganAMNIST it increases strong attack success from $89.7\%$ to $99.3\%$ (paired difference $+9.57$ points; 95\% hierarchical bootstrap CI $[+5.52,+14.03]$). At $c=1$, $40$-$47\%$ of clean Poincare features are hard-clipped, the radial Jacobian of the inherited map is nearly zero, and dimensionless attack trajectories are unusually long and inefficient. The spherical head provides a control: its curvature change is an exact scale gauge to floating-point precision and produces much smaller attack differences. These results do not establish intrinsic hyperbolic robustness. They identify an implementation-sensitive regime in which curvature, scale, and proximity to the Poincare boundary jointly organize clean recognition and adversarial representation motion.

</details>


### [423] [Grand Canonical Generators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00683)
*Andreas Burger,Malte Franke,Luka Mucko,Kjell Jorner,Alan Aspuru-Guzik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GCG extends Boltzmann generators to the grand canonical ensemble, enabling joint sampling of particle number and configuration conditioned on chemical potential, with two designs: a conditional variable-size model and a factorized approach using existing canonical Boltzmann generators with analytical chemical potential encoding and tractable likelihood supporting self-normalized importance sampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Boltzmann generators are powerful for sampling canonical ensembles but are limited to fixed particle numbers. Many physical and chemical systems (e.g., adsorption, phase equilibria) require the grand canonical ensemble where particle number fluctuates based on chemical potential. This work addresses the need to extend generative models to handle variable particle numbers while maintaining physical accuracy and computational efficiency.

Method: Two complementary designs: (1) A conditional approach that directly conditions a variable-size generative model on chemical potential, enabling joint sampling of particle number and configuration. (2) A factorized approach that decomposes the grand canonical distribution into a particle-number distribution and canonical Boltzmann density, allowing integration with existing Boltzmann generators while analytically encoding chemical potential dependence and supporting self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS).

Result: Empirical validation on two test systems: (1) Lennard-Jones fluid - accurate reproduction of grand canonical observables across different chemical potentials. (2) Methane adsorption in a zeolite - demonstrated generalization across chemical potentials and effective correction via SNIS and grand canonical Monte Carlo.

Conclusion: GCG successfully extends Boltzmann generators to the grand canonical ensemble, providing a principled framework for variable-particle-number systems. The factorized formulation offers particular advantages by leveraging existing canonical models and enabling rigorous importance sampling. The method shows strong empirical performance on both simple fluids and complex adsorption problems, suggesting broad applicability in computational chemistry and materials science.

Abstract: We introduce Grand Canonical Generators (GCG), a generative framework that extends Boltzmann generators to the grand canonical ensemble. We present two designs. The first conditions a variable-size generative model on the chemical potential, sampling particle number and configuration jointly. The second factorizes the grand canonical distribution into a particle-number distribution and the corresponding canonical Boltzmann density. This factorized formulation can use any existing Boltzmann generator for the canonical component, encodes the known linear chemical-potential dependence analytically, and yields a tractable likelihood that supports self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS). Empirically, GCG accurately reproduces grand canonical observables on a Lennard--Jones fluid and methane adsorption in a zeolite, demonstrating generalization across chemical potentials and correction via SNIS and grand canonical Monte Carlo.

</details>


### [424] [SkillSpec: Consensus-Gated Agent Skill Evolution via Representation Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00704)
*Huancheng Chen,Xiaodi Sun,Zhaoqiong Huang,Shenyang Huang Shreya Singhal,Jingwen Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SkillSpec is a two-phase framework for optimizing natural-language skills (textual procedural memories) in LLM agents. It combines consensus-gated evolution (requiring paired evaluations to reach consensus before committing updates) with representation specialization (selecting flat, graph, or hybrid representations based on optimization trajectory signals). The method improves average success rate by 6.89% over SkillOpt across six benchmarks and three language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing methods treat skills as static artifacts or monolithic documents optimized using aggregate validation scores. This restricts optimization to textual content without modeling the structure through which procedural knowledge is retrieved and executed. The key insight is distinguishing between what knowledge to retain and how to organize it—textual updates should be validated through execution evidence before structuring retained knowledge according to procedural dependencies and retrieval requirements.

Method: SkillSpec employs a two-phase approach: (1) Consensus-gated evolution: complementary editing intents generate candidate skills; updates are committed only when paired evaluations reach consensus, requiring sufficient overall improvement and non-negative aggregate paired gain in every repeated evaluation. (2) Representation specialization: signals of process and redundancy sensitivity derived from the full optimization trajectory (including accepted and rejected candidates) guide selection of flat, graph, or hybrid representation.

Result: SkillSpec improves average success rate over SkillOpt by 6.89%, averaged across three target language models, evaluated on six benchmarks.

Conclusion: Reliable skill evolution and representation specialization address complementary objectives: deciding what knowledge to retain and how to structure it for inference. The two-phase approach effectively separates the validation of textual content from the organization of retained knowledge, leading to consistent performance improvements.

Abstract: Natural-language skills are textual procedural memories through which large language model (LLM) agents retain reusable task knowledge without updating model weights. Existing methods typically treat skills as either static artifacts or monolithic documents optimized using aggregate validation scores as feedback. However, representing a skill as a monolithic document restricts optimization to its textual content, without explicitly modeling the structure through which procedural knowledge is retrieved and executed. We identify a key distinction between learning what knowledge to retain and determining how to organize it: textual updates should first be validated through execution evidence, after which the retained knowledge should be structured according to its procedural dependencies and retrieval requirements. To this end, we introduce SkillSpec, a two-phase framework comprising consensus-gated evolution and representation specialization. In the consensus-gated phase, complementary editing intents generate complete candidate skills.
