An update is committed only when paired evaluations reach consensus, requiring sufficient overall improvement and non-negative aggregate paired gain in every repeated evaluation. In the specialization phase, signals of process and redundancy sensitivity derived from the full optimization trajectory, including accepted and rejected candidates, guide the selection of a flat, graph, or hybrid representation.Across six benchmarks and three target language models, SkillSpec improves average success rate over SkillOpt by 6.89%, averaged across the three models. These results demonstrate that reliable skill evolution and representation specialization address complementary objectives: deciding what knowledge to retain and how to structure it for inference.

</details>


### [425] [Initialization Improves LLM-Driven Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00707)
*Mansi Sakarvadia,Marco Ciccone,Colin Raffel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies how harness design affects LLM-driven discovery (algorithms, theorems, drugs). The authors developed 12 Modular harnesses and tested them across 5 tasks, finding discovery success is brittle and sensitive to design choices. Mode collapse (loss of iterate diversity) is a common failure mode. Popular harnesses and diversity interventions yield inconsistent results. However, early discovery performance predicts eventual success.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand why LLM-driven discovery success is inconsistent and to develop better harness designs that improve success rates. The authors aim to generalize past work on harness design and characterize performance across diverse discovery tasks.

Method: The authors developed a suite of 12 harnesses called 'Modular' and characterized their performance across 5 diverse discovery tasks. They studied mode collapse as a failure mode and tested various diversity-inducing interventions.

Result: Discovery success is brittle and sensitive to harness design. Mode collapse (dramatic drop in iterate diversity) is a common failure. Popular state-of-the-art harnesses and diversity interventions yield inconsistent gains. Early discovery performance is predictive of eventual success.

Conclusion: The authors propose a universally applicable intervention using initial parallel exploration to initialize subsequent iterative optimization. This method provides consistent gains across many harnesses and target applications, confirming the importance of initialization in LLM-driven discovery.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been used for novel discovery of algorithms, theorems, drugs, and other tasks through the use of harnesses that prompt an LLM to iteratively optimize an objective. In this work, we study the relationship between the population of previous iterates and eventual discovery success. We generalize past work on harness design to develop a suite of 12 harnesses called 'Modular' and characterize their performance across 5 diverse discovery tasks, finding that discovery success is brittle and sensitive to harness design. We uncover mode collapse, characterized by a dramatic drop in the diversity of iterates, as a common failure mode. We find that popular state-of-the-art harnesses and diversity-inducing harness interventions, which aim to prolong this collapse, yield inconsistent gains. Our results instead uncover that the performance of early discoveries is predictive of eventual success. We therefore propose a universally applicable intervention that performs an initial stage of parallel exploration in order to initialize subsequent iterative optimization. Our method provides consistent gains across many harnesses and target applications, confirming the importance of initialization in LLM-driven discovery.

</details>


### [426] [Beyond Unimodal Bases: Pullback Geometry for Multimodal Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00708)
*Honglei Brinkmann,Lucas Ng,Georgios Batzolis,Mark Girolami,Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb,Willem Diepeveen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces a pullback Riemannian geometry for multimodal data supported on mixtures of manifolds, extending scalable geometric representations beyond single-manifold assumptions. The method uses a latent Gaussian mixture with a responsibility-weighted expected component precision metric, and is implemented in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing scalable pullback geometries assume unimodal Gaussian latent distributions, which fails for multimodal data. Mapping separated modes into one Gaussian region causes substantial transport deformation and compromises geometry. The authors seek to create geometric representations that traverse high-likelihood regions for multimodal data.

Method: 1) Define Riemannian metric as matrix square of responsibility-weighted expected component precision from Gaussian mixture latent distribution
2) For structured overlapping mixtures, establish conditions for log-density concavity along geodesics
3) Instantiate in normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning to allow number of components to emerge from data

Result: Experiments on synthetic geometric data, controlled multi-view image setting with known reference trajectory, and MNIST demonstrate: reduced transport distortion, competitive path support, close reference-trajectory recovery, and improved interpolation realism.

Conclusion: The proposed geometry extends scalable pullback geometry beyond single-manifold datasets while retaining tractable and interpretable local structure. It successfully handles multimodal data without requiring substantial transport deformation.

Abstract: Data-driven Riemannian geometry provides nonlinear interpolation and geometric representations of high-dimensional data. For these operations to be statistically meaningful, paths between observations should preferentially traverse high-likelihood regions. Existing scalable pullback constructions typically use a unimodal Gaussian latent distribution, assuming that the data reside close to a single manifold. For multimodal data, mapping separated modes or local structures into one Gaussian region can require substantial transport deformation and compromise the resulting geometry.
  We introduce a pullback geometry for data supported on mixtures of manifolds. Using a latent Gaussian mixture, we define its Riemannian metric as the matrix square of the responsibility-weighted expected component precision. The metric is smooth and positive definite and recovers the existing Gaussian construction in the single-component limit. For structured overlapping mixtures, we establish conditions under which the log-density is concave along geodesics, providing a formal connection between the proposed geometry and paths through high-likelihood regions, and derive the corresponding local curvature relations.
  We instantiate this geometry in a normalizing flow with adaptive mixture learning, allowing the number of active components to emerge from the data and supporting component-wise reconstruction and local effective-dimension estimation. Experiments on synthetic geometric data, a controlled multi-view image setting with a known reference trajectory, and MNIST show reduced transport distortion, competitive path support, close reference-trajectory recovery, and improved interpolation realism. These results extend scalable pullback geometry beyond datasets that reside close to a single manifold while retaining tractable and interpretable local structure.

</details>


### [427] [WOMBAT: Whitebox Oracle for Molecular Benchmarking and Attribution Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00713)
*Dominik Matuszek,Bartosz Zieliński,Tomasz Danel,Dawid Rymarczyk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WOMBAT is a benchmark of 14 whitebox GNNs with handcrafted message-passing weights designed to detect specific SMARTS motifs. It provides attribution ground truth to distinguish between when GNN explainers fail versus when models learn shortcuts, addressing a critical gap in evaluating explainability methods for molecular graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When GNN explainers produce unexpected attributions, it's unclear whether the explainer failed or the model learned a shortcut. Existing benchmarks lack ground truth about model decision rules, making it impossible to diagnose explainer errors. The authors needed a way to systematically evaluate whether explainers correctly identify the actual reasoning behind model predictions.

Method: The authors constructed 14 whitebox GNN models with known decision rules by manually setting message-passing weights to detect specific SMARTS motifs. They validated these models on millions of PubChem molecules and evaluated post-hoc explainers (GNNExplainer, PGExplainer, Integrated Gradients) against the known ground truth. They also constructed a model that causes Integrated Gradients to spread attribution incorrectly.

Result: The benchmark successfully identifies explainer errors by comparing attributions against known decision rules. The authors demonstrated a case where Integrated Gradients spreads attribution across the graph even though the model reliably detects the intended motif, revealing a failure mode of that explainer.

Conclusion: WOMBAT provides a valuable benchmark for evaluating GNN explainers by providing ground truth about model decision rules. This enables researchers to better understand explainer failures and develop more reliable XAI tools for GNNs in molecular applications. The dataset, models, and evaluation code are released to support future research.

Abstract: When a graph neural network (GNN) explainer produces an unexpected attribution on a molecule, the attribution alone cannot reveal whether the explainer has failed or the model has learned a shortcut. We introduce WOMBAT, a benchmark of 14 whitebox GNNs, each with message-passing weights set by hand to detect a specific SMARTS motif. Each model's decision rule is known by construction, providing attribution ground truth against which explainer errors can be identified and studied. We validate the models on millions of PubChem molecules and evaluate post-hoc explainers including GNNExplainer, PGExplainer, and Integrated Gradients. Guided by our qualitative analysis, we construct a model that causes Integrated Gradients to spread attribution across the graph, even though the model reliably detects the intended motif. We release the dataset, models, and evaluation code to help researchers in the development of newer XAI tools for GNNs.

</details>


### [428] [JEPA-TTT: Persistent Test-Time Training of Latent World Models for Planning under Dynamics Shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00722)
*Zheyuan Zhang,Suyu Ye,Nakul Agarwal,Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub,Ehsan Moradi Pari,Daniel Khashabi,Tianmin Shu,Vaishnav Tadiparthi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: JEPA-TTT is a method that adapts a pretrained action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model during test time to handle dynamics shifts. It uses self-supervised updates on the latent dynamics predictor while keeping the visual encoder and reward head fixed, employing dense replay to form prediction windows at every temporal offset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: World models enable agents to plan by predicting future states, but their predictions become unreliable when test-time dynamics differ from training dynamics. This is a critical problem for deploying agents in real-world scenarios where environment dynamics may change.

Method: JEPA-TTT adapts the latent dynamics predictor of a pretrained action-conditioned JEPA world model throughout test time using self-supervised updates. The visual encoder and reward head remain fixed to preserve pretrained representations and task objectives. The method uses dense replay, which forms prediction windows at every temporal offset, retains them in a growing buffer, and samples minibatches for predictor updates. Planning requires no goal image or online environment reward.

Result: Across eight dynamics shifts in four continuous-control environments, JEPA-TTT improves planning on every shift. After 500 test-time episodes, it reduces autoregressive latent prediction error by 83% on average and improves planning performance by 153% over the frozen JEPA world model.

Conclusion: Persistent self-supervised test-time training can effectively adapt a pretrained latent world model under changed dynamics, demonstrating that JEPA-TTT successfully bridges the gap between training and test-time environment dynamics.

Abstract: World models enable agents to plan by predicting future states of the environment, but their predictions can become unreliable when test-time dynamics differ from those seen during training. We present JEPA-TTT, which adapts the latent dynamics predictor of a pretrained action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture world model throughout test time. Self-supervised updates accumulate across episodes, while the visual encoder and reward head remain fixed, preserving the pretrained representation and task objective. Planning requires neither a goal image nor online environment reward. JEPA-TTT uses dense replay, which forms prediction windows at every temporal offset, retains them in a growing buffer, and samples minibatches from that buffer for predictor updates. Across eight dynamics shifts in four continuous-control environments, JEPA-TTT improves planning on every shift. After 500 test-time episodes, it reduces autoregressive latent prediction error by 83% on average and improves planning performance by 153% over the frozen JEPA world model. These results show that persistent self-supervised test-time training can adapt a pretrained latent world model under changed dynamics.

</details>


### [429] [Benchmarking Generative Models for Weather Data Assimilation on Real Station Observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00728)
*Ruizhe Huang,Qidong Yang,Jonathan Giezendanner,Sherrie Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first controlled benchmark evaluating generative AI models for weather data assimilation on real NOAA weather station observations. It compares major design choices (diffusion vs flow matching, pixel vs latent-space, conditioning strategies) against 3D-Var baseline, finding that learned generative priors outperform Gaussian priors (35.7% vs 33.3% RMSE reduction), full-gradient guidance is most effective, while other choices like diffusion vs flow matching show minimal difference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weather reanalysis currently relies on computationally intensive numerical weather predictions followed by data assimilation. Deep generative models offer a cheaper alternative, but existing approaches have only been evaluated on synthetic data or under inconsistent evaluation schemes, making it unclear which design choices actually improve real-world data assimilation performance.

Method: The authors conducted the first controlled benchmark using 11,849 NOAA MADIS stations across the contiguous United States with four weather variables. They held dataset, observation operator, and deep learning architecture fixed while comparing major design choices: diffusion versus flow matching, pixel versus latent-space formulations, and multiple inference-time conditioning strategies (full-gradient guidance vs stop-gradient vs initial-noise optimization). They evaluated against a classical 3D-Var baseline in both dense and sparse station settings.

Result: Three key findings emerged: (1) Learned generative priors outperform the Gaussian prior of 3D-Var (35.7% vs 33.3% RMSE reduction over ERA5) despite using no ERA5 background field at inference; (2) Full-gradient guidance consistently outperforms stop-gradient and initial-noise optimization; (3) Other choices provide minimal benefit - diffusion and flow matching perform nearly identically, and latent-space variable mixing does not help. The advantages from generative AI and full-gradient guidance are more pronounced under sparse station conditions.

Conclusion: This work identifies which components of generative weather data assimilation actually improve performance on real station observations: learned generative priors and full-gradient guidance are the key effective components. The study establishes a standardized benchmark for future work and demonstrates that generative AI approaches can outperform classical 3D-Var methods, particularly in challenging sparse observation scenarios.

Abstract: Weather reanalysis products rely on computationally intensive numerical weather predictions followed by data assimilation that corrects the forecast toward observations. Deep generative models offer a cheaper alternative that shifts much of this cost from inference to offline training. However, existing generative approaches have been evaluated on synthetic observations or under different datasets and evaluation schemes, making it unclear which design choices actually improve real-world data assimilation. We present the first controlled benchmark of generative weather data assimilation on real weather station observations. Using 11,849 NOAA MADIS stations across the contiguous United States and four weather variables, we evaluate methods while holding the dataset, observation operator, and deep learning architecture fixed. The benchmark compares the major design choices, including diffusion versus flow matching, pixel versus latent-space formulations, and multiple inference-time conditioning strategies, against a classical 3D-Var baseline. The benchmark reveals three clear conclusions. First, learned generative priors outperform the Gaussian prior of 3D-Var (35.7% vs. 33.3% RMSE reduction over ERA5) despite using no ERA5 background field at inference. Second, full-gradient guidance consistently outperforms stop-gradient and initial-noise optimization. Third, other choices provide little measurable benefit: diffusion and flow matching perform nearly identically under matched conditions, and latent-space variable mixing does not help. We further evaluate both dense and sparse station settings and find advantages from generative AI and full-gradient guidance more pronounced under sparsity. Together, these results identify which components of generative weather data assimilation improve performance on real station observations and establish a standardized benchmark for future work.

</details>


### [430] [Reward as Observation: Learning Reward-Based Policies for Rapid Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00729)
*Morgan Byrd,Maks Sorokin,Robert Wright,Sehoon Ha*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reward-based policy for zero-shot transfer between environments with completely different observation spaces. The policy is conditioned only on rewards and actions, enabling adaptation to new environments without requiring sample-intensive retraining. The approach is demonstrated across multiple environments (Pointmass, Cartpole, 2D Car Racing) and transferred to diverse observations including different color palettes, 3D rendering, and robot navigation in Habitat-Sim.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the observation that while humans demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies struggle to adapt to new environments and require substantial samples for successful transfer. The key challenge is achieving zero-shot transfer when source and target environments have completely different observation spaces.

Method: The authors propose a novel reward-based policy conditioned only on rewards and actions (rather than observations). They discuss the challenges and feasibility of such an approach and develop a practical training algorithm. The method enables zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations.

Result: The paper demonstrates that: (1) a reward policy can be trained within three different environments (Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing); (2) the trained policy can be transferred to completely different observations (different color palettes, 3D rendering, Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim) in a zero-shot manner; (3) the reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.

Conclusion: The proposed reward-based policy approach provides a viable solution for zero-shot transfer across environments with radically different observation spaces. This work bridges the gap between human-like adaptation capabilities and machine learning policies, with potential applications in sim-to-real transfer and multi-environment generalization.

Abstract: This paper explores a reward-based policy to achieve zero-shot transfer between source and target environments with completely different observation spaces. While humans can demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies often struggle to adapt to a new environment and require a considerable amount of samples for successful transfer. Instead, we propose a novel reward-based policy only conditioned on rewards and actions, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations. We discuss the challenges and feasibility of a reward-based policy and then propose a practical algorithm for training. We demonstrate that a reward policy can be trained within three different environments, Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing, and transferred to completely different observations, such as different color palettes or 3D rendering, or Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim, in a zero-shot manner. We also demonstrate that a reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.

</details>


### [431] [Reformulation-Contrastive Learning for Mixed Integer Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00730)
*Ousema Bouaneni,Mathis Le Bail,Clément Elliker,Maël Jenny,Sonia Vanier*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces ReMILP, a self-supervised learning framework that leverages MILP reformulations (integrality-preserving variable changes and redundant constraints) to learn general-purpose representations of MILP variables and constraints. The method uses graph neural networks and hypernetworks to predict how variable embeddings transform under changes of variables, without requiring solver-derived labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MILPs model many real-world decision problems, but solving them is computationally expensive. The authors aim to exploit recurring structure to accelerate MILP solving by learning useful representations. The key insight is that MILPs admit many equivalent formulations, and these reformulations can serve as a source of self-supervision for representation learning.

Method: The paper characterizes valid affine reformulations (distinguishing re-descriptions from substitutions), then builds on equivariant self-supervised learning to propose ReMILP. This framework jointly trains a graph neural network (for encoding MILP structure) and a hypernetwork (for predicting variable embedding transformations under changes of variables). The learned representations are designed to be invariant to re-descriptions and equivariant to substitutions.

Result: ReMILP learns representations that exhibit the intended invariance and equivariance properties on unseen problem classes without solver-derived labels. Across three downstream tasks (binary solution prediction, constraint activity prediction, and integrality gap prediction), these frozen representations carry task-relevant information and provide useful initialization for fine-tuning.

Conclusion: The self-supervised approach using MILP reformulations is effective for learning general-purpose representations. The learned representations transfer well to unseen problem classes and improve performance on various MILP prediction tasks, demonstrating the potential of leveraging mathematical structure for representation learning in optimization.

Abstract: Mixed-integer linear programs (MILP) model many real-world decision problems, motivating machine-learning methods that exploit recurring structure to accelerate MILP solving. MILPs can admit many equivalent formulations: integrality-preserving changes of variables and the addition of redundant constraints can alter their formulations while preserving the optimization problem. We leverage these reformulations as a source of self-supervision for learning general-purpose representations of MILP variables and constraints. We characterize the affine reformulations that are valid for every input instance, and distinguish re-descriptions, which leave variables unchanged, from substitutions, which transform them predictably. Building on equivariant self-supervised learning, we introduce ReMILP (reformulation-contrastive MILP representation learning), which jointly trains a graph neural network and a hypernetwork to predict how variable embeddings transform under changes of variables. Without solver-derived labels, ReMILP learns representations that exhibit the intended invariance and equivariance on unseen problem classes. Across binary solution, constraint activity and integrality gap prediction, these representations carry task-relevant information when frozen and provide a useful initialization for fine-tuning.

</details>


### [432] [Signal-Noise Factorization Isolates Nuisance Variation into Removable Subspaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00751)
*Sakin Kirti,Joel Zylberberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces two geometric regularizers (SNF and SSF) to shape representation geometry in deep neural networks. SNF regularization improves performance on CIFAR-100 and BloodMNIST with corruptions, while SSF shows no benefit. SNF models isolate noise in separate subspaces, allowing projection-based corruption removal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding how representation geometry affects neural network inference ability, particularly for handling out-of-distribution distortions in biomedical applications.

Method: Built regularizers enforcing Signal-Noise Factorization (SNF) and Signal-Signal Factorization (SSF) during training. Tested on CIFAR-100 and BloodMNIST with MedMNIST-C corruptions. Analyzed nuisance subspaces and performed projection-based corruption removal.

Result: SNF regularization improved model performance on both tasks, with larger gains on corrupted biomedical data. SSF regularization provided no improvement. SNF models represent noise in distinct subspaces, enabling projection-based corruption removal that substantially boosted accuracy.

Conclusion: Regularizers enforcing signal-noise factorization produce significant improvements on vision tasks with out-of-distribution distortions. Isolating nuisance variables from categorical ones is more important than maintaining factorized representations of categorical variables.

Abstract: Recent theoretical work identified fundamental properties of representation geometry that shape inference ability of deep neural networks. These include signal-noise factorization (SNF), the ability to segregate signal from noise, and signal-signal factorization (SSF), the ability to segregate task-specific and task-irrelevant signals. Here, we built regularizers that reinforce these two properties during training. We compared networks trained with these regularizers to $L_2$-regularized baseline networks on the CIFAR-100 classification task to understand how our regularizers shape representation geometry and impact performance on a well-known computer vision baseline. Enhancing SNF via regularization improved model performance but enhancing SSF did not. Motivated by biomedical applications, we investigated how our regularizers affected performance on the BloodMNIST dataset treated with MedMNIST-C corruptions at five severity levels, and found even larger performance gains using the SNF regularizer. To understand the mechanism by which SNF-regularization produces improved performance, we analyzed the nuisance subspaces across regularization regimes, finding that the SNF-regularized models represent noise in distinct subspaces, separate from class-relevant signal. Because this geometry is explicit, the dominant corruption-induced directions can be estimated on held-out data and projected out of the representations. This manipulation led to a substantial gain in accuracy. These results show that regularizers that enforce signal-noise factorization can produce substantial improvements on computer vision tasks that contain out-of-distribution image distortions at inference time. They also highlight how shaping representations affects model performance: isolating nuisance variables from categorical ones is more important than maintaining factorized representations of categorical variables.

</details>


### [433] [Increasing Width Allows Greedy Layer-wise Training to Rival End-to-End Backpropagation in Self-Supervised Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00753)
*Syon Mansur,Joel Zylberberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates how network width and depth affect the performance of greedy layer-wise training versus end-to-end backpropagation in self-supervised learning. The key finding is that width compensates for restricted credit assignment: in wider networks, the performance gap between greedy and end-to-end training shrinks, and in some cases, greedy training actually outperforms end-to-end training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the conditions under which locally optimized networks (avoiding end-to-end backpropagation) can learn representations comparable to end-to-end training, particularly in the context of self-supervised learning for large-scale pretraining.

Method: The authors conducted experiments comparing greedy layer-wise and end-to-end self-supervised training across convolutional networks with varying widths and depths. They analyzed the representational geometry of the learned representations.

Result: In wider networks, the benefits of end-to-end backpropagation over greedy layer-wise training diminish. In relatively shallow but very wide networks, greedy layer-wise training even achieved higher performance than end-to-end training. Analysis showed that wide greedy-trained networks exhibit more favorable representational geometry than end-to-end trained networks.

Conclusion: Width can compensate for restricted credit assignment in greedy layer-wise training. Differences in representational geometry represent a potential mechanism for the improved performance of wide greedy-trained networks. This work identifies architectural conditions where simpler training mechanisms can match or exceed end-to-end backpropagation.

Abstract: End-to-end backpropagation has been the dominant mode of training in deep learning, allowing for the coordination of parameter updates across layers of a neural network. Prior studies have explored alternative -- and, in some cases, simpler -- training mechanisms, showing that they can sometimes achieve performance similar to backpropagation. However, the architectural conditions under which locally optimized networks, which avoid end-to-end backpropagation of error, can learn representations comparable to those learned through end-to-end training remain unclear. We aim to answer this question in the context of self-supervised learning, an important framework for large-scale pretraining in artificial intelligence. Here, we investigate how network width and depth affect the efficacy of greedy layer-wise and end-to-end self-supervised training in convolutional networks. We find that in wider networks, the benefits of end-to-end backpropagation over greedy layer-wise training shrink: in relatively shallow and very wide networks, we even observed higher performance in models trained with greedy layer-wise training. Subsequent analysis of the representations formed by these networks shows that very wide greedy-trained networks exhibit more favorable representational geometry than do networks trained end-to-end with backpropagation. This work shows that width can compensate for restricted credit assignment and identifies differences in representational geometry as a potential mechanism for their improved performance.

</details>


### [434] [Scalable Multi-Task Inverse Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00758)
*Allen Tran,Jia Wan,Nathan Kallus,Aurélien Bibaut*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Multi-task inverse reinforcement learning method that learns transferable rewards across multiple agents by leveraging a low-rank assumption, reducing coverage requirements and computational cost while enabling policy transfer to new environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current IRL methods face strict coverage requirements where target environments must cover all relevant state occupancies. Additionally, per-task planning becomes computationally expensive as the number of tasks grows. The goal is to develop a method that alleviates coverage requirements and offers scalable evaluation across multiple tasks.

Method: Proposes a multi-task IRL method that pools data across multiple agents with different rewards in the same environment under a low-rank assumption. This approach allows each task to not need full state coverage as long as other tasks cover those states. The computational complexity scales with rank rather than the number of tasks.

Result: The method provides finite sample guarantees on reward recovery and on policy learning in new environments. Experiments demonstrate: (1) robustness to limited coverage, (2) ability to recover rewards both on and off each task's support, (3) transfers to target environments with lower regret than baselines, (4) computational advantage that widens as the number of tasks increases.

Conclusion: The proposed multi-task IRL method successfully addresses coverage limitations and computational scalability in IRL. By leveraging low-rank structure across tasks, it enables efficient reward learning and policy transfer with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance compared to baseline approaches.

Abstract: By learning transferable rewards, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) enables counterfactual evaluation of agents under modified environments. Such transfer places strict requirements on coverage since target environments affect agents' state occupancy. We propose a multi-task IRL method that pools data across multiple agents with different rewards in the same environment under a low-rank assumption. In addition to alleviating coverage requirements, so each task need not visit every state as long as others do, the method offers scalable evaluation of multiple tasks under new environments as computationally intensive planning scales with rank rather than the number of tasks. We provide finite sample guarantees on reward recovery and on policy learning in new environments. Experiments show our method is robust to limited coverage, recovers rewards on and off of each task's support, transfers to target environments at lower regret than baselines, with its computational advantage over per-task methods widening as tasks grow.

</details>


### [435] [Pre-training interventions, ex post facto: Grafting model beliefs across checkpoints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00767)
*Peter Nutter,Dani Roytburg,Clément Dumas,Jinghua Ou,Shi Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "grafting," a method to apply synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF) interventions at the pre-training stage while reusing existing post-trained models. The approach trains an SDF adapter on the pre-trained checkpoint, then grafts the learned weights onto the post-trained model, addressing the "reality drift" problem where models treated fabricated entities as real when SDF is applied post-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to solve the inefficiency in alignment research where pre-training corpus changes require full post-training runs to measure effects. Current practice applies SDF to already post-trained models, which leaves artifacts, degrades capabilities, and causes "reality drift" - treating fabricated entities unrelated to training documents as real.

Method: The proposed "grafting" method works in two steps: (1) train the SDF adapter on the pre-trained checkpoint, then (2) add the learned weight update to the post-trained model. This approximates the faithful approach of applying SDF during pre/mid-training while reusing existing post-training. Experiments were conducted across model families up to 284B parameters, including installing false facts, training misaligned model organisms, and applying constitutional mid-training intervention.

Result: Grafting installs target beliefs as strongly as SDF on post-trained models while reducing both reality drift and loss of preference coherence by more than half on average. It also stays closer to a faithful mid-training run. The method enables rapid iteration on pre-training interventions at the cost of a single fine-tuning run, as the same adapter can be applied to any later checkpoint.

Conclusion: Grafting provides an effective solution for applying pre-training interventions without requiring full post-training runs. It significantly reduces reality drift and capability degradation compared to post-training SDF, while maintaining the target belief installation effectiveness. This enables researchers to iterate quickly on alignment interventions at minimal computational cost.

Abstract: Pre-training interventions are critical to alignment research, since beliefs formed during pre-training shape how a model generalizes from later training. One recently popular technique for such interventions is synthetic document fine-tuning (SDF), which aims to alter what the model believes. Ideally, synthetic documents would be mixed into pre- or mid-training, but every change to a pre-training corpus must be followed by a full post-training run before its effect can be measured, making iteration slow and expensive. Common practice instead applies SDF to an already post-trained model. This is known to leave artifacts and degrade capabilities, and, as we show, it makes the model treat fabricated entities unrelated to the documents as real, a failure we call reality drift. We propose grafting: train the SDF adapter on the pre-trained checkpoint, then add the learned weight update to the post-trained model, which approximates the faithful approach while reusing the existing post-training. We demonstrate this by installing false facts, training misaligned model organisms and applying a constitutional mid-training intervention, across model families up to 284B parameters. Grafting installs the target belief as strongly as SDF on the post-trained model while reducing both reality drift and the loss of preference coherence by more than half on average, and it stays closer to a faithful mid-training run. Because grafting requires no post-training, the same adapter can be applied to any later checkpoint, enabling researchers to iterate quickly on pre-training interventions at the cost of a single fine-tuning run.

</details>


### [436] [Localizing Transfer Between Memorization Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00771)
*Yimiao Yu,Florentin Guth*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the mechanisms underlying transfer learning by examining transfer between memorization tasks of random input-output mappings. The authors discover two surprising transfer patterns: equivalent transfer (each pre-training epoch saves approximately one fine-tuning epoch) and non-equivalent transfer (pre-training on mismatched tasks can outperform direct training on the target task). Through ablation experiments, they decompose transfer into two components: a "trivial" magnitude-driven effect in the last layer and a "non-trivial" structure-driven effect attributable to the covariance of other layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The central puzzle in transfer learning is understanding why pre-training on one task accelerates training or improves performance on another task, and what mechanisms underlie this transfer. The authors aim to decompose and localize these transfer effects to advance understanding of transfer learning mechanisms.

Method: The authors conduct experiments using memorization tasks of random input-output mappings. They perform ablation experiments to decompose and localize the transfer effects into separate components.

Result: Two surprising transfer patterns were discovered: (1) Equivalent transfer - each additional pre-training epoch saves approximately one downstream fine-tuning epoch; (2) Non-equivalent transfer - pre-training on a mismatched task can be more efficient than directly training on the downstream task. The transfer was decomposed into two effects: a "trivial" magnitude-driven transfer in the last layer, and a "non-trivial" structure-driven transfer partially attributable to the covariance of other layers.

Conclusion: Transfer learning effects can be decomposed into trivial (magnitude-driven) and non-trivial (structure-driven) components. The non-trivial transfer is partially attributable to the covariance of layers other than the last layer. These findings advance understanding of transfer learning mechanisms and have potential to guide principled pre-training strategies.

Abstract: A central puzzle in transfer learning is why pre-training on one task can accelerate training or improve performance on another task, and what mechanisms underlie this transfer. In this work, we examine the transfer between memorization tasks of random input-output mappings. We find two surprising transfer patterns: equivalent transfer, where each additional pre-training epoch saves approximately one downstream fine-tuning epoch; and non-equivalent transfer, where pre-training on a mismatched task can be even more efficient than directly training on the downstream task itself. Through ablation experiments, we decompose and localize the transfer into two separate effects: a "trivial" magnitude-driven transfer in the last layer, and a "non-trivial" structure-driven transfer, partially attributable to the covariance of the other layers. These results advance our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of transfer learning and have the potential to lead to principled pre-training strategies.

</details>


### [437] [Learning Goal-Reaching Quasimetric Geometry From Finite-Time Reachability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00778)
*Daisuke Yamada,Travis Pence,Vikas Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReQRL is a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning method that uses finite-horizon reachability to constrain value gradients in quasimetric learning, decoupling dynamical reachability from boundary geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing quasimetric approaches in GCRL use local constraints that fail to capture direction-dependent effects of control composition over finite horizons and environmental feasibility. A method that properly incorporates these aspects was needed.

Method: ReQRL constrains the critic's value gradients through finite-horizon reachability, drawing on state-constrained optimal control. It decouples dynamical reachability from boundary geometry and estimates both from data.

Result: On OGBench benchmark, ReQRL outperforms or rivals existing quasimetric approaches and other offline GCRL methods.

Conclusion: The proposed finite-horizon reachability constraint effectively improves goal-conditioned RL by properly modeling direction-dependent control costs and environmental feasibility, demonstrating superior performance on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: In goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL), quasimetric learning models goal-reaching costs as quasimetric distances, connecting local constraints to global value geometry. Its local constraints, however, should reflect the direction- dependent effects of control composition over a finite horizon together with environmental feasibility. We propose ReQRL, which constrains the critic's value gradients through finite-horizon reachability. Drawing on state-constrained optimal control, we decouple dynamical reachability from boundary geometry, estimating both from data. On OGBench, our method outperforms or rivals existing quasimetric approaches and other offline GCRL methods.

</details>


### [438] [Training-Aware Target Coverage for Synthetic Data Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00814)
*Yang Ba,Michelle V. Mancenido,Rong Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of determining when and how much synthetic data should be used for LLM training. The authors develop a linear theory to characterize the tradeoff between beneficial information and synthetic errors, and introduce TATC (Training-Aware Target Coverage), a method that selects synthetic data by identifying candidates whose training effects benefit the target task while expanding coverage of underrepresented target-relevant directions. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks show TATC outperforms alternative selection methods on GSM8K.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic data is increasingly used to scale LLM training, but more synthetic data does not necessarily produce better models. The key challenge is that useful synthetic data must add information relevant to the target task without introducing errors that offset their benefit. Additionally, the value of an example can change as the training set grows, making it difficult to determine when synthetic data is useful, how much should be added, and what the marginal value of adding one example is.

Method: The authors develop a linear theory that characterizes the tradeoff between the benefits of relevant information and the costs of synthetic errors. This theory determines where synthetic data are useful, how much should be added, and the marginal value of adding one example. Based on this theory, they introduce Training-Aware Target Coverage (TATC), a synthetic data selection method for LLM fine-tuning that identifies candidates whose training effects are beneficial to the target task and selects among them to expand coverage of target-relevant directions not already represented by available data.

Result: Experiments on text and image data verify the linear theory. With mathematical reasoning tasks, TATC selects synthetic solutions for fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and outperforms alternative synthetic-data selection methods on GSM8K across selection budgets.

Conclusion: This work provides a principled approach to synthetic data selection by quantifying and maximizing its value to the target task. The linear theory characterizes the conditions when input coverage alone is sufficient and when synthetic errors must also be considered.

Abstract: Synthetic data are increasingly used to scale LLM training, yet more synthetic data do not necessarily produce better models. Useful synthetic data must add information relevant to the target task without introducing errors that offset their benefit, and the value of an example can change as the training set grows. We develop a linear theory that characterizes this tradeoff and determines where synthetic data are useful, how much should be added, and the marginal value of adding one example to an existing set. The analysis shows the conditions when input coverage alone is sufficient and when synthetic errors must also be considered. Guided by these results, we introduce \emph{Training-Aware Target Coverage} (TATC), a synthetic data selection method for LLM fine-tuning. TATC identifies candidates whose training effects are beneficial to the target task and selects among them to expand coverage of target-relevant directions not already represented by the available data. Experiments on text and image data verify the linear theory. With mathematical reasoning tasks, TATC selects synthetic solutions for fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct and outperforms alternative synthetic-data selection methods on GSM8K across selection budgets. In summary, we provide a principled approach to synthetic data selection by quantifying and maximizing its value to the target task.

</details>


### [439] [Quantifying the Impact of Ambulance Ramping: A Multi-Year Analysis of Victorian Emergency Medical Services Cases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00818)
*Ayesha Tanveer,Khandakar Ahmed,Assefa Teshome,Oyetunde Gbadeyan,Ziad Nehme*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This study analyzes 2,026,569 emergency department transports across Victoria, Australia from 2020-2024 to characterize ambulance ramping (delay between hospital arrival and patient handover). Key findings: 1.49 million ambulance hours lost (equivalent to ~96 ten-hour shifts lost daily), 57% increase in annual losses to 2022 peak, with 10 of 59 hospitals accounting for 57.8% of lost hours. Handover duration increases with concurrent ambulance arrivals but varies little with patient acuity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ambulance ramping is a critical operational bottleneck in EMS, yet its systemic magnitude and dynamics remain inadequately characterized at scale. The study aims to quantify the scale, trajectory, and operational correlates of ramping across an entire statewide EMS system.

Method: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) of 2,850,575 ambulance attendances in Victoria, Australia from January 2020 to March 2024. After preprocessing, 2,026,569 ED transports across 59 hospitals and 79 Local Government Areas were analyzed using: interval decomposition, Pareto concentration, hourly cross-correlation, hospital arrival concurrency, and priority-stratified operational comparisons.

Result: Cumulative Ambulance Hours Lost (AHL) totaled 1,491,127 hours (~96 ten-hour shifts lost daily). Ten hospitals accounted for 57.8% of lost hours from 50.9% of cases. Annual losses rose 57% to a 2022 peak while transported demand fell 3.7%, indicating deterioration in per-case handover rather than demand growth. Handover duration varies little with patient acuity but rises monotonically with concurrent ambulance arrivals in the preceding hour. Hourly demand is moderately correlated with ramping 2-4 hours later (r = 0.365).

Conclusion: The findings establish empirical preconditions for hospital-state aware ambulance routing, suggesting that routing decisions should account for hospital-level concentration of delays and temporal patterns in ramping.

Abstract: Ambulance ramping, the delay between hospital arrival and patient handover, is a critical operational bottleneck in Emergency Medical Services (EMS), yet its systemic magnitude and dynamics remain inadequately characterised at scale. This paper quantifies the scale, trajectory, and operational correlates of ramping across an entire statewide EMS system, analysing 2,850,575 ambulance attendances in Victoria, Australia from January 2020 to March 2024 using an Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA). After systematic preprocessing, an analytical cohort of 2,026,569 Emergency Department (ED) transports across 59 hospitals with ED and 79 Local Government Areas (LGA) was examined through interval decomposition, Pareto concentration, hourly cross-correlation, hospital arrival concurrency and priority-stratified operational comparisons. Cumulative Ambulance Hours Lost (AHL) totalled 1,491,127 hours, equivalent to approximately 96 ten-hour ambulance shift lost every day of the study window. Ten of 59 hospitals account for 57.8% of lost hours from 50.9% of cases. Annual losses rose 57% to a 2022 peak while transported demand fell 3.7%, indicating deterioration in per-case handover rather than growth in demand. Handover duration varies little with patient acuity, but rises monotonically with the number of ambulances arriving at the same hospital in the preceding hour, an effect persisting within every hour of the day. Hourly demand is moderately associated with ramping two to four hours later (r = 0.365). These findings establish the empirical preconditions for hospital-state aware ambulance routing.

</details>


### [440] [On-the-fly Weight Generation: A Hypernetwork Proof of Concept on ARC-1D](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00820)
*Fabio J. Fehr,Philip Torr*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents a proof-of-concept approach for generating compact, task-specific specialist models on-the-fly from few-shot demonstrations using a hypernetwork, demonstrating that the resulting weight space can support reuse and generalisation beyond known functions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors address the challenge of obtaining specialized models without task-specific training or adaptation. They explore whether specialists can be generated directly from a few demonstrations, combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with the efficiency of specialized models.

Method: Using ARC-1D as a controlled testbed, the authors employ a hypernetwork that generates parameters for tiny specialist models from context (few-shot demonstrations). They investigate compositional generalisation and generalisation to unseen transformations, while testing the effect of removing explicit task identifiers.

Result: The generated parameters form a structured weight space. The resulting specialists show partial compositional generalisation and can generalise to transformations not seen during training. Removing explicit task identifiers improves generalisation beyond the training transformations.

Conclusion: Few-shot task context can be compiled on-the-fly into compact executable model parameters, and the resulting weight space can support reuse and generalisation beyond known functions. This provides a proof of concept for meta-learning of task-specific specialists.

Abstract: General-purpose models can adapt to many tasks from context, while specialised models can execute individual functions with less capacity. Yet obtaining such specialists requires task-specific training or adaptation. We ask whether they can instead be generated directly from a few demonstrations. Using ARC-1D as a controlled testbed, we show that individual transformations can be represented by tiny specialist models, and that a hypernetwork can generate their parameters from context. The generated parameters form a structured weight space, while the resulting specialists show partial compositional generalisation and generalisation to transformations not seen during training. In both settings, removing explicit task identifiers improves generalisation beyond the training transformations. Together, these results provide a proof of concept that few-shot task context can be compiled on-the-fly into compact executable model parameters, and that the resulting weight space can support reuse and generalisation beyond known functions.

</details>


### [441] [AnyJev Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00831)
*Jiamu Zhang,Tianze Yang,Yucheng Shi,Evan Chen,Zixiang Nie,Kelly Wan,Liangjie Hong,Ninghao Liu,Liang Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AnyJev is a system that reads typed decisions (probability distributions over fixed options) from a single prefill of a pretrained instruction-tuned language model, without requiring specially trained models. It corrects two defects (label priors and position bias) through label prior estimation and cyclic rotation averaging, achieving accuracy improvements on 11 of 11 models tested.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current systems for typed decisions require models trained specifically for that purpose. This report proposes reading typed decisions directly from pretrained instruction-tuned language models, which would be more efficient and flexible.

Method: AnyJev reads a typed decision from one prefill by restricting the next-token distribution at the answer position to the option tokens. Two corrections are applied: (1) dividing out label prior estimated from unlabeled inputs to address model bias toward certain labels, and (2) averaging log-probabilities over K cyclic rotations of the option list to address position bias. A stopping rule is used to reduce the number of rotations needed.

Result: On two 20-option tasks, cyclic rotations lowered the order-flip rate from 0.33 to 0.14 and from 0.33 to 0.18, and raised accuracy on 11 of 11 models on both tasks. Using threshold selection on one unlabeled split and bounding disagreement on a second, it reads 10.6 rotations of 18 at a verified 0.008 bound on two of four cells. With selection and bounding on one split (serving run), it reads 7.3 rotations and serves 2.2 times as many decisions per second on vLLM.

Conclusion: AnyJev successfully reads typed decisions from pretrained language models without gradient steps or parameter changes. The method corrects label priors and position bias, achieving improved accuracy across multiple models while maintaining computational efficiency through a stopping rule that reduces the number of rotations needed.

Abstract: A typed decision is a choice among a fixed set of options, returned as a probability rather than as text. Systems that need typed decisions today use models trained for that purpose. This report describes AnyJev, which reads a typed decision from one prefill of a pretrained instruction-tuned language model. The readout restricts the next-token distribution at the answer position to the option tokens. It has two defects: the model assigns higher probability to some labels whatever the input, and to some positions in the option list. AnyJev corrects both with no gradient steps and no parameter changes: it divides out a label prior estimated from unlabelled inputs, and it averages log-probabilities over the K cyclic rotations of the option list. On two 20-option tasks the rotations lower the order-flip rate from 0.33 to 0.14 and from 0.33 to 0.18, and raise accuracy on 11 of 11 models on both. Reading every rotation requires K prefills. A stopping rule selected against the full-rotation decision on unlabelled states cuts that. Selecting the threshold on one unlabelled split and bounding its disagreement on a second, it reads 10.6 rotations of 18 at a verified 0.008 bound on two of four cells; selected and bounded on one split, as our serving run did, it reads 7.3 and serves 2.2 times as many decisions per second on vLLM. The code is open source.

</details>


### [442] [TrueMuse: A Benchmark for Data Attribution in Text-to-Music Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00835)
*Jiawei Yu,Jian Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TrueMuse is a benchmark dataset for evaluating data attribution methods in text-to-music generation models. It addresses the lack of reliable ground truth for evaluating attribution methods by creating controlled test cases through fine-tuning three diffusion-based models on known attribution samples.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-to-music generation models are trained on massive music collections, creating a need for data attribution methods to quantify training sample contributions. However, existing attribution methods cannot be rigorously evaluated due to the lack of reliable ground truth, making it difficult to assess their actual effectiveness.

Method: TrueMuse is constructed by fine-tuning three diffusion-based text-to-music models on carefully curated attribution samples with known inclusion in fine-tuning. The benchmark covers four attribution settings: melodic structure, timbral characteristics, artist-level stylistic signatures, and genre-level shared patterns. It includes 133 attributes, 648 fine-tuned models, and 95,456 generated samples across two prompt types. Existing black-box attribution methods are evaluated along four dimensions: fine-tuning improvement, prompt-type difficulty, multi-task training, and fine-tuning data size.

Result: Attribution remains challenging with existing methods exhibiting substantial variation across evaluation settings.

Conclusion: There is a need for more reliable and generalizable attribution methods for text-to-music generation. The TrueMuse benchmark provides a controlled evaluation framework to drive progress in this area.

Abstract: Text-to-music generation models are trained on massive music collections, creating a growing need for data attribution methods that can quantify the contribution of individual training samples. However, existing attribution methods are difficult to rigorously evaluate due to the lack of reliable ground truth, making it challenging to reliably assess their actual effectiveness. To address this gap, we introduce TrueMuse, a controlled dataset and benchmark for text-to-music data attribution. TrueMuse is constructed by fine-tuning three diffusion-based text-to-music models on carefully curated attribution samples, whose known inclusion in fine-tuning provides controlled attribution targets for evaluation. The benchmark covers four attribution settings, spanning melodic structure, timbral characteristics, artist-level stylistic signatures, and genre-level shared patterns, and includes 133 attributes, 648 fine-tuned models, and 95,456 generated samples across two prompt types. Using TrueMuse, we systematically evaluate existing black-box attribution methods along four dimensions: fine-tuning improvement, prompt-type difficulty, multi-task training, and fine-tuning data size. Our results show that attribution remains challenging, with existing methods exhibiting substantial variation across evaluation settings, highlighting the need for more reliable and generalizable attribution methods for text-to-music generation. Code and Dataset will be released upon acceptance.

</details>


### [443] [SHARPO: Segment-Level Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00838)
*Xinchen Du,Zhengze Zhou,Wenhui Zhu,Han Yu,Sen Na,Rohit Jain,Alborz Geramifard*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SHARPO is a credit-assignment mechanism for agentic reinforcement learning that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the segment level. It computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within segments to compute bounded multipliers on GRPO advantages, allowing credit to vary across different segments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In agentic RL where LLMs act over long multi-step interactions, a single localized error can cause task failure. Trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions, making it difficult to identify which specific decisions led to success or failure.

Method: SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each environment-facing segment (inspired by on-policy self-distillation/OPFD). These gaps are used to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage, which is shared by all tokens within that segment. This allows credit assignment to vary across different segments.

Result: With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

Conclusion: Segment-level credit assignment via SHARPO effectively improves agentic RL performance by allowing the model to learn more granular feedback from individual decisions within multi-step interactions.

Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher-student log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.

</details>


### [444] [Fixing a Model That Learned Worse Cancer Means Lower Risk: Monotonic Constraints in Bladder Cancer Recurrence Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00858)
*Saram Abbas,David Thomas,Naeem Soomro,Rishad Shafik,Rakesh Heer,Kabita Adhikari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A UK multicentre trial (BOXIT, n=435) found that an unconstrained XGBoost model learned counter-intuitive relationships where higher tumor stage and carcinoma in situ predicted lower recurrence risk. Conventional validation methods (AUC, calibration, SHAP) failed to detect this inversion. The authors developed a counterfactual direction test to detect this failure and monotonic constraints to correct it, with no loss in discrimination performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinicians expect recurrence risk to increase with cancer severity, but machine learning models can learn counter-intuitive patterns. The study was motivated by the observation that a trial-validated XGBoost model learned that higher tumor stage and carcinoma in situ predicted lower recurrence risk - opposite to medical intuition. Conventional validation methods (discrimination, calibration, SHAP) all failed to detect this concerning failure.

Method: BOXIT trial enrolled 472 patients across 51 UK sites (2007-2012); 435 had at least 2 years follow-up (153 recurrences, 35.2%). The study developed: (1) a counterfactual direction test that worsened each patient on one directed feature at a time to check whether risk fell as expected; (2) a monotonic-constraint correction using constraint directions from EORTC and EAU risk systems. Both were evaluated against unconstrained XGBoost and logistic regression on 18 predictors (7 directed) over 50 cross-validation folds. SHAP direction and calibration were also assessed.

Result: Tumor stage and carcinoma in situ were associated with lower recurrence risk, opposite to medical intuition. The unconstrained model reversed carcinoma in situ counterfactuals in 90.2% of cases and stage in 74.3%. Discrimination (ΔAUC 0.005, p=0.47), calibration, and SHAP magnitude were all blind to the inversion. Monotonic constraints eliminated every violation at no cost to discrimination (0.723 vs 0.718) and outperformed EORTC (p=8.9e-16).

Conclusion: A model that learned counter-intuitive inversions passed every conventional check (discrimination, calibration, SHAP). A counterfactual direction test, run as a single refit with pre-specified monotonic constraints, catches this failure at no cost to performance and should be routine before clinical deployment. Limitations: single trial, internal-external validation only.

Abstract: Background and Objective: Clinicians expect recurrence risk to climb with cancer severity. In a UK multicentre trial, an unconstrained XGBoost model learnt that higher tumour stage and carcinoma in situ predicted lower recurrence risk, and discrimination, calibration, and SHAP were all blind to it. We developed a counterfactual testing framework to detect this inversion and a monotonic-constraint framework to remove it without hurting performance. Methods: BOXIT enrolled 472 patients with protocol-mandated cystoscopy across 51 UK sites (2007-2012); 435 had at least two years' follow-up (153 recurrences, 35.2%). We developed a counterfactual direction test and a monotonic-constraint correction, with constraint directions drawn from the EORTC and EAU risk systems, and evaluated both against unconstrained XGBoost and logistic regression on 18 predictors (seven directed) over 50 cross-validation folds. The test worsened each patient on one directed feature at a time to check whether risk fell; SHAP direction and calibration were also assessed. Key Findings and Limitations: Tumour stage and carcinoma in situ were associated with lower recurrence, opposite to medical intuition; the unconstrained model reversed carcinoma in situ counterfactuals in 90.2% of cases and stage in 74.3%. Discrimination ($Δ$AUC 0.005, p=0.47), calibration, and SHAP magnitude were all blind to the inversion. Monotonic constraints eliminated every violation at no cost to discrimination (0.723 vs 0.718) and outperformed EORTC (p=8.9e-16). Limitations: single trial, internal-external validation only. Conclusions and Clinical Implications: A model that had learned this inversion passed every conventional check. A counterfactual direction test, run as a single refit with pre-specified monotonic constraints, catches this failure at no cost to performance and should be routine before clinical deployment.

</details>


### [445] [Don't Waste the Noise: Importance-Guided Perturbation Allocation under Joint Global and Local Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00861)
*Melika Shirian,Kianoosh Vadaei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses adversarial optimization under a shared ℓ1 budget with local magnitude constraints, introducing an importance-guided allocation mechanism that uses clean-gradient priors to steer perturbation toward model-sensitive regions while redistributing rather than enlarging the available budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When adversarial perturbations are limited by both a global ℓ1 budget and local magnitude constraints, the allocation of this limited budget across input coordinates becomes critical. The authors identify that existing methods don't adequately address where to spend the perturbation budget.

Method: The proposed method uses a fixed clean-gradient prior to identify model-sensitive regions and steers perturbation toward them through a centered allocation objective. This encourages perturbation at above-average importance locations while discouraging unnecessary expenditure elsewhere, effectively redistributing the budget without increasing total ℓ1 consumption.

Result: Across ten robust model-dataset configurations under capacity-limited threat settings, the method improves attack success over APGD- and PMA-based baselines by 2.52 to 17.70 percentage points. Allocation analysis shows greater perturbation mass in high-importance regions without increased global ℓ1 consumption.

Conclusion: Perturbation allocation is a distinct and practically relevant dimension of adversarial optimization under shared-budget, locally constrained threat models. Both centered non-uniform redistribution and model-derived importance contribute to the performance gains.

Abstract: Adversarial optimization under a shared $\ell_1$ budget requires deciding not only how much perturbation to use, but also where that limited budget should be spent. This allocation problem becomes particularly important when individual input coordinates are subject to local magnitude constraints, which restrict the extent to which perturbation can be concentrated on a small number of locations. We introduce an importance-guided allocation mechanism that uses a fixed clean-gradient prior to steer perturbation toward model-sensitive regions while leaving the feasible perturbation set unchanged. A centered allocation objective encourages perturbation at above-average importance locations and discourages unnecessary expenditure elsewhere, thereby redistributing rather than enlarging the available budget. Across ten robust model--dataset configurations under a common capacity-limited threat setting, the proposed method improves attack success over matched APGD- and PMA-based baselines by $2.52$ to $17.70$ percentage points. Allocation analysis shows that these gains are accompanied by substantially greater perturbation mass in high-importance regions without increased global $\ell_1$ consumption. Mechanism ablations further show that centered non-uniform redistribution provides part of the benefit, while model-derived importance yields an additional improvement. These results identify perturbation allocation as a distinct and practically relevant dimension of adversarial optimization under shared-budget, locally constrained threat models.

</details>


### [446] [Rethinking Data Augmentation under Covariate Shift: Invariant-Guided Diffusion and Prototype Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00873)
*Hongyu Cao,Xinyuan Wang,Arun Vignesh Malarkkan,Kunpeng Liu,Haifeng Chen,Yanjie Fu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses the Augmented and Weighted Learning under Covariate Shift (AWL-CS) problem, where industrial applications face challenges of scarce/imbalanced tabular data, covariate shift between training and deployment, and distribution drift. The proposed IGDPR framework combines invariant-guided diffusion for task-relevant synthetic data generation with prototype-based reweighting for stable adaptation against validation noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial applications suffer from: 1) scarce and imbalanced tabular data requiring synthetic expansion; 2) covariate shift between training and deployment; 3) validation-test distribution divergence; 4) generative models mimicking outdated source distributions. These issues limit stability of augmentation and adaptation pipelines.

Method: IGDPR (Invariant-Guided Diffusion with Prototype Reweighting) has two components: 1) Invariant-guided diffusion sampling - steers the diffusion process using invariant potentials to ensure synthetic samples align with stable decision boundaries rather than outdated correlations; 2) Prototype-based reweighting - assesses sample reliability through structural clusters instead of isolated points to filter validation noise.

Result: Extensive experiments on real data demonstrate improved data quality by augmenting the most beneficial data for robust learning.

Conclusion: IGDDR provides a unified framework that synergizes stable synthesis and structural adaptation, effectively addressing misleading generative guidance and structural instability of distributional density in AWL-CS settings.

Abstract: In many industrial applications, 1) tabular data is scarce and imbalanced and thus requires synthetic expansion; 2) input distributions drift between training and deployment (covariate shift); 3) validation sets often diverge from unseen test environments; or 4) standard generative models simply mimic outdated source distributions. This learning setting limits the stability of standard augmentation and adaptation pipelines. We generalize the task under such setting as the Augmented and Weighted Learning under Covariate Shift problem (AWL-CS). AWL-CS imposes two critical challenges on existing methods: 1) misleading generative guidance where models optimize for source similarity rather than downstream task relevance, and 2) structural instability of distributional density where reweighting mechanisms overfit to noisy validation signals. To tackle these challenges, we propose IGDPR (Invariant-Guided Diffusion with Prototype Reweighting), a unified framework that synergizes stable synthesis and structural adaptation: i) To achieve task-relevant generation, we steer the diffusion sampling process using invariant potentials to ensure synthetic samples align with stable decision boundaries rather than outdated correlations. ii) To ensure stable adaptation, we develop a prototype-based reweighting strategy that assesses sample reliability through structural clusters instead of isolated points, effectively filtering validation noise. Extensive experiments on real data demonstrate our method improves data quality by augmenting the most beneficial data for robust learning.

</details>


### [447] [Match the Distribution, Not the Compute: Post-Training Multi-Token Prediction Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00888)
*Prachi Badarayani,Aidan Jay,Chenghui Zhou,Dayquan Julienne,Yuan Gao,Tianwei Chen,George Zerveas,Ishmam Zabir,Xiren Zhou,Chris Quirk,Xia Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a lightweight post-training approach for Multi-token Prediction (MTP) that achieves comparable throughput speedup to jointly trained models (MiMo-7B, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3) using 10³-10⁴× fewer training tokens, along with two serving-time optimizations: chain-aware verification relaxation and adaptive MTP head engagement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Jointly trained MTP models require training heads over tens of trillions of tokens throughout pretraining. This work investigates whether a lightweight post-training pass on target-generated chain-of-thought can achieve the same throughput speedup on a frozen reasoning model, potentially reducing computational costs dramatically.

Method: 1) Post-training recipe using plain cross-entropy on ~2.5B tokens with chained MTP heads (K=3) on frozen Qwen3-8B. 2) Chain-aware relaxation of draft token verification allowing bounded drift from backbone LM distribution. 3) Adaptive controller that dynamically selects number of MTP heads at inference time.

Result: 1) Post-training on ~2.5B tokens reaches or exceeds expected speedup of jointly trained MiMo-7B on math, coding, and knowledge benchmarks while using 10³-10⁴× fewer MTP-training tokens. 2) Chain-aware relaxation increases expected speedups by +12 to +16% per benchmark while preserving task accuracy. 3) Adaptive controller recovers 11-14% loss in speedup compared to fixed maximum MTP draft length.

Conclusion: Lightweight post-training is sufficient to achieve comparable MTP speedups to joint pretraining, and serving-time optimizations (chain-aware verification and adaptive head engagement) can further enhance throughput by 12-16% and recover 11-14% speedup loss respectively.

Abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) improves the throughput of autoregressive generation by enabling the language model to draft multiple next tokens per forward pass, while a verification step over draft tokens ensures that token distribution of the backbone is preserved. Every open MTP-family release (MiMo-7B, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3) trains its heads jointly with the backbone over the full pretraining run of tens of trillions of tokens, thus setting the drafter quality at pretraining time. We ask whether a lightweight post-training pass on target-generated chain-of-thought is enough to reach the same expected throughput speedup on a frozen reasoning model, and study how a serving-time system built on such a checkpoint can be optimized. We present three findings. 1) On a frozen Qwen3-8B with $K{=}3$ chained MTP heads, we show that a post-training recipe with plain cross-entropy on $\approx\!2.5$B tokens reaches or exceeds the expected speedup of jointly trained MiMo-7B on math, coding and knowledge benchmarks. Our post-training recipe utilizes $10^3$-$10^4\times$ less MTP-training tokens as compared with joint pre-training of MiMO-7B MTP baseline. 2) We propose a chain-aware relaxation of draft token verification rule that allows a bounded drift from backbone language model token distribution.
