We show that this relaxation lifts expected speedups by $+12$ to $+16\%$ per benchmark while preserving task accuracy. 3) We propose an adaptive controller that dynamically chooses the number of MTP heads to be engaged at inference time and demonstrate recovery of upto $11$--$14\%$ loss in speedup using fixed maximum MTP draft length.

</details>


### [448] [Clock Diffusion: Efficient Semi-Autoregressive Continuous Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00894)
*Yair Schiff,Omer Belhasin,Roy Uziel,Matan Rusanovsky,Ran Zilberstein,Marianne Arriola,Gilad Turok,Guanghan Wang,Volodymyr Kuleshov,Michael Elad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Clock Diffusion introduces position-dependent noise schedules to enable semi-autoregressive continuous diffusion language models with variable-length generation and KV-cache support, achieving state-of-the-art results on OpenWebText and GSM8K benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continuous diffusion models for discrete data (language) lack two essential features for practical use: variable-length generation and key-value cache support. Additionally, they lag behind autoregressive and discrete diffusion models in quality.

Method: The paper introduces a novel model parameterization using position-dependent noise schedules to define semi-autoregressive (SAR) continuous diffusion language models (DLMs). This framework, called Clock Diffusion, includes two special cases: block and sliding window generation. Efficient training and sampling algorithms are proposed, along with Cache Grab samplers that adapt techniques from accelerated discrete diffusion inference (confidence thresholding and self-speculative decoding).

Result: ClockDLMs achieve state-of-the-art diffusion likelihood bounds on OpenWebText, outperforming block SAR discrete diffusion models. On GSM8K, ClockDLMs substantially outperform continuous baselines and match/exceed comparable SAR discrete diffusion models. Cache Grab samplers further improve quality and efficiency.

Conclusion: Clock Diffusion successfully bridges the gap between continuous diffusion and practical language modeling by enabling variable-length generation and KV-cache support while achieving superior performance on standard benchmarks.

Abstract: Recent works on continuous diffusion for discrete data have demonstrated performance on par with comparable discrete diffusion models. However, these continuous counterparts lack key features that are essential to practical use as language models, namely variable-length generation and support for a key-value cache, and they still lag behind the frontier of autoregressive and discrete diffusion quality. In this work, we address these limitations. We do so by introducing a model parameterization that uses position-dependent noise schedules to define semi-autoregressive (SAR) continuous diffusion language models (DLMs). Together with efficient training and sampling algorithms, we call this framework Clock Diffusion, and we present two special cases of our method: block and sliding window generation. We then define ClockDLMs, a family of Gaussian DLMs based on sliding window Clock Diffusion that attain state-of-the-art diffusion likelihood bounds on OpenWebText, even beating the performant block SAR discrete diffusion models. ClockDLMs trained on TinyGSM also substantially outperform continuous baselines on the GSM8K benchmark and match and exceed comparable SAR discrete diffusion models. Finally, building on our parameterization, we propose more efficient samplers that we dub Cache Grab, which adapt techniques from accelerated inference in discrete diffusion, such as committing tokens whose probabilities exceed a confidence threshold and self-speculative decoding, further improving our models' quality and efficiency.

</details>


### [449] [Towards Fast and Disentangled Counterfactuals for Visual Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00895)
*Sidney Bender,Benedikt Kunz,Ahmed Zeid,Shinichi Nakajima,Klaus-Robert Müller,Marco Morik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DiDAE (Disentangled Diffusion Autoencoders) is a method for generating counterfactual explanations for foundation models by wrapping a frozen model in a conditional diffusion decoder and using disentangled dictionary learning. It achieves up to 2000x speed improvement over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining or improving quality on six datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Foundation models remain vulnerable to spurious correlations and "Clever Hans" strategies. While explainable ML can address these issues for classifiers with metadata, no equivalent solution exists for foundation models. This work aims to fill this gap by providing a method to identify and remove such strategies.

Method: DiDAE wraps a frozen foundation model in a conditional diffusion decoder. Counterfactuals are generated through closed-form edits along directions of a disentangled dictionary, which can be supervised (Procrustes) or unsupervised (SVD, Sparse Autoencoders). No gradients are needed, enabling high-speed processing. The method also includes Counterfactual Knowledge Distillation (CFKD) for repairing downstream classifiers and a workflow to rank a pretrained dictionary against a trained classifier.

Result: On six datasets (2 synthetic, 4 real-world), DiDAE's counterfactuals are on par with or better than the state of the art in desiderata-driven benchmarks. Through CFKD, it outperforms metadata-based correction. The method can identify the few directions a classifier actually uses, causally verify them with counterfactuals, and repair classifiers along spurious directions.

Conclusion: DiDAE provides an efficient, plug-and-play solution for identifying and removing spurious correlations in foundation models. The open-source Pearl library enables practical application with just a linear distillation and fine-tuning of the classifier.

Abstract: Foundation models remain vulnerable to spurious correlations and ``Clever Hans'' strategies. Explainable machine learning can find and remove such strategies for classifiers without metadata. For foundation models, no such option exists yet. We propose Disentangled Diffusion Autoencoders (DiDAE). DiDAE wraps a frozen foundation model in a conditional diffusion decoder. A counterfactual is one closed-form edit along a direction of a disentangled dictionary, followed by decoding. The dictionary can be supervised (Procrustes) or unsupervised (Singular Value Decomposition, Sparse Autoencoders). No gradients are needed, so DiDAE is up to 2000 times faster than the state of the art. We evaluate on six datasets, two synthetic and four real-world. In a desiderata-driven benchmark on three of them, its counterfactuals are on par with or better than the state of the art, and they repair downstream classifiers through Counterfactual Knowledge Distillation (CFKD), where they beat metadata-based correction. The same machinery can rank a pretrained dictionary against a trained classifier. It returns the few directions the classifier actually reads, each causally verified by a counterfactual that flips the decision, and repairs the classifier along those a teacher marks spurious. The workflow is plug-and-play in our open-source Peal library we publish alongside the paper. With a public dictionary and a pretrained decoder, all that remains is a cheap linear distillation of the classifier and its own fine-tuning.

</details>


### [450] [When Do Biological Reasoning Models Use Their Biological Inputs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00898)
*Ada Fang,Nikitha Thoduguli,Lukas Fesser,Hanlin Zhang,Sham M. Kakade,Marinka Zitnik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the assumption that biological reasoning models actually reason over biological inputs (foundation model representations). Through extensive experiments on six models across DNA, protein, and single-cell tasks, the authors find that most models (BioReason, BioReason-Pro) rely primarily on text rather than biological representations, despite benchmark accuracy claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biological reasoning models claim to use post-training to connect LLMs to biological foundation model representations. However, the benchmark accuracy is taken as evidence that LLMs actually reason over these inputs. This paper questions this assumption and aims to test whether these models truly utilize biological representations or merely rely on text.

Method: The authors used four main methods: (1) perturbing one biological input while holding query and other inputs fixed; (2) constructing evidence conflicts by pairing foundation model representation of one genome/protein/cell with text of another; (3) fitting linear probes to representations the language model receives; (4) analyzing reasoning traces against biological inputs. They tested six models across DNA, protein, and single-cell tasks.

Result: Key findings: (1) Evo2 and ESM3 contribute little to BioReason and BioReason-Pro performance; (2) Shuffling DNA sequence barely changes BioReason disease prediction accuracy; (3) In evidence conflicts, BioReason models follow text in 97.9% and 99.7% of cases; (4) Linear probes can predict task targets from foundation model representations, showing they encode relevant info, but don't improve performance; (5) ChatNT, Prot2Text-V2, CellWhisperer, and Cell2Sentence-Scale show genuine contributions from biological inputs; (6) Accuracy increases don't imply greater contributions from biological inputs across checkpoints; (7) Reasoning traces misstate or omit information.

Conclusion: Current post-training strategies do not ensure that foundation model representations contribute to task performance. Many biological reasoning models primarily rely on text rather than biological representations, despite using foundation models in their architecture. This challenges the validity of benchmark accuracy as evidence for biological reasoning.

Abstract: Biological reasoning models use post-training to connect LLMs to biological foundation model representations and biological text. Their benchmark accuracy is taken as evidence that LLMs reason over these inputs. We test this assumption in six biological reasoning models across DNA, protein, and single-cell tasks. We perturb one biological input while holding the query and other inputs fixed, construct evidence conflicts that pair the foundation model representation of one genome, protein, or cell with the text of another, fit linear probes to the representations the language model receives, and analyze reasoning traces against the biological inputs. Evo2 and ESM3 contribute little to BioReason and BioReason-Pro performance on the evaluated tasks. Shuffling the DNA sequence barely changes BioReason disease prediction accuracy, and in evidence conflicts the two models follow the text in 97.9% and 99.7% of cases. Linear probes trained on the Evo2 and ESM3 representations predict the task targets, so these foundation models encode information relevant to the task, but provide limited overall performance improvement to BioReason and BioReason-Pro. In contrast, foundation model inputs contribute to ChatNT, Prot2Text-V2, and CellWhisperer performance, and differentially expressed genes in the gene sentence contribute to Cell2Sentence-Scale performance. Across SFT and RL checkpoints of BioReason-Pro and 42 BioReason checkpoints, increases in accuracy do not imply greater performance contributions from biological inputs. BioReason traces misstate nucleotide changes, while BioReason-Pro traces describe functions omitted from final predictions under evidence conflicts. We find that current post-training strategies do not ensure that foundation model representations contribute to task performance.

</details>


### [451] [Sharpen Before You Adapt: Data-Free Entry-State Sharpening for Test-Time Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00903)
*Zhanming Zhang,Vinoth Selvendran*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes "entry-state sharpening" - using data-free training before test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) to prepare a language model checkpoint in a state that subsequent label-free adaptation can exploit more efficiently. The key insight is that entry policy entropy strongly predicts TTRL conversion efficiency (Spearman ρ=-0.90).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In TTRL, the checkpoint's entry state is consequential because a diffuse policy provides noisier self-supervision and may waste adaptation budget concentrating probability mass before reliably expressing capability. The authors argue that entry-state preparation is a critical but overlooked factor in TTRL success.

Method: The authors derive five different data-free checkpoints from Qwen3-4B using different training objectives, then evaluate them under an identical 15-step TTRL protocol. They measure entry policy entropy and correlate it with endpoint conversion efficiency. They also perform an in-domain label-free self-distillation intervention.

Result: Entry policy entropy strongly rank-orders endpoint conversion efficiency (Spearman ρ=-0.90; ρ=-0.99 after controlling for entry reachability). R-Zero remains diffuse at 3.39 nats and finishes below the untuned base in 6/6 matched comparisons across MATH, GPQA, and AMC. SPIRAL reaches 0.07 nats and achieves the highest post-TTRL accuracy on MATH and GPQA despite using no math training data in its self-play stage.

Conclusion: The authors propose treating checkpoint preparation as a state-control problem: use data-free training to improve TTRL readiness, with entry entropy as a label-free control signal and reachable capability as the constraint. The entry state can be deliberately sharpened through interventions like self-distillation.

Abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts language models on unlabeled test problems using supervision derived from their own samples. This makes the checkpoint's \emph{entry state} consequential: a diffuse policy provides noisier self-supervision and may spend much of a limited adaptation budget merely concentrating probability mass before reliably expressing capability it already possesses. We propose \textbf{entry-state sharpening}: use data-free training \emph{before} TTRL to prepare a general-purpose checkpoint in a state that subsequent label-free adaptation can exploit more efficiently. The idea is not tied to one training recipe; different data-free objectives can move the same base model to different entry states. Across five data-free checkpoints derived from Qwen3-4B and evaluated under an identical 15-step TTRL protocol, entry policy entropy strongly rank-orders endpoint conversion efficiency, a reliability-to-reachability measure (Spearman $ρ=-0.90$; $ρ=-0.99$ after controlling for entry reachability). The contrast across objectives is striking: R-Zero remains diffuse at $3.39$ nats and finishes below the untuned base in 6/6 matched comparisons across MATH, GPQA, and AMC, whereas SPIRAL reaches $0.07$ nats and achieves the highest post-TTRL accuracy on MATH and GPQA despite its self-play stage using no math training data. An in-domain label-free self-distillation intervention further shows that the entry state can be deliberately sharpened. These results motivate treating checkpoint preparation as a \emph{state-control problem}: use data-free training to improve TTRL readiness, with entry entropy as a label-free control signal and reachable capability as the constraint.

</details>


### [452] [In CEM, a World Model Is Also a Proposal Mechanism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00921)
*Oliver Obst,Frieder Stolzenburg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the dual role of scoring in the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM): selecting action sequences and updating proposal distributions. The authors evaluate whether predictive model scores reliably guide both present decisions and future candidate generation across Walker and Cheetah robotic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CEM uses world-model scores to both select action sequences and fit the distribution for the next iteration. A scoring error can therefore affect both current decisions and future search candidates. The motivation is to understand whether these two roles are equally affected by model errors and whether model-based scoring actually improves optimization outcomes.

Method: Four types of predictive models generate CEM traces on 12 independently trained task-seed units (Walker and Cheetah). Every model rescores every saved candidate pool. Environment execution provides reference elite sets for comparison. A one-update intervention replaces the first model-ranked update with an environment-ranked update on six units, then tested on six held-out units.

Result: 1) Proposal distance consistently falls from first to final CEM iteration across all units. 2) Proposal widths contract and fitted means separate relative to remaining search width. 3) Pairwise ranking agreement stays near chance on Walker and declines on Cheetah. 4) Elite-set agreement does not improve. 5) Cheetah shows greater variation between scorers than between pool sources; Walker shows variation in both. 6) Replacing model-ranked update with environment-ranked update lowers final realized selected-sequence cost in both original and held-out units.

Conclusion: Model-based scoring in CEM performs poorly for both its roles - selecting elite candidates and updating proposal distributions. The intervention experiment shows that environment-based ranking can outperform model-based ranking, suggesting that CEM's reliance on imperfect world models may be fundamentally limiting optimization performance. The lack of improvement in elite-set agreement indicates that model scores fail to identify truly beneficial action sequences.

Abstract: The cross-entropy method (CEM) uses world-model scores to select action sequences and fit the distribution sampled in its next iteration. A scoring error can therefore change both the present decision and the candidates considered later. We evaluate these two roles separately. Four types of predictive model generate CEM traces, and every model rescores every saved candidate pool. Executing the same candidates in the environment provides a reference elite set and proposal update.
  Across twelve independently trained task-seed units on Walker and Cheetah, the pre-specified proposal distance falls from the first to the final CEM iteration in every unit. Proposal widths contract and fitted means separate relative to the remaining search width. Pairwise ranking agreement stays near chance on Walker and declines on Cheetah; elite-set agreement does not improve. This comparison shows greater variation between scorers than between pool sources on Cheetah; Walker has variation in both and in their pairings. We use the original six units to select Random nonlinear for a one-update intervention, without inspecting intervention outcomes. Replacing its first model-ranked update with an environment-ranked update lowers final realised selected-sequence cost in those six units and in six further units held out from the selection.

</details>


### [453] [Rate-Optimal Algorithm for Adversarial Linear CMDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00927)
*Kihyun Yu,Honghao Wei,Dabeen Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses episodic adversarial linear constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) with unknown transitions, where both loss and constraint functions can vary adversarially across episodes. The authors develop a new primal-dual algorithm that achieves O(√K) regret and cumulative constraint violation, improving upon the previous O(K^{3/4}) bound and closing the gap to optimality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The best previous algorithm achieves O~(K^{3/4}) regret and cumulative constraint violation, leaving a gap to the optimal O~(√K) dependence on the number of episodes K. The authors aim to close this gap without assuming Slater's condition.

Method: The algorithm combines adaptive Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL), contracted value estimation, and an exponential Lyapunov function. An adaptive dual regularizer offsets the dependence on the dual weights in the primal regret bound, removing the need for policy mixing. The normalization in the FTRL update bounds policy parameters independently of dual weight magnitudes.

Result: The proposed algorithm achieves O~(√K) regret and cumulative constraint violation without assuming Slater's condition. Under feature access, computational complexity is independent of the state space size.

Conclusion: This work closes the gap between previous O~(K^{3/4}) results and the optimal O~(√K) dependence for episodic adversarial linear CMDPs. The key insight is that FTRL normalization keeps the policy class compatible with uniform concentration, avoiding the complexity issues caused by policy mixing in standard constrained online learning techniques.

Abstract: We study episodic adversarial linear constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) with unknown transitions, where both the loss and constraint functions may vary adversarially across episodes. The best previous algorithm achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{3/4})$ regret and cumulative constraint violation, leaving a gap to the optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ dependence on the number of episodes $K$. We close this gap by proposing a new primal dual algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{K})$ regret and cumulative constraint violation without assuming Slater's condition. The main challenge is that learning linear CMDPs requires uniform concentration over a value function class with a controlled covering number, whereas standard techniques in constrained online learning, such as policy mixing, can make this class more complex. Our algorithm combines adaptive Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL), contracted value estimation, and an exponential Lyapunov function. An adaptive dual regularizer offsets the dependence on the dual weights in the primal regret bound, removing the need for policy mixing. We further show that the normalization in the FTRL update bounds the policy parameters independently of the magnitudes of the dual weights, which explains why the resulting policy class remains compatible with uniform concentration. Under feature access, the computational complexity is independent of the size of the state space.

</details>


### [454] [Platonic Task Arithmetic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00929)
*Junghwan Park,Woojin Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "Universal Task Descriptors" - architecture-independent matrices that capture task knowledge and enable transfer across heterogeneous models. Two realization methods are proposed: a linear least-squares approach and a low-rank adapter approach. Experiments across six model families show 74-80% retention of performance gains when transferring task knowledge across different architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that models specialized for the same task converge to similar behavior, but their parameter updates exist in different coordinate systems (model-specific), making cross-architecture transfer impossible. The authors hypothesize, inspired by Plato's allegory of the cave, that these model-specific updates are "shadows" of a shared, model-agnostic underlying object - the "platonic task vector."

Method: 1) Universal Task Descriptors: architecture-independent matrices that record a task's functional effect, supporting addition and negation as matrix operations. 2) Transfer mechanism: editing target model to reproduce the descriptor on unlabeled probe images and class-name prompts. 3) Two realizations: (a) Factorization into shift field on image embeddings - single least-squares solve yields linear operator folded into last layer as weight edit; (b) Low-rank adapter trained on same objective reaching every layer.

Result: Cross-model transfer retains 74-80% of the gain compared to the target's own descriptors. Experiments across six model families, eight classification tasks, and an audio-text setting demonstrate successful task knowledge transfer and composition across heterogeneous models.

Conclusion: The platonic task vector hypothesis is validated - there exists a model-agnostic representation of task knowledge that can be captured by Universal Task Descriptors. This enables transfer learning across heterogeneous architectures without requiring per-image labels, with only modest performance loss (20-26%) compared to within-model transfers.

Abstract: Models specialized for the same task converge to similar behavior, yet the parameter updates that produce it share no common coordinate system, so weight-space task arithmetic stays confined to a single model and cannot cross architectures without a structural correspondence. Drawing on Plato's allegory of the cave, we hypothesize that these model-specific updates are shadows of one shared, model-agnostic object, which we call the platonic task vector. To make it operational for models that pair an image or audio encoder with a text encoder, we introduce Universal Task Descriptors: matrices whose shape is independent of architecture and embedding dimension, which record a task's functional effect and support addition and negation as matrix operations. Transferring a descriptor into a target means editing the target until it reproduces the descriptor on the task's unlabeled probe images and class-name prompts, requiring no per-image labels. We realize this edit in two ways. First, the descriptor factorizes into a shift field on image embeddings, so a single least-squares solve yields a linear operator that folds into the target's last layer as a weight edit; by linearity, a bank of such operators admits any composition at any strength as a signed sum. Second, a low-rank adapter trained on the same objective reaches every layer and fits compositions jointly, at the cost of one optimization per edit. Heterogeneous models share this object only partially, with a model-specific residual comparable in norm to the shared component, yet cross-model transfer still retains 74-80 percent of the gain of the target's own descriptors. Experiments across six model families, eight classification tasks, and an audio-text setting show that task knowledge transfers and composes across heterogeneous models under both realizations.

</details>


### [455] [GUI-HARVEST: Self-Improving GUI Agents through Evidence-Driven Harness Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00948)
*Geyi Yang,Zikun Qu,Xiang Li,Zhiyong Wang,Min Zhang,Shipei Zeng,Zhongxiang Dai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GUI-HARVEST is an automatic harness optimizer that enables self-improving GUI agents with frozen backbone models by diagnosing failures, identifying recurring failure patterns, and translating them into reusable runtime changes through bounded source-code edits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current harness optimization for GUI agents faces three coupled challenges: reconciling model intent with observed visual effects, diagnosing failures under variable execution outcomes, and identifying recurrent failure patterns across tasks to translate them into reusable runtime changes. Existing harness optimization methods (Self-Harness, Meta-Harness) fail to address GUI-specific diagnosis and validation.

Method: GUI-HARVEST addresses these challenges through three key components: (1) Grounding diagnosis in observed action effects by aligning model outputs and executed actions with before-and-after screenshots; (2) Treating repeated runs of the same task as a joint evidence unit to locate outcome-relevant behavioral differences through within-task comparisons; (3) Consolidating verified findings across tasks into recurring failure patterns, mapping them to bounded source-code edits with predictions recorded before evaluation, and checking predicted behavioral effects through repeated execution.

Result: On OSWorld-Verified, GUI-HARVEST shows consistent held-out gains across six backbone models (general-purpose open, GUI-specialized open, and proprietary). Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct gains 12.33 points on the full suite. Frozen-harness transfer improves GPT-5 by 13.87 percentage points on WindowsAgentArena at 50 steps. It outperforms Self-Harness and Meta-Harness with the same backbone and initial harness.

Conclusion: GUI-specific diagnosis and validation help harness improvements generalize to unseen tasks. The approach successfully enables self-improving GUI agents with frozen backbone models, demonstrating significant performance gains across diverse model architectures and transferability to new benchmarks like WindowsAgentArena.

Abstract: The executable harness surrounding a GUI model determines how observations are assembled, actions are executed, and verification, recovery, and termination are controlled. Compared with harness optimization for non-GUI agents, automatically optimizing this harness poses three coupled challenges: reconciling model intent with observed visual effects, diagnosing failures under variable execution outcomes, and identifying recurrent failure patterns across tasks and translating them into reusable runtime changes. We introduce GUI-HARVEST, an automatic harness optimizer that enables self-improving GUI agents with frozen backbone models. First, to ground diagnosis in observed action effects, it aligns model outputs and executed actions with before-and-after screenshots, tying findings to specific interface transitions. Second, to account for execution variability, it treats repeated runs of the same task as a joint evidence unit, using within-task comparisons to locate outcome-relevant behavioral differences. Third, it consolidates verified findings across tasks into recurring failure patterns, maps them to bounded source-code edits with predictions recorded before evaluation, and checks the predicted behavioral effects alongside task performance through repeated execution. Experiments on OSWorld-Verified show consistent held-out gains across six general-purpose open, GUI-specialized open, and proprietary backbone models; Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct gains 12.33 points on the full suite. Frozen-harness transfer improves GPT-5 by 13.87 percentage points on WindowsAgentArena at 50 steps without further optimization. With the same backbone and initial harness, GUI-HARVEST outperforms Self-Harness and Meta-Harness, suggesting that GUI-specific diagnosis and validation help harness improvements generalize to unseen tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/GaryYang12345/GUI-HARVEST.

</details>


### [456] [Structure-agnostic Causal Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00968)
*Arman Behnam,Binghui Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SaCRL is a novel causal representation learning framework that jointly identifies causal structure and learns invariant representations without prior structural knowledge, using HSIC-based violation metrics with adaptive weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing causal representation learning methods require specifying causal structure a priori, but different structures demand incompatible invariance constraints, and misspecification leads to representations that discard predictive information.

Method: The approach formulates structure selection as a soft optimization over candidate invariances using HSIC-based violation metrics, with adaptive weights that automatically concentrate on the achievable structure. Theoretical guarantees are provided for structure identification, including under random-feature approximation, invariance satisfaction, and out-of-distribution generalization.

Result: Empirically, SaCRL recovers the true structure on synthetic and semi-synthetic Bayesian-network benchmarks, outperforms fixed-invariance baselines on Colored MNIST, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three DomainBed benchmarks (PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome), and degrades gracefully under structural misspecification and limited environment diversity.

Conclusion: SaCRL successfully addresses the challenge of unknown causal structure in invariant representation learning, providing a principled approach that jointly optimizes structure identification and representation learning without prior knowledge.

Abstract: Causal representation learning aims to discover robust features by exploiting the causal structure underlying data generation. Existing methods require specifying the causal structure a priori, yet different structures demand fundamentally incompatible invariance constraints, and misspecification leads to representations that discard predictive information. We introduce SaCRL, a framework that jointly identifies the causal structure and learns the corresponding invariant representation without prior structural knowledge. Our approach formulates structure selection as a soft optimization over candidate invariances using HSIC-based violation metrics, with adaptive weights that automatically concentrate on the achievable structure. We provide theoretical guarantees for structure identification, including under random-feature approximation, invariance satisfaction, and out-of-distribution generalization. Empirically, SaCRL recovers the true structure on synthetic and semi-synthetic Bayesian-network benchmarks, outperforms fixed-invariance baselines on Colored MNIST, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three DomainBed benchmarks (PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome), and degrades gracefully under structural misspecification and limited environment diversity. Code is available at: https://github.com/ArmanBehnam/sacrl.

</details>


### [457] [Variational Streaming Flow: Probabilistic Forecasting in Physical Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00976)
*Hans Hao-Hsun Hsu,Minseon Gwak,Soon Hoe Lim,Pan Li,N. Benjamin Erichson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces Variational Streaming Flow (VSF), a method that extends deterministic Streaming Flow (SF) for probabilistic forecasting in complex dynamical systems. VSF learns a latent distribution conditioned on dynamics to enable multiple plausible future predictions while maintaining SF's computational efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Probabilistic forecasting is essential for complex dynamical systems due to intrinsic randomness and incomplete observations. While flow matching is flexible, it's computationally expensive. Streaming Flow (SF) improves efficiency but remains deterministic, providing only a single future trajectory per initial state. This limitation prevents capturing the inherent uncertainty in dynamical systems.

Method: VSF learns a latent distribution conditioned on the dynamics of interest, enabling probabilistic forecasting while retaining SF's computational efficiency through generation in physical time. The approach can be integrated into JEPA-based world models as a plug-and-play predictor.

Result: VSF demonstrates superior predictive accuracy and distributional fidelity across deterministic and stochastic dynamical systems. It successfully handles long-horizon rollouts exceeding 1,000 steps and settings with bifurcating dynamics. When integrated into JEPA-based world models, it improves temporal dynamics and goal-directed success rate in navigation, motion planning, and manipulation tasks.

Conclusion: VSF successfully bridges the gap between probabilistic forecasting and computational efficiency in modeling dynamical systems. Its ability to generate multiple plausible futures while maintaining computational tractability makes it valuable for applications requiring uncertainty quantification, and its compatibility with JEPA-based world models enables practical deployment in robotics and control tasks.

Abstract: Probabilistic forecasting is important for predicting complex dynamical systems because intrinsic randomness and incomplete observations can cause the same observed state to evolve into multiple plausible futures. While flow matching is a flexible approach for probabilistic forecasting, it is computationally expensive. Streaming flow (SF) reformulates this approach to model temporal evolution efficiently by learning a continuous velocity field directly in physical time. However, SF learns a deterministic velocity field. Thus, it provides only a single future trajectory for a given fixed initial state and observation history. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Variational Streaming Flow (VSF). Our approach learns a latent distribution that is conditioned on the dynamics of interest. In turn, this enables probabilistic forecasting. Importantly, we retain the computational efficiency of SF by generating in physical time. Across deterministic and stochastic dynamical systems, VSF demonstrates superior predictive accuracy and distributional fidelity. We demonstrate the advantage for both long-horizon rollouts exceeding 1,000 steps, and settings with bifurcating dynamics. Moreover, VSF can be integrated into existing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA)-based world models as a plug-and-play predictor to improve temporal dynamics and goal-directed success rate in navigation, motion planning, and manipulation.

</details>


### [458] [Generalist Representation, Specialist Detection: TS-Router for Time-Series Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00978)
*Tian Lan,Yifei Gao,Yimeng Lu,Xuming An,Meng Wang,Yue Pan,Wenjun He,Chenghao Liu,Chen Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TS-Router is a generalist-representation, specialist-detection framework for time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) that uses pretrained foundation models to coordinate heterogeneous anomaly detectors rather than imposing a universal scoring mechanism. It estimates the relative competence of different anomaly detectors from temporal representations and selects suitable specialists for each target series, using soft competence supervision derived from simulated tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Time-series anomaly detection is difficult to generalize across datasets because heterogeneous temporal dynamics imply different notions of normality and favor different detection criteria. Existing approaches that couple foundation models with fixed anomaly-scoring mechanisms overlook this variation. The authors propose a different perspective: using foundation models to coordinate specialized anomaly criteria rather than directly imposing a universal one.

Method: TS-Router estimates the relative competence of heterogeneous anomaly detectors from pretrained temporal representations and selects suitable specialists for each target series. It derives soft competence supervision from specialists' relative performance on labeled simulated tasks (avoiding reliance on real task labels). At deployment, routing requires no target anomaly labels, and only selected specialists are fitted unsupervisedly on the target series. The method bounds Top-k set-competence regret under representation coverage and conditional competence stability.

Result: Across 16 real-world benchmarks and four complementary evaluation metrics, TS-Router achieves the best overall average rank. Controlled ablations with multiple frozen TSFM encoders support the use of pretrained representations for competence estimation and adaptive specialist selection.

Conclusion: The proposed TS-Router framework successfully addresses the challenge of generalizing time-series anomaly detection across heterogeneous datasets by coordinating specialized detectors through foundation models. The approach demonstrates strong empirical performance and provides theoretical guarantees through bounds on set-competence regret.

Abstract: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) is difficult to generalize across datasets because heterogeneous temporal dynamics imply different notions of normality and favor different detection criteria. While time-series foundation models provide transferable representations, coupling them with a fixed anomaly-scoring mechanism can overlook this variation. This motivates a different perspective on foundation-model-based TSAD: using foundation models to coordinate specialized anomaly criteria rather than directly imposing a universal one. Based on this view, we propose \textbf{TS-Router}, a generalist-representation, specialist-detection framework that estimates the relative competence of heterogeneous anomaly detectors from pretrained temporal representations and selects suitable specialists for each target series. To avoid relying on specialist-performance labels from real tasks, we derive soft competence supervision from specialists' relative performance on labeled simulated tasks. At deployment, routing requires no target anomaly labels, and only the selected specialists are fitted unsupervisedly on the target series. We bound Top-\(k\) set-competence regret under representation coverage and conditional competence stability. Across 16 real-world benchmarks and four complementary evaluation metrics, TS-Router achieves the best overall average rank. Controlled ablations with multiple frozen TSFM encoders further support the use of pretrained representations for competence estimation and adaptive specialist selection. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TS-Router-D8FF.

</details>


### [459] [HADRec: A Hierarchy-Aware Drug Recommendation Framework by Fusing Molecular Knowledge and Electronic Health Record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00984)
*Junke Wang,Hongshun Ling,Li Zhang,Jinjing Wu,Tong Shao,Fang Wang,Yuan Gao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HADRec is a hierarchy-aware drug recommendation framework that integrates molecular knowledge (via ChemBERTa encoding drug SMILES) with electronic health records (via LLaMA-7B encoding clinical notes) using cross-attention fusion and ATC-hierarchical consistency constraints to achieve state-of-the-art medication recommendation performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing drug recommendation methods have two key limitations: (1) drugs are represented as discrete tokens without capturing molecular structures and pharmacological mechanisms, and (2) the "flat" recommendation paradigm ignores the hierarchical structure of the ATC classification system used internationally.

Method: HADRec employs: (1) LLaMA-7B for encoding clinical notes into rich patient representations; (2) ChemBERTa for encoding drug SMILES strings into a global molecular knowledge base; (3) a cross-attention mechanism for deep multimodal fusion between patient states and drug features; (4) a hierarchical predictor with a novel consistency constraint loss to enforce ATC logical dependencies.

Result: Experiments on MIMIC-III show state-of-the-art performance across Jaccard, F1, and PR-AUC metrics. External validation on MIMIC-IV confirms strong generalization under distribution shifts. Calibration analysis shows well-calibrated predictions (ECE = 0.04, Brier = 0.06). Counterfactual evaluation reveals clinically aligned reasoning that disentangles disease-specific treatments from general care.

Conclusion: HADRec establishes a high-performance, interpretable, and clinically grounded pathway toward safe and reliable AI-driven medication recommendation by effectively integrating molecular knowledge with EHR data while respecting ATC hierarchical structure.

Abstract: Accurate medication recommendation is central to clinical decision-making, directly determining therapeutic efficacy and patient safety. However, existing methods suffer from two key limitations: drugs are often abstracted as discrete tokens, ignoring their molecular structures and pharmacological mechanisms, and the commonly used "flat" recommendation paradigm fails to leverage the hierarchical logic of the internationally standardized Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system. To address these issues, we propose HADRec, a Hierarchy-Aware Drug Recommendation framework that integrates molecular knowledge with electronic health records (EHRs). HADRec employs LLaMA-7B to encode clinical notes for rich patient representations and ChemBERTa to encode drug Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System strings, building a global molecular knowledge base. A cross-attention mechanism then performs deep multimodal fusion between patient states and drug features. The framework further incorporates a hierarchical predictor and a novel consistency constraint loss to enforce strict adherence to ATC logical dependencies. Extensive experiments on MIMIC-III demonstrate that HADRec achieves state-of-the-art performance across Jaccard, F1, and PR-AUC. External validation on MIMIC-IV confirms strong generalization under distribution shifts, and calibration analysis shows well-calibrated predictive confidence on MIMIC-IV with ECE = 0.04, and Brier = 0.06. Counterfactual evaluation reveals clinically aligned reasoning, disentangling disease-specific treatments from general care. Together, these results establish HADRec as a high-performance, interpretable, and clinically grounded pathway toward safe and reliable AI-driven medication recommendation.

</details>


### [460] [Neural scaling laws and evolution of learnable activation functions of Kolmogorov-Arnold networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00985)
*Tilen Cadez,Sanghoon Lee,Kyoung-Min Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates neural scaling laws of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) across image classification and scientific regression tasks, revealing a broken neural scaling law (BNSL) behavior where test loss transitions from faster to slower scaling as dataset size increases, with exponents dependent on architecture and task type.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional MLPs use fixed activation functions, while KANs employ learnable activation functions offering better interpretability. However, understanding how KANs scale with data and how their activation functions evolve is crucial for practical applications in scientific domains.

Method: Three KAN variants (BSRBF-KAN, Gottlieb-KAN, Faster-KAN) were evaluated on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and a magnetic parameter estimation task. The study analyzed test loss scaling behavior and structural evolution of activation functions across different dataset sizes.

Result: Test loss exhibits BNSL behavior with two scaling regimes: faster scaling (L ∝ N_D^(-α), α = 0.4-1.5) followed by slower scaling (L ∝ N_D^(-β), β = 0.06-0.6) for image classification. The magnetic regression task shows a single scaling law with exponent 1.28-2.59. Activation functions transition from linear-like to stable symbolic forms as data increases.

Conclusion: KANs follow architecture- and task-dependent scaling laws with broken power-law behavior. The evolution of activation functions from simple to symbolic forms provides a roadmap for efficient KAN application while balancing model expressivity and computational overhead.

Abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) represent a compelling alternative to traditional Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)-based neural networks. By employing activation functions as learnable elements, KANs offer superior interpretability, making them suited for scientific domains. In this work, we investigate the neural scaling laws of KANs and the structural evolution of their learnable activation functions under dataset expansion. Specifically, we evaluate the scaling behavior of three KAN variants---BSRBF-KAN, Gottlieb-KAN, and Faster-KAN---across standard image classification benchmarks (MNIST and Fashion-MNIST) and a specialized scientific regression task (magnetic parameter estimation from domain images of moiré magnetic textures). Our results demonstrate that the test loss ${\cal L}$ exhibits a broken neural scaling law (BNSL) behavior as a function of the dataset size $N_D$. After passing through a random-guess regime, the loss follows architecture- and task-dependent scaling behavior. The loss crosses from a faster- to a slower-scaling branch, ${\cal L}\propto N_D^{-α}$ and ${\cal L}\propto N_D^{-β}$ with $α>β$ for image classification tasks. The exponents $α$ and $β$ depend strongly on both the specific network architecture and the dataset-size regime, ranging from 0.4 to 1.5 and from 0.06 to 0.6, respectively. For the magnetic parameter-regression task, the loss follows a single scaling law with its exponent ranging from 1.28 to 2.59. Additionally, we provide a structural analysis of how activation functions refine their complexity as data volume increases, finding that dataset expansion drives a transition from simple linear-like approximations toward stable, interpretable symbolic forms. These findings provide a quantitative roadmap for the efficient application of KANs while managing the trade-off between model expressivity and computational overhead.

</details>


### [461] [Auditable Algebraic Counting Field for Cryptic-Pocket Detection from Apo Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00988)
*Shan Yu,Xuening Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ACF is a supervised machine learning method that predicts cryptic ligand-binding pocket residues from apo protein structures using explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features compiled into compact lookup tables, without requiring sequence searches or protein language models at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cryptic ligand-binding pockets are not visible in apo (unbound) protein structures, making them difficult to identify. Existing methods lack inspectability—users cannot easily trace predictions back to the underlying structural measurements and training data. This work aims to address both challenges: accurate prediction with fully transparent prediction logic.

Method: The method compiles explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features into compact integer-weighted lookup tables (algebraic counting fields). Each prediction score can be reconstructed from feature values, training counts, table weights, and spatial aggregation. No sequence search, structural-template transfer, or protein language model is used at inference.

Result: On an external set of 57 post-CryptoBench apo-holo units, ACF exceeded P2Rank by +0.044 in mean paired ROC-AUC (95% CI [+0.010, +0.079]). However, the advantage was dataset-dependent: on official folds, ROC-AUC and matched-budget F1 differences against P2Rank remained unresolved, and a second external evaluation did not confirm gains from added structural features.

Conclusion: ACF provides a compact predictor with externally validated signal and an inspectable path from structural measurements and training counts to residue scores. The method shows promise but with dataset-dependent performance, suggesting careful validation is needed for new target families.

Abstract: Cryptic ligand-binding pockets are not apparent in experimentally determined apo structures, making them difficult to identify from unbound receptor geometry. A complementary challenge is to make the structural measurements and learned evidence behind each prediction directly inspectable. We introduce a supervised algebraic counting field (ACF) for predicting cryptic-pocket residues from apo structures. ACF compiles explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features into compact, integer-weighted lookup tables. Each prediction score can be reconstructed from feature values, training counts, table weights, and spatial aggregation, without sequence search, structural-template transfer, or a protein language model at inference. We evaluate ACF on CryptoBench and two locked external collections, separating ranking performance from the effects of residue-calling budgets. On an external set of 57 post-CryptoBench apo-holo units, ACF exceeded P2Rank by +0.044 in mean paired ROC-AUC (multiplicity-adjusted 95% CI [+0.010, +0.079]). The advantage was dataset-dependent: official-fold ROC-AUC and matched-budget F1 differences against P2Rank remained unresolved, and a second external evaluation did not confirm gains from added structural features. ACF thus provides a compact predictor with externally validated signal and an inspectable path from structural measurements and training counts to residue scores.

</details>


### [462] [Adapter Thickets: Splitting an RLVR Budget Beats Concentrating It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00991)
*Jonathan Williams,Esin Tureci Karthik R. Narasimhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper reveals a critical flaw in the standard test-time scaling pipeline: combining RLVR training with majority voting. RLVR sharpens policy samples to make similar errors, so voting cannot correct them. The solution is an "adapter thicket" - splitting training budget across K independent LoRA adapters instead of one fully trained adapter, which maintains diversity and improves majority vote accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The standard pipeline for test-time scaling combines RLVR (to improve each completion) with majority voting (to aggregate multiple samples). The authors discovered this composition is "lossy" - while RLVR improves single-sample accuracy, it actually harms majority vote performance because the trained policy makes more correlated errors, preventing voting from correcting mistakes.

Method: The authors conducted experiments across 4 models (1.5B-8B parameters) with 160 completions per problem. They compared: (1) single LoRA adapter trained on full RLVR budget, (2) an "adapter thicket" - K separate LoRA adapters each trained on disjoint data shards, (3) early-stopped single adapter as control. They tracked voter error correlation and majority vote accuracy throughout training.

Result: Training a single LoRA adapter improved single-sample accuracy on all models but reduced majority vote accuracy below the base model in 3/4 models (by up to 4.8 points). During training, voter errors became increasingly correlated, causing majority vote accuracy to peak early then decline by up to 7.0 points. The adapter thicket approach outperformed the fully trained adapter in all 16 (model, K) settings. For K≥4, thickets stayed within 0.8 points of base model or above. The thicket's advantage grew from 1.3 points (16 votes) to 3.3 points (160 votes).

Conclusion: When the plan is to sample and vote, RLVR training budget should be spent "broad" (across multiple diverse adapters) rather than "deep" (intensively training one adapter). The concentration of errors in strongly trained policies is the fundamental cause, not RLVR itself. This insight suggests a paradigm shift in how to apply RLVR for test-time scaling scenarios.

Abstract: Majority voting over sampled completions is the workhorse of test-time scaling, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is the workhorse for making each completion better. The standard pipeline composes the two: train one policy with RLVR, then sample it many times and vote. We show that this composition is lossy. A vote can only overturn mistakes that its voters do not share, and RLVR sharpens a policy so that its samples increasingly make the same mistakes. With every method drawing exactly $160$ completions per problem, training a single LoRA adapter on the full RLVR budget raises single-sample accuracy on every model we test ($1.5$B-$8$B). Yet on three of four models it leaves the majority vote below that of the untrained base model, by up to $4.8$ points. The damage builds during training: voter errors grow steadily more correlated, and the majority vote accuracy peaks early before falling by up to $7.0$ points. The cause is concentration, not RLVR itself. We split the same data and training budget across $K$ LoRA adapters, each trained on its own random disjoint shard, and call the result an adapter thicket. Thickets out-vote the fully trained adapter in all $16$ (model, $K$) settings, and for $K{\geq}4$ they stay within $0.8$ points of the base model or above it. A single adapter stopped early, at a thicket member's step count, is a strong control that matches thickets for small $K$. For $K{\geq}8$, thickets keep more of RLVR's single-sample gain and out-vote this control in six of eight settings. The cost of concentration also grows with the number of votes: from $16$ to $160$ votes, the thicket's lead over the fully trained adapter widens from $1.3$ to $3.3$ points. When the plan is to sample and vote, an RLVR budget is better spent broad than deep.

</details>


### [463] [Reliability-aware short-term roll prediction for unmanned surface vehicles via multi-task learning and adaptive centralization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00996)
*Kaizhen Li,Xi Zhou,Zihao Wang,Dan Zhang,Jianjian Liu,Xiaowei Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a reliability-aware prediction paradigm for unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) roll prediction, integrating confidence assessment into the predictive pipeline using a multi-task learning architecture with dual heads for simultaneous prediction and reliability quantification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While existing studies focus on improving prediction accuracy for USV roll prediction, the quantification of prediction reliability remains insufficiently addressed. This gap limits risk-sensitive downstream applications and autonomous decision-making.

Method: The proposed architecture uses a multi-task learning structure with: 1) A shared feature extraction backbone feeding into dual heads - a regression head for precise roll prediction and a quantification head for confidence scoring. 2) An adaptive centralization strategy tailored for short-term real-time roll prediction to improve model generalization under varying operational conditions.

Result: Experiments on a real-sea dataset demonstrate that the proposed method effectively quantifies the reliability of prediction results and maintains superior generalization under varying conditions.

Conclusion: The reliability-aware prediction paradigm offers significant potential for practical engineering applications by providing both accurate predictions and corresponding confidence scores for risk-sensitive downstream tasks.

Abstract: Reliable roll prediction of unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) is essential for ensuring navi?gational safety and enhancing autonomous decision-making. While existing studies primarily focus on improving prediction accuracy, the quantification of prediction reliability remains insufficiently addressed. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a reliability-aware prediction paradigm that integrates confidence assessment into the predictive pipeline. The architecture utilizes a multi-task learning structure where a shared feature extraction backbone feeds into dual heads: a regression head for precise roll prediction and a quantification head for confidence scoring. This configuration provides accurate prediction and corresponding confidence for risk?sensitive downstream tasks. In addition, an adaptive centralization strategy tailored for short?term real-time roll prediction is introduced to improve model generalization under varying operational conditions. Experiments conducted on a real-sea dataset demonstrate that the proposed method effectively quantifies the reliability of prediction results and maintains superior generalization under varying conditions, offering significant potential for practical engineering applications.

</details>


### [464] [Optimal Transport Reweighting for Robust Learning under Spurious Correlations and Label Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01028)
*Sung Ho Jo,Seonghwi Kim,Wonsang Yun,Minwoo Chae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: POTER is a reweighting framework that uses optimal transport to address performance degradation under subpopulation shift, particularly when label noise is present. It constructs a reference distribution from limited validation group annotations and derives sample importance from transport geometry between training and reference distributions, requiring only a single ERM training stage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Machine learning models often rely on spurious correlations (shortcut features) that fail to generalize across subgroups, causing performance degradation under subpopulation shift. Existing loss-based methods to identify informative samples become distorted under label noise, as mislabeled samples may also incur large losses and contaminate reweighting. This intersection of subpopulation shift and label noise remains underexplored.

Method: POTER uses optimal transport to derive sample importance by measuring alignment at the individual-sample level between the training distribution and a reference distribution constructed from limited validation group annotations. It downweights mislabeled or strongly bias-aligned samples while assigning higher importance to samples better aligned with the reference distribution. The method requires only a single ERM training stage, moving beyond the retraining paradigm common in prior work.

Result: POTER achieves state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy across standard benchmarks and noisy-label settings, including cases where label corruption is concentrated within minority subgroups.

Conclusion: The optimal transport-based reweighting approach effectively addresses both subpopulation shift and label noise simultaneously by leveraging transport geometry rather than relying on loss signals, offering a practical single-stage solution that outperforms existing methods.

Abstract: Machine learning models often suffer performance degradation under subpopulation shift, particularly when spurious correlations cause models to rely on shortcut features that fail to generalize across subgroups. A recent line of work mitigates this issue by using loss-based signals to identify informative samples, but these signals can become severely distorted under label noise: mislabeled samples may also incur large losses and contaminate subsequent reweighting or retraining. Despite its practical importance, this intersection remains largely underexplored. We propose POTER, a reweighting framework based on optimal transport that derives sample importance from the transport geometry between the training distribution and a reference distribution constructed from limited validation group annotations. By measuring alignment at the individual-sample level rather than relying on loss, POTER downweights mislabeled or strongly bias-aligned samples while assigning higher importance to samples better aligned with the reference distribution. In addition, POTER requires only a single ERM training stage, moving beyond the retraining paradigm common in recent work. Across standard benchmarks and noisy-label settings, POTER achieves state-of-the-art worst-group accuracy, including cases where label corruption is concentrated within minority subgroups.

</details>


### [465] [SLIM: Simplex-Lattice Interpolation Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01037)
*Seongcheol Jeong,Masahiro Suzuki,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SLIM (Simplex-Lattice Interpolation Merging) is a method that uses classical mixture design to construct a quadratic surrogate model for optimizing merging coefficients in large language models, requiring only minimum evaluations of individual experts and equal-weight pairs to accurately predict multi-expert mixture performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Optimizing merging coefficients for large language models requires many costly benchmark evaluations, making it expensive and time-consuming to find optimal combinations of expert models.

Method: SLIM constructs a quadratic surrogate of aggregate performance on the coefficient simplex using classical mixture design. The method determines the surrogate with the minimum number of measurements by evaluating individual experts and equal-weight pairs, then optimizes the surrogate without further target-metric evaluations.

Result: Experiments on two model architectures demonstrate accurate prediction of unseen multi-expert mixtures and competitive merge performance under limited evaluation budgets. Matched-budget comparisons show that structured evaluation points improve prediction fidelity over random designs, including those using regularized fitting.

Conclusion: Structured evaluation points (as in SLIM) significantly improve prediction fidelity over random designs, even when compared to regularized fitting approaches, enabling efficient LLM merging under limited evaluation budgets.

Abstract: Optimizing merging coefficients for large language models can require many costly benchmark evaluations. We propose \textbf{Simplex-Lattice Interpolation Merging (SLIM)}, which constructs a quadratic surrogate of aggregate performance on the coefficient simplex using a classical mixture design. Evaluations of individual experts and equal-weight pairs determine the surrogate with the minimum number of measurements needed to identify a general quadratic on this domain. SLIM then optimizes the surrogate without further target-metric evaluations. Experiments on two model architectures demonstrate accurate prediction of unseen multi-expert mixtures and competitive merge performance under limited evaluation budgets. Matched-budget comparisons show that structured evaluation points improve prediction fidelity over random designs, including those using regularized fitting.

</details>


### [466] [Kernelized Activation Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01062)
*Laziz U. Abdullaev,Minh-Hieu Pham,Bach Do,Khoat Than,Tan M. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KAS introduces kernelized activation steering, lifting traditional input-independent activation steering (like DiM) into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space to enable locally adaptive, geometry-aware interventions across activation space.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard activation steering methods like Difference-in-Means apply a single input-independent steering vector across all activations, limiting expressivity and ignoring the local geometry of the activation space. This restricts the ability to perform nuanced, context-aware interventions.

Method: KAS formulates steering as an optimization problem expressed purely via kernel evaluations, yielding an implicit, activation-dependent steering score without constructing explicit feature maps. It uses kernel functions to capture local geometry, where DiM is recovered as a special case under a linear kernel, while richer kernels enable geometry-aware interventions.

Result: Across standard activation steering tasks, including jailbreaking LLMs and image style control, KAS outperforms or is on par with existing methods.

Conclusion: KAS provides a unifying framework that generalizes standard activation steering while enabling locally adaptive, nonlinear steering fields. The kernel-based approach successfully captures activation space geometry and achieves superior or comparable performance across diverse tasks.

Abstract: Activation steering provides a simple, training-free mechanism for controlling attributes of generative models such as sentiment, style, and helpfulness. However, standard approaches such as Difference-in-Means apply a single input-independent steering vector across all activations, limiting expressivity and ignoring the local geometry of the activation space. We propose Kernelized Activation Steering (KAS), a unifying framework that lifts activation steering into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. KAS formulates steering as an optimization problem expressed purely via kernel evaluations, yielding an implicit, activation-dependent steering score without constructing explicit feature maps. Unlike DiM, KAS induces locally adaptive steering: each activation is modified according to its relative position with respect to source and target reference sets, producing a nonlinear steering field over the representation space. Importantly, DiM is recovered as a special case under a linear kernel, while richer kernels enable geometry-aware interventions. Across standard activation steering tasks, including jailbreaking LLMs and image style control, KAS outperforms or is on par with the existing methods.

</details>


### [467] [GLoC-EHR: Evidence-Cited Clinical Reasoning over Global Context and Local EHR Events](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01076)
*Chaiho Shin,Kwangsoo Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GLoC-EHR is a multimodal language model for clinical EHR records that uses global and local memory mechanisms to generate hospital-course summaries and answer clinical questions with evidence citation. It outperforms zero-shot LLMs on MIMIC-IV outcome tasks and transfers well to EHRSHOT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical EHR records contain sequential clinical codes representing patient trajectories. Answering clinical questions requires understanding both the overall context and specific supporting events. Existing methods either lack the ability to cite evidence or cannot effectively capture the full trajectory context.

Method: GLoC-EHR uses a dual memory architecture: (1) Global memory encoding the entire trajectory as fixed-size context, and (2) Local memory of selected events. The model is trained to generate hospital-course summaries from global memory and describe masked concepts from local memory, aligning both with clinical text. Training involves rationale fine-tuning followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rewards for correct answers and record-supported evidence.

Result: On three MIMIC-IV outcome tasks, GLoC-EHR achieves the highest macro AUROC among compared models when answering directly. Zero-shot LLMs reading serialized records fall far behind. With evidence-cited reasoning, it maintains performance close to its direct multi-task counterpart. Evidence terms reduce unsupported evidence without detectable macro AUROC change. Local memory adds distinct supported findings, especially under strict matching. Without retraining, it transfers to EHRSHOT on par with EHR-BERT and answers two unseen laboratory questions better than zero-shot prompting.

Conclusion: GLoC-EHR effectively combines global trajectory context with local event memory for clinical question answering. Its evidence-cited reasoning mechanism maintains performance while providing supporting citations. The model demonstrates strong transfer learning capabilities to unseen datasets and tasks without retraining.

Abstract: Structured electronic health records (EHRs) contain a patient's clinical trajectory as a sequence of clinical codes. Answering clinical questions from such records requires both the context of the whole trajectory and the specific events that support the answer. We introduce GLoC-EHR, a multimodal language model that reads a contextual encoding of the record through a fixed-size global memory of the trajectory and a local memory of selected events. The model learns to generate hospital-course summaries from the global memory and descriptions of masked concepts from the local memory, aligning both with clinical text. It is then trained to cite evidence before answering, through rationale fine-tuning followed by group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with rewards for correct answers and record-supported evidence. On three MIMIC-IV outcome tasks, GLoC-EHR attains the highest macro AUROC among the compared models when it answers directly, whereas zero-shot LLMs reading the serialized record fall far behind. With evidence-cited reasoning, it stays close to its direct multi-task counterpart in macro AUROC, and the evidence terms of the objective reduce unsupported evidence at a similar macro AUROC. The local memory adds distinct supported findings, particularly under strict matching, without a detectable change in macro AUROC. Without retraining, GLoC-EHR transfers to EHRSHOT on par with EHR-BERT and answers two unseen laboratory questions better than zero-shot prompting of its own backbone.

</details>


### [468] [Dataset Identity, Not Novelty: The Source of an Inflated OOD Detection Gain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01096)
*Donghoon Lee,Shinjin Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper reveals a fundamental flaw in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection evaluation: current benchmarks report inflated performance by fitting on OOD dataset identity rather than true novelty detection. The authors introduce "inflation" as the gap between reported performance (fitting on partial OOD data) and actual performance (holding out the entire OOD dataset).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current OOD detection benchmarks fit detectors on OOD data and validate on held-out samples of the same OOD dataset. This validation only rules out memorizing individual images, but fails to detect when the detector has learned to recognize which dataset it is (dataset identity) rather than detecting genuine novelty. The practical implication is that a detector installed by a practitioner will encounter OOD data from sources never used in fitting, making the reported numbers misleading.

Method: The authors measure "inflation" by holding out the entire OOD dataset (instead of just samples) during validation. They test across a range of combiners on ImageNet and CIFAR-100 backbones. They also perform controlled experiments varying whether the input exposes class identity to isolate the source of inflation. They derive a closed-form solution to compute inflation from fitting rows.

Result: Most of the gain reported by standard protocols comes from dataset identity recognition rather than novelty detection. The effect is not ordinary overfitting (varying fit size doesn't change what survives). The inflation depends on whether the input exposes class identity, and controlled experiments separate the inflation on every backbone of both benchmarks. A closed-form solution accurately predicts which fits will inflate. Only the single constant fit on a designated validation dataset survives; anything above it reports gains not returned by the hold-out protocol.

Conclusion: The standard OOD detection evaluation protocol produces severely inflated numbers. Only the baseline constant fit (already used in the field) provides honest performance. A practitioner can use the closed-form solution to identify inflated fits without running the hold-out protocol. On one benchmark, what survives actually falls while what is reported climbs, indicating the problem is getting worse with more complex methods.

Abstract: A post-hoc out-of-distribution (OOD) detector reads the activations of a trained classifier and returns a score. It fits that score on in-distribution data, and the benchmarks that evaluate it supply a second piece of OOD data for the fitting itself. Some detectors tune a constant on it. Others fit a direction in feature space or train a flexible combiner and report the number that it reaches as the gain that is still available. Every such fit is validated on held-out samples of the same OOD dataset. That check rules out memorizing individual images. It says nothing about a fit that has instead learned which dataset it is looking at, and a direction that recognizes one OOD dataset rather than novelty passes it perfectly. The detector that a practitioner installs meets OOD data from a source that nobody fitted it on, so the difference decides what the reported number is worth. We measure it by holding out the whole OOD dataset rather than a sample of it, and we call that gap the inflation. We read it across a range of combiners on ImageNet and CIFAR-100 backbones. Most of the gain that the usual protocol reports turns out to be dataset identity rather than novelty. The size of the fit does not move what survives, so the effect is not ordinary overfitting. The share depends instead on whether the input exposes class identity, and two controls that vary that property alone separate the inflation on every backbone of both benchmarks. A closed form accounts for the effect and computes it from the fitting rows, so a practitioner can tell which fits will inflate without running the hold-out protocol. One of these fits survives, namely the single constant that the field already picks on a designated validation dataset. Anything above it reports a gain that the hold-out protocol does not return, and on one benchmark what survives falls while what is reported climbs.

</details>


### [469] [How Much Can Language Models Gain from Test-Time Computation?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01110)
*Bangji Yang,Jingyuan Li,Jiajun Fan,Yi Evie Zhang,Ruihan Guo,Hongba Ma,Neil He,Chumeng Liang,Qinglong Zheng,Zhanghan Ni,Ge Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SELF-POT is a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures test-time scaling potential across competition mathematics, competitive programming, and agentic workflows. It compares direct inference with parallel sampling and self-revision under unified budget rules, charging all model calls (including selection and critique) in dollars to provide accurate cost-benefit analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The research addresses a critical gap in understanding test-time scaling: how much can additional inference computation improve a language model, and at what cost? Previous comparisons evaluated one domain at a time and rarely accounted for selection costs in the budget.

Method: The framework separates candidate coverage from final accuracy, tracks correctness transitions under revision, and measures protocol completion alongside task success. It evaluates five low-cost reasoning models on 350 sealed tasks using Claude Opus 5.5 Direct as reference, comparing direct inference against parallel sampling and self-revision under fixed budget multiples.

Result: For programming tasks, public-example selection increased correct submissions from 376 to 453 while saving 12-49% of API cost. Retaining available candidates when judging fails recovered 61 submissions. For mathematics, judging with fallback yielded 186 correct submissions versus 182 for voting, while voting saved 12-21% of API cost.

Conclusion: Test-time scaling returns are highly domain-dependent and depend on selection rules and failure handling. The controlled replays demonstrate how selection and failure handling significantly change gains from generated candidates, and quantify the marginal value of a model judge.

Abstract: How much can test-time computation improve a language model, and at what cost? Test-time scaling is widely proposed as a substitute for larger models, but existing comparisons mostly evaluate one domain at a time and rarely charge selection to the budget. We introduce SELF-POT, a benchmark and evaluation framework that measures the test-time potential of a model across competition mathematics, competitive programming, and agentic workflows. SELF-POT separates candidate coverage from final accuracy on static tasks, tracks correctness transitions under revision, and measures protocol completion alongside task success in agentic environments. Under a unified budget rule, it compares Direct inference with parallel sampling and self-revision under fixed multiples of the Direct budget, and charges every model call, including selection and critique, in dollars.
