This design supports two kinds of comparison: the gain a model obtains from additional inference, and a lower-cost model with additional inference against a stronger model. Across five low-cost reasoning models on 350 sealed tasks, with Claude Opus 5.5 Direct as the reference, the returns depend on the domain, the selection rule, and failure handling. When we replay the retained programming candidate pools, public-example selection raises correct submissions from 376 to 453 of 500 scheduled cells while saving 12-49% of logical API cost across models, and simply retaining an available candidate when judging fails recovers 61 submissions at unchanged cost. On identical mathematics pools, judging with fallback yields 186 correct submissions versus 182 for voting, while voting saves 12-21% of logical API cost. These controlled replays show how selection and failure handling change the gains realized from the same generated candidates, and they quantify the marginal value of a model judge.

</details>


### [470] [Latent Information Sharing for Accelerating Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01126)
*Seungjun Lee,Ensieh Khazaei,Dimitrios Hatzinakos,Baturalp Buyukates,Sunwoo Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel latent information sharing scheme for federated learning that addresses client drift by sharing hidden-layer activations. The method mitigates data heterogeneity across clients while preserving convergence guarantees and data privacy, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to existing methods like FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedPVR, FedProto, and SplitFed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated learning faces significant challenges from client drift caused by data heterogeneity across clients, which hinders efficient training of a global model. Existing approaches have limitations in addressing this issue comprehensively.

Method: The proposed method shares a small amount of hidden-layer activations (latent information) directly between clients to mitigate data heterogeneity. This approach preserves convergence guarantees and data privacy while reducing communication overhead.

Result: The method demonstrates superior model accuracy compared to existing FL approaches (FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedPVR, FedProto, SplitFed) under fixed round budget without incurring excessive communication overhead. Theoretical and empirical results confirm improved training efficiency.

Conclusion: This work presents a promising new knowledge aggregation scheme for federated learning and provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of activation sharing on federated optimization, offering a viable solution to the client drift problem.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a communication-efficient distributed learning paradigm. However, client drift remains one of the most critical challenges, hindering the efficient training of a global model. In this study, we propose a novel latent information sharing scheme that directly mitigates data heterogeneity across clients. Our theoretical and empirical results show that sharing a small amount of hidden-layer activations significantly improves training efficiency while preserving convergence guarantees and data privacy. Furthermore, we compare our method with existing FL approaches designed to address client drift, including FedProx, SCAFFOLD, FedPVR, FedProto, and SplitFed, and demonstrate superior model accuracy under a fixed round budget without incurring excessive communication overhead. Overall, this work presents a promising new knowledge aggregation scheme and provides a comprehensive analysis of the impact of activation sharing on federated optimization.

</details>


### [471] [Does Scaling Reinforcement Learning Really Require More Training?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01133)
*Bangji Yang,Jiajun Fan,Hongba Ma,Ruihan Guo,Ge Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SURGE achieves policy-space scaling by combining two RL checkpoints (anchor + donor) through spectral decomposition, creating stronger single policies without additional training or inference compute. Results: 54.17% on DeepSeek AIME24 (vs 50.83% native max) and 83.7% on OLMo HumanEval+ (vs 82.8%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current reasoning scaling relies on RL training or increased inference compute. This work shows that a completed RL training history contains deployable policies stronger than any single checkpoint, enabling scaling without additional training or inference costs.

Method: SURGE combines two checkpoints from the same RL run: a high-accuracy anchor and a competitive donor with shorter responses. It expresses both as changes from shared initialization, spectrally decomposes the anchor's update to retain its dominant component, then incorporates the donor's complementary component. Block size is determined from weights without testing candidate policies.

Result: DeepSeek AIME24: 54.17% vs 50.83% native maximum; OLMo HumanEval+: 83.7% vs 82.8%. Gains exceed observed training curves while using fewer reasoning tokens than the anchor.

Conclusion: Stored RL history is a reusable scaling resource—the capability available from a training run need not end at its best checkpoint. Policy-space scaling can extract stronger policies from fixed RL histories without extending training or increasing per-query inference.

Abstract: Scaling reasoning typically spends more compute on reinforcement learning (RL) or on inference. We show that a completed RL training history can yield policies stronger than the checkpoints visited by its optimizer. We call this policy-space scaling: expanding the deployable policy set accessible from a fixed RL history, without extending training or increasing per-query inference computation. We instantiate it with SURGE (Scaling Up RL Gradient-free via Eigenspace fusion). SURGE combines two checkpoints from the same RL run: a high-accuracy anchor and a competitive donor that generates shorter responses. It expresses both checkpoints as changes from their shared initialization, then spectrally decomposes the anchor's update to retain its dominant component and incorporate the donor's complementary component. With a fixed target for how much of the anchor update to retain, SURGE determines the block size from the weights without testing candidate policies. We evaluate two 1.5B mathematical-reasoning histories, DeepSeek and Nemotron, and one 7B coding history, OLMo. SURGE improves benchmark-average accuracy over both input checkpoints while using fewer reasoning tokens than the anchor. It reaches 54.17% on DeepSeek AIME24 against a measured native maximum of 50.83%, and 83.7% on OLMo HumanEval+ against 82.8%. These gains exceed the observed training curves. Geometric controls support the importance of RL-update structure beyond weight displacement or token reduction alone. Each constructed model runs as a single policy. Our findings identify stored RL history as a reusable scaling resource: the capability available from a training run need not end at its best checkpoint.

</details>


### [472] [Parameter-Efficient Distributionally Robust Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models under Subpopulation Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01143)
*Seonghwi Kim,Sung Ho Jo,Minwoo Chae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DR-TFM is a parameter-efficient distributionally robust adaptation framework for tabular foundation models that addresses poor performance on underrepresented groups under subpopulation shift without requiring true group annotations. It fine-tunes a query scaling network (updating only 0.016% of parameters for TabPFN-3) while keeping all other parameters fixed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite strong mean accuracy, tabular foundation models (TFMs) perform poorly on underrepresented groups when group proportions change between training and deployment (subpopulation shift). Existing methods either require true group annotations or are not parameter-efficient.

Method: DR-TFM adjusts attention to labeled context examples by fine-tuning an existing query scaling network or adding and training one, while keeping all other parameters fixed. The framework uses two robust objectives: estimated groups or source conditional distributions derived from training data.

Result: DR-TFM achieves substantially higher average worst-group accuracy than pretrained TFMs and robust baselines across five tabular benchmarks, while maintaining competitive mean group accuracy. It also improves average worst-group accuracy on ACS Income and across four additional TFMs.

Conclusion: DR-TFM provides an effective parameter-efficient solution for improving robustness to subpopulation shift in tabular foundation models without requiring true group annotations, demonstrating versatility across multiple TFMs and benchmarks.

Abstract: Despite strong mean accuracy, tabular foundation models (TFMs) can perform poorly on underrepresented groups under subpopulation shift, where group proportions change between training and deployment. We propose DR-TFM, a parameter-efficient distributionally robust adaptation framework that requires no true group annotations. DR-TFM adjusts attention to labeled context examples by fine-tuning an existing query scaling network or adding and training one, while keeping all other parameters fixed. We instantiate the framework with two robust objectives using estimated groups or source conditional distributions derived from training data. For TabPFN-3, adaptation updates only 0.016% of the pretrained model's parameters. Across five tabular benchmarks, DR-TFM achieves substantially higher average worst-group accuracy than pretrained TFMs and the compared robust baselines without true group annotations, while maintaining competitive mean group accuracy. DR-TFM also improves average worst-group accuracy on ACS Income and across four additional TFMs.

</details>


### [473] [Looping Beyond Twice: A Scalable Recipe for Looped Mixture-of-Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01153)
*Di He,Pengxiang Li,Da Chang,Qingyan Meng,Lu Yin,Shiwei Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LOOM addresses scaling issues in looped MoE transformers by stabilizing recurrence through residual scaling and input re-injection, and diversifying computation via per-loop routers and Looping Residual, achieving up to 9-12 loops with significant perplexity and zero-shot accuracy improvements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While looped Transformers add recurrent depth without increasing parameters, the benefits diminish for large MoE LLMs due to two main obstacles: (1) the curse of depth causing hidden-state variance growth, and (2) expert selection collapse where routers repeatedly select the same experts across loops, wasting computation.

Method: LOOM introduces three key mechanisms: (1) Scaled residual updates to bound variance growth, (2) Input embedding re-injection at every loop to maintain stability, (3) Per-loop routers that engage different experts and a Looping Residual mechanism that carries earlier outputs forward to increase computational diversity.

Result: Under near-iso-FLOP conditions, the 700M model with 5 loops reduces perplexity from 18.36 to 16.54 and improves average zero-shot accuracy from 38.84% to 39.53%. Without FLOP matching, the 1.7B model trained on 60B tokens peaks at 9 loops, reducing perplexity from 9.62 to 7.77 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 42.4% to 47.7%. Stable scaling to 9-12 loops is achieved across 100M-1.7B models.

Conclusion: LOOM successfully enables stable scaling of looped MoE transformers by addressing both the variance growth and expert selection collapse problems. The approach demonstrates that recurrent depth can be effectively scaled in large MoE LLMs, with substantial improvements in both perplexity and zero-shot capabilities.

Abstract: Looped Transformers introduce recurrent depth as a new scaling axis for LLMs: by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, they increase effective depth without increasing parameter count. However, the benefits of looping remain unclear for large MoE LLMs under FLOPs-matched comparisons. The main reason is that the gains from additional iterations diminish quickly and can even turn into degradation, so the extra FLOPs spent on looping yield little substantial improvement. Consequently, prior work typically settles on two loops. We identify two main obstacles to scaling looped MoE. First, looping inherits and amplifies the curse of depth: hidden-state variance grows with each iteration as residual updates accumulate, which destabilizes deep recurrence and causes representations to drift. Second, looped MoE suffers from expert selection collapse: routers repeatedly select the same experts across loops, so extra iterations add computation without adding computational diversity. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose LOOM, built on a single principle: each loop should contribute new computation while keeping the recurrent state stable. LOOM stabilizes recurrence by scaling residual updates to bound variance growth and re-injecting the input embedding at every loop, and diversifies it through per-loop routers that engage different experts and a Looping Residual that carries earlier outputs forward. Experiments across 100M-1.7B models show stable scaling to 9-12 loops. Under near-iso-FLOP, the 700M model performs best at 5 loops, reducing perplexity from 18.36 to 16.54 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 38.84% to 39.53% over the non-looped baseline. Without FLOP matching, the 1.7B model trained on 60B tokens peaks at 9 loops, reducing perplexity from 9.62 to 7.77 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 42.4% to 47.7%. Code is available https://github.com/hed-ucas/LOOM.

</details>


### [474] [Persistent Depth Ordering amid Shifting Block-Bypass Responses in Language Model Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01165)
*Shengye Tao,Yinzhu Cheng,Haihua Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates how layer intervention responses in language models evolve throughout pretraining, rather than just examining single checkpoints. Using single-block identity bypass experiments across five model trajectories and 11 model-domain combinations, the authors find that while depth ordering remains recognizable, the magnitudes of responses redistribute over training. Nearby checkpoints show stronger rank correspondence than distant ones, with large changes concentrating at recurrent positions across text samples. Different models (Pythia vs OLMo-2 7B) show distinct patterns in how bypass effects relate to downstream sensitivity, suggesting that intervention responses should be interpreted in the context of training evolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most layer intervention studies examine only single training checkpoints, leaving open whether observed patterns reflect persistent organization or transient training effects. The authors aim to understand which depth-dependent intervention responses are stable throughout pretraining and which are temporary consequences of training dynamics.

Method: The study uses single-block identity bypass on fixed teacher-forced contexts across five released trajectories (Pythia, OLMo, etc.) and 11 model-domain combinations. They conduct controlled experiments with replicated Pythia runs and OLMo-2 7B to examine how bypass effects change and relate to downstream sensitivity across training.

Result: Block-bypass responses retain recognizable depth ordering while magnitudes redistribute over training. Nearby checkpoints preserve stronger rank correspondence than distant ones. Large changes concentrate at positions that recur across text samples and transfer across evaluation domains. In Pythia runs, local missing-update magnitude grows while pooled matched downstream response decreases; OLMo-2 7B exhibits a different balance. Responses depend on perturbation strength and direction without targeted compensation.

Conclusion: Longitudinal layer sensitivity is structured but not static. Single-checkpoint intervention responses should be interpreted in the context of how the underlying perturbation pathway evolves during training. The study emphasizes the importance of considering training dynamics when analyzing internal model organization through interventions.

Abstract: Layer interventions are widely used to probe the internal organization of language models, yet most analyses examine a single training checkpoint even though model representations and computations evolve throughout pretraining. This leaves open which depth-dependent intervention responses reflect persistent organization and which are transient consequences of training. We study this question using single-block identity bypass on fixed teacher-forced contexts across five released trajectories and 11 model-domain combinations. We find that block-bypass responses retain recognizable depth ordering while their magnitudes redistribute: nearby checkpoints preserve stronger rank correspondence than distant ones, and large changes concentrate at positions that recur across text samples and transfer across evaluation domains. Controlled experiments further show that changes in the natural bypass effect cannot be reduced to a single downstream sensitivity: in replicated Pythia runs, local missing-update magnitude grows while the pooled matched downstream response decreases, whereas OLMo-2 7B exhibits a different balance. These matched responses also depend on perturbation strength and direction, without identifying targeted compensation. Together, our results show that longitudinal layer sensitivity is structured but not static, and that single-checkpoint intervention responses should be interpreted in the context of how the underlying perturbation pathway evolves during training.

</details>


### [475] [Detect, Explain, Interpret: An End-to-End Benchmark for Time Series Anomaly Detection, Explainability and Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01168)
*Roberto Stanzione,Jules Barbe,Magali Parrino,Jérémie Fourmann,Paul Boniol*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SHAD is a new benchmark for time series anomaly detection that addresses the lack of explainability and interpretability in existing methods. It contains 215 multivariate, high-dimensional time series from real-world cloud storage systems with rich semantic annotations. The benchmark evaluates detection methods, explainability (dimension contribution analysis), and interpretability (frozen LLM baselines).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the gap between current TSAD methods and practical needs: most detectors ignore domain context, lack explainability and interpretability, and existing benchmarks focus mainly on detection accuracy without adequate semantic annotations for human-understandable interpretations of anomalies.

Method: The paper introduces SHAD benchmark with 215 multivariate, high-dimensional time series from Scality's cloud storage systems, containing rich contextual information and three families of anomalies with varying severity. They evaluate baseline methods across three dimensions: (1) Detection - benchmarking existing anomaly detectors; (2) Explainability - evaluating dimension contribution to anomaly scores; (3) Interpretability - testing frozen LLM baselines for localizing and interpreting anomalies.

Result: The paper provides a comprehensive benchmark dataset and baseline evaluations across detection, explainability, and interpretability dimensions. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed benchmark for evaluating TSAD pipelines and highlight the potential of LLM-based approaches for interpretability tasks.

Conclusion: SHAD fills a critical gap in TSAD research by providing a fully annotated benchmark with rich semantic information that supports evaluation of detection, explainability, and interpretability. This enables more holistic evaluation of time series anomaly detection methods and paves the way for developing more interpretable and explainable anomaly detection systems.

Abstract: Time Series Anomaly Detection has received increasing attention, driven by the growing availability of complex time series data. This surge has led to the development of numerous detection methods, as well as a variety of benchmarks aimed at thoroughly evaluating their performance. However, most existing detectors remain largely agnostic to domain context, overlooking explainability and interpretability. One of the main reasons for this gap is that current benchmarks primarily focus on detection accuracy, and only few of them evaluate spatial explainability. Moreover, no benchmark currently provides sufficiently rich semantic annotations to support the generation of human-understandable interpretations of anomalies. To address these limitations, we introduce SHAD (Scality High-dimensional Anomaly Detection benchmark), a fully annotated benchmark composed of 215 multivariate, high-dimensional time series collected from real-world distributed cloud storage systems operated by Scality. The proposed dataset includes rich contextual information, covering three families of anomalies with varying degrees of severity. As further contribution, we provide a foundation for future work by evaluating baseline methods for Detection, Explainability, and Interpretability, covering all stages of a TSAD pipeline. For Detection, we benchmark a wide range of existing anomaly detectors, testing their effectiveness on the proposed real-world dataset. Then, we consider explainability by evaluating whether measuring the contribution of each dimension in the generated anomaly score can provide accurate anomaly attributions. Finally, for interpretability, we investigate the effectiveness of frozen LLM baselines in localizing and interpreting anomalies.

</details>


### [476] [Learning Rate Transfer for Hybrid Transformer-SSM Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01172)
*Jimin Seo,Gyubok Lee,Yeonsik Jo,Kiwoong Yoo,Yeongoon Kim,Minhae Oh,Jin Woo Koo,Suhwan Kim,Nakyung Lee,Minsik Seol,Idris Nechnech,Jaehyeon Kim,Giho Lee,Jungwoo Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates learning rate scaling for hybrid Transformer-State-Space Model (SSM) architectures, finding that despite theoretical predictions suggesting LR transfer should fail, practical implementations achieve near-zero LR transfer gap across widths 256-2048 and depths 4-32 up to billion-parameter scale using only the original μP prescription.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The gap between theoretical scaling rules derived for SSMs under zero-order-hold discretization at infinite width and practical implementations using simplified-ZOH Mamba at fixed state size. The authors seek to understand why practical hybrid architectures work despite falling outside standard μP representability conditions.

Method: Empirical testing of various parameterizations across different widths (256-2048), depths (4-32), sequence lengths, batch sizes, and Transformer-to-SSM ratios. They used the coordinate-check diagnostic to test μP correctness and attributed the success to a two-condition decomposition: global update-to-weight invariance (enforced by μP's initialization and LR scaling) and local per-component balance (provided by AdamW's per-parameter normalization).

Result: Optimal LR is invariant to width up to 8×, and this width invariance holds across depth, sequence length, batch size, and Transformer-to-SSM ratio. The findings transfer to Nemotron-H, a production hybrid outside the custom architecture set.

Conclusion: The gap between theoretical scaling rules and practical hybrid implementations can be bridged through understanding the two-condition decomposition of LR transfer. The work provides practical guidance for scaling hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures and stimulates further research in this direction.

Abstract: We study learning rate (LR) scaling for hybrid architectures combining Transformer and State-Space Model (SSM) blocks, a class adopted by several recent production language models. In particular, we focus on the gap between the theoretical scaling rules derived for SSMs under zero-order-hold (ZOH) discretization at infinite width with growing state size, and the field-standard practical implementations using simplified-ZOH Mamba at fixed state size. Surprisingly, in this practical regime hybrid architectures achieve a near-zero LR transfer gap across widths 256-2048 and depths 4-32 up to billion-parameter scale using only the original $μ$P prescription, even though SSM operations fall outside its Tensor Programs representability conditions and every parameterization we test fails the standard coordinate-check diagnostic of $μ$P correctness. We attribute this to a two-condition decomposition of LR transfer in hybrid architectures: a global update-to-weight invariance, enforced by $μ$P's initialization and LR scaling; and a local per-component balance, provided by AdamW's per-parameter normalization. Our observations show that the optimal LR is invariant to width up to 8$\times$, that this width invariance holds across depth, sequence length, batch size, and Transformer-to-SSM ratio, and that it transfers to Nemotron-H, a production hybrid outside our custom architecture set. We hope these findings fill the gap between theoretical scaling rules and practical hybrid implementations, and stimulate further research toward bridging it.

</details>


### [477] [CAGE-NAS: Certified Functional Descent for Efficient Model Growth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01173)
*Santiago Florido Gomez,Stéphane Rivaud*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CAGE-NAS is a neural architecture search method that decides when to expand a network by checking if the current representation can support a certified Functional Gradient Descent step. When the admissibility criterion fails, a function-preserving expansion is applied.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The progressive growth of neural networks requires determining when the current representation is sufficient for optimization and when it should be expanded. Existing methods lack a principled criterion for this decision in function space.

Method: CAGE-NAS formulates the expansion decision through an admissibility criterion on approximations of the functional gradient. The method uses the tangent space family with regularized projection of the functional gradient. As long as the representation enables a certified Functional Gradient Descent step, the architecture remains fixed; when the criterion fails, a function-preserving expansion is applied.

Result: In controlled settings with exact certification, CAGE-NAS produces architectures positioned above the 99.8th performance percentile by held-out RMSE among all admissible alternatives within the same parameter budget, without enumerating them during the growth trajectory.

Conclusion: The function-space-based admissibility criterion provides a principled approach to neural architecture growth, achieving state-of-the-art performance efficiently without exhaustive search over admissible alternatives.

Abstract: The progressive growth of neural networks requires deciding when the current representation remains sufficient for optimization and when it should be expanded. CAGE-NAS formulates this decision in function space through an admissibility criterion on approximations of the functional gradient. As long as a representation enables a certified Functional Gradient Descent step, the architecture remains fixed; when the criterion fails, a function-preserving expansion is applied and the resulting representation is evaluated again. As the main instance, we study the family induced by the tangent space, using a regularized projection of the functional gradient. In a controlled setting with exact certification, CAGE-NAS produces architectures positioned above the 99.8th performance percentile by held-out RMSE among all admissible alternatives within the same parameter budget, without enumerating them during the growth trajectory.

</details>


### [478] [Rethinking the Information Bottleneck: Structured Decomposition under Label-Induced Partitions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01175)
*Jingyao Zhang,Yuxuan Li,Lu Han,Ali Anaissi,Nguyen H. Tran*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a dual-bottleneck regularization method that extends standard Information Bottleneck by explicitly separating label-relevant structure from nuisance variation through a conditional KL term, showing improved performance in low-data classification and dense prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard IB regularization treats all information homogeneously via a single scalar I(Z;X), coupling label-relevant structure with residual within-condition variation. This allows nuisance information (e.g., acquisition conditions, background factors in medical imaging) to persist in learned representations, particularly problematic in data-limited settings where models overfit such variation.

Method: The paper proposes a dual-bottleneck formulation based on a label-induced partition: (1) A standard KL term controls global information capacity, and (2) A conditional KL term targets within-condition information. The conditional KL decomposes into a within-condition information term and a prior-mismatch term. Using a simplex-structured conditional prior provides controllable latent geometry and integrates with existing pipelines.

Result: Experiments on classification and segmentation show the clearest gains in low-data classification and consistent improvements across dense prediction benchmarks.

Conclusion: The dual-bottleneck approach successfully separates nuisance-like variation from task-supporting structure, providing explicit control over representation geometry and improving generalization in data-limited scenarios.

Abstract: Standard information bottleneck (IB) regularization constrains representations via a single scalar I(Z;X), implicitlytreating all information as homogeneous. However, a single global compression control couples label-relevant structurewith residual within-condition variation, rather than regulating their allocation independently, allowing nuisanceinformation to persist in learned representations. For example, in medical imaging applications, residual variation oftenstems from acquisition conditions, background factors, or subject-specific appearance. This issue becomes particularlypronounced in data-limited settings, where models tend to overfit such variation, hindering generalization. While existingregularization methods can stabilize training, control capacity, or shape representation geometry, they do not explicitlyseparate nuisance-like variation from task-supporting structure. To address this limitation, we revisit IB from a structuredperspective based on a label-induced partition, where condition-level structure and within-condition information playdistinct roles. This leads to a dual-bottleneck formulation: a standard KL term controls global information capacity, while aconditional KL term targets within-condition information. We show that the conditional KL admits an exact decompositioninto a within-condition information term and a prior-mismatch term, explaining its alignment with the design objective.With a simplex-structured conditional prior, the method provides controllable latent geometry and integrates seamlesslyinto existing pipelines. Experiments on classification and segmentation show the clearest gains in low-data classificationand consistent improvements across dense prediction benchmarks.

</details>


### [479] [Fully Online Decentralized Learning in Stochastic Games with Unknown Independent Chains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01181)
*S. Rasoul Etesami*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper develops a fully online, decentralized mirror-descent algorithm for stochastic games with independent controlled chains and unknown transition kernels. The algorithm operates in the dual space of occupancy measures to approximate stationary Nash equilibria, achieving O(T^{-1/2}) regret decay while avoiding exponential dependence on the number of players through exploiting local structure.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stochastic games with multiple players face the curse of dimensionality when the joint state space grows exponentially with the number of players. Existing methods often require centralized coordination, coverage of the joint state space, or synchronized episodes. This work aims to develop a scalable, fully online learning framework that exploits the independence of players' controlled transition chains to avoid exponential complexity.

Method: The algorithm uses a primal-dual mirror-descent approach operating in the dual space of occupancy measures. It requires only a single transition/reward sample at each time step, relies on local information only, and needs neither joint state space coverage nor synchronized episodes. The analysis relies on uniform-ergodicity and finite-coverage assumptions, with an additional global variational-stability condition for asymptotic convergence.

Result: With high probability, the time-averaged fixed-comparator regret decays at O(T^{-1/2}) rate (up to logarithmic factors and polynomial dependence on game parameters). The complexity depends on cover times of individual local state spaces rather than the product state space. The algorithm provides approximate coarse-correlated-equilibrium guarantees and, under a variational-stability condition, converges asymptotically in the last iterate to a stationary ε-NE.

Conclusion: This work provides a fully online and scalable learning framework for stochastic games with unknown independent chains, exploiting independence and local structure to avoid exponential dependence on the number of players. The algorithm bridges the gap between practical scalability and theoretical guarantees in multi-agent reinforcement learning.

Abstract: We consider stochastic games with independent controlled chains and unknown transition kernels, where players observe only their local states and realized payoffs. We develop a fully online, decentralized, and uncoordinated mirror-descent algorithm that operates in the dual space of occupancy measures for approximating stationary Nash equilibrium (NE) policies. The algorithm uses a single transition/reward sample at every primitive time step, relies only on local information, and requires neither coverage of the joint state space nor synchronized episodes. Under uniform-ergodicity and finite-coverage assumptions, we show that, with high probability, the time-averaged fixed-comparator regret decays at the canonical $O(T^{-1/2})$ rate, up to logarithmic factors and polynomial dependence on the game parameters. In particular, the complexity depends on the cover times of the individual local state spaces rather than the product state space, avoiding exponential dependence on the number of players and the sizes of the joint state and action spaces. The resulting finite-time regret bound further yields an approximate coarse-correlated-equilibrium guarantee, which is natural for arbitrary reward functions since computing a stationary $ε$-NE is PPAD-hard in this setting. Under an additional global variational-stability condition, we show that the same fully online algorithm converges asymptotically in the last iterate to a stationary $ε$-NE. Our results provide a fully online and scalable learning framework for stochastic games with unknown independent chains. The algorithm can also be viewed as a primal-dual framework for Markov games that exploits the independence and local structure of the players' controlled transition chains.

</details>
