# cs.SD [[Back]](#toc)

### [480] [High-Value Synthetic Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of a Compact Japanese Speech Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00026)
*Sidi Chang,Peiying Zhu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a parameter-efficient approach for adapting a compact 1.47B audio model to transform Japanese care handoff speech into six-field structured notes using synthetic data. Using only 182 synthetic training clips, full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA both achieve significant improvements over the unadapted baseline, with LoRA reaching 97.7% of full-tuning performance while using only 0.85% of trainable parameters (12.4M).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from two key challenges: (1) the difficulty of collecting and redistributing private domain speech data, and (2) the need for task-specific supervision in compact models. The study aims to develop an auditable synthetic pipeline that can acquire audio-to-structure transformation capabilities from synthetic examples without relying on real private speech data.

Method: The study uses 182 synthetic training and development clips to adapt a 1.47B audio model via two approaches: full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation). Evaluation is conducted on a 39-clip scenario-seed-disjoint synthetic test set. The primary metric is model-judged factuality-recall score.

Result: On the synthetic test set, the unadapted model achieves a factuality-recall score of 0.0500, full fine-tuning achieves 0.8664, and LoRA achieves 0.8461. LoRA reaches 97.7% of full-tuning performance as a descriptive ratio while using only 12.4M trainable parameters (approximately 0.85% of the backbone). The full-versus-LoRA interval crosses zero, meaning no statistically significant difference can be claimed between the two methods.

Conclusion: The evidence demonstrates that a compact model can acquire a narrow audio-to-structure transformation from a few hundred synthetic examples. However, the authors explicitly note this is a parameter-efficient capability-acquisition result, not a device-performance result—latency, memory, energy, and real-time factor were not measured. The study does not establish clinical validity, real-speech transfer, or superiority to clean cloud systems. All evaluation data and targets are synthetic, references are model-proposed, and the judge is uncalibrated.

Abstract: Private domain speech is difficult to collect and redistribute, while compact models need task-specific supervision. We study an auditable synthetic pipeline that maps Japanese care handoffs directly to six-field structured notes. Using 182 synthetic training and development clips, we adapt a 1.47B audio model by full fine-tuning and rank-16 LoRA. On a 39-clip scenario-seed-disjoint synthetic test, an unadapted model obtains a model-judged factuality-recall score of 0.0500, full tuning 0.8664, and LoRA 0.8461. LoRA reaches 97.7% of the full-tuning aggregate as a descriptive ratio while project telemetry reports 12.4M trainable parameters, about 0.85% of the backbone. Both adaptations show large paired gains over the same base; the full-versus-LoRA interval crosses zero, and differing optimization settings preclude an equivalence claim. This is a parameter-efficient capability-acquisition result, not a device-performance result: latency, memory, energy, and real-time factor were not measured. All evaluation speech and targets are synthetic, references are model-proposed, and the judge is uncalibrated. The evidence shows that a compact model can acquire a narrow audio-to-structure transformation from a few hundred provenance-linked synthetic examples; it does not establish clinical validity, real-speech transfer, or superiority to a clean cloud system.

</details>


### [481] [PLACE: Positional Latent Adaptation via Conditioned Embeddings for Binaural Audio Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00630)
*Tiernon Riesenmy,You Zhang,Gautam Bhattacharya,Andrea Fanelli*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: PLACE is a binaural audio generation method that extends the pretrained AudioX model to generate audio from arbitrary combinations of text, video, and optional audio prompts. It uses Perception Encoder Core features, aligns text-video representations for spatial cues, and applies conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation to generated latents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to enable flexible multimodal control for binaural audio generation, allowing generation from various input combinations (text, video, audio) while maintaining spatial consistency and improved spatial quality compared to existing methods.

Method: PLACE augments video conditioning with Perception Encoder Core features, aligns text and video representations to derive spatial cues, and applies a conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation to the generated latent. The adapter is supervised via decoded-audio interaural level difference (ILD) and interaural time difference (ITD) objectives. The model is trained on the MRSAudio dataset.

Result: PLACE improves most metrics over ViSAGe on FAIR-Play and achieves an improved SpatialCLAP score over SpatialSonic on the BEWO-1M Single Static test split. Listener evaluations favor PLACE for video-to-audio and out-of-distribution text-to-audio generation.

Conclusion: PLACE demonstrates flexible multimodal control and improved spatial consistency, making it effective for both video-to-audio and text-to-audio generation tasks, including out-of-distribution scenarios.

Abstract: We present PLACE, a method that extends the pretrained any-to-audio model AudioX for binaural generation from arbitrary combinations of text, video, and optional audio prompts. PLACE augments video conditioning with Perception Encoder Core features, aligns text and video representations to derive spatial cues, and applies a conditioning-dependent low-rank transformation to the generated latent. The adapter is supervised via decoded-audio interaural level and time difference objectives. Trained on MRSAudio, PLACE improves most metrics over ViSAGe on FAIR-Play and achieves an improved SpatialCLAP score over SpatialSonic on the BEWO-1M Single Static test split. Listener evaluations favor PLACE for video-to-audio and out-of-distribution text-to-audio generation, demonstrating flexible multimodal control and improved spatial consistency.

</details>


### [482] [How Robust Are Neural Audio Codecs for African Speech? A Multi-Task Benchmark and the Limits of Perceptual Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00154)
*Chibuzor Okocha,Christan Earl Grant*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks seven open-source neural audio codecs on three African speech datasets, evaluating signal-level quality metrics and downstream ASR/ASV tasks. The study reveals that reference-based metrics (ViSQOL, STOI) and F0-RMSE predict downstream performance better than neural MOS predictors, and that domain-dependent degradation can be partially recovered through efficient codec adaptation (LoRA).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural audio codecs are increasingly used for low-bitrate speech compression and tokenization, but their robustness on accented and multilingual speech (particularly African languages) remains under-evaluated. This lack of evaluation risks perpetuating biases in speech technology for underrepresented populations.

Method: The authors benchmarked seven open-source neural codecs (DAC, EnCodec, FocalCodec, LanguageCodec, SemantiCodec, UniCodec, WavTokenizer) on three African speech datasets: afrinames, afrispeech dialog, and afrispeech multilingual. They evaluated using signal-level quality metrics (NISQA, UTMOS, ViSQOL, STOI, F0-RMSE) and two downstream tasks: automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker verification (ASV). They also tested parameter-efficient codec adaptation using LoRA (~1-3% of parameters) on ~35 hours of African speech.

Result: Four key findings: (1) Reference-based structural/intelligibility metrics (ViSQOL, STOI) and prosodic error (F0-RMSE) track ASR and ASV degradation more reliably than neural MOS predictors (NISQA, UTMOS); (2) Intelligibility and speaker-identity preservation diverge across architectures, with identity ranking depending on ASV backend; (3) Degradation is strongly domain-dependent, largest for conversational dialog; (4) LoRA adaptation on ~35 hours of African speech partially recovers compression-induced WER gap, approaching uncompressed baseline performance.

Conclusion: Task-aware, domain-representative, and adaptation-aware evaluation of speech codecs is essential for inclusive deployment. The study demonstrates that neural codecs perform unevenly across accents/languages and that efficient adaptation can mitigate degradation, highlighting the importance of evaluating speech technologies on diverse, underrepresented datasets before deployment.

Abstract: Neural audio codecs enable low-bitrate speech compression and tokenization, yet their robustness on accented and multilingual speech remains under-evaluated. We benchmark seven open-source neural codecs (DAC, EnCodec, FocalCodec, LanguageCodec, SemantiCodec, UniCodec, WavTokenizer) on three African speech datasets afrinames, afrispeech dialog, afrispeech multilingual, reporting signal-level quality (NISQA, UTMOS, ViSQOL, STOI, F0-RMSE) alongside two downstream tasks: automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker verification (ASV). Our analysis yields four findings. First, signal metrics differ sharply in downstream validity: reference-based structural/intelligibility measures (ViSQOL, STOI) and prosodic error (F0-RMSE) track ASR and ASV degradation far more reliably than neural mean-opinion-score predictors (NISQA, UTMOS). Second, intelligibility and speaker-identity preservation diverge sharply across architectures, and the apparent identity ranking itself depends on the ASV backend. Third, degradation is strongly domain-dependent and largest for conversational dialog. Fourth, the resulting degradation is partly recoverable: parameter-efficient \emph{codec} adaptation (LoRA, $\sim$1--3\% of parameters) on roughly 35 hours of African speech reduces the compression-induced word-error-rate gap, recovering recognition toward the uncompressed baseline (developed in companion work). These results motivate task-aware, domain-representative, and adaptation-aware evaluation of speech codecs as a prerequisite for inclusive deployment.

</details>


### [483] [ProxyMOS: Label-Free Speech Quality Assessment by Multi-Teacher Distillation with Adaptive Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00419)
*Maxim Trokunov,Kirill Borodin,Nikita Vasiliev,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: ProxyMOS combines multiple public MOS predictors into a stronger model without human labels by using ensemble routing, then uses the ensemble to pseudo-label 807k utterances for training a wav2vec 2.0 student that achieves ρ=0.802 on URGENT and ρ=0.636 on a new Russian TTS benchmark (mos260).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human MOS collection is costly, and non-intrusive MOS predictors degrade outside their training domain. This work aims to create a better MOS predictor without requiring new human labels.

Method: 1) Benchmarked 8 public MOS predictors against human ratings; 2) Selected 5 most informative predictors via subset search under 5 routing strategies (uniform, correlation-weighted, error-weighted, MSE-optimized, adaptive per-utterance); 3) Used best 4-model ensemble to pseudo-label 807k unlabeled utterances; 4) Trained wav2vec 2.0 student on these labels.

Result: On URGENT: student achieves ρ=0.802 vs 0.773 for best teacher. On mos260 (4,600 utterances, 38 Russian TTS conditions): achieves ρ=0.636 per utterance and 0.95 per condition. Adaptive routing is the only method that doesn't degrade when weak predictors are added.

Conclusion: ProxyMOS effectively combines multiple weak MOS predictors into a stronger model through adaptive routing, achieving better performance than any individual predictor without requiring additional human labels. The method generalizes well to new domains (Russian TTS) and releases resources (model, ONNX exports, mos260 dataset).

Abstract: Human mean opinion scores (MOS) are costly to collect, and non-intrusive MOS predictors degrade sharply outside their training domain. ProxyMOS turns a pool of public MOS predictors into a single stronger model without new human labels. Eight predictors are benchmarked against human ratings; the five most informative enter a subset search under uniform, correlation-weighted, error-weighted, MSE-optimised and adaptive per-utterance routing; and the best routed four-model ensemble labels 807k unlabeled utterances that train a wav2vec 2.0 student. On URGENT the student reaches Spearman $ρ=0.802$ against $0.773$ for the best teacher. On mos260, a new Russian TTS benchmark of 4,600 utterances from 38 synthesis conditions, it reaches $ρ=0.636$ against $0.613$ per utterance and $0.95$ per condition, matching its own routed ensemble in one forward pass. Adaptive routing is the only rule that does not degrade when weak predictors are added. Model, ONNX exports and mos260 are released. It's about 950 characters; arXiv's limit is 1,920. I kept $ρ$ because arXiv renders it on the abstract page. If you'd rather avoid math, replace $ρ=0.802$ with rho = 0.802 and do the same for the other $...$ values.

</details>


### [484] [Collapse, Not Invariance: Diagnosing Auxiliary Objectives in Speech Anti-Spoofing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00539)
*Ksenia Lysikova,Kirill Borodin,Maxim Maslov,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether auxiliary objectives (e.g., cosine consistency, angular margin) can improve speech anti-spoofing countermeasure robustness against generator, codec, and channel changes. Through 113 experimental runs across five corpora, the authors find that while some auxiliary objectives appear effective due to embedding space compression, none consistently outperform standard cross-entropy training when the space is properly normalized.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures suffer performance degradation when the generator, codec, or channel changes. The field assumes that auxiliary objectives shape the embedding space to be more robust, but this assumption was never directly validated since EER (Equal Error Rate) is a pure ranking metric insensitive to embedding space characteristics.

Method: The authors conducted 113 experimental runs across five corpora, comparing seven auxiliary objectives against cross-entropy baseline. They tested AASIST3 architecture with three random seeds plus four pre-trained detectors, and directly measured the embedding space properties of 24 AASIST3 runs to understand what the training actually achieves.

Result: Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency appear effective, but the actual gain is a smaller embedding space, not a more stable one. When normalized by spread, no configuration consistently improves over cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by a single decision axis (expected for binary classification), and training-set structure does not transfer to test scenarios. Four experimental runs collapsed to near-constant outputs that displacement rewards and EER reports as poor accuracy. No auxiliary objective maintains advantage across different architectures, corpora, and random seeds.

Conclusion: Auxiliary objectives that claim to improve robustness through embedding space shaping do not provide consistent benefits over standard cross-entropy training. Apparent gains are artifacts of embedding space compression rather than genuine stability improvements. The field should reconsider the use of such objectives and focus on other approaches for improving anti-spoofing robustness.

Abstract: Speech anti-spoofing countermeasures degrade when the generator, codec or channel changes, and a common remedy is an auxiliary objective that shapes the embedding space; whether it does is invisible to EER, a pure ranking metric. We compare seven such objectives with cross-entropy over 113 runs on five corpora, AASIST3 at three seeds plus four pre-trained detectors, and measure the embedding space of the 24 AASIST3 runs directly. Raw augmentation displacement makes cosine consistency look effective, but the gain is a smaller space, not a more stable one: normalised by the spread, no configuration consistently improves on cross-entropy. Every trained space is dominated by the single decision axis expected for two classes, whose training-set structure does not transfer, and four runs collapse to a near-constant output that displacement rewards and EER reports as poor accuracy. No auxiliary objective keeps an advantage over cross-entropy across architectures, corpora and seeds.

</details>


### [485] [On Evaluating Quantum Kernel Robustness for Low-Resource Cross-Corpus Audio Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00649)
*Lisan Al Amin,Lei Zhang,Vandana P. Janeja*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This study compares quantum kernel methods (QSVM) with classical SVM and MLP for cross-corpus audio deepfake detection under severe data constraints (200 training samples). Under extreme domain shift, QSVM significantly outperforms MLP, but advantages are inconsistent across transfer directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic speech detection performance degrades when labeled data are scarce and evaluation conditions differ from training (cross-corpus setting). This study investigates whether quantum kernel methods can provide advantages under such challenging conditions.

Method: Compare QSVM, classical SVM, and MLP all trained on frozen wav2vec 2.0 embeddings with 200 training samples. Embeddings reduced to 4 dimensions using PCA to match near-term quantum hardware qubit budget. Experiments across ASVspoof 2019, ASVspoof 5, ADD 2023 Challenge, and In-the-Wild datasets.

Result: Under severe domain shift (ASVspoof 2019 → ADD 2023): MLP degrades to near-random (AUC ~50%, EER 50.0%), while QSVM maintains AUC 76.0%, EER 27.0%. However, when trained on ADD 2023, QSVM falls below chance on 2/3 transfers while MLP performs better.

Conclusion: Quantum kernel methods can be competitive under severe cross-corpus shifts and strict low-resource constraints, but do not provide consistent advantage under near-domain transfer. Results characterize quantum kernel inductive bias under distribution shift rather than demonstrating quantum advantage (4-qubit kernel is classically simulable).

Abstract: Synthetic speech detection is critical for audio security, but performance can degrade when labeled data are scarce and evaluation conditions differ from training. This study examines quantum kernel methods and lightweight neural models for cross-corpus audio deepfake detection under limited training data. We compare a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM), a classical support vector machine (SVM), and a multilayer perceptron (MLP), all trained on frozen wav2vec 2.0 embeddings using a strict budget of 200 training samples. To match the qubit budget of near-term quantum hardware, embeddings are reduced to four dimensions using principal component analysis, and all models use the same reduced features. Experiments on ASVspoof 2019, ASVspoof 5, the ADD 2023 Challenge, and the In-the-Wild dataset show that under severe domain shift from ASVspoof 2019 to ADD 2023, the MLP degrades to near-random performance, with an area under the curve of approximately 50% and an equal error rate of 50.0%. In contrast, the QSVM maintains meaningful discrimination, achieving an area under the curve of 76.0% and an equal error rate of 27.0%. This advantage is not consistent across transfer directions. When trained on ADD 2023, the QSVM falls below chance on two of three transfers, while the MLP performs better. These results suggest that quantum kernel methods can be competitive under severe cross-corpus shifts and strict low-resource constraints, but do not provide a consistent advantage under near-domain transfer. We interpret these findings as an empirical characterization of quantum kernel inductive bias under distribution shift, rather than evidence of quantum advantage, since the four-qubit kernel can be simulated exactly on classical hardware.

</details>


### [486] [Balalaika-Longform: A Russian Speech Corpus for Continuous Long-Form Text-to-Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00658)
*Nikita Vasiliev,Kirill Borodin,Vasilii Kudryavtsev,Maxim Maslov,Grach Mkrtchian*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces Balalaika-Longform, a 189-hour Russian corpus for long-form text-to-speech evaluation, and demonstrates that training sequence length critically affects TTS performance in continuous generation scenarios, with CosyVoice3 achieving 16.6% WER with properly formatted transcripts vs 99.9% with short-window fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-form TTS systems must retain requested words over extended generations, but conventional sentence-level training and evaluation masks critical issues like word omissions and early stops that only appear in continuous synthesis scenarios.

Method: The authors created Balalaika-Longform, an open Russian corpus of 189 hours with continuous units (30 seconds to 15 minutes) plus matched short windows for comparison. They fine-tuned four TTS models (CosyVoice3, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2, F5-TTS) on both short and long views, then tested continuous synthesis on 50 text-voice pairs with unseen voices at ~75, 300, and 1,200 words.

Result: At 1,200 words, CosyVoice3 WER dropped from 99.9% (short-window fine-tuning) to 47.3% (long targets) to 16.6% (punctuated, format-matched transcripts). Long targets improved Qwen3-TTS and VoxCPM2, while F5-TTS showed only marginal improvement with WER remaining above 90%.

Conclusion: Training sequence length has a critical impact on long-form TTS performance under continuous-generation protocols. Proper transcript formatting (punctuation, format-matching) provides additional significant gains, and not all TTS models benefit equally from long-target training.

Abstract: Long-form text-to-speech must retain requested words over extended generations, yet sentence-level training and evaluation can hide omissions and early stops. We introduce Balalaika-Longform, an open Russian corpus of 189 hours in continuous units of 30 seconds to 15 minutes. Long units and matched short windows support fine-tuning comparisons on the same source recordings, and the accompanying evaluation retains every synthesis attempt. We fine-tune CosyVoice3, Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2 and F5-TTS on either view and test continuous synthesis on 50 text-voice pairs with voices unseen in fine-tuning, at about 75, 300 and 1,200 words. At 1,200 words, CosyVoice3 WER falls from 99.9% after short-window fine-tuning to 47.3% with long targets, and to 16.6% with punctuated, format-matched transcripts; paired intervals favor long targets for Qwen3-TTS and VoxCPM2, and by a small margin for F5-TTS, whose absolute WER stays above 90%. The results isolate the effect of training sequence length under a fixed continuous-generation protocol.

</details>


### [487] [AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00706)
*Pooneh Mousavi,Amir Ivry,Mirco Ravanelli,Cem Subakan*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AnchorPrompt is an efficient adaptation method for Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) that addresses sensitivity to input perturbations (noise, corruption, adversarial injections) by learning prompt vectors through self-distillation, using clean audio predictions as targets and assigning refusal targets when evidence is insufficient.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large audio-language models are sensitive to input perturbations like noise, waveform corruption, and adversarial injections, leading to hallucinations and inconsistent answers. Existing methods typically require perturbation detection at inference or don't generalize to unseen distortions.

Method: AnchorPrompt keeps the model frozen and learns a single block of prompt vectors inserted at the decoder input between audio and question embeddings. Training uses self-distillation over diverse audio and text perturbations. The model's prediction on clean recordings serves as the target for answerable inputs, while a refusal target is assigned when audio lacks sufficient evidence to answer. The method is perturbation-agnostic at inference, requiring no prior perturbation detection.

Result: Evaluated on three LALMs across three benchmarks, AnchorPrompt improves answer consistency in most conditions. Clean accuracy improves in six of nine model-benchmark pairs, with minimal impact on the remainder (1.2% max). It reduces hallucinations under severe audio corruption while keeping false refusals on clean audio rare. Consistency gains transfer to unseen perturbations including choice permutations and reverberation.

Conclusion: AnchorPrompt provides an effective solution for improving robustness of LALMs against various input perturbations without requiring perturbation detection at inference. The method achieves zero-shot transfer to unseen distortions and maintains clean accuracy while significantly reducing hallucinations in corrupted audio scenarios.

Abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) are sensitive to input perturbations, such as noise, waveform corruption, and adversarial injections. We propose AnchorPrompt, an efficient adaptation method that keeps the model frozen and learns a single block of prompt vectors inserted at the decoder input, between the audio and question embeddings. We train these vectors through self-distillation over diverse audio and text perturbations. To improve answer consistency and mitigate hallucination, we use the model's prediction on the clean recording as the target for answerable inputs, and assign a refusal target when the audio lacks sufficient evidence to answer. Furthermore, AnchorPrompt is perturbation-agnostic at inference, requiring no prior detection of perturbations and enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen distortions. We evaluate three LALMs across three benchmarks and show that AnchorPrompt improves answer consistency in most tested conditions. Clean accuracy improves in six of nine model-benchmark pairs, with minimal impact on the remainder of 1.2% at most. Crucially, AnchorPrompt reduces hallucinations under severe audio corruption while keeping false refusals on clean audio rare. Finally, these consistency gains transfer to unseen perturbations, such as choice permutations and reverberation.

</details>


### [488] [Where the Body Keeps the Beat: Structured Motion Conditioning and Music Dynamics Supervision for Dance-to-Music Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00726)
*Changchang Sun,Lu Cheng,Yan Yan*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Dyna2Music is a latent flow-matching framework for dance-to-music generation that addresses limitations in existing methods by incorporating structured motion conditioning across body parts and frequency bands, along with a novel latent dynamics consistency (LDC) objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics. The method achieves improved rhythmic alignment and audio quality on AIST++ and TikTok datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing dance-to-music (D2M) methods do not explicitly distinguish motion cues across different body parts and frequency bands, and standard flow matching lacks a dedicated objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics. These limitations lead to suboptimal alignment between dance movements and generated music.

Method: Dyna2Music uses a latent flow-matching framework with two key components: (1) Structured motion conditioning - decomposes joint velocities into slow and fast components, applies spatial partitioning and frequency separation, and hierarchically fuses part-wise motion energy with pretrained joint features; (2) Latent dynamics consistency (LDC) - an auxiliary objective that matches adjacent-frame change magnitudes between single-step clean-latent estimates and paired references, making local music-latent variation explicit without adding parameters or inference computation.

Result: Empirical analysis on AIST++ quantifies how spatial partitioning and frequency separation affect raw music-to-kinematic beat alignment and motion-reference density. Experiments on AIST++ and TikTok demonstrate improved rhythmic alignment and audio quality over representative D2M baselines.

Conclusion: Dyna2Music successfully addresses the limitations of prior D2M methods through structured motion conditioning and explicit supervision of music-latent dynamics via LDC, achieving superior performance in rhythmic alignment and audio quality.

Abstract: Dance-to-music (D2M) generation aims to synthesize musically plausible soundtracks whose temporal structure aligns with a given dance performance. Representative D2M methods do not explicitly distinguish motion cues across body parts and frequency bands, while standard flow matching lacks a dedicated objective for supervising local music-latent dynamics. To address these issues, we propose Dyna2Music, a latent flow-matching framework that combines structured motion conditioning with explicit supervision of music-latent dynamics. An empirical analysis on AIST++ quantifies how spatial partitioning and frequency separation affect raw music-to-kinematic beat alignment and motion-reference density, informing the conditioning design. Accordingly, Dyna2Music decomposes joint velocities into slow and fast components and hierarchically fuses the resulting part-wise motion energy with pretrained joint features to condition music generation. To complement this representation, we introduce latent dynamics consistency (LDC), an auxiliary objective that matches adjacent-frame change magnitudes between a single-step clean-latent estimate and the paired reference. LDC makes local music-latent variation an explicit training target without adding trainable parameters or inference computation. Dyna2Music supports variable-length music generation, and experiments on AIST++ and TikTok demonstrate improved rhythmic alignment and audio quality over representative D2M baselines.

</details>


### [489] [RMS-AQA: A Two-Stage Spatial Audio Question Answering Benchmark for Real-World Domestic Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00935)
*Peihao Chen,Qing Wang,Lichun Fan,Yufeng Hao,Zhifeng Kong,Mengyao Zhu,Hengyi Hong,Hang Chen,Hang Su,Yujie Jian,Chao-Han Huck Yang,Shichao Hu,Jun Du,Jian Luan,Ke Li*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: RMS-AQA is a new spatial audio question answering (SAQA) benchmark for embodied assistants in domestic environments, featuring a two-stage QA format to assess audio-language models' ability to ground sound events and perform spatio-temporal reasoning. The benchmark combines real-world FOA recordings with synthetic data using measured room impulse responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodied assistants in domestic environments need to infer what happened, where and when it occurred, and how to respond. Existing benchmarks lack comprehensive assessment of spatial audio understanding and spatio-temporal reasoning in real-world domestic settings.

Method: The benchmark combines authentic real-world first-order Ambisonics (FOA) recordings with high-fidelity synthetic data generated using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). A lightweight spatial plug-in was developed to inject FOA-format data into frozen audio-language backbones. The two-stage QA format first grounds audible sound events, then performs complex spatio-temporal reasoning.

Result: Experimental results reveal three primary challenges: (1) concurrent sources, (2) far distance, and (3) sim-to-real domain gap between RIR-synthesized and authentic recordings.

Conclusion: The benchmark provides a comprehensive testbed for evaluating audio-language models' spatial understanding in domestic environments, though significant challenges remain in handling multiple concurrent sources, distant sounds, and bridging the simulation-to-reality gap.

Abstract: Embodied assistants in domestic environments must infer what happened, where and when it occurred, and how to respond. To address this, we introduce RMS-AQA, a spatial audio question answering (SAQA) benchmark for real-world domestic environments. The benchmark features a two-stage question-answering (QA) format to comprehensively assess the ability of audio-language models (ALMs) to first ground audible sound events and subsequently perform complex spatio-temporal reasoning based on that grounding. To maximize acoustic realism, our dataset combines authentic real-world first-order Ambisonics (FOA) recordings with high-fidelity synthetic data generated using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). Furthermore, we provide a lightweight spatial plug-in that injects FOA-format data into frozen audio-language backbones. Experimental results reveal that the primary challenges stem from concurrent sources, far distance, and sim-to-real domain gap between RIR-synthesized and authentic recordings.

</details>


### [490] [Toward Elastic Speech Inference: Training-Free Wake-Word Detection from Pretrained ASR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01182)
*Hwayeon Kim,Youngwon Choi,Hyeonyu Kim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper explores using pretrained ASR models (Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 and Moonshine-base) for wake-up word detection without gradient-based fine-tuning, using PCA-based structured pruning (SliceGPT) to extract compact encoders. Results show WuW detection performance remains stable with 50% channel dimension reduction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the need for ASR models to generalize across diverse domains and acoustic conditions, and to explore whether task-specific compact encoders can be derived from pretrained ASR models without requiring fine-tuning, which would be more efficient and adaptable.

Method: The method uses SliceGPT, a PCA-based structured pruning approach, to extract compact encoders from pretrained ASR models (Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 and Moonshine-base) for wake-up word detection without gradient-based fine-tuning.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that WuW detection performance remains relatively stable when the encoder channel dimension is reduced by 50%, suggesting that task-relevant compact encoders can be derived from pretrained ASR models without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: The conclusion is that task-relevant compact encoders can be successfully extracted from pretrained ASR models for wake-up word detection without requiring fine-tuning, maintaining acceptable performance even with significant dimension reduction.

Abstract: Recent ASR development has placed growing emphasis on generalization across diverse domains and acoustic conditions. Existing approaches typically adapt pretrained ASR models to front-end functions such as wake-up word (WuW) detection through additional training or task-specific modules. In this work, we explore the use of a shared pretrained ASR backbone for WuW detection without gradient-based fine-tuning and examine whether a compact encoder can be extracted using the PCA-based structured pruning approach of SliceGPT. Experiments with Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 and Moonshine-base show that WuW detection performance remains relatively stable when the encoder channel dimension is reduced by 50%. These results suggest that task-relevant compact encoders can be derived from pretrained ASR models without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [491] [AudioJev: Direct Audio Decisions with Order-Calibrated Probabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01293)
*Sihan Lv,Zhen Li,Zhiqi Cao,Jinshan Zhang,Ying Li,Meng Xi,Jianwei Yin*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: AudioJev is a model for audio question answering that directly maps waveforms, questions, and answer alternatives to a candidate distribution through a single shared full-parameter model. It addresses order sensitivity (where probability estimates depend on option ordering) through random-derangement SKL training, achieving 68.88%/55.33% accuracy on MMAU/MMAR benchmarks while reducing order-related calibration errors by 43.8%/60.5%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio decisions often depend on evidence that text transcripts cannot preserve. Additionally, probability estimates in multiple-choice audio QA can be artificially influenced by how answer options are ordered (position bias). The authors sought to establish a "direct audio interface" that maintains calibration across meaning-preserving option permutations.

Method: The approach uses: (1) A shared full-parameter model that maps waveform, question, and alternatives directly to candidate distributions; (2) Order calibration as a preservation property where answer probability remains consistent under meaning-preserving option permutations; (3) Random-derangement SKL training that pairs each question with a reordered view where every alternative changes position, supervises both answers, aligns the two distributions, and applies a symmetric KL penalty; (4) Single forward pass inference without calibration head or order ensemble.

Result: Across three training seeds, AudioJev achieves 68.88% mean accuracy on MMAU and 55.33% on MMAR. It reduces random-order SKL (a measure of order-induced probability distortion) by 43.8% relative to single-view removal on MMAU and 60.5% on MMAR. The same model handles multiple audio understanding tasks: intent recognition, environmental sound classification, note properties, speech activity detection, and conversational transitions.

Conclusion: AudioJev demonstrates that a single model can handle diverse audio QA tasks while maintaining probability stability across option orderings. The random-derangement SKL training approach effectively reduces order-related calibration errors, establishing a direct audio interface whose calibration objective acts on candidate meaning rather than presentation position. The model weights and inference code are publicly available.

Abstract: Audio decisions often depend on evidence that a transcript does not preserve, while their probability estimates can depend on how answer options are ordered. AudioJev maps a waveform, question and supplied alternatives directly to a candidate distribution through one shared full-parameter model. We define order calibration as preserving an answer's probability under meaning-preserving option permutations. Random-derangement SKL training pairs each question with a reordered view in which every alternative changes position, supervises both answers, and aligns the two distributions before applying a symmetric KL penalty. Inference retains a single candidate-scoring forward, with no calibration head or order ensemble. Across three training seeds, AudioJev reaches 68.88%/55.33% mean accuracy on complete MMAU/MMAR and reduces random-order SKL by 43.8%/60.5% relative to the single-view removal ablation. The same model handles intent, environmental sound, note properties, speech activity and conversational transitions. Paired removal ablations and multi-order evaluation measure predictive accuracy and probability stability together, establishing a direct audio interface whose calibration objective acts on candidate meaning rather than presentation position. Inference code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SihanLv/AudioJev-Inference and https://huggingface.co/shlv/AudioJev.

</details>


### [492] [Multi-Party Backchannel Prediction: a Diagnosis, a Benchmark, and a Ceiling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01488)
*Mohammed Hafsati,Ahmed Loughzali*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces the first multi-party benchmark for backchannel prediction, revealing that state-of-the-art dyadic models fail in multi-party settings (AUROC 0.499) and that speaker identity is entangled with useful backchannel cues, making it difficult to transfer predictions to unseen listeners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Backchannel prediction has been studied almost entirely in dyadic conversation, leaving a gap in understanding how listeners respond in multi-party meetings. The authors aim to create a benchmark and investigate whether dyadic models generalize to multi-party settings.

Method: The authors created a multi-party benchmark using the AMI corpus with 682 masked-listener views from 171 meetings, 190 speakers, and 18,697 backchannel events. They tested a state-of-the-art dyadic model zero-shot, then used linear probes and retraining. They also experimented with capacity reduction, listener-adversarial training, per-listener adaptation, and oracle lexical conditioning. They compared backchannel prediction with turn-onset prediction as a within-model control.

Result: Zero-shot dyadic model performed at chance (AUROC 0.499). Linear probe reached 0.704, and retraining raised performance to 0.751. Listener conditioning improved prediction for seen listeners but not unseen listeners. The gap persisted across all interventions. Adversarial training removed only part of speaker-identity information, while stronger removal hurt prediction. Turn-onset prediction transferred to unseen listeners, but backchannel prediction did not. Backchannel rates varied about twice as much across individuals as turn-onset rates.

Conclusion: Speaker identity is entangled with cues useful for backchanneling, making it difficult to generalize to unseen listeners. The authors release the benchmark and evaluation tools to facilitate further research in multi-party backchannel prediction.

Abstract: Backchannel prediction has been studied almost entirely in dyadic conversation. We introduce a multi-party benchmark based on the AMI corpus, comprising 682 masked-listener views from 171 meetings, 190 speakers, and 18,697 backchannel events, with a person-disjoint held-out split. A state-of-the-art dyadic model applied zero-shot to meeting audio performs at chance (AUROC 0.499); nevertheless, its frozen acoustic features remain informative: a linear probe reaches 0.704, and retraining the predictor raises performance to 0.751. Retraining reveals a second limitation. Listener conditioning improves prediction for listeners seen during training but not for unseen listeners, and the gap remains under capacity reduction, listener-adversarial training, per-listener adaptation, and oracle lexical conditioning. Adversarial training removes only part of the speaker-identity information, while stronger removal hurts prediction, suggesting that identity is entangled with cues that are useful for backchanneling. A within-model control helps explain this pattern: with the same features and data splits, turn-onset prediction transfers to unseen listeners, while backchannel prediction does not. Backchannel rates also vary about twice as much across individuals as turn-onset rates. Since backchannels occupy only about 1% of frames, frame-level F1 is strongly affected by the base rate. We therefore report AUROC alongside event-F1 on listener-active regions. We release the benchmark and evaluation tools at https://github.com/HafsatiMohammed/bc_multiparty_release.

</details>


### [493] [Q-SPT: Learnable Query-Based Compression for Low-Frame-Rate Speech Tokenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01492)
*Jeeyoung Yun,Seohwan Yun,Sungwoong Kim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: Q-SPT is a low-frame-rate dual-stream speech tokenizer that uses separate, context-aware, learnable query-based compressors for semantic and acoustic representations, achieving superior reconstruction quality and downstream performance for speech language models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lowering the frame rate in neural speech codecs reduces computational and memory costs for SLMs, but makes it difficult to preserve both linguistic information and acoustic detail. Existing rule-based compression methods (average pooling or similarity-based merging) have limitations in maintaining both aspects.

Method: Q-SPT uses queries at a fixed rate that independently attend to semantic and acoustic streams as separate key-value sources, enabling stream-specific, context-aware aggregation through two separately learned compressors. Additionally, an autoregressive text loss explicitly supervises the semantic compressor to preserve linguistic information.

Result: Q-SPT achieves the best reconstruction quality among evaluated codecs at the same frame rate. In downstream SLMs, it yields the best speech recognition accuracy and text-to-speech perceptual quality with competitive intelligibility.

Conclusion: The proposed dual-stream approach with separate learnable compressors and text supervision effectively balances linguistic preservation and acoustic quality at low frame rates, making it a promising tokenizer for speech language models.

Abstract: Neural speech codecs increasingly serve as tokenizers for speech language models (SLMs). Lowering the frame rate reduces the computational and memory costs of SLMs, but makes it difficult to preserve both linguistic information and acoustic detail. Existing approaches rely on rule-based compression: average pooling can discard linguistic information, whereas similarity-based merging uses a fixed threshold on adjacent-frame similarity and applies the resulting boundaries to the acoustic stream. We propose Q-SPT, a low-frame-rate dual-stream speech tokenizer with separate, context-aware, learnable query-based compressors specialized for semantic and acoustic representations. In particular, queries at a fixed rate independently attend to the semantic and acoustic streams as separate key-value sources, enabling stream-specific, context-aware aggregation through two separately learned compressors. In addition, an autoregressive text loss explicitly supervises the semantic compressor to preserve linguistic information. Experimental results show that Q-SPT achieves the best reconstruction among the evaluated codecs at the same frame rate. In downstream SLMs, it yields the best speech recognition accuracy and text-to-speech perceptual quality with competitive intelligibility.

</details>


### [494] [Beyond Decodability: Do Acoustic Factors Drive Predictions in Speech-Based Alzheimer's Assessment?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01846)
*Serli Kopar,Alkis Koudounas,Roshan P. Rane,Sam Gijsen,Paula A. Perez-Toro,Kerstin Ritter*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether recording factors (noise, reverberation) in speech-based Alzheimer's disease (AD) assessments using self-supervised learning (SSL) models merely encode information or systematically alter predictions. Using ADReSSo dataset and three SSL backbones, the study applies controlled acoustic interventions and finds that these interventions alter AD predictions, with noise showing the strongest effects despite having no significant diagnostic-group difference in original data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech-based AD assessments increasingly use pretrained SSL models that learn directly from raw audio, exposing models to recording factors. The researchers wanted to determine whether these factors are merely encoded in SSL representations or can systematically alter predictions, which is critical for clinical trustworthiness.

Method: The study used ADReSSo dataset and three large SSL backbones. They applied controlled noise and reverberation interventions to participant-speech-only, non-speech, and full-recording audio. Methods included layer-wise linear decoding, input- and representation-space interventions, and geometric alignment analysis to distinguish acoustic decodability from influence on AD prediction.

Result: Controlled acoustic interventions alter AD predictions across all three SSL backbones. Noise produces the strongest intervention effects despite showing no significant diagnostic-group difference in the original data. These effects are systematically structured relative to the classifier's decision direction, replicate on held-out test set, and reverse when representation-space intervention direction is reversed.

Conclusion: High predictive performance and the absence of a significant diagnostic-group difference in a measured acoustic factor are not sufficient for robustness. The authors argue that intervention-based robustness tests should become standard for trustworthy clinical speech models.

Abstract: Speech-based Alzheimer's disease (AD) assessments increasingly rely on pretrained self-supervised learning (SSL) models that learn acoustic representations directly from raw audio, exposing the model to recording factors. We ask whether such factors are merely encoded in SSL representations or can systematically alter predictions. Using ADReSSo and three large SSL backbones, we apply controlled noise and reverberation interventions to participant-speech-only, non-speech, and full-recording audio. We combine layer-wise linear decoding, input- and representation-space interventions, and geometric alignment analysis to distinguish acoustic decodability from influence on AD prediction. Our results show that controlled acoustic interventions alter AD predictions across all three SSL backbones. Noise, despite showing no significant diagnostic-group difference in the original data, produces the strongest intervention effects. Importantly, these effects are systematically structured relative to the classifier's decision direction, replicate on the held-out test set and reverse when the representation-space intervention direction is reversed. Together, these findings show that high predictive performance and the absence of a significant diagnostic-group difference in a measured acoustic factor are not sufficient for robustness. We argue that intervention-based robustness tests should become standard for trustworthy clinical speech models.

</details>


### [495] [From Isolated Feature to Orbits: Discovering Music Concepts via Multi-SAE Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01864)
*Liwei Lin,Gus Xia*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces a structure-based interpretability framework for music foundation models, moving beyond feature identification to analyze structured relations in inner representations. The method uses pitch transposition as an inductive bias with multi-view SAE alignment to discover organized orbits of pitch-related features, recovering structures corresponding to chords, keys, and melodic patterns.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current interpretability approaches (probing, SAEs) focus on identifying individual features with minimal structural assumptions. However, in music, concepts like chords and keys are naturally expressed as structured sets (e.g., 12 transpositions of a chord, diatonic system within a key) rather than isolated features. The authors argue that understanding learned representations requires analyzing structured relations rather than just isolated features.

Method: The framework uses pitch transposition as an inductive bias to induce ordered orbits via multi-view SAE alignment. They generate pitch-shifted input pairs and align their Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) representations to discover structured groups of pitch-related features. This approach requires only minimal grounding (e.g., a few anchor examples) to interpret entire concept families.

Result: Experimental results show that the approach recovers orbit structures corresponding to chords, keys, and melodic patterns across two state-of-the-art music foundation models. The method requires only minimal grounding to interpret entire concept families.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that music foundation models learn organized structures over features, not just isolated features. The proposed structure-based analysis framework provides a way to understand the internal organization of musical concepts in foundation models, with potential applications in model interpretability and music understanding.

Abstract: How can we understand what a music foundation model has learned \textit{internally}? Most interpretability approaches, such as probing and Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), focus on identifying individual features with minimal structural assumptions. We argue that many concepts are better understood as \textit{structured relations} rather than isolated features. This is especially prominent in music, where tonal structures are organized in the space of pitch and time. For example, concepts such as chords or keys are naturally expressed as structured sets (e.g., the 12 transpositions of a chord or the diatonic system within a key), rather than isolated features. In this study, \textbf{we shift from feature identification to structure-based analysis}, asking whether the learned inner representations of music foundation model emerge as organized structures over features. To this end, we introduce a framework that uses pitch transposition as an inductive bias to induce ordered orbits via multi-view SAE alignment. Concretely, we generate pitch-shifted input pairs and align their SAE representations to discover structured groups of pitch-related features. Experimental results show that this approach recovers orbit structures corresponding to chords, keys, and melodic patterns across two state-of-the-art music foundation models, while requiring only minimal grounding (e.g., a few anchor examples) to interpret entire concept families.

</details>


### [496] [LAST: Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01926)
*Haider Al-Tahan,Sean O'Brien,Anastasia Razdaibiedina,N. Apurva Ratan Murty*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper proposes Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer (LAST), which reuses the same transformer blocks to refine only the class token over fixed audio features, enabling efficient depth through iterative passes rather than adding more layers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Increasing the depth of transformer models improves recognition accuracy but comes with substantial computational costs due to increased parameters. The authors investigate whether additional processing can focus on integrating features already computed rather than adding more layers.

Method: LAST first processes all tokens (full audio spectrogram), then reuses the same transformer blocks in subsequent passes to refine only the class token over fixed audio features. This makes later passes computationally inexpensive since the audio features are not re-processed.

Result: Ten-pass LAST achieves 0.345 mean average precision on AudioSet, exceeding a twelve-layer sequential transformer by 2.1% relative while using 49.4% fewer parameters, 42% fewer multiply-accumulate operations, and 9.8% higher measured throughput. Increasing pass count from 2 to 10 improves accuracy while adding only 1.2% computation. The method shows improved robustness to temporal masking and various auditory augmentations, with better generalization on music, environmental, and event sound classification tasks.

Conclusion: The looped architecture with class token refinement over fixed audio features is an effective approach for improving transformer efficiency. It achieves better accuracy than deeper sequential models while being significantly more computationally efficient, with additional benefits of improved robustness and generalization.

Abstract: Increasing depth of transformer models improves recognition, but it comes at a substantial cost. Each additional layer requires more parameters, which makes the process computationally inefficient. We ask whether additional processing can focus on integrating features already computed. Looped Audio Spectrogram Transformer (LAST) first processes all tokens, then reuses the same blocks to refine only the class token over fixed audio features, thereby making later passes inexpensive. On AudioSet, ten-pass LAST achieves 0.345 mean average precision, exceeding a twelve-layer sequential transformer by 2.1% relative with 49.4% fewer parameters, 42% fewer multiply-accumulate operations, and 9.8% higher measured throughput. Across separately trained models, increasing the pass count from two to ten improves accuracy while adding only 1.2% computation. Further evaluations show improved robustness to temporal masking and various other auditory augmentations, with better generalization on classification tasks with music, environmental, and event sounds.

</details>
